It first clips the input raster to its own extent (effectively copying it), then rasterizes the input vector polygons onto that copy using the matched lc_value as the burn-in value, producing a modified land cover raster where overlapping pixels are replaced.

name: Modify land cover raster
desc: The script modifies pixels in an input land cover raster (e.g., NLCD or C-CAP) within polygon areas defined by a vector layer, overwriting them with a user-selected land cover class value (e.g., 'Developed, High Intensity' → value 24). It first clips the input raster to preserve its extent and data type, then rasterizes the input vector polygons using a fixed land cover code derived from CSV-sourced NLCD/C-CAP classification coefficients. The output is a modified land cover raster where overlapping pixels are replaced with the selected class’s numeric code. No time-series analysis, spectral computation, or classification modeling is performed — it is a deterministic spatial overwrite operation. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; the algorithm is generic and data-source-agnostic, relying solely on user-provided raster and vector inputs and local CSV coefficient files.

name: Rasterize hydrologic soil group and K-factor
desc: The script converts a vector polygon layer representing soil properties into two raster outputs: (1) a Hydrologic Soil Group (HSG) raster where categorical HSG values ('A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'A/D', 'B/D', 'C/D', 'W', or Null) are mapped to integer codes (1–9) via field calculation and then rasterized; and (2) a K-Factor raster where numeric erodibility values from a user-specified attribute field are directly rasterized. Input validation ensures HSG field values conform strictly to USDA NRCS-approved codes. Both rasters inherit the input layer’s CRS and are generated at a user-defined cell size using GDAL’s rasterize algorithm.

name: Estimate annual erosion volume
desc: The script estimates annual erosion volume (in kg/year per cell and Mg/year accumulated) using the RUSLE (Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation) and Sediment Delivery Ratio (SDR) models. Key workflow steps include: (1) preprocessing K-factor raster by replacing zero values with DEFAULT_URBAN_K_FACTOR_VALUE = 0.3; (2) generating C-factor raster via lookup-table-based reclassification of land cover raster; (3) computing LS-factor using GRASS r.watershed on elevation raster; (4) calculating RUSLE soil loss (ton/acre/year, then converted to kg/year); (5) computing Relief Length Ratio from elevation; (6) generating Curve Number (CN) raster from land cover and hydrologic soil group rasters, with configurable handling of dual-category soils (A/D, B/D, C/D); (7) computing SDR using empirical power-law expression combining RL ratio and CN; (8) multiplying RUSLE by SDR to yield local sediment yield (kg/year); (9) converting to Mg/year and accumulating downstream using GRASS material transport (single-flow-direction routing); (10) saving outputs—including 'Sediment Local' and 'Sediment Accumulated' GeoTIFFs—and a JSON configuration file documenting inputs, outputs, and run metadata. The script operates entirely on user-provided local raster/vector inputs (no GEE server-side assets), and all geospatial operations are performed via QGIS Processing algorithms (e.g., qgis:rastercalculator, grass7:r.watershed, custom raster math). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code — all inputs are generic file paths or QGIS layer references.

name: Convert radar reflectivity to GeoTIFF
desc: The script converts NetCDF-formatted meteorological radar data (specifically 'Band1', representing radar reflectivity in dBZ) into a georeferenced GeoTIFF file projected to WGS84 UTM Zone 17S (EPSG:32717). It applies a user-defined NoData threshold (default 25 dBZ) to mask low-reflectivity values as NaN, computes geographic transform from latitude/longitude arrays, writes the masked reflectivity array to a temporary GeoTIFF in WGS84 lat/lon, then attempts robust reprojection to UTM 17S using multiple fallback GDAL/QGIS methods. Finally, it loads the output raster into QGIS with a custom pseudo-color ramp optimized for precipitation intensity (0–250 dBZ), applying transparency for near-zero values and setting CRS explicitly to EPSG:32717.

name: Locate nearest meteo stations
desc: The script computes the centroid of a user-provided basin polygon, then identifies the N (default 4) meteorological stations nearest to that centroid using a distance matrix and spatial join. It outputs a vector layer of the selected stations, enriched with distance and association attributes from the distance matrix.

name: Compare park cooling effects on air temperature
desc: The script compares two urban microclimate scenarios (reference vs. alternative) to quantify differences in park-induced cooling effects—specifically the spatial pattern and magnitude of air temperature modification (ΔT) and absolute temperature (T) at day (14:00) and night (2:00) hours, as well as derived building energy savings and thermal discomfort reduction. It validates geometric consistency between scenarios (park boundaries must be identical; building footprints/heights may differ only for 'buildings characteristics' change), computes raster-based differences, generates isovalue contour layers (geojson) for visualization, and returns aggregated city-scale metrics including mean ΔT per scenario, total energy saved, and degree-hour comfort improvements.

name: Generate Curve Number layer
desc: The script generates a Curve Number (CN) raster layer for a user-defined Area of Interest (AOI) in the contiguous United States by combining ESA World Cover 2021 land cover data and ORNL Hydrologic Soil Groups (HYSOGs250m) soil data. It applies a lookup-based CN assignment using either built-in hydrologic condition (HC: Poor/Fair/Good) and antecedent runoff condition (ARC: I/II/III) tables or a custom CSV lookup mapping ESA land cover codes concatenated with HSG values (e.g., '110A') to CN values. Optional outputs include aligned and clipped ESA Land Cover and HSG rasters, and a vectorized (polygonized) CN layer. The workflow includes GDAL-based clipping, WCS download of ORNL soils, reprojection/resampling (gdalWarp), raster algebra via perform_raster_math using generated CN expressions, and optional polygonization.

name: Convert building plan boundary to XPlanGML
desc: The script converts one or more user-drawn or loaded polygon features (Bebauungsplan umring / building plan boundary) from a QGIS vector layer into a standards-compliant XPlanung GML v5.4 file (xplan.gml), embedded in a ZIP archive. It performs geometry preprocessing (reprojection to specified CRS, CCW orientation enforcement, duplicate vertex removal, Z/M dropping), validates input constraints (character set, length, required fields), injects metadata (name, number, AGS, plan type, legal status, dates, municipality/Ortsteil, planner), replaces placeholder GML geometries and bounding boxes with actual feature geometry and extent, assigns UUID-based gml:id and xlink:href attributes per XPlanGML v5.4 schema requirements, and sanitizes filenames for xPlanBox compatibility (German umlauts → ae/oe/ue/ss, non-alphanumeric → underscore). The output is a ZIP archive named after the sanitized plan name containing exactly one xplan.gml file.

name: Convert building plan boundary to XPlanGML
desc: The script converts one or more polygon features representing the boundary (Umring) of a German Bebauungsplan (development plan) from QGIS vector layers into a valid XPlanung GML v6.0 file embedded in a ZIP archive. It performs geometry preprocessing (reprojection to user-specified CRS, enforcing counter-clockwise polygon orientation, removing duplicate vertices, dropping Z/M values), validates and sanitizes input strings (e.g., plan name character set and length per xPlanBox requirements), injects user-provided metadata (name, number, AGS, plan type, legal status, dates, municipality/Ortsteil, plangeber), replaces placeholder GML geometry with actual WGS84/GML3-compliant geometry derived from the input layer’s first feature, updates bounding box coordinates, assigns UUIDs to all gml:id and xlink:href attributes, and writes the final XML to 'xplan.gml' inside a ZIP file. The study area is implicitly defined by the input vector layer’s geometry and CRS; no remote sensing data or time-series analysis is involved.

name: Clip raster plan by polygon boundary
desc: The script clips a provided raster layer (e.g., a digital XPlan raster map) to the exact geometry of an input polygon vector layer, optionally setting palette index 0 as NoData (commonly used for white background transparency in XPlanBox compliance). It first retains only necessary fields from the polygon, then segments its boundaries at 0.01 map units to ensure topological robustness for GDAL clipping, and finally executes gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer with compression (DEFLATE) and configurable NoData handling — producing a georeferenced, masked raster output suitable for official spatial planning publication.

name: Subtract polygon from raster plan
desc: The script performs a geospatial raster masking operation: it takes an input raster layer (representing a planning document, e.g., a zoning or development plan) and subtracts (i.e., masks out) the area covered by a user-provided polygon vector layer. Internally, it first generates a bounding extent layer from the raster, segments the polygon for geometric robustness, computes a vector difference (extent minus polygon), then uses that resulting geometry as a mask to clip the original raster — optionally setting palette index 0 as NoData. The output is a new raster where the polygon area is removed (transparent/NoData), preserving only the original raster outside the polygon. This is intended for XPlan-compliant digital planning documents (e.g., German Bauleitplanung), specifically for generating 'Umring' (outline/perimeter) rasters in KRZN-XPlanBox.

name: Convert plan boundary to XPlanGML
desc: The script converts one or more user-provided polygon vector layers (representing Flächennutzungsplan 'Umring' boundaries) into a valid XPlanung GML v6.0 XML file embedded in a ZIP archive. It performs geometric preprocessing (reprojection to specified CRS, CCW orientation enforcement, duplicate vertex removal, Z/M dropping), extracts the bounding box and GML3 geometry of the first feature, populates an XPlanGML template with user inputs (name, AGS, planart, rechtsstand, dates, etc.), dynamically assigns UUIDs to GML elements, updates srsName and bounding coordinates, conditionally removes or populates date fields based on Rechtsstand selection, sanitizes the plan name for xPlanBox compliance, and writes the final GML to 'xplan.gml' inside a ZIP archive. The study area is not defined by remote sensing data but by the input vector layer provided by the user in QGIS; no satellite, sensor, or band processing occurs.

name: Convert landscape plan boundary to XPlanGML
desc: The script converts one or more polygon features representing landscape plan boundaries (Umringpolygon(e)) from a QGIS vector layer into a valid XPlanung GML v6.0 XML file, packaged in a ZIP archive. It performs geometric preprocessing (reprojection to user-specified CRS, CCW polygon orientation enforcement, duplicate vertex removal, Z/M value dropping), validates input constraints (character set and length of plan name for xPlanBox compatibility), injects user-provided metadata (name, number, Bundesland, AGS, planart, Rechtsstand, dates, etc.), replaces template placeholders with real geometry (GML3-encoded MultiSurface/Polygon), updates UUIDs and xlink references, adjusts bounding box coordinates from the input geometry, and handles conditional date fields (aufstellungsbeschlussDatum, inkrafttretenDatum, untergangsDatum) based on Rechtsstand selection. The output is a standards-compliant XPlan-Archiv (.zip containing xplan.gml) ready for ingestion into xPlanBox or other XPlanung-compliant systems. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis is involved — it is a vector-based metadata + geometry serialization workflow.

name: Replace spatial extent geometry
desc: The script replaces the raeumlicherGeltungsbereich (spatial extent) geometry in an XPlanGML file with a new polygon geometry provided as a QGIS vector layer, while preserving all other attributes and metadata; it validates XPlanGML structure (single *_Bereich, correct namespace, srsName), reprojects and cleans the input polygon (force CCW winding, remove duplicate vertices, drop Z/M), updates both the root and plan-level boundedBy envelopes, replaces the existing raeumlicherGeltungsbereich element with a newly generated GML3 MultiSurface/Polygon conforming to GML 3.2 and the original coordinate reference system, and writes the modified XPlanGML to the specified output file.

name: Extract local elevation maxima
desc: The script identifies local elevation maxima (spot heights) within user-defined circular neighborhoods across a digital elevation model (DEM). It first computes the maximum value in each neighborhood using GRASS r.neighbors, then isolates cells where the original DEM value equals that neighborhood maximum (i.e., local peaks), nulls all zero-valued pixels, converts remaining pixels to vector points, and finally filters those points to retain only those intersecting the input coastline polygon—yielding on-land spot height candidates as point features with elevation values.

name: Generate distance-based environmental variable
desc: The script generates a continuous raster surface representing Euclidean distance from vector features (e.g., rivers, roads, urban nuclei) within user-defined territorial boundaries and maximum distance. It rasterizes clipped input vector features to a zero-initialized reference grid, computes proximity (distance) raster up to a specified maximum distance, fills null values with a user-defined fill value, and masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster—producing a standardized distance raster suitable for MaxEnt species distribution modeling.

name: Delimit habitat suitability zones
desc: The script reclassifies a Maxent-generated ASCII habitat suitability raster into discrete ecological or management zones (e.g., 'High', 'Medium', 'Low' suitability) using user-defined thresholds (Min/Max value ranges per category) from a CSV-based typology layer; it then converts the reclassified raster to vector polygons, producing both a thematic raster and a polygon vector layer where each feature represents a spatially contiguous zone of uniform suitability class.

name: Generate distance-based environmental variable raster
desc: The script generates a continuous raster surface representing Euclidean distance from input vector features (e.g., rivers, roads, urban nuclei) within user-defined territorial boundaries. It rasterizes clipped vector features to a zero-initialized reference raster grid, computes proximity (distance) up to a specified maximum distance, fills null pixels with a user-defined control value, and masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster layer. The output is a standardized-resolution distance raster suitable for Maxent species distribution modeling. No satellite imagery, time-series, or spectral analysis is involved; all operations are vector-to-raster conversion and distance transformation using QGIS Processing algorithms (qgis:rastercalculator, native:clip, gdal:rasterize, gdal:proximity, grass7:r.null, saga:rastermasking). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Compute zonal statistics for environmental variables
desc: The script computes comprehensive zonal statistics (mean, median, min, max, std, variance, sum, count, range, minority, majority, uniqueness) of a continuous environmental raster variable within circular buffers (user-defined radius) centered on species occurrence point locations. It outputs a point feature layer where each original occurrence point is replaced by its buffer centroid and enriched with the computed raster statistics as attributes prefixed with 'Sta_'. The workflow consists of three deterministic QGIS native processing steps: (1) buffering input points, (2) computing zonal statistics over the buffered polygons using the environmental raster, and (3) computing centroids of the buffered polygons to return point geometry aligned with original occurrences while retaining all statistics.

name: Delimit raster variable by negative buffer zone
desc: The script processes an input environmental raster (e.g., for MaxEnt modeling) by first generating a zero-valued raster of identical extent, converting it to a polygon, applying a *negative* distance buffer (i.e., an inward shrinkage) to create a perimeter mask, and finally clipping the original raster to that buffered polygon. This effectively removes peripheral pixels — such as coastal edges, administrative boundaries, or island fringes — to avoid edge artifacts in species distribution modeling. The output is a spatially constrained raster where only the interior region (retracted by the specified negative distance) remains, with outer pixels masked out.

name: Rasterize and fill linear or isolated environmental features
desc: The script converts linear or isolated vector-based environmental features (e.g., rivers, roads, protected areas, settlements) into a standardized raster layer for Maxent modeling. It first clips the input vector layer to territorial influence boundaries, then rasterizes it using a specified numeric field and user-defined pixel resolution, fills NoData cells with a user-controlled fill value, and finally masks the result to the spatial extent of a reference raster—producing a ready-to-use, spatially constrained environmental variable raster aligned with Maxent requirements.

name: Rasterize categorical vector variable
desc: The script rasterizes a categorical environmental vector layer (e.g., land cover, habitat type, or administrative zoning) into a standardized-resolution raster aligned to a territorial boundary mask, specifically for Maxent species distribution modeling. It first clips the input vector layer to a territorial influence boundary using spatial intersection, then rasterizes the clipped features using a specified numeric field (categorical ID), and finally masks and resamples the resulting raster to match the extent, resolution, and geometry of the provided territorial limits layer — ensuring pixel alignment and NoData handling suitable for ecological niche modeling.

name: Generate microshed basins
desc: The script runs GRASS r.watershed on a user-provided DEM raster to compute watershed basins using a user-specified cell-count threshold (e.g., minimum exterior basin size of 1000 cells, recommended for ~2–3 km²). It outputs a uniquely labeled integer raster where each pixel value corresponds to a distinct microshed basin ID. Optionally, it polygonizes that raster into a vector layer (GeoPackage or similar) with a 'basin_id' attribute. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is embedded in the code — inputs are generic QGIS raster layers supplied by the user at runtime. The workflow relies entirely on local DEM input and GRASS GIS hydrological modeling, not remote sensing imagery or temporal analysis.

name: Compute network betweenness centrality
desc: The script computes betweenness centrality for road/path network segments within 30 selected municipalities in the Madrid region (Comunidad de Madrid, Spain), using a pre-existing vector network layer and administrative boundary polygons. It first filters the polygon layer to retain only municipalities with specific INE boundary codes (e.g., '28005', '28006', ...), splits the network layer along those municipal boundaries, then iteratively applies GRASS v.net.centrality (betweenness mode) to each municipality’s subset of the split network. Outputs include individual GeoPackage layers per municipality containing centrality values (as attribute 'centrality'), and a final merged GeoPackage layer aggregating all municipal centrality results for downstream spatial analysis and visualization in QGIS.

name: Integrate LULC with water and farm layers
desc: The script integrates high-resolution (10m) IITD-generated LULC maps for Raichur district (Karnataka, India) with spatially aligned water network and farm plot vector layers. It clips LULC rasters to a distributary-specific AOI (D10), generates a pixel-skeleton polygon layer from the clipped LULC, overlays water/farm features to assign thematic values (e.g., 100 for water), rasterizes those assignments at ~10m resolution (0.00009° ≈ 10 m at equator), null-corrects generated rasters, sums them with original LULC rasters to produce fused thematic rasters (e.g., LULC + water + farm), and exports each final raster’s pixel matrix as a separate Excel sheet (named by fiscal year, e.g., '2022-2023') — enabling pixel-wise tabular analysis of land–water–agriculture interactions in the Prarambha distributary system.

name: Generate village interior sampling polygons
desc: The script generates a set of non-overlapping 100 m × 100 m rectangular polygons distributed randomly inside the interior (buffered-in) boundary of a selected village polygon. It first extracts one selected (or first) village feature from an active QGIS vector layer, applies an inward buffer (−70 m), generates random points inside that buffered area, then converts each point into a centered rectangle. The final output is a shapefile of these rectangles stored in a predefined local folder (e.g., 'C:\Users\atree\Desktop\QC_polygons') named after the village (e.g., 'village_name_polygons.shp'). This is intended for spatial sampling or field survey planning within village boundaries.

name: Delineate catchments and correct structure locations
desc: The script processes point-based water-harvesting structure locations (anicut, pokher, taal) in Karauli district, Rajasthan, India. It first corrects each input point’s location by identifying the nearest high-flow-accumulation pixel within a 200m buffer of the original point using FABDEM-derived flow accumulation raster. Then, for pokher and taal structures, it traces upstream drainage lines by iteratively stepping to the lowest-flow-accumulation pixel within successive 25m buffers along the flow path (using FABDEM drainage direction), generating polylines of specified lengths (300m for pokher, 1000m for taal). Finally, it delineates the contributing catchment for each corrected point using GRASS r.water.outlet on the drainage direction raster, polygonizes the catchment, and outputs combined vector layers: original points, corrected points, structure-specific buffers (250m for anicut/pokher/taal), drainage lines (for pokher/taal), and catchment polygons — all georeferenced in EPSG:4326.

name: Estimate water storage volume
desc: The script estimates the volume of water that can be stored by a check dam or johad structure (a traditional rainwater harvesting structure) based on high-resolution elevation data (FABDEM, ALOS, or CartoSat), flow accumulation, and drainage direction rasters. It first corrects the outlet point using flow accumulation thresholding, delineates the upstream catchment via r.water.outlet, masks the elevation raster to that catchment, identifies the lowest elevation (outlet), computes depth per pixel as (lowest_elev + effective_height − pixel_elevation), filters pixels where depth > 0 and < effective_height+50, and sums depth × pixel_area across all ponding pixels to compute total storage volume in m³ (reported also in crore litres). Outputs include a pandas DataFrame with counts of ponding pixels and storage volume per structure and effective height.

name: Fill DEM and generate hillshade
desc: The script fills depressions in a digital elevation model (DEM) using the Wang & Liu sink-filling algorithm, computes flow accumulation using GRASS r.watershed with a threshold of 500,000 cells, and generates a hillshade raster from the filled DEM using specified azimuth (315°), vertical angle (45°), and user-defined Z factor. Outputs are three rasters: filled DEM, flow accumulation, and hillshade.

name: Derive stream reach and sub-catchments
desc: The script identifies main stream reaches from an input flow network vector layer using a user-defined numeric field threshold (e.g., flow accumulation ≥ ClassValue), rasterizes the filtered reaches, reclassifies a D8 flow direction raster to TauDEM-compliant coding, computes flow accumulation via TauDEM’s AreaD8, then executes TauDEM’s StreamNet to generate topologically correct stream reaches (vector) and corresponding sub-catchment polygons (raster → polygonized + dissolved by catchment ID). Outputs are two vector layers: 'Output Stream Reach' (line features with original attributes plus ID) and 'Output Sub-catchments' (polygon features with dissolved Value = catchment ID).

name: Extract flow pathways from flow accumulation
desc: The script processes a precomputed flow accumulation raster to extract stream networks (flow pathways) by applying a user-defined area threshold (in hectares), converting the thresholded raster to binary, thinning the raster cells to single-pixel width using GRASS r.thin, and vectorizing the result into polylines. The output is a line vector layer representing approximate flow pathways; the script explicitly notes that line direction may be incorrect and that this tool is intended for rapid visualization rather than hydrologically rigorous analysis.

name: Generate polygon-based sampling points
desc: The script implements a QGIS Processing algorithm to generate spatial sampling points inside user-provided polygon geometries, supporting two methods: (1) random point placement within buffered polygons (to avoid edge effects), and (2) regular grid-based point placement with optional minimum inter-point distance enforcement. It applies an inward buffer (negative distance) to the input polygon layer to constrain sampling away from boundaries, then either runs 'qgis:randompointsinsidepolygons' or constructs a regular point grid clipped to the buffered geometry and converts multipart results to single parts. Finally, it adds X/Y coordinate fields to the output point layer. The output is a vector point layer suitable for field sampling design in precision agriculture applications.

name: Correct building geometry errors
desc: The script performs topological quality assurance and correction on a vector layer of buildings in Delhi, identifying and fixing invalid geometries (e.g., self-intersections, ring orientation errors), snapping vertices to eliminate micro-gaps/overlaps within a 1.0-unit tolerance, and removing small interior holes (gaps < 10.0 sq units). It outputs before-and-after diagnostic layers — Invalid Geometries, Overlapping Areas, and Gaps/Holes — along with quantitative summaries comparing feature counts, invalid geometry counts, overlap counts/areas, and gap counts/areas before and after correction.

name: Clip rasters to homogeneous region
desc: The script clips multiple input raster layers to the geometry of a vector layer named 'homo_region' (homogeneous region), reprojecting them from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:32632 and cropping strictly to the cutline. It outputs a list of clipped rasters — one per input raster — each masked and resampled to the target CRS. The subsequent pixel-to-points conversion block is unreachable (due to early return) and thus not executed; only the clipping step runs.

name: Rasterize categories and compute basin zonal statistics
desc: The script rasterizes a categorical vector layer (e.g., biome classes) using a specified field (e.g., 'BIOME_INT') into a categorical raster at user-defined resolution, then computes zonal statistics (count, minority, majority) and zonal histograms for each input basin polygon layer against that raster. Outputs are GeoPackage files per basin layer containing added attribute columns summarizing the distribution and dominant classes of the categorical surface within each basin polygon.

name: Aggregate clipped map area by administrative unit
desc: The script clips multiple input vector layers (e.g., land use or risk maps) to a user-defined mask polygon, intersects the clipped layers with administrative units (e.g., municipalities), computes the area (in km²) of overlapping geometries, and aggregates the total area per administrative unit (grouped by ISTAT code), joining results across scenarios (e.g., 'alta', 'media', 'bassa') as separate columns into a final vector layer where each row is an administrative unit and columns include ISTAT, Comune, Provincia, and scenario-specific area sums.

name: Aggregate land cover area by administrative unit
desc: The script clips multiple input vector layers (e.g., land cover or hazard scenario maps) to a mask layer, intersects them with administrative units (e.g., Italian municipalities), computes the area (in km²) of intersected geometries, and aggregates the total area per administrative unit (grouped by ISTAT code). It then joins these aggregated area values — one per input layer, labeled by the 'per' field value (e.g., 'alta', 'media', 'bassa') — onto a master administrative units layer. The final output is a single vector layer (e.g., 'COM' polygons) enriched with columns like 'ISTAT', 'Comune', 'Provincia', and scenario-specific area sums (e.g., 'alta', 'media', 'bassa'). No raster data, time-series analysis, or classification is performed; all operations are vector-based geometric clipping, intersection, area calculation, and attribute aggregation/joining. Study area and data sources are not specified in the code — only generic parameter names ('LHP', 'REG', 'COM') and field names ('ISTAT', 'NOME_C', 'SG_PRV') suggest Italian administrative geography (e.g., ISTAT codes, province abbreviations), but no explicit region, time range, satellite, or sensor is referenced.

name: Aggregate land cover area by administrative unit
desc: The script clips multiple input vector layers (e.g., land cover or hazard scenario maps) to a mask layer, intersects them with administrative units (e.g., municipalities), computes the area (in km²) of overlapping geometries, and aggregates total area per administrative unit (grouped by ISTAT code). It then joins all scenario-specific area sums (e.g., 'alta', 'media', 'bassa') as separate fields onto a single administrative boundary layer (e.g., 'COM' — likely Italian comuni). The final output is a vector layer where each administrative unit has one row and columns for ISTAT, COMUNE, PROVINCIA, and one area field per input scenario layer. Study area and data sources are not embedded in the script — it is a generic GIS workflow tool operating on user-provided vector layers; no satellite imagery, time-series, or raster processing occurs. All operations are vector-based (clip, intersection, field calculation, aggregation, table join).

name: Extract cities within area of interest
desc: The script extracts point features representing cities that intersect with a user-provided polygon layer 'Area of interest', clips two polygon layers ('Regional Boundary' and 'Catchment area') to that same area, applies predefined QGIS style files to all layers for cartographic consistency, and exports a print layout as a PDF map. The core geoprocessing outputs are: (1) a clipped regional boundary layer, (2) a clipped catchment area layer, (3) a subset of cities located inside the area of interest, and (4) a georeferenced PDF map combining these layers with standardized symbology.

name: Extract hydrological network from DEM
desc: The script computes a hydrological network (stream vector layer) from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) using GRASS GIS r.watershed to derive flow accumulation and stream raster, then converts the stream raster to vector lines via r.to.vect. The watershed size parameter controls the minimum contributing area (in cells) required to initiate a stream. Input is a user-provided DEM raster; no time-series, cloud masking, or spectral bands are involved. Output is a vector layer of stream segments (hydro network), with no explicit study area, time range, satellite, or sensor information embedded in the code.

name: Model hydro network dispersion
desc: The script models the dispersion of an alien species along a hydrological network by delineating the total watershed upstream of a given occurrence point (using GRASS r.watershed and r.water.outlet), vectorizing stream networks and sub-watersheds, and clipping those features to the affected watershed. It outputs three vector layers: (1) the hydro network (streams) affected by the species, (2) the sub-watersheds intersecting the affected watershed, and (3) the full upstream watershed polygon derived from the occurrence point and DEM.

name: Model watershed dispersion upstream
desc: The script calculates the upstream watershed area (dispersion zone) from a user-specified species occurrence point using a digital elevation model (DEM). It first computes flow direction with GRASS r.watershed, then delineates the contributing (upstream) watershed using r.water.outlet. The output is a binary raster indicating the watershed dispersion area — i.e., all cells draining to or upstream of the input point. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic extent is encoded in the script; it is a generic hydrological delineation tool requiring user-provided DEM and point location. Input DEM source, CRS, resolution, and point coordinate system are not specified.

name: Create species distribution grid
desc: The script creates a regular vector grid (rectangular cells) aligned to the extent of an input species distribution or occurrence layer, with user-defined horizontal and vertical spacing. It then extracts only those grid cells that intersect the input species distribution geometry, producing a clipped, species-relevant grid layer for spatial analysis (e.g., occupancy, density, or overlay statistics). Key workflow steps: (1) generate a full-extent fishnet grid using QGIS native:creategrid with specified HSPACING/VSPACING; (2) spatially filter grid cells using 'intersects' predicate against the input species layer via native:extractbylocation. Output is a vector feature sink containing the subset of grid cells overlapping species presence.

name: Identify hydro network monitoring points
desc: The script computes intersection points between a line layer representing the affected hydro network and the boundary lines derived from watershed or administrative management polygon boundaries. It converts the input polygons to lines, performs line-line intersection to locate where the hydro network crosses administrative/watershed boundaries, then adds X/Y coordinate fields to the resulting point geometry. The output is a vector point layer ('Monitoring points') containing the geographic coordinates of these crossing locations, intended for field monitoring of alien species along hydrological networks at jurisdictional boundaries.

name: Model species range expansion
desc: The script models the potential geographic range of a species by buffering its known distribution points or polygons by a user-defined dispersal distance, then intersecting the buffered area with a reference grid or administrative boundary layer to extract only those grid cells/boundaries that overlap the buffered zone. The output is a vector layer containing the subset of the reference grid or boundaries that fall within the species' theoretical dispersal envelope.

name: Model species range from dispersal and grid
desc: The script calculates the potential distribution area (range) of a species by first buffering its known distribution polygon by a user-defined dispersal distance, then generating a regular grid (with specified horizontal and vertical spacing) covering that buffered area, and finally extracting only those grid cells that intersect the buffered distribution. The output is a vector layer of grid cells representing the modeled species range, intended for distribution analysis and spatial planning.

name: Model species range with ineffective barriers
desc: The script calculates the potential distribution range of a species by buffering its known distribution by a user-defined dispersal distance, intersecting that buffer with a reference grid (e.g., administrative units or ecological grid cells), then excluding areas influenced by ineffective zones (e.g., barriers, unsuitable ecosystems) via buffering those zones by an 'ineffective distance' and subtracting the resulting buffered ineffective grids from the initial range grids. The final output is a vector layer ('Range') representing the refined, barrier-adjusted species range at the resolution of the reference grid.

name: Delineate watershed basin
desc: The script delineates a watershed (catchment) basin for a given point observation using digital elevation model (DEM) and flow direction (D8) raster data. It first snaps the input point to the nearest stream or flow path using the DEM, then uses the snapped location as an outlet point in GRASS r.water.outlet to generate the contributing upstream area (basin) raster, which is subsequently polygonized into a vector boundary. The workflow integrates hydrological analysis (snap-to-stream, flow accumulation-derived D8, watershed delineation) with GIS vector-raster operations (spatial join, buffering, reclassification, polygonization) to produce a vectorized basin boundary for environmental assessment.

name: Clip raster by vector features
desc: The script clips a single input raster layer to the geometry of each individual feature in an input polygon vector layer, producing one clipped raster per feature (stored in a specified output folder), then builds a virtual raster (VRT) mosaic from all clipped rasters as the final output. It enforces a maximum of 100 features, dissolves and converts multipart polygons to singleparts before processing, and uses custom helper functions (feature2Layer, clipRaster4) for geometry-based raster clipping.

name: Calculate ecological values for forest points
desc: The script calculates ecological indicator values (nutrient retention, soil moisture, biodiversity, and deadwood potential) for user-provided point locations in Finnish forests. It retrieves spatial data via OGC WMS/WCS/REST services—including CHM (canopy height model), grid cell attributes (fertility class, stem counts), DTW (depth-to-water), biogeographical zones (MKasviv), and Euclidean distance to water protection areas—then joins and samples these layers at input points. Finally, it applies the ESS (Ecological Site Suitability) model using species and diameter inputs and outputs a point layer enriched with ecological scores and derived attributes.

name: Identify ecological value trees
desc: The script identifies individual trees with high ecological value (e.g., for retention as conservation trees — 'säästöpuut') within forestry cutting areas ('leimikko') in Finland. It integrates LiDAR-derived canopy height model (CHM) to detect tree tops, clips and samples raster layers (DTW — depth-to-water, Euclidean distance to water, vegetation zones, forest grid cells), joins tabular forest inventory attributes (fertility class, development class, stem counts, mean diameters/heights), and applies a weighted ecological scoring model (NP/phosphorus retention, BIO/biodiversity, LP/deadwood potential, DTW/moisture) to rank trees. Outputs are: (1) a point layer of ecologically scored trees ('Puiden ekologiset arvot'), styled with 'reTree3.qml'; and (2) a polygon layer aggregating these points into conservation area proposals ('Säästöpuuehdotus'), generated via point-to-area buffering ('point2area' with radius 1 m), styled with 'retreet_areas.qml'.

name: Identify ecological tree retention areas
desc: The script identifies ecologically valuable trees for retention (säästöpuut) within forest stands (leimikko) in Finland. It ingests a user-provided polygon layer of forest stands, then fetches geospatial data via OGC WMS/WCS/WFS endpoints: (1) Canopy Height Model (CHM) raster from Metsäkeskus' 'CHM_newest' service; (2) Stand-level vector attributes (e.g., SPECIALFEATURECODE, STEMCOUNTSPRUCE) from 'stand' service; (3) Grid-cell level forest inventory data (e.g., FERTILITYCLASS, MEANHEIGHTPINE) from 'gridcell' service; (4) Digital Terrain Wetness Index (DTW) raster from CSC's 'luke_dtw_04' WCS; (5) Biogeographical region ('eliogeoalue') vector from Ympäristöministeriön WMS; (6) Euclidean distance to water bodies raster from Metsäkeskus' 'euclidean' ImageServer; and (7) Protected sites vector layer. It vectorizes the CHM into individual tree crowns (createTreeMap), spatially joins all attribute layers, samples DTW and Euclidean rasters, applies an ecological scoring model (runEssModel) weighted by user-specified importance levels for phosphorus retention (FOSFORI), soil moisture (DTW), biodiversity (BIOD), and deadwood potential (LAHOP), and outputs two products: (a) a point layer ('Puiden ekologiset arvot') with ecological scores per retained tree, and (b) a polygon layer ('Säästöpuuehdotus') derived from buffering and aggregating those points. All operations occur on-the-fly via QGIS Processing algorithms and custom SMK Python modules; no explicit time-series or satellite imagery processing is performed — inputs are static, near-real-time national forest and terrain datasets.

name: Condition DEM for hydrological modeling
desc: The script performs hydrological conditioning of a digital elevation model (DEM) to prepare it for watershed delineation and stream network extraction. It supports optional resampling, stream carving using user-provided blue lines (with configurable depth), and walling using user-provided linear barriers (e.g., levees or embankments). Key workflow steps include: (1) optional resampling of input DEM to a specified output resolution (km); (2) saving an unconditioned copy ('_DEMraw.tif'); (3) rasterizing vector blue lines and subtracting a uniform carving depth from the DEM where streams are located; (4) rasterizing vector walls and adding a large elevation offset (5000 m) to enforce flow barriers; (5) running GRASS r.watershed to compute flow accumulation and extract streams based on a user-defined threshold in km², converted to cell count using the DEM’s ground resolution; and (6) exporting the conditioned DEM ('_DEMconditioned.tif') and derived stream raster ('_streams.tif'). All operations are performed locally using QGIS Processing with GDAL and GRASS 7 algorithms. No satellite, time-series, or external geospatial datasets beyond user-supplied inputs (DEM, Bluelines, Walls) are used — all data sources are user-provided and format-agnostic (raster/vector).

name: Compute hydrological derivatives alpha and beta
desc: The script computes hydrological conditioning parameters (alpha and beta) for the Continuum hydrological model using a conditioned DEM and raw DEM. It performs watershed delineation (flow accumulation, drainage direction, stream network), generates ancillary rasters (mask, latitude, longitude, area cell, choice map, pointers), and implements a custom iterative algorithm to compute alpha (local slope angle over a defined elevation drop DD=50 m along flow paths) and beta (smoothed channel slope). Outputs include ASCII grid files (.txt) for dem, area, choice, pnt, mask, lat, lon, areacell, alpha, and beta, all formatted for Continuum 3.1.6 input.

name: Propagate rupture probabilities along lines
desc: The script computes cascading failure probabilities by combining polygon-based rupture probabilities (e.g., from infrastructure or geological sources) with line-based propagation probabilities (e.g., fault traces, flow paths, or hazard corridors). It spatially splits rupture polygons using propagation lines, identifies which polygon subparts lie left-of each line (using single-sided buffering), and assigns an accumulated probability of occurrence (acca_prob) by indexing into a pre-defined domain matrix (domains.MATRIX_BREAKING) that maps rupture × propagation probability pairs to final event likelihoods. Output is a polygon layer enriched with a 'periodo_ritorno' field and the computed 'acca_prob' per feature.

name: Derive salinity indices from Landsat bands
desc: The script computes 10 spectral indices (SI1–SI10) from Landsat Band 2 (blue), Band 3 (green), Band 4 (red), and Band 5 (NIR) to serve as proxies for sea surface salinity (SSS), using raster algebra in QGIS. It then samples these indices against SSS values extracted from SMAP-derived NetCDF files (via VRT/XYZ conversion), merges the sampled results into a unified CSV per scene with longitude, latitude, SSS, and all 10 SI values, and exports them to 'C:/Users/MLMan/Desktop/CSVs/'. The workflow is fully local-file-based, operating on pre-downloaded Landsat Level-1 or TOA imagery and co-located SMAP SSS NetCDF products.

name: Fill no-data gaps in RF_NCSS land cover layers
desc: The script processes 10 pre-generated RF_NCSS raster layers (each with 6 bands), extracts and fills nodata regions band-by-band using GRASS r.fill.stats (with uncertainty estimation), then merges the filled bands into two multi-band GeoTIFFs per layer: one containing the filled classification bands ('_filled.tif') and one containing the corresponding uncertainty surfaces ('_uc.tif'). It is a post-classification gap-filling and uncertainty quantification workflow for multi-band land cover probability or confidence outputs.

name: Fill gibbsite raster bands
desc: The script processes a 10-band input raster named 'RF_Gibbsite.tif', where each band represents a spatial prediction (likely from a Random Forest model) of gibbsite — a clay mineral indicator in soil science. For each band, it extracts the band as a single-band GeoTIFF, then applies GRASS 'r.fill.stats' to fill NoData (void) pixels using inverse-distance-weighted interpolation with distance=3, power=2, and 8-directional search cells; uncertainty rasters ('uc') are simultaneously generated. Finally, all filled bands are merged into two multi-band outputs: 'RF_Gibbsite_filled.tif' (filled predictions) and 'RF_Gibbsite_uc.tif' (filled uncertainty estimates). The workflow is purely raster post-processing — no time-series, no external GEE image collections, no classification or modeling logic — and operates entirely on a precomputed local raster file. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code; the only domain-specific clue is the variable name 'Gibbsite', indicating a soil mineralogical target within pedology/soil mapping.

name: Calculate satellite visibility C-index
desc: The script computes the radar-based C-index raster (ranging from -1 to +1) that quantifies the geometric sensitivity of satellite SAR (e.g., Sentinel-1) line-of-sight (LOS) measurements to ground movement along terrain slope direction. It derives this index using DTM-derived slope and aspect, plus user-provided satellite acquisition geometry (incidence angle θ and track/azimuth angle φ) to compute directional cosines (H, N, E). The workflow includes: (1) generating constant rasters for θ and φ; (2) computing azimuth-corrected φ (φ+90); (3) calculating H = cos(θ), N = cos(π/2−θ)·cos(π−φ), E = cos(π/2−θ)·cos(3π/2−φ); (4) extracting slope and aspect from the input DTM; (5) evaluating the full C-index formula: C = N·cos(S)·sin(A−π/2) + E·(−1)·cos(S)·cos(A−π/2) + H·sin(S); (6) converting C to absolute percentage (|C|×100); and (7) reclassifying the percentage into five ordinal visibility classes (0–20%, 20–40%, ..., 80–100%). Outputs are three co-registered rasters: C_index (unitless, −1 to +1), Percentage_c_index (0–100%), and Class_of_visibility (integers 1–5).

name: Model shallow landslide susceptibility
desc: The script implements the SHALSTAB (SHAllow Landslide STABility) physically-based model to assess spatially distributed shallow landslide susceptibility. It computes absolute stability and instability conditions using infinite slope stability theory combined with steady-state hydrological modeling. Key outputs include: (1) Critical_rainfall (mm/day) — raster of daily critical infiltrated rainfall required to reach factor-of-safety = 1, where absolute stable cells are masked (NoData) and absolute unstable cells are assigned 0; (2) StabilityCells — binary raster identifying topographically stable cells (value = 9999) under full saturation; (3) InstabilityCells — binary raster identifying topographically unstable cells (value = −9999) even under zero rainfall; (4) Susceptibility — a 7-class reclassified raster based on log₁₀(qₜᵣ/T), following Montgomery & Dietrich (1998), representing relative landslide hazard classes derived from the ratio of critical rainfall to hydraulic transmissivity.

name: Generate street area and boundary from snapped centerlines
desc: The script processes manually edited street centerlines (snapped_streets.geojson) to generate: (1) a buffered street area polygon (street_area.geojson) via lane-aware buffering; (2) island polygons (islands_full.geojson) representing non-street, non-building, non-green open spaces within the map extent; (3) street boundary representations — both original (street_boundary_original.geojson) and filled/unioned with islands (street_boundary_filled.geojson); and optionally (4) sidewalk-derived street area and generalized sidewalk geometry (sidewalk_gen.geojson) when sidewalk_area.geojson is present. All outputs are georeferenced GeoJSONs organized by map scale (1:500 or 1:1000) and used for cartographic production.

name: Generate street area and boundary polygons
desc: The script processes manually edited street centerlines (snapped_streets.geojson) to generate buffered street area polygons, smooth them, extract urban islands (non-street land parcels within the extent), and derive both original and filled street boundaries — with conditional logic for sidewalk-informed refinement. Inputs include building footprints, green space, and extent geometries; outputs are GeoJSON files: street_area.geojson, islands_full.geojson, street_boundary_original.geojson, street_boundary_filled.geojson, street_from_sidewalk.geojson, street_boundary_filled.geojson (sidewalk path), and sidewalk_gen.geojson. All operations occur in a user-defined CRS (epsg from param.json), at either 1:500 or 1:1000 scale depending on size_code ('A3' → 500, else 1000), using geometric buffering, hole removal, smoothing, boolean difference/union, and disjoint/intersection filtering. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used — all inputs are static vector layers stored locally under 'data/' subfolders. The study area is implied by input file paths and geometry but not named explicitly.

name: Propagate rupture probability along lines
desc: The script computes propagation-based occurrence probabilities by combining rupture probabilities from polygon features (e.g., infrastructure or hazard zones) with propagation probabilities from line features (e.g., fault traces, flow paths, or transmission corridors). It spatially splits rupture polygons using propagation lines, then assigns a combined probability to each resulting polygon fragment based on a lookup matrix (domains.MATRIX_BREAKING) indexed by rupture probability and propagation probability values. The output is a polygon layer with original attributes plus a new 'periodo_ritorno' (return period) integer field and a computed probability attribute (acca_prob), derived from domain-specific coupling logic. No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or spectral processing is involved — inputs are user-provided vector layers with pre-assigned numeric/string fields; study area, time range, and sensor data are not specified in the code.

name: Convert ice-water boundary rasters to polylines
desc: The script processes a sequence of GeoTIFF raster files representing detected ice-water boundaries (binary masks) and converts them into vector polyline layers. It first masks out NoData values (setting 0 as nodata), then applies morphological thinning (using GRASS r.thin with 200 iterations) to reduce the raster boundary to single-pixel width, followed by raster-to-vector conversion (GRASS r.to.vect) to extract centerline polylines. Finally, it reprojects each resulting polyline shapefile from its native CRS to EPSG:3413 (NSIDC Sea Ice Polar Stereographic North), and loads the reprojected vector layer into the QGIS map canvas. Input rasters are located in 'edges/water_ice/', and outputs include masked, thinned, vectorized, and reprojected files organized in subdirectories.

name: Convert ice-water boundaries to polylines
desc: The script processes pre-classified raster files representing detected ice-water boundaries (stored in 'water_ice/*.tif') and converts them into vector polyline layers. It applies GDAL nodata masking (setting 0 as NoData), GRASS r.thin to skeletonize the binary boundary raster (200 iterations), GRASS r.to.vect to raster-to-vector conversion (line type, value column), and reprojects the resulting shapefiles from an unspecified input CRS to EPSG:3413 (NSIDC Polar Stereographic North, used for Arctic cryosphere applications). The final outputs are reprojected polyline shapefiles named 'wil_edge_line_{counter}.shp' → 'wil_line_repr_{counter}.shp', loaded as vector layers in QGIS. The study area is implied to be a glacier in Oregon (per Dropbox path), and the time range is indicated by the folder '2003/Classified/', confirming data from 2003. No satellite, sensor, or band information is present — the input rasters are already classified outputs ('Classified/edges/water_ice/'), so the script performs post-classification geometric processing only. Input CRS is not specified; output CRS is EPSG:3413 with explicit proj pipeline definition.

name: Convert ice-water boundary rasters to polylines
desc: The script converts pre-generated binary raster files representing water-ice boundaries (stored in 'edges/water_ice/*.tif') into vector polyline layers. It applies GDAL nodata masking (setting 0 as NoData), morphological thinning using GRASS r.thin (200 iterations) to reduce raster edges to 1-pixel width, raster-to-vector conversion via GRASS r.to.vect (line type), and reprojection from an unspecified input CRS to EPSG:3413 (NSIDC Polar Stereographic North). The final outputs are individual Shapefile polyline layers named 'wil_edge_line_{counter}.shp', reprojected to EPSG:3413 as 'wil_line_repr_{counter}.shp', and added to the QGIS map canvas. The study area is implied to be a glacier or ice-covered region in Oregon (per Dropbox path), with data dated 2019; however, the script itself does not generate or access satellite imagery — it processes already-classified edge rasters. Input rasters originate from prior classification (not shown), and no satellite, sensor, or band information is present in this script.

name: Generate urban activity spaces
desc: The script automates the creation of individualized urban activity spaces by processing survey-derived segment identifiers (e.g., street segments visited) against a road network. It uses GRASS v.net.steiner to compute least-cost Steiner trees connecting selected segments, buffers those routes to define activity space extents, clips original point segments to those buffers, and exports georeferenced shapefiles and CSVs per respondent — all tagged with unique RSP_ID identifiers. Outputs include Steiner route layers, buffered activity zones, clipped activity points, and tabular exports in structured folder hierarchy (Steiner_routes/, Buffers/, Activity Spaces/, csvs/).

name: Compute interior and exterior buffer zones
desc: The script computes a D=20 unit buffer around the RVFundamental vector layer, then clips it with the RPFGC_PPSM layer to extract the interior (overlap) region, computes the difference (RPFGC_PPSM minus interior) to extract the exterior region, merges interior and exterior into a single layer named 'IntExt_20', and exports it as a GeoPackage file. All operations are performed using QGIS Processing algorithms on local vector data; no remote sensing imagery or time-series analysis is involved. The study area is implied by the input geopackage filenames but not explicitly defined in code; inputs are local file paths pointing to 'RPFGC_PPSM.gpkg' and 'RVFundamental.gpkg'. No satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or coordinate reference system metadata is present in the script — all geospatial operations are purely geometric (buffer, clip, difference, merge).

name: Convert contours to true 3D LineStringZ
desc: The script converts 2D contour lines (from either a generated DEM-derived layer or an existing vector layer) into true 3D geometries (LineStringZ or MultiLineStringZ) by assigning Z-values from an elevation attribute (e.g., 'ELEV'), then exports the result as a GeoPackage with Z-enabled geometry and a SketchUp-compatible DXF file preserving 3D line geometry. It validates CRS alignment, handles reprojection, skips null/invalid elevations, and verifies Z-geometry integrity before output.

name: Generate professional topographic contour maps
desc: The script generates a publication-ready topographic contour map from either a DEM raster or existing contour vector data. It applies LandWise’s survey-grade styling: (1) classifies index/intermediate contours using user-specified interval and indexing rule; (2) optionally smooths contours for visual professionalism; (3) filters out short segments (<5 m); (4) applies white-glow line symbology with precise widths and colors (Deep Forest Green for index, Slate Grey for intermediate); (5) places curved, repeat-interval elevation labels (e.g., '12.5m') only on index or all contours per user choice; (6) integrates optional hillshade (auto-generated or user-provided) and orthomosaic with controlled opacity and desaturation; (7) styles boundary polygons with dashed red lines; and (8) exports A3 landscape print layouts with branded sidebar, coordinate grid, legend, scale bar, north arrow, and project metadata — plus high-res PNG/PDF deliverables and a comprehensive text/JSON report with contour statistics, elevation range, CRS, and processing parameters.

name: Generate terrain analysis from DEM
desc: The script processes a user-provided DEM/DTM raster to generate a standardized terrain analysis dataset in EPSG:32647 (UTM Zone 47N), including multi-angle hillshades (NW, NE, SE, SW), raw and classified slope (5 classes: Very Gentle to Very Steep), aspect, and optional client-specific clipped rasters; it skips hydrological processing (flow direction/accumulation/streams) per explicit design, delegating those to a separate 'Drainage Script.py', and produces a professionally branded QGIS print layout with elevation legend, scale bar, north arrow, and project metadata.

name: Classify solar orientation from terrain aspect
desc: The script performs true solar geometry analysis by calculating site-specific sunrise/sunset times, azimuths, and solar noon altitudes for solstices and equinoxes using pysolar. It generates aspect and slope rasters from a DEM, then classifies terrain into five client-meaningful solar exposure zones (Neutral Terrain, Cooler Slopes/North-facing, Morning Sun/East-facing, Full Sun/South-facing, Afternoon Heat/West-facing) based on aspect ranges and slope threshold (>2°). Outputs include: (1) classified solar orientation raster with LandWise color styling; (2) multi-angle hillshades (morning/midday/afternoon, terrain, and seasonal solstice hillshades); (3) polar sun path diagram showing seasonal sun trajectories; (4) professional A3 print layout with sidebar metadata, legend, scale bar, north arrow, and sun path inset; (5) high-res PNG (4000px) and PDF (300 DPI) exports; (6) comprehensive text and JSON reports containing solar geometry statistics, elevation metrics, exposure distribution (%/ha/pixels), and design recommendations.

name: Analyze ocean visibility from terrain
desc: The script computes terrain-based line-of-sight visibility from observer points (or a site grid) to the ocean using a dual-DEM architecture: a high-resolution drone DEM for local elevation sampling and a regional SRTM 30m DEM for terrain between the site and coast. It auto-detects coastline pixels below 3.0 m, selects N representative coast points by bearing, and performs ray-cast LOS checks from each observer/grid point to those coast targets. Outputs include: (1) a binary ocean-view coverage raster (1=visible, 0=blocked), (2) per-observer ocean view confirmation (✓/✗), (3) vectorized premium view zones (contiguous visible areas ≥50 m²), (4) styled QGIS layers with LandWise-compliant symbology, (5) professional A3 print layout with title, scale bar, north arrow, ocean direction indicator, legend, and visibility summary, and (6) deliverables folder with PNG (4000px), PDF (300 DPI), report (.txt), and statistics (.json).

name: Generate accessibility cost surface
desc: The script generates a cost surface for accessibility analysis by combining population density (inverted to represent travel cost) with administrative boundary lines (buffered and rasterized) to penalize crossing boundaries. It then runs GRASS r.cost to compute least-cost paths from settlement points (afg_pplp_SUBSET_proj.shp) across this combined cost raster, followed by polygonization and generalization of the resulting cost map. The study area is Afghanistan (inferred from 'afg_pplp_subset_proj.shp', 'afg_adm2_new_proj.shp', and 'bbox.shp'); inputs include a clipped/resampled population raster ('pop_clipped_qgis_resamp.tif') and vector administrative boundaries; no satellite or time-series data are used — all inputs are static, pre-processed geospatial datasets. Final outputs are: (1) 'admin_lines_v21.tif' (rasterized 100m-buffered admin boundaries), (2) 'combined_cost_v21.tif' (inverted population + boundary penalty), (3) 'out.tif' (GRASS r.cost output), (4) 'cost_map.tif' (nearest cost distance raster), (5) 'cost_map.shp' (polygonized cost zones), and (6) 'cost_map_gen.shp' (generalized polygons).

name: Compute rotated minimum bounding box
desc: The script computes a rotated minimum bounding box (RMBB) for the active QGIS vector layer by calculating convex hull vertices, then iteratively evaluating all vertex pairs to identify two parallel 'horizontal' lines (at user-defined rotation angle) and two parallel 'vertical' lines (orthogonal to horizontal) that maximize perpendicular distances between opposing lines. It solves line intersection equations to obtain four corner coordinates, sorts them clockwise, and constructs a memory polygon layer representing the tightest-fitting rotated rectangle aligned to the specified angle. Output is a single QgsVectorLayer polygon added to the QGIS project.

name: Compute watershed outlets
desc: The script iterates over a point layer (stop points), executes GRASS GIS's r.water.outlet on a flow direction raster for each point to delineate the upstream contributing area, polygonizes each resulting raster outlet mask, and merges all polygonized features into a single output vector layer. Each polygon is attributed with the original point's fid (and optionally 'hoyde', though that field is not defined in inputs). The workflow relies on local QGIS processing algorithms (GRASS r.water.outlet and GDAL polygonize) and does not use Google Earth Engine—despite the user prompt mentioning 'GEE script', the provided code is a QGIS Processing Algorithm written in Python for QGIS, with no Earth Engine API calls, ee.* imports, or GEE-specific syntax. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor information are not present in the script; it operates on user-provided local vector points and a precomputed flow direction raster (e.g., from SRTM or other DEM-derived hydrology). Output is a merged vector layer of watershed polygons, one per input point.

name: Calculate Curve Number
desc: The script calculates the USDA Soil Conservation Service (SCS) Curve Number (CN) for a user-defined polygon study area using global land cover and hydrologic soil group datasets. It processes ESA WorldCover 2021 (10 m) land cover raster via VRT clipping, retrieves ORNL HYSOG Global Hydrologic Soil Groups (A/B/C/D) via WCS download from ORNL’s webmap broker, aligns both rasters to matching extent and resolution, performs pixel-wise CN lookup using hydrologic condition (Poor/Fair/Good) and antecedent runoff condition (I/II/III) parameters, clips the final CN raster to the input polygon, and reports statistics including mean CN, potential retention (S), and direct runoff (Q) under an assumed rainfall depth. Outputs include optional intermediate rasters (land cover, soil groups) and mandatory final CN raster.

name: Delineate watershed basin
desc: The script delineates a watershed basin polygon from a user-provided Digital Elevation Model (DEM) and a single pour point coordinate using GRASS GIS hydrological tools (r.fill.dir, r.watershed, r.water.outlet). It optionally clips an input stream network to the derived basin boundary and applies geometric smoothing (iterations and offset) to the basin polygon. Outputs are a smoothed vector polygon layer representing the watershed basin and — if provided — a clipped line layer of the stream network within that basin.

name: Map weathering zones in watersheds
desc: The script computes a quantitative weathering index raster by integrating five geospatial inputs—watershed polygons, slope, moisture, lithology index, and temperature amplitude rasters—using domain-specific weighting and normalization logic (encapsulated in `compute_weathering_index`). It then derives a binary weathering mask by thresholding the index at a user-defined percentile (e.g., 85th), polygonizes the mask to generate weathering zone geometries, and intersects those zones with input watershed boundaries to produce attribute-rich, basin-constrained weathering polygons. Outputs are: (1) a GeoTIFF weathering index raster, and (2) a vector layer of weathering zones clipped to and attributed by watershed units.

name: Calculate pond stage storage volume
desc: The script calculates stage-storage relationships for individual pond polygons by slicing the ground elevation raster at regular vertical intervals (storage_interval) to generate contour polygons, clipping them to each pond boundary, and computing incremental and cumulative volumes and surface areas per elevation slice. It outputs a GeoPackage vector layer containing polygon slices with attributes including ssMIN, ssMAX (capped at pond RLmax), ssAREA, ssINCVOL, ssCUMVOL, ssMINDPTH, ssMAXDPTH, and all original pond attributes; plus an optional HTML report summarizing depth, RL, area, incremental volume, and cumulative volume per pond.

name: Compute shortest paths from origins to POIs
desc: The script preprocesses origin-destination (DeSO centroids and OSM POIs) and street network layers, then computes shortest path routes over the network using QGIS processing tools; it outputs a vector layer ('Result network') containing routed geometries (e.g., least-cost paths) linking each origin to its nearest or matched destinations, based on attributes like 'Totalt' (origin population) and 'fclass' (POI type), enabling accessibility or service area analysis.

name: Model bike and e-bike destination choice
desc: The script processes pre-calculated shortest path networks between origins and points of interest (POIs) to model destination choice and mode choice for bicycle and electric bicycle travel. It joins origin population sizes ('Totalt') to path features, applies a gravity-based exponential distance-decay function (parameterized per purpose: Leisure, Shopping, Services, Touring), computes mode-specific choice probabilities using a sigmoid function (with distinct parameters for bike vs. e-bike), and calculates weighted path flows ('Weight_bike', 'Weight_ebike') by normalizing the product of origin size, mode probability, and decay weight by the sum of decay weights per origin (i.e., destination choice normalization over destinations sharing the same origin). Outputs are finalized shapefiles (/tmp/WeightedPathsFinal_*.shp) containing these flow weights per path segment, loaded as vector layers in QGIS.

name: Sample landslide points by grid
desc: The script randomly samples landslide point locations into training and validation subsets using a regular grid-based stratification method. It rasterizes input landslide points within a user-defined polygon mask, resamples the raster to a specified pixel width/height (w/h), clips the raster to the polygon extent, and then assigns each point to a grid cell. A percentage (train%) of grid cells is randomly selected for training; all points in those cells form the training set, while remaining points form the validation set. Outputs are two vector layers: one containing training points ('Layer of sample') and one containing validation points ('Layer of 1-sample'). The script operates entirely on local vector/raster I/O (e.g., /tmp/inv_sampler.tif, /tmp/invq_sampler.tif) and uses QGIS Processing and GDAL — no Earth Engine server-side operations are present. No satellite imagery, time series, or cloud-based GEE assets are used; inputs are local shapefiles (points + polygon). Study area, time range, and sensor data are not specified.

name: Compute LS factor for erosion modeling
desc: The script computes the LS (slope-length and steepness) factor used in the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and USPED erosion models. It takes a filled DEM as input, derives slope (in degrees) and flow accumulation (using SAGA's Multiple Flow Direction top-down algorithm), then applies a raster calculation implementing the standard LS formula: LS = m × (A / 22.1)^m × (sin(θ) / 0.09)^n, where A is upstream contributing area per unit contour width (derived from flow accumulation and cell size), θ is slope angle in radians, and m and n are user-defined sheet and rill erosion exponents. Outputs are three georeferenced rasters: the final LS factor map, the intermediate slope raster (degrees), and the flow accumulation raster (cell count or area units depending on input DEM resolution).

name: Compute USPED erosion potential
desc: The script computes the Universal Soil Loss Equation-based Sediment Potential (USPED) raster, a spatially distributed estimate of net soil erosion/deposition derived from topographic, hydrological, and land cover factors. It first calculates flow accumulation and topographic derivatives (slope, aspect) from a filled DEM; then constructs a flow-slope topographic index (sflowtopo); multiplies it by R, K, and C factors (either as rasters or scalar values) and directional components (cosine/sine of adjusted aspect) to derive sediment transport components qsx and qsy; computes their spatial gradients (qsx_dx, qsy_dy) via slope/aspect of those components; and finally sums them (with optional 10× scaling for sheet erosion) to produce the final USPED raster output representing predicted sediment flux magnitude and directionality.

name: Calculate slope unit aspect segmentation metric
desc: The script computes the Alvioli et al. (2016) segmentation aspect metric for landslide susceptibility modeling, specifically calculating three components per input slope unit (SU) polygon layer: (1) V — a normalized variance-like index quantifying intra-unit aspect dispersion using sin/cos of aspect raster sums weighted by area; (2) I — an adjacency-weighted inter-unit aspect coherence index derived from teta angles and Queen contiguity adjacency; and (3) F — a composite, normalized, additive score combining standardized V and I values. Outputs are a CSV file containing one row per slope unit with columns 'name', 'V', 'I', and 'F'.

name: Generate parcel boundary stroke geometry
desc: The script generates a vector layer ('stroke_geom_layer') representing stylized boundary strokes for parcels, rivers, and lakes within a defined raster extent. It computes inner and outer buffers around non-road parcels to create a 'stroke' (difference between outer and inner buffer), applies a uniform buffer to road parcels, clips rivers and lakes to the extent with additional buffering for visual stroke width, dissolves all resulting geometries, and finally clips the dissolved stroke layer to the original raster extent. The output is a single dissolved, clipped polygon layer rendered with light gray fill and no border, intended for cartographic stroke representation of hydrographic and cadastral features.

name: Generate elevation contour stroke layers
desc: The script generates a vector layer ('stroke_geom_layer') composed of buffered contour lines derived from an input elevation vector layer ('area5_for_script'), where two sets of contours are extracted based on specific elevation values (460 m and [20, 240, 680, 1000] m), buffered at different widths (thick_stroke_width and thin_stroke_width) to create visually distinct contour strokes; the final output is a memory-based polygon layer filled with light gray (#dcdcdc) and no border, clipped to the extent of a raster layer ('area5_rectangle1'), intended for cartographic rendering as stylized elevation contours.

name: Generate contour stroke geometry
desc: The script generates a vector layer ('stroke_geom_layer') containing buffered contour lines and buffered coastlines, styled as filled polygons with no fill and black borders (later set to light gray fill with no border), clipped to the extent of a raster layer named 'rata_rectangle1'. It selects two contour elevation classes: thick strokes for contours where elevation modulo 160 equals zero, and thin strokes for contours where elevation modulo 80 equals zero but modulo 160 does not — effectively generating hierarchical contour line symbology (e.g., index and intermediate contours). Coastlines are similarly buffered and clipped to produce a consistent stroke width matching the thin contour style. The final output is a single memory-based polygon layer whose geometry represents the union of all buffered-and-clipped contour and coastline features, intended for cartographic stroke rendering (e.g., as a mask or outline layer in print/map production).

name: Compute symmetrical difference of two polygon layers
desc: The script computes the symmetrical difference (XOR) between two vector layers representing an exterior extent and a survey mosaic, after dissolving each layer to single-part geometries. It outputs a new vector layer containing areas present in either the exterior extent or the survey mosaic but not in both — i.e., the non-overlapping portions — and adds this result as a map layer in QGIS.

name: Generate contour stroke geometry
desc: The script generates a vector layer ('stroke_geom_layer') composed of buffered contour lines and buffered coastlines, styled as a solid gray fill with no border. It processes contour lines from 'harakeke_contours_250' (elevation contours at 250 m intervals) and coastline from 'harakeke_coast', both clipped to the extent of 'harakeke_rectangle1'. Thick contours (multiples of 1000 m elevation) are buffered at scale-adjusted width (0.4 mm map units → ~thick_stroke_width), thin contours (multiples of 500 m but not 1000 m) at half that width, and coastlines buffered identically to thick contours. All buffered geometries are merged into a single memory polygon layer. The study area is Harakeke (a locality in New Zealand), inferred from layer names and CRS EPSG:2193 (NZGD2000 / New Zealand Transverse Mercator). No satellite or raster analysis is performed — all operations are vector-based GIS processing using QGIS native algorithms. Final output is a styled polygon layer added to the QGIS project for cartographic rendering.

name: Generate river water race lake stroke geometry
desc: The script constructs a buffered 'stroke' geometry layer representing the visual stroke (outline) of hydrographic features — rivers, water races, lakes, and river polygons — clipped to a raster extent. It buffers linear features (rivers, water races) by a scale-dependent width (0.2 mm at 1:100,000), retains lake and river polygon geometries as-is (no buffering), merges all into a single memory vector layer, dissolves overlapping geometries, then clips the result to the exact extent of the input raster layer 'kahikatea_rectangle1'. The final output is a dissolved, extent-clipped polygon layer rendered with light gray fill and no border, intended for cartographic stroke/outline representation of hydro features in a map layout.

name: Convert parcel stroke to polygon geometry
desc: The script converts vector parcel boundaries (e.g., 'kanuka_parcel') into filled stroke polygons by buffering selected features (non-Road and Road parcels) with positive and negative offsets, computing geometric differences (for non-Road) or single positive buffers (for Road), unioning all stroke geometries via dissolve, and clipping the final stroke layer to a predefined raster-derived boundary polygon ('kanuka_area'). The output is a single, topologically clean, fill-ready QGIS vector layer ('clipped_layer') styled with solid gray fill and no border, intended for export to SVG/Inkscape without requiring 'stroke to path' conversion.

name: Convert road stroke to polygon geometry
desc: The script converts linear vector features (specifically 'Road' and other parcel intents) into polygonal representations by buffering each line feature outward by half the stroke width and subtracting an inward buffer of equal magnitude, effectively turning strokes into filled polygons. For 'Road' features, only the outer buffer is retained (no inner subtraction), while for non-Road features (e.g., 'Agriculture', 'Forest'), the stroke is represented as a ring-shaped polygon via outer_buffer.difference(inner_buffer). All resulting geometries are unioned (dissolved) into a single seamless polygon layer clipped to the extent of a reference raster layer ('area3_rectangle2'), producing a clean, fill-ready QGIS memory layer without reliance on SVG stroke rendering or Inkscape's unstable 'stroke to path' function.

name: Generate contour stroke geometry
desc: The script generates a stylized vector stroke layer representing topographic contours and river polygons, with differentiated line weights: thick strokes for every 180 m elevation (e.g., 0, 180, 360 m), thin strokes for specific elevations (20, 100, 260, 340 m), and buffered river polygons — all clipped to a raster extent and dissolved into a single filled polygon layer with light gray fill (#dcdcdc) and no border, intended for cartographic base mapping or thematic overlay.

name: Extract urban core-adjacent built-up areas
desc: The script processes Urban Atlas 2018 vector data for Poznań, Poland, to identify and isolate built-up areas (code_2018) belonging to selected functional urban zones (e.g., 21000–24000, 13400), then spatially refines them by intersecting with a buffered Urban Core layer (attached buffer: 200 m) and excluding areas overlapping with a separately buffered detached zone (code 12230, buffer: 250 m); finally, it filters resulting geometries to retain only those with area >10 ha (100,000 m²), outputs a cleaned single-part polygon layer of urban-periurban built-up patches adjacent to—but not overlapping—the Urban Core and detached functional zones.

name: Clip land cover raster by point buffers
