It first cleans existing LW-prefixed fields (e.g., 'LWD', 'LWE', 'LWN') from the input road layer, then performs a PK-based attribute join between the cleaned road layer and the Groovy-processed LW_ROADS.geojson output, producing a joined road layer enriched with emission/level attributes. The final output is a vector feature sink containing the original road geometry plus appended emission-related fields.

name: Generate river sampling points
desc: The script generates regularly spaced point features along a user-provided river network vector layer at a specified distance interval (in meters), assigns unique IDs and distance attributes, reprojects them to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), appends geometry attributes (x/y coordinates), and exports the resulting points to an Excel file (River_points.xlsx). If user-provided searching points (Excel/ODS) are supplied instead, it copies them to the working directory. Subsequently, it executes external Python modules ('extraction' and 'translation') to fetch geotagged Twitter posts near those points using a provided API key and optional keyword filters, then translates non-English tweets — producing a final translated tweet dataset (export_dataframe.xlsx).

name: Join features by transit time
desc: The script performs a spatial join between two vector layers (input and join layers) based on real-world multimodal transit travel time (e.g., walking, cycling, driving) using the OpenRouteService (ORS) Matrix API. It computes origin-destination travel durations from each input feature centroid to all join feature centroids, filters pairs within user-defined min/max time thresholds (in minutes or hours), selects the nearest join feature per input, copies specified attributes with optional prefixing, and optionally appends the computed transit time as a new field. The output is a new vector layer where input features are enriched with joined attributes and (optionally) transit time, retaining only matches satisfying the time constraints.

name: Print water mains map layout
desc: The script connects to a PostGIS database to load a 'water_mains' vector layer (with geometry column 'geometry' and primary key 'id'), validates and inspects its features, styles it categorically by 'material' field (PVC, STEEL, IRON, COPPER, OTHER) with colored line symbols and labels pipe size, adds an OpenStreetMap basemap (reprojected if needed), creates a print layout from a QPT template ('watermain_layout_1.qpt'), sets the map extent to match the water mains layer's bounding box with padding and aspect-ratio adjustment, and exports the final layout as a PDF ('water_mains.pdf').

name: Densify lines with nearest points by attribute condition
desc: The script densifies input line geometries by inserting new vertices derived from a point layer. It supports two methods: (1) using the nearest points themselves as new vertices (modifying line paths), or (2) interpolating points onto the original lines at the distances where nearest points project onto them (preserving original line paths). Crucially, it applies optional, configurable attribute-based filtering—using up to two comparison expressions (one per layer) combined via logical operators (AND/OR/XOR/etc.)—to determine which point–line pairs qualify for densification. Input lines can be ordered (e.g., for sequential processing like river networks), filtered, and constrained by maximum search distance. Output is a new line layer with added vertices; duplicate nodes can be optionally removed. The algorithm requires projected CRS for geometric accuracy and handles reprojection, multipoint conversion, and spatial indexing for efficiency.

name: Extend lines to nearest points
desc: The script extends line geometries (or parts of multiline geometries) to the nearest point features based on configurable geometric rules (start/end of line or part) and optional attribute-based conditional matching between line and point features. It supports filtering source lines and points via expressions, ordering source lines, setting maximum extension distance and minimum required distance, allowing or disallowing self-crossing of extended segments, and controlling point reuse (per layer, per feature, or per part). The output is a new vector layer of modified line geometries with vertices extended toward qualifying nearest points.

name: Join attributes by nearest with condition
desc: The script performs a conditional spatial join between a source vector layer and a join vector layer, finding the nearest neighbors based on geometry (or centroids) and optionally applying user-defined attribute-based conditions (e.g., field comparisons using operators like '=', '!=', 'contains'). It supports multiple comparison expressions with logical concatenation (AND/OR/XOR), filtering before join, ordering of source features, limiting by count or distance, prefixing joined fields, and handling duplicate joins. Outputs include a copy of the source layer with joined attributes, plus two added fields: shortest Cartesian distance and shortest line geometry as WKT.

name: Snap line vertices to points
desc: The script snaps specified vertices (start, end, or mid-vertices) of line geometries in a source vector layer to the nearest point from a points layer, optionally constrained by attribute-based conditions (e.g., field comparisons using operators like '=', '!=', 'contains') and maximum snapping distance. It supports advanced matching logic (AND/OR/XOR combinations of two conditions), configurable reuse of points (once per layer/feature/part), spatial indexing for efficiency, reprojection if CRS mismatched, and multipoint-to-singlepoint conversion. Output is a new vector layer with modified geometries preserving original attributes.

name: Split lines at nearest points by condition
desc: The script splits line geometries at locations determined by the nearest points from a separate point layer, optionally applying attribute-based conditions (using expressions and comparison operators) to filter which line-point pairs trigger a split. It supports two methods: modifying line paths by inserting vertices at the nearest points themselves, or interpolating points along the existing line geometry closest to those points. The algorithm handles filtering, reprojection, spatial indexing, expression evaluation for conditional logic, duplicate node removal, and optional dropping of resulting line segments shorter than a specified length. Outputs are new line features representing the original lines segmented at the computed split points.

name: Create perpendicular lines from points
desc: The script creates perpendicular lines from input points to the nearest line features, optionally filtered by attribute conditions. It uses QgsGeometry.nearestPoint() and QgsGeometry.interpolateAngle() to locate intersection points and compute perpendicular orientation; supports dynamic parameters (max distance, max neighbors, line length) via expressions per point; adds metadata fields including source/overlay IDs, WKT geometries, intersection distance along line, interpolated angle, and 3D distance; requires projected CRS for accuracy; handles multipoint-to-singlepoint conversion and optional reprojecting of overlay layer.

name: Refine forest patch density
desc: The script refines a primary-forest candidate raster by applying a neighbourhood density filter (circular or square kernel) to remove isolated small forest patches, followed optionally by a minimum patch size sieve filter. It computes local forest pixel proportion within a user-specified radius (in meters), thresholds pixels below a density threshold (0–1), and masks results back to the input forest extent. For large radii (>5000 m) or when 'Fast approximation' is enabled, it uses an area-corrected square kernel; otherwise, it uses exact circular convolution (via FFT if scipy is available, else integral image). Output is a binary refined forest raster (primary_forest.tif).

name: Vectorize primary forest raster
desc: The script converts a binary or coded PFF (Primary Forest Finder) raster into vector polygons for selected pixel values (e.g., '1' for primary forest or '1,2,3' for broader forest classes), optionally simplifies geometries using Douglas-Peucker with a user-defined tolerance in metres, and produces a dissolved multipart polygon suitable as a sampling-area boundary for validation workflows (e.g., Collect Earth Online). It uses GDAL polygonize (4-connected), QGIS native simplifygeometries, and native dissolve — all operating on a masked raster where only specified pixel values are retained and background is set to nodata. Outputs are GeoPackage or Shapefile layers: one simplified vector layer and one dissolved single-feature multipart layer.

name: Join field boundaries to point locations
desc: The script performs a spatial join between a point layer named '2025' and a polygon layer named 'POLA' using the 'intersects' predicate. It first ensures both layers share the same CRS by reprojecting the points if necessary, then joins all attributes from the polygon layer to the points, prefixing them with 'pole_'. The output is a GeoPackage file ('punkty_z_numerami_pol2025.gpkg') containing the original points augmented with attributes (e.g., field IDs, names, or parcel numbers) from the intersecting polygons — enabling attribution of cadastral or agricultural field identifiers to survey/GPS points.

name: Convert heat density raster to vector polygons
desc: The script converts a raster file representing current heat demand density (heat_res_curr_density_clip.tif) into vector polygon features using GDAL's polygonize algorithm, then reprojects the resulting GeoJSON from its native CRS to EPSG:25830 (ETRS89 / UTM zone 30N), and — though commented out — indicates intent to spatially join the reprojected heat-density polygons with building footprint data (buildings_inspire_clip_oxarkoaga+census.shp) to transfer heat demand attributes (HDemProj/HDem) to buildings. The final output is a vector layer where each polygon represents a contiguous area of homogeneous heat demand density, georeferenced in ETRS89 UTM 30N, suitable for urban energy planning and infrastructure analysis.

name: Reproject layer to TransCAD CRS
desc: The script reprojects an input vector layer through a three-step coordinate transformation workflow: (1) reprojection from the input CRS to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), (2) reprojection from EPSG:4326 to the custom TransCAD Israel TM CRS (retrieved via get_transcad_crs()), and (3) assignment of EPSG:2039 as the declared CRS without altering coordinates — effectively overriding the CRS metadata to match Israel’s official geodetic system (Israeli Transverse Mercator, ITM), which is equivalent to EPSG:2039. The output is a vector layer with geometry coordinates transformed to ITM and CRS explicitly set to EPSG:2039.

name: Convert GDB layers to GeoPackage
desc: The script converts specified vector layers from an ESRI File Geodatabase (.gdb) to a single GeoPackage (.gpkg) file using PyQGIS's 'native:package' processing algorithm. It initializes QGIS in headless mode, validates and loads input layers via OGR URI syntax (e.g., 'gdb_path|layername=layer_name'), optionally handles CRS reprojection, deletes any existing output GeoPackage before writing, and logs success or failure per layer. Outputs include a GeoPackage containing the selected layers, with optional CRS alignment.

name: Reproject vector layer
desc: The script reprojects a vector layer ('brgm.shp') from its native CRS to EPSG:3460 using QGIS's native reprojection algorithm. It initializes the QGIS application, loads the vector layer via QgsVectorLayer, sets up processing with QgsNativeAlgorithms, configures parameters including input layer and target CRS, executes 'native:reprojectlayer', and captures the output shapefile ('outputfile.shp'). Error handling logs messages via QgsMessageLog connection.

name: Generate perpendicular lines along line
desc: The script generates perpendicular line segments at regular intervals along input line or polygon boundary geometries. It first reprojects the input layer to a specified CRS (e.g., UTM), then places points along the lines using user-defined distance, start offset, and end offset parameters. For each point, it constructs a perpendicular line segment using a geometry expression that projects from the point at an angle 90° offset from the local line direction (via 'radians("angle"-90)'). The resulting lines are optionally reprojected to a final output CRS. The output is a vector layer of perpendicular line features.

name: Interpolate surface property values
desc: The script performs Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation on point vector features to generate a continuous raster surface representing a specified attribute (e.g., elevation, soil moisture, temperature). It optionally clips the resulting interpolated raster to a polygon mask layer. Key workflow steps include: (1) reading an input point vector layer and selecting a numeric attribute by index for interpolation; (2) configuring IDW parameters — distance coefficient P, output extent, and pixel size; (3) executing QGIS’s native 'qgis:idwinterpolation' algorithm; and (4) conditionally applying GDAL’s 'gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer' using a user-provided mask polygon layer, with advanced options for CRS handling, nodata value, and compression. Outputs are either the raw interpolated raster ('Interpolated') or the clipped version ('Clipped'), both as GeoTIFFs with configurable creation options.

name: Join vector layers by spatial relationship
desc: The script performs sequential spatial joins of multiple vector layers onto a first (base) layer using QGIS's native 'joinattributesbylocation' algorithm. It iteratively joins each subsequent layer to the accumulating result (starting from the first layer), applying user-specified geometry predicates (e.g., 'intersects', 'contains'), join type (e.g., one-to-one, one-to-many), field selection, prefixing, and optional non-matching record discarding. The final output is a single vector layer with attributes from all input layers appended according to their spatial relationships.

name: Generate offset line arrays
desc: The script generates a series of parallel offset lines from an input line vector layer, using a user-defined mapping of (spacing, count) tuples to iteratively apply the native QGIS 'offsetline' algorithm. Each tuple defines a spacing distance and number of offsets to generate consecutively — with optional half-spacing for the first offset and an extra half-offset after the last in a group. The resulting offset lines are merged into a single output vector layer ('Array of offset lines'), optionally including the original input line ('Keep first'). This is a deterministic geometric transformation workflow for creating corridor buffers, lane delineations, or multi-track centerlines (e.g., for road widening, pipeline routing, or survey transect design).

name: Georeference and merge port locations
desc: The script georeferences two port location datasets (one from a CSV with lat/lon coordinates, another from a shapefile joined with an auxiliary CSV), fixes geometries, reprojects both to ESRI:54034 (Equal Earth Cylindrical Equal Area), merges them into a single vector layer, and adds an auto-incrementing ID field. The final output is a unified, projected, topologically cleaned point layer of port locations (ports.shp → ports_id.shp) suitable for spatial analysis or cost raster integration.

name: Prepare CAR KML exports
desc: The script prepares KML files for the Brazilian Rural Environmental Registry (Cadastro Ambiental Rural – CAR) by extracting only the features from visible vector layers in the QGIS project that intersect with selected polygon features (e.g., rural property boundaries) from an input polygon layer. It filters overlay layers by spatial containment, reprojects them to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and exports each as a named KML file (e.g., 'roads_<property_name>.kml') into a user-specified folder. Output includes one KML per visible vector layer, each containing only geometries within the selected property boundary and named using a user-specified attribute field.

name: Generate building detection training chips
desc: The script generates synthetic training chip pairs (satellite image PNG + binary building mask PNG) for deep learning models (e.g., Mask R-CNN, U-Net). It loads a satellite GeoTIFF basemap and an OSM building vector layer, reprojects the vector to match the raster CRS, rasterizes buildings into a pixel-aligned binary mask GeoTIFF, computes a regular grid of chip extents over a user-defined AOI, clips and resizes both image and mask to fixed dimensions (e.g., 256×256 px), filters out chips with insufficient building coverage (< min_positive_ratio), and logs dataset statistics including total chips, exported count, skip/fail rates, and average building pixel coverage.

name: Update urban point attributes
desc: The script updates a point layer representing current land surface conditions by identifying points located within future urbanization polygons, then modifies their attributes: (1) sets 'ALB' (albedo) to the value from the 'ALBFUT' field of the intersecting urban polygon; (2) sets 'HAUTA' (tree height) to 0; (3) sets 'URB' (urban flag) to 1; (4) sets 'OCCSOL' (land cover class) to 6 (indicating an urban class); finally merges updated points with unmodified points (those outside future urban zones) and removes the temporary 'ALBFUT' join field, producing a fully updated point layer with consistent urban attribute assignments.

name: Extract UHI predictor variables
desc: The script extracts a comprehensive set of geospatial predictor variables for Urban Heat Island (UHI) modeling, including Land Surface Temperature (LST) from Landsat 9 Band 7, elevation (ALT), slope (PENTE), aspect/exposition (EXP), land cover (OCCSOL), soil type (NATSOL), tree height (HAUTA), hydrologic class (CATHYD), climatic zone (ZONECL), and urban-rural classification (URB), all sampled at LST pixel locations; it computes albedo (ALB) from Landsat 9 reflectance bands (LS1–LS6) and outputs a cleaned point vector table (CSV-compatible) with all attributes aligned to the same spatial extent and CRS (EPSG:4326), ready for machine learning input.

name: Compute LST and vegetation/urban/water indices
desc: The script processes locally stored Landsat Level-1 or Level-2 surface reflectance and thermal raster files (B2–B8, B10) to compute five geospatial raster outputs per scene: NDVI (using B4/red and B5/near-infrared), NDBI (using B5/NIR and B6/shortwave infrared), NDWI (using B5/NIR and B3/green), LST in Celsius (converted from B10 thermal band in Kelvin), and a pansharpened true-color RGB image (B2/B3/B4 merged + B8 panchromatic sharpening). All outputs are saved as GeoTIFFs in individual date-named subfolders under the Santa Marta study directory.

name: Extract LST and environmental variables
desc: The script extracts Land Surface Temperature (LST) from Landsat 9 imagery (band specified by user parameter 'numro_de_bande_de_la_lst', default=7) and co-locates it with 10 ancillary geospatial rasters: digital elevation model (DEM), land cover (DWV1), soil type, tree height, hydrologic category, climate zone (LCZ), slope, aspect (exposure), urban-rural classification, and albedo. Workflow includes reprojection (all rasters to EPSG:4326), spatial clipping to user-defined extent ('emprise_de_calcul_de_luhi'), raster-to-point conversion of LST pixels, sampling of all rasters at those points, field renaming, urban-rural binary derivation (class 6 → 1, else 0), and albedo calculation using a weighted linear combination of Landsat bands 1–6. Final output is a point vector layer (feature sink) with attributes: LST, LAT/LON, ALT, OCCSOL, URB, PENTE, EXP, NATSOL, HAUTA, CATHYD, ZONECL, ALB, and LS1–LS6 — exported as CSV for AI modeling. No explicit study area, time range, or satellite metadata (e.g., acquisition date) is present in the code; all inputs are preloaded raster layers with no temporal filtering or dynamic collection handling.

name: Estimate floodwater depth
desc: The script estimates floodwater depth using a digital elevation model (DEM) and a user-provided inundation polygon. It follows the FwDET v2.1 method (Cohen et al., 2022): (1) clips the DEM to the inundation polygon extent; (2) rasterizes the inundation boundary (polygon-to-line → raster); (3) samples DEM elevations along that boundary; (4) smooths boundary elevations via iterative neighborhood maximum filtering; (5) applies slope-based filtering using GRASS r.slope.aspect (with threshold in percent); (6) grows the smoothed boundary outward using GRASS r.grow.distance with configurable distance metric (euclidean, squared, etc.); (7) computes water depth as the difference between the grown distance surface and the clipped DEM; (8) masks depths to the inundation area; and (9) optionally applies a low-pass 3×3 average filter. Outputs are three rasters: shore-boundary elevation, interpolated water depth, and smoothed water depth. No satellite or time-series data is used — inputs are static local raster (DEM) and vector (inundation polygon) layers. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified in the code.

name: Download Copernicus land cover product
desc: The script downloads Copernicus Global Land (CGL) products — specifically NetCDF-formatted land surface thematic datasets (e.g., LAI, FAPAR, land cover, soil moisture) — by programmatically navigating the VITO CGL manifest directory structure; it selects the manifest file corresponding to the user-specified product collection and date, identifies the nearest-availability NetCDF file via date parsing in HTML-manifest paths, downloads it, extracts the first geospatial subdataset (e.g., 'lccs_class' or 'LAI_10D'), and converts it to a compressed GeoTIFF with GDAL Translate. Outputs include the final GeoTIFF file and the original downloaded NetCDF URL.

name: Compute slope and aspect from DTM
desc: The script processes raw digital terrain model (DTM) GeoTIFF files by reprojecting them to EPSG:7791, then computing slope and aspect rasters for each input DTM tile; it also derives and exports the spatial extent of each reprojected DTM as a shapefile. Outputs include per-tile slope rasters, aspect rasters, and tile boundary shapefiles, organized in dedicated subfolders (slope/, aspect/, tile/, dtm/).

name: Clip raster by vector mask
desc: The script clips an input raster file to the spatial extents and geometry of a provided vector mask layer (Shapefile), reprojecting the raster to the mask layer's coordinate reference system first. It produces a single clipped GeoTIFF output file ('clipped.tif') and removes the intermediate reprojected raster. The operation is projection-aware and handles format-agnostic rasters using GDAL-based QGIS processing algorithms.

name: Model school suitability location
desc: The script computes a final school suitability map by integrating normalized population density, road proximity, slope, land use/land cover suitability, and water body proximity rasters. It applies a custom weighted formula that reduces city-center bias via a Gaussian-adjusted population term (penalizing high-density areas), then normalizes the raw output to 0–1. Outputs are two GeoTIFFs: an unnormalized raw suitability raster and a normalized 0–1 suitability raster for decision support in educational infrastructure planning.

name: Aggregate flood hazard layers
desc: The script performs spatial upscaling (coarsening) of high-resolution flood modeling outputs—specifically DEM (digital elevation model), WSE (water surface elevation), and WSH (water surface height/depth)—using two physics-informed averaging methods from Bryant et al. (2023): (1) 'WSH Averaging', where WSH is directly averaged and WSE is reconstructed as DEM + WSH; and (2) 'WSE Averaging', where WSE is first averaged, then filtered against the coarsened DEM to retain only wet cells (WSE > DEM), and WSH is derived as WSE − DEM. Outputs are three coarsened rasters at user-specified scale: DEM_s2, WSE_s2, and WSH_s2, all aligned and consistent with hydrologic constraints.

name: Apply linear fuzzification to indicator raster
desc: The script performs spatial fuzzification of a geospatial indicator (e.g., soil moisture, temperature, or land degradation index) by converting its crisp raster values into fuzzy membership values between 0 and 1 using a linear membership function. It first extracts a user-defined WKT polygon area, reads indicator point data from a PostGIS table ('pixels') filtered by 'indicator_id', spatially joins those points to a regular grid (cell size configurable), rasterizes the joined grid with indicator 'value' as burn-in, applies either direct or inverse linear fuzzification based on 'relationship' (mapping [min,max] → [0,1] or [max,min] → [0,1]), converts the resulting fuzzy raster back to points, appends the 'indicator_id', and exports the fuzzy point layer to the 'fuzzy_view' table in PostGIS. The output is a georeferenced point layer where each point holds a fuzzy membership value and its associated indicator ID.

name: Convert raster pixels to point features
desc: The script processes a raster input layer by reprojecting it to EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator), clipping it to a user-provided polygon study area, converting the resulting clipped raster pixels to vector point features (one point per pixel, retaining pixel values in a 'VALUE' field), adding a constant integer attribute 'project_indicator_id' to all points, and finally appending those points to a PostGIS table named 'pixels' in the 'integral' database under the 'public' schema. The output is a persistent spatial table of georeferenced pixel points with indicator metadata, enabling subsequent SQL-based aggregation or spatiotemporal analysis.

name: Convert indicator raster to points
desc: The script processes a raster input layer by reprojecting it to EPSG:4326, clipping it to a user-provided polygon study area, converting the clipped raster pixels to point features (one point per pixel), adding an integer 'indicator_id' field with a user-specified value, and exporting the resulting point vector layer to a PostGIS table named 'pixels' in the 'integral' database. It then queries min/max pixel values for that indicator_id from the inserted points and updates the 'Indicators' table with those statistics plus a randomly selected palette code and fixed pixel_size=0.05. No classification, time-series, or spectral analysis is performed; the input raster is treated as a static, precomputed indicator surface. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the script.

name: Convert CHM to forest polygons
desc: The script converts a Canopy Height Model (CHM) raster into a binary forest/non-forest raster using height and density thresholds, followed by morphological closing/opening (with adaptive kernel size derived from minimum width and area constraints), removal of small connected components (< minArea m²) in both forest and non-forest masks, optional integration of user-provided forest/no-forest mask rasters (e.g., SIBOSCO/NOBOSCO), and final vectorization into polygon features with area (ha) attribute and style application. Outputs include a classified forest raster layer and an optional smoothed, single-part polygon layer with area calculation.

name: Estimate glacier thickness distribution
desc: The script estimates spatially distributed glacier ice thickness for the Juncal Norte glacier system (Chilean Andes) using Farinotti et al. (2019) gridded thickness data, reprojects and masks it to EPSG:32719, replaces zero values with NaN, and integrates it with Landsat-derived NDSI, Random Forest classification, DEMs, model ID rasters, and debris cover to generate a structured CSV containing per-pixel glacier attributes: U_ID, MOD_ID, GLAC_ID, MOD_H (model DEM elevation), GLAC_H (glacier surface elevation), DEB (debris flag), FRAC_GLAC (glacier coverage fraction), and ICE_DEPTH (thickness). This CSV serves as input for glacio-hydrological modeling (e.g., in PCRaster).

name: Package layers to KMZ
desc: The script packages multiple QGIS vector and raster layers into a single KMZ file. It reprojects layers to a user-specified or project CRS, exports vector layers to KML using QgsVectorFileWriter with optional symbology export, converts raster layers to KML ground overlays via GDAL warp + translate (using KMLSUPEROVERLAY), and composes a master doc.kml that aggregates Folder elements from each input layer’s KML into a ZIP-compressed KMZ archive. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing is performed; the workflow is purely geospatial packaging and format conversion within QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not involved — this is a desktop GIS export utility, not an Earth Engine (GEE) script despite the prompt's mischaracterization.

name: Reclassify and smooth NLCD land cover
desc: The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) raster data for Alaska, specifically the 2016 Tree Canopy and Land Cover layers. It performs a sequence of geospatial operations: (1) reprojecting the input NLCD Land Cover raster to EPSG:4326; (2) reclassifying land cover classes into simplified grass-dominated values using a pixel-wise arithmetic expression mapping 20 original NLCD classes (e.g., 21=Developed, Open Space → 26; 41=Deciduous Forest → 23) to new integer codes; (3) separately reclassifying urban classes (21,22,23,24) into urban-subtype codes (10,1,1,2); (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to denoise and remove road/clutter artifacts from the urban layer; (5) compositing the cleaned urban layer over the grass-only layer using conditional pixel replacement (urban pixels override grass where present); (6) upscaling (8× finer resolution) via GDAL Warp with resampling; (7) spatially smoothing the high-resolution composite using GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and (8) compressing and exporting as an 8-bit LZW-compressed GeoTIFF. The final output is a smoothed, high-resolution, urban-prioritized, grass-background land cover raster in WGS84, named 'NLCD_2016_Alaska_SaintPaul-Island_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff'. Input filenames and paths confirm the source is NLCD 2016, and the processing is explicitly scoped to Alaska, specifically Saint Paul Island and adjacent longitude bands (e.g., 'Alaska141-140_60').

name: Reclassify NLCD land cover
desc: The script reclassifies and processes the NLCD (National Land Cover Database) 2016 land cover raster for Alaska's Diomede Island region. It performs a sequence of geospatial operations: (1) warping the input NLCD raster to EPSG:4326; (2) reassigning NLCD class values to simplified 'grass-only' categories using a deterministic pixel-wise expression mapping 20 original NLCD classes (e.g., 21=Developed, Open Space → 26; 41=Deciduous Forest → 23) to new land-cover-representative codes; (3) isolating urban classes (NLCD 21–24) into a binary/multi-value reclassified urban layer; (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to clean urban features by removing small clutter/road artifacts; (5) combining the cleaned urban layer with the grass-only layer via conditional raster algebra (urban pixels override grass where present); (6) upscaling (8× higher spatial resolution) the combined raster using GDAL Warp; (7) smoothing the high-resolution result with GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and (8) compressing to 8-bit GeoTIFF with LZW. The study area is explicitly Diomede Island, Alaska; the time range is fixed to 2016; the source is NLCD 2016 — a USGS-conducted, multi-source (Landsat-derived + ancillary) land cover product — not a raw satellite acquisition. No satellite or sensor metadata is embedded in the script; the input is a pre-processed, classified raster dataset.

name: Reclassify and smooth NLCD tree canopy and land cover
desc: The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) raster data for Alaska to generate a smoothed, high-resolution, reclassified land cover product. It specifically combines tree canopy layers (NLCD Tree Canopy classes 41–43: Deciduous Broadleaf, Evergreen Forest, Mixed Forest) with base NLCD Land Cover, replaces non-forest urban/clutter classes with grass or other vegetation proxies, reclassifies urban subclasses (21–24) into simplified urban codes (10,1,1,2), removes noise using GRASS r.neighbors median filtering (7×7 then 11×11 windows), upsamples resolution by factor of 8, and compresses output as LZW-compressed Byte GeoTIFF in EPSG:4326. Input data paths explicitly reference NLCD 2016 Alaska tile '162-154_56', confirming the source is NLCD 2016 — a USGS-conducted, multi-source (Landsat-derived + ancillary) land cover product. No satellite imagery is directly accessed or processed in GEE; instead, the script operates on pre-generated NLCD rasters stored locally. All geospatial operations are local GDAL/QGIS/GRASS-based (gdal_calc.py, gdal:warpreproject, grass7:r.neighbors, gdal:translate), not Earth Engine API calls. The final output is a single compressed GeoTIFF: 'NLCD_2016_Alaska162-154_56_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff'.

name: Reclassify and combine NLCD land cover and tree canopy
desc: The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) data for Alaska in 2016 to produce a refined, high-resolution, EPSG:4326-aligned land cover raster. It first reclassifies NLCD Tree Canopy (input: NLCD_2016_Tree_Canopy_Alaska162-154_56.tiff) into a single forest class (value 43) where canopy > 0; warps both tree canopy and NLCD Land Cover (input: NLCD_2016_Land_Cover_Alaska162-154_56.tiff) to WGS84 (EPSG:4326); combines them using conditional logic that prioritizes tree canopy over land cover except where land cover is already forest (41–43); replaces non-forest urban/clutter classes (e.g., 11, 21–24, 31, 51–52, 71–75, 81–82, 90, 95) with grass- or vegetation-appropriate NLCD codes (e.g., 41→23, 21→10, etc.); reclassifies urban classes (21–24) into simplified urban types; applies GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=7) to clean urban pixels; merges cleaned urban with grass-reclassified raster; upsamples the result by factor of 8 using gdal.Warp; smooths again with GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11); and compresses to 8-bit LZW GeoTIFF. The final output is NLCD_2016_Alaska162-154_59_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff — a high-definition, visually smoothed, reclassified land cover raster for flight simulation scenery generation. Study area is Alaska, tile identifier '162-154_56'; time range is 2016; no satellite/sensor is involved — inputs are derived NLCD raster products (not raw satellite imagery).

name: Reclassify and smooth NLCD land cover
desc: The script processes the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) 2016 land cover raster for Alaska (specifically the Diomede Island subregion) to produce a smoothed, high-resolution, compressed GeoTIFF in EPSG:4326. Key steps include: (1) reprojecting the input NLCD land cover raster to WGS84; (2) reclassifying all NLCD classes into simplified vegetation/land-type codes (e.g., urban → 26, forest → 23–25, grass → 18–19, wetlands → 30–32, etc.) using gdal_calc.py; (3) separately reclassifying urban classes (21–24) into three urban subclasses (10, 1, 2); (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to clean urban pixels and remove roads/clutter; (5) combining the cleaned urban layer with the grass-only reclassified layer via conditional pixel-wise replacement; (6) upscaling (8× finer resolution) using GDAL Warp; (7) applying a second GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11) for spatial smoothing; and (8) compressing to 8-bit LZW GeoTIFF. The study area is explicitly Alaska, Diomede Island; the source data is NLCD 2016 Land Cover; no satellite/sensor/bands are involved — this is a vector-to-raster derived thematic product processed entirely via raster algebra and filtering.

name: Reclassify and smooth NLCD land cover
desc: The script processes the NLCD 2016 Land Cover dataset for Alaska (specifically the Diomede-Island tile, identified by 'Alaska152-142_59') to produce a high-resolution, cleaned, and smoothed land cover raster suitable for scenery generation. Key steps include: (1) warping the input NLCD raster to EPSG:4326; (2) reclassifying all non-urban NLCD classes (e.g., 11, 12, 21–24, 31, 41–43, etc.) to grass-representative values using a deterministic lookup expression; (3) isolating and reclassifying urban classes (21, 22, 23, 24) into three urban types (10, 1, 1, 2); (4) applying GRASS r.neighbors (median filter, size=7) to remove clutter/roads from the urban layer; (5) combining the cleaned urban layer with the grass-only layer via conditional pixel-wise replacement (urban pixels override grass where present); (6) upscaling (8×) the combined raster using GDAL Warp with nearest resampling; (7) applying a second GRASS r.neighbors (median, size=11) for spatial smoothing; and (8) compressing to 8-bit GeoTIFF with LZW. The final output is 'NLCD_2016_Alaska152-142_59_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff'. Input data source is the NLCD 2016 Land Cover product — a USGS-conducted, multi-source (Landsat-derived + ancillary) thematic classification — not satellite-native imagery. No spectral bands, cloud masking, or time-series analysis are involved.

name: Reclassify and smooth NLCD tree canopy and land cover
desc: The script processes NLCD (National Land Cover Database) raster data for a specified U.S. state and year to generate a smoothed, high-resolution, reclassified land cover product. It begins with NLCD Tree Canopy and Land Cover rasters (e.g., 'NLCD_2021_Tree_Canopy_California-Southern.tiff' and 'NLCD_2021_Land_Cover_California-Southern.tiff'), reclassifies forest types (41–43) into a unified tree class, reprojects both layers to EPSG:4326, combines them prioritizing tree canopy over conflicting land cover classes, replaces non-forest urban/clutter classes with grass-like or vegetation-appropriate classes (e.g., 21→10, 22→1, 81→18), applies GRASS median filtering to clean urban features and remove roads/clutter, merges cleaned urban and grass-reclassified layers, upsamples the result by factor 8 (not interpolation but resolution refinement via gdal.Warp), applies further GRASS median smoothing (size=11), and compresses to 8-bit LZW GeoTIFF. The final output is 'NLCD_2021_California-Southern_Smoothed-HD-Compressed_4326.tiff'. Study area is California (Southern portion); time range is single-year (2021); data source is NLCD — a USGS-produced, multi-source, Landsat-derived land cover product; no satellite/sensor/bands are directly accessed in code — all inputs are pre-processed rasters.

name: Compute raster statistics in geosquare grids
desc: The script converts an input raster layer into a vector grid of equal-area geosquares (hierarchical H3-like or custom geohash-based polygons) aligned to a user-defined grid size (50 m to 10 km), clips the raster to a boundary polygon, and computes per-grid zonal statistics (Sum, Mean, Median, St Dev, Min, Max) for a selected raster band. It uses a two-level tiling strategy: first partitions the boundary into ~10 km parent cells (via `polyfill`), then subdivides each into child grids at the specified resolution (`parrent_to_allchildren`), filters children intersecting the boundary, and applies `zonalstatisticsfb` to assign the chosen statistic value to each grid cell. Output is a vector polygon layer with fields 'gid' (geosquare identifier) and 'value' (computed statistic).

name: Identify nearest gas leak to schools
desc: The script identifies the publicly reported gas leak closest to each Massachusetts school by converting KML gas leak data to shapefile, reprojecting both gas leak and school point layers to EPSG:3857, performing a nearest-neighbor spatial join to assign the nearest gas leak (by 'Name' attribute) to each school, visualizing both layers in QGIS, and exporting the joined result—including school attributes and nearest leak name—as a CSV table with XYZ geometry coordinates.

name: Derive stream network and catchment velocity
desc: The script performs hydrological terrain analysis on a DEM to derive flow direction, flow accumulation, Strahler stream order, and channel networks; it snaps a user-defined pour point to the extracted channels, computes the upslope contributing catchment, calculates a slope-area term (sqrt(slope) × sqrt(flow accumulation)) as a proxy for flow velocity potential, clips it to the catchment, computes its mean statistic, then derives a normalized velocity layer and its inverse (weight grid) for downstream hydrological modeling. Outputs include filled DEM, flow direction/accumulation rasters, Strahler-order rasters (full and thresholded ≥6), vectorized channels and catchment, slope raster, slope-area term raster (clipped), velocity raster, and weight raster.

name: Project urban area demand
desc: The script projects future urban land use demand using a genetic algorithm (GA) optimization framework. It loads current land cover (LC) raster data, agriculture/conservation/urban suitability rasters, and a study area boundary (e.g., 'kumasi_area' or custom shapefile). It clips the LC raster to the study area, computes zonal mean suitability values and majority land cover per MGRS grid cell (using pylusat.zonal.zonal_stats_raster), classifies suitability into preference tiers (1–3), calculates urban land-use conflict via lucis.LandUseConflict, and configures GA parameters (population size, crossover/mutation rates, generations, initial sampling probabilities) from GUI inputs. The GA (ga.main()) optimizes new land use allocation to meet projected population growth (e.g., PPL_GROWTH = proj_pop − curr_pop) under temperature constraint (TEMP_TARGET) and conflict minimization. Outputs include a GeoDataFrame with a new land use column (e.g., 'FUTURE_SCENARIO') exported as Shapefile or GeoPackage, visualized as a QGIS vector layer. Study area is implied to be Kumasi (Ghana) based on 'kumasi_area' layer name and config region/district lists (e.g., Ashanti, Greater Accra); input data sources are local files (no GEE server-side assets), including population.csv, slope CSV, and raster files (no satellite metadata in code).

name: Calculate Euclidean distance to vector sources
desc: The script computes a raster where each cell contains the Euclidean distance (in ground units, using geographic coordinates with DISTUNITS=GEO) to the nearest non-zero (i.e., source) cell in a rasterized input vector layer. It rasterizes the input vector layer to a temporary byte raster (burn value = 1), then applies GDAL's ComputeProximity to generate the distance raster. The output is a user-specified raster (e.g., Float32/Float64/Int32) with configurable extent, cell size, and maximum distance cutoff. No satellite imagery, time-series, or spectral analysis is involved — the input is purely vector-based (e.g., points, lines, polygons representing sources), and all operations are deterministic GIS proximity computations. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Extract raster pixels by attribute expression
desc: The script performs pixel-wise conditional filtering of a single-band raster layer using a user-defined QGIS expression (e.g., 'value > 0'). It reads the input raster band via GDAL, iterates row-by-row, evaluates the expression for each pixel value (with NoData handling), and writes output pixels retaining original values where the expression evaluates to True, otherwise assigning NoData. The output is a georeferenced GeoTIFF raster with identical spatial extent, resolution, projection, and data type as the input. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic classification is involved — it is a generic, local, attribute-based raster masking tool operating entirely on pre-loaded QGIS raster layers. All parameters (input layer, band number, expression, output path) are user-provided at runtime; no hardcoded datasets, dates, locations, or sensors appear in the code.

name: Apply fuzzy membership transformation
desc: The script transforms a user-provided input raster layer into a 0–1 (or scaled) fuzzy membership raster, where each pixel value represents the degree of membership in a user-defined set. It supports three fuzzification functions — Linear, J-shaped, and Sigmoidal — applied to the normalized range [min, max] of the selected band. The output is a single-band GeoTIFF raster (GDAL Float32) with identical georeferencing and projection as the input. The script performs full-pixel-by-pixel GDAL-based raster I/O, computes min/max by scanning all valid pixels (excluding nodata), applies the chosen function, optionally inverts (decreases) the membership curve, and scales the result by an integer 'Degree Of Membership' parameter. No remote sensing data ingestion, time-series, or cloud masking occurs — it is a deterministic, band-level, local fuzzy scaling operation on arbitrary raster data. Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; the input is generic and provided via QGIS Processing interface.

name: Convert vector to raster
desc: The script converts an input vector layer (e.g., polygons or lines) into a georeferenced single-band raster dataset using GDAL's RasterizeLayer. It supports burning either a specified numeric attribute field value or a constant value (1) into the raster cells overlapping vector features. The output raster is GeoTIFF-formatted, with user-configurable extent, cell size, data type (Float32/Float64/Int32), and nodata value (-9999). No study area, time range, satellite data, or external imagery is involved — it is a pure vector-to-raster geometric conversion operating solely on QGIS vector layers. Input CRS and extent are preserved; if no extent is provided, the source layer’s full extent is used. Cell size defaults to ~1/250th of the smaller dimension of the extent.

name: Rasterize building and tree height polygons
desc: The script converts vector polygon layers representing buildings and trees—each with an associated height attribute—into two aligned raster layers (BuildingTerrain_raster.tif and Tree_raster.tif) using GDAL's rasterize algorithm. Both rasters share the same spatial extent (user-defined analysis extent), resolution (0.5 m pixel size), data type (Float32), and nodata value (0); they encode height values (in meters) from the respective 'Height [m]' fields, burning them into rasters where polygons overlap the extent. The output rasters are saved to a 'Step_2' subdirectory within the QGIS project’s absolute path.

name: Compute ground surface temperature
desc: The script computes hourly ground surface temperature (in °C) for a grid of points across a user-defined study area, using material properties (albedo, emissivity, thermal conductivity, volumetric heat capacity, thickness), solar radiation and weather data (air temperature, humidity, sky temperature), shadow duration from precomputed rasters, ground heat conduction (using annual temperature wave propagation at 20 cm depth), and evapotranspiration (Penman-Monteith). It solves a nonlinear energy balance equation (radiation + convection + conduction + storage + latent heat) iteratively per hour per material-shadow combination, outputs a CSV with x/y coordinates and hourly/mean/min/max temperatures, and loads it as a styled point layer in QGIS.

name: Compute ground surface temperature
desc: The script computes hourly ground surface temperature (in °C) for a grid of points across a user-defined study area, using material properties (albedo, emissivity, thermal conductivity, volumetric heat capacity, thickness), local shadowing derived from precomputed rasters (Step_3/*.tif), and EPW weather data (dry bulb temperature, global horizontal radiation, relative humidity, etc.). It solves a transient energy balance equation incorporating solar absorption, longwave radiation exchange with sky, convective heat transfer with air, conductive heat transfer to subsurface, thermal inertia effects, and evapotranspiration (Penman-Monteith). Outputs include a CSV file (ComputedPoints.csv) with per-point, per-hour temperatures and summary statistics (min/mean/max daily), loaded as a QGIS point layer styled with 'point_style.qml'. The study area is defined by the user-provided 'Ground description layer' and 'Buildings layer'; no fixed geographic extent is hardcoded. Weather data is read from an external EPW file specified by the user. Shadow rasters are assumed pre-generated in ProjectPath/Step_3/ and named with hour identifiers (e.g., 'shadow_07.tif').

name: Calculate centerline distance metrics
desc: The script calculates four distance metrics along vector centerlines: (1) Distance (cumulative distance from the startpoint), (2) RDistance (reverse cumulative distance from the endpoint), (3) SP_Dist (shortest path distance from the startpoint of the longest shortest path), and (4) SP_RDist (reverse shortest path distance from the endpoint of the longest shortest path). It operates on input line features (centerlines), optionally densifying vertices at a user-specified interval or exploding lines at each vertex. It constructs a networkx graph where nodes are rounded coordinate endpoints of line segments and edges represent segments with weight = geometry length. Using Dijkstra’s algorithm, it identifies the two endpoints of the longest shortest path in each connected component, then computes distances relative to those endpoints. Outputs are line features with original attributes plus the four new numeric fields, preserving geometry. No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite imagery is involved — input is purely vector line geometry. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate polygon centerlines
desc: The script calculates centerline(s) for each input polygon feature using Voronoi diagram-based skeletonization and graph-theoretic shortest-path analysis. It supports three methods: (1) 'Centerlines' — single shortest path between two endpoints derived from the largest connected component of the trimmed Voronoi graph; (2) 'All' — all shortest paths after iterative dangle trimming; (3) 'Circles' — edges belonging to cycles (loops) in the pruned graph. Input polygons are optionally simplified (Douglas-Peucker) and densified before vertex extraction. Outputs are line features with attributes: ID, Distance (distance from first endpoint), RDistance (distance from reverse endpoint), SP_Dist (shortest path distance from startpoint), and SP_RDist (reverse shortest path distance). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms (SAGA Thiessen polygons, polygon-to-lines, explode lines, select by location) and NetworkX for graph operations. No satellite or remote sensing data is used — input is vector polygon geometry only. Study area, time range, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Calculate centerline width and deviation
desc: The script calculates geometric attributes—including width, centerline deviation (symmetry distance from centerline to polygon boundary), left/right width components, and width asymmetry—along a user-provided centerline within matching polygons. It supports two modes: (1) 'Fast Compute', which estimates width as twice the distance from each centerline endpoint to the nearest polygon vertex; and (2) standard mode, which constructs perpendicular transects at sampled points along the centerline, intersects them with the polygon, and measures left/right widths via geometry decomposition. Inputs require matching 'ID' fields between centerline (LineString) and polygon layers, same CRS, and pre-processed single-part geometries (e.g., after 'Explode Tool'). Outputs are LineString features with attribute fields including Distance, SP_Dist, Width, Deviation, DWidthL, DWidthR, WidthL, WidthR, and Diff (width ratio %). No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite processing is involved—the tool operates purely on vector geometry in QGIS Processing Framework using PyQGIS.

name: Skeletonize raster centerlines
desc: The script creates vector centerlines from a binary raster image by applying morphological skeletonization (either 'lee' or 'medial axis' method from scikit-image), followed by raster-to-vector conversion (GRASS r.to.vect), line splitting, exploding, and network-based topological cleaning to resolve spurious cycles and node intersections. The output is a vector line layer representing centerlines of rasterized linear features (e.g., rivers, roads, or other binary-valued linear objects). Input must be a single-band binary raster (values 0/1); no thresholding is performed internally — the script explicitly requires prior binarization via a separate 'Thresholding tool'. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic coordinates are embedded in the code; it is a generic, local raster processing algorithm operating on user-provided QGIS raster layers.

name: Calculate line network tortuosity
desc: The script computes tortuosity (ratio of shortest-path distance to Euclidean distance) and shortest-path distances along a linear network (e.g., rivers, faults, or roads) between source points and optional target points. It constructs a NetworkX graph from an input linestring layer, optionally weighted by a numeric field (e.g., slope, resistance, or impedance), then solves shortest-path problems using Dijkstra's algorithm. Input requires a line layer (exploded into segments), a source point layer with 'ID' attribute, and an optional target point layer also with matching 'ID'. Output is a line vector layer where each segment represents an edge in the shortest path, attributed with source ID, accumulated path distance ('Distance'), and straight-line distance from first to last node ('SP_Dist'). No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite-derived inputs are used — all operations are vector-based geometric and graph-theoretic. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Generate perpendicular transects
desc: The script generates perpendicular line transects along input centerline features at user-specified sampling intervals. It first optionally densifies the centerlines to improve sampling accuracy, then explodes multilines into single-part segments, constructs a networkx graph to model line connectivity and lengths, identifies the longest path in each connected component, and iteratively places perpendicular transects (of specified width) at cumulative distances along that path. Output is a line vector layer of transects, with original attribute fields preserved and optionally an added 'Distance' field representing cumulative distance from path start. No remote sensing data, time series, or classification is involved — it is a pure geometric vector processing tool operating on user-provided line features.

name: Create land cover lookup table template
desc: The script creates a copy of a pre-packaged CSV-based land cover characteristics template file (e.g., 'Agriculture.csv', 'Forest.csv') from QNSPECT's local resources directory. It reads the selected CSV as a delimited text vector layer and writes it to a new vector feature sink (e.g., GeoPackage or CSV), preserving all original fields and rows. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, or Earth Engine server-side computation is performed — the entire workflow operates client-side in QGIS using local filesystem paths. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations are not specified because the script does not access or process any geospatial raster or time-series data; it only copies static coefficient tables.

name: Detect buildings in satellite imagery
desc: The script detects buildings in a user-provided satellite raster image using Modzy's pre-trained deep learning model (model ID '07cda3cad0'). It accepts a single raster layer as input, validates its dimensions (must be ≤300×300 pixels), submits it to the Modzy API for inference, parses the JSON output containing bounding box coordinates and confidence scores for detected buildings, and renders them as vector polygons (with score attribute) in the QGIS map canvas. The output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer of building footprints (axis-aligned bounding boxes) with opacity, fill color, and border styling applied; no raster outputs, exports, or time-series analysis are performed. Input CRS is preserved (defaulting to EPSG:4326 if projection parsing fails); georeferencing uses GDAL GeoTransform to convert pixel coordinates to map coordinates. The script does not specify any study area, time range, satellite, sensor, or bands — it operates on arbitrary local raster files (e.g., GeoTIFF) provided by the user via QGIS interface.

name: Detect objects in satellite imagery
desc: The script performs general object detection on a user-provided satellite raster image using Modzy's hosted deep learning model (model ID 'zi2wvziln1', version '0.0.2'). It validates input image dimensions (must be ≤416×416 pixels), submits the local raster file to Modzy’s inference API, waits for job completion, parses the JSON output containing bounding box coordinates (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) and class labels with probabilities, then converts those pixel-based bounding boxes into georeferenced polygon vector features aligned with the input raster’s CRS and geotransform. The output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer of polygons added to the QGIS project, with attributes 'className' and 'probability'; the algorithm returns the count of detected objects. No specific study area, time range, or satellite/sensor metadata is extracted or used — the input is a generic local raster file (e.g., GeoTIFF) with no temporal or mission-specific constraints enforced in code. Geospatial operations include GDAL-based coordinate transformation (if non-WGS84), bounding box to polygon conversion, and CRS-aware geometry creation. Final product is a vector layer of object outlines rendered with semi-transparent cyan fill.

name: Detect vehicles in satellite imagery
desc: The script detects and localizes vehicles in a user-provided satellite raster image using Modzy's cloud-hosted deep learning model (model ID 'l5lhvcgzt4', version '0.0.1'). It validates input image dimensions (must be ≤416×416 pixels), submits the image file to Modzy for inference, retrieves bounding box coordinates and confidence scores from the model’s JSON output ('results.json'), converts pixel-based bounding boxes to georeferenced polygons using GDAL geotransform metadata, and renders them as a memory vector layer with fill styling and score attribute. The output is a QGIS vector layer named '<image_basename> Vehicles' added to the project, with opacity 0.65 and cyan fill; no raster outputs, exports, or time-series analysis are performed. Input data source, study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code — only a generic raster file path is used.

name: Execute SQL query on vector layers
desc: The script executes a user-defined SQL query over one or more input vector layers using QGIS's virtual layer provider. It supports referencing layers as 'input1', 'input2', etc., in the SQL; handles geometry field specification, UID field assignment, geometry type (autodetect, point, polygon, etc.), and CRS definition; and outputs the result as a new vector layer (feature sink). No raster data, time-series analysis, remote sensing calculations, or satellite imagery is involved — it is purely a vector SQL execution tool operating within QGIS Processing Framework. All inputs are arbitrary vector layers provided by the user; no fixed study area, time range, or sensor data is embedded.

name: Generate hypsometric curves
desc: The script computes hypsometric curves (elevation-area distribution and cumulative area-elevation relationships) for polygon features (e.g., watersheds, administrative units) overlaid on a digital elevation model (DEM). It rasterizes each input polygon to mask the DEM, extracts elevation values within the masked region, bins them at user-defined elevation intervals (STEP), and outputs CSV files containing cumulative area (either in absolute units — m² — or as percentage of total area) versus elevation. The workflow includes GDAL-based raster I/O, OGR vector geometry handling, NumPy array masking and binning, and CRS-aware reprojection/intersection. Input data sources are user-provided: a single DEM raster layer and a vector polygon layer; no time-series or multi-temporal processing is performed. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified — the script is generic and agnostic to source origin, relying solely on QGIS-provided raster and vector layers.

name: Export vector layer to SpatiaLite
desc: The script exports a QGIS vector layer (e.g., points, lines, polygons) into a SpatiaLite database file (.sqlite), creating or overwriting a specified table with optional spatial index, geometry column naming, field name case conversion, string length constraint dropping, and single-part geometry enforcement. It uses QgsVectorLayerExporter with SpatiaLite provider, handles encoding, primary key assignment, and geometry column configuration. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or geospatial modeling is performed — it is purely a database export utility within QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified because the script operates on arbitrary user-provided vector layers without intrinsic spatiotemporal or spectral constraints.

name: Generate points along line
desc: The script converts vector line features into a set of point features located at the centroids of raster pixels intersected by each line segment. It uses a raster layer’s geotransform to map line vertices to pixel coordinates, then applies a modified Bresenham’s line algorithm to traverse all pixels crossed by each line segment (including diagonal steps), and generates one point per traversed pixel centroid. Points are attributed with sequential 'id', 'line_id', and 'point_id' fields. The output is a point vector layer in the same CRS as the input raster, with no temporal or thematic analysis — purely geometric sampling of lines against a raster grid. Input data sources, study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Execute and load PostgreSQL SQL query
desc: The script executes a user-provided SQL query against a configured PostgreSQL/PostGIS database connection and loads the resulting spatial table as a valid QGIS vector layer. It constructs a QgsDataSourceUri from the connection, wraps the SQL in a subquery, sets the geometry and ID fields via uri.setDataSource(), instantiates a QgsVectorLayer with 'postgres' provider, validates it, and registers it in the processing context for output. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed — the script is purely a database interface tool. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Generate isovalue polygons
desc: The script generates vector isovalue polygons (or polylines) from an input raster layer by performing contouring via bilinear interpolation across raster cells. It processes each 2x2 pixel neighborhood to compute intersection points of contour lines with cell edges, groups line segments by isovalue, and optionally converts contours into polygons using spatialite's ST_Polygonize. Input parameters include min/max contour values, interval step, no-data value, band selection, and options for polygon vs. polyline output and individual-value (non-interpolated) mode. The output is a vector layer (MultiPolygon or LineString geometry) with an 'id' attribute representing the isovalue. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or external datasets are embedded in the code—the algorithm is generic and operates on any user-provided raster layer loaded in QGIS.

name: Generate isovalue polygons
desc: The script generates vector isovalue (contour) polygons or polylines from an input raster layer, using linear interpolation between adjacent pixel values to compute contour lines at user-defined intervals. It processes raster cells in a grid-based manner (2x2 pixel neighborhoods), computes edge intersections for each isovalue step, constructs line segments, and optionally converts them into closed polygons via spatial polygonization using SpatiaLite. The output is a vector layer (MultiPolygon or MultiLineString) with attributes containing the isovalue (or mapped individual raster values if 'individual values' is enabled), projected in the input raster's CRS. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or external datasets are used—the algorithm operates purely on a generic user-provided raster layer loaded in QGIS.

name: Compute network-based travel time raster
desc: The script computes a raster representing interpolated travel times across a geographic window, based on a linear network (e.g., roads or paths), using node-specific costs (i-cost and j-cost), directional flow constraints, lateral diffusion rules, and optional impassable barriers. It performs geometric proximity analysis (closest segment, buffering, distance-to-line), spatial discretization into a regular grid, per-pixel travel time accumulation (weighted by segment length ratio and sqrt(distance) × speed factor), and outputs two rasters: (1) a primary raster of computed travel times (in seconds or minutes, derived from speed in km/h and distance in meters), and (2) an auxiliary distance-to-network raster; both in ASCII Grid format with accompanying .prj and dictionary (.dic) files mapping individual values (e.g., station IDs). The algorithm operates entirely on vector input — no satellite or remotely sensed data is loaded, processed, or referenced. All parameters (e.g., radius, speed, pixel size) are user-defined at runtime; the study area, time range, and data sources are not embedded in the code.

name: Aggregate population to isochrone polygons
desc: The script performs spatial aggregation of a variable (e.g., population) from a source polygon layer (e.g., municipalities) onto an isovalue polygon layer (e.g., travel-time isochrones such as 30-minute accessibility areas). It computes weighted or unweighted statistics (mean, sum, min, max) based on geometric intersection area proportions — specifically using ST_Intersection and ST_Area to proportionally allocate the source variable across target polygons. The output is a new vector layer with identical geometry to the input isopolygons layer, but with aggregated attribute values per polygon ID. No satellite, temporal, or external geospatial data sources are used; all operations occur in-memory via SpatiaLite SQL within QGIS Processing, using only user-provided vector layers and field names. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified.

name: Geocode address list
desc: The script performs forward geocoding of addresses from a vector table field using the HERE Geocoding API. It reads an input vector layer (e.g., CSV, TXT, or database table), extracts address strings from a user-specified string field, sends HTTP GET requests to 'https://geocode.search.hereapi.com/v1/geocode', parses the JSON response to extract coordinates (lat/lng), address components (country, city, street, etc.), quality metrics (relevance, field scores), and match type. It outputs a new point vector layer in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) with attributes including original ID, input address, geometry, parsed address fields, and geocoding quality indicators. Credentials are loaded from QGIS global settings under 'HQGIS/api_key'. No study area, time range, satellite data, or Earth observation processing is involved — this is purely a web-based geocoding utility.

name: Convert raster to PCRaster format
desc: The script converts an input GDAL-supported raster layer into PCRaster format, with user-selectable output data type (Boolean, Nominal, Ordinal, Scalar, Directional, or LDD). It uses GDAL Translate with specific metadata options (e.g., 'VS_SCALAR') and output data types (e.g., GDT_Float32 for Scalar) to ensure PCRaster compliance. No spatial or temporal analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — only format and datatype translation. Input source, study area, time range, satellite, sensor, or bands are not referenced or inferred from the code.

name: Calculate passive viewshed and depth below horizon
desc: The script computes passive viewshed and depth-below-horizon (DBH) raster outputs from observer points and a digital elevation model (DEM) in QGIS Processing. It first calculates angular difference rasters (DBH) using viewshed_raster with curvature and refraction corrections, then applies a raster calculator threshold (DBH <= observer height) to derive the passive viewshed. Inputs include a point layer (with 'observ_hgt' and 'radius' fields), DEM raster, observer height, Earth curvature toggle, and atmospheric refraction coefficient. Outputs are two rasters: OUTPUT_DBH (angular difference in radians × distance, i.e., vertical drop below horizon) and OUTPUT_PASSIVE (binary mask where DBH ≤ observer height).

name: Calculate passive viewshed and depth below horizon
desc: The script computes a 'depth below horizon' (DBH) raster from observer points and a digital surface model (MNS), then derives a passive viewshed raster by combining DBH with a digital elevation model (MNE) using the condition DBH[j] + MNE[j] <= Hobs (observer height). It uses geospatial visibility analysis with Earth curvature correction and atmospheric refraction modeling. Inputs include vector observer points (with mandatory 'observ_hgt' and 'radius' fields), MNS and MNE rasters, and parameters for observer height, curvature, and refraction. The workflow involves raster-based viewshed computation per observer point via angular difference calculation, buffering, masking, and raster algebra (GDAL raster calculator). No satellite imagery, time-series, or classification is involved — it is a static terrain visibility analysis. Study area, time range, and satellite data sources are not specified in the code.

name: Compute passive visibility zones from viewpoints
desc: The script computes passive visibility zones (i.e., areas visible *from* each observer point) and depth-below-horizon (DBH) rasters using a digital elevation model (DEM) and a set of observer points with unique 'ID' attribute. It first generates viewpoint features via the 'Choucas:Création de point de vue' algorithm (likely extending observer locations with azimuth/elevation sampling), then iteratively runs 'Choucas:Calcul de la vision active, passive et le raster depth below horizon...' for each viewpoint to produce per-point passive visibility rasters (binary or Boolean-like, as multiplied in raster calculator) and DBH rasters. Finally, it multiplies all passive visibility rasters together (using GDAL Raster Calculator) to obtain a composite raster where pixel value = 1 only where *all* viewpoints share mutual visibility — i.e., intersection of passive visibility zones. Outputs include: (1) a vector layer of generated viewpoints ('OUTPUT_VIEWPOINTS'), (2) individual DBH and passive visibility GeoTIFFs per viewpoint stored in the specified output folder, and (3) a concatenated raster 'Concatenation_Visi_Passive_Pts.tif' representing the spatial intersection of all passive visibility zones. No satellite imagery, time series, or classification is involved; input is strictly static terrain (raster DEM) and observer point geometry. Study area, time range, and satellite data sources are not specified in the code.

name: Compute passive visibility rasters
desc: The script computes multiple passive visibility raster maps (GeoTIFF) by systematically varying observer height, target height, number of observation points (for polygon inputs), and surface elevation adjustments (MNS/MNE variations). For polygon inputs, it first samples points along the perimeter, computes individual viewsheds per point, then aggregates them into binary (full visibility), count-based, and fuzzy-logic visibility rasters. Outputs are stored in user-specified directories with structured filenames encoding parameter combinations (e.g., 'vpass_nbpt3_Hcible0_Hobs160_sursol_code1var5.tif'), and optionally launches a web interface for visualization.

name: Calculate passive visibility rasters with parameter variations
desc: The script computes multiple passive visibility raster maps (GeoTIFF) by systematically varying observer height, target height, number of contour points (for polygon inputs), and surface elevation (MNS/MNE) parameters—either uniformly across all built/vegetation features or differentially per land cover type (using CSV-specified codes). For polygon inputs, it first generates random contour points, computes individual visibility rasters per point, then aggregates them via logical AND (pixel sees polygon only if it sees all points). Outputs include a folder of visibility rasters (1 = visible, 0 = not visible), optional web-visualizable GeoJSON points and EPSG:3857-reprojected rasters, and intermediate MNE/MNS rasters reflecting surface height perturbations.

name: Segment lines by length and assign point counts
desc: The script segments input line features (e.g., roads) into fixed-length segments (e.g., 200 m), then spatially joins point features (e.g., crime incidents or sensors) to those segments within a user-defined maximum distance (e.g., 100 m); it outputs (1) a graduated segmented line layer where each segment is attributed with a count of associated points (e.g., 'NUMPOINTS'), and (2) a point layer symbolically linked to the nearest segment — enabling graduated thematic mapping of linear infrastructure based on point density or event frequency.

name: Simulate snow slide runout
desc: The script executes snow slide simulations using the AvaFrame com5SnowSlide module. It accepts a digital elevation model (DEM), one or more release area vector layers, and an optional resistance layer as inputs; copies them into a standardized AvaFrame project folder structure; invokes the external AvaFrame Python module via subprocess ('python -m avaframe.runCom5SnowSlide'); then converts resulting raster peak files (e.g., ppr, pft, pfv) into styled vector polygon layers using 'native:pixelstopolygons' and applies QGIS layer styles (pprSnowSlideShape.qml, etc.). Outputs are vector layers representing simulated snow slide deposition (ppr), flow thickness (pft), and flow velocity (pfv) — all derived from AvaFrame's com1DFA-based snow slide modeling. No satellite data, time series, or explicit study area is used; inputs are local GIS layers provided by the user in QGIS. The workflow is purely deterministic physical simulation driven by topography and user-defined release/resistance geometries.

name: Convert vector layers to raster
desc: The script performs Boolean overlay analysis by converting multiple input vector layers into binary (0/1) rasters at a user-specified cell size and extent, then sums them pixel-wise to produce a single output raster where pixel values represent the count of overlapping vector layers. It uses GDAL's rasterize algorithm via QGIS Processing, with no classification, fuzzy logic, or thematic interpretation — only geometric rasterization and arithmetic summation. The study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and thematic content are not specified; inputs are generic vector layers with no inherent temporal or sensor-based attributes.

name: Calculate morphological quality index
desc: The script computes the Morphological Quality Index (MQI), specifically the IQM9* composite index, for river segments (UEAs) in a watershed. It calculates nine individual indices (A1–A4 and F1–F5) representing morphological integrity drivers: A1 (longitudinal continuity of riparian forest), A2 (lateral connectivity via floodplain forest extent), A3 (barrier density and land-use impact near dams), A4 (longitudinal gradient smoothness of channel width), F1 (structural obstruction density from bridges/tunnels), F2 (road proximity impact on floodplain forest), F3 (road proximity impact on agricultural/anthropogenic floodplain), F4 (channel width variability), and F5 (riparian band integrity). Each index is scored 0–10; the final IQM9* score per segment is computed as 1 − (sum of all nine indices)/40, yielding a normalized morphological quality score between 0 and 1. Output is a line vector layer (stream network) enriched with attribute fields for each index and the final 'Score IQM9'.

name: Extract OSM roads and railways
desc: The script extracts road and railway line features from an OpenStreetMap (.osm) vector layer based on user-selected highway and railway types (e.g., 'motorway', 'rail', 'cycleway'), clips them to a user-provided watershed polygon, and appends a 'demi_emp' (half-width in meters) attribute derived from standardized width values per feature type (e.g., 22.5 m for motorway, 5.486 m for rail), producing a new metric-projected line vector layer representing the morphologically relevant transport infrastructure within the watershed for MQI (Morphological Quality Index) calculation.

name: Snap stream network outlets to DEM-derived flow paths
desc: The script extracts the downstream endpoints (outlets) of each river segment (UEA) from a vector stream network, interpolates points near the end of each line (at ~90% or length−30 m), rasterizes the stream network using a LiDAR-derived 10-m DEM, then snaps those interpolated points to the nearest stream pixel within 40 m using a flow-path-aware algorithm (JensonSnapPourPoints); finally, it joins the original segment ID attribute from the stream layer to the snapped points. The output is a point vector layer where each feature represents a topologically consistent outlet location for an ecological aquatic unit (UEA), correctly aligned with the hydrologically conditioned DEM for subsequent MQI (Morphological Quality Index) computation.

name: Extract road railway cycleway network
desc: The script extracts and filters road, railway, and cycleway vector layers from Quebec’s AQréseau+ geospatial datasets (MRNF and MELCCFP sources), clips them to a user-provided watershed polygon (or processes all features if the watershed is empty), applies attribute-based filtering to retain only morphologically relevant linear infrastructure (e.g., excluding tunnels, ferries, unmarked/unbuilt cycleways, and ferry railways), merges the three filtered line layers into a single unified transport network layer, and appends a 'demi_emp' (half-right-of-way) width attribute using rule-based lookup tables derived from official Quebec transportation design standards (Ministère des Transports du Québec, 2012). The output is a metric-projected QgsVectorLayer of lines with geometry and a calculated decimal width field, intended for use in computing the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) of river systems.

name: Extract sub-watershed land use areas
