desc: The script computes morphologically relevant sub-watershed polygons (one per river segment, identified by 'Id_UEA' or user-specified field) from a D8 flow direction raster and snapped stream network outlets; reclassifies a 10-m resolution land use raster (MELCCFP) into four thematic classes (forest, agriculture, anthropogenic, water); calculates area (m²) of each class within each sub-watershed; computes total watershed area and land area; and optionally aggregates dam drainage area (from CEHQ dam points) per sub-watershed. Outputs a vector polygon layer with attributes including 'Id_UEA', 'watershed_area', 'forest_area', 'agri_area', 'anthro_area', 'water_area', 'land_area', and 'dam_area_sum' — serving as the foundational input for IQM indices A1 (land use composition) and A2 (anthropogenic pressure).

name: Filter river-proximate structures
desc: The script identifies and filters point-based infrastructure structures (e.g., bridges, culverts, tunnels) and road-river intersections that are spatially coincident with or within 100 m of a river network. It first computes line intersections between roads and rivers, merges those intersection points with existing MTMD point structures, applies a 2 m buffer to each point, dissolves overlapping buffers, computes centroids of dissolved polygons (to aggregate nearby structures), then extracts only those centroids within 100 m of the river network. Finally, it assigns a unique integer ID (fid) to each retained point. The output is a cleaned, de-duplicated point layer of anthropogenic structures directly associated with the fluvial system for Morphological Quality Index (MQI) assessment.

name: Calculate Morphological Quality Index A1
desc: The script calculates the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) component 'Indice A1' for river segments (UEAs) by quantifying upstream watershed land cover composition—specifically forest and agricultural area proportions—and applying a rule-based classification to assign an integer score (0–5) reflecting hydrogeomorphic alteration. It requires either a precomputed sub-watershed polygon layer with land-use attributes or generates it on-the-fly using a D8 flow direction raster, dam point layer, and land-use raster; then joins computed watershed-area, forest-area, and agri-area metrics back to the input stream network (line features), appending them along with the final A1 index to the output vector layer.

name: Calculate dam impact index A2
desc: The script calculates the Morphological Quality Index (MQI) component 'Indice A2', which quantifies the hydrogeomorphological impact of upstream dams on river segments by computing the ratio of total dam-affected drainage area to total watershed area per segment. It uses a pre-segmented stream network (CRHQ UEA layer), optionally provided sub-watershed polygons (with land use), or generates them using a D8 flow direction raster (WBT D8 Pointer), dam point locations (CEHQ), and land use raster (MELCCFP). The workflow includes: (1) validating input fields (e.g., 'Id_UEA'); (2) generating sub-watersheds if not provided; (3) computing 'dam_area_sum' per watershed via spatial join/summarize; (4) applying a rule-based classification formula to derive integer 'Indice A2' scores (0–4) based on dam-area-to-watershed-area ratio thresholds; and (5) joining results back to the original stream network. Study area is implied to be Québec, Canada (via CEHQ, MELCCFP, CRHQ, LERGA/UQAC); data sources are provincial/national administrative datasets — no satellite imagery or time-series analysis is used. Outputs are a line vector layer (UEA segments) enriched with 'dam_area_sum_m2' and 'Indice A2' attributes.

name: Compute spectral index layer
desc: The script computes a user-specified or predefined spectral index (e.g., NDVI) from an input spectral raster layer using band arithmetic. It supports automatic band mapping based on central wavelength matching to ASI-defined spectral bands (e.g., 'R', 'N', 'B'), manual band/constant mapping via matrix parameter, and dynamic band referencing via regex patterns (e.g., 'r123' for nearest band to 123 nm, 'r@42' for band index 42). The output is a virtual raster layer generated via QGIS's 'native:virtualrastercalc', with metadata (e.g., SI:formula, SI:application_domain) stored as custom layer properties. No specific study area, time range, or satellite data source is embedded in the script — it is a generic, sensor-agnostic raster calculator for spectral indices operating on any QgsRasterLayer provided as input.

name: Compute class fraction raster
desc: The script computes a class fraction raster from a categorized input layer (vector or raster) by first rasterizing/resampling it at a 10× finer resolution grid, then aggregating pixel counts per class into percentage-based fractions at the target grid resolution. It excludes pixels where total class coverage falls below a user-defined threshold (0–100%). Output is a multi-band raster where each band corresponds to one category, storing integer percentages (0–100), with NoData=255, band names set to category names, colors preserved, and scale factor 0.01 (i.e., stored values × 0.01 = actual fraction). The script uses EnMAP-Box QGIS processing algorithms (CreateGridAlgorithm, RasterizeCategorizedVectorAlgorithm, TranslateCategorizedRasterAlgorithm) and does not involve time-series, spectral indices, or external Earth Engine assets — it operates purely on user-provided local or QGIS-loaded categorized layers and a target grid raster. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Import EMIT reflectance raster
desc: The script imports and orthorectifies NASA's EMIT L2A Reflectance (RFL) NetCDF product, applying GLT-based geolocation to produce a georeferenced spectral raster in GeoTIFF format. It scales reflectance values to 0–1 range, embeds wavelength and FWHM metadata per band, filters out bad bands if requested, sets no-data value (−9999), assigns WKT CRS from NetCDF metadata, and configures a default RGB renderer using approximate red/green/blue wavebands mapped to EMIT’s hyperspectral bands. The output is a single multi-band raster layer with embedded spectral metadata, ready for spectral analysis or visualization in EnMAP-Box. Study area, time range, and geographic extent are fully determined by the input EMIT NetCDF file (e.g., 'EMIT_L2A_RFL_001_20220815T042838_2222703_003.nc'), whose metadata provides bounding coordinates, temporal coverage, and sensor parameters. No classification, modeling, or statistical analysis is performed — only data ingestion, orthorectification, metadata injection, and rendering setup.

name: Import EnMAP L2A spectral raster
desc: The script imports and prepares an EnMAP Level 2A (L2A) hyperspectral product as a georeferenced raster layer with calibrated spectral metadata. It reads the XML metadata (or ZIP archive) to extract per-band wavelength, FWHM, gain, offset, and statistics; selects bands based on detector type (VNIR/SWIR), overlap handling option, and no-data filtering; stacks the selected bands from the SPECTRAL_IMAGE.vrt source; writes wavelength, FWHM, scale, and offset into the output raster’s band metadata; and configures a default RGB renderer using red/green/blue waveband mapping (e.g., ~650 nm, ~550 nm, ~480 nm) with cumulative cut stretch (2–98%) for visualization. The output is a VRT or GeoTIFF raster layer with embedded spectral attributes, ready for spectral analysis or index computation in EnMAP-Box.

name: Import Landsat L2 surface reflectance
desc: The script imports and prepares a Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 (L2SP) surface reflectance product from a local *_MTL.txt metadata file. It validates the input filename against Landsat 4–9 sensor prefixes (LT04, LT05, LE07, LC08, LC09) and collection 2 requirement; constructs a VRT or GeoTIFF stack from SR_B*.TIF band files; applies radiometric scaling (gain = 0.0000275, offset = -0.2) to convert DN to surface reflectance in [0,1]; embeds ENVI-compliant wavelength metadata (e.g., '{443, 482, 562, 655, 865, 1610, 2200}' for Landsat 8); assigns band descriptions with nanometer units; and configures a default RGB renderer using automated cumulative cut stretch (2–98%) on bands mapped to red, green, and blue wavebands (e.g., B4/B3/B2 for Landsat 8). Outputs include a georeferenced raster layer (GeoTIFF or VRT) with spectral metadata and a saved QGIS rendering style. No cloud masking, time-series processing, classification, or analysis beyond preparation is performed.

name: Import PlanetScope surface reflectance
desc: The script imports and prepares PlanetScope L1/L3 scene collections (PSScene_collection.json) into georeferenced, wavelength-calibrated, scaled surface reflectance (SR) and usable data mask (UDM2) raster layers. It validates the input JSON file, extracts metadata (band names, center wavelengths, FWHM, scales, nodata values) from associated assets (e.g., 'AnalyticMS', 'ortho_analytic_8b_sr', 'ortho_udm2'), converts non-GDAL-compatible GeoTIFFs (e.g., lacking spatial reference) to GDAL-compliant TIFFs using QGIS raster pipe, builds VRTs for multi-band stacking, applies scaling and spectral metadata via RasterWriter, sets band names/wavelengths/fwhm (converted to nm), assigns no-data values, and configures a default RGB renderer using red/green/blue bands mapped by wavelength (e.g., ~660 nm, ~550 nm, ~480 nm). Outputs are a surface reflectance raster (TIFF or VRT) and a UDM2 QA raster (VRT or TIFF), both with embedded spectral metadata and styling. Study area, time range, and geographic extent are not specified — they are fully determined by the input PSScene_collection.json and its linked assets, which are external to the script.

name: Import Sentinel-2 L2A spectral raster
desc: The script imports a Sentinel-2 Level-2A (atmospherically corrected, surface reflectance) product by parsing its MTD_MSIL2A.xml metadata file or associated ZIP archive. It identifies and stacks user-selected spectral bands (e.g., B1–B12) from the three resolution groups (10 m, 20 m, 60 m), resampling all to the finest selected pixel size. It sets ENVI-compliant metadata including wavelength (in nanometers) and units, applies a scale factor of 0.0001 (converting quantized integers to physical reflectance in 0–1 range), assigns band descriptions, and configures a default RGB renderer using red (B4), green (B3), and blue (B2) bands with 2–98% cumulative histogram stretches. The output is a single multi-band GeoTIFF (or VRT) raster layer with embedded spectral metadata, ready for spectral analysis or visualization in EnMAP-Box. No study area, time range, or classification/analysis beyond import and scaling is performed — the script is purely a data ingestion and preprocessing utility.

name: Create spectral library from classification dataset
desc: The script creates a spectral library vector layer from a classification dataset file (e.g., classifier dump). It reads spectral profiles (X) and class labels (y), maps labels to category names, constructs point geometries (either dummy points if no locations exist or real coordinates from dump.locations), assigns a CRS (WKT or default EPSG:4326), writes the data as a vector layer with categorized rendering based on 'CategoryValue', and saves the default style. The output is a QGIS vector layer file (.gpkg or similar) containing spectral profiles as attributes and point geometries.

name: Create spectral library from regression dataset
desc: The script creates a QGIS vector-based spectral library from a regression dataset file (e.g., .pkl), extracting spectral profiles (X) and target values (y) as attributes, associating each profile with a point geometry (either dummy or from provided locations), and writing the result to a vector layer file with CRS handling. It logs processing steps, validates CRS consistency, and ensures the output layer is valid.

name: Rasterize categorized vector layer
desc: The script rasterizes a categorized vector layer (e.g., land cover or land use polygons) into a categorized raster layer aligned to a user-specified grid. It preserves original category names and colors from the vector’s categorized renderer. When majority voting is enabled, it uses a two-step resampling: first burns classes at 10× finer resolution (via RasterizeVectorAlgorithm), then aggregates back using mode resampling (TranslateRasterAlgorithm with ModeResampleAlg) and applies pixel coverage masking (using AverageResampleAlg on a binary mask) to exclude pixels where polygon coverage falls below a user-defined threshold (e.g., 50%). Outputs include a georeferenced GeoTIFF with paletted renderer configured for visualization in QGIS, plus auxiliary files (VRTs, logs). No satellite imagery, time series, or spectral analysis is involved — input is purely vector + grid; no study area, time range, or sensor data is referenced in the code.

name: Rasterize vector layer
desc: Converts vector geometries (points, lines and polygons) into a raster grid using a user-specified target grid, burn values (fixed, attribute-based, or feature ID), initialization value, and optional GDAL rasterization flags (e.g., -at for all-touched, -add for additive burning). The script handles CRS reprojection of the input vector to match the grid, optionally creates a temporary FID field, and invokes GDAL's rasterize algorithm via QGIS Processing with custom command-line argument patching (e.g., fixing -ts precision). Outputs a georeferenced raster file in GTiff format with user-defined data type and filename.

name: Tile raster into tiling scheme
desc: The script tiles an input raster layer into user-defined polygon tiles from a vector tiling scheme layer. It first warps the source raster to match the tiling scheme’s CRS and spatial extent (using GDAL Warp), then computes a bounding polygon of the warped raster, and finally extracts each intersecting tile using GDAL Translate with projWin. For existing tile files, it performs pixel-wise update (non-overwrite: new pixels replace nodata in existing tiles). Outputs are GeoTIFF tiles organized in subfolders named after tile attributes, with preserved metadata and band names. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification methods are involved — this is a pure geospatial data structuring/management operation on arbitrary raster inputs.

name: Translate raster layer
desc: The script performs raster format conversion and preprocessing operations including spatial subsetting (by extent or pixel window), band subsetting/reordering (including spectral matching by center wavelength), data scaling/offset application, no-data value handling, resampling, reprojection, bad band exclusion (via BBL metadata or derived NaN/inf/no-data detection), metadata/style copying, and optional ENVI header generation. It uses GDAL Translate or Warp under the hood depending on CRS/resampling compatibility, and outputs a new raster file in the specified format (e.g., GeoTIFF) with updated georeferencing, bands, data type, and metadata. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification logic is embedded — it is a generic raster I/O and transformation utility operating on arbitrary QGIS raster layers provided as inputs.

name: Compute monthly climate anomaly
desc: The script computes a monthly climate anomaly raster by subtracting a long-term monthly mean raster from a given monthly raster (e.g., temperature, precipitation, or other climate variable). It uses GDAL's raster calculator with formula 'A-B', where input A is the target month's raster and input B is the corresponding climatological mean raster for that month. Both rasters are expected to be co-registered, same resolution and projection. The output is a single-band Float32 raster labeled 'Monthly_Anomaly'. No spatial or temporal filtering, cloud masking, or sensor-specific preprocessing is performed — the operation is purely arithmetic differencing of two aligned rasters. Study area, time range, data sources, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Estimate land surface temperature
desc: The script computes Land Surface Temperature (LST) and NDVI from Landsat 7 ETM+ top-of-atmosphere (TOA) or calibrated radiance raster inputs. It first converts band 6 (TIR) digital numbers to at-sensor spectral radiance using Landsat 7 ETM+ calibration parameters (gain = (12.650 − 3.200)/(255 − 1), offset = 3.200), then applies a single-channel LST algorithm: LST = (1282.71 / ln(666.09 / L) + 1) − 273.15, where L is the calculated radiance — consistent with the mono-window algorithm for Landsat 7 ETM+ band 6 (10.4–12.5 µm). Simultaneously, it computes NDVI using band 3 (red) and band 4 (NIR) as (B4 − B3)/(B4 + B3), clips both outputs to a user-provided ROI polygon, and applies pre-defined QGIS layer styles for visualization.

name: Estimate land surface temperature
desc: The script computes Land Surface Temperature (LST) and NDVI from Landsat 8 thermal infrared (B10) and optical bands (B4, B5), using a single-channel algorithm that incorporates atmospheric correction via brightness temperature (TOABT), NDVI-derived vegetation proportion (PV), and emissivity estimation (E = 0.004×PV + 0.986). It outputs two clipped, ROI-masked rasters: NDVI (unitless, −1 to 1) and LST (in °C), both styled with predefined QML files for visualization.

name: Generate styled density grid
desc: The script computes a point density heatmap by aggregating input point features into a regular (rectangle/diamond/hexagon) grid, counting points per cell (optionally weighted), filtering cells by minimum count, and applying a graduated color ramp style to the resulting polygon layer. It outputs a styled vector polygon layer representing spatial density distribution, with configurable grid geometry, units, color ramp, classification mode, and outline visibility.

name: Rasterize polygon density
desc: The script converts an input polygon vector layer into a raster density heatmap by rasterizing polygons onto a regular grid. It computes cell dimensions in user-specified measurement units (e.g., meters, feet), adjusts for CRS unit conversion, enforces maximum output image dimensions, and uses GDAL's rasterize algorithm with BURN=1, INIT=0, and -add to accumulate overlapping polygon coverage (i.e., count of polygons per cell). The output is a single-band Float32 raster where pixel values represent the number (or density) of overlapping polygons per grid cell. No time-series, spectral analysis, classification, or external satellite data is involved — it is a pure vector-to-raster spatial aggregation workflow operating on arbitrary user-provided polygon geometry. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate polygon overlap density
desc: The script computes the spatial density of overlapping polygons in a vector layer by performing a union operation to split all intersecting polygons into non-overlapping atomic parts, then aggregates each resulting geometry to count how many original input polygons contributed to it (NUMPOINTS), optionally listing their unique IDs (ID_LIST); finally, it filters out parts where the overlap count is below a user-defined threshold, outputting a cleaned polygon layer where each feature represents a spatially distinct zone with its associated overlap count and optional source ID list.

name: Generate styled kernel density heatmap
desc: The script computes a kernel density estimation (KDE) raster from an input point vector layer using QGIS's native 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm, then applies a pseudocolor raster style (including user-selected color ramp, inversion, interpolation mode, classification method, and number of classes) via the 'densityanalysis:rasterstyle' algorithm. It dynamically converts pixel size and kernel radius from user-specified measurement units (e.g., meters, feet) into the layer’s CRS units, validates output raster dimensions against a maximum allowed size, and reports errors if grid cells become too coarse (zero dimension) or exceed image limits. The final output is a styled, georeferenced raster heatmap with quantitative density values rendered using a customizable color gradient.

name: Buffer water point features
desc: The script performs a vector buffer operation on the active QGIS layer named 'Water Point' (referred to as 'OMP waterpoint layer'), using a fixed distance of 0.01 map units, 25 segmentation points, round end caps, miter joins, and no dissolve. It loads the buffered output as a temporary vector layer, prints the feature count, and iterates over each buffered feature to print its 'Waterpoint' attribute value and geometry object. The script is purely geometric — no remote sensing data, no time series, no classification, no raster operations, and no GEE-specific code (despite the prompt context mentioning GEE; this is actually PyQGIS code for QGIS processing). All operations are local vector GIS workflows within QGIS desktop. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods beyond buffering are not specified.

name: Generate geodesic buffer polygon
desc: The script constructs a geodesically accurate circular buffer polygon centered at (30.0, 12.0) with radius 9,000,000 meters (≈9,000 km), using an azimuthal equidistant projection (AEQD) centered on the point to ensure true-distance buffering on the ellipsoid. It transforms the center point to AEQD space, creates a planar buffer, reprojects back to WGS84, and handles antimeridian crossing by inserting artificial vertices near ±179.9° longitude and ±85° latitude to prevent invalid geometry splitting. The final output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer named 'Geodesic_Buffer' containing a single polygon feature, added to the QGIS project. No satellite imagery, time-series data, classification, or external datasets are used — the entire workflow is synthetic geometric construction in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS).

name: Generate geodesic buffer geometry
desc: The script computes a geodesically accurate circular buffer (5,000,000 m radius) centered at (168°E, 48°S) in WGS84, explicitly handling antimeridian crossing by projecting to Azimuthal Equidistant (centered on point), then to Pacific-centered EPSG:3832, performing geometric difference with a buffered antimeridian line, and intersecting with a global geographic extent polygon (±179.9° longitude, ±85° latitude). The output is a single QgsGeometry object representing the buffered area clipped to valid geographic bounds, added as a feature to a memory vector layer 'Geodesic_Buffer' in QGIS. No remote sensing data, time-series, or classification is involved — it is purely a coordinate geometry operation for accurate large-scale buffering on the ellipsoid.

name: Generate geodesic buffer geometry
desc: The script creates a geodesically accurate circular buffer polygon around a given Cartesian (map canvas) coordinate point, using an azimuthal equidistant projection centered at the WGS84-transformed location. It transforms the input canvas coordinates (x, y) to WGS84 lat/lon, constructs a custom PROJ4-based aeqd CRS with those center coordinates, generates a planar buffer of specified radius (in meters) in that local projection, then reprojects the resulting geometry back to the map canvas CRS. The output is a single QgsGeometry polygon added to a memory vector layer named 'Geodesic_Buffer' in QGIS. No time-series, raster data, classification, or external datasets are involved — it is purely coordinate transformation and geometric buffering. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Generate geodesic buffer polygon
desc: The script constructs a geodesically accurate circular buffer polygon centered at (135.0, -78.0) with a 500,000-meter radius, using an azimuthal equidistant projection (aeqd) to preserve true distances from the center point. It transforms the center point to the custom aeqd CRS, buffers in that projected space, then reprojects the buffered geometry back to WGS84 (EPSG:4326). To handle antimeridian crossing (longitude discontinuity), it inserts artificial vertices near ±179° and ±89° to ensure valid WKT polygon geometry across the dateline. The final output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer named 'Geodesic_Buffer' containing the corrected polygon feature, added to the QGIS project. No satellite data, time-series, classification, or external datasets are used — this is purely a vector geometry generation and reprojection workflow.

name: Extract zonal maximum elevation points
desc: The script extracts raster pixel locations (as point features) where the raster value equals the zonal maximum within each input polygon feature. It outputs a point layer with one or more points per polygon: multiple points if tied maxima exist; a single centroid point if all pixels in the polygon share the same value (min == max). The output attribute 'Elev' stores the maximum raster value. The workflow includes clipping the raster to each polygon’s bounding box, computing zonal min/max statistics via QgsZonalStatistics, and — when min ≠ max — reading the clipped raster array with GDAL, identifying all pixel indices equal to the max, converting those indices to map coordinates (center-aligned), and filtering for points strictly within the polygon geometry. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is embedded in the code — it is a generic QGIS Processing algorithm operating on user-provided raster and polygon layers.

name: Geocode address points
desc: The script geocodes street addresses from a user-provided CSV file using the ArcGIS Online geocoding service (via the `geocoder.arcgis` Python package), creates point features in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) with attributes including the original address, latitude, and longitude, and outputs a memory-based QGIS vector layer of geocoded points. It handles empty or non-string addresses gracefully, reports geocoding success/failure per address via QGIS feedback, and supports field selection for the address column. No study area, time range, satellite data, or remote sensing operations are involved — this is a pure client-side geocoding workflow within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Identify high-altitude and steep-slope areas
desc: The script identifies two distinct terrain-based environmental constraint zones within a user-defined rural property boundary: (1) areas with elevation > 1800 m above sea level, derived by binary thresholding a reprojected Digital Terrain Model (MDT), and (2) areas with slope > 45°, computed from the same MDT using the native slope algorithm; both outputs are vectorized, attribute-filtered (DN = 1), and clipped to the input property polygon, yielding two separate polygon layers suitable for APP (Permanent Preservation Area) identification under Brazilian environmental regulation (e.g., CAR/APP criteria).

name: Query Rural Environmental Registry parcels
desc: The script queries and downloads Cadastro Ambiental Rural (CAR) property polygons from WFS services (official SICAR or GeoOne-hosted) within a user-defined rectangular extent. It transforms the input extent to EPSG:4674, intersects it with Brazilian state boundaries (BR_UF_2020.shp), constructs per-state WFS URIs (e.g., 'sicar_imoveis_ac' for Acre), and fetches only features intersecting the extent. The output is a single merged vector layer of CAR-imóveis polygons clipped to the query rectangle, loaded into QGIS with post-processed layer naming. No remote sensing imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations are performed — it is purely a WFS-based vector data retrieval and integration tool. Study area is Brazil (inferred from BR_UF_2020.shp and SICAR domain); data source is official Brazilian CAR database served via WFS; no satellite/sensor/bands involved.

name: Identify 25°–45° slope areas
desc: The script computes terrain slope from a user-provided Digital Terrain Model (MDT) raster, reprojects it to a projected CRS (e.g., UTM), calculates slope in degrees using QGIS native:slope, applies a raster algebra condition '(A>=25)*(A<=45)' to isolate pixels within the 25°–45° range, converts the binary raster to polygons via gdal:polygonize, filters for DN=1 polygons (i.e., slope-valid areas), and clips the result to the input property boundary ('Área do imóvel'), producing a vector layer of polygons where terrain inclination falls strictly between 25 and 45 degrees — intended for identifying potential Areas of Permanent Preservation (APP) under Brazilian environmental regulation (Resolução CONAMA 303/2002).

name: Generate CAR KML files
desc: The script exports vector layers from the current QGIS project to KML format, specifically targeting layers with names containing 'Geo', 'CAR', or 'INCRA' (though these are actually excluded via 'continue'), reprojection to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and automatic cleanup of intermediate Shapefile artifacts. It operates on all non-empty vector layers in the project, filters by layer name heuristics (excluding layers with 'Geo', 'CAR', or 'INCRA' in name), writes each to a .kml file in the user-specified output folder, and reports success or error per layer. No remote sensing data, image processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — it is a GIS export utility for Cadastro Ambiental Rural (CAR) compliance visualization in Google Earth. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band usage are not involved or specified.

name: Download LiDAR elevation data
desc: The script downloads French national LiDAR HD elevation and point cloud data from IGN's Géoplateforme WFS service (https://data.geopf.fr/wfs/ows) based on an input Area of Interest (AOI). It queries the WFS for tiles intersecting the AOI in EPSG:2154 (Lambert-93), filters by four data types — MNT (Digital Terrain Model), MNS (Digital Surface Model), MNH (Digital Height Model), or raw LIDAR point clouds (COPC/LAZ) — and applies user-selected merge strategies (download all, merge all intersecting, or select tile with maximum AOI coverage). Outputs include downloaded files (TIF or LAZ) in a user-specified folder, optionally merged rasters (via GDAL) or merged point clouds (via PDAL), and automatic loading into QGIS as raster or classified point cloud layers. The study area is implicitly France (via IGN’s national dataset), with no temporal dimension (static archival data). Data sources are exclusively WFS-delivered tiles from IGNF_MNT-LIDAR-HD, IGNF_MNS-LIDAR-HD, IGNF_MNH-LIDAR-HD, or IGNF_NUAGES-DE-POINTS-LIDAR-HD — no satellite, sensor, or bands involved.

name: Calculate public transport accessibility index
desc: The script calculates a Public Transport Accessibility Level (PTAL) layer by aggregating EDF (Effective Distance Factor) values from a relationships table ('POI_SAP_Relationships') grouped by POI_ID and route_type ('bus' or 'trein'). For each POI in the base 'POI' point layer, it computes AI_bus and AI_trein as weighted sums of EDF values (largest EDF + 0.5 × sum of remaining EDFs), then derives PTAI as their sum. The output is a new in-memory point layer named 'PTAL' with fields POI_ID, AI_bus, AI_trein, and PTAI, retaining the geometry and CRS of the input POI layer.

name: Generate network-based isochrones
desc: The script generates isochrone polygons by computing concave hulls around service access points (SAPs) that intersect each individual line segment of an input transportation or utility network layer. For every network line feature, it spatially extracts SAPs that intersect that line, counts them, and—if at least three points are found—computes a concave hull using a user-defined alpha parameter; the resulting polygon inherits the original network line’s attributes plus a new 'point_count' field. Output is a polygon vector layer where each feature represents a localized isochrone zone bounded by the concave hull geometry.

name: Correct surface elevation model
desc: The script corrects an input raster surface (e.g., DEM or seismic horizon) using point-based control measurements (e.g., well tops or interpreted horizon picks), accounting for geological faults. It first samples the input raster at point locations to compute residuals (observed minus modeled elevation), then interpolates those residuals into a delta surface—constrained by fault lines via the custom 'PUMAplus:creategridwithfaults' algorithm—then adds the delta surface to the original to produce a fault-aware corrected surface. A quality control vector layer is generated containing both original residuals (Delta1) and post-correction residuals (Delta2) for validation. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and specific geospatial parameters are not specified in the code; all inputs are user-provided layers (raster surface, point vector, fault lines), with no embedded temporal, geographic, or sensor metadata.

name: Compute precipitation event variability
desc: The script computes pixel-wise standard deviation of precipitation maxima (15-minute events) across multiple input raster layers, then optionally applies local spatial smoothing (via scipy's generic_filter with a user-defined window size) and exports the result as a GeoTIFF. The output raster represents spatial variability of precipitation intensity across events — not temporal change over time, but inter-event dispersion at each location. Input rasters are read via QGIS raster layer providers; no reprojection or resampling is performed — all rasters must share identical extent, resolution, and CRS. The script does not generate vector points despite the class name 'Raster_to_points'; the 'Output' parameter is declared as TypeVectorPoint but the implementation writes a GeoTIFF and returns a GDAL dataset object — indicating a critical mismatch between declared interface and actual behavior. No point vector is created or exported. The HelpString explicitly states: 'Spatial variability of precipitation maxima (15 min) by means of standard deviation pixel-per-pixel for different events'. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and projection details are inferred only from input file paths and GDAL metadata — none are hardcoded or specified in the script.

name: Compute basin-averaged precipitation from gridded data
desc: The script computes spatially weighted average precipitation over a catchment area using a gridded precipitation dataset. It reprojects the grid to EPSG:32632, clips it to the catchment boundary, calculates cell area, appends a constant field with total catchment area, computes weighting factors (cell area / catchment area), and then generates new weighted precipitation fields (e.g., 'DATA_20230101_pesata') by multiplying each 'DATA*' precipitation value by its corresponding weight. Outputs include: (1) clipped & reprojected grid, (2) clipped grid with area, catchment area constant, and weight fields, and (3) final layer with original precipitation fields plus their basin-weighted versions for downstream aggregation (e.g., summing weighted values yields basin-mean precipitation).

name: Derive waste dump elevation model
desc: The script processes a DEM raster clipped to a waste dump polygon, computes the minimum positive elevation value within that clipped area, creates a constant raster layer with that minimum value, subtracts it from the clipped DEM to generate a relative elevation (height-above-base) raster, and then — though incorrectly configured — attempts to compute surface volume (but misuses the 'Create Constant Raster Layer' algorithm in place of 'raster surface volume'). The final output is a 'DerivedDem' raster representing elevation relative to the lowest positive terrain point inside the waste dump boundary.

name: Connect points to path by distance
desc: The script connects input point features into line paths based on iterative nearest-neighbor search: starting from an initial point (optionally ordered by expression), it repeatedly finds the nearest unused point within a configurable maximum distance and group constraint, appends it to the path, and marks both points as used. Points are grouped optionally by a user-defined expression (e.g., field or category), and paths can be limited by max distance between consecutive points, max number of points per path, and self-crossing avoidance (computationally expensive). Input MultiPoint geometries are cast to SinglePoints. Outputs include a LineString layer with fields for group ID/name, vertex count, path length, start/end feature IDs, optional custom ID strings (cid), and optional semicolon-separated lists of visited feature IDs and inter-vertex distances. No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite-derived inputs are involved — it is a pure vector geometric processing algorithm operating on arbitrary QGIS point layers.

name: Compute zonal mean temperature
desc: The script computes zonal statistics (mean) for all bands of an input raster layer named 'temperatureorarie' over polygon features in a vector layer named 'comuni'. It iteratively applies 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' — one band per iteration — updating the vector layer with new mean-value fields prefixed by the band identifier (e.g., 'temperatureorarie@1_'). The final output is a vector layer ('Tempcomuni') containing all computed band-wise mean temperature values as attributes for each polygon. No study area, time range, satellite, sensor, or band names are explicitly specified in the code; the raster is treated as a generic multi-band temperature raster, and the vector layer appears to represent administrative units ('comuni' = Italian for 'municipalities'), but no geographic extent, CRS, or data provenance is encoded in the logic.

name: Clip administrative boundaries and water bodies
desc: The script performs vector clipping operations to extract portions of two input polygon layers—'Oria Diamerismatwn' (Administrative Boundaries) and 'Ydatika' (Water Bodies)—that intersect with a user-defined area of interest ('Perioxi endiaferontos'). It outputs two clipped vector layers: 'OriaDiamerismatwn_clip' containing only the administrative boundary segments within the area of interest, and 'Ydatika_clip' containing only the water body polygons overlapping that same area. No raster processing, classification, or temporal analysis is performed; the workflow is purely geometric overlay (clip) using QGIS native vector tools.

name: Calculate street openness ratio
desc: The script computes the street openness ratio (h/d ≤ 1) for urban blocks, where h is building height (derived from floor count × 3 m) and d is the perpendicular distance between opposing building façades across streets. It identifies façade segments perpendicular to street centerlines using azimuth matching (±6° and ±174°–186°), generates transects, clips them against buildings, retains only segments intersecting exactly two buildings (i.e., spanning the street width), measures their length (d), computes h/d, filters segments where h/d ≤ 1, and finally calculates the percentage of total block perimeter length covered by such favorable segments — outputting a grid-based polygon layer with the computed IA06 indicator value per cell.

name: Calculate pedestrian intersection density
desc: The script computes pedestrian intersection density as a connectivity indicator for urban areas, by extracting street network intersections from OpenStreetMap (OSM) line data, filtering out dead-ends (intersections with <3 connected segments), aggregating remaining intersections into clusters to resolve topological noise, counting them per grid cell, and normalizing by grid cell area (km²) to produce a density metric (intersections/km²). Output is a vector feature class (polygon grid) with an attribute field named per NAMES_INDEX['IA12'][0] containing the computed density values.

name: Compute coastal elevation change
desc: The script computes vertical change (erosion/accretion) between two point cloud datasets representing coastal topography at different times. It merges multiple old and new point clouds separately, converts each merged set to a 1-m resolution DEM raster (using Z attribute), assigns the project's CRS, then calculates the difference (New − Old) to produce a continuous-change raster ('temp.tif') representing elevation change in meters. The result is loaded into QGIS with a predefined style (style.qml) and exported as a styled GeoTIFF named after the user-specified 'Erosion Map Layer Name'.

name: Estimate mean flow and low flow
desc: The script estimates Mean Flow and Mean Low Flow for ungauged subcatchments using a Random Forest regression model trained on geofactors (e.g., elevation statistics, slope, land cover, precipitation) from gauged subcatchments. It supports two modes: (1) training a new model on user-provided gauged subcatchment geofactors (‘Estimate from gauged_subcatch_geofactors.shp’), or (2) applying pre-trained regional models (e.g., ‘[Pre-trained] Warnow catchment (Germany)’). Predicted flows are distributed to river sections proportionally to segment length, then accumulated downstream along a topologically structured river network (using NET_ID/NET_TO fields). Outputs include: (a) a polygon layer of ungauged subcatchments with fields CATCH_ID, Mean_Flow, M_Low_Flow, acc_Mean, acc_M_Low, CATCH_TO, and flow_unit; and (b) a line layer of river sections with the same flow fields plus distributed and accumulated values. The study area is implicitly the Warnow catchment (Germany), as it is the only enabled pre-trained region and used as default in variable names (e.g., warnow_subcatch_gf), file prefixes ('Warnow'), and plugin documentation. No satellite, sensor, or time-series data are used — all inputs are static vector layers (subcatchments, river network) containing derived geofactor attributes. The workflow relies entirely on scikit-learn (RandomForestRegressor, StandardScaler), geometric operations (length-based flow distribution), and custom topological accumulation logic over directed acyclic networks.

name: Calculate cumulative risk quotient
desc: The script calculates individual Risk Quotients (RQ = PEC/PNEC) for selected APIs across river sections (lines or polygons), using concentration fields (e.g., 'conc_Carb', 'conL_Carb') from an input accumulation layer and PNEC values from a user-provided table. It then computes a Cumulative Combined Risk Index (CCRI) per risk assessment type (ERA, HHRA, AMR-RA) as CCRI = log(RQ_sum + 1) × (1 + (RQ>1)_sum / RQ_sum), where RQ_sum is the sum of all RQs per prefix (e.g., 'era_', 'hhraL_') and (RQ>1)_sum is the sum of RQs exceeding 1. Outputs include a vector layer with original geometry plus new RQ fields (one per API–RA combination) and CCRI fields (e.g., 'CCRI_era', 'CCRI_hhraL'). The tool supports both line-based river networks and polygon-based subcatchments (e.g., Finnish hydrological model output); no satellite, temporal, or explicit geographic extent is used — it operates purely on local QGIS vector layers loaded in the project (e.g., 'River accumulation', 'PNEC').

name: Calculate surface runoff
desc: The script implements the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) Curve Number (CN) method to estimate surface runoff (Q in mm), potential retention (S), initial abstraction (Io), runoff coefficient (CE %), infiltration coefficient (CF %), and initial abstraction coefficient (CIo %) for a user-defined study area. It integrates vector layers of soil hydrologic groups and land use/vegetation cover, intersects them to derive combined CN codes, applies antecedent moisture condition (CHA I/II/III) lookup tables to assign CN values, computes S = 254×(100/CN − 1), Io = 0.2×S, and then applies the standard CN runoff equation Q = (P − Io)²/(P + 0.8×S) when P > Io (else Q = 0). Outputs are five thematic vector layers: GeoQ (full attribute result), NC (Curve Number), CE (runoff coefficient), CF (infiltration coefficient), and CIo (initial abstraction coefficient), each styled with predefined QML symbology.

name: Calculate solar energy potential on rooftops
desc: The script computes rooftop solar irradiation potential and shading exposure for building roofs in a defined local extent. It processes high-resolution DSM/DTM LiDAR data to derive roof slope and aspect rasters, classifies roof planes by slope and aspect, calculates annual solar irradiance using the UMEP SEBE model with meteorological EPW data, and computes seasonal shadow binary rasters (March, June, September, December) to derive a composite shade index. Final outputs include vector layers of processed roof planes enriched with attributes: mean roof aspect (via sin/cos zonal stats), mean slope, mean annual solar irradiance (kWh/m²), and mean shade fraction (0–1).

name: Extract roof planes from DSM and DTM
desc: The script identifies candidate roof planes within building footprints by processing high-resolution digital surface (DSM) and terrain (DTM) models. It computes DSM−DTM to isolate above-ground structures, filters for heights ≥2 m, calculates slope and aspect rasters, reclassifies them into ordinal classes (aspect: N/NE/E/SE/S/SW/W/NW → 1–4; slope: 0–20°/20–40°/40–60° → 1–3), applies sieve filtering to remove noise, clips and polygonizes both rasters within buffered building footprints, intersects the resulting aspect and slope polygons to derive roof plane geometries, applies morphological cleaning (buffer-debuffer cycles), and appends zonal statistics (mean cosine and sine of aspect, mean slope) as attributes to the final vector layer of processed roof planes.

name: Identify candidate roof planes
desc: The script identifies candidate roof planes by processing DSM and DTM raster data to derive building-height rasters (DSM−DTM), filtering for structures ≥2 m above ground, computing slope and aspect, reclassifying both into ordinal classes (slope: 1–3; aspect: 1–4), applying sieve filtering to remove small noisy patches, clipping the reclassified rasters to buffered building footprints, polygonizing the clipped rasters, intersecting aspect- and slope-derived polygons to produce roof plane candidates, applying morphological cleaning (buffer/debuffer cycles) to regularize geometry, and attaching zonal statistics (mean cosine and sine of aspect, mean slope) as attributes to the final vector layer of processed roof planes. Inputs include user-provided building vector layers, local extent polygons, and raster DTM/DSM layers — no satellite imagery or time-series data are used. Outputs are shapefiles: clipped DSM/DTM, DSM−DTM rasters, slope/aspect rasters (full and ≥2 m), reclassified and sieved rasters, clipped and polygonized rasters, validated and intersected roof plane polygons, and the final cleaned 'PROCESSED_ROOF_PLANES_LAYER_NAME' vector layer with statistical attributes. The study area is implicitly constrained by user-supplied 'LOCAL_EXTENT' and 'BUILDINGS_LAYER', with CRS assumed to be BRITISH_NATIONAL_GRID (EPSG:27700) based on explicit reference in code. All operations are local GIS raster/vector workflows in QGIS Processing using GDAL, SAGA, and native algorithms — no GEE server-side computation occurs.

name: Calculate annual solar shadow patterns
desc: The script calculates solar shadow rasters for four key dates (March 20, June 21, September 23, and December 22, 2020) using a Digital Surface Model (DSM) and optional roof plane vector data. It generates continuous-shadow rasters via geometric shadow casting (using the external ShadowGenerator class), reclassifies them into binary shadow/no-shadow rasters, multiplies them to produce a composite annual shadow mask (where 1 = persistently sunlit, 0 = shaded on ≥1 date), and finally computes mean shade values per roof plane polygon using zonal statistics. Outputs include four date-specific shadow rasters, four binary rasters, one final multiplied binary shadow layer, and updated roof vector attributes ('Shade_mean').

name: Calculate annual shadow patterns
desc: The script calculates solar shadow rasters for four key solstice/equinox dates (2020-03-20, 2020-06-21, 2020-09-23, 2020-12-22) using a high-resolution DSM clipped to a local area and optionally enhanced with a low-resolution wide-area DSM context. It reclassifies each shadow raster into binary (shadow/no-shadow), multiplies them to produce a composite annual shadow mask (where 1 = consistently sunlit across all four dates), and computes mean shade values per roof polygon via zonal statistics. Outputs include four date-specific shadow rasters, four binary rasters, one final binary shadow raster, and updated roof vector layer with 'Shade_' attributes.

name: Calculate solar irradiation on roofs
desc: The script calculates annual solar energy (irradiation) raster for rooftops in a local area, using DSM/DTM-derived elevation data, wall height/aspect rasters, processed meteorological data (EPW format), and SEBE (Solar Energy Balance Engine) modeling. Key steps include: (1) preprocessing EPW meteorological data; (2) computing wall height and wall aspect rasters from a DSM-minus-DTM difference layer (named 'dsm_minus_dtm_1m_clipped.tif'); (3) initializing solar parameters (slope, aspect, albedo, radiation matrices) from a 1m-clipped DSM raster ('dsm_1m_clipped.tif'); (4) running the SEBE worker to compute solar energy array accounting for direct, diffuse, and reflected irradiance; (5) writing the result as a GeoTIFF ('annual-solar-energy.tif'); and (6) performing zonal statistics to assign mean irradiation values to roof polygon features (from 'processed_roof_planes.shp'). The study area is not specified in the code; inputs are file-path-based and user-provided via QGIS Processing interface. No satellite or remote sensing imagery is used — all geospatial inputs are local raster/vector files (DSM, DTM, roof polygons) and meteorological time-series (EPW).

name: Prepare solar PV roof layers for web mapping
desc: The script transforms solar-suitable rooftop polygons from British National Grid (EPSG:27700) to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), filters attributes to retain only 'id', 'latitude', 'longitude', 'Num_panels', and 'Output_kwh' (rounded to 2 significant figures), and clips the full buildings layer to a user-defined local boundary. It does not perform any Earth observation analysis, classification, or time-series processing — it is a coordinate transformation and attribute reduction workflow for QGIS2WEB deployment. The study area is implicitly Cumbria, UK (per copyright and author affiliation), and inputs are precomputed shapefiles (e.g., SUITABLE_ROOF_PLANES_LAYER_NAME, LOCAL_EXTENT_LAYER_NAME, FULL_AREA_BUILDINGS_LAYER_NAME), not satellite imagery. No remote sensing data, sensors, bands, or temporal filtering are used.

name: Generate linear referencing marks
desc: The script creates a point vector layer of linear referencing marks placed along input line geometry, with mandatory marks at distance = 0 (start) and full line length (end), plus inner marks either at fixed map-unit intervals or equally spaced by count. Each output point contains a numeric 'distance' field (accumulated length from line start) and a formatted 'label' string field (e.g., '123.45'), and is automatically styled with black cross markers (2 mm) and white Arial labels (8 pt) with black 0.8 mm buffer.

name: Calculate AWEIsh water index
desc: The script computes the Automated Water Extraction Index shadow (AWEIsh) using Landsat 8 Surface Reflectance bands B2 (blue), B3 (green), B5 (NIR), B6 (SWIR1), and B7 (SWIR2) from a single scene with acquisition date 2019-03-12 (inferred from filename LC08_L2SP_169062_20190312_20200829_02_T1_SR_*.tif). It applies the AWEIsh formula: A + 2.5B − 1.5(C + D) − 0.25E, where A=blue, B=green, C=NIR, D=SWIR1, E=SWIR2; then masks negative values to -9999. The output is a single-band GeoTIFF raster (AWEIsh_masked.tif) representing water likelihood with non-water pixels set to -9999. No spatial extent or geometry is defined programmatically — the calculation uses the NIR band’s extent as reference. Study area and projection are not specified beyond file paths; no temporal filtering or compositing is performed — only one static scene is used.

name: Split multipart geometry parts
desc: The script splits a single vector layer feature containing multiple geometry parts (e.g., disconnected polygons) into separate shapefiles — one per part — named 'Pugu_part_1.shp', 'Pugu_part_2.shp', etc. It uses QGIS's native 'multiparttosingleparts' algorithm to decompose the geometry, then exports each resulting single-part feature as an individual ESRI Shapefile with preserved attributes and CRS. The study area is implied by the output filename prefix 'Pugu', but no raster data, satellite imagery, time series, classification, or geospatial analysis beyond geometry decomposition is performed. Input is a local vector layer identified by name or source containing substring 'pug'; no remote sensing data, bands, sensors, or temporal filtering is involved.

name: Calculate NDVI from Landsat surface reflectance
desc: The script calculates the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) using pre-downloaded Landsat 8 Surface Reflectance (SR) band files: red band (B4) and near-infrared band (B5), corresponding to the scene LC08_L2SP_169062_20190312_20200829_02_T1. It loads the two GeoTIFFs as QGIS raster layers, validates them, adds them to the QGIS project, and applies a raster calculator expression '(nir@1 - red@1) / (nir@1 + red@1)' using the NIR layer’s extent, CRS, and pixel size. The output is a single-band GeoTIFF (LC08_169062_20190312_NDVI.tif) containing float-valued NDVI pixels ranging from -1 to 1, with NoData set to -9999. The scene ID implies path/row 169/062, acquisition date 2019-03-12, and processing level L2SP (Level 2 Science Products). Study area and exact geographic bounds are not specified in the code; satellite sensor and bands are explicitly identified via filenames (B4 = red, B5 = NIR), and no classification, time-series, or masking steps are performed — only a single-date, band-based arithmetic index calculation.

name: Calculate water quality index
desc: The script computes a Water Quality Index (WQI) raster using Landsat 8 Surface Reflectance bands (B2/blue, B3/green, B4/red, B6/swir1) and a precomputed AWEIsh (Automated Water Extraction Index shadow-adjusted) mask. The WQI formula is ((GREEN + (BLUE − RED) − SWIR1) / (GREEN + (BLUE − RED) + SWIR1)), applied only where AWEIsh ≥ 0; pixels with AWEIsh < 0 are assigned nodata value −9999. Input rasters are local GeoTIFFs derived from LC08_L2SP_169062_20190312_20200829_02_T1_SR (Landsat 8 OLI Surface Reflectance Level 2, Path 169 Row 062), indicating acquisition on 2019-03-12. The output is a single-band masked WQI raster saved as LC08_169062_20190312_WQI_masked.tif. No cloud masking, temporal compositing, or spatial subsetting is performed — all operations are pixel-wise raster algebra using QGIS Raster Calculator on preloaded local layers.

name: Classify temperature and precipitation bivariate classes
desc: The script generates three-quantile (tercile) classifications (1/2/3) for two input rasters — e.g., temperature (Raster A) and precipitation (Raster B) — then combines them into a bivariate integer code raster with values 11–33 (e.g., 11 = low temp + low precip, 33 = high temp + high precip). It optionally divides Raster B (e.g., to convert monthly total mm to mm/day), reprojects and aligns both rasters to a common grid/CRS, computes quantiles on valid pixels only, applies raster algebra for reclassification and combination, and outputs three GeoTIFFs (A-class, B-class, bivariate code) plus an exact paletted QML style file with predefined labels and colors for visual interpretation in QGIS.

name: Create map extent polygon
desc: The script creates a single rectangular polygon shapefile representing the current QGIS map canvas extent. It retrieves the canvas extent as a QgsRectangle, converts it to a QgsGeometry polygon, writes it to a user-specified Shapefile path using QgsVectorFileWriter, and optionally loads the resulting layer into the QGIS project. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or external geospatial datasets are used — the input is purely the interactive map view state. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Calculate distance to nearest waterpoint
desc: The script computes the Euclidean distance from each input GPS collar point feature to the nearest waterpoint feature (e.g., borehole, dam, river crossing) in a user-provided waterpoint layer. It outputs a new point layer with added attributes: distance in meters and kilometers, the waterpoint’s type (if specified in the source waterpoint layer), and its name/ID. All distance calculations are performed in a user-specified projected CRS to ensure metric accuracy; geographic CRS is explicitly rejected. The workflow includes geometry validation (fixing invalid geometries), spatial indexing for efficient nearest-neighbor lookup, on-the-fly reprojection of input layers if needed, and attribute preservation from the source GPS layer. No remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite-derived products are used — inputs are purely vector-based (GPS points and waterpoint points), and no study area, time range, or satellite data is referenced in the code.

name: Clip GPS collar points to paddocks
desc: The script clips raw GPS collar point GeoPackage files (vector point layers) from an input folder to a user-provided paddock or buffered paddock polygon layer (vector polygon), producing clipped GeoPackage outputs saved in an output folder. The workflow uses QGIS native:clip processing algorithm, iterates over all .gpkg files in the source directory, materializes the clip polygon layer for reproducibility, and saves each clipped result with the same filename in the output folder. No satellite imagery, time-series filtering, classification, or spectral analysis is performed; it is a pure vector overlay (clipping) operation on field-collected GPS point data. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Summarize watered land type areas
desc: The script computes, for each paddock polygon, the area (km²) and percentage of each intersecting land type that falls within 3km and 5km watered zones — using either buffered water points (3 km and 5 km buffers) or pre-defined watered area polygons. It calculates a weighted watered area as 100% of the 3km zone plus 50% of the annular 3–5km zone, then outputs a vector layer with per-paddock-per-land-type attributes (ID, Paddock, Land_Type, Pdk_LT_area_km2, 3km_WA_LT_area_km2, 5km_WA_LT_area_km2, Watered_LT_area, Pcnt_LT_watered) and optionally exports a spreadsheet summary. Input layers are CRS-aligned on-the-fly; geometries are made valid, intersected, dissolved, and converted to MultiPolygon where needed. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or spectral analysis is performed — all inputs are user-provided vector layers (polygons for land types/paddocks/watered areas, points for waterpoints). Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Clip pastoral district rasters
desc: The script clips four types of Australian grassland monitoring rasters — growth probability, growth percentile (at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months), total standing dry matter (TSDM), and TSDM percentile — to individual pastoral district boundaries using vector polygon masks. It outputs ERDAS IMAGINE (.img) raster files named by district (e.g., 'Barkly_GROWTHPROB.img', 'Barkly-6.img', 'Barkly_TSDM.img', 'Barkly_TSDMPCNT.img') into user-specified output folders, preserving nodata as -999 and enforcing cutline-based cropping. The workflow iterates over each district feature, selects it individually, and applies GDAL’s cliprasterbymasklayer algorithm with consistent resampling and data type (Float32, DATA_TYPE=5).

name: Calculate daily distance to water statistics
desc: The script calculates daily statistics (maximum time gap between consecutive GPS points in minutes, minimum/maximum/mean distance-to-water in meters) from a GPS collar point layer containing datetime and distance-to-water fields. It filters features by a user-specified datetime range, groups them by date, computes time deltas and DTW values for consecutive chronological features per day, aggregates statistics per date, and exports results to an Excel spreadsheet with fields: Paddock, Collar_No, Date, Max_T_Delta_mins, Min_DTW_m, Max_DTW_m, Mean_DTW_m. The input layer is a vector layer (not satellite-derived), and no remote sensing imagery or GEE server-side processing is performed — this is a QGIS Processing algorithm operating entirely on local vector data.

name: Calculate daily movement statistics
desc: The script calculates daily GPS collar-derived movement statistics for livestock, including total daily track distance (km), maximum time gap between pings (minutes), minimum/maximum/mean inter-ping distances (m), and minimum/maximum/mean speeds (km/h). It outputs a line vector layer ('Daily Tracks') where each feature represents a daily trajectory with attached statistics, and an Excel spreadsheet containing the same tabular results. Input is a user-provided GPS point layer with datetime stamps; no remote sensing data is used—only vector geometry and attribute processing. The script performs chronological sorting per day, polyline construction, coordinate transformation to a user-specified projected CRS, pairwise distance/speed computation between consecutive points (with <5-minute gaps filtered), and statistical aggregation (min/max/mean). Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Summarize daily livestock movement
desc: The script calculates daily movement statistics (max, min, mean total distance in km) for GPS-collared livestock across paddocks, using line vector layers representing animal tracks. It extracts paddock name, collar ID, and date attributes from input layers; computes duration between first and last track dates; slices off the last feature per layer (treated as incomplete day); aggregates Total_distance_km values per day; identifies dates of max/min daily distances; and exports a summary table to Excel with fields: Paddock, Collar, Start Date, End Date, Duration, Max Daily Total (km), Max On, Min Daily Total (km), Min On, Mean Daily Total (km). Input data sources are user-provided vector line layers (not satellite-derived), with no geospatial raster operations, cloud masking, classification, or spectral analysis performed. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and explicit geometry are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate time per watered band
desc: The script calculates the time (in hours) that GPS-collared animals spend within each predefined distance-to-water (DTW) band (e.g., '1000-1500m') using a point-layer of GPS collar fixes with datetime and DTW attributes, intersected against a polygon layer of watered bands. It computes daily time-in-band by linearly interpolating time between consecutive chronological GPS points across band boundaries using geometric line-polygon intersection to apportion time proportionally to segment length within each band. Outputs are written to an Excel spreadsheet (.xlsx or .ods) with one row per observed date and a final summary row for the entire collar deployment period. Input layers are user-provided local vector layers — no remote sensing imagery or GEE server-side assets are used; all operations occur client-side in QGIS using PyQGIS geometry and attribute logic. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Delineate watershed subbasins
desc: The script delineates a watershed basin and its internal subbasins from a digital elevation model (DEM), using GRASS GIS hydrological tools (r.fill.dir, r.watershed, r.water.outlet) in QGIS Processing. It snaps an outfall point to the nearest stream network, extracts streams at high resolution (r.stream.extract), and characterizes subbasins by intersecting them with reprojected and geometry-fixed land cover and soil vector layers. It computes hydrologic parameters including Manning’s n, retardance coefficient, runoff coefficient class, Hydrologic Soil Group (HSG), SCS Curve Number (CN), and area (ha) for each subbasin polygon — outputting three vector layers: Streams (detailed stream network), Basin (delineated watershed boundary), and Subbasins (attribute-rich, clipped, and area-calculated subbasin polygons).

name: Calculate SCS curve number and lag time
desc: The script computes the Soil Conservation Service (SCS) Curve Number (CN) and time of concentration (lag time) for each subbasin by integrating land cover, soil hydrologic group (HSG), and topographic parameters derived from a filled DEM. It first reprojects and fixes geometries of input vector layers (subbasins, land cover, soil type), then performs sequential intersections to spatially associate land cover classes and soil types per subbasin polygon. Using lookup rules, it assigns retardance coefficients, runoff coefficients (e.g., 'AS', 'CN', 'GPF'), HSG values ('A'–'D') based on soil texture, Manning’s n, and CN values per land-cover–HSG combination. It calculates weighted-average CN and n per subbasin using area-weighted aggregation. Then, using WhiteBoxTools, it clips the DEM to each subbasin, computes the longest flow path and average slope along that path, and applies the SCS lag equation: tc = (60 × (L × 3.28084)^0.8 × (1000/CN − 9)^0.7) / (1900 × S^0.5), clamping minimum tc to 5 minutes. Final output is a CSV file ('basin_summary.csv') containing per-subbasin records with ID, area (ha), weighted CN, weighted n, longest flow path (m), average slope (%), and lag time (min).

name: Delineate catchments and compute discharge
desc: The script delineates watersheds and subbasins from a user-provided DEM using WhiteBoxTools (Wang & Liu depression filling, D8 flow routing, Jenson Snap Pour Points, Watershed, Subbasins, LongestFlowpath). It intersects land cover and soil vector layers with subbasins to compute weighted hydrological parameters (CN, Manning’s n, retardance coefficient, runoff coefficient) per subbasin. For each return period (from user-supplied regression CSV), it computes time of concentration (tc) using five empirical methods (Kirpich, Izzard, FAA, SCS Lag, Kinematic Wave), selects the minimum tc, then applies the Rational Method (Q = 0.278 × C × i × A) to compute peak discharge. Outputs a CSV ('basin_summary.csv') containing subbasin ID, area, weighted CN/n/retardance, longest flow path, average slope, return period, runoff coefficient, selected tc (value and method name), rainfall intensity, and peak discharge.

name: Delineate catchment basins
desc: The script delineates catchment basins and subbasins from a digital elevation model (DEM) using hydrological terrain analysis. It reprojects the DEM to a specified CRS, fills sinks, computes flow direction and accumulation, extracts stream networks using a minimum contributing area threshold, vectorizes streams and basin raster outputs, snaps an outfall point to the nearest stream, derives the upstream contributing basin from that outfall using r.water.outlet, clips subbasins to the main basin boundary, and generates refined stream vectors within the delineated basin. Outputs include: (1) a vector layer of the full catchment basin, (2) a clipped vector layer of subbasins within that basin, and (3) a detailed stream network vector layer confined to the basin extent.

name: Classify river water quality from tweets
desc: The script classifies geolocated social media (Twitter) posts about rivers into n categories (default 3) based on a training dataset (.xlsx), using an external Python module 'Predictions.predict'. It reads translated and filtered tweet data from 'Data/Data_translated.xlsx', applies classification with user-specified allowed error (%) and number of categories, then generates a point vector layer ('Mapces') from the resulting histogram file 'Data/PointsHistogram.xlsx' containing xcoord/ycoord columns. The output layer is in EPSG:4326 and represents classified river observation points. No satellite imagery, remote sensing indices, or geospatial filtering by region/time is performed in the script — all processing is tabular/statistical/machine learning–based on pre-geocoded tweet metadata. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and explicit spatial filtering are not present in the code.

name: Extract slope-derived road candidate points
desc: The script processes a precomputed slope raster (in degrees) to generate point shapefiles stratified by slope ranges (0–24°, 24–32°, 32–40°, 40–45°, and 0–45°), then excludes points within a 10-meter buffer of existing streams to produce a final shapefile of potential road alignment points ('GENERATED ROAD POINTS.shp') suitable for civil infrastructure planning.

name: Convert 2D lines to 3D arcs
desc: The script converts input 2D vector line geometries into 3D polyline geometries (LineStringZ) by generating smooth arc-like vertical profiles along each line segment. It uses a custom geometric method (imported from arc_3d_methods.generate_3d_polyline_from_geometry) that takes user-defined parameters — number of interpolation segments (3–15), Y-axis rotation angle (10°–90°), and Z-scale factor (0–1) — to compute z-values per vertex. Input CRS is optionally transformed to EPSG:3857 for computation, then back-transformed; output is a new vector layer with LineStringZ geometry in the original CRS. No remote sensing data, time-series, or classification is involved — purely deterministic 2.5D/3D vector geometry transformation. Study area, time range, satellite data, and external datasets are not specified.

name: Convert 2D lines to 3D arcs
desc: The script converts input 2D line vector geometries into 3D (LineStringZ) polyline geometries by applying arc-based vertical deformation: it generates smooth 3D curves using user-specified per-feature parameters — number of segments (controling curve resolution), Y-angle (controlling vertical angular deviation in the y-axis plane), and Z-scale (controlling vertical exaggeration/magnitude). The workflow includes optional on-the-fly CRS transformation to EPSG:3857 for computation, calls an external method `generate_3d_polyline_from_geometry` (defined in `arc_3d_methods.py`, not provided here) to compute the 3D geometry, then transforms back to the input CRS. Output is a new vector layer with LineStringZ geometry, preserving original attributes. No remote sensing data, time series, or classification is involved — it is purely geometric vector processing within QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Generate 3D arc geometry
desc: The script generates a 3D polyline (LineStringZ) representing an arc derived from input 2D line geometries. It computes a circular arc approximation using the start/end points to estimate radius, buffers a point to create a circle polygon, applies sequential 3D affine transformations (rotation around y/z axes, z-axis scaling, and translation), aligns the result to the original geometry's centroid and bearing, and appends the resulting 3D geometry to a new memory layer with matching attributes. Input parameters control segmentation count, y-axis rotation angle (degrees), and vertical scaling factor.

name: Identify disconnected network segments
desc: The script analyzes topological connectivity of a line-based river or transport network layer relative to an initial 'River Mouth' point/geometry. It iteratively selects connected line segments by vertex proximity and spatial adjacency, starting from the River Mouth, using dissolve-by-ID, vertex extraction, selection-by-location, and iterative expansion until no new features are selected. It outputs two vector layers: (1) 'Excerpt Disconnected' — line segments with no topological path to the River Mouth (i.e., isolated branches), and (2) 'Connected section' — line segments reachable via shared vertices/intersections from the River Mouth, representing the topologically continuous upstream/downstream network.

name: Count vertex connections in line networks
desc: The script identifies topological vertices in input line vector layers where more than one line segment meets (i.e., degree > 1), counts the number of incident line segments per vertex, and outputs a point layer containing only those high-degree vertices with an integer attribute 'Vertice' indicating the connection count. It operates purely on vector geometry (no raster or time-series data), using coordinate-based vertex aggregation and topological counting logic. The input must be a line-type vector layer (e.g., roads, rivers, utility networks); no study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are involved — all processing is local, CRS-aware vector topology within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Identify dangle line endpoints
desc: The script identifies dangles (unconnected line endpoints) in an input vector line layer using QGIS's 'Identify Dangles' algorithm. It then spatially evaluates each dangle point against user-selected vector layers (points, lines, or polygons) by generating small buffers (0.000001 decimal degrees) around non-polygon layers and merging all candidate overlap layers. Using intersection and extract-by-location operations, it classifies dangles into two outputs: (1) 'DANGLES_Overlapping' — dangle points that intersect/overlap with any of the selected layers (with attribute 'layer_overlap' populated from the overlapping layer's 'layer' field), and (2) 'DANGLES_Non_Overlap' — dangle points that do not intersect any selected layer. The workflow preserves original dangle geometry (as points) and attributes, and handles mixed geometry types via buffering and spatial indexing for performance.

name: Identify line layer dangles
desc: The script identifies dangle features (loose endpoints of line segments) in a user-provided vector line layer. It does so by splitting input lines at their mutual intersections using QGIS's 'native:splitwithlines' algorithm, then counting vertex occurrences across all resulting line segments; vertices appearing exactly once are classified as dangles and output as point features preserving original attributes. The workflow is purely vector-based, requires no raster data or time-series analysis, and operates entirely within QGIS Processing Framework using native algorithms and QgsGeometry operations. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are involved — input is an arbitrary local or loaded vector line layer with unspecified CRS and extent.

name: Extract headwater sources
desc: The script identifies and extracts headwater (spring) locations from a linear stream/river network vector layer. It first identifies dangle vertices (unconnected endpoints) as candidate headwaters, then filters them by length criteria (minimum, maximum, or all), removes false positives near river mouths using a buffer-based spatial exclusion, and outputs two products: (1) Headwater_Lines — line segments representing the upstream-most reaches of headwater streams, attributed with their length ($length); and (2) Headwater_Points — point features at the upstream endpoints of those lines, inheriting original layer attributes plus length. The core logic relies on topological analysis (dangle detection via 'Identify Dangles'), network splitting, and spatial filtering (extract-by-location with NOT_INTERSECTS predicate against river mouth buffer).

name: Detect pseudo-node topological connectivity
desc: The script identifies pseudo-nodes (line endpoints that are not properly connected to other line vertices) in an input polyline layer, then determines whether each pseudo-node spatially coincides with any vertex from user-selected vector layers (points, lines, or polygons). It outputs two point layers: (1) 'Pseudo-node Non_Overlap' — pseudo-nodes with no topological coincidence to any vertex of the selected layers; and (2) 'Pseudo-node Overlapping' — pseudo-nodes that do coincide with at least one vertex, enriched with a 'Layer_Name' attribute identifying which source layer contributed the coincident vertex. The workflow involves generating pseudo-nodes via a custom 'Continuous_Network_Analysis:Pseudo-node' algorithm, extracting all vertices from selected layers (handling multipoint, polyline, and polygon geometries by densifying to points), building a unified vertex layer with layer attribution, and performing spatial intersection/extract-by-location operations to classify pseudo-nodes based on vertex overlap.

name: Download flood hazard zones
desc: The script downloads FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) flood hazard data for a user-defined Area of Interest (AOI) using the FEMA ArcGIS REST API. It retrieves vector layers (e.g., Flood Hazard Zones, Base Flood Elevations, Levees) as GeoJSON, converts them to QGIS vector layers, optionally clips them to the AOI geometry, converts Unix timestamp fields (e.g., EFF_DATE, REV_DATE) to QDate format, and saves them as shapefiles in WGS84 (EPSG:4326). Outputs include clipped/unclipped shapefiles per selected layer, a README.txt with AOI bounds and metadata, and optional auto-loading into the QGIS project. Data source is exclusively the FEMA NFHL MapServer (ID-based layer access), not satellite or remote sensing imagery; no classification, modeling, or time-series analysis is performed.

name: Model rockfall energy propagation
desc: The script implements the DROKA BASIC method to model rockfall hazard propagation from source points across a terrain. It computes a 3D energy cone defined by lateral spreading angle and energy angle, samples terrain elevation at source and potential impact points, calculates the energy line (delta = start_elev − distance × tan(shadow_angle) − final_elev), filters for physically feasible impacts (delta > 0), derives velocity (sqrt(2×g×delta)) and kinetic energy (delta × g × mass / 1000), aggregates results onto a regular grid (cell size configurable), and outputs a point vector layer where each point represents a DTM cell centroid within the affected area, annotated with count of overlapping cones, percent frequency, min/mean/max energy (kJ), and min/mean/max velocity (m/s).

name: Simulate rockfall energy and velocity paths
desc: The script simulates rockfall propagation paths from user-defined source points using a hydrological flow tracing approach (GRASS r.drain) on five perturbed DTM variants generated via Monte Carlo sampling from a normal distribution (mean = original DTM elevation, user-specified standard deviation). For each traced path point, it computes the vertical difference between the ground surface and an energy cone defined by the user’s energy angle (ϕp), then derives kinetic energy (kJ) and velocity (m/s) per point. Results are aggregated spatially into a regular grid (cell size = input cell_size), computing min/max/mean energy and velocity per grid cell; the final output is a vector point layer (grid cells) with fields: 'energy_min', 'energy_max', 'energy_mean', 'velocity_min', 'velocity_max', 'velocity_mean'.

name: Generate SHALSTAB input rasters
desc: The script generates six constant-value raster layers required as inputs for the SHALSTAB landslide susceptibility model: friction angle (°), soil cohesion (N/m²), root cohesion (N/m²), unit weight (N/m³), depth of unstable layer (m), and permeability (m/h).
