Each raster is created with the same spatial extent, resolution (cell size), and CRS as the input DTM using QGIS's native:createconstantrasterlayer algorithm. The workflow processes parameters sequentially, creating one raster per step, and supports user-defined default values for all geotechnical and hydrological parameters.

name: Characterize pockmark depressions
desc: The script characterizes delineated pockmark polygons (submarine or terrestrial depressions) using an input DEM by computing a comprehensive suite of morphometric, geometric, and volumetric attributes. It rasterizes pockmark polygons, fills DEM depressions to compute relative depth (depth below local spill point), calculates zonal statistics (mean, min, max, std dev, range, sum) on slope, absolute elevation, and relative depth rasters; derives Minimum Bounding Geometry (MBG) metrics (width, height, angle); computes shape descriptors (compactness, circularity, convexity, solidity, eccentricity, roughness index, dissection index, profile index, relief-area ratio); estimates pockmark volume in m³ from summed relative depths and pixel area; and optionally extracts pockmark centroids and intra-polygon local minima points (deepest points) via minimum filtering, raster comparison, point extraction, buffering/dissolving, and spatial joining with polygon attributes. Outputs include a fully attributed polygon layer, optional centroid points, and optional local minima points — all enriched with quantitative descriptors for geomorphic analysis.

name: Enable vector file editing
desc: The script creates an editable copy of a locked vector layer by applying a trivial expression-based filter ($id is not null) to extract all features. It does not perform geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations; it is a data preparation utility for GIS editing workflows. The input is a blocked vector source (e.g., read-only, zipped, or externally locked), and the output is a new, fully editable vector layer with identical geometry and attributes. No study area, time range, satellite data, or spectral processing is involved — the operation is purely local, attribute-agnostic, and geometry-preserving.

name: Fetch administrative boundary data
desc: The script fetches administrative boundary geometries (e.g., country-level ADM0 boundaries) from the GeoBoundaries API (geoboundaries.org) using a specified ISO-3 country code, boundary type (e.g., 'ADM0'), and release type (e.g., 'gbOpen'). It downloads GeoJSON files via URLs provided in the API response, converts them into a QGIS memory vector layer with EPSG:4326 CRS, adds an 'id' attribute, and loads the layer into the current QGIS project. The study area is defined solely by the `country_code` parameter (e.g., 'DEU'), no time dimension is involved, and no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used — this is purely vector boundary data ingestion. Output is a polygon vector layer named '{country_code}_{boundary_type}_{release_type}_geoBoundaries' visible in QGIS.

name: Fetch administrative boundary polygons
desc: The script fetches administrative boundary polygons (ADM0–ADM5) for a specified country (ISO-3 code) from the geoBoundaries API. It constructs a QGIS vector layer in EPSG:4326 from GeoJSON downloads, validates geometry integrity (via shapely WKT conversion), appends metadata, and adds the resulting memory layer to the QGIS project. The study area is defined solely by the user-provided ISO-3 country code (e.g., 'DEU'), with no temporal component, no satellite/sensor involvement, and no geospatial analysis or classification — only HTTP retrieval, GeoJSON parsing via geopandas, and QgsGeometry conversion. Data source is the geoBoundaries REST API (https://www.geoboundaries.org/api/current/), with release types gbOpen/gbHumanitarian/gbAuthorative.

name: Convert raster to PCRaster format
desc: The script converts an input GDAL-supported raster layer into PCRaster format, with user-selectable output data types (Boolean, Nominal, Ordinal, Scalar, Directional, or LDD). It uses GDAL's Translate function with specific metadata options (e.g., 'VS_SCALAR') and output data types (e.g., GDT_Float32 for Scalar) to ensure PCRaster compliance. The workflow reads the source raster via GDAL Open, applies format translation with type- and semantics-aware metadata, writes to the specified output path, and properly closes datasets. No spatial or temporal filtering, classification, modeling, or analysis is performed — it is purely a format and data-type conversion utility. Input study area, time range, satellite/sensor, bands, and geographic context are not specified in the code.

name: Burn drainage into DEM
desc: The script burns vector-based drainage features (e.g., rivers, canals, ditches) into a digital elevation model (DEM) by lowering elevation values along buffered drainage corridors using a two-stage vertical drop: a gradual (smooth) drop over a user-defined buffer distance, followed by an additional sharp drop directly on the drainage centerline. It rasterizes and aligns vector drainage layers to the DEM’s CRS and resolution, converts both DEM and drainage rasters to PCRaster format, applies PCRaster’s burndem operator with custom parameters (buffer size, smooth drop depth, sharp drop depth), and outputs a modified DEM raster where drainage networks are topographically enforced — critical for hydrological modeling accuracy.

name: Calculate stream subcatchments
desc: The script calculates vector subcatchments from a PCRaster flow direction (LDD) raster using Strahler stream ordering. It first computes Strahler orders, thresholds to extract rivers (≥ user-defined order), identifies junctions as cells where downstream flow does not retain the same river order, assigns unique outlet IDs to junctions, and then iteratively computes individual catchments for each outlet using the PCRaster `catchment()` function. Each subcatchment is rasterized, polygonized into a shapefile, cleaned (invalid geometry handling, part union), reprojected to the user-specified destination CRS, and written as a multi-polygon feature with `catchment_id` attribute. Outputs include optional boolean rasters for rivers, junctions, and outlets, plus a mandatory vector layer of subcatchment polygons. No satellite imagery, time series, or external geospatial datasets beyond the input LDD raster are used; all processing is deterministic hydrological modeling using PCRaster operators. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified — the input is a static, precomputed local drain direction map.

name: Calculate subcatchments from outlets
desc: The script calculates vector subcatchment polygons for each outlet location using a PCRaster-based hydrological workflow. It takes a local drain direction (LDD) raster and a nominal raster of outlet identifiers as inputs, computes catchments via the PCRaster `catchment()` function for each outlet ID, polygonizes each resulting binary catchment raster, unions multipart geometries per outlet, transforms to the specified destination CRS, and outputs a single vector layer (MultiPolygon) with one feature per subcatchment, each attributed with a 'catchment_id' field. The script uses QGIS Processing Framework integration, GDAL/OGR for raster-to-vector conversion, and PCRaster for core hydrological routing — no satellite imagery or time-series analysis is involved; all operations are static, deterministic, and based on precomputed raster inputs. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor information are not specified in the code.

name: Delineate stream network and catchment
desc: The script delineates a stream network and its corresponding upstream catchment boundary for a user-defined outlet point within a specified study extent. It downloads a DEM from OpenTopography (e.g., SRTM or Copernicus), reprojects and converts it to PCRaster format, computes flow direction (LDD) using lddcreate, derives Strahler stream order, thresholds streams by order (e.g., ≥5), snaps the user-provided outlet point to the nearest stream cell within a tolerance buffer using flow accumulation maxima, computes the contributing catchment with catchment(), and outputs vectorized streams (as polylines) and a polygonized catchment boundary — all in the user-specified CRS.

name: Burn drainage into DEM
desc: The script burns vector-based drainage features (e.g., rivers, canals, ditches) into a digital elevation model (DEM) by modifying elevation values along and near the drainage network. It first merges input vector drainage layers, rasterizes them to match the DEM’s resolution and extent, converts both DEM and rasterized drainage to PCRaster format, prepares a spatially aligned boolean drainage mask using `cover`, then applies the custom `burndem` PCRaster script to lower elevations: a smooth linear drop over a user-defined buffer distance (e.g., 100 map units), plus an additional sharp vertical drop directly on the drainage line (e.g., 30 map units). The output is a modified DEM raster in PCRaster scalar format where drainage paths are topographically enforced — critical for hydrological flow routing. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are referenced; inputs are generic local raster/vector layers provided by the user.

name: Calculate stream subcatchments
desc: The script calculates vector subcatchments from a PCRaster flow direction (LDD) raster using Strahler stream ordering. It first computes Strahler orders, thresholds to extract rivers (≥ user-defined order), identifies junctions as cells where downstream flow does not retain the same river order, assigns unique outlet IDs to junctions, and then iteratively computes individual catchments for each outlet using the PCRaster `catchment()` function. Each subcatchment is rasterized, polygonized into a shapefile, cleaned (invalid geometry handling, part union), reprojected to the user-specified destination CRS, and written as a multi-polygon feature with `catchment_id` attribute. Outputs include optional boolean rasters for rivers, junctions, and outlets, plus a mandatory vector layer of subcatchments. No satellite imagery, time series, or external geospatial datasets beyond the input LDD raster are used; all processing is deterministic hydrological modeling using PCRaster operators. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified — the input is a static, precomputed local drain direction map.

name: Calculate subcatchments from outlets
desc: The script calculates vector subcatchments for each outlet using a PCRaster flow direction (LDD) raster and a nominal outlet raster. It iterates over each unique outlet ID (1 to maximum outlet value), computes the contributing catchment area using PCRaster's `catchment()` function, converts each resulting catchment raster to vector polygons via GDAL polygonization, unions fragmented parts, validates geometry, transforms coordinates to the specified destination CRS, and writes each subcatchment as a feature in a single output MultiPolygon vector layer with 'catchment_id' attribute. The workflow relies entirely on local raster hydrological modeling (no time-series or remote sensing analysis); inputs are precomputed static rasters (flow direction and outlet locations), and no study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial boundaries are referenced in the code — all spatial context is implicit in the input raster layers' extent and CRS.

name: Generate ISO XML task file
desc: The script converts a QGIS vector layer of field boundary polygons into an ISO 11783-compliant TASKDATA.XML file for agricultural machinery (specifically AGOpenGPS). It iterates over input polygon features, extracts vertex coordinates (lat/lon in WGS84), and serializes them into XML elements <PFD>, <PLN>, <LSG>, and <PNT> with prescribed attributes. If the input layer is not in EPSG:4326, it reprojects to WGS84 first. The output is a UTF-8 encoded XML file conforming to ISO 11783-10 (VersionMajor=3, VersionMinor=3) with no embedded time-series, raster, or satellite data — purely geometric vector-to-XML translation. Study area is not specified; no temporal filtering, classification, or remote sensing analysis occurs.

name: Adjust raster georeferencing with GCPs
desc: The script performs geometric adjustment of an arbitrary input raster using user-provided ground control point (GCP) vectors (line features with exactly two vertices representing displacement vectors). It supports three coordinate transformation models: Translation (1–2+ vectors), Helmert 2D (Conformal, 2–3+ vectors), and Affine (3–4+ vectors). The workflow includes CRS validation, computation of forward/inverse transformation parameters (via Ajust2D and ValidacaoVetores), resampling of the input raster (nearest/bilinear/bicubic) into a newly computed bounding box aligned to the transformed geometry, and generation of three outputs: (1) a GeoTIFF raster with updated geotransform and projection, (2) a point vector layer containing adjusted GCP coordinates and per-point planimetric precisions (σₓ, σᵧ), and (3) an HTML report summarizing residuals, statistics, and transformation parameters. Input data sources are local (not GEE-hosted): a user-specified raster file (e.g., drone orthomosaic) and a QGIS vector layer of lines; no satellite, sensor, or band information is involved — this is a local georeferencing correction tool, not a remote sensing analysis script. Study area, time range, and geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Remove alpha band from raster
desc: The script removes the 4th (alpha) band from a 4-band input raster (e.g., RGBA GeoTIFF), optionally converting transparent pixels (alpha = 0) to NoData values in the output 3-band RGB GeoTIFF. It reads the input via GDAL, validates that exactly 4 bands are present, extracts and interprets the alpha band as a binary transparency mask, applies it to set null values in RGB bands where alpha is zero, writes the result to a new GeoTIFF with proper geotransform and projection, and optionally loads the output into QGIS. The tool is designed for drone-derived or orthophoto rasters with embedded alpha channels — no satellite imagery, time-series, classification, or external geospatial analysis is performed.

name: Convert raster to JPEG
desc: The script converts an input 8-bit RGB or RGBA raster layer (3 or 4 bands) into a compressed JPEG file using GDAL's lossy JPEG compression. It optionally generates a world file (.jpw) for georeferencing and loads the output into QGIS. The workflow reads the source raster via GDAL, validates band count (3 or 4) and data type (GDT_Byte), applies gdal.Translate with '-of JPEG' and '-ot Byte' options, writes a .jpw file if requested using the original GeoTransform parameters, and handles CRS preservation. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification logic is involved — it is a pure format conversion and compression tool operating on arbitrary local raster files loaded in QGIS. Input is a user-selected raster layer (e.g., drone-captured orthomosaic), not a cloud-hosted Earth Engine image collection.

name: Adjust DEM vertical bias
desc: The script performs vertical adjustment of a user-provided Digital Elevation Model (DEM) raster using Ground Control Points (GCPs) with known Z values. It supports two adjustment methods: constant offset (global shift) and plane-based (affine vertical surface fit). For each GCP, it interpolates the original DEM value at the point’s XY location (using nearest/bilinear/bicubic resampling), computes residuals (delta_z), fits the model, applies correction to the full raster, and outputs (1) the adjusted GeoTIFF DEM, (2) a vector layer of GCPs augmented with adjusted_z, delta_z, and precision_z, and (3) an HTML report summarizing statistics, residuals, and model parameters. Input CRS validation is optional but enforced by default. No satellite, time-series, or automated cloud masking is involved — all inputs are local/user-supplied files (raster + vector).

name: Evaluate vertical positional accuracy
desc: The script evaluates the altimetric (Z) positional accuracy of a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) by computing Z-discrepancies between reference ground control points (with known elevation values in a user-specified field) and interpolated DEM elevations at those point locations. It performs bilinear/bicubic/nearest-neighbor interpolation on the input raster DEM using GDAL, computes RMSE (Root Mean Square Error) of discrepancies, and classifies accuracy against Brazil’s Cartographic Accuracy Standard (PEC-PCD) across multiple map scales (1:500 to 1:250,000). Outputs include: (1) a vector layer with added 'discrep_Z' attribute containing per-point elevation differences; (2) an HTML report containing RMSE, descriptive statistics (mean, std, min, max), and a PEC-PCD compliance table mapping each scale to quality class (A–D or R). Input requirements are strictly a raster DEM layer and a point vector layer with a numeric elevation field — no satellite imagery, time-series, or classification logic is involved. All geospatial operations are local (point-in-raster sampling + interpolation), CRS validation is enforced (projected only), and no study area, time range, or external satellite data is referenced or used.

name: Create RGB composite from bands
desc: The script combines three user-provided single-band raster layers (Red, Green, Blue) into a single 3-band GeoTIFF file where Band R is written to the first raster band, Band G to the second, and Band B to the third. It preserves georeferencing (geotransform and projection) from the input Red band. No spatial or temporal filtering, cloud masking, normalization, or classification is performed — it is a pure band stacking operation using GDAL. The output is saved as a GeoTIFF and optionally loaded into the QGIS project. All inputs are arbitrary local raster files (e.g., GeoTIFFs), with no constraints on satellite origin, sensor, or acquisition date; the script does not access GEE servers or remote image collections. Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and band identities are not specified in the code — only generic band roles (R/G/B) are enforced by parameter labels.

name: Match raster histogram
desc: The script performs histogram matching of an input raster to a reference raster using statistical normalization and calibration. It reads both rasters via GDAL, computes mean and standard deviation for each band (excluding alpha if present), normalizes the input band, scales and shifts it to match the reference's statistics, enforces 8-bit radiometric limits (0–255), and writes the result as a GeoTIFF. Input and reference rasters are provided as QGIS raster layer parameters; no cloud masking, temporal filtering, or spatial subsetting is applied. The output is a single GeoTIFF file with matched histograms per band (RGB + optional alpha), and optionally loaded into the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor metadata, and geographic extent are not specified in the code — it is a generic, local-file-based raster processing tool operating on user-provided GeoTIFFs or similar GDAL-readable formats.

name: Split raster into tiles
desc: The script splits a single input raster dataset into smaller rectangular tiles (sub-rasters) by dividing it along the X (horizontal) and Y (vertical) axes into user-specified numbers of columns and rows. It reads the input raster using GDAL, computes tile boundaries based on pixel dimensions, extracts each tile’s array data band-by-band, preserves georeferencing (geotransform and projection), honors NoData values, and exports each tile as a separate GeoTIFF file to a user-defined output folder. The script supports multi-band rasters and loads the resulting rasters into QGIS if requested. No spatial filtering, temporal analysis, classification, or external dataset access occurs — it is purely a geometric partitioning operation on an existing local raster file. Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not specified because the script operates generically on any user-provided raster layer without referencing remote sensing collections, dates, or geographic extents.

name: Calculate raster band statistics
desc: The script calculates user-selected statistics (count, sum, mean, median, std, min, max) for raster band values intersecting polygon features. It uses pixel-center sampling: only raster cells whose center falls exactly inside each polygon are included. Input is a generic raster layer (any source) and a vector polygon layer; output is an augmented polygon feature class with new attribute fields prefixed by user-defined string and named per band and statistic (e.g., 'stat_band1_mean'). The algorithm performs coordinate transformation if CRS mismatch exists, computes bounding-box-optimized raster clipping per polygon ring (including hole handling via Path.contains_points), applies nodata masking, and aggregates values before computing statistics. No specific study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is embedded — it is a generic GDAL-based local zonal statistics tool operating on file-based rasters loaded via QgsRasterLayer and processed with numpy/gdal/path.

name: Calculate vegetation index
desc: The script performs band arithmetic on user-provided raster inputs to compute custom spectral indices (e.g., GLI, NDVI, NDWI, VARI, VIgreen) using algebraic formulas referencing bands b1, b2, b3 (and optionally b4). It reads the input raster via GDAL, parses and evaluates the user-defined formula string by substituting band arrays (e.g., 'b1' → array of band 1), handles nodata and alpha transparency (if enabled), avoids division-by-zero, and writes the resulting single-band float32 GeoTIFF output with -9999 as NoData. The script operates entirely on local raster files supplied by the user in QGIS; no remote sensing data collection, time-series processing, cloud masking, or classification is performed. All parameters — input raster, formula, alpha handling, output path — are interactive QGIS Processing inputs. Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and geographic location are not specified in the code and are fully user-determined at runtime.

name: Binary thresholding of raster values
desc: The script creates a binarized raster (GeoTIFF) by classifying input raster pixel values into two classes (0 or 1) based on user-defined or statistically derived lower and upper thresholds. Thresholds are computed either from sample polygons/points (e.g., NDVI-rich vegetation areas) using methods including Min/Max, 2–98% quantiles, or mean ± 2/3 standard deviations — explicitly cited in documentation for NDVI-based vegetation identification (França et al., 2017). Input is a single-band raster (e.g., NDVI, but no specific index is hardcoded); samples may be vector polygons or points; output is a byte-typed GeoTIFF with 0 (outside threshold range) and 1 (within range). No study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is embedded in the code logic — it is a generic, local raster processing tool operating on any loaded QGIS raster layer. The workflow includes GDAL-based raster I/O, polygon-based pixel sampling via matplotlib.path.Path, point interpolation via custom Interpolar, statistical aggregation, and binary masking using NumPy boolean indexing. Final output is optionally loaded into QGIS.

name: Compress RGB raster with JPEG
desc: The script performs lossy JPEG compression on an input RGB (3-band) or RGBA (4-band) GeoTIFF raster to reduce file size (~10%), using GDAL's Translate with configurable compression type (JPEG, PHOTOMETRIC=YCBCR, or JPEG_PHOTOMETRIC), quality level (65%, 75%, or 85%), and tiling. It validates that the input has exactly 3 or 4 bands and is 8-bit; if Photometric compression is selected, it enforces exactly 3 bands. The output is a compressed GeoTIFF file with specified creation options, optionally loaded into the QGIS project. No remote sensing analysis, classification, time-series, or geospatial modeling is performed — only raster encoding optimization.

name: Create raster holes from polygons
desc: The script creates 'holes' (no-data or transparent pixels) in an input raster by masking out areas defined by a polygon vector layer. It reads the raster as a GDAL array, transforms polygon geometries to match the raster's CRS if needed, converts polygon vertices to pixel coordinates, uses matplotlib's Path.contains_points to identify interior pixels, and assigns nodata values (or sets alpha=0 for 4-band rasters) to those pixels. The output is a new GeoTIFF raster with modified pixel values reflecting the masked regions. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is specified—the tool is generic and operates on user-provided local raster and vector layers.

name: Define null raster cells
desc: The script processes a user-provided input raster to reclassify pixel values outside a specified numeric interval [MIN, MAX] as null (NoData) using a custom null value. It reads the raster via GDAL, iterates over all bands, applies a conditional mask ((band>=MIN)*(band<=MAX))*band + (band<MIN or band>MAX)*NULLVALUE, writes the result to a new GeoTIFF, and sets the NoData value accordingly. The output is a GeoTIFF raster with null cells defined per user parameters; no study area, time range, satellite data, or classification model is involved — it is a generic raster preprocessing operation operating on local file-based rasters loaded in QGIS.

name: Extract raster band
desc: The script extracts a single user-specified band from a multiband raster file (e.g., GeoTIFF) using GDAL. It reads the input raster via GDAL.Open(), selects the band by index (1-based), reads its array, preserves georeferencing (projection and geotransform), and writes a new single-band GeoTIFF. No spatial or temporal filtering, classification, or spectral index computation is performed. The output is a standalone GeoTIFF file containing only the selected band, optionally loaded into the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor metadata, and band names are not specified in the code — the tool is generic and agnostic to data origin, relying solely on local raster layer input provided by the user.

name: Fill raster no-data patches
desc: The script fills null/no-data pixels in an input raster using data from one or more smaller overlapping raster layers ('patches'), applying resampling (nearest, bilinear, or bicubic) during spatial interpolation. It handles 1-band (grayscale), 3-band (RGB), and 4-band (RGBA) rasters, respects nodata values, and outputs a patched GeoTIFF. The workflow includes georeferenced pixel-wise interpolation via the external `Interpolar` function, bounding-box-aligned patch application, and progressive feedback. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external GEE collections are involved — all inputs are local QGIS raster layers (e.g., drone mosaics, orthophotos, or manually prepared patches); the script operates purely on file-based GDAL raster I/O within QGIS Processing Framework. Output is a single patched GeoTIFF file, optionally loaded into the QGIS project.

name: Interpolate raster pixel values at point locations
desc: The script estimates raster cell values at user-provided point geometries using spatial interpolation (nearest neighbor, bilinear, or bicubic) based on GDAL raster reading and custom interpolation logic. It supports single-band or multi-band rasters, handles coordinate reference system transformation between point layer and raster, preserves original point attributes, appends interpolated values as new double-precision fields (e.g., 'sample_band_1'), and outputs a new point vector layer with interpolated values. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or classification method is embedded—the tool is generic and data-agnostic, relying entirely on user-supplied raster and vector inputs.

name: Inventory raster file metadata
desc: Creates a vector layer (Point or Polygon geometry) containing metadata for raster files in a specified folder: filename, extension, path, resolution (resX/resY), dimensions (n_cols, n_rows), CRS description, number of bands, and data type. Geometry is either the bounding box polygon or centroid point of each raster, reprojected to a user-specified CRS.

name: Load raster files by location
desc: The script loads raster files (e.g., GeoTIFFs) that spatially intersect the geometries of an input vector layer. It scans a user-specified folder (optionally including subfolders) for files matching a given format (default '.tif'), reads each raster’s geotransform and projection via GDAL, constructs its bounding polygon, reprojects that polygon to match the vector layer’s CRS, and tests intersection with each feature in the vector layer. Rasters intersecting at least one feature are selected. Optionally, selected rasters are copied to a destination folder. Finally, all selected rasters are loaded as QgsRasterLayer instances into the QGIS project. No classification, time-series analysis, band math, or modeling is performed — only spatial selection and loading based on geometry overlap. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; the script is purely file-system and geometry-driven, agnostic to content.

name: Mosaic raster images
desc: The script creates a raster mosaic by combining two or more input GeoTIFF rasters into a single seamless output GeoTIFF. It supports user-defined spatial resolution, null value handling, clipping to a vector polygon frame, and multiple overlap resolution strategies (first, average, median, min, max) applied per-pixel in overlapping regions. Interpolation methods (nearest neighbor, bilinear, bicubic) are used during resampling. Input rasters must share the same CRS, number of bands, data type (GDT), and NoData value. The workflow includes geometry extraction from each raster’s geotransform, union/intersection/difference operations to partition coverage areas by combinatorial overlap classes, pixel-wise coordinate mapping, and band-wise interpolation/aggregation. Output is a georeferenced GeoTIFF with user-specified projection, extent (either union of inputs or clipped to frame), resolution, and NoData value. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or spectral bands are referenced — it is a generic GDAL/QGIS-based raster mosaicking tool operating on local file paths.

name: Rescale raster to 8 bits
desc: The script rescales input raster pixel values—regardless of original radiometric resolution (e.g., 16-bit, 8-bit, or float)—to the exact 0–255 range using one of three linear stretch methods: (1) global min/max, (2) 2nd–98th percentile quantiles, or (3) mean ± 2×stdDev. It supports per-band or global rescaling, optional null-pixel handling (mapping NoData to 0), and outputs a GeoTIFF with GDT_Byte data type, preserved geotransform, projection, and (if enabled) NoData value set to 0. The operation is purely radiometric and pixel-wise; no spatial filtering, classification, compositing, or temporal aggregation is performed. Input raster path is read via GDAL; output is written using GDAL’s GTiff driver. No study area, time range, satellite metadata, or spectral analysis is involved—the script is a generic raster bit-depth reduction utility for QGIS Processing Toolbox.

name: Convert RGB to HSV components
desc: The script converts a 3-band (RGB) or 4-band (RGBA) input raster into three separate GeoTIFF outputs: Hue (H), Saturation (S), and Value (V) rasters, preserving georeferencing (projection and geotransform). It reads the raster using GDAL, stacks the first three bands as an RGB array, applies a custom `rgb2hsv` transformation function (imported from `lftools.geocapt.dip`), and writes each HSV component as a single-band float32 GeoTIFF. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification logic is involved — it is a pixel-wise color space transformation applied to any georeferenced RGB raster provided by the user.

name: Perform supervised raster classification
desc: The script performs pixel-wise supervised classification of a multi-band raster image using user-provided polygon training samples and one of four statistical methods: Parallelepiped, Ellipsoid, Euclidean Distance, or Mahalanobis Distance. It reads the input raster (via GDAL), extracts spectral values from each training polygon per band, computes class statistics (mean, standard deviation, covariance matrix), and assigns each pixel to the class with highest likelihood or minimum distance — prioritizing classes by descending trace of covariance matrix for Parallelepiped/Ellipsoid. Outputs a classified GeoTIFF raster where pixel values correspond to integer class IDs from the user-specified 'Class Field'. No specific study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is embedded in the code; it is a generic, local-file-based QGIS Processing algorithm operating on arbitrary raster and vector inputs provided by the user.

name: Calculate DEM difference
desc: The script computes the pixel-wise arithmetic difference between two input Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), supporting coordinate transformation when CRSs differ, resampling (nearest/bilinear/bicubic) during interpolation, and optional sign inversion. It outputs a GeoTIFF raster where each pixel value equals (Minuend − Subtrahend) or (Subtrahend − Minuend) depending on the selected reference grid, with NoData handling (-9999 default) and progress feedback. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification is involved — it is a generic raster algebra tool operating on user-provided local raster files loaded via QGIS Processing interface.

name: Download digital elevation model
desc: The script downloads and clips Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for a user-defined extent in QGIS, supporting five global/regional datasets (SRTM, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, FABDEM, ANADEM, GMTED2010); it automatically identifies required tiles, fetches them from public repositories (Hugging Face or AWS S3), decompresses SRTM .hgt.gz files, merges overlapping tiles into a virtual mosaic (VRT), and clips the result precisely to the input extent in WGS84; outputs a single GeoTIFF DEM file with optional styling applied upon load.

name: Apply raster filtering to DEM
desc: The script applies spatial filtering (mean, median, minimum, or maximum convolution kernels of size 3×3 or 5×5) pixel-by-pixel to a single-band input raster (e.g., DEM/DTM/DSM), preserving NoData values and adjusting geotransform to account for edge loss. It outputs a filtered GeoTIFF with reduced dimensions (rows and columns decreased by kernel_size−1), same projection and resolution, and optional automatic loading into QGIS. The script uses GDAL and NumPy for low-level array-based convolution — no GEE API calls, satellite data, or temporal logic are present; it is a local raster processing tool implemented in QGIS Processing Framework (not Google Earth Engine).

name: Generate spot elevations from contours and DEM
desc: The script generates a point layer of spot elevations by sampling a Digital Terrain Model (DTM) raster at the location of local maxima/minima within closed contour polygons. It first identifies closed contour lines (rings), filters out nested contours, then for each remaining contour polygon, it extracts the raster values within the polygon boundary, computes the mean elevation, compares it to the contour's labeled elevation field to classify the feature as a peak (type=1) or depression (type=-1), and places a point at the pixel with the extreme value (max for peaks, min for depressions) inside the polygon. Outputs include a point vector layer with attributes 'elevation' (cota) and 'type' (peak/depression).

name: Trim and extend fracture networks
desc: The script performs topological editing of line vector layers representing fracture or lineament networks. It identifies and removes short isolated fractures (I-I branches), trims dangling line ends (I-C branches) within a user-defined distance, and extends dangling ends to intersect nearby lines within another user-defined distance. The workflow includes splitting lines at intersections, building a node degree graph to classify endpoints (isolated vs. connected), spatial indexing for efficient nearest-neighbor queries, geometry extension using QgsGeometry.extendLine(), intersection detection, and final line reconstruction. Outputs are a cleaned, topologically improved line vector layer with preserved attributes. No satellite imagery, temporal data, or raster processing is involved — this is a pure vector GIS topology repair tool operating on user-provided line features. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial data sources are not specified in the code.

name: Digitise fracture network
desc: The script digitises a fracture network from a user-provided binary raster input by applying morphological skeletonization (either 'lee' thinning or medial axis transform), vectorizing the skeleton into linestrings, simplifying geometries using Douglas-Peucker if specified, splitting lines at intersections to ensure topological consistency, and pruning short isolated branches below a user-defined length threshold. The output is a topologically cleaned line vector layer representing fracture traces with x-node (crossing) intersections resolved into four-segment junctions. The script requires pre-processed binary input — no satellite data processing, thresholding, or temporal analysis is performed within this code; it operates purely on an existing raster layer supplied by the user.

name: Repair fracture network topology
desc: The script repairs common topological errors in digitized fracture (e.g., fault or joint) networks. It merges V-shaped nodes (two-line endpoints meeting at a vertex), extends lines at sharp-angle vertices using a user-defined angle threshold and distance, optionally creates X-nodes (four-way intersections) at such vertices, removes closed loops/circles, and fixes multiple intersections (>4 line endpoints coincident at one location) by iteratively removing the shortest segment(s) associated with the smallest grouped fracture length (using 'Fault No' attribute if present). Input is a vector line layer; outputs are a repaired line layer and optionally an intermediate layer showing multiple-intersection repair steps. No satellite, image, or temporal data is involved — it is a pure vector topology correction tool for GIS digitization workflows.

name: Simplify fracture network geometry
desc: The script simplifies a vector-based fracture (line) network while preserving original geometry and length attributes. It performs topological graph operations using NetworkX to identify and optionally remove dangles (unconnected line endpoints), isolated fractures (I-I branches), and to extract shortest pathways between user-selected or boundary-defined dangles. Simplification reduces each line to its start/end vertices while storing the original length in an 'origLen' field. The extent option clips the network to a user-defined rectangle, and boundary direction (left-right or bottom-top) controls which dangles are preserved during dangle removal. Outputs include a new vector line layer ('Simplified Network') with updated geometry and attribute table containing 'origLen' and all original non-'origLen' fields.

name: Snap fracture network nodes
desc: The script snaps isolated (I) nodes in a vector-based fracture network line layer by creating new short connecting line segments between endpoints that meet spatial (distance), angular (orientation consistency), and topological (node degree: I, V, or Y type) criteria. It first explodes input multilinestrings into simple linestrings, builds a node-degree graph by counting endpoint occurrences, then iteratively searches for candidate connection targets within increasing distance thresholds (controlled by 'Distance to Connect' and 'Number of Distance Iterations'), validates angular alignment between original and candidate segments, and ensures target nodes satisfy the specified 'Snap Node Count' (1=I only, 2=I/V, 3=I/V/Y). Output is a new line layer containing both the original lines and the newly generated snapping connector lines. No remote sensing data, time series, or raster operations are involved — it is purely vector geometric/topological processing on user-provided line features.

name: Simulate 1D fracture flow
desc: The script solves for one-dimensional fluid flow across a user-provided fracture network linestring, using PorePy to construct a meshed discrete fracture network (DFN), apply pressure boundary conditions (low/high pressure), compute pressure distribution, Darcy flux (m/s), and flow azimuth (degrees). It optionally simulates tracer transport over user-defined time steps, outputting time-series concentration values (0–1) per fracture segment. Input requires a line layer with a 'Transmisiv' field (in mD·m); output is a LineString feature class with attributes: ID, Pressure (Pa), Flux (m/s), Azimuth (deg), Tracer (per timestep), StartTime, EndTime. No satellite or remote sensing data is used — input is vector-based geological/fracture geometry. Study area, time range, and geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Plot cumulative fracture frequency
desc: The script computes cumulative fracture frequency along line samples (e.g., scanlines or grid lines) intersecting a fracture network. It uses geometric intersection and network-based shortest-path distance calculation (via NetworkX) to assign distances along each sample line to fracture intersection points. Fracture frequencies can be weighted by user-specified numeric attributes (e.g., aperture, displacement) and grouped by categorical fields (e.g., orientation set). Outputs include interactive Plotly line plots showing cumulative frequency vs. distance, plus a summary table quantifying spatial heterogeneity (Vf) using Kolmogorov–Smirnov–style D+ and D− deviations from uniform distribution. The analysis assumes input vector layers: a 'Line Grid' (sample lines) and a 'Fracture Network' (linestring fractures), both in arbitrary projected coordinate system (no CRS validation or reprojection in code). No remote sensing data is used — all inputs are local vector layers provided by the user; study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not applicable.

name: Measure fracture network tortuosity
desc: The script computes tortuosity of pathways along a user-provided fracture network vector layer by modeling it as a weighted graph (using NetworkX), identifying source and target points via spatial proximity to network vertices, calculating shortest paths (Dijkstra), and deriving two key metrics: (1) Tortuosity Index = straight-line distance between source and target divided by the total length of the shortest path; and (2) Deviation = perpendicular distance of each segment midpoint from the source–target baseline, aggregated cumulatively. Outputs include a line feature sink with attributes 'Value' (cumulative path length), 'Line' (sequential ID), 'Deviation' (per-segment deviation), and 'Tort Index' (global tortuosity ratio). Optionally, it generates an interactive Plotly plot showing cumulative deviation vs. distance and a summary statistics table including CoV, percentiles, and Vf (deviation envelope). Input data are strictly vector-based: a polyline fracture network, and two point layers (sources and targets) linked by a shared 'ID' field — no raster, satellite, or temporal data are used or referenced.

name: Calculate contour grid statistics
desc: The script computes per-sample-no statistical summaries (e.g., mean, min, max, std, quantile, median, mode, kurtosis, skew) across a user-provided list of vector polygon contour grids. It requires all input grids to share the same 'Sample_No_' integer field and identical numeric attribute fields (e.g., elevation, depth, or model output values). For each unique Sample_No_, it aggregates values from corresponding polygons across all grids, computes the selected statistic per attribute, and outputs a new polygon layer where each feature represents one sample ID and contains the computed statistics as attributes. The geometry is inherited from the first input grid. No raster data, satellite imagery, time-series filtering, or spatial interpolation is performed — the operation is purely tabular aggregation over aligned vector contours.

name: Generate contour grid polygons
desc: The script creates a rotated, spaced polygon grid (contour grid) for sampling a fracture network or interpretation boundary. It generates square/rectangular grid cells at user-defined spacing and rotation, then clips each cell’s centroid-based circular buffer (with user-specified radius) against the input fracture linestring or boundary polygon to compute sampled length (fracture trace intersection) and area. Outputs are polygon features with attributes: Sample_No_, Area, Circ (length), Radius, Rotation, Spacing. The grid is constrained optionally to lie within the interpretation boundary. No satellite imagery, time-series, or spectral analysis is involved — it is a vector-based geometric sampling tool operating purely on user-provided vector layers in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Generate parallel line grid for fracture sampling
desc: The script generates a vector layer of equally spaced, parallel line segments oriented at a user-specified rotation angle, clipped to the spatial extent of an input fracture network (linestring) or interpretation boundary (polygon). It computes the bearing of each line segment and retains only those aligned (within rounding tolerance) to the specified rotation. Output is a linestring feature class with integer 'Sample_No_' attribute, intended for geological fracture network sampling. No remote sensing data, time-series, or raster processing is involved — it is purely vector-based geometric construction and clipping using QGIS Processing algorithms ('qgis:creategrid' and 'native:rotatefeatures'). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and sensors are not specified.

name: Identify fracture-enclosed blocks
desc: The script identifies polygonal rock or geological blocks bounded by fracture lines (input as a linestring layer) within user-defined sample areas (input as polygons). It performs topological polygonization of the fracture network using QGIS's 'polygonize' algorithm after extending line endpoints to ensure proper closure. Blocks are intersected with sample polygons (optionally buffered by a 'Radius' field value) to compute per-sample statistics: minimum, mean, maximum, sum, count, and count of non-fully-contained blocks. Outputs include (1) a polygon layer of all identified blocks with FID and area attributes, and (2) an updated or new sample polygon layer with six appended statistical fields. No remote sensing data, time-series, or spectral analysis is involved; the workflow is purely vector-based topological GIS processing in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Extract fracture network branches and nodes
desc: The script extracts topological elements (branches and nodes) from a user-provided vector-based fracture network (linestring) within a specified sample area polygon (or contour grid), optionally constrained by an interpretation boundary polygon. It classifies node types (I, Y, X, U for unknown, E for edge, or numeric error codes) and branch connection types (e.g., 'I - I', 'I - Y', 'X - X') based on intersection degree and spatial containment. Outputs are two vector layers: (1) a line layer ('Branches') with attributes including 'Class' (node-pair topology), 'Connection', 'Weight', 'Sample_No_', and 'Length'; and (2) a point layer ('Nodes') with 'Class' and 'Sample_No_'. Symbology is applied via external QML files ('branches.qml', 'nodes.qml'). All inputs must share the project's CRS. No remote sensing imagery or time-series analysis is performed — the workflow is purely vector topology processing using QGIS native algorithms (e.g., splitwithlines, intersection, buffer, multiparttosingleparts, centroids). Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified.

name: Calculate shortest pathway along fracture network
desc: The script computes the shortest geometrical or weighted cost distance pathway from source points (or polyline vertices) to edges in a fracture network vector layer. It builds a NetworkX graph where nodes are rounded coordinate pairs of line endpoints and source points, and edges are fracture segments with weights equal to their Euclidean length (or field-weighted length if a 'Weight Field' is provided). Source points are snapped to the nearest fracture endpoint using spatial indexing and distance minimization. For polyline sources, optional vertex densification is applied before extraction. The output is a line feature sink containing each fracture segment edge annotated with the minimum distance (or weighted distance) from any source point — i.e., the shortest path length to reach that segment from the nearest source. No raster data, time series, or satellite imagery is involved; input is purely vector-based (line and point/polyline layers), and all operations occur within QGIS Processing using native algorithms ('explodelines', 'densifygeometriesgivenaninterval', 'extractvertices') and NetworkX graph analysis. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Identify railway junction nodes
desc: The script generates a point layer of railway transport nodes ('Nós transporte ferroviário') by extracting start and end vertices of railway line segments, removing duplicates, counting how many segments meet at each vertex (via spatial join summary), classifying nodes based on connection count (1 = 'fim de via' / end-of-line, 2 = 'pseudo-no' / pseudo-node, ≥3 = 'juncao' / junction), and clipping the result to a user-provided polygonal work area. The output is a vector point layer with attribute 'valor_tipo_no_trans_ferrov' encoding node type as string values '4', '3', or '1' respectively.

name: Classify hydrographic nodes
desc: The script generates a vector layer of hydrographic nodes (points) derived from stream centerlines (eixo), classifying each node into one of six types based on topological connectivity (number of incident segments) and spatial overlap with auxiliary layers: '1' = upstream start, '2' = downstream end, '3' = confluence (≥3 connections), '4' = pseudo-node (2 connections, no overlap with barriers/waterfalls/wetlands), '5' = flow variation node (2 connections + overlap with waterfall or wetland), '6' = flow regulation node (2 connections + overlap with barrier). The workflow includes Z-aware geometry orientation, vertex extraction (start/end points), deduplication, spatial joining with input layers (barrier, waterfall, wetland), clipping to the working area, and attribute-driven classification using conditional logic on count and presence fields.

name: Identify road transport nodes

The output is a point layer with attribute ‘valor_tipo_no_trans_rodov’ encoding node type as string values ‘4’, ‘3’, or ‘1’. All operations are purely vector-based; no raster or remote sensing data is used. Input data sources are two local vector layers: a line layer ‘segmentovia’ (road segments) and a polygon layer ‘readetrabalho’ (study area boundary). No time dimension, satellite, sensor, or band information is present.

It refactors the input layer to add a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') and a 'valor_tipo_no_trans_ferrov' field — either a fixed enumerated value selected via UI (e.g., 'Estação Ferroviária') or dynamically populated from an existing string field in the input layer (e.g., 'tipo_no'). The input must be a 3D point layer. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, or classification is performed; it is a metadata-aware vector data export workflow targeting RECART — a Portuguese national cartographic database. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Export road transport node
desc: The script exports point features representing road transport nodes (e.g., intersections, terminals, or access points) from a QGIS vector layer to the 'no_trans_rodov' table in a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART schema). It adds a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') and populates the 'valor_tipo_no_trans_rodov' field either with a user-selected enumerated value (mapped via get_lista_codigos('valorTipoNoTransRodov')) or dynamically using the content of a user-specified string field from the input layer. The workflow consists of two key steps: (1) refactoring the input point layer to add/replace fields using 'qgis:refactorfields', and (2) appending the result to the target PostGIS table 'public.no_trans_rodov' via GDAL's 'importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. Input must be a 3D point vector layer; no raster, satellite, or time-series processing is involved. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Export infrastructure polygon layer
desc: The script exports a user-provided vector polygon layer (intended for 3D polygons representing civil engineering structures) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'obra_arte' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'valor_tipo_obra_arte' (a categorical string value selected from a predefined enumerated list via QGIS Processing UI, mapped using get_lista_codigos('valorTipoObraArte')). The export uses GDAL's 'importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' algorithm with append mode, no overwrite, and geometry column named 'geometria'. The input layer must be a polygon layer; no raster, satellite, or time-series processing occurs. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification, or analysis methods are not involved — this is a pure vector data export and field augmentation workflow.

name: Export pipeline infrastructure data
desc: The script exports vector line features representing oil pipelines, gas pipelines, or chemical substance transport infrastructure from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART) using predefined categorical attribute values. It adds two mandatory attributes—'valor_gasoduto_oleoduto_sub_quimicas' and 'valor_posicao_vertical'—mapped from user-selected enumeration options (retrieved via external utility 'get_lista_codigos'), and timestamps the record with 'inicio_objeto' = current time. The output is a persisted table 'oleoduto_gasoduto_subtancias_quimicas' in the 'public' schema of the target PostgreSQL connection. No remote sensing, image processing, or geospatial analysis is performed—the workflow is purely vector data ETL (Extract-Transform-Load) with field refactoring and PostGIS insertion. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Export point of interest
desc: The script exports vector features (points or polygons) from a QGIS input layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'ponto_interesse' in the 'public' schema, adding two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_tipo_ponto_interesse' (a categorical value selected from a predefined enumerated list via get_lista_codigos('valorTipoPontoInteresse')). It uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'qgis:refactorfields' and 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. The target database connection is user-selected via a configured PostgreSQL provider connection. No remote sensing, image processing, or geospatial analysis is performed — only vector field augmentation and database export. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not involved or specified in the code.

name: Export 3D point elevation data
desc: The script exports 3D point vector features (with Z/elevation values) from a QGIS input layer to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS table named 'ponto_cotado' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp) and 'valor_classifica_las' (a user-selected LAS classification code from a predefined list, e.g., ground, vegetation, building). The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms: 'qgis:refactorfields' to inject metadata fields, then 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections' to append the enriched 3D points to the RECART database. Input must be a 3D point layer; no raster, satellite, or time-series processing occurs. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Export waterfall point data
desc: The script exports a vector point layer representing waterfall features ('queda_de_agua') from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'queda_de_agua'), using an existing configured connection. It first adds a timestamp field 'inicio_objeto' with the current time via 'qgis:refactorfields', then imports the modified layer into PostGIS using 'gdal:importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. The input layer must be 3D point geometry, and the target database is named 'RECART' per the parameter label and help text. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing occurs — it is purely a data export and schema enrichment workflow.

name: Export cable transport route segments
desc: The script exports vector line features representing 'Segmento da via por cabo' (cable transport route segments) from a QGIS input layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'seg_via_cabo' in the 'public' schema. It adds a timestamp field 'inicio_objeto' with the current time using QgsProcessing's refactorfields algorithm, then imports the modified layer into the RECART geodatabase via GDAL's PostGIS import algorithm. The input must be a 2D line vector layer; no remote sensing, classification, or temporal analysis is performed. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code — it is a generic database export tool dependent on user-provided input geometry and preconfigured PostgreSQL connection.

name: Export railway segment attributes
desc: The script exports a user-provided vector line layer (representing railway segments) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'seg_via_ferrea' in the 'public' schema, enriching it with standardized categorical attribute values selected via QGIS Processing enum parameters (e.g., bitola category, line status, vertical position, line type, track type) and a boolean 'eletrific' flag. It adds a timestamp field ('inicio_objeto') with current time and maps input geometry unchanged. The input must be 3D line geometry. No remote sensing or Earth observation data is used; all inputs are local vector layers and user-selected categorical codes sourced from an external utility function 'get_lista_codigos', implying lookup tables stored outside the script (e.g., RECART domain value lists). The target database connection is preconfigured in QGIS as a PostgreSQL provider connection.

name: Export road segment attributes
desc: The script exports vector line features representing road segments to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'public', table 'seg_via_rodov') using a preconfigured connection. It refactors the input line layer by injecting standardized attribute values—derived from QGIS enum parameters mapping to controlled vocabularies (e.g., 'valorEstadoViaRodov', 'valorSentido')—along with computed fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'num_vias_transito' (user-provided integer), and 'pavimentado' (boolean). The input layer must be 3D line geometry. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing is performed; the workflow is purely data structuring and database ingestion. Study area, time range, satellite data, and imagery processing are not involved—this is a GIS data publishing tool for the RECART national cartographic database.

name: Export geodetic signal points
desc: The script exports point features representing geodetic signals (e.g., survey markers, benchmarks) from a QGIS vector layer into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'sinal_geodesico' in the 'public' schema. It appends standardized attribute values — 'valor_local_geodesico', 'valor_ordem', 'valor_tipo_sinal_geodesico', and 'data_revisao' — derived from user-selected enumerations and a string input, along with a timestamp ('inicio_objeto') set to 'now()'. The input layer must be 3D point geometry, and the export relies on an existing PostgreSQL connection configured in QGIS. No remote sensing or Earth observation data is used; all operations are vector-based attribute assignment and database ingestion.

name: Export road boundary geometry
desc: The script exports a user-provided vector line layer (expected to be 3D line geometry) to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database table named 'via_rodov_limite' in the 'public' schema. It adds two fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp, type DateTime) and 'valor_tipo_limite' (a categorical string value selected from a predefined enumeration list 'valorTipoLimite'). The workflow consists of two main steps: (1) refactoring the input layer to inject these new fields using QGIS 'refactorfields', and (2) appending the resulting layer to the target PostGIS table via GDAL's 'importvectorintopostgisdatabaseavailableconnections'. No spatial filtering, reprojection, or geometric transformation is applied beyond what GDAL handles by default (e.g., dimension handling with DIM=1). The study area, time range, satellite data, and remote sensing operations are not involved — this is a pure vector data ingestion workflow for cartographic infrastructure features.

name: Export wetland polygons
desc: The script exports user-provided polygon vector layers representing wetlands to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (RECART) with standardized attribute fields: 'inicio_objeto' (current timestamp), 'valor_zona_humida' (a categorical code mapped from an enumerated UI parameter), and 'mare' (a boolean flag). It performs field refactoring using QGIS's 'refactorfields' algorithm, then appends the result to the 'zona_humida' table in the 'public' schema. The input layer must be a 3D polygon vector layer; no remote sensing or raster processing is performed. All operations are vector-based and database-oriented. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified — the script is purely a metadata-enriched vector export workflow for a national cartographic database (RECART, Portugal).

name: Evaluate predicted depth model
desc: The script evaluates a predicted bathymetric (depth) raster against unseen validation points from a vector layer. It extracts predicted depth values at each point's location (with optional CRS transformation), computes residuals, and calculates accuracy metrics (RMSE, MAE, R², Bias). Outputs include: (1) a text report with metadata and metrics, (2) a scatter plot of true vs. predicted depths with 1:1 line, and (3) a CSV file containing all evaluated point attributes, coordinates, true depth, predicted depth, and error. The workflow uses rasterio to read the predicted raster, pandas for tabular aggregation, scikit-learn for metric computation, and matplotlib for visualization. No satellite data ingestion or preprocessing occurs in this script — it is purely an *evaluation* step operating on pre-generated model output and independent validation points. Study area, time range, satellite sources, and sensor/band information are not present in the code and cannot be inferred.

name: Adapt species occurrence coordinates
desc: The script processes point-based species occurrence records by clipping them to a user-defined influence boundary polygon, removing specified attribute fields (e.g., species name columns), and appending X/Y coordinate fields in the project CRS — producing a cleaned, Maxent-compatible CSV-ready point layer with geographic coordinates explicitly as attributes.

name: Rasterize categorical environmental variable
desc: The script converts a vector polygon layer representing an environmental variable into a raster layer using a specified categorical attribute field. It uses GDAL's rasterize algorithm with user-defined pixel resolution, burns the field values into the raster, sets NoData to 0, and outputs a single-band raster where pixel values correspond to the categorical class identifiers from the input vector's attribute field. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are involved — the input is purely a local vector layer provided by the user in QGIS; all parameters (input layer, field name, resolution, output path) are runtime user inputs with no hardcoded geographic or temporal constraints.

name: Standardize raster environmental variables
desc: The script standardizes a continuous environmental raster variable by clipping it to a polygon boundary layer and resampling it to a user-specified pixel resolution. It uses GDAL's cliprasterbymasklayer algorithm with 'CROP_TO_CUTLINE=True', 'SET_RESOLUTION=True', and matching X/Y_RESOLUTION. The output is a masked, resampled raster file suitable for Maxent species distribution modeling. No reprojection is performed (SOURCE_CRS and TARGET_CRS are both 'ProjectCrs'). Input data sources, time range, study area geometry, satellite/sensor/band information, and classification methods are not specified in the code — only generic QGIS processing parameters are defined.

name: Generate styled density grid
desc: The script computes a point density heatmap by aggregating input point features into a regular or hexagonal grid, counting points per cell (optionally weighted), filtering cells by minimum count, and applying a graduated color ramp style to the resulting polygon layer. It supports rectangle, diamond, and hexagon grid types; unit-aware cell sizing; extent customization; and advanced styling options including invert, number of classes, color ramp mode (e.g., quantile), and outline suppression. The output is a styled vector polygon layer ('Output density heatmap') with attribute 'NUMPOINTS', where styling is applied via a custom 'densityanalysis:graduatedstyle' algorithm — not exported as raster or statistics table. No remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite processing occurs; input is purely vector point geometry. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Rasterize polygon density
desc: The script converts an input polygon vector layer into a raster density heatmap by rasterizing the polygons onto a regular grid. It computes grid cell dimensions based on user-specified measurement units (e.g., meters, feet) and extent, optionally constrained by a maximum image dimension. The core geospatial operation is GDAL's 'rasterize' algorithm with BURN=1, INIT=0, and EXTRA='-add', producing a floating-point raster where pixel values represent the count (or additive sum) of overlapping polygons per cell. No time-series, spectral analysis, classification, or satellite data is involved — it is a pure vector-to-raster conversion for spatial density representation. Input CRS handling includes coordinate transformation of the extent to match the layer CRS. Outputs include a single GeoTIFF raster file ('OUTPUT') representing polygon density.

name: Calculate polygon overlap density
desc: The script computes the spatial density of overlapping polygons in a vector layer by performing a union operation to split intersecting polygons, then aggregating to count how many original polygons contribute to each resulting fragment. It optionally retains a list of unique IDs from the contributing source polygons and filters output fragments to only those with overlap counts greater than or equal to a user-defined threshold. The output is a new polygon layer where each feature represents a non-overlapping geometric fragment annotated with 'NUMPOINTS' (count of overlapping input polygons) and optionally 'ID_LIST' (comma-separated string of source polygon IDs). No raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, or external geospatial datasets are used — the entire workflow operates on the input vector layer only. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Generate point density heatmap
desc: The script computes a kernel density estimation (KDE) heatmap from an input vector point layer, producing a raster density surface that visualizes the spatial concentration of point features (e.g., population centers, infrastructure points, or event locations). It applies configurable kernel shapes (Quartic, Triangular, etc.), radius and pixel size in user-specified measurement units (converted to CRS units), and optional decay for triangular kernels. The output raster is then styled with a pseudocolor ramp (user-selectable from a predefined list), invertible, interpolated (Discrete/Linear/Exact), classified by mode (Continuous/Equal Interval/Quantile), and discretized into a specified number of gradient classes. All parameters—including coordinate reference system handling, extent-based grid dimensioning, and max-image-dimension safety checks—are derived solely from the input vector layer’s geometry and CRS. No time-series, satellite imagery, or external geospatial datasets are involved; the analysis is purely vector-to-raster density transformation.

name: Evaluate segmentation accuracy
desc: The script evaluates semantic segmentation model outputs against ground-truth polygon masks following Brazil's ET-CQDG (Especificação Técnica para a Cartografia Digital e Geoespacial) standards. It processes quadrilateral tile layers (ET-CQDG tiles) with fields 'mi', 'quadricula', and 'fuso_utm'; rasterizes ground-truth polygons per tile using class integer values (0 = Background, nodata = 255); clips and reprojects inferred segmentation rasters to match each tile’s UTM zone; computes per-tile and per-class metrics including Accuracy, IoU, Precision, Recall, and F1-score; and exports structured evaluation reports. Outputs include: (1) per-experiment folders containing ground-truth and predicted GeoTIFFs per tile, (2) CSVs for tile-level, MI-level, and overall metrics, and (3) consolidated CSVs across all experiments — 'consolidated_all_metrics.csv', 'per_class_metrics.csv', 'consolidated_tile_metrics.csv', and 'consolidated_mi_metrics.csv'. The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms (e.g., reprojection, clip, dissolve, join by location) and rasterio-based parallel tile processing via ThreadPoolExecutor. No satellite imagery or time-series analysis is performed — inputs are static vector masks and precomputed segmentation rasters.

name: Generalize landing strip polygons
desc: The script processes polygon layers representing landing strips and generalizes them into centerlines when their area or width falls below user-defined cartographic thresholds (scaled by map scale). It computes the pole of inacessibility to estimate width, filters polygons based on scaled area and half-width criteria, applies Voronoi skeletonization and simplification, trims endpoints, extends lines to match bounding box height, intersects with original geometry, and outputs resulting centerlines while deleting the original polygons from the input layer.

name: Split polygons by grid subdivision
desc: The script splits input polygon features into a regular grid of smaller polygons based on a user-selected factor (1×1, 2×2, 3×3, 4×4, or 5×5 subdivisions), applies an overlap buffer to each grid cell, intersects buffered cells with the original dissolved input geometry, and assigns a sequential priority integer attribute to non-empty intersected output polygons. The workflow uses QGIS native vector geometry operations (bounding box extraction, rectangle creation, buffering, spatial indexing, intersection, unary union) — no raster, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is performed. All operations are purely geometric and topological; no study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are referenced or implied in the code.

name: Load raster layer from PostgreSQL server
desc: The script loads a raster layer stored in a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database with raster support (via the postgresraster provider) by connecting to a remote server using provided credentials, querying the raster_columns metadata table to retrieve schema, table, and raster column names, constructing a QgsDataSourceUri for the raster, and creating a QgsRasterLayer instance. The layer is then added to the QGIS project and optionally loaded into the map canvas. Inputs include server IP, port, database name, table name, user, and password; output is a raster layer ID registered in the QGIS project.

name: Merge shapefile layers into GeoPackage
desc: The script merges multiple zipped shapefiles into a single GeoPackage file, grouping layers by case-insensitive name and consolidating them using QGIS native merge functionality; it reprojects all layers to a user-specified CRS (default EPSG:4674) and drops fields named 'layer', 'path', 'ID', or 'id'. The output is a single .gpkg file containing one layer per unique shapefile basename, with all original attributes preserved (except dropped fields). No remote sensing, raster, or time-series processing occurs — the script operates purely on local vector file I/O and QGIS processing algorithms. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis methods are not involved or specified.

name: Generate systematic grid frames
desc: The script generates a systematic grid of polygonal map frames (e.g., INOM/MI-indexed cartographic frames) constrained to the spatial extent of an input vector or raster layer. It derives the grid geometry from the input layer’s bounding extent (or buffered geometry for point/line layers), applies scale-dependent subdivision logic (e.g., 2×2 for 1:50k, 4×4 for 1:100k, 12×8 for 1:250k), and optionally filters output frames to retain only those intersecting the original input geometry (especially critical for raster inputs, where only frames overlapping the raster extent are kept). The output is a vector layer of polygons with attributes 'inom' (map sheet identifier) and 'mi' (map index), in the same CRS as the input. No remote sensing analysis, time-series processing, or classification is performed — it is purely a cartographic tiling/grid generation algorithm.

name: Export vector layer to memory
desc: The script exports a user-provided vector layer to a QGIS memory layer with optional styling. It creates a new QgsVectorLayer of the same geometry type and CRS as the input layer, imports a QML style (if provided), copies all fields and features from the input layer, registers the resulting layer in the processing context's temporary layer store, and adds it to the load-on-completion list for display in QGIS. No geospatial analysis, remote sensing, classification, or time-series operations are performed; the script is purely a QGIS processing utility for model chaining. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations beyond feature copying are not specified.

name: Raise geospatial validation flags
desc: The script transfers flag annotations (text-based validation or quality control messages) from an input vector layer to a target PostgreSQL vector layer, preserving geometry and attribute values. It reads features from the input layer, transforms coordinates if needed using a specified CRS, maps them to a destination PostGIS table schema/name/geometry column, and writes each feature with its original flag text value into the output layer's designated flag text field. The process occurs within a QGIS Processing Algorithm context, using DsgTools' FeatureHandler and LayerHandler for geometry conversion and database parameter handling. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations are involved; it is purely a vector attribute and geometry transfer workflow for cartographic quality assurance. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and visualization/export beyond the PostGIS layer are not specified.

name: Package raster files for BDGEx
desc: The script packages input GeoTIFF raster files into BDGEx-compliant format: (1) groups rasters by seamline geometry derived from associated shapefiles (_SEAMLINES_SHAPE and _TILE_SHAPE), (2) builds VRTs from grouped rasters, (3) clips rasters to seamline polygons (splitting large rasters >2 GB into tiled sub-geometries), (4) exports clipped rasters in JPEG-compressed GeoTIFF format with specific GDAL options (TILED=TRUE, PHOTOMETRIC=YCbCr for multiband), and (5) generates metadata XML files per clipped raster using a user-provided template and feature attributes (e.g., 'acquisitio', 'source', 'productTyp', '_filename') from the seamline shapefile. Outputs are written to a user-specified folder preserving relative input directory structure. The process is sensor-aware ('Imagens BECA' or 'Imagens MAXAR') for XML metadata tagging.

name: Prepare raster seamlines for packaging
desc: The script unzips input ZIP archives containing geospatial raster delivery packages, locates DeliveryMetadata.xml files to extract sensor vehicle, acquisition time, catalog identifier, and relative directory metadata, then identifies corresponding *_PRODUCT_SHAPE.shp files and generates new *_SEAMLINES_SHAPE.shp files. Each output shapefile retains original geometry and attributes, and appends five new fields: 'sensorVeh', 'acquisitio', 'catIdent', 'relDir', and '_filename' — the last constructed from metadata and a regex-modified bandInfo field (e.g., stripping 'T.*' from timestamps, removing hyphens/spaces). The process is designed for BDGEx (Brazilian Department of Geosciences and Strategic Resources) raster packaging workflows; no classification, modeling, or image analysis is performed — only metadata-driven vector file transformation and renaming. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code — all inputs are file-system–based and agnostic to location or temporal bounds.

name: Identify line layer dangles
desc: The script identifies geometric dangle features (unconnected line endpoints) in a user-provided vector line layer. It builds an endpoint dictionary by extracting boundaries of input lines, then filters candidate dangles using spatial relationships with optional filter layers (line or polygon), the input layer itself, and an optional geographic boundary layer for output clipping. Key methods include boundary extraction, spatial indexing, buffer-based intersection testing, and concurrent multi-threaded point-in-buffer evaluation. The output is a point-based flag layer containing geometries of detected dangles, each labeled with a descriptive message referencing the input layer name. No raster data, time series, satellite imagery, or classification models are involved; the analysis is purely vector topological and geometric. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Rasterize channel cross-sections
desc: The script rasterizes 1D channel networks into 2D elevation rasters using geometric cross-section definitions.
