It reads vector layers representing channels (lines) and cross-section locations (points), constructs triangulated 3D geometries (points, triangles, outlines) from channel centerlines and cross-sectional width/height tables, generates temporary UGRID mesh layers, rasterizes them at a specified pixel size (or derived from input DEM), clips outputs to channel outlines, and merges all channel rasters—optionally with a background DEM—using a 'deepen-only' (min-aggregation) approach. Outputs include a final merged raster layer representing the 2D topographic representation of channels (e.g., for hydrodynamic modeling), plus optional debug outputs: point features (channel vertices), polygon features (triangles), and polygon features (channel outlines). The workflow is designed for Rana schematisations and supports open rectangle, tabulated trapezium, tabulated rectangle, and YZ cross-section types; it performs geometric validation (e.g., non-intersecting sides, increasing widths with height) and reports errors/warnings per channel ID. No satellite or time-series data is involved; inputs are static vector and raster GIS layers.

name: Setup TUFLOW hydrodynamic project
desc: The script sets up a TUFLOW Catch (hydrodynamic) modeling project by generating folder structures, initializing configuration files (e.g., tfsettings.json), creating domain check GIS layers, generating empty model input files (e.g., .mif, .asc, .csv), and populating control file templates (e.g., .tcf). It dynamically loads existing project settings from 'tfsettings.json' when a project folder is selected, auto-fills executable paths, CRS, GIS format, and output format configurations, and optionally applies QGIS styling to domain check layers using a predefined QML file.

name: Create geospatial empty files
desc: The script creates empty geospatial datasets (e.g., vector layers with schema but no features) for predefined 'empty types' (e.g., TGC, TBC, BC, etc.) within a TUFLOW project structure. It dynamically populates available empty types based on the project folder contents, supports export to GeoPackage (separate, grouped, or all-to-one), or Kart repository, and loads generated layers into QGIS. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing is performed — it is purely a GIS scaffolding/initialization utility for hydrodynamic modeling setup.

name: Assign elevation values to polygon vertices
desc: The script processes input polygon vector layers and a digital elevation model (DEM) raster layer to generate two outputs: (1) a point layer containing densified or original polygon vertices with Z-elevation values sampled from the raster, and (2) a polygon layer with a 'Shape_Width' field set to -1 to indicate TUFLOW-compatible TIN polygon formatting. It uses QGIS native algorithms — Densify by Interval (optional), Extract Vertices, Delete Duplicate Geometries, Raster Sampling, Field Calculator (to copy sampled elevations into a 'Z' field), and Retain Fields — ensuring topologically clean, elevation-annotated vertices snapped to the source polygons for TIN generation.

name: Convert TMO time-series points
desc: The script converts a binary TMO (TUFLOW Model Output) file into a vector point layer, where each point represents a model output location with attributes 'Value' (real-valued result, e.g., water level or velocity magnitude) and 'Domain' (integer domain index). It reads the TMO file using a custom `TMO` class, extracts data for a user-selected time step (e.g., 'max', 'min', or a specific numeric time), iterates over all model points, and writes them as OGR features with WKB point geometry. The output is a vector file (e.g., GeoPackage) containing spatialized time-slice values; no raster, classification, satellite data, or temporal aggregation is performed — only direct spatialization of precomputed 1D time-series per point. Study area, coordinate reference system, time units, and physical variable type are not specified in the code and are fully determined by the external TMO file.

name: Generate LiDAR-derived terrain and density rasters
desc: The script processes airborne LiDAR point cloud data (LAS/LAZ format) to generate four core raster products: (1) a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN)-based digital elevation model (DEM), (2) an Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)-interpolated surface, (3) ground point density (GPD) raster, and (4) low vegetation density (LVD) raster. It first optionally classifies unclassified input point clouds using LAStools, converts LAZ to LAS if needed, then applies WhiteboxTools algorithms (LidarTINGridding, LidarIdwInterpolation, LidarPointDensity with class exclusions) to compute surfaces and densities at a user-defined cell size. All outputs are resampled to the target resolution and reprojected to the specified CRS before being loaded into QGIS as named layers (e.g., 'TLI', 'IDW', 'Ground Point Density').

name: Generate digital feature model
desc: The script processes airborne LiDAR point cloud data (LAS/LAZ format) to generate a Digital Feature Model (DFM), an archaeology-specific elevation model that integrates ground surface and built structures (e.g., buildings, walls). Key workflow steps include: (1) optional classification of unclassified LAS/LAZ input using an external tool ('ToClassLas'); (2) generation of base elevation products (DEM, Ground Point Density 'GPD', Low Vegetation Density 'LVD', IDW, TIN) via 'basedata'; (3) computation of a DFM confidence map using the DEM, GPD, and LVD layers; and (4) hybrid interpolation combining the confidence map with TLI (TIN-based Linear Interpolation) and IDW to produce the final DFM raster. Outputs include the DFM raster ('DFM'), optionally loaded into QGIS as a layer named with a user-defined prefix. The script relies entirely on local LiDAR files — no satellite, aerial imagery, or time-series data is used. Study area, time range, coordinate reference system (CRS), and cell size are user-provided parameters; no default or hardcoded location, date, or CRS is present in the code. All geospatial operations are performed via QGIS Processing algorithms from the Open LiDAR Toolbox (e.g., 'DFM confidence map', 'Hybrid interpolation'), which internally leverage LASTools, Whitebox Tools, GDAL, GRASS GIS, and QGIS core tools. No satellite/sensor/band information is present — input is exclusively point cloud data.

name: Generate DFM and visualizations from LiDAR point cloud
desc: The script processes raw or pre-classified LAS/LAZ LiDAR point cloud data to generate a high-resolution Digital Feature Model (DFM) using hybrid interpolation (combining TIN-based DFM and IDW with a confidence map), then produces multiple topographic visualizations including Hillshade, Openness, Sky View Factor (SVF), Visual Assessment Technique (VAT), and DME (Depth of Multi-scale Edge). It also outputs classified LAS/LAZ, Ground Point Density (GPD), Low Vegetation Density (LVD), and a Confidence Map (CFM) as intermediate or optional products.

name: Generate archaeological terrain visualisations
desc: The script takes a digital feature model (DFM) or DEM as input and generates five archaeologically significant terrain visualisations: Sky-View Factor (SVF), Visual Assessment Technique (VAT) via RVT Blender, Openness (OPN), Difference-from-Mean Elevation (DfME), and Hillshade (HS). Each output is saved as a temporary GeoTIFF, styled where applicable (e.g., DfME uses a predefined QML style), and loaded into the QGIS project with a user-defined prefix. The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms interfacing with Relief Visualization Toolbox (RVT) and WhiteboxTools (wbt:DiffFromMeanElev), along with native QGIS hillshading.

name: Calculate watershed elongation index
desc: The script calculates the morphometric elongation index (Re) for hydrographic watersheds by computing the ratio of equivalent diameter (2√(Area/π)) to the 3D Euclidean distance between the highest and lowest elevation points within each watershed polygon. It requires two user-provided vector layers: (1) watershed polygons with an area field (e.g., 'Shape_Area'), and (2) point features with X, Y, and Z (elevation) coordinates — automatically detected from common field name variants (e.g., 'X','Y','Z' or 'POINT_X','POINT_Y','elevation'). The workflow includes spatial containment testing (using `geometry.contains()` and `intersects()`), extremum point selection (max/min Z, with tie-breaking by X-coordinate), 3D distance calculation, classification into 8 Schumm (1956)-based morphological categories (e.g., 'Muy alargada', 'Ensanchada', 'Rodeando el desagüe'), and attribution of results to a new output layer. Outputs include: (a) a vector layer (Shapefile or GeoPackage) enriched with fields such as VALOR_ELON, CLASIF_ELON, DIST_MAX, MINPOINT_X/Y/Z, MAXPOINT_X/Y/Z, DIAMETRO_EQ, and NUM_PUNTOS; (b) categorized symbology applied in QGIS based on CLASIF_ELON; (c) comprehensive statistics (mean, median, std, min/max indices, area totals, classification frequencies); and (d) an interactive HTML report with Plotly bar/circle charts, tabular watershed details, classification legend, and automated geomorphic interpretation — all generated in the system's temp directory and opened in the default web browser. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or satellite data is used; all inputs are local vector layers. The script is explicitly developed for UTPL (Universidad Técnica Particular de Loja) and references Ecuadorian academic context but does not constrain input data geographically.

name: Convert layout items to map bounds
desc: The script converts the bounding boxes and geometries of QGIS layout items (QgsLayoutItemMap, QgsLayoutItemShape, QgsLayoutItemPicture, QgsLayoutItemLabel) from layout scene coordinates into real-world map coordinates using linear transformation relative to a reference QgsLayoutItemMap. It constructs a memory vector layer of polygon features representing the spatial extent of each processed layout item in the project's CRS. The output is a QGIS vector layer named 'Layout_Bounds' added to the current project, styled with an external QML file (layoutItemsStyle.qml), containing one polygon per supported layout item — including the reference map’s full extent and transformed bounding rectangles or polygons for other items.

name: Place hydrographic element border
desc: The script computes the boundary segments of hydrographic elements (e.g., rivers, lakes) from a polygon layer, identifies which of those segments spatially coincide with water body boundaries (from a separate 'massa d'água' polygon layer), filters segments by specific feature types (rocha em agua → tipo 8, recife contiguo/afastado → tipo 18/19), maps them to new symbol codes (1 or 2), and inserts the resulting line geometries into an editing layer ('edicao_borda_elemento_hidrografico_l'). It uses QGIS native and DSGTools processing algorithms — including polygons-to-lines, explode lines, spatial join by location (with 'within' and 'contains' predicates), and geometry merging — but no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or Earth observation data. All inputs are local vector layers with fixed default names (e.g., 'elemnat_elemento_hidrografico_a', 'cobter_massa_dagua_a'), indicating a Brazilian cartographic production workflow; no study area extent, temporal scope, satellite data, or raster operations are present.

name: Place master contour labels
desc: The script places cartographic labels for master (index) contour lines in Brazilian Army topographic mapping workflows. It identifies master contours (e.g., every 10th, 25th, or 50th meter depending on scale), extracts QGIS-rendered label bounding polygons from map layers within geographic boundaries, buffers interpolated midpoints of clipped master contour segments, and selects contour line fragments that intersect those small buffers to serve as candidate symbol placements. It then populates a dedicated vector layer (edicao_simb_cota_mestra_l) with these geometry fragments and their elevation values (cota), while clearing the 'texto_edicao' field on the original contour layer for master contours. The workflow is fully vector-based, uses QGIS native and DSGTools processing algorithms, and operates on pre-existing local vector layers — no raster or remote sensing data is loaded, processed, or exported.

name: Validate cartographic grid alignment
desc: The script validates the geometric and attribute correctness of a user-provided cartographic grid (line layer) and grid numbering points (point layer) against a reference grid generated from a frame polygon and selected map scale (e.g., 1:5,000–1:250,000). It computes grid errors via symmetrical difference between reference and input grids, and identifies three types of point errors — missing points (present in reference but absent in input), incorrect points (mismatched 'numero' or 'direcao' attributes within tolerance), and extra points (present in input but not matched to any reference point within tolerance). Outputs are two error layers: a line layer of grid discrepancies labeled 'erro_grid', and a point layer of validation failures labeled 'ponto_faltante', 'ponto_incorreto', or 'ponto_extra', each retaining relevant attributes ('numero', 'direcao').

name: Classify land cover classes
desc: The script performs supervised classification of a multiband raster image (e.g., Sentinel-2) using Random Forest machine learning trained on user-provided vector polygons with class labels (e.g., 'LABEL' field). It computes image statistics, trains an OTB RandomForest classifier (1000 trees, depth 10, min samples 10), and applies it to generate a 12-class integer raster output where each pixel is assigned one of the following thematic classes: 1-construction, 2-vialidad (roads), 3-vegetation, 4-water body, 5-bare soil, 6-crop, 7-low vegetation, 8-shadow, 9-clouds, 11-medium vegetation, 12-high vegetation. The output includes a classified raster file and automatic QML styling for visualization in QGIS.

name: Preprocess wildfire exposure elements
desc: The script preprocesses geospatial inputs for wildfire risk analysis, specifically generating categorized and spatially filtered shapefiles for Points of Interest (POI) and roads based on user-defined attribute tables, rasterizing land cover (from either Corine-like raster or vector), deriving fuel model codes by joining vegetation classes with an Excel lookup table, computing urban-wildland interface zones using vegetation codes flagged as urban in the Excel table, and saving all outputs (POI layers, road layers, fuel model raster, and urban interface raster) to a local Downloads\Layer_processed directory. The workflow relies entirely on local QGIS layers (DEM, land cover raster/vector, POI/roads shapefiles) and an Excel file mapping vegetation classes to fuel models; no Earth Engine server-side computation is performed—the script is a QGIS Processing algorithm wrapper that uses GDAL, NumPy, and QGIS processing tools. Study area, time range, satellite data, and cloud masking are not involved—this is a desktop GIS preprocessing step, not a remote sensing analysis.

name: Model wildfire hazard intensity
desc: The script models wildfire hazard by combining susceptibility (derived from DEM-derived topography, land cover/vegetation, historical fire locations, and optional user-provided raster features) with fuel type (mapped from vegetation classes using an Excel lookup table). It computes susceptibility via Random Forest classification trained on burned/unburned pixels, classifies susceptibility into three quantile-based classes, aggregates vegetation into fuel types, then combines them via a hazard matrix (2×6 and 2×12 configurations) to produce hazard maps. Finally, it estimates annual fire probability by scaling the 12-class hazard map with historical fire density over N years. Outputs are five GeoTIFFs saved to ~/Downloads/Hazard_output: susceptibility (continuous), susceptibility_classes (1–3), fuel_type, hazard (6-class), hazard_12cl (12-class), and probabilities (annualized). Input data sources are local files (DEM, land cover rasters/shapes, fire polygons, roads, optional rasters); no GEE assets or satellite imagery are used — all processing occurs locally in QGIS using GDAL, NumPy, and scikit-learn. Study area is defined by user-provided mask or inferred from layer names (e.g., 'dem', 'corine', 'fire'); time range is defined only by the user-input NFIRES parameter (default 15 years) applied to historical fire data, but no temporal filtering or date metadata is parsed from inputs.

name: Evaluate wildfire risk exposure
desc: The script evaluates wildfire risk by integrating hazard (wildfire hazard map), exposure (POIs, roads, vegetation, population, urban interface), and vulnerability (element-specific vulnerability coefficients from input tables) to compute potential damage degree (PDD) per exposed element and a total classified risk map. Key methods include: (1) reprojection and clipping of all inputs to match the hazard raster’s CRS and extent; (2) max-sliding-window filtering (3×3) applied to hazard, fuel type, and probability rasters to capture local neighborhood effects; (3) raster–vector overlay for POIs (point-based) and roads (linear/polygon-based) to derive spatial exposure masks; (4) element-specific risk evaluation using vulnerability vectors (V1–V4) and exposure values (E) from user-provided matrix tables; (5) summation and classification of total potential damage; (6) optional population risk scaling (if 'Rescale' selected) and urban interface risk masking. Outputs include: a merged shapefile of POIs with 'Damage' and 'Risk' attributes; per-element damage/risk rasters (e.g., 'hospitals_damage', 'primary_roads_risk'); a total damage map ('total_damage_map'); a classified total risk map ('total_risk_map'); optional population risk ('POP') and urban interface risk ('URB_risk'). Study area is implicitly Albania (from path comment: 'assets_albania'), but no explicit geometry or AOI definition is enforced — mask is optional. Data sources are entirely user-provided local files (no GEE asset IDs, no satellite imagery loading); no time range is used or referenced.

name: Calculate water table depth
desc: The script calculates the depth to the water table (i.e., vertical distance from ground surface to groundwater level) by subtracting a water table elevation raster from a digital terrain model (DTM) raster. It performs spatial alignment (clipping and resampling to common extent, CRS, and cell size), raster arithmetic using QgsRasterCalculator, and outputs the result as an ASCII (.asc) grid with user-specified precision. Input rasters must be co-registered or are reprojected/clipped via GDAL translate; the output is a continuous-depth raster where positive values indicate depth below surface (e.g., 2.5 m), and negative values indicate perched or surface water conditions.

name: Create irrigation district database
desc: The script creates a SQLite/GeoPackage database for the IdrAgra water demand simulation model. It populates the database with sample parameter tables (crop types, irrigation methods, soil types, soil profiles, soil uses) and optional geospatial and time-series data (weather stations, nodes, links, soil maps, use maps, irrigation maps, distribution maps, control points, meteorological time series, and discharge time series). All data are loaded from local CSV and parameter files bundled in the plugin’s 'sample/' subdirectory. The script does not access or process any remote sensing imagery, GEE assets, or online Earth observation data — it is a local database initialization tool for a QGIS plugin. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis operations (e.g., masking, classification, NDVI) are performed in this script.

name: Classify hydrologic soil groups
desc: The script creates a raster map of Hydrologic Soil Groups (HSG) — classified as A (1), B (2), C (3), or D (4) — by integrating soil property data (soil ID, maximum depth, minimum saturated hydraulic conductivity at 0–0.5 m, 0–0.6 m, and 0–1.0 m depths) with spatial rasters: a soil distribution map (thematic), digital elevation model (DEM), and water table elevation map. It first reclassifies the soil map using lookup tables derived from the source table to generate per-pixel max depth and min Ksat rasters; then computes water table depth as elevation minus water table elevation; finally applies the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) HSG classification logic from the National Engineering Handbook (Mockus et al., 2009), which conditions group assignment on combinations of soil depth, water table depth, and hydraulic conductivity thresholds — outputting a single-band integer raster (values 1–4, nodata = -9) in ASCII Grid or GDAL-compatible format.

name: Extract elevation and slope from DTM
desc: The algorithm extracts elevation values at weather station points and mean slope values within crop field polygons using a digital terrain model (DTM) raster. It supports conditional filling (only null fields) and applies a tangent-of-radians transformation to slope values (degrees → tan(slope)). Inputs are a polygon layer (crop fields), a point layer (weather stations), and a DTM raster; outputs are in-place attribute updates to existing fields 'slope' and 'alt' in the respective layers, returning the total count of edited features.

name: Aggregate irrigation water demand variables
desc: The script calculates zonal statistics (e.g., mean, sum, min, max) of IdrAgra-simulated hydrological variables (e.g., caprise, evap, precip) over user-defined vector aggregation areas (e.g., irrigation units or watersheds). It parses an IdrAgra parameter file (*.txt) to locate output raster files (ASCII .asc format), extracts timestamps from filenames (either monthly or step-based), performs zonal statistics using QGIS’s native:zonalstatisticsfb algorithm, and outputs a vector table with fields: timestamp (date), wsid (aggregation ID), recval (aggregated value), and count (number of valid pixels). The study area, satellite data, and geospatial extent are not specified — inputs are local file paths and user-provided vector layers; no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, image collections, or remote sensing data ingestion occur in this script. This is a QGIS Processing algorithm, not a GEE script.

name: Rasterize domain map
desc: The script creates a binary raster domain map (value = 1 inside the domain, 0 outside) by combining multiple input raster layers (e.g., soiluse, irr_eff, irr_meth, Meteo_*) — excluding time-dependent or meteo matrix rasters — using a multiplicative Boolean formula ('raster0@1' * 'raster1@1' * ... * 0 + 1) within a user-specified extent and cell size. It then exports the result as an ASCII (.asc) raster file. The algorithm operates entirely on pre-existing local raster layers provided by the user via QGIS Processing interface; no remote sensing data ingestion, time-series analysis, cloud masking, or classification is performed. All inputs are assumed to be co-registered rasters covering the same geographic domain, and the output represents the spatial footprint (intersection envelope) of valid non-excluded rasters, resampled to the specified resolution and extent. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor information are not involved — this is a pure GIS raster algebra and export workflow.

name: Rasterize vector map area
desc: The script converts a user-provided polygon vector layer (e.g., irrigation district boundary or model domain) into a raster grid by burning a specified numeric field value into each pixel. It uses GDAL’s rasterize algorithm with user-defined extent, square cell size, and nodata value (-9), then saves the result as an ASCII (.asc) raster file via a custom QGIS processing algorithm ('IdragraSaveAscii'). The output is a georeferenced raster representing spatial domain discretization for the IdrAgra irrigation water demand model.

name: Rasterize soil table fields
desc: The script rasterizes numeric fields from a tabular dataset (e.g., soil properties) by spatially distributing their values across polygon features in a vector map (e.g., soil units or land parcels), using a reference raster’s georeferencing parameters (origin, cell size, extent). It performs a table-vector join on matching ID fields, then executes GDAL rasterization for each numeric field (excluding string and 'fid' fields), exporting each as an ASCII (.asc) raster file in the specified output folder. The workflow is designed for generating spatially explicit raster layers of agronomic or pedological attributes from IdrAgra database tables.

name: Rasterize time-series irrigation data
desc: The script converts a vector layer containing polygons with temporal (datetime) and numeric attribute fields into a series of time-stamped raster maps — one per specified year — using GDAL rasterization. It selects features by year (via SQL-like datetime field filtering), writes year-specific subsets to temporary GeoPackage files, then burns the numeric data field values into rasters aligned to a user-defined extent and cell size. Outputs are ASCII (.asc) raster files named with a base name and year suffix (e.g., 'output_2000.asc'), each representing spatially distributed values (e.g., water demand, crop ID, or irrigation volume) for that year.

name: Aggregate irrigation water demand variables
desc: The script creates a time series of aggregated statistics (e.g., mean, sum) for a selected hydrological or agronomic variable (e.g., irrigation demand, evapotranspiration) from IdrAgra model output files, using user-defined vector aggregation zones (e.g., irrigation districts or water user associations). It parses the IdrAgra parameter file (*.txt) to extract simulation metadata (start/end dates, monthly flag, input/output paths), reads gridded domain and meteo data (e.g., *.asc, *.dat files), performs zonal aggregation via an internal 'IdragraGroupStats' algorithm, and outputs a vector table with fields: 'timestamp' (daily or monthly date), 'wsid' (water source/zone ID), and 'recval' (aggregated value). The time series is constructed by distributing values across days/months based on IdrAgra’s timestep logic (e.g., uniform distribution between consecutive timestamps), using cell size from the domain.asc raster for unit conversion (e.g., mm → m³). No satellite or remote sensing data is used — inputs are strictly model-derived ASCII grids and tabular meteo files. Study area, coordinate system, and exact spatial extent are not specified in the code.

name: Conditional vector intersection
desc: The script performs a spatial intersection between two vector layers (source and overlay), optionally filtered by user-defined attribute expressions and comparison operators. It supports single or dual conditional logic (e.g., 'source_field = overlay_field AND source_field2 > overlay_field2') to determine whether an intersection is retained. Features can be ordered (by expression) and intersected only once (first match) or multiple times. Output is a new vector layer containing intersected geometries and merged attributes — with optional prefixing and field conflict resolution — preserving all source fields and selected/filtered overlay fields. The algorithm handles on-the-fly reprojection, spatial indexing for performance, and self-intersection (when source and overlay layers are identical, excluding self-matches). No raster, time-series, or satellite data is involved; it is purely vector-based GIS processing within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Count features by geometric category
desc: This algorithm counts features from an overlay vector layer within or related to features of a source vector layer, grouped by a user-defined category expression (e.g., field or expression result) on the overlay layer. It supports configurable geometric predicates (e.g., 'within', 'intersects', 'disjoint'), logical combination (AND/OR), single- vs. multiple-counting per overlay feature, and three output structures: (1) one output feature per source–category pair (with fields for category name and count), (2) one output feature per source feature with a separate count field per unique category, or (3) one output feature per source feature with a single string field containing a Python dictionary mapping categories to counts. Input layers can be any geometry type (point/line/polygon); reprojection is performed if CRSs differ; spatial indexing accelerates intersection queries; expressions are evaluated per-feature using QgsExpression with full context support. No raster, time-series, or satellite data is involved — it is purely vector-based geometric counting with categorical aggregation.

name: Count features in features with condition
desc: The script implements a QGIS Processing algorithm that counts how many features from an overlay vector layer satisfy specified geometric predicates (e.g., 'within', 'intersects') and optional attribute-based logical conditions (e.g., field equality, comparison operators) relative to each feature in a source vector layer. It supports advanced configuration including multiple geometric predicates (combined via AND/OR), dual conditional expressions with operators (e.g., '=', 'contains'), spatial index acceleration, reprojection handling, ordering, filtering, and deduplication control ('count multiple' toggle). The output is a copy of the source layer with an added integer count field (default 'count_n'), where each feature’s attribute reflects the number of matching overlay features. No remote sensing imagery, time-series analysis, or raster operations are involved — it is purely vector-based spatial and attribute relational counting. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic coordinates are not specified, as the algorithm operates on user-provided vector layers without embedded spatiotemporal constraints.

name: Count nearest features by category
desc: The script counts, for each feature in a source vector layer, the number of nearest features from an overlay vector layer grouped by a user-defined category (evaluated via expression or field). It supports three output structures: (1) one output feature per source-feature–category pair with fields for max distance, category name, and count; (2) one output feature per source feature with a separate integer field for each distinct category (e.g., 'category_count_n_cat_a'); (3) one output feature per source feature with a single string field containing a Python dictionary mapping categories to counts (e.g., '{"cat_a":0,"cat_b":13}'). Distance is computed in CRS units, supports dynamic per-feature maximum distance via expression, optional filtering on both layers, reprojection if CRS mismatched, spatial indexing for efficiency, and configurable counting logic (allowing or disallowing multiple counting of the same overlay feature). Input geometries can be points, lines, or polygons; no raster, time-series, or satellite data is involved — it is purely vector-based spatial proximity analysis within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Count nearest features by condition
desc: This algorithm counts nearest features in an overlay layer for each feature in a source layer, based on a maximum search distance and optional attribute-based logical conditions (up to two comparison expressions per layer, combined with AND/OR/XOR). It supports filtering both layers via expressions, reprojecting the overlay layer to match the source CRS, building a spatial index for efficient nearest-neighbor queries, and optionally allowing multiple counting or restricting to the single nearest match. The output is a copy of the source layer with an added integer count field (e.g., 'count_n') indicating how many qualifying overlay features fall within the specified distance and satisfy the conditional logic. No remote sensing data, time series, or raster operations are involved — it is purely vector-based geoprocessing within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Count points in polygons with condition
taskType: Count Features in Features with Condition
desc: This algorithm counts 2D single-point features from an overlay layer that fall within polygon features of a source layer, optionally applying geometric predicates (within/intersects), attribute-based filtering on both layers, and up to two conditional expressions (with configurable operators and logical concatenation) to restrict which point-polygon pairs contribute to the count. The output is a copy of the source polygon layer with an added integer field containing the count per polygon. The script explicitly states it does not support MultiPoints, 2.5D, or 3D points, and uses QgsSpatialIndexKDBush for acceleration. No remote sensing data, time series, or spectral analysis is involved — it is a pure vector overlay and conditional counting operation in QGIS Processing.

name: Count points in time-interval polygons
desc: The script creates time-sliced polygon features by duplicating input polygons for each time interval (in seconds) between a user-defined start and end datetime. For each polygon-interval combination, it counts how many points (from a separate point layer) fall both spatially within the polygon and temporally within the interval (i.e., point datetime > interval start AND ≤ interval end). It outputs a new vector layer with original polygon attributes plus three added fields: 'from_datetime', 'to_datetime', and 'pointcount'. The point layer’s datetime is evaluated via a QGIS expression (e.g., field reference or function), and optional de-duplication (removing counted points from the spatial index) is supported. No remote sensing imagery, spectral indices, or satellite-derived data are used — only vector geometry and attribute-based datetime logic.

name: Connect points to path by distance
desc: The script connects input point features into linear paths based on nearest-neighbor spatial proximity, grouping points by optional expressions (e.g., categorical fields), maximum inter-point distance, and/or maximum number of points per path. It processes points sequentially—ordered optionally by an expression—and iteratively appends the nearest unassigned point within max_dist that satisfies group membership and (optionally) non-self-crossing constraints. Outputs are LineString features with attributes including path_group_id, path_group_name, path_n_vertices, path_length, start/end feature IDs (fid), optional custom ID strings (cid), and semicolon-separated lists of visited fids/cids/dists (if enabled). Input MultiPoint geometries are cast to SinglePoints. The algorithm is purely vector-based, operates on user-provided QGIS layers, and contains no remote sensing or time-series logic.

name: Extract longest flow path
desc: The script computes the longest hydrological flow path within a watershed by identifying the channel network segment with the maximum network distance from a user-specified discharge (pour) point. It first spatially filters channels intersecting the watershed basin, extracts start vertices (proxy for upstream endpoints/springs), computes Euclidean distances from those vertices to the pour point, selects a subset of farthest vertices based on the chosen method (Custom Ranges, Linear 10%, or Brute Force), then calculates actual on-network shortest paths (using graph-based routing on the channel layer) from the pour point to those candidate upstream vertices; finally, it selects the path with the greatest network cost (distance) as the longest flow path, appends elongation ratio metrics, and outputs a single-line vector layer representing that path.

name: Derive upslope basin and terrain attributes
desc: The script computes the upslope contributing area (watershed) for a user-specified discharge point using a filled DEM via SAGA's deterministic 8-direction flow routing. It then polygonizes and cleans the upslope area, clips the DEM and channel network to that basin, generates contour lines at 100 m intervals, and computes watershed-level hydrological attributes (area, perimeter), CN values (using soil and Corine land cover inputs), and land use/land cover class distributions. Outputs include: (1) raw and cleaned basin polygons, (2) clipped basin DEM raster, (3) basin contour lines, (4) clipped basin channel network, (5) basin-wide Curve Number (CN) polygon layer, (6) Corine-based and SCS-based land cover classification layers within the basin.

name: Calculate watershed curve number
desc: The script calculates the spatially weighted average Curve Number (CN) for a user-defined watershed by intersecting Corine Land Cover (CLC) and soil/geology map layers, assigning SCS hydrologic soil groups (A–D) and land use classes (1–7), then combining them to retrieve CN values from condition-specific lookup tables (unfavorable/mean/favorable). It outputs: (1) a vector layer with per-polygon CN, land cover description, soil group, and basin percentage; (2) clipped Corine and soil layers; and (3) a detailed UTF-8 log file reporting class-wise coverage percentages, CN distribution, weighted mean CN, and urban cover quantification.

name: Validate vector layer naming
desc: The script validates QGIS vector layers for compliance with IGN Geoplateforme submission requirements. It checks for consistent CRS across all input layers, absence of invalid characters (<>"&') in layer names, file names, and field names; ensures only QgsVectorLayer types are used; verifies geometry validity using QGIS's 'qgis:checkvalidity' algorithm; and confirms each layer contains at least one feature. The output is a bitmask result code (ResultCode) indicating which validation failures occurred (e.g., CRS_MISMATCH=1, INVALID_LAYER_NAME=2), returned as a numeric processing output. No geospatial data is generated, transformed, or exported — the script performs purely metadata/structural validation within QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and geographic coordinates are not involved or specified.

name: Upload vector layers delivery
desc: The script uploads vector layers to a geospatial platform (Geoplateforme) as a delivery (livraison). It accepts multiple vector layers (GPKG, ESRI Shapefile, GeoJSON), validates their CRS consistency, handles associated files (e.g., .shx/.dbf for shapefiles), exports unsupported or multi-layer sources (e.g., GPKG with multiple layers) to temporary single-layer GPKG files, aggregates all input files and associated files into a semicolon-separated list, and delegates the actual upload to the GpfUploadFromFileAlgorithm. Outputs include the created upload ID string.

name: Update pipeline flow rates
desc: The script updates flow rate attributes in a vector layer (e.g., pipelines or network segments) by joining and recalculating flow values from a separate flow rate data layer. It applies unit conversions (volume: e.g., L → m³ via user-defined conversion factors; time: day/hour/minute/second → seconds), optionally multiplies by fluid density (retrieved via `get_fluid_parameter` using ambient temperature/pressure and selected fluid), and outputs a new vector layer with updated flow rate values. The workflow includes scenario-based filtering of flow data, field calculation, column deletion, and attribute join — all performed using QGIS native processing algorithms (`extractbyexpression`, `fieldcalculator`, `deletecolumn`, `joinattributestable`).

name: Compute antipodal point locations
desc: The script computes the antipodal (diametrically opposite) geographic coordinates for each vertex in input vector geometries (points, polylines, polygons), preserving geometry type and attributes. It reprojects non-geographic CRS inputs to EPSG:4326, applies the antipode transformation using the becagislibrary.latlong.antipode function (which inverts latitude and adds/subtracts 180° from longitude), and outputs a new vector layer with transformed geometries. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are involved — it is a pure coordinate transformation algorithm operating on user-provided vector layers. The output is a feature sink (QgsFeatureSink) containing antipodal geometries identical in structure (single/multi, parts, rings) to the input.

name: Compute antipodal point locations
desc: The script computes the antipodal (diametrically opposite) geographic coordinates for each vertex in input vector features (points, polylines, polygons), reprojects input to EPSG:4326 if needed, and outputs a new vector layer with geometries transformed such that every coordinate (lat, lon) is replaced by its antipode (−lat, (lon + 180) % 360). It handles single-part points, lines, and polygons; multi-part geometries are skipped. No raster data, time-series, or classification is involved — it is a pure coordinate transformation algorithm operating on vector geometry vertices using the becagislibrary.latlong.antipode function. The output is a QGIS feature sink (vector layer) with identical schema and CRS (WGS84) as input, but with antipodally reversed vertices.

name: Compute largest empty circle
desc: The script computes the Largest Empty Circle (LEC) for a given point layer — i.e., the largest possible circle that can be inscribed in the convex hull of the point set without containing any input points in its interior. It first calculates the LEC center and radius using a Voronoi-based geometric algorithm (imported from becagislibrary.voronoi), then adjusts the radius for geographic CRS by converting meters to degrees using Gaussian mean Earth radius approximation, and finally outputs two vector layers: (1) a point feature representing the LEC center (with duplicate geometries removed), and (2) a buffered polygon (circle) centered at that point with radius equal to the LEC radius (64-segment approximation, dissolved).

name: Reverse X coordinate of vector features
desc: The script reverses the X (longitude) coordinate of vector geometry points, polylines, and polygons using a custom `reversed_x` function imported from `becagislibrary.latlong`. It first reprojects input vector layers to EPSG:4326 if not already geographic, then applies coordinate reversal per vertex: for each point (lon, lat), it computes a reversed longitude while preserving latitude (exact reversal logic is external in `reversed_x`, but based on name and usage, it likely reflects longitude across a central meridian—e.g., 180° or 0°—though implementation details are opaque). The output is a new vector layer with identical schema and geometry type but transformed X coordinates. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification is involved—the operation is purely geometric and coordinate-based. Input is any QGIS vector layer (points, lines, polygons); output is a feature sink with reversed-X geometries.

name: Reverse Y coordinate axis
desc: The script reverses the Y-coordinate (latitude) of vector geometry features in an input layer, effectively flipping the vertical axis of point, line, and polygon geometries. It first checks if the input CRS is geographic (EPSG:4326); if not, it reprojects to EPSG:4326. Then, for each feature — whether selected or all — it applies a custom `reversed_y` function (imported from `becagislibrary.latlong`) to transform each vertex’s latitude/longitude pair into a reversed latitude (e.g., `reversed_lat = 90 - lat` or similar geodetic inversion logic, though exact implementation is external). The output is a new vector layer with identical attributes and geometry types but with Y-coordinates inverted. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification is involved — this is a pure coordinate transformation algorithm operating on user-provided vector layers in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Swap XY coordinates
desc: The script swaps the X and Y coordinates of vector geometry features (points, polylines, polygons) in a QGIS processing algorithm. It first checks if the input layer is in a geographic CRS; if not, it reprojects to EPSG:4326. Then, for each feature, it reverses latitude and longitude (i.e., treats current X as longitude and Y as latitude, then outputs X = original Y, Y = original X) using the external `swap_xy` function from `becagislibrary.latlong`. The output is a new vector layer with transformed geometries, preserving all original attributes. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic analysis is involved — it is a pure coordinate transformation utility for vector layers.

name: Calculate watered land type area
desc: The script computes, for each paddock polygon, the area (km²) of intersecting land types both within the paddock and within 3 km and 5 km buffer zones around water points. It calculates a weighted watered area (full 3 km + 50% of the 3–5 km annulus) and the percentage of each land type that is watered. Outputs include: (1) a vector output layer with per-paddock-per-land-type features containing geometry (intersection), ID, paddock name, land type name, areas (paddock-only, 3 km WA, 5 km WA, weighted watered), and percentage watered; and (2) an Excel/ODS spreadsheet summary derived from that output layer. All spatial operations are performed using QGIS native vector geometry methods (buffer, intersection, unaryUnion, area); no raster or satellite data is used — inputs are user-provided vector layers (land types, paddocks, water points). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate paddock area by distance-to-water bands
desc: The script calculates the area of paddocks (agricultural land parcels) falling within user-defined distance bands (e.g., 0–500 m, 500–1000 m, etc.) from water sources, using a precomputed raster layer representing Euclidean distance to water ('Water proximity' rasters). It reads each raster as a GDAL array, computes pixel area from geotransform, classifies pixels into non-overlapping distance intervals (band_dist = 500 m), sums pixel counts per band, converts to area units (m², ha, km²), computes percentage of total paddock area, and outputs a memory vector layer with attributes: 'Pdk Name', 'PdkArea Ha', 'DTW Band', 'Area m2', 'Area ha', 'Area km2', 'Percent'. These layers are then exported collectively to an Excel spreadsheet. The study area is implied by the input raster source path '/home/ben/DITT/Mulga_Park/For_Robyn/MDTW_test/...', and no satellite or time-series data is used — inputs are static, locally stored raster files generated externally (e.g., via QGIS or GEE distance tools). No classification model, temporal filtering, or spectral band processing occurs; only raster algebra (thresholded binning) and area aggregation.

name: Extract GPS geotags from drone images
desc: The script extracts EXIF GPS metadata (latitude, longitude, altitude, and timestamp) from JPG images captured by a DJI drone, converts DMS coordinates to decimal degrees, and creates a QGIS memory vector layer of point features representing image locations with attributes for name, time, latitude, longitude, and altitude. The study area is implied by the folder path 'gate-pdk_drone\DJI_202305191306_003_gate-pdk1', indicating drone imagery over a site named 'gate-pdk1'; no satellite or Earth observation data is used — only embedded camera EXIF/GPS metadata. The output is a QGIS vector layer added to the current project.

name: Extract drone image GPS locations
desc: The script extracts EXIF GPS metadata (latitude, longitude, altitude, and timestamp) from JPEG images captured by a DJI drone, converts DMS coordinates to decimal degrees, and creates a QGIS memory vector layer of point features with attributes (Name, Time, Latitude, Longitude, Altitude). The study area is implied by folder paths containing 'Beatrice_Gate_Paddock_2023' and 'gate-pdk1', indicating a specific paddock (pasture field) named 'Beatrice Gate Paddock'; the images are from three time-stamped DJI flight folders on 2023-05-19. No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used — data source is ground-based drone RGB imagery. Outputs are a QGIS point layer ('RGB_img_locations') added to the current project, with geometry including Z (altitude) values.

name: Extract drone image GPS coordinates
desc: The script extracts geolocation metadata (latitude, longitude, altitude) from DJI drone-captured TIFF images stored in three specific local folders. It parses XMP metadata embedded in each TIFF file to retrieve GPSLatitude, GPSLongitude, and AbsoluteAltitude values, then constructs a QGIS memory vector layer of 3D point features (WGS84, EPSG:4326) with attributes for image name, latitude, longitude, and altitude. The output is a QGIS vector layer named 'MS_img_locations' added to the current project. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or satellite data processing occurs — only local geotag extraction and GIS point layer creation. Study area and time are inferred from folder paths; sensor is DJI camera (not satellite); no bands, indices, or temporal filtering are used.

name: Generate grid cell polygons
desc: The script generates a regular rectangular grid of polygon features covering the extent of an existing QGIS vector layer named 'rbg_image_locations'. It divides the layer's bounding box into a fixed number of rows (2) and columns (3), computes cell dimensions, and constructs WKT Polygon geometries for each cell in EPSG:4326. The output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer named '6_cell_grid' with two attributes ('ID' and 'CELL_REF'), added to the current QGIS project. No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or geoprocessing beyond geometry creation is performed. The study area is implicitly defined by the extent of the 'rbg_image_locations' layer; no temporal filtering, remote sensing data, or thematic analysis is present.

name: Extract land type polygons within station boundaries
desc: The script extracts and clips land type polygons from three regional land mapping layers (vrd_100, mtrid_250, owsp_250) to buffered boundaries of three Australian research stations: Kidman Springs Research Station, Mount Riddock, and Old Man Plains Research Station. It performs spatial intersection between each land type layer and a 5 km buffer around the respective station boundary (in EPSG:7845), reprojects geometries as needed for coordinate compatibility (EPSG:7845 ↔ EPSG:4283), computes clipped polygon areas in km², and populates a new memory vector layer ('Land_Types') with attributes including SURVEY_ID, LAND_TYPE (mapped from source fields like 'LAND_UNIT', 'LandSystem'), MAP_UNIT, CLASS (e.g., 'LF_CLASS', 'MapClass'), SOIL_DESC, VEG_DESC (e.g., 'VEG_DESC_1', 'VegDesc'), and AREA_KM2. The output is a single merged vector layer added to the QGIS project. All operations are vector-based; no raster or time-series analysis is performed. Study area is confined to three named pastoral research stations in Australia; no temporal dimension is present. Data sources are local vector layers loaded into QGIS — not GEE assets — so this is a QGIS Python (PyQGIS) workflow, not a Google Earth Engine script despite the user’s mislabeling.

name: Generate paddock boundaries from source layers
desc: The script constructs a new memory-based polygon layer 'Pdk_Boundaries' in EPSG:7845, aggregating and reprojecting paddock geometries from three input layers: 'Kidman_Paddocks', 'mrk_pdks_slct', and 'OMP_PDKS'. It applies CRS transformation using QgsCoordinateTransform, removes interior rings via removeInteriorRings(), filters by minimum area (1,000,000 m² for Kidman and OMP layers), handles missing name attributes by generating fallback identifiers (e.g., 'KDM_no-name_1'), assigns fixed district and property values per source layer, computes area in km² rounded to 5 decimals, and adds the resulting features to the output layer which is then added to the QGIS project.

name: Compile waterpoint infrastructure locations
desc: The script compiles point-based water infrastructure (waterpoints and troughs) from three local vector layers — 'KID_WATERPOINTS', 'mrk_wpts', and 'OMP_TROUGHS' — into a single standardized memory layer named 'Waterpoints' in EPSG:7845. It reprojects each input layer's geometries to the target CRS, harmonizes attribute fields ('FEATURE', 'NAME', 'DISTRICT', 'PROPERTY'), applies consistent labeling logic (e.g., hardcoding 'Trough' for OMP_TROUGHS, 'VRD' and 'Kidman' for KID_WATERPOINTS), and appends all features to a new QgsVectorLayer. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations are performed; the workflow is purely vector data integration and reprojection. Study area and time range are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate water-accessible paddock area
desc: The script computes the area of each paddock (from 'Kidman_Paddocks' layer) that lies within a 500-meter buffer of designated water points (e.g., troughs, tanks, waterholes) specified per paddock name in the pdk_wpts dictionary. It intersects buffered water point geometries with each matching paddock geometry, calculates area metrics (m², ha, km²), and outputs a new memory vector layer ('temp_wa') containing one feature per matched paddock with attributes: Pdk_Name, Pdk_ID, Water pts (original string), Area_m2, Area_ha, Area_km2. The study area is implicitly Kidman pastoral properties; data sources are local QGIS vector layers — no satellite, sensor, or temporal data are used. All operations are vector-based geometric buffering, unary union, intersection, and area calculation in EPSG:7845 (GDA2020 / MGA zone 52).

name: Map waterpoint-to-paddock access lines
desc: The script generates vector line features representing straight-line connections from waterpoints to paddocks within a 1500-meter buffer, based on a predefined mapping of waterpoint IDs to paddock names. It uses two local QGIS vector layers: 'Kidman_Paddocks' (polygon layer with 'NAME' attribute) and 'Kidman_Waters' (point layer with 'FEATURE' attribute), both assumed to be in EPSG:7845 (GDA2020 / MGA zone 45). For each waterpoint ID referenced in the pdk_wpts dictionary, the script buffers the point by 1500 m, intersects that buffer with the corresponding paddock polygon(s), computes the centroid of the intersection geometry as the endpoint, and creates a line from the original waterpoint to that centroid. Attributes include source waterpoint name ('FEATURE') and target paddock name ('NAME'). No satellite, raster, or temporal data is used; all operations are vector-based geometric computations in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS). Study area is implicitly Kidman pastoral station in Australia, but no coordinate extent or time dimension is present.

name: Extract waterpoint infrastructure features
desc: The script extracts a subset of waterpoint features from the 'Kidman_Waters' vector layer in QGIS based on a predefined dictionary (pdk_wpts) mapping site names to waterpoint IDs. It parses numeric IDs from string-encoded waterpoint descriptors (e.g., 'Trough(45); Tank(17)'), collects all unique IDs, and uses QgsVectorLayer.getFeatures() with that ID list to retrieve matching features. A new memory layer 'temp_wpts' is created with identical schema and CRS (EPSG:7845), populated with the selected features’ geometries and attributes, then added to the QGIS project.

name: Calculate time per watered band
desc: The script calculates the time (in hours) that GPS-collared animals spend within each distance-to-water (DTW) band (e.g., '1000-1500m') defined in a polygon layer. It processes chronological GPS point data with datetime and numeric DTW fields, interpolates time allocation across bands when GPS points straddle adjacent bands using line-segment intersection with band polygons, and aggregates results per calendar date. Outputs are written to an Excel spreadsheet (.xlsx or .ods) with one row per date (including total time in each band, checksum), plus a final row for the entire collar period. Input layers are user-provided vector layers (GPS points and DTW bands); no satellite or raster data is used — all operations are vector-based geometric and temporal computations in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Calculate distance to waterpoints for cattle GPS tracks
desc: The script processes cattle GPS collar CSV data (latitude/longitude, timestamp) to compute distance-to-water (DTW) for each point within a specified paddock boundary. It first clips the GPS points to a 100-m buffer around the paddock polygon, then calculates the shortest Euclidean distance from each point to the nearest waterpoint (e.g., bores, dams, waterholes) within that paddock. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage (.gpkg) with original attributes plus 'q_datetime' (QDateTime), 'Date' (date-only), and 'dist_to_water_m' fields; (2) an Excel spreadsheet (.xlsx) exporting the DTW GeoPackage; and (3) daily movement statistics (distance traveled, speed, time spent near water) saved as both a tracks GeoPackage and Excel file.

name: Calculate distance to water points
desc: The script processes GPS collar CSV data (e.g., No4_1168_20240715_132300.csv) to compute point-to-water distances for animal movement analysis within a defined paddock. It clips the GPS points to a buffered paddock boundary ('No_4_plus_100'), adds a QDateTime field from the 'Time' column, appends a Date field for Excel compatibility, computes Euclidean distance from each GPS point to all clipped waterpoints (from 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes' layer) in EPSG:9473 (GDA2020 MGA Zone 53), saves results as a GeoPackage (.gpkg), exports it to Excel (.xlsx), and further derives daily movement statistics (track length, displacement, etc.) with paddock name and collar ID metadata.

name: Calculate distance to water points
desc: The script processes GPS collar data (CSV) from an antelope GPS collar (No. 4) deployed in the 'No_4_and_No_5_West' paddock area. It clips the GPS points to a buffered paddock boundary ('No_4_plus_100_asymmetrical'), adds a QDateTime field parsed from a 'Time' column in the CSV, appends a Date field for Excel compatibility, computes distance-to-water (DTW) for each point using clipped waterpoints (from layer 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes') intersecting the physical paddock ('No_4'), and exports results to GeoPackage and Excel. It then generates daily movement statistics (tracks, distances, speeds) using the DTW-augmented points, outputting both GeoPackage and Excel files. The study area is implicitly the paddock system managed by Anthony (likely in Australia, given EPSG:9473 — GDA2020 / MGA zone 53), with time inferred only from filename ('20240715'). No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used — all inputs are vector layers (paddock boundaries, waterpoints) and tabular GPS logs.

name: Calculate distance to water points
desc: The script processes GPS collar data from a wildlife tracking device (collar ID '0236', associated with paddock 'No. 4') to compute point-to-water distances and derive daily movement statistics. It loads a CSV of GPS points (with Latitude, Longitude, and ISO Zulu-formatted Time), clips it to a buffered paddock boundary ('No_4_plus_100'), joins it with clipped waterpoint features (from layer 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes' intersecting physical paddock 'No_4'), adds a QDateTime field ('q_datetime') and a Date field, computes distance-to-water (DTW) in meters using EPSG:9473 (GDA2020 / MGA zone 53), exports the DTW-annotated points to GeoPackage and Excel, then generates daily movement statistics (track segments, distances, speeds) and saves them as a second GeoPackage and Excel file. The study area is implicitly tied to Australian pastoral land (GDA2020 CRS, paddock naming convention 'No. 4', 'No. 5 West'), and all spatial operations are vector-based — no satellite or raster data is used. Inputs: local CSV, QGIS project layers ('No_4', 'No_4_plus_100', 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes'); outputs: two GeoPackages (.gpkg), two Excel spreadsheets (.xlsx), and intermediate in-memory layers.

name: Calculate distance to water points
desc: The script processes GPS collar data (CSV) from an antelope collar (No. 5) to compute distance-to-water (DTW) for each recorded location within a buffered paddock boundary ('No_5_plus_100'). It clips the GPS points to the buffered paddock, adds QDateTime and Date fields from the 'Time' column (formatted as ISO Zulu time), clips waterpoints (from 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes') to the physical paddock boundary ('No5_both'), projects all layers to EPSG:9473 (GDA2020 / MGA zone 53) for accurate distance calculation, computes DTW using a custom QGIS algorithm ('ditt-lid:adddist2water'), exports results to GeoPackage and Excel (.xlsx), then generates daily movement statistics (including tracks and summary metrics) using the DTW-enhanced layer. The study area is implicitly the No. 5 paddock in Australia’s arid rangelands (inferred from GDA2020 CRS and paddock naming convention), with input CSV timestamped '20240715' — indicating a single-day observation. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are vector-based field/GIS layers and tabular GPS logs.

name: Calculate distance to water points
desc: The script processes GPS collar data from an antelope (Ant) collar (No5_West_1159_20240715_132642.csv) to compute distance-to-water (DTW) for each recorded location within a buffered paddock boundary ('No_5_West_plus_100'). It clips the GPS points to the buffered paddock, adds a QDateTime field parsed from the 'Time' column (format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%SZ'), appends a Date field for Excel compatibility, then calculates Euclidean distance (in EPSG:9473 — GDA2020 / Australian Albers) from each point to clipped waterpoints (from layer 'ANT_waters_plus_waterholes' intersecting the physical paddock 'No5_West'). Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage (.gpkg) containing all attributes plus DTW, (2) an Excel spreadsheet (.xlsx) of the DTW layer, and (3) daily movement statistics (track segments, distances, speeds) exported as both a GeoPackage and Excel file. The study area is the 'No. 5 West' paddock in Australia (inferred from EPSG:9473 CRS and paddock naming convention), and the input CSV timestamp is 2024-07-15.

name: Calculate daily livestock track distance
desc: The script processes GPS-derived line geometry data from cattle collars to compute daily movement distances. It reads GeoPackage files containing GPS point tracks (with 'Date' or 'Time' fields), groups points by date, constructs daily polyline geometries, reprojects from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:28352 (GDA94 / MGA zone 52), computes planimetric length in meters, converts to kilometers (rounded to 3 decimals), and stores results as memory vector layers with attributes: Paddock, Collar No, Date (formatted YYYY-MM-DD), and Distance (km). The study area is implied to be Conkerberry station in Australia’s Northern Territory (inferred from folder path 'Conkerberry' and CRS EPSG:28352 — MGA zone 52, covering NT/WA). Input data are ground-based GPS point logs (not satellite-derived); no remote sensing imagery, bands, or classification methods are used. Output is a set of daily track line features added to the QGIS project for visualization and further GIS analysis.

name: Interpolate GPS collar point gaps
desc: The script performs spatial and temporal linear interpolation of GPS collar point data to fill temporal gaps exceeding one minute. It processes vector layers containing GPS points with datetime stamps ('date_time'), geometry, and attributes including 'Index', 'Distance', 'Latitude', 'Longitude', and 'Azimuth'. For each consecutive pair of points, it computes the time delta in minutes; if >1 minute, it generates intermediate points at 1-minute intervals along the great-circle (ellipsoidal) line segment between them, using QgsDistanceArea for geodetic length measurement and QgsGeometry.interpolate() for spatial interpolation. Azimuth is computed from current to next point and assigned to all interpolated features. Output is saved as GeoPackage (.gpkg) files in a local folder 'Paddock_Power_GPS\GPS Data Aug21-March22\gps_layers_final', with new attributes: ID (sequential integer), gpx_index (original index + offset), Distance (interpolated segment length in meters), Latitude/Longitude (WGS84 coordinates), date_time (QDateTime at 1-min increments), and Azimuth (degrees). Study area is implied by layer naming ('BigMudgee') and output folder path; no satellite, sensor, or band usage — purely vector-based GPS point processing in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS).

name: Clip GPS tracks to paddock boundary
desc: The script clips raw GPS track vector layers (stored as GeoPackages) to a specific paddock boundary defined in a buffered paddock layer (Paddocks_buffered_350.gpkg). It filters the paddock layer to retain only the 'Conkerberry' paddock using an SQL subset string, then iteratively applies vector clipping ('native:clip') to each GPS GeoPackage file in the source folder, producing clipped GeoPackage outputs in the destination folder. The study area is the Conkerberry paddock; time range is not specified in the code; data sources are local vector files (no satellite, sensor, or bands involved); no raster processing, classification, or temporal filtering occurs — only geometric clipping of point/line GPS features to a polygon boundary.

name: Process GPS collar location data
desc: The script processes raw CSV files containing GPS collar telemetry data, filtering out rows with zero latitude or longitude values, constructing point geometries in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and saving each cleaned dataset as a separate GeoPackage (.gpkg) file. The input data resides in a local Windows directory path referencing 'FireGraze dry season 2023 GPS data' and 'Box', indicating field-collected animal movement data from a fire-grazing ecological study. No remote sensing imagery, cloud processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — only tabular-to-vector conversion and spatial validation. Outputs are individual geopackages named after the source CSV files, stored in a designated local output folder. All attribute types and precision are explicitly defined (e.g., Latitude as QVariant.Double with prec=6), and coordinate parsing includes cleaning (e.g., stripping null bytes, handling Excel-formatted time strings like '="12:03:45"').

name: Batch rasterize vector fields
desc: The script performs batch rasterization of selected attribute fields from an input vector layer onto a template raster grid (defined by 'likeraster'). It iterates over user-specified fields, uses GDAL's rasterize algorithm to convert each field’s vector features into a separate GeoTIFF raster where pixel values correspond to the field’s attribute values (burned), aligned spatially and dimensionally to the like raster (extent, resolution, CRS). No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic classification is involved — it is a pure vector-to-raster conversion workflow. Outputs are one raster per selected field, saved to a user-defined directory or loaded as temporary layers in QGIS. All parameters (extent, pixel size, nodata, data type) are derived solely from the provided 'likeraster'; no filtering, masking, temporal aggregation, or spectral analysis occurs.

name: Load raster layers from folder
desc: The script loads all raster files (e.g., GeoTIFF, IMG) from a user-specified local directory into QGIS as QgsRasterLayer instances using GDAL. It validates each layer, adds them to the temporary layer store and layer-to-load-on-completion queue, and triggers a post-processor that moves all loaded raster layers into a newly created 'Group1' at the top of the layer tree. No geospatial computation, filtering, reprojection, or classification is performed — it is purely an I/O and layer organization workflow. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and analysis methods are not specified because the script operates on arbitrary local raster files with no embedded temporal/spatial metadata parsing or remote sensing logic.

name: Package rasters into Geopackage
desc: The script packages multiple input raster layers as sub-dataset raster tables in an existing GeoPackage file using GDAL's translate algorithm with APPEND_SUBDATASET=YES. It iterates over each raster layer, determines its band count and NoData value (defaulting to None if NaN, or 0 for multi-band rasters), sets the appropriate GDAL data type (6 for single-band, 1 for multi-band), and appends each raster as a named subdataset (using the layer name) via the RASTER_TABLE creation option. The output is a GeoPackage containing all input rasters as embedded raster tables.

name: Load raster layers from folder
desc: The script loads multiple raster files (e.g., GeoTIFF, etc.) from a user-specified local directory into the QGIS project. It validates each file as a GDAL-supported raster layer, adds valid layers to the project’s temporary layer store and layer-to-load-on-completion registry, and triggers a post-processor that moves all loaded rasters into a new layer tree group named 'group1' at the root level. No geospatial analysis, classification, time-series processing, or remote sensing computation is performed — the script is purely a QGIS processing algorithm for batch raster import and layer organization. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations are not specified because the script operates on arbitrary local raster files with no embedded temporal, spatial, or sensor metadata constraints.

name: Style raster layers with pseudocolor
desc: The script applies a single-band pseudocolor renderer to multiple raster layers loaded from a user-specified local folder. It computes band statistics (min/max) for band 1 of each raster, creates a linear blue-to-red gradient color ramp, and assigns a QgsSingleBandPseudoColorRenderer to each valid raster layer. The output consists of styled raster layers added to the QGIS project’s layer panel with visual rendering applied; no geospatial analysis, classification, or export is performed — only client-side visualization styling. No study area, time range, satellite data, or remote sensing operations are involved; all inputs are local GDAL-supported rasters (e.g., GeoTIFF) whose content, origin, and metadata are not inspected or constrained by the script.

name: Style raster layers with pseudocolor ramp
desc: The script loads multiple raster files from a user-specified local directory and applies a single-band pseudocolor renderer using a linear gradient color ramp (blue to red) based on the full data range (min/max statistics of Band 1). It does not perform any geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing computation — only visualization post-processing within QGIS. No study area, time range, satellite data, or analytical method is involved; inputs are generic local GDAL-readable rasters (e.g., GeoTIFFs), and outputs are styled QgsRasterLayer instances added to the QGIS project. The script operates entirely client-side in QGIS Processing, with no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, imagery loading, filtering, or export logic — despite the prompt’s reference to 'GEE script', this is purely a QGIS Python Processing algorithm.

name: Filter GPS points by Northern Territory extent
desc: The script processes CSV files containing GPS point data (with 'Longitude' and 'yField=Latitude' columns) and filters them spatially to retain only those falling within a predefined rectangular extent corresponding to Australia's Northern Territory (NT). It reads each CSV as a delimited text layer in QGIS, validates it, then uses a QgsSpatialIndex to intersect features with the NT bounding box (QgsRectangle with coordinates approximating NT’s geographic bounds: ~129°E–138°E, ~−26°S–−11°S). Valid points are written to individual GeoPackage (.gpkg) files under a 'gps_points' subdirectory. No time filtering, classification, or remote sensing analysis is performed — the core operation is spatial subsetting of tabular GPS point data using a fixed AOI. Satellite imagery, bands, temporal filtering, or thematic modeling are absent; the only geospatial operation is vector point-in-polygon (via rectangle intersection) using QGIS Python API.

name: Filter point features by spatial extent
desc: The script processes CSV files containing latitude/longitude point data, converts them into QGIS vector layers, and filters features to retain only those intersecting a predefined Northern Territory (NT) bounding box (xmin=129.000476, ymin=-25.998618, xmax=138.001200, ymax=-10.965914). It writes the filtered points to ESRI Shapefile format in the specified output directory. The input CSVs are assumed to contain georeferenced observations (e.g., field measurements or sensor readings), but no metadata about their origin, time, or thematic content is present in the code. No classification, modeling, temporal aggregation, or satellite-derived analysis occurs — only spatial subsetting using a fixed rectangle. The study area corresponds to the approximate extent of Australia’s Northern Territory, though no explicit NT label or administrative logic is used — only coordinate bounds. All operations occur client-side in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), not in Google Earth Engine (GEE); despite the prompt stating 'You are a professional GEE developer', the provided script contains zero GEE calls (no ee.Initialize(), no ee.ImageCollection, no .map(), etc.) and is purely a QGIS processing workflow.

name: Filter and export GPS points
desc: The script processes CSV-formatted GPS point data (with Latitude/Longitude columns) by reading them as delimited text layers in QGIS, filtering features spatially to retain only those intersecting a predefined Northern Territory bounding rectangle (nt_extent), converting the 'Time' field (in '%d/%m/%Y %I:%M:%S%p' format) into a QDateTime attribute, and exporting the cleaned, georeferenced points to GeoPackage (.gpkg) files in a 'gps_points' subdirectory. No satellite, remote sensing, or GEE-specific operations are performed—the script runs entirely in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), not Google Earth Engine. The study area is implicitly constrained by nt_extent (Northern Territory, Australia), and only the first CSV file in the directory is processed due to the 'break' statement. Output products are per-file GeoPackage point layers with added DateTime attribute.

name: Process GPS point locations
desc: The script processes CSV-formatted GPS track logs (with Latitude/Longitude columns) into geopackage (.gpkg) point layers, filtering points to those intersecting a predefined Northern Territory bounding box (nt_extent), converting 'Time' strings to QDateTime objects, and appending them as a 'Date_Time' attribute. Input files are read from '/home/ben/DITT/Pain_Trial_GPS/csv_files', and outputs are written to '/home/ben/DITT/Pain_Trial_GPS/gpkg/gps_points/'. No satellite, raster, or remote sensing analysis is performed; the workflow is purely vector-based GPS data ingestion, spatial subsetting, and format conversion. The study context ('Pain_Trial_GPS') and file path suggest clinical/mobile health GPS monitoring data collected during a pain trial, but no time range, sensor metadata, or classification/analysis beyond spatial filtering and datetime parsing is present in the code.

name: Quantify land condition within watered zones
desc: The script computes the proportional area of each land condition class (from 'Landcon_no456' layer, field 'LCOverall_') intersecting three hydrologically defined zones—0–3 km, 3–5 km, and unwatered (tobufdist = -99)—around paddocks in the 'ANT_NO5_SPLIT_GR3_TOP_WATER' layer. It performs spatial intersection and area calculation in EPSG:7845 (GDA2020 / MGA zone 53), using coordinate transformation for both layers, spatial indexing for efficiency, and geometry collection for multi-part features. Outputs are a memory vector layer ('Watered Land Condition') containing polygon features per land condition class per zone, with attributes: Property ('ANTHONY_LAGOON'), Paddock (name), Water_Dist (zone label), Land_Condition (LCOverall_), Area_m2/ha/km2, and Percent (of zone area). The script validates results via percentage checksums per zone (targeting 100%). Study area is Anthony Lagoon in northern Australia; data sources are local QGIS vector layers—not satellite-derived—so no sensor, bands, or time range are involved.

name: Execute SQL on vector layers
desc: The script executes a user-provided SQL query against one or more input vector layers using QGIS's virtual layer provider. It constructs a QgsVirtualLayerDefinition from the input layers (referenced as 'input1', 'input2', etc.), sets the SQL query, optional UID field, geometry field, geometry type (including 'No geometry'), and CRS. It then creates a temporary virtual vector layer, validates it, and writes the resulting features to an output vector layer. No raster data, time-series filtering, spatial extent constraints, or satellite-derived inputs are involved — this is purely a vector SQL query execution tool operating within QGIS Processing Framework. All parameters (datasources, query, UID, geometry field/type/CRS) are user-defined at runtime; no hardcoded study area, time range, or external datasets appear in the code.

name: Identify EV charging station candidate locations
desc: The script estimates optimal locations for new electric vehicle (EV) charging stations by analyzing spatial gaps in existing coverage using Voronoi diagrams, road proximity, population density, and land value. It computes weighted scores combining consumer-oriented factors (population density, distance to roads) and investor-oriented factors (land value, distance to existing stations), then filters high-scoring candidate points. Outputs include: Voronoi polygons of existing stations; Voronoi vertices as initial candidates; buffered coverage gaps; roadside-aligned candidate points; population- and land-value-weighted metrics per candidate circle; normalized multi-criteria scores; and a final filtered layer of high-potential candidate points (>0.3 weighted score).

name: Apply binary closing morphological operation
desc: The script performs binary morphological closing on a user-provided raster layer using SciPy's `binary_closing`. It reads a specified band from the input raster, replaces NoData values with 0, generates a disk-shaped structuring element based on a user-defined map-distance parameter (converted to pixels using the raster's geotransform), applies the closing operation for a specified number of iterations, and writes the result to a GeoTIFF output layer. The workflow relies entirely on local raster I/O via GDAL and SciPy morphology — no Earth Engine server-side operations, no time-series analysis, no cloud platform execution, and no satellite imagery processing logic. All parameters (band number, distance in map units, iterations) are user-configurable via QGIS Processing interface. Study area, time range, satellite data sources, and geographic extent are not involved or referenced in the code.

name: Compute differential DEM threshold mask
desc: The script computes the difference between an input DEM and a reference DEM, then generates a binary raster mask where pixel values are 1 if the difference falls within a user-defined threshold range (min_value < (DEM − REF_DEM) ≤ max_value), and 0 otherwise. It reads both DEMs using GDAL, handles NoData values via masked arrays, performs element-wise subtraction, applies a bitwise AND condition for the inclusive-exclusive threshold interval, and writes the resulting uint8 mask to a GeoTIFF output raster. The script operates entirely on local raster files provided as QGIS processing inputs; no remote sensing data ingestion, time-series analysis, cloud masking, or satellite-derived indices are involved.
