All parameters (thresholds, input paths, output path) are user-specified at runtime; no hardcoded study area, time range, or sensor metadata is present in the code.

name: Map subgrid outlet watersheds
desc: The script generates a subgrid map raster where each pixel is assigned the feature ID of the nearest upstream watershed outlet point, using flow direction to delineate contributing areas. It reads vector point features (subgrid outlets), a precomputed flow direction raster (e.g., D8 or D-infinity), converts outlet coordinates to pixel indices via affine geotransform, initializes a target array with outlet IDs at their pixel locations, then executes a watershed delineation function (from terrain_analysis.watershed) that propagates those IDs downstream/upstream (depending on implementation logic — standard watershed labeling typically fills basins upstream from pour points). The output is a GeoTIFF raster with float32 values representing outlet feature IDs (0 for no assignment), spatially aligned with the input flow raster, and with matching CRS and geotransform. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific terrain dataset (e.g., SRTM, MERIT) is specified in the code — all inputs are user-provided via QGIS Processing interface; the only explicit geospatial operation is world-to-pixel coordinate conversion using GDAL’s GetGeoTransform().

name: Identify subgrid topographic outlets
desc: The script identifies subgrid topographic outlet points for polygon features (e.g., hydrologic response units or grid cells) using flow direction and flow accumulation rasters. It computes the local contributive area (LCA) for candidate pixels within each polygon, selects the pixel with maximum LCA as the outlet, then traces downstream to identify the receiving feature (graph linkage). Outputs are point features with attributes including outlet coordinates (OX,OY), downstream neighbor coordinates (NX,NY), NODEID, LINKID, drainage area (DRAINAGE), local contributive area (LOCALCA), and net contributive area (CONTRIB). The algorithm supports two implementations: pure Python (raster masking + heap-based LCA search) and Cython-accelerated (via external terrain_analysis module). No study area, time range, satellite data, or explicit geographic extent is specified — inputs are generic raster layers (flow direction, flow accumulation) and vector polygons provided by the user.

name: Analyze land cover continuity from streams
desc: The script computes a land cover continuity map by performing shortest-path exploration from stream pixels across a valley bottom domain, using land cover classes as an ordered gradient (e.g., natural → artificialized). It modifies land cover values based on discontinuities (e.g., remapping classes 51/53 to 2, assigning 40/53 to discontinuity codes 3/4), applies spatial masking to valley bottom only, defines a tiered cost matrix (1.0 for classes 1–29, 10.0 for 30–49, 100.0 for ≥50), and runs a custom `ta.shortest_max` function that propagates the maximum land cover class encountered along the least-cost path from streams. Outputs a raster where each pixel holds the maximum land cover class value along its shortest path from the nearest stream, with stream pixels set to 1 and non-valley-bottom pixels masked to nodata. Input rasters are read via GDAL; no time-series or satellite processing is performed — all inputs are static, pre-classified rasters. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Burn streams into DEM for flow direction
desc: The script computes a flow direction raster and optionally a depression-filled DEM by integrating vector stream networks into a digital elevation model (DEM) using a priority-flood algorithm that processes stream cells first. It rasterizes input LineString streams (with optional primary key ordering), identifies stream junctions via backward traversal to resolve link collisions, and applies the 'burnfill' algorithm from the FCT terrain_analysis library — a topological variant of Wang & Liu’s priority flood method with minimum Z-delta enforcement (0.0005 default). Inputs are a GDAL-readable DEM raster and a QGIS vector layer of streams; outputs are a signed 16-bit flow direction raster (D8 encoding, -1 for no data) and an optional float32 filled-DEM raster. No study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is referenced — it operates on generic local raster/vector inputs.

name: Compute flow accumulation raster
desc: The script computes a flow accumulation raster from an input flow direction raster using a terrain analysis function (flow_accumulation). It reads the flow direction raster via GDAL, applies the flow_accumulation algorithm (imported from ...lib.terrain_analysis), masks out NoData cells by setting accumulation to zero where input flow equals NoData, and writes the result as a UInt32 GeoTIFF with tiling and DEFLATE compression. The output is a single-band raster where each cell value represents the number of upstream cells draining through it (i.e., contributing area in cell counts). No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are referenced — the input is a generic local raster layer provided by the user (QgsProcessingParameterRasterLayer named 'Flow Direction'), and all operations are deterministic, pixel-based hydrological computations. The CRS and geotransform are inherited from the input flow raster.

name: Compute D8 flow direction
desc: The script computes D8 flow direction from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) input raster using the `flowdir` function from the local `...lib.terrain_analysis` module. It reads the DEM as a NumPy array via GDAL, preserves its georeferencing (geotransform and CRS), applies flow direction calculation handling nodata values, and writes the result as a signed 16-bit integer GeoTIFF with nodata value -1. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external imagery is involved — the input is a generic raster layer provided by the user in QGIS; the operation is purely deterministic terrain analysis on elevation data.

name: Calculate height above nearest drainage
desc: The script computes a relative digital elevation model (DEM) by calculating the height of each cell above the nearest stream cell within its watershed, using a combination of raster and vector inputs. It reads a DEM, stream network (as LineString features), watershed boundaries raster, D8 flow direction raster, and slope class raster. The workflow includes: (1) rasterizing the stream network to identify stream cell elevations; (2) propagating the nearest stream elevation across each watershed using a shortest-path algorithm (via external terrain_analysis module); (3) applying a slope-based mask to exclude steep non-stream areas (slope > 2 → set refz = -99999); (4) performing watershed-based filling of reference elevations using flow direction; and (5) subtracting the final reference surface from the original DEM to produce 'Relative Elevation'. Outputs are a single-band GeoTIFF raster with same geotransform and projection as input DEM, preserving nodata values. No study area, time range, satellite data, or explicit geographic coordinates are specified in the code — all inputs are generic raster/vector layers provided by the user at runtime.

name: Calculate height above nearest drainage
desc: The script computes a Relative Digital Elevation Model (DEM), also called a detrended DEM or Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) within the same watershed. It rasterizes input stream line features onto the DEM grid, marks stream cell elevations, then applies a terrain analysis function (shortest_ref_ws) to propagate the minimum stream elevation across each watershed — effectively computing, for each non-stream pixel, the elevation difference between its DEM value and the elevation of the nearest upstream or same-watershed stream cell. The output is a raster where each pixel value equals (original DEM elevation − propagated reference stream elevation), with NoData preserved from the input DEM. Input data includes a DEM raster, a vector layer of stream centerlines (LineString geometry), and a raster layer of delineated watersheds (integer-coded basin IDs). All geospatial operations are performed using GDAL and NumPy in-memory raster processing — no GEE server-side operations occur; this is a QGIS Processing algorithm wrapper relying on local Python terrain libraries (e.g., ...lib.terrain_analysis.shortest_ref_ws). No satellite imagery, time-series, or cloud-based Earth Engine calls are present — it is purely a desktop GIS raster-vector hydro-terrain workflow.

name: Compute mask-based flow accumulation
desc: The script computes a flow accumulation raster where accumulation is constrained by a binary (or integer) mask raster, using D8 flow direction as input. It reads the flow direction raster and mask raster as NumPy arrays, passes them to an external `flow_accumulation` function (from `...lib.terrain_analysis`), and writes the resulting accumulated values (stored in the modified `mask` array) to a GeoTIFF output with UInt32 data type, same geotransform and projection as the flow input. The mask values are interpreted as unit-contributing cells (i.e., each masked cell contributes 1 unit upstream), and accumulation follows D8 routing. No study area, time range, satellite data, or explicit geographic extent is defined in the script — it operates purely on user-provided local raster layers loaded via QGIS Processing Framework. Output is a single-band UInt32 GeoTIFF accumulation raster with NoData=0.

name: Calculate stream-relative elevation
desc: The script computes a Relative Digital Elevation Model (DEM) — i.e., a detrended DEM where each cell’s elevation is subtracted by the elevation of the nearest stream cell (projected onto the DEM grid). It rasterizes input vector stream LineString features onto the DEM grid using Bresenham’s line algorithm, filters for valid (non-no-data) stream pixels, removes duplicate vertices, builds a cKDTree spatial index over stream pixel coordinates and elevations, then for every DEM cell computes the Euclidean distance to the nearest stream pixel and subtracts that stream cell’s elevation from the local DEM value. The output is a GeoTIFF raster of the same extent, resolution, and projection as the input DEM, with no-data values preserved. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets (e.g., GEE image collections) are used — inputs are local QGIS raster and vector layers provided by the user.

name: Compute D8 flow direction
desc: The script computes D8 flow direction raster from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) and a rasterized stream network input. It uses an external terrain analysis function `stream_flow` (imported from `...lib.terrain_analysis`) that takes elevation array, streams array, nodata value, and QGIS feedback. The output is a signed 16-bit integer raster where cell values encode the D8 flow direction (e.g., 1=East, 2=Southeast, ..., 8=Northeast), with nodata set to -1. No DEM source metadata (e.g., resolution, origin), stream delineation method, or hydrological conditioning logic is visible in the script — all preprocessing is assumed completed prior to execution. The script operates entirely on locally loaded GDAL raster datasets within QGIS Processing Framework; no GEE server-side computation occurs.

name: Vectorize stream networks
desc: The script vectorizes stream networks from raster inputs: flow direction and flow accumulation rasters, optionally incorporating elevation data to produce 3D line features (LineStringZ) or 2D lines (LineString). It applies a minimum contributing area threshold (in km²) to filter stream segments, converts pixels above the threshold into connected line segments using an external terrain_analysis.stream_to_feature function, and attributes each segment with upstream contributing areas (CONTAREA1 at head, CONTAREA2 at penultimate pixel). Outputs are QGIS vector line features with GID, CONTAREA1, and CONTAREA2 fields. No study area, time range, satellite data, or explicit geographic extent is specified in the code — all inputs are generic raster layers provided by the user via QGIS processing interface; the algorithm operates purely on local raster arrays using GDAL and NumPy, with no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, imagery collections, or temporal filtering.

name: Propagate Strahler order to delineate watersheds
desc: The script performs watershed delineation by propagating Strahler order values from stream cells (in the Target Raster) upstream along inverse D8 flow paths defined in the Flow Direction raster. It uses a custom terrain_analysis.watershed() function to fill NoData cells in the target raster by tracing flow direction backward (i.e., against flow), assigning each cell the Strahler order of its downstream stream cell. The output is a continuous raster where each watershed is labeled by its outlet’s Strahler order — effectively producing a Strahler-order–coded watershed map. Input rasters are read via GDAL; no cloud masking, temporal filtering, or satellite-derived bands are involved. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code — it is a generic, local raster-based hydrological processing algorithm operating on precomputed flow direction and stream order inputs.

name: Propagate Strahler order upstream
desc: The script fills no-data cells in a target raster (e.g., Strahler order values on stream cells) by propagating non-null values upstream along the inverse D8 flow direction defined in a separate flow direction raster. It uses a reference raster to optionally guide or constrain propagation, and replaces filled cells with a user-specified fill value (default -99999), later resetting those cells to the original target raster’s NoData value. The output is a watershed-identifying raster where each watershed is labeled by the Strahler order of its outlet stream cell — effectively generating a Strahler-order–based watershed delineation map. No study area, time range, satellite data, or explicit geographic extent is specified in the code; all inputs are generic raster layers provided by the user via QGIS Processing interface.

name: Cut and rotate polygon rings
desc: The script cuts polygon rings (interior or exterior boundaries) at user-provided point features, identifies the nearest point on each ring segment to each cut point, sorts cut points along the ring’s vertex sequence, splits the ring into linestrings between successive cut points, and rotates the original ring so that it starts and ends at the first cut point—avoiding duplication at ring closure. It outputs a line vector layer where each feature is either a cut segment (between two cut points), the rotated full ring (starting/ending at first cut point), or the original uncut ring if no cut points match. Input is a polygon vector layer and a point vector layer; output is a LineString vector layer with same attributes and CRS as input. No raster, time-series, remote sensing, or classification logic is present—pure vector geometry manipulation in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Segment linear and polygonal features
desc: The script segments input vector features (either LineString or Polygon geometries) into smaller, regularly spaced segments based on a user-defined step distance. For polygons, it requires a centerline and uses the 'fct:disaggregatepolygon' algorithm to partition the polygon along the centerline at intervals equal to the segmentation step; for lines, it applies 'fct:segmentize' to break the line geometry into segments of approximately the specified length. Outputs are segmented vector features (LineString or MultiLineString) with topology preserved and spatially aligned to the input geometry’s structure.

name: Generate DGGS grid layer
desc: The script generates discrete global grid system (DGGS) vector layers—specifically H3, S2, A5, or rHEALPix grids—at user-specified resolutions over the current QGIS map canvas extent. It uses the vgrid QGIS processing provider (e.g., 'vgrid:h3_gen') to create polygonal grid cells, reprojects the extent from canvas CRS to project CRS for correctness, handles antimeridian wrapping, and adds the resulting memory layer to the QGIS project. No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, or classification is performed; the core functionality is on-the-fly vector grid generation driven by natural-language prompts parsed via regex and backed by Hugging Face LLM inference for intent detection and resolution extraction.

name: Rasterize XYZ bathymetry data
desc: The script converts one or more plain-text XYZ files (containing Easting, Northing, and Depth/Elevation values) into georeferenced GeoTIFF raster layers. For each input file, it auto-detects or applies a user-specified grid resolution, preserves original Z values in direct rasterization mode, or fills gaps via IDW interpolation, outputs rasters with Float32 precision and optional LZW compression, and adds them to the QGIS project. It uses a robust VRT+GDAL bridge for reliable coordinate-aware rasterization and handles multiple files individually with per-file parameter optimization.

name: Import GeoMedia MDB feature tables
desc: The script imports vector feature tables (Point, LineString, Polygon, MultiPoint) from Microsoft Access (.mdb/.accdb) databases generated by Intergraph GeoMedia. It parses binary BLOB geometry fields using a custom 3D-aware binary format decoder, reconstructs WKT geometries (including Z/depth values), and creates QGIS memory layers with added 'depth' (average Z-coordinate) and 'source' (filename) attributes. It relies on GeoMedia system metadata tables (GFeatures, FieldLookup, AttributeProperties) to discover feature classes and attribute schemas. Outputs are in-memory QgsVectorLayer objects added to the QGIS project via QgsProcessingContext, with no raster or satellite data involved — exclusively vector database import and conversion.

name: Import ship outline geometry
desc: The script imports a ship outline from a user-provided DXF file, applies geometric transformations (scale, rotation, and CRP offset), reprojects to a user-specified CRS, merges all features into a single geometry, and outputs a new QGIS vector layer (polygon or polyline) with metadata attributes including source file name, scale, rotation, CRP offsets, and output CRS. The layer is automatically renamed to match the input DXF filename.

name: Integrate GPX farm track data with CSV attributes
desc: The script integrates GPX-formatted GPS track or route files (from field surveys) with tabular farm metadata from a CSV file, producing two polygon vector layers: one for PPI (presumably 'Precision Planting Input' or similar farm operation type) and one for DA (presumably 'District/Area' or 'Data Acquisition' unit). It parses filenames to extract identifiers (e.g., 4th underscore-separated part for PPI, full stem for DA), matches them against 'FARMID' and 'GEOREF ID' fields in the CSV, loads line-based GPX sublayers ('tracks' or 'routes'), converts each line geometry into a closed polygon (using all points as a single ring), and appends both filename, source type, parsed ID, and all CSV attributes as feature properties. Outputs are EPSG:4326 polygon layers named 'joined_PPI_polygons' and 'joined_DA_polygons'. No satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or explicit geographic extent is used — input is local file system GPX/CSV; CRS is fixed to WGS84 but no spatial filtering or reprojection logic is applied. Study area, time range, and satellite data are not specified.

name: Extract KML KMZ ground overlays
desc: The script parses KML or KMZ files to locate GroundOverlay elements, extracts embedded or referenced raster images (e.g., JPEG, PNG), georeferences them using geographic bounding boxes (LatLonBox) or quadrilateral coordinates (gx:LatLonQuad), applies optional rotation correction via GCPs, and exports them as GeoTIFFs with EPSG:4326 spatial reference. Outputs include georeferenced TIFF files written to a user-specified folder, optionally auto-loaded into QGIS; non-georeferenceable or network-hosted images are reported as errors and skipped.

name: Convert ground overlay to GeoTIFF
desc: The script converts a georeferenced raster image (e.g., from KML/KMZ GroundOverlay) into a properly georeferenced GeoTIFF file using GDAL's translate tool. It supports two modes: (1) axis-aligned georeferencing via bounding box (north/south/east/west lat/lon) with EPSG:4326 spatial reference, and (2) rotated georeferencing using four ground control points (GCPs) derived from rotating the bounding box corners around its center point by a user-specified angle. Outputs include a GeoTIFF with embedded geotransform, projection (EPSG:4326), and optional GDAL creation options.

name: Create lane polygon from lane lines
desc: The script creates lane polygons by identifying left and right adjacent lane line features from a PostgreSQL/PostGIS layer (vw_lane_lines), computing their spatial relationship (proximity, azimuth alignment), buffering one side, detecting intersections, and invoking a database function (lane_poly_generate_auto) to generate polygon geometry. It relies on user selection of lane line features in QGIS, reads configuration (database connection, schema) from AppConfig.json, and uses QGIS processing tools (single-sided buffer) and PostGIS spatial functions. The output is a polygon layer generated server-side and stored in the database; no satellite or Earth observation data is used—the input is vector road infrastructure data.

name: Analyze watershed morphometric parameters
desc: The script performs watershed morphometric analysis using a basin polygon, stream network line layer, and DEM raster. It clips the DEM to the basin, calculates slope, identifies the pour point from the highest-order Strahler stream segments, computes morphometric parameters (e.g., basin area, length, relief, hypsometric integral), and generates an interpreted report with units and qualitative interpretations. It also optionally produces a hypsometric curve HTML visualization. All operations are CRS-aware and require projected coordinates (meters).

name: Simulate dam flood water depth
desc: The script simulates flood inundation depth by subtracting pixel-wise DEM elevation from a user-defined flood level (computed as DEM minimum elevation + input water level in meters). It processes a local raster DEM layer (not satellite-derived), optionally clips it to a user-provided extent, computes per-pixel water depth (zero or positive where elevation < flood level; NoData otherwise), and outputs a GeoTIFF raster of water depth. It also reports total flooded area (m²), total stored water volume (m³), and maximum water depth (m). The algorithm uses direct raster algebra on a single-band elevation raster — no time-series, no classification, no spectral indices, no external satellite data ingestion. All inputs are local QGIS raster layers; no GEE server-side operations occur — this is a QGIS Processing algorithm that runs locally using GDAL and QgsRasterBlock. Study area, DEM source, and water level are fully user-defined at runtime; no fixed geographic scope or temporal component is embedded in the code.

name: Classify land surface classes
desc: The script performs supervised machine learning classification of a multiband raster image using training points with class labels. It supports four algorithms: Random Forest (with feature importance analysis), Gaussian Mixture Model, Support Vector Machine, and K-Nearest Neighbors. Input includes a point vector layer (training data), a classification field, and a source multiband raster. It extracts spectral values at training points, validates sample size and class balance per scientific standards (e.g., ≥10×bands or ≥30 total points, ≥max(10, bands) per class), trains the selected classifier, evaluates accuracy using test split and optional k-fold cross-validation, computes Overall Accuracy, Cohen’s Kappa, and Balanced Accuracy, and outputs a classified GeoTIFF with a populated raster attribute table mapping integer class IDs to original class names. An optional HTML scientific report is generated with metrics, confusion matrix, class distribution, and (for Random Forest) band importance. The script uses GDAL for robust raster I/O and lazy imports of scikit-learn/numpy to avoid QGIS startup freeze. No specific study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is encoded — it operates on arbitrary user-provided raster and vector layers.

name: Calculate Curve Number
desc: The script calculates the USDA Soil Conservation Service (SCS) Curve Number (CN) for a user-defined study area using two global raster datasets: ESA WorldCover 2021 (land cover classification) and ORNL HYSOG (Hydrologic Soil Groups). It reprojects the input polygon to EPSG:4326, clips ESA WorldCover from a local VRT file (esa_worldcover_2021.vrt), downloads required HYSOG soil tiles dynamically via HTTP from 'https://arcgeek.com/hysog_tiles/' using bounding box intersection logic, merges and clips them to the study area, fills NoData with GDAL FillNodata, standardizes soil group values (mapping invalid codes >4 and 13–14 to Group C), aligns the soil raster to match the land cover raster’s extent and resolution using GDAL Warp, performs pixel-wise CN lookup using hydrologic condition (Poor/Fair/Good) and antecedent runoff condition (I/II/III) parameters via CSV-based lookup tables (e.g., 'default_lookup_f_ii.csv'), and outputs a final clipped CN raster. Optional intermediate rasters (land cover, soil groups) are also generated. Statistics (mean CN, S, Q) are computed post-processing. Data sources are static (ESA WorldCover 2021) and dynamic (HYSOG tiles); no satellite imagery or time-series analysis is performed — all operations are raster algebraic and geoprocessing-based.

name: Generate topographic profile
desc: The script generates an interactive HTML topographic profile by sampling elevation values from a user-provided DEM raster along a vector line feature. It computes distance-normalized elevation points, optionally applies moving-average smoothing based on total line length (window=1/3/7), supports labeling of nearby vector points (within user-defined threshold) using direct DEM sampling at their coordinates, and outputs a Plotly-based HTML file containing a chart (with smoothed elevations), summary statistics (min/max/difference, count, total distance), a toggleable table (using raw DEM values for accuracy), and a downloadable CSV. All layers must share the same CRS; automatic CRS alignment is attempted only for the line layer if mismatched with the DEM. No time-series, classification, or satellite-derived processing occurs — it is a static, single-scene terrain visualization tool operating entirely on local QGIS layers.

name: Extract upstream catchment polygons
desc: The script processes a river network vector layer and a point sites layer to extract, fix, and dissolve upstream catchment polygons for each site based on the RSC_NUMNA (lower Strahler order) and RSC_UNUMNA (upper Strahler order) attributes. It filters river segments within the Strahler order range associated with each site, repairs geometries, dissolves the resulting segments into a single polygon per site, and outputs a feature layer where each feature is a dissolved upstream catchment polygon attributed with the site’s code field value.

name: Extract upstream catchment polygons
desc: The script generates a vector layer of dissolved upstream catchment polygons for each input point site, using river network features filtered by the 'RSC_NUMNA' (lower Strahler order) and 'RSC_UNUMNA' (upper Strahler order) attributes. It applies QGIS geometry fixing and dissolution to produce topologically clean, single-part polygon features per site, each attributed with the original 'Site code'. The workflow relies entirely on vector-based hydrographic network analysis — no raster or remote sensing operations are performed. Input data sources are user-provided vector layers (river network as polygon, sites as point), with no embedded spatial extent, time range, satellite, or sensor information. All processing is local to QGIS Processing Framework using built-in algorithms ('qgis:extractbyexpression', 'qgis:fixgeometries', 'qgis:dissolve'); no GEE (Google Earth Engine) API calls or cloud-based geospatial computation occurs despite the prompt’s mischaracterization — the script is purely QGIS Python Processing, not GEE.

name: Compute route directions from polyline layers
desc: The script computes routing directions (e.g., fastest, shortest, or recommended paths) for input LineString or MultiLineString features using the openrouteservice (ORS) API. It processes each line geometry by transforming coordinates to WGS84, then sends them as ordered waypoints to ORS’s /directions or /optimization endpoints depending on configuration. Key workflow steps include: (1) extracting and reprojecting line geometries; (2) building ORS request parameters (profile, preference, extra_info, CSV weighting); (3) handling Traveling Salesman optimization per feature when enabled; (4) parsing JSON responses to generate output vector features (lines or points) with attributes like distance, duration, geometry, and optional extra info (e.g., elevation, waytype); (5) optionally exporting an ordered point layer of route steps. Outputs include a GeoJSON-compatible vector layer (QgsVectorLayer sink) in EPSG:4326 with direction attributes, and — if EXPORT_ORDER is enabled — a separate memory point layer showing step-by-step locations with sequence IDs. No study area, time range, satellite data, or local geospatial datasets are used; routing is purely API-driven and geometry-input-dependent. All data sources and processing are external to GEE — this is a QGIS plugin, not a Google Earth Engine script.

name: Compute point-to-point travel directions
desc: The script computes route geometries (LineString) between points in a QGIS vector layer using the openrouteservice (ORS) API. It supports two modes: standard point-sequence routing (e.g., A→B→C) and Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) optimization over waypoints within each (Multi)Point feature. Inputs include a point/multipoint layer, optional ID/sort fields, travel profile (e.g., driving-car), preference (fastest/shortest), extra info (e.g., elevation, waytype), and CSV-based weighting parameters. Outputs are a GeoJSON-compatible LineString layer in EPSG:4326 with attributes including distance, duration, geometry, and optionally extra info fields (e.g., elevation gain); when TSP is enabled, it also optionally exports an in-memory point layer showing optimized step order. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is involved — it is purely a web-service-driven routing algorithm integrated into QGIS processing framework.

name: Calculate network-distance interpolation iso-area
desc: The script computes an iso-area (service area) raster representing network-distance interpolation from a user-specified start point on a vector line network layer. It builds a graph using QNEAT3’s network analysis framework, calculates reachable vertices up to a maximum cost (distance or time), generates a point cloud of interpolated cost values, and produces a raster output via either QGIS TIN interpolation (faster, approximate) or QNEAT3’s custom bilinear edge-based interpolation (slower, more exact). The output is a GeoTIFF raster where each cell value represents the minimum network-based cost (distance or time) from the start point to that cell’s midpoint, accounting for entry/exit costs, directionality, speed fields, and topology tolerance. All operations assume a projected CRS; WGS84 is explicitly prohibited. No satellite, remote sensing, or temporal data is involved — input is purely vector-based (line network + point).

name: Calculate NDVI from multispectral raster
desc: The script calculates NDVI from a single input GeoTIFF file assumed to contain at least red and NIR spectral bands. It first splits the input raster into constituent bands (red, green, NIR) using a custom QGIS processing algorithm 'uas:Split_bands', explicitly routing the red band to 'R_conv.tif' and NIR band to 'B_conv.tif'. Then, it computes NDVI using the standard formula (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red) via QgsRasterCalculator, exporting the result as a GTiff to the specified output path. No satellite metadata, temporal filtering, cloud masking, or spatial subsetting is performed — the input is a local file path only. The study area, time range, sensor identity, and exact band mapping are not specified in the code; band assignment ('Red' → red.sdat, 'Blue' → nir.sdat) suggests non-standard band ordering (e.g., likely a custom UAV or multispectral camera where the third band is NIR), but no dataset name, satellite, or acquisition date is referenced.

name: Calculate NDVI from NIR and red bands
desc: The script computes the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) raster by applying the standard NDVI formula (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red) to two user-provided input rasters representing the near-infrared (NIR) and red spectral bands. It uses QGIS’s native raster calculator algorithm with no additional preprocessing (e.g., no cloud masking, no temporal filtering, no projection resampling beyond default CRS handling). The inputs are generic raster layers — no satellite metadata, acquisition dates, or georeferencing assumptions are embedded in the code. The output is a single-band floating-point raster (values typically in [−1, 1]) written to the specified destination path. All parameters — including extent, cell size (30), and CRS — are either user-defined or inherited from context (e.g., 'ProjectCrs'); no study area, time range, sensor, or data source is hardcoded or inferred from the script.

name: Calculate NDVI from bands
desc: The script computes the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) raster by applying the standard NDVI formula (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red) using two user-provided single-band raster layers: one representing the near-infrared (NIR) band and one representing the red band. It uses QGIS’s native raster calculator algorithm with explicit band referencing via layer names ('INPUT_NIR_BAND@1' and 'INPUT_RED_BAND@1'), float casting for safe division, fixed cell size (0.03), and inherits CRS and extent from the NIR input raster. No cloud masking, temporal filtering, spatial subsetting, or classification is performed — it is a direct pixel-wise algebraic operation on two aligned rasters. The output is a floating-point NDVI raster written to the specified destination path. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor identity, and geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Generate proximity distance raster
desc: The script creates a rasterized proximity layer where each pixel value represents the Euclidean distance (in meters) to the nearest input polygon feature boundary. It achieves this by iteratively buffering input polygons at decreasing distances (from user-specified maximum down to zero in equal steps), merging all buffered geometries into an in-memory vector layer with a 'BURN' attribute encoding the buffer distance, and then rasterizing that layer using GDAL's rasterize algorithm. The output is a single-band raster with values corresponding to distance intervals (e.g., 5000, 4750, ..., 0), nodata = -1, and resolution specified in degrees. Input must be in a geographic CRS (WGS84 implied), and the algorithm uses azimuthal equidistant projection centered on each feature’s centroid for accurate meter-based buffering. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are involved — it is a pure vector-to-raster distance transformation workflow operating solely on the provided polygon layer.

name: Topologise transit graph
desc: The script topologises, optimises line ordering, and computes octilinear layouts for transit network graphs using the loom backend (topo, loom, and octi stages). It accepts QGIS vector layers of nodes (points) and edges (lines), converts them to GeoJSON FeatureCollection format, passes them with JSON configuration to external C++ functions (run_topo, run_loom, run_octi), and returns processed node and edge layers. The workflow includes robust QVariant-to-Python type conversion, JSON-aware property parsing (e.g., preserving nested 'lines' arrays), null-geometry filtering, and memory-layer reconstruction with geometry-type–specific QgsGeometry construction. No satellite, temporal, or georeferenced study area is involved — inputs are generic vector layers in EPSG:4326; outputs are updated QGIS vector layers with modified geometries and attributes. All operations occur client-side within QGIS Processing Framework; no GEE server-side computation is performed.

name: Model forest road wood flux
desc: The script models the flow of harvested timber through a forest road network by generating wood-source points inside harvest polygons, assigning wood volume to the nearest road segments, and propagating flux downstream toward designated ending points (e.g., main road connections). It computes per-segment wood flux values, resolves network topology via k-d tree–accelerated spatial adjacency detection, infers directional flow using Dijkstra-based least-cost path search from line endpoints to user-provided termination points, and outputs a line vector layer with attributes: segment ID, total wood flux (volume or density-derived), upstream neighbor IDs, and downstream neighbor IDs. The algorithm enforces topological consistency by processing segments only after all upstream contributors have been resolved, preventing cycles and ensuring mass conservation in directed acyclic network traversal.

name: Generate parallel offset lines
desc: The script generates an array of adjacent parallel lines by offsetting input line features symmetrically to the left and right using configurable spacing and counts. It supports two modes: centered (with a central line plus equal numbers of lines on each side) or non-centered (offsets starting from half-spacing outward). The workflow uses two instances of a custom 'Mapped multiple offsets' script to generate right-side and left-side offset lines separately, then merges the resulting vector layers. No remote sensing data, imagery, or time-series analysis is involved; it is purely a vector geometric operation on user-provided line features. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and sensor information are not specified.

name: Retract line endpoints
desc: The script retracts (shortens) the start and end segments of input line features by specified distances. It computes vertex offsets between original and extended lines, then calculates new first and last vertex coordinates to produce a modified line geometry where the start and end portions are removed—effectively 'retracting' the line inward along its direction. The output is a vector line layer with retracted geometries, supporting only single-part (non-multi-part) lines.

name: Fetch Japanese population data
desc: The script fetches and rasterizes municipal-level population statistics for Japan using the e-Stat API (Japan's official statistics portal). It computes JIS standard 5th-level mesh codes (20m × 20m resolution in lat/long, but derived from 1/4° × 1/6° base mesh) covering the user-specified extent, groups them into 1st-level mesh codes (corresponding to ~80 km × 80 km blocks), queries the e-Stat REST API with statsDataId mapped from a local lookup file (estatId_mesh_list.txt), parses JSON responses containing population values per mesh code, converts mesh codes to centroid coordinates (using cal_meshcode5 and meshcode_to_latlong), creates a point vector layer with 'population' attribute, and rasterizes it at fixed resolution (7.5″ latitude × 11.25″ longitude ≈ 230 m × 230 m at equator) into a single-band integer raster output. The final product is a pseudo-colored population density raster with opacity 0.5 and a diverging color ramp (light purple to dark red), rendered automatically post-processing. Study area is defined by user input extent; no temporal filtering is applied — the API returns the latest published dataset for each mesh. Data source is statistical (not remote sensing), and CRS handling includes optional reprojection via TARGET_CRS and FETCH_CRS (default EPSG:6668, JGD2011 / Japan Plane Rectangular CS VIII).

name: Shift raster geolocation
desc: The script performs geospatial coordinate adjustment of raster data by applying user-defined X/Y shifts (in meters) to the raster's geotransform, optionally preceded by CRS reprojection (e.g., from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:2180). It uses GDAL Warp for reprojection and GDAL CreateCopy + SetGeoTransform for pixel grid translation. Input is any QGIS-loaded raster layer; output is a new GeoTIFF with updated georeferencing. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic analysis is involved — it is a pure georeferencing correction tool for misaligned rasters. Author-specified default target CRS is EPSG:2180 (Poland's national coordinate system), and default Y-shift is 50.0 m.

name: Download GeoDanmark infrastructure data
desc: The script downloads and unpacks official Danish geospatial vector datasets from the Dataførderen API (GeoDanmark) for a user-specified entity (e.g., 'Vejmidte', 'Bygning', 'Jernbane') and temporal variant ('current', 'bitemporal', or 'temporal'), returning a QGIS feature layer (vector) in GeoPackage format. It performs HTTP GET authentication using username/password, downloads a zipped GeoPackage, unzips it via a custom 'Unzipper' script, and outputs the first extracted layer after applying a trivial filter ('1=1') to ensure valid feature sink handling.

name: Download cadastral parcel data
desc: The script downloads and processes cadastral vector data from the Danish Datafordeler API, specifically targeting one of 20 predefined cadastral entity types (e.g., 'Jordstykke', 'Matrikelskel', 'BygningPaaFremmedGrundFlade') in either current, bitemporal, or temporal version. It performs an HTTP GET request to retrieve a GeoPackage (.gpkg) file, unzips it (via a custom 'Unzipper' script), and extracts all features (using expression '1=1') into a QGIS feature sink. The output is a vector layer containing the full geometry and attributes of the selected entity — no spatial subsetting, temporal filtering, or attribute transformation is applied. Study area is Denmark (inferred from 'datafordeler.dk', 'Matriklen', and entity names like 'Ejerlav', 'Sogn', 'Kommune'); time range is determined by the 'type' parameter ('current', 'bitemporal', 'temporal') but no explicit dates are hardcoded; data source is the Danish national cadastre (Matriklen2), delivered via REST API; no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — this is authoritative vector cadastral data.

name: Download geocoded place names
desc: The script downloads Danish topographic place name data (e.g., 'Stednavn', 'Bygning', 'Vej') from the official Danish Datafordeler API as GeoPackage files, authenticates via username/password, selects a specific entity type and temporal variant (current/bitemporal/temporal), downloads the file via HTTP GET, then unzips and loads the resulting vector layer into QGIS as a feature sink output.

name: Convert CSV WKT to PointZ
desc: The script converts a CSV file containing WKT-formatted POINT geometries and a Z (elevation) field into a QGIS vector layer of type PointZ. It auto-detects the CSV delimiter and WKT/Z field names using flexible naming conventions (e.g., 'GEOMETRIA_WKT', 'COTA', 'Z'), validates geometry type (rejecting non-POINT features), parses and normalizes Z values (handling comma decimal separators), and constructs 3D points (x, y, z). Outputs are a QgsVectorLayer with QgsWkbTypes.PointZ geometry, preserving all original attributes and CRS (epsg:4674 — SIRGAS 2000, Brazil’s official geodetic datum). No remote sensing data, time series, or classification is involved; it is a pure vector geometry transformation and elevation attribution workflow.

name: Query rural property boundaries
desc: The script queries and loads vector layers of rural properties from Brazilian land registry sources (INCRA and GeoOne) using WFS requests. It accepts a user-defined extent rectangle, transforms it to EPSG:4326 (or EPSG:4674 for GeoOne), and retrieves features intersecting that geometry. The data sources include SIGEF-certified parcels (private/public), SNCI-certified properties, settlements, quilombola territories, and pending titulation parcels. Outputs are a QGIS vector layer with added HTML-formatted attribute fields containing direct links to SIGEF for downloading CSV vertices, SHP boundaries, parcel shapefiles, and detailed parcel information. No raster processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — it is strictly a spatial query and metadata enrichment workflow for cadastral/fundiary boundaries.

name: Import SIGEF ODS parcel geometry
desc: The script imports and converts an ODS spreadsheet conforming to the Brazilian INCRA/SIGEF rural property georeferencing standard into three QGIS vector layers: (1) VERTICE (3D points with attributes like vertex code, positioning method, and sigma uncertainties), (2) LIMITE (3D line segments representing boundary segments, categorized by confrontant-type combinations), and (3) PARCELA (3D multipolygon representing the rural property perimeter). It extracts coordinate reference system (CRS) metadata from the ODS content.xml (e.g., UTM zone derived from meridian and hemisphere), parses geographic or projected coordinates (handling DMS for lat/lon), reads property metadata from an 'identificacao' sheet via OGR, applies standardized symbology (red circles for vertices, categorized colored lines for boundaries, semi-transparent pink fill for parcel), and auto-labels layers using attribute expressions. The output layers are grouped under 'Camadas da planilha ODS' at the top of the QGIS layer tree. No remote sensing data, time-series, or classification is performed — this is a structured file import and cartographic rendering workflow specific to Brazilian rural land registry documentation.

name: Download WFS layers for rural property georeferencing
desc: The script downloads and exports selected WFS layers (e.g., municipalities, conservation areas, RBMC stations, DNIT road right-of-way) within a user-defined rectangular extent using QGIS Processing Framework. It applies spatial filtering via QgsFeatureRequest.setFilterRect(), handles CRS transformation between project and source layer, and post-processes specific layers (RBMC and GPS stations) with custom symbology, labeling, and web actions. Outputs include a vector feature sink layer named after the selected layer (e.g., 'RBMC 2024') with attribute-based rendering and interactive actions.

name: Aggregate route segments by spatial coordinates
desc: The script processes a vector line layer of routes by (1) exploding each line into its constituent segments, (2) grouping segments using a custom spatial key — the concatenation of the minimum x and maximum y coordinate of each segment's geometry (i.e., 'x_min($geometry)-y_max($geometry)'), and (3) computing per-group statistics: a count of features based on a user-specified identifier field and an optional numeric sum (e.g., traffic flux). The output is a new line vector layer where each feature represents a spatially grouped segment with attached count and sum attributes.

name: Convert naturalist observations to SINP format
desc: The script converts vector-based naturalist observation data (e.g., avifauna, chiroptera, fauna) from a QGIS vector layer (shapefile, GeoPackage, etc.) into a standardized SINP-compliant output file — either a CSV or Excel (.xlsx) file conforming to the DEPOBIO V2 schema. Key steps include: (1) reprojection to EPSG:2154 (Lambert-93); (2) TAXREF taxonomic lookup using a provided CSV to assign cdNom and normalize nomCite; (3) parsing and normalizing dates (to 'DD/MM/YYYY'), times (to 'HH:MM:SS'), and effectif values (e.g., '2–5', '>10', '≈3') into denbrMin/denbrMax integers; (4) mapping ocStade values (e.g., 'adulte'→'2', 'juvénile'→'3') using a built-in dictionary; (5) generating or preserving permId (UUID v4); (6) exporting geometry as normalized WKT (e.g., 'POLYGON' in uppercase); (7) optional simplification of non-point geometries; and (8) inclusion of default SINP metadata fields (e.g., statObs='Pr', typDenbr='Co', observer='ANONYME (INDDIGO)'). Outputs are written to user-specified .csv or .xlsx (with worksheet 'DEPOBIO_V2'), optionally added to the QGIS project. No remote sensing imagery, satellite data, or time-series analysis is involved — all inputs are local vector files and reference CSVs. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified in the script.

name: Model least-cost path network
desc: The script computes a least-cost path (LCP) network between user-provided origin and destination point layers using a cost surface raster. It implements Dijkstra’s algorithm to generate cumulative cost distance maps from each origin point, then backtracks optimal paths from each origin to all destinations (excluding self-pairs). Outputs include: (1) individual GeoTIFF cost-distance rasters (named 'lcp_network_distances_N.tif') for each origin point; (2) a single memory-based line vector layer ('least cost path network') containing all computed LCPs as polylines; and (3) an exported ESRI Shapefile ('least_cost_path.shp') of the full LCP network. The script uses GDAL for raster I/O, QGIS vector geometry operations, and custom raster coordinate transformations — no Earth Engine API calls or cloud processing. All inputs (vector layers, raster) are local file paths provided via QGIS Processing parameters; no remote sensing data ingestion, time-series analysis, or satellite-derived indices are performed.

name: Calculate network-distance interpolation
desc: The script computes an iso-area (service area) raster representing interpolated network-distance or travel-time cost from a user-specified start point on a vector line network layer. It first builds a network graph using QNEAT3, then calculates reachable vertices up to a maximum cost (distance in meters or time in seconds), generating a point cloud of vertex locations and their accumulated costs. Finally, it performs spatial interpolation — either via QGIS TIN interpolation (faster, approximate) or a custom QNEAT3 method (slower, more exact) — that estimates cost values at regular raster cells by computing the shortest path distance from each cell midpoint to the nearest network edge segment, incorporating both edge-traversal cost and perpendicular distance to the segment. The output is a single-band GeoTIFF raster where pixel values represent interpolated shortest-path cost (meters or seconds). No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is involved; input is strictly a local projected vector network layer and a point coordinate. All geospatial operations are vector-network-based (graph construction, Dijkstra-like shortest paths, spatial indexing, closest-segment geometry calculations) and raster-based (grid generation, GDAL GeoTIFF writing). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Buffer vector layer geometry
desc: The script performs a geometric buffer operation on an input vector layer, creating polygon features at a user-specified distance around each input feature. It uses QGIS's native buffer algorithm with round end caps and join styles, 10 segmentation points per curve, no dissolve, and no separation of disjoint geometries. The output is a new vector polygon layer. No study area, time range, satellite data, bands, or external geospatial datasets are referenced — the script operates purely on arbitrary user-provided vector input and produces a geometrically transformed vector output. All parameters (e.g., 'distance2', 'input_layer') are abstract and runtime-defined; no hardcoded locations, dates, or data sources appear in the code.

name: Dissolve polygon boundaries
desc: The script performs a vector-based dissolve operation on an input polygon layer, merging adjacent or overlapping polygons that share the same value in a specified attribute field. It uses QGIS's native:dissolve algorithm with 'SEPARATE_DISJOINT' set to False, meaning disjoint geometries with identical attribute values are merged into single multipart features. No raster data, time-series processing, spectral analysis, classification, or external geospatial datasets are involved; the workflow is purely vector geometry aggregation. Input layer type is constrained to QgsProcessing.TypeVectorPolygon, and output is a vector feature sink of type QgsProcessing.TypeVectorAnyGeometry. All parameters (input layer, attribute field, output sink) are user-defined at runtime; no hardcoded study area, time range, satellite data, or sensor information is present in the code.

name: Reproject vector layer coordinate system
desc: The script reprojects a user-provided vector layer from its native CRS to a target CRS specified by the user (default EPSG:28992). It uses QGIS's native:reprojectlayer algorithm with no geometry conversion or additional processing. The output is a new vector layer in the target CRS, written to a feature sink. No study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification, or analysis methods are involved — this is a pure coordinate reference system transformation of vector geometries.

name: Convert PCRaster LDD to GRIB flow vectors
desc: The script converts a PCRaster-formatted Local Drainage Direction (LDD) raster into a two-band GRIB file encoding x- and y-components of flow direction. It reads the input raster's directional codes (values 1–9 per PCRaster LDD convention), maps each code to corresponding unit vector components (e.g., code 8 → (1e-7, 1)), writes them into two bands of an intermediate GeoTIFF, then rewrites that as GRIB using GDAL with band-specific metadata ('x-flow', 'y-flow'), setting GRIB band descriptions and grib_comment. The output is a single GRIB file (.grb) containing flow vector components; no study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial analysis is involved — it is a deterministic raster format conversion for hydrological flow representation.

name: Convert SAGA flow direction to GRIB
desc: The script converts a single-band raster representing SAGA flow direction indices (0–7, plus 255 for no-data) into a two-band GRIB file encoding orthogonal x-flow and y-flow components. It maps each 8-direction index to unit-vector approximations (e.g., index 1 → (√2/2, √2/2)), writes them as Band 1 (x-flow) and Band 2 (y-flow) in a temporary GeoTIFF, then re-encodes the result as GRIB using GDAL with band-specific metadata (grib_comment, description, NoDataValue=255). The output is a GRIB file compliant with MDAL 0.2.0 requirements for vector flow visualization, with no explicit study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic bounds — it operates generically on any user-provided input raster layer.

name: Calculate hypsometric curves
desc: The script computes hypsometric curves (elevation-area distribution) for polygon features intersecting a digital elevation model (DEM). It rasterizes each input polygon, clips the DEM to the polygon’s bounding box, masks DEM values outside the polygon geometry, bins elevation values into user-defined step intervals (e.g., 100 m), and accumulates area (or percentage) cumulatively from lowest to highest elevation. Outputs are CSV files per feature containing two columns: cumulative area (or %) and corresponding elevation threshold (upper bound of bin). The script uses GDAL/OGR and NumPy for raster-vector operations and does not perform classification, modeling, or time-series analysis — it is strictly a static terrain morphometric analysis tool operating on a single DEM and vector boundary layer.

name: Generate points along line
desc: The script converts vector line features into a set of point features located at the centroids of raster pixels intersected by the lines. It uses a raster layer to define the pixel grid and performs raster-to-vector coordinate conversion (mapToPixel/pixelToMap) to snap line segments to the raster grid, then applies a modified Bresenham’s line algorithm to generate one point per traversed pixel centroid along each line segment. Input is a line vector layer and a raster layer; output is a point vector layer with attributes 'id', 'line_id', and 'point_id'. No classification, time-series analysis, or thematic modeling is performed — it is strictly a geometric sampling operation. Study area, time range, satellite data, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Generate points pixel centroids inside polygons
desc: The script converts raster pixel centroids that fall within input polygon geometries into point vector features. It reads a raster layer to obtain its geotransform and CRS, then for each polygon feature (reprojected to the raster's CRS), computes the bounding box, maps it to raster pixel indices, iterates over all pixels in that bounding box, converts each pixel center to map coordinates, and tests whether that point lies inside the polygon using a prepared geometry engine. Output is a point vector layer with attributes 'id', 'poly_id', and 'point_id', where each point corresponds to a raster pixel centroid fully contained within a polygon. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification methods are involved — the script is purely geometric and raster-vector spatial intersection logic. Input sources are generic user-provided raster and polygon layers; no specific dataset paths, dates, locations, or sensors are referenced in the code.

name: Calculate network service area
desc: The script computes service areas (isochrones) from a vector line network layer (e.g., roads) and a vector point layer of start locations, using graph-based shortest-path or fastest-path analysis. It builds a directed graph with configurable directionality (forward/backward/both), optional speed-based costing, topology tolerance, and outputs: (1) boundary nodes (points) representing reachable vertices within the travel cost threshold, including interpolated edge endpoints where the cost limit intersects edges, and (2) line segments representing all traversed network edges fully or partially within the cost limit. The script also optionally includes upper/lower bound points at cost-limit intersections on edges. No remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite-derived inputs are used — it operates purely on user-provided vector layers in QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified.

name: Calculate service area from point
desc: The script computes a network-based service area from a user-specified start point on a vector line network layer, using either shortest-distance or fastest-time routing strategies. It constructs a graph from the input network with configurable directionality (forward/backward/both), optional speed fields, and topology tolerance; performs Dijkstra's algorithm to determine reachable vertices within a given travel cost; interpolates boundary points where edges exceed the cost threshold; and outputs both boundary nodes (points) and traversed edges (lines), optionally including upper/lower bound points. The algorithm is implemented via QGIS Processing using QgsVectorLayerDirector, QgsGraphBuilder, and QgsGraphAnalyzer.

name: Execute SQL on vector layers
desc: The script executes a user-defined SQL query over one or more input vector layers using QGIS's virtual layer provider. It supports aliasing input layers as 'input1', 'input2', etc., in the query, handles geometry type and CRS specification, optional UID field definition, and outputs a new vector layer (feature sink) containing the SQL result. The workflow includes: (1) validating and optionally persisting memory layers to disk for stability in modeler contexts; (2) constructing a QgsVirtualLayerDefinition with sources and expanded (expression-resolved) SQL; (3) instantiating a temporary virtual vector layer; (4) validating its geometry and attribute schema; and (5) copying features to the output sink. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, raster operations, classification, or geospatial modeling beyond SQL-based vector feature selection/join/aggregation is performed. All inputs and outputs are vector layers; no study area, time range, satellite data, or domain-specific analysis (e.g., agriculture, climate) is encoded in the script.

name: Export vector layer to SpatiaLite
desc: The script exports a QGIS vector layer (e.g., points, lines, polygons) into a SpatiaLite database file (.sqlite), optionally overwriting the table, creating a spatial index, converting field names to lowercase, dropping string length constraints, forcing single-part geometries, and specifying geometry column name, primary key field, and encoding. It uses QgsVectorLayerExporter with Spatialite provider and handles connection setup, feature iteration, and error reporting. No remote sensing data processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — it is purely a database export utility for vector data.

name: Execute and load PostgreSQL SQL query
desc: The script executes a user-provided SQL query against a configured PostgreSQL/PostGIS database connection and loads the resulting table as a valid QGIS vector layer. It constructs a QgsDataSourceUri with the SQL subquery as a virtual table, specifies geometry and ID fields for GIS interpretation, validates the resulting layer, and registers it in the QGIS project's temporary layer store and layer loading queue. No spatial or temporal filtering, classification, or analysis is performed — the task is purely database query execution and vector layer instantiation. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations are not specified because the script operates entirely on external PostGIS data without embedding or referencing any Earth observation datasets.

name: Compute average elevation
desc: The script computes the mean elevation value (in meters) over the currently visible map canvas extent using the 'srtm' raster layer loaded in the QGIS project. It creates a temporary memory vector layer representing the canvas extent as a polygon, then runs QGIS's 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' algorithm with statistic ID 2 (mean) on the SRTM raster (band 1). The result is extracted from the output feature attributes and displayed as an info message in the QGIS message bar. No time dimension, no explicit study area, no satellite/sensor/band specification in code — the SRTM source is assumed to be preloaded by the user and named 'srtm'; its provenance (e.g., SRTM v3 1-arcsec, COPERNICUS DEM) is not specified.

name: Extract zoning classification values
desc: The script extracts unique categorical values from the 'zoning' attribute field of a vector layer named 'zoning' loaded from a GeoPackage file (sf.gpkg). It uses QGIS's 'qgis:listuniquevalues' processing algorithm to enumerate distinct values in that field. The study area is implied by the dataset filename 'sf.gpkg', commonly referencing San Francisco, and the layer name 'zoning' indicates municipal land-use zoning designations. No time range, satellite data, imagery, or temporal analysis is involved — the input is a static vector dataset. Output is a Python list of unique strings (e.g., 'RESIDENTIAL', 'COMMERCIAL') printed to console and optionally saved to 'unique_values.csv'. No geospatial operations beyond attribute enumeration are performed; no classification, modeling, or raster analysis occurs.

name: Compute average elevation
desc: The script computes the mean elevation value (in meters) over the currently visible map canvas extent using a locally loaded SRTM raster layer named 'srtm'. It creates a temporary memory polygon layer from the canvas extent (reprojected to EPSG:4326), runs zonal statistics (mean only, statistic code 2) on the SRTM raster (band 1), and displays the result as a message bar notification. No time dimension is involved; the analysis is static, instantaneous, and driven solely by the user’s current QGIS map view. The study area is dynamic and undefined in code — it is whatever region is currently visible in the QGIS interface. Data source is an unnamed local raster layer named 'srtm', assumed to be SRTM-derived elevation data (e.g., SRTM v3 1-arcsecond or similar), with no explicit satellite, sensor, or band metadata provided in the script.

name: Extract ignition points from fire simulation log
desc: The script parses a text-based fire simulation log file (LogFile.txt) to extract ignition point identifiers and their corresponding raster cell indices, then converts those cell indices to geographic coordinates using the geotransform of a provided base raster layer (e.g., fuel or elevation map). It creates a QGIS vector point layer with attributes: simulation ID, 1-based cell index, pixel column (x_pixel), and pixel row (y_line), and applies a predefined QML style. The output is a styled point layer loaded into the QGIS project under a configurable group name; no satellite imagery, cloud masking, temporal filtering, or classification algorithms are used — only deterministic coordinate transformation and regex-based log parsing.

name: Match raster geotransform to reference grid
desc: The script performs a two-step GDAL-based geospatial raster alignment: (1) clips the input 'modify' raster to the exact extent of the 'matchto' raster using gdal:translate with -projwin, and (2) resizes and overwrites the geotransform of the clipped raster to precisely match the pixel size, origin, rotation, and dimensions of the 'matchto' ASCII raster using -a_gt and -outsize. Outputs a new .asc file with identical spatial metadata (origin, resolution, extent, size) as the reference raster, enabling direct pixel-wise comparison or integration in fire modeling workflows requiring consistent AII (Area of Interest Index) grids.

name: Optimize raster treatment allocation
desc: The script solves a multi-dimensional integer programming optimization problem to determine, for each pixel in an input raster stack, the optimal treatment (from a set of alternatives) and optionally the optimal team to assign, maximizing the net value gain (target_value − current_value) subject to spatial, budgetary, and capacity constraints. It reads current treatment, current value, and multiband target value rasters; cost, area, and budget parameters per treatment and per team; and outputs two classified rasters: one encoding selected treatments per pixel (with labels like 'unable', 'unchanged', or treatment names), and another encoding selected teams per pixel (with labels like 'unable', 'unchanged', or team names). Both outputs are GeoTIFFs (or GPKG rasters) styled with categorized legends matching the encoded labels.

name: Calculate self-sourced wastewater volume
desc: The script computes the volume of wastewater generated within each rioleringsgebied (sewerage area) based on three primary sources: (1) residential wastewater from BAG verblijfsobjecten (dwellings), using a configurable per-address inhabitant count (inw_per_adres) and a standard per-capita wastewater generation rate (12 L/capita/hour); (2) industrial/commercial wastewater inferred from VE (verontreinigende emissies) point sources, scaled by GRONDSLAG values; and (3) planned future wastewater from plancap (development plans), with period-specific extra DWA volumes (ExAFW_2124, ExAFW_2529, etc.) aggregated per Bemalingsgebied_ID. It also calculates theoretical POC (punt van ontlasten/point of discharge) flow rates for mixed and VGS (verbeterd hemelwater) systems based on hardened surface area (GEM_ha, VGS_ha) and runoff coefficients. Outputs include spatial layers with attributes for DWA_BAG_m3h, DWA_VEs_m3h, Extra_DWA_Periode_*_m3h, POC_Theorie_Totaal_m3h, Aangesloten_Oppervlak_Stelsel_ha, and joined hydrological infrastructure attributes (e.g., drinkwater consumption, BGT-derived surface types).

name: Calculate upstream wastewater contribution
desc: This script computes upstream wastewater contributions to rioleringsgebieden (sewer catchments) in the Dutch GeoDyn GWSW framework. It processes hydrological flow networks (afvoerboom, afvoerrelatie, afvoerpunten) and sewer catchment polygons to identify upstream contributing areas using topological relationships (e.g., 'Onderbemalingsgebied_IDs' fields), then aggregates wastewater generation estimates — derived from BAG (address-based), drinkwater consumption, and VE (verhard oppervlak / impervious surface) data — across both direct ('Eigen_Gebied') and upstream ('Onderbemalingen') sources. Key outputs include: (1) enriched upstream catchment layers with summed wastewater volumes per source (BAG/Drinkwater/VE) and POC (Piekafvoercapaciteit) theory/practice metrics; (2) identification of catchments where total wastewater demand exceeds available capacity ('Gebieden_waar_afvalwateraanbod_groter_is_dan_afvoercapaciteit'); (3) derived hydraulic performance indicators (e.g., 'Maximale_Vultijd_Droogweer_h', 'Stelselberging_mm'); and (4) standardized kengetallen (key figures) for both rioleringsgebieden and afvoerpunten, including per-hectare POC rates (mm/h). The workflow relies on custom GeoDynTools algorithms ('lis2graph', 'calc fields upstream', 'calc fields upstream POC with iteration') for graph-based upstream accumulation and iterative POC allocation.

name: Aggregate plancap-derived exfiltration per drainage area
desc: The script spatially links plancaps (planning capacity units) and other point-based infrastructure datasets (VEs, BAG verblijfsobjecten, drinkwater connections) to drainage areas (bemalingsgebieden) using geometric intersection and spatial joins. It computes summary statistics—including counts and sums of exfiltration values (ExAFW_2124, ExAFW_2529, etc.) per BEM_ID—by first intersecting plancaps with drainage polygons, filtering for largest-area plancaps per drainage area (to resolve one-to-many), aggregating exfiltration by BEM_ID, and then joining these results with statistical summaries from VEs, VBOs, and drinkwater points. Outputs include: (1) ExAFW_per_bem_id — aggregated exfiltration and concatenated PC_IDs per drainage area; (2) Meerdere_plancaps_in_bemalingsgebied — drainage areas containing ≥2 plancaps; (3) Plancap_in_meerdere_bemalingsgebieden — plancaps overlapping ≥2 drainage areas; (4) PLANCAP_PC_ID — plancaps with auto-generated PC_ID field; (5) Bemalingsgebieden_joined_stats — final joined layer with all infrastructure statistics (VE counts/sums, VBO counts, drinkwater counts/sums, and plancap exfiltration); plus auxiliary stats layers for each source.

name: Model sewer system storage capacity
desc: This script processes GWSW (Groundwater and Surface Water) sewer network data to compute total storage capacity (in m³) per drainage area (bemalingsgebied), integrating geometry-based spatial joins, buffer analysis, and volumetric calculations for pipes and manholes. It identifies and attributes key infrastructure elements (pumps, overflows, weirs, and pipe segments) to drainage areas, computes maximum allowable storage levels based on maaiveld (ground level) statistics and overflow thresholds, calculates pipe and manhole storage volumes using geometric formulas (circular, rectangular, egg-shaped cross-sections), aggregates storage per system segment (STELSEL_ID), and outputs standardized feature classes for downstream GeoDyn hydraulic modeling—including point-based area characteristics (Gebiedsgegevens_punt_tbv_stap2), line-based attributes (Gebiedsgegevens_lijn_tbv_stap2), buffered sewer networks (Rioolstelsel_buffer_10m), and summary tables of system features (Stelselkenmerken), all tagged with BEM_ID_SP identifiers linking drainage areas to sewer subsystems.

name: Convert kikker network to GeoDyn input
desc: The script converts municipal sewer infrastructure data (kikker punten/lijnen) into GeoDyn-compatible input layers by spatially joining point features (e.g., manholes, pumps) and line features (e.g., pipes, channels) to drainage catchments (bemalingsgebieden), assigning standardized BEM_ID identifiers, retaining only required hydrological and infrastructural attributes (e.g., BERGING_M3, NUMMER, VAN_KNOOPN, NAAR_KNOOP, TTOTAAL_M3), and outputting three cleaned, attribute-joined layers: (1) polygon catchments with BEM_ID, (2) point features enriched with BEM_ID_SP and original kikker attributes, and (3) line features joined with BERGING_M3 and structural identifiers — all structured for direct ingestion into the GeoDyn hydraulic modeling suite.

name: Generate drainage relationships for catchments
desc: The script constructs hydrological drainage networks (afvoerrelaties) between catchment areas (bemalingsgebieden) using linear infrastructure (leidingen/pipe networks) and point infrastructure (gebiedsgegevens_punt, e.g., manholes, storage). It identifies flow direction by extracting start/end vertices of lines, spatially joining them to catchment polygons to assign upstream (VAN_BEM_ID) and downstream (NAAR_BEM_ID) catchment IDs, filters out self-loops (drukriolering), resolves one-to-many ambiguities via sorting (by VAN_NAAR string, BERGING_M3 descending, length ascending) and deduplication, then builds a hierarchical drainage tree (afvoerboom) using hub-and-spoke lines from catchment centroids. Outputs include: (1) enriched catchment polygons with drainage attributes, (2) a cleaned VAN_NAAR relation table, (3) the selected infrastructure lines, (4) end-point features within terminal catchments, and (5) a visual drainage tree layer linking catchments by flow direction.

name: Calculate wastewater discharge prognosis
desc: The script computes a wastewater discharge prognosis for Dutch drainage basins (bemalingsgebieden) by integrating and spatially joining multiple municipal infrastructure and demographic datasets—including BGT inlooptabel (land use/infrastructure), BAG verblijfsobjecten (residential units), drinkwater connections, VE's (wastewater treatment facilities), and plancap (capacity planning zones). It applies a multi-step field calculation workflow using CSV-defined formulas (st2a, 01_ber through 11_ber, 03_obm, 09_obm, etc.) to derive per-basin metrics such as population-equivalent wastewater volumes (e.g., AW_21_24_G), infiltration/inflow (INF_HA_sum), surface water contributions (HWA_HA_sum), capacity deficits (POC_O_M3_O), and undercapacity indicators (BERGING_M3, PAR_RESULT, ZAK_RESULT). Outputs include a fully attributed polygon layer (Result_all_fields), a simplified final result (Eindresultaat) with empty fields dropped, intermediate statistics layers (Stats_vbo, Stats_drinkwater, etc.), and spatial intersection products (Bgt_intersect, Plancap_pc_id). The workflow handles optional inputs via fallback empty layers and enforces data hygiene by replacing None values with zero across >30 domain-specific fields.

name: Select points within polygons
desc: The script performs a spatial selection of point features (knooppunten) that intersect with polygon features (bemalingsgebieden) using QGIS's 'selectbylocation' algorithm. It loads a point shapefile and a polygon shapefile, runs the selection, writes the selected points to a new shapefile ('test_selection.shp'), loads a QGIS project file, adds the point layer to the project, and saves the updated project. The core operation is a vector-based spatial join/selection based on geometry intersection.

name: Validate WaPOR raster data integrity
desc: The script validates downloaded WaPOR (Water Productivity through Remote Sensing in Open access) raster datasets for common data quality issues. It scans all product subdirectories (e.g., 'AETI', 'T', 'NPP', 'RET', 'PCP', 'BF', 'Adequacy', 'CV', 'RWD', 'Biomass', 'Yield', 'WPb', 'WPy') within a user-specified local folder, performing five evidence-based checks: (1) file integrity (via QgsRasterLayer.isValid()), (2) NoData coverage percentage using GDAL (flagged if > threshold %), (3) value range validation against predefined bounds per product (e.g., AETI: 0–500 mm/dekad; BF: 0–1.5 ratio), (4) CRS consistency across all rasters, and (5) dekadal date gap detection via filename parsing (e.g., 'AETI_2020-01-D1.tif'). Outputs include a status string ('PASSED', 'WARNING', or 'FAILED'), total/valid file counts, issue count, and a detailed log with warnings. No remote GEE assets are accessed — all operations are local-file-based using QGIS Processing and GDAL. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and geometry are not specified in the script; it is a generic post-download validation tool for locally stored WaPOR Level 1 and Level 2 raster products.

name: Model coastal inundation extent
desc: The script models incremental coastal inundation extents under rising sea levels by performing raster-based elevation thresholding (using a DTM), followed by cost-distance accumulation from a shoreline vector line to simulate overland flow paths across low-lying terrain. For each sea level increment (e.g., 2.1 m → 2.3 m), it generates: (1) a binary inundation mask (1 = below/equal to sea level, else NoData), (2) a distance accumulation raster measuring shortest path cost (in cells) from the densified shoreline to each inundated cell, (3) a final inundation raster where values represent the sea level elevation (in cm) assigned only to cells reachable within the cost distance, and (4) a vector polygon layer (GeoPackage) of the inundated area. Temporary rasters are cleaned up after each iteration.

name: Hydrologically condition DTM with burned streamlines
desc: The script hydrologically conditions a digital terrain model (DTM) by burning linear hydrological adaptation features (e.g., streams, canals, or drainage lines) into it. It achieves this by: (1) dissolving input vector polylines; (2) extracting start/end vertices and sampling their Z-values from the DTM; (3) assigning linearly interpolated Z-values along each line segment based on distance from the start point and slope (ΔZ/length); (4) rasterizing the interpolated points; and (5) replacing original DTM pixel values with the interpolated Z-values where burn-in occurs, producing a hydrologically corrected DTM raster (e.g., 'DTM_with_hydro_adaptations.tif'). The output is a seamless, depression-free, flow-enforced elevation model suitable for hydrological modeling.

name: Burn building footprints into DTM
desc: The script burns building footprint polygons into a Digital Terrain Model (DTM) raster by assigning a uniform elevation value (e.g., 20 m) to each building polygon, rasterizing the buildings to match the DTM’s resolution and extent, filling NoData cells with 0, and then summing the building-raster layer with the original DTM to produce an updated DTM where buildings are elevated as impermeable barriers — resulting in a modified terrain model (DHyM_with_buildings.tif) suitable for hydrological modeling requiring explicit representation of built infrastructure.

name: Convert horseshoe adaptations to stamping lines
desc: The script converts manually digitized horseshoe-shaped hydrological adaptation features (vector polylines representing drainage or infiltration structures) into evenly spaced parallel line segments optimized for 'stamping' onto a digital height model (DHM).
