It computes DHM cell size from raster metadata, derives line spacing as 0.7× cell size, and for each valid 4-vertex horseshoe (interpreted as a trapezoidal opening), generates interpolated transverse lines between the two opposing sides (vertices 0→3 and 1→2). Features with >4 or <4 vertices are flagged, temporarily saved, simplified using the DHM cell size as tolerance, and reprocessed. Outputs are a single ESRI Shapefile ('HorseshoeLines.shp') containing all generated LineString features with integer 'id' attribute. The study area is implied by file paths but not explicitly defined in code logic; data sources are local filesystem paths — no satellite, sensor, or band information is present.

name: Model coastal storm surge inundation
desc: The script models coastal flood extents for multiple sea-level rise scenarios using a digital terrain model (DTM) and a coastline (Line At Sea). For each scenario, it first identifies all raster cells at or below the specified sea level (e.g., 1.0 m, 1.2 m, ..., up to N iterations), then computes cost-distance accumulation from the Line At Sea across those inundatable cells (using GRASS r.cost), producing a distance-accumulated raster where non-negative values indicate connected inundation pathways. It finally generates binary inundation rasters (1 = inundated, 0 = not) and converts them to vector polygons (.gpkg), exporting both .tif and .gpkg outputs per scenario.

name: Burn buildings onto DTM
desc: The script burns building footprints (as vector polygons) onto a digital terrain model (DTM) or digital height model (DHyM) by rasterizing building polygons with a user-specified height value, filling NoData cells with zero, and summing the resulting building-height raster with the input DTM to produce an augmented surface model where buildings are elevated above ground level. Inputs are a local DTM raster file (path provided), a vector layer of building polygons (OGR-readable, e.g., Shapefile or GeoPackage), and a scalar height value (e.g., 20.0 m). The workflow includes: (1) adding an 'elevation' attribute field to the building layer and populating it uniformly with the height value; (2) rasterizing the building layer using GDAL's rasterize algorithm aligned to the DTM’s extent, resolution, and CRS; (3) replacing NoData values in the rasterized output with 0 using QGIS's Fill NoData tool; (4) summing the processed building raster and the original DTM via raster calculator. Outputs are three geotiff files in the specified output folder: 'Building_raster.tif', 'Building_raster_NONull.tif', and 'DHyM_with_buildings.tif'. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial identifiers are referenced — all inputs are local file paths provided at runtime. The script operates entirely within QGIS Processing Framework using GDAL and native QGIS algorithms, with no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls or cloud-based assets.

name: Trace coastal line segment
desc: The script extracts a line segment from a vector layer named 'kystlinje' (Danish/Norwegian for 'coastline') between one or two user-provided point features ('trace_start' and optionally 'trace_end'), supporting both open polylines and closed polygons. It performs spatial proximity search using bounding boxes, geometry normalization (converting polygons to boundary polylines, handling multi-part geometries), closest-segment snapping, index-based directional tracing (forward/backward along vertices), and length-aware path selection for closed loops (e.g., choosing shortest or longest arc between start/end on a polygon). The output is a new vector layer (GeoPackage/Shapefile/GeoJSON) containing a single traced LineString feature with attributes: id (1) and shape_len (length in map units), added to the QGIS project and zoomed to. Study area is implied by layer names and file path but not explicitly defined; no satellite, temporal, or raster data is involved — this is purely vector geometry processing within QGIS desktop.

name: Extract tent structures
desc: The script identifies tent-like structures (e.g., IDP camp shelters) in RGB satellite imagery by computing two spectral indices — F1 (green/red/blue ratio-based edge contrast) and F3 (green minus min(red,blue), thresholded to zero) — normalizing them using linear fuzzy membership, applying Otsu thresholding and segmentation, intersecting the resulting binary built-up masks, masking out bare soil areas (derived from Soil Brightness Index sampled from user-provided bare-ground points), performing morphological opening to refine tent-shaped objects, and finally polygonizing and filtering for DN=1 to output a vector layer of tented structures. The workflow is explicitly designed for rapid identification of temporary shelters in humanitarian response contexts, with post-processing guidance for rectanglify and manual cleaning.

name: Extract tented structures in IDP sites
desc: The script extracts temporary shelter (tent) structures within known Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites using RGB satellite imagery. It computes two spectral indices—F1 (based on normalized green/red/blue ratios and their absolute deviations) and F3 (a vegetation-suppressed brightness index derived from green minus min(red,blue))—normalizes them via linear fuzzy membership, thresholds them using Otsu’s method, segments the resulting layers, intersects the segmented built-up candidates with buffered known IDP site polygons, optionally removes overlapping known buildings, and outputs cleaned polygon geometries representing probable tented areas. The workflow includes bare soil sampling to mask non-urban surfaces, morphological opening to regularize binary structures, polygonization, geometry cleaning (fixing, multipart-to-singlepart, hole removal), and conditional output routing based on availability of IDP site boundaries and building footprints.

name: Convert raster to PCRaster format
desc: The script converts an input GDAL-supported raster layer (e.g., GeoTIFF, etc.) into the PCRaster format, preserving spatial metadata and applying user-specified PCRaster data types (Boolean, Nominal, Ordinal, Scalar, Directional, or LDD) via GDAL Translate with appropriate output data types and VS_* metadata options. It does not perform geospatial analysis, classification, modeling, or time-series processing — only format conversion. Input source, study area, time range, satellite/sensor, bands, and geographic extent are not referenced, used, or inferred in the code.

name: Fix vector layer geometries
desc: The script runs QGIS's native 'fix geometries' algorithm on an input vector file (e.g., shapefile, GeoPackage) to repair invalid or malformed geometries (e.g., self-intersections, unclosed rings, duplicate nodes) and writes the cleaned result to a specified output file. It initializes QGIS in headless mode, registers native processing algorithms, loads the input as a QgsVectorLayer, and executes the 'native:fixgeometries' algorithm with no additional parameters beyond INPUT and OUTPUT. No study area, time range, satellite data, classification, or visualization is involved — it is purely a geometric validation and correction utility. All inputs and outputs are file paths provided via command-line arguments; no geospatial metadata, CRS handling, or attribute manipulation is present in the code.

name: Extract pavement edge vertices
desc: The script processes a vector layer named 'PAVEMENT_EDGE' to generate a coarse grid (2500 m spacing) over a fixed coordinate range in EPSG:2263 (NAD83 / NY Long Island), intersects the pavement edges with each grid cell, extracts all geometry vertices from the intersection result, and exports the vertex coordinates (as X,Y) to individual CSV files named '<i>_<j>.csv'. The grid is hardcoded to cover a region starting at (910000, 115000) with row/column indices i∈[0,4] and j∈[0,9], but the y-range calculation erroneously reuses 'i' instead of 'j', indicating an intent to tile a rectangular AOI — likely NYC metro area given EPSG:2263 and coordinate magnitudes. Output is a set of point-coordinate CSVs for downstream pavement geometry analysis or digitization QA.

name: Assess autobahn impact on valuable habitats
desc: The script performs a spatial impact assessment of an autobahn infrastructure project on ecologically valuable habitats in Switzerland. It loads vector layers for environment (habitat classification with attributes 'ffh_typ_nr', 'geschuetzt_biotop', 'bedeutend_gruenland_typ') and autobahn linear infrastructure; creates nested buffers (20 m, 100 m, 300 m) to model physical footprint and broader ecological disturbance zones; unions these buffers into cumulative impact areas; intersects them with the environment layer to isolate affected habitat polygons; subsets and intersects valuable vs. non-valuable habitats using attribute queries; applies categorized symbology by habitat type ('ffh_typ_text', 'bfn_biotop_text') for visual differentiation; and overlays a semi-transparent raster basemap. Outputs include styled map layers: 'Impact Area Intersected', 'Valuable Intersected', and 'Non-Valuable Intersected' — enabling spatial quantification and visualization of habitat loss/fragmentation due to road construction.

name: Analyze autobahn impact on habitats
desc: The script analyzes the spatial impact of Autobahn (highway) construction on terrestrial habitats in a Swiss study area using vector geoprocessing. It loads an Environment layer (containing habitat attributes such as 'ffh_typ_nr', 'geschuetzt_biotop', and 'bedeutend_gruenland_typ') and an Autobahn linear layer from local GeoPackage files. It creates three concentric buffers (20 m, 100 m, and 300 m) around the Autobahn to represent physical footprint and cumulative ecological impact zones, then unions them into a single 'Impact Area'. It intersects this impact zone with the Environment layer to extract 'Impact Area Intersected'. It then subsets valuable habitats (using attribute queries for FFH sites, protected biotopes, and significant grassland types) and non-valuable habitats, intersecting each with the impact area to produce 'Valuable Intersected' and 'Non-Valuable Intersected' layers. Final outputs include categorized symbology by habitat type (e.g., 'ffh_typ_text', 'bfn_biotop_text'), opacity-adjusted visual layers, and layer reordering for cartographic clarity — all within QGIS Desktop. No time-series analysis or remote sensing data is used; inputs are static vector layers. Study area is implied to be in Switzerland (CH) via file path '\svm-c113.hsr.ch\zkang\Desktop\QGIS-Steilkurs_MSE_Maerz_2017\...' and CRS EPSG:31467 (DHDN / Gauss-Krüger zone 3, used in Germany and parts of Switzerland).

name: Assess autobahn infrastructure impact on environment
desc: The script performs a spatial impact assessment by generating concentric buffer zones (20m, 100m, 300m) around an Autobahn vector layer, unions them to create a cumulative 'Impact Area', and intersects this area with an 'Environment' vector layer to identify spatially overlapping zones — producing a final 'Intersected' vector layer representing environmentally sensitive areas affected by autobahn proximity.

name: Export terrain for FDS simulation
desc: The script exports geospatial terrain data (DEM, landuse, texture, wind, fire layers) into Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) input format. It reprojects inputs to UTM, clips and interpolates a DEM to user-specified resolution (pixel_size), aligns domain extent to DEM pixel grid, generates sampling points, computes terrain geometry (OBST or GEOM), defines FDS MESH parameters (cell_size, nmesh), and writes FDS input files (.fds) including &OBST, &SURF, &GEOM, &WIND, &INIT, and texture image assets. Inputs are QGIS project layers (raster/vector); outputs are FDS case files in the specified fds_path folder. No satellite imagery processing occurs — all inputs are local GIS layers; no time-series analysis is performed.

name: Rasterize species range polygons
desc: The script converts vector-based species range polygons into individual species-specific raster layers, where each raster encodes presence (value 1) for a single species within its geographic range; it first adds a presence field to the input polygon layer, then iterates over unique species values in the Species_Attribute field, exports one shapefile per species, and rasterizes each using GDAL with fixed dimensions (2000×1000 pixels), producing one GeoTIFF per species named after the species (with spaces replaced by underscores) in the specified output directory.

name: Model noise exposure levels
desc: The script computes acoustic noise levels (Lgeneric, Lday, Levening, Lnight, Lden) at receiver points using source emissions from point and line (road) layers, incorporating geometric spreading, atmospheric absorption, diffraction (2D and 3D), and terrain/building obstruction modeling. It supports multiple noise emission models: POWER_P/POWER_R, CNOSSOS (road and generic), NMPB, and frequency-based octave-band inputs. Outputs include updated receiver point layers with computed noise levels, optional ray-tracing shapefiles (direct, diffracted, and 3D vertical diffraction paths), and automatic symbology application in QGIS. Input data are local vector layers (receivers, sources, obstacles) — no remote sensing or satellite data are used; all processing is deterministic acoustic propagation in GIS space.

name: Extract building diffraction points
desc: The script processes a vector layer of building footprints to identify and extract geometric vertices (points) that serve as acoustic diffraction points for noise modeling. It reads building polygons, handles multipart geometries, removes pseudo-vertices by angular coefficient comparison (with tolerance m_delta = 0.01), eliminates duplicate coordinates within each building (via set() conversion), then filters across all buildings to retain only vertices appearing exactly once (i.e., non-shared corners — likely exterior, non-adjacent building corners). The output is a point shapefile containing these unique, non-coincident building corner points, intended as input for opeNoise — a QGIS plugin for environmental noise computation. No satellite or raster data is used; inputs are local OGR-readable vector files (e.g., shapefiles), with CRS preserved from the input buildings layer. Study area, time range, sensor, bands, and satellite are not specified in the code.

name: Generate road emission points for noise modeling
desc: The script processes vector layers representing noise sources (e.g., roads) and receivers (e.g., buildings or monitoring points) to generate a memory-based point layer of emission points along source lines. It computes the minimum distance from each source feature to nearby receiver points within a user-defined search radius ('research_ray'), derives a segment length (half the minimum distance, clamped to ≥2 m), and densely samples the source line geometry (polyline vertices and interpolated points) at that spacing. Each emitted point is attributed with unique IDs (global and per-source) and the computed segment length ('d_rTOe'). The output is a QgsVectorLayer in memory containing these emission points — intended as input for subsequent acoustic propagation modeling (e.g., in opeNoise). No raster data, satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or classification is involved; all operations are vector-based geometric sampling and spatial indexing using QGIS Python API. Study area, time range, satellite data, and coordinate reference system are inherited from input layers but not specified in the script.

name: Create viewport polygon layer
desc: The script creates a memory-based polygon vector layer representing the current QGIS map canvas extent (viewport), defined by its four corner coordinates. It constructs a single rectangular polygon feature from the canvas's minimum and maximum x/y coordinates, commits it to a new memory layer with the project's CRS, and adds it to the QGIS project. No analysis, classification, time-series processing, or external data ingestion occurs — the task is purely cartographic/geometry generation for spatial context visualization or masking. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification methods, and exported products are all not specified.

name: Copy and clip vector feature class
taskType: Exporting a layer to the geopackage format
desc: The script copies a source vector layer (e.g., from a shapefile or GeoPackage) to a new GeoPackage file at a specified output path. If a mask tuple is provided, it clips the source features to the geometry of a filtered 'sample_frame_features' layer (filtered by 'sample_frame_id'), performing coordinate transformation and intersection-based clipping. The output is a GeoPackage layer containing either the full source layer or its spatially clipped subset. No raster data, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived products are involved — this is purely a vector I/O and geometric clipping operation within QGIS using GDAL/OGR-backed QgsVectorFileWriter and QgsVectorLayer APIs.

name: Import vector layer to GeoPackage
desc: The script imports a QGIS vector layer into a GeoPackage file, performing optional attribute injection, field mapping, metadata JSON serialization, geometry clipping, reprojection to EPSG:4236, and feature filtering. It supports direct field copying, value mapping via ImportFieldMap, and conditional layer creation/appending in the target GeoPackage. Outputs include a written GeoPackage layer (or new file), with logging and signal emission of input/output/skipped feature counts. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing occurs — it is purely a GIS data ingestion and transformation utility for QGIS vector layers.

name: Load vector layer from PostgreSQL
desc: The script loads a vector layer into QGIS by executing a user-defined SQL query against a configured PostgreSQL/PostGIS database connection. It validates the database connection, constructs a QgsDataSourceUri with the SQL as a subquery, creates a QgsVectorLayer object, applies a simple black line symbology, and registers the layer in the QGIS processing context for output. The outputs include a status code (integer), a message string, the layer ID, and the layer name (either user-specified or default). No geospatial analysis, classification, time-series processing, or remote sensing operations are performed — it is purely a data retrieval and layer registration utility for the RAePa (Réseau d’Assainissement et d’Eau Potable) QGIS plugin. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Resample Copernicus vegetation products
desc: The script resamples Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) vegetation biophysical variables (e.g., NDVI, LAI, FAPAR) from native 333 m resolution to a consistent 1 km spatial resolution while preserving the original 1 km time-series spatial extent (−180° to 180° longitude, −60° to 80° latitude). It applies two parallel resampling pathways: (1) 'average' resampling for continuous variables (e.g., NDVI), including scaling and georeferenced cropping; (2) 'mode' resampling on a reclassified version of the input (using user-defined class intervals, e.g., [-1,1,1,1,255,0]) for categorical or integer-coded data. The final output is the pixel-wise multiplication of the average-resampled and mode-resampled rasters — effectively blending continuous-value smoothing with dominant-class preservation — then compressed and exported as a GeoTIFF.

name: Resample Copernicus vegetation product to 1km
desc: The script resamples high-resolution (333m) Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) vegetation biophysical products (e.g., NDVI, LAI, FAPAR) — originally derived from Sentinel-3 — to a consistent 1 km spatial resolution matching legacy PROBA-V time series. It applies a two-path resampling workflow: (1) an 'average' resampling for continuous variables (preserving radiometric integrity via scaling and offset correction), and (2) a 'mode' resampling for categorical or integer-coded layers (e.g., land cover flags or quality masks); then combines them via raster algebra to produce a final 1 km output with UInt32 encoding, DEFLATE compression, and proper nodata handling. The reclassification step (using user-defined thresholds like [-0.08,0.92,1,0.92,255,0]) converts floating-point reflectance/indices into discrete classes before mode resampling, while the final formula applies offset removal and scaling (e.g., (PVo − (1−offset) − offset) × scaling) to restore integer physical units (e.g., scaled LAI × 250).

name: Resample Copernicus land cover raster
desc: The script resamples input Copernicus Global Land (CGLS) vegetation-related rasters (e.g., NDVI, FAPAR, LAI) from native 333 m resolution to 1 km resolution while preserving the standard global spatial extent (−180° to +180° longitude, −60° to +80° latitude). It applies two parallel resampling workflows: one using 'average' (for continuous variables) and another using 'mode' (for categorical or discrete classes), followed by pixel-wise multiplication of the two outputs. The final output is a compressed GeoTIFF at 1 km resolution with DEFLATE compression. The script explicitly targets Copernicus GL products distributed via QGIS plugin interface, and references PROBA-V (pre-July 2020) and Sentinel-3 (post-July 2020) as underlying sensors — though no actual GEE data loading occurs in this code, as it operates purely on user-provided local raster layers within QGIS. All geospatial operations (reclassify, translate, clip, raster calculator) are executed via GDAL/QGIS Processing algorithms, not Earth Engine APIs. No time-series processing, cloud masking, or temporal filtering is performed — the script is strictly spatial resampling and reclassification.

name: Resample Copernicus land cover raster
desc: The script resamples an input Copernicus Global Land (CGLS) raster (e.g., NDVI, FAPAR, LAI at 333 m) to 1 km resolution while preserving the spatial extent and temporal consistency of existing 1 km time series. It applies a two-path resampling workflow: (1) 'average' resampling for continuous variables (e.g., NDVI), and (2) 'mode' resampling for categorical or integer-coded layers (after reclassification via user-defined table), then multiplies the two outputs. The final output is a compressed GeoTIFF at 1 km resolution (pixel size = 1/112° ≈ 0.00893°, ~1 km at equator), clipped to global bounding box [−180, −60, 180, 80] (WGS84). Input raster statistics (min/max) are auto-detected; reclassification table and resampling method are user-configurable parameters. No explicit time filtering or temporal aggregation is performed — the script operates on a single static raster layer provided as input.

name: Clip raster by vector mask
desc: The script clips the input raster 'AestheticMax.tif' to the spatial extent defined by the vector layer 'TestVectorExtent.shp' using GDAL's cliprasterbymasklayer algorithm. It applies nodata value -9999, preserves original resolution, and outputs a georeferenced GeoTIFF at '/Users/ep9k/Desktop/output_clip.tif'. The operation is a geometric masking (not classification or temporal analysis), with no reprojection, resampling, or spectral processing. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified — the inputs are local file-based rasters and vectors with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata.

name: Reclassify aesthetic suitability raster
desc: The script applies a conditional reclassification to the input raster 'AestheticMax.tif', where pixel values equal to 255 are set to 0, and all other values are preserved unchanged. This is implemented using GDAL's raster calculator with the formula '(A != 255) * A', operating on Band 1 of the input raster. The output is written to '/Users/ep9k/Desktop/reclassoutput.tif' and loaded into QGIS. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis methods (e.g., classification algorithms, masking, compositing) are present in the script — it is a simple per-pixel arithmetic reclassification of a pre-existing local GeoTIFF file. Data source is a local file with no temporal or sensor metadata evident in the code; the raster appears to represent an aesthetic suitability index (possibly derived from landscape metrics), but its origin, spatial extent, resolution, projection, and generation method are not specified.

name: Classify bicycle network suitability
desc: The script classifies road segments from the Swedish National Road Database (NVDB) into bicycle infrastructure suitability categories (VGU and LTS) using geometric, traffic, speed, and functional attributes. It buffers existing bike infrastructure to detect proximity, applies rule-based logic to assign VGU (required infrastructure level) and LTS (Level of Traffic Stress) scores, and computes a stress ratio. Inputs include a line network layer with fields like 'vagtr_474' (road type), 'vagha_6' (operational status), 'klass_181' (class), 'f_hogst_225'/'b_hogst_225' (speed limits), and 'adt_f_117' (annual daily traffic). The output is a vector layer with new attributes: rlid, from_measure, to_measure, oper, class, speed, adt, vgu, lts, ratio, and gc (boolean indicating proximity to existing bike infrastructure). No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are vector layers (network, origins, destinations, work, school) and optional CSV socio-economic data — all assumed to be local/regional administrative or transport datasets. Study area and time range are not specified.

name: Calculate origin-destination job flow matrices
desc: The script calculates Euclidean distance-based origin-destination (OD) relation matrices for 15 job types (SNI_01 to SNI_15) within a 20 km threshold. It processes two QGIS vector layers — origins (Centroids_A3.shp) and destinations (Centroids_A5.shp) — both containing centroid geometries and job-count fields. For each job type field (indexed i=2 to 16 in the layer’s field list), it selects only origin features where that job count > 0, creates subset shapefiles (O{i}.shp and D{i}.shp), then runs the SAGA 'pointdistances' algorithm to compute pairwise distances from selected origins to selected destinations (not all destinations — critically, destinations.selectByIds([k for k in id_list]) reuses the *same* origin ID list, implying destination selection is misaligned and likely erroneous, but the intent is symmetric filtering per job type). Output is a DBF file (OD{i}.dbf) per job type containing distance records up to 20,000 m. The study area is implied by file paths and layer names but not geographically bounded in code; no temporal data is used — the SCB dataset (Statistics Sweden) is static tabular data joined to centroids. No satellite, imagery, or time-series processing occurs.

name: Delineate forest stands from canopy height models
desc: The script performs automated forest stand delineation using a 10m-resolution Vegetation Height Model (VHM) as primary input. It applies a hierarchical classification algorithm (run_stand_classification) that segments the VHM into homogeneous height-based stands, incorporating optional coniferous proportion and vegetation zone rasters for stratification. The workflow includes post-processing steps: simplification and elimination of small polygons, merging of geometrically and structurally similar neighboring stands (based on hdom relative difference), clipping to a user-provided perimeter boundary, gap elimination, calculation of dominant height (DG) using a higher-resolution (150 cm) VHM, addition of coniferous proportion attributes, attribution with forest site and vegetation zone codes via spatial join, and final cleanup (field removal, project packaging). Outputs include a GeoPackage vector layer (TBk_Bestandeskarte.gpkg) containing stand polygons with attributes such as DG, coniferous proportion, VegZone_Code, ForestSite, area, perimeter, and geometry; auxiliary files (log, config, tmp layers); and a QGIS project file.

name: Export forest stand map for WIS2
desc: The script exports a QGIS vector layer of forest stands into a WIS2-compliant XML file (wis2_stands_export_YYYYMMDD-HHMM.xml) containing per-stand attributes: ID, area_m2, DG (dominant height), hdom (mean dominant height), ddom (0), age (0), ten tree species proportions (p100–p800), and siteCategory. It supports spatial joining of forest site categories from an external polygon layer, handles missing/NULL field values via defaults (e.g., '7a' for site category, 'NH' for tree species), enforces sum-to-100 normalization of species proportions with rounding correction, and writes standardized XML with <Stand> elements under a <dataroot> root. The script operates entirely on user-provided vector inputs (no raster or remote sensing data); no study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is involved — it is a postprocessing/export tool for existing stand maps. All logic is evidence-based from parameter definitions (e.g., FIELD_P100, FIELD_FOREST_SITE_CATEGORY), join operations ('native:joinattributesbylocation'), and XML structure generation.

name: Calculate area-weighted average perimeter
desc: The script computes the Area-weighted Average Perimeter (AwaP) metric for urban blocks intersecting or contained within user-defined boundary polygons. It processes vector layers of urban blocks and boundaries through geometry cleaning (fix geometries, dissolve, multipart-to-singlepart, delete holes), optional dead-end removal via buffer-in/buffer-out morphological filtering, and spatial selection (intersection/within/partial overlap based on user thresholds). For each boundary polygon (or dissolved union), it calculates AwaP = Σ(Perimeter × Area) / Σ(Area) across qualifying blocks, then outputs either: (1) a set of styled block layers annotated with AwaP value per block (when coloring by Area or Perimeter), or (2) a boundary layer where each feature is attributed with its computed AwaP value (when coloring 'by AwaP', i.e., grid-cell-level AwaP mapping). Outputs are emitted as QgsVectorLayer objects with attribute tables containing 'awap_id', 'Area', 'Perimeter', and 'AwaP' fields.

name: Model reservoir inundation and dam-modified DEM
desc: The script models the construction of a dam on an existing digital elevation model (DEM) by first buffering the dam crest vector layer, computing elevation-dependent fill levels along buffer rings using dam wall slope geometry (1:H), rasterizing those fill levels to create a water-surface elevation surface, then merging it with the original DEM via conditional raster algebra (keeping the higher of DEM or fill level at each cell) to produce a new DEM containing the raised dam structure. Finally, it uses GRASS r.lake to simulate flooding from a user-provided interior point up to a specified water level (dam top minus water depth), generating a raster of the resulting lake extent/depth. Outputs are (1) a new lake raster layer representing flooded area/depth, and (2) a modified DEM raster layer incorporating the engineered dam structure.

name: Generate sidewalk network from OSM data
desc: The script generates a full sidewalk network (as LineString features in EPSG:4326) within a user-specified bounding box by fetching and processing OpenStreetMap (OSM) road and optional building data. Key workflow steps include: (1) parsing the input extent (QgsRectangle) and transforming it to EPSG:4326; (2) computing a local UTM CRS for internal metric operations; (3) querying OSM Overpass API for highway=* ways using a bbox-based query string with configurable highway type filters (e.g., motorway, residential, footway); (4) cleaning, clipping, and reprojecting fetched road data; (5) assigning street widths (default or per-class); (6) generating protoblocks via polygonization of street networks; (7) filtering protoblocks based on pre-existing sidewalk density (footway=sidewalk); (8) optionally fetching and clipping OSM building footprints for exclusion zone logic; (9) calling the core sidewalk generation function (generate_sidewalk_geometries_and_zones) which produces sidewalk lines, exclusion/sure zones, and width-adjusted streets — all in local TM; (10) generating crossings and kerbs by detecting street endpoint intersections and constructing perpendicular crossing geometries with kerb points at 25% interpolation; and (11) reprojecting final outputs (sidewalks, crossings, kerbs) back to EPSG:4326. Debug layers (protoblocks, exclusion zones, sure zones, width-adjusted streets) are optionally saved in their native CRS (EPSG:4326 for protoblocks, local TM for others). No satellite, sensor, or time-series data is used — inputs are exclusively vector OSM data fetched live via Overpass API.

name: Generate sidewalk network from polygon
desc: The script generates a full sidewalk network (sidewalk lines, crossings, kerbs, and debug protoblocks) for a user-provided input polygon area by fetching OpenStreetMap (OSM) road, building, and address data. It performs OSM query construction via bbox-based Overpass API calls (using osm_query_string_by_bbox and get_osm_data), clips and filters roads by highway type and width, removes dead-end streets, polygonizes the street network into 'protoblocks', filters protoblocks based on pre-existing sidewalks (footway=sidewalk), and runs a custom sidewalk generation logic (generate_sidewalk_geometries_and_zones) that computes buffered sidewalk centerlines with curve radii, building-aware width adjustments, and exclusion/sure zones. Outputs are delivered in EPSG:4326 (sidewalks, crossings, kerbs) and optionally local transverse Mercator CRS (protoblocks debug). No satellite, aerial, or time-series imagery is used — exclusively vector OSM data. Study area is defined dynamically by the input polygon; no fixed location or time range is embedded.

name: Generate protoblocks from OSM street network
desc: The script generates protoblocks — polygonal parcels representing urban blocks — by fetching OpenStreetMap (OSM) street centerlines within a user-provided input polygon, filtering them by highway type (e.g., motorway, residential, footway) using configurable boolean checkboxes, clipping to the polygon, reprojecting to a local transverse Mercator CRS for metric accuracy, removing unconnected line segments (dangles), and polygonizing the cleaned street network. The final output is a vector layer of polygons in EPSG:4326, with no attributes. Data sources are exclusively OSM query results (no satellite or remote sensing data); the study area is fully user-defined via an input polygon layer; time range is not applicable (OSM is versioned but no temporal filter is applied); and all geospatial operations are vector-based (reprojection, clipping, topology cleaning, polygonization).

name: Generate urban protoblocks from OSM street network
desc: The script generates polygonal 'protoblock' units by fetching OpenStreetMap (OSM) street centerline data (ways) within a user-provided bounding box (extent), filtering by highway type (e.g., motorway, residential) and minimum width threshold (≥0.5 m), removing unconnected line segments, and polygonizing the cleaned street network. It further analyzes pre-existing mapped sidewalks (highway=footway AND footway=sidewalk) to compute per-protoblock sidewalk length and classifies protoblocks as having 'existing sidewalks' if the normalized sidewalk coverage ratio exceeds cutoff_percent_protoblock. The final output is a vector layer of polygons in EPSG:4326 with attributes 'existing_sidewalks' (Boolean) and 'existing_sidewalks_length' (meters). Input extent CRS is transformed to EPSG:4326 if needed; OSM data is fetched via Overpass API using a bbox query string; reprojection uses a local Transverse Mercator (TM) CRS centered on the bbox longitude for geometric operations; no satellite, aerial, or temporal imagery is used — only vector OSM data. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified.

name: Select forest contour and isolated trees
desc: The script processes pre-generated tree crown polygons and treetop point layers to identify trees located on the forest contour (i.e., edge trees) and isolated trees. It uses zonal statistics (max value extraction) from a binary forest-selected raster (forestSelectedPath) over crown polygons to flag crowns intersecting forest edges; selects crowns where '_max' == 1.0; then joins treetops to crowns via spatial intersection to assign treetop IDs ('tid') to crowns; generates Delaunay triangulation of treetops; filters out triangles whose perimeter exceeds a user-defined threshold ('MaxTrianglePerimeter'); and finally deletes unselected crowns and corresponding treetops. Inputs are file-based (not GEE ImageCollections): precomputed 'crowns.shp', 'treetops.shp', and 'forest_selected.tif' — implying prior remote sensing or LiDAR-based tree detection and forest masking. No satellite imagery, cloud masking, spectral indices, or time-series analysis occurs in this script — it is a post-processing workflow for structural forest segmentation. Study area, time range, sensor, bands, and satellite are not specified in the code.

name: Generate street lane markings
desc: The script processes OpenStreetMap (OSM) road network data to generate detailed, geometry-accurate street lane markings for cartographic rendering in the Berlin 'Straßenraumkarte' micromap. It parses OSM highway line features with complex tagging (e.g., `lanes`, `turn:lanes`, `width:lanes`, `cycleway:left`, `placement`, `lane_markings`), resolves directional and topological relationships between adjacent segments (including dual carriageways and placement transitions), computes per-lane offsets using precise width and buffer attributes, generates parallel lane centerlines via array offsetting, assigns lane-specific properties (access type, turn direction, marking style, surface colour), clips markings at junctions and crossings, and outputs a final GeoJSON layer (`marked_lanes.geojson`) containing individual lane geometries with rich semantic attributes for stylized vector rendering.

name: Calculate water depth from bathymetric point cloud
desc: The script processes an airborne LiDAR point cloud (COPC format) classified with standard ASPRS classes to derive water depth. It first separates bathymetric points (Class 40) and water surface points (Class 41), then generates a 1 m resolution DTM (from Class 2 + 40) and a 1 m watersurface raster (from Class 2 + 41); computes water depth as the difference (watersurface − DTM); derives 1 m depth contours; calculates point density at 2 m resolution over bathymetric points (Class 2 + 40); masks depth to 0.5–2.5 m range; masks density to ≥20 pts/4 m²; and finally applies a boolean AND to produce a 2 m resolution raster indicating locations where both sufficient density and valid depth co-occur — used for quality control of topobathymetric products.

name: Extract land markers subset
desc: The script loads a WFS layer named 'landemaerker' from the URL 'https://rida-services.test.septima.dk/ows?map=land_attraktioner' with CRS EPSG:25832. It defines a rectangular bounding box using explicit UTM coordinates (minx=710320, miny=6170841, maxx=728036, maxy=6186120) in EPSG:25832, selects features intersecting that rectangle, materializes the selection into a new in-memory vector layer, validates it, adds it to the QGIS project, and then exports the subset to a GeoPackage file at '/data/WFS_subset.gpkg'. The final output is a saved GeoPackage layer named 'saved_subset' containing the spatially filtered landemaerker features. No time filtering, spectral analysis, classification, or satellite data is involved — this is a static WFS feature subsetting and export workflow.

name: Buffer vector features
desc: The script performs a geometric buffer operation on an input vector layer (points, lines, or polygons) using a user-specified integer distance in map units. It applies the native QGIS buffer algorithm with round end caps and join styles, no dissolve, and 4 segmentation segments per quarter circle. The output is a new polygon vector layer representing the buffered zones around the input features. No raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, classification, or thematic analysis is involved — it is purely a deterministic geoprocessing operation on vector geometry. Study area, time range, data sources, sensors, bands, and satellite information are not specified in the code.

name: Compute viewshed visibility
desc: The script performs iterative viewshed analysis for each observer point in the 'observers' vector layer against the 'HELIX_test' DEM raster. For each observer, it first creates a temporary single-point layer, then runs the 'visibility:Viewshed' algorithm (QGIS Visibility plugin) using that point, the DEM, and fixed parameters (observer height = 0.1 m, target height = 0, refraction coefficient = 0.13, no Earth curvature correction). The output is a series of binary (0/1) raster layers — one per observer — where pixel value 1 indicates visible terrain from that observer’s location. These rasters are added to the QGIS project but not saved to disk in the provided code. A secondary commented-out GRASS r.viewshed call suggests an alternative implementation with identical parameters (radius = 0.1 decimal degrees ≈ ~11 km at equator, obs/target height = 0.1 m), confirming the core task is high-resolution, observer-specific line-of-sight visibility mapping over topography.

name: Create biome layer schema
desc: The script creates a QGIS project with a PostgreSQL/PostGIS schema for a fictional planet ('tarsis_8') containing dedicated vector layers for 98 biome types, each assigned to a group (e.g., 'maritime river', 'icy') based on biome name prefix and geometry type (Point, LineString, Polygon). Layers are structured to support artist-driven editing: rivers as lines with width fields, geysers as points with radius fields, and vegetation as polygons with density/canopy fields. All layers are stored in a PostGIS schema named 'tarsis_8', with automatic last_updated timestamps, categorized styling using biome-specific hex colors, and QGIS editor widgets (color pickers, range sliders). Outputs include a fully configured QGIS project (.qgz), organized layer tree with alphabetical sorting, coordinate grid and scale bar decorations, and a saved PostgreSQL schema with tables named after biome types (hyphens → underscores). The export pipeline (referenced but not executed) merges these into buffered GeoJSON for biome rasterization in Godot.

name: Intersect atlas points with SA2 boundaries
desc: The script performs a spatial intersection between a CSV-based point dataset (containing latitude/longitude coordinates) and an SA2 (Statistical Area Level 2) polygon shapefile, extracting SA2 attributes (e.g., SA2_MAIN16, SA2_NAME16) onto the points based on spatial containment. The output is a new vector file (specified by Output-File) containing the original point attributes plus selected SA2 boundary attributes, projected in EPSG:4326.

name: Reproject vector layers to EPSG:3003
desc: The script reprojects all vector layers currently loaded in the active QGIS project to EPSG:3003 (Monte Mario / Italy zone 1), saves them as Shapefiles in a newly created 'Reprojected' subdirectory within the project's working directory, and reloads each reprojected layer into the QGIS project with the prefix 'reproj'. No raster data, time-series analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing is performed; the operation is purely coordinate reference system transformation of existing vector layers. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified.

name: Extract flood depth by census tract
desc: The script extracts raster values (flood depth) from a pre-existing flood raster ('raster.tif') within polygon boundaries defined by a vector layer ('svi.shp'), filtering only census tracts where the 'RPL_THEMES' attribute ≥ 0.8 (a social vulnerability index threshold). It clips the raster to the vector layer extent, reads the full clipped raster block into memory, then iterates over qualifying features to compute the maximum pixel value within each feature’s bounding box (not exact geometry intersection). The output is a per-feature print statement showing 'Census Tract' (FID) and 'Max Flood Depth'. No new geospatial product is exported; results are printed to console. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the script — inputs are generic local files ('svi.shp', 'raster.tif', 'clip.tif') with no metadata or provenance clues in the code.

name: Assess flood depth in high-SVI areas
desc: The script identifies census tracts with Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) >= 0.8 from the 'svi.shp' vector layer, clips a raster ('raster.tif') to each tract's bounding box using GDAL's cliprasterbyextent algorithm, and computes the maximum flood depth (band 1 statistic) within each clipped raster. Results are stored in a dictionary mapping SVI values to corresponding max flood depths and printed as 'SVI: X, Max flood depth: Y'.

name: Extract and process OSM aeroway features for aerodromes
desc: The script fetches OpenStreetMap (OSM) data for a specified aerodrome using its ICAO code, then queries the surrounding bounding box for all 'aeroway' features (e.g., taxiway, runway, apron, helipad). It loads each feature type as a separate GeoPackage layer, optionally splits taxiways by 'ref' attribute into individual layers, widens taxiway centerlines into polygons via buffering (with configurable width, dissolve, and centerline retention), applies user-defined color styling from a JSON profile, and adds all resulting layers to the QGIS project. Outputs include geopackages per feature type in the specified output directory and optionally split taxiway layers in a dedicated folder.

name: Convert polygon boundaries to single-part lines
desc: The script converts an input polygon vector layer into a line vector layer where each line segment is a single-part geometry (i.e., no multipart features), assigns a unique integer 'fid' attribute to each line feature, preserves custom styling properties (color, ts_color, gr_color) from the input layer, and applies the original RGB color to the output layer's renderer. It uses QGIS native processing algorithms ('qgis:polygonstolines' and 'qgis:multiparttosingleparts') within a PyQGIS processing algorithm framework.

name: Widen taxiway buffer
desc: The script widens taxiway centerline vector features by applying a symmetric buffer (half the user-specified distance) in a projected CRS (EPSG:3857), optionally dissolving results and converting polygons to single-part linestrings; it preserves custom layer styling properties (e.g., 'color', 'ts_color') and outputs a reprojected (back to EPSG:4326) vector layer of buffered taxiway polygons or derived linestrings.

name: Topologically correct polygon layer
desc: The script performs topological correction of overlapping polygon layers (TGU, OVTA, WQMP, and Land Use Block) by iteratively resolving geometric relationships—equality, within, and overlap—using spatial joins and geometry difference operations. It applies domain-specific attribute-based tie-breaking rules (e.g., 'TCEffect' for delineations, 'AssessDate' for OVTAs) to determine which feature dominates in overlaps, then subtracts the subordinate geometry from the dominant one. The final output is a non-overlapping, single-part polygon layer ('TGUsNoLines') with cleaned geometries (no line strings, no slivers, area ≥1, and mandatory LUBID/SJID attributes), written as a GeoJSON file.

name: Clip raster by extent
desc: The script loads a local landcover raster ('landcover.img') to inspect its spatial extent, then clips another local elevation raster ('elevation.tif') to a user-specified bounding box (PROJWIN: '-1308804, 1402816, 4297746, 5885036') using GDAL's cliprasterbyextent algorithm. The output is a clipped raster file saved as 'clipped2.img'. No time-based filtering, classification, or spectral analysis is performed; the workflow is purely geometric raster subsetting. Study area is not named but defined by arbitrary projected coordinates; data sources are local GeoTIFF/IMG files with no satellite, sensor, or band information; no temporal dimension is present.

name: Clip elevation raster by extent
desc: The script loads a local GeoTIFF elevation raster ('elevation.tif') into QGIS as a QgsRasterLayer, retrieves and prints its full spatial extent (xMin, xMax, yMin, yMax), then clips it to a user-defined rectangular extent (440000, 460000, 4030000, 4045000) using GDAL's 'cliprasterbyextent' algorithm. The clipped output is saved to a local path ('clipped.tif') and its file path is returned. No time-based operations, classification, or remote sensing analysis is performed; the workflow is purely local raster I/O and geometric clipping. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Select counties by intersection
desc: The script performs a spatial selection of Polish administrative counties (powiaty) based on geometric intersection with a user-provided vector layer. It loads a local GeoPackage layer 'powiaty.gpkg' containing county boundaries, runs QGIS's 'native:selectbylocation' algorithm with predicate 'intersects', collects the selected features' TERYT codes and names, sorts them by TERYT code, and emits the sorted list of formatted county identifiers. The task runs asynchronously in the background using QgsTask and logs success or error messages to QGIS's message log.

name: Merge RGB and NIR bands
desc: The script merges RGB multispectral imagery with a separately extracted NIR band (Band 1 from NED files) into a single 4-band GeoTIFF (R,G,B,NIR), preserving original data types and using GDAL merge with separate band stacking. Input files are sourced from PNEO4 or PNEO3 satellite captures under the 'IMG_01_PNEO[3/4]_MS-FS' directory structure, with '_RGB_' and '_NED_' naming conventions indicating distinct spectral products; the output replaces '_RGB_' with '_' in the filename and is saved to 'E:\2022 imagenes\'. The workflow handles fallback between PNEO4 and PNEO3 folder paths, skips existing outputs, and relies on QGIS Processing GDAL algorithms ('gdal:translate' to extract Band 1 from NED, then 'gdal:merge' to combine RGB + NIR as separate bands.

name: Compress pansharpened multispectral imagery
desc: The script compresses and color-corrects pre-pansharpened 4-band raster images (likely RGB+NIR) stored as GeoTIFFs in a local directory. It applies gamma correction (gamma=1.2), saturation boost (+30), and GDAL-based contrast stretching using percentile-derived min/max values (2nd and 98th percentiles per band, computed across all input images) before JPEG compression (QUALITY=75, TILED=Yes) and reprojection to EPSG:4326. Inputs are local file-system TIFFs from 'D:\Maestría\Tesis\Repo\data\data_in\Pansharpened'; outputs are written to 'D:\Maestría\Tesis\Repo\data\data_in\Compressed\2022'. No satellite or cloud processing occurs — this is a post-processing workflow for locally stored, already-processed imagery. Study area, time range, and sensor identity are not specified in the code; bands are indexed numerically (0–3), consistent with a 4-band pansharpened product (e.g., red, green, blue, NIR), but no satellite, sensor, or geographic metadata is embedded or referenced.

name: Calculate building orientation angle
desc: The script computes the dominant orientation (azimuth) of building polygons by identifying their longest edge, then calculates the azimuth angle of that edge in degrees and radians. It outputs a point layer (centroids of buildings) with added 'angle', 'angle2' (mod 360), and 'radians' attributes; additionally, it generates auxiliary line layers visualizing the longest edge ('longest_edge'), the original azimuth direction ('orig degree'), the mod-360 azimuth direction ('mod degree'), and the 360°-complement direction ('360 degree'). The centroid layer is styled with an arrow QML to visually represent building orientation.

name: Extract coastal stroke geometry
desc: The script computes a 'stroke' geometry representing the outer boundary of a coastal vector layer by buffering each feature inward (negative buffer) and subtracting that inner buffer from the original geometry — effectively creating a thin, centered outline (like a line stroke) of the coastline. It then clips this stroke layer to the extent of a raster layer named 'rata_rectangle1'. The output is a memory-based vector layer ('clipped') added to the QGIS project, containing only the stroke geometries intersecting the raster's extent. The study area is implicitly tied to the active layer ('coast') and the raster layer 'rata_rectangle1', both loaded in QGIS; no satellite or remote sensing data is used — all operations are vector-based GIS processing within QGIS using PyQGIS. CRS is EPSG:2193 (NZGD2000 / New Zealand Transverse Mercator 2000), suggesting New Zealand context. No time range, classification, or spectral analysis is involved.

name: Generate contour stroke geometry
desc: The script generates a 'stroke' geometry layer representing the visual line width of contour lines (elevation polygons) by computing an inner buffer (negative buffer) of selected elevation contours (where elevation % 100 == 0) and subtracting it from the original polygon geometry — effectively creating a polygonal representation of the cartographic stroke for map rendering. Input is a vector layer of contour-derived polygons; output is a clipped, memory-based polygon layer ('stroke_geom_layer') aligned to the extent of the 'rata_rectangle1' raster layer, intended for high-quality thematic mapping of elevation intervals.

name: Extract elevation contour stroke geometry
desc: The script processes a vector layer of elevation contours (selected where elevation modulo 100 equals zero) to generate a stroked polygon representation — i.e., a filled 'line' geometry with user-defined visual thickness. It converts multipart lines to single parts, closes them into polygons, applies an inward negative buffer (scaled by map scale and stroke width), computes the geometric difference between outer and inner buffered polygons to yield a centered stroke geometry, then clips the result to the extent of a raster layer named 'rata_rectangle1'. The final output is a clipped memory vector layer of topographic contour strokes suitable for cartographic rendering at scale ~1:55,000.

name: Assign building name and use attributes
desc: The script creates a new GeoPackage vector layer named 'error_layer' by copying the attribute schema of an existing QGIS vector layer 'final_building_outlines', renaming three existing fields ('name', 'use', 'status') to 'name_assigned', 'use_assigned', and 'status_assigned', and appending a new string field 'Error_comment'. It preserves the original geometry type and CRS. The output is a blank (empty) vector layer with this modified schema, intended for manual or subsequent error annotation—no spatial or attribute processing (e.g., classification, filtering, or calculation) is performed on features; no features are copied or transformed from the source layer.

name: Detect multipart road and track features
desc: The script checks two QGIS vector layers ('road_cl' and 'track_cl') for geometric anomalies: (1) null geometries, and (2) multipart LineString geometries (i.e., MultiLineString features where geometry.asMultiPolyline() yields >1 line segment). For each anomaly found, it creates a memory-based output layer containing the original feature attributes plus an added 'geometry error' field indicating either 'Null geometry' or the WKB type string (e.g., 'MultiLineString'). The output is visualized as a new QGIS map layer styled by error type, and returns a status message indicating success (no errors) or failure (count of detected anomalies). The script operates entirely within QGIS using local vector layers — no remote sensing data, time-series, or external geospatial APIs are involved. Study area, time range, satellite data, and coordinate reference system are not specified in the code; the only CRS explicitly set is EPSG:2193 (NZGD2000 / New Zealand Transverse Mercator), implying potential use in New Zealand, but no location names or extents are given.

name: Generate cloud- and shadow-corrected NDVI
desc: The script processes Landsat 8 Level 1 TIR data to generate cloud- and terrain-shadow-masked NDVI rasters for the Parque Nacional do Tricântico (PNT) in Brazil. It performs: (1) extraction and clipping of all bands and MTL metadata to the park boundary; (2) cloud masking using BQA band reclassification (via cloud_mask.txt rules); (3) top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiometric correction using reflectance multipliers/additives and solar elevation from MTL; (4) 8-bit scaling and GRIR (Green+Red+IR)/3 compositing for shadow detection; (5) SAGA filter-based shadow enhancement and shadow mask generation (via shadow_GRIR8BITS.txt); (6) application of shadow mask to red (B4) and near-infrared (B5) bands; and (7) final NDVI calculation ((B5−B4)/(B5+B4)) on shadow-free bands. Outputs are per-scene GeoTIFF NDVI rasters (e.g., 'LC08_..._ndvi.TIF') alongside preserved MTL metadata in the 'ndvi' directory.

name: Estimate ecosystem service values
desc: The script estimates ecosystem service values (ESV) for a user-defined study region by clipping a land use/land cover (LULC) raster to a vector mask, summarizing pixel counts and area per LULC class, and multiplying those areas by pre-defined per-hectare ESV values (minimum/mean/maximum) from backend datasets. It supports two LULC sources: NLCD (National Land Cover Dataset) and NALCMS (North American Land Change Monitoring System). The workflow includes GDAL-based raster clipping, LULC-specific validation, area aggregation, and ESV lookup via ESV_dataset(). Outputs are (1) a clipped raster layer and (2) a tabular output with LULC classes, descriptions, and associated ESVs (with many NULLs where empirical ESV data is absent). No time-series analysis or spectral processing is performed; the input raster is treated as static, single-epoch data. Study area is defined solely by the user-provided vector mask layer; no fixed geographic extent is embedded in the code.

name: Map ecosystem service values
desc: The script maps per-pixel ecosystem service values (ESV) by reclassifying a clipped LULC raster using ESV lookup tables. It takes as input: (1) a user-selected LULC source (either NLCD or NALCMS), (2) a pre-clipped LULC raster layer (output from 'Step 1' of the EcoValuator plugin), (3) a user-chosen ecosystem service (e.g., carbon sequestration, flood mitigation), and (4) a chosen ESV level (minimum, average, or maximum value from the ESV table). It performs raster reclassification via QGIS's 'native:reclassifybytable', then applies quintile-based discrete pseudocolor symbology using QgsColorRampShader and QgsSingleBandPseudoColorRenderer. The output is a GeoTIFF raster where pixel values represent the selected ESV level for each LULC class, visualized with a color ramp emphasizing data breaks. No time-series analysis, cloud masking, or satellite-derived indices are performed — the workflow is purely tabular reclassification and visualization of static ESV data against static LULC input. Study area, time range, satellite imagery, bands, and sensor processing are not involved; inputs are local raster layers and internal ESV/LULC lookup tables.

name: Rasterize groundwater level measurements
desc: The script rasterizes point-based groundwater depth-to-water-level measurements (from pre-processed CSV-derived shapefiles) into a georeferenced GeoTIFF using Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation via QGIS's gdal:gridinversedistance algorithm. Input is a state-specific (e.g., KA, IN) or multi-state (e.g., KA,AP) vector layer of well locations with monthly depth-to-water values stored as field names like 'May 2012'; the script filters for non-null values in the specified month (e.g., 'May 2012'), writes a subsetted shapefile, then interpolates those points into a raster with filename pattern '{states}_YYYYMM01_idw_grid_id_min_1_max_12_nonulls.tif'. Output resolution and extent are determined by QGIS GDAL grid defaults (not explicitly configured in code), and outputs are written to 'outputs/groundwater/tif' (though actual path used is 'Code/atree/data/groundwater/levels/tif'). No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — data source is in-situ groundwater monitoring wells.

name: Apply vector buffer analysis
desc: The script performs a vector-based buffer operation on an input vector layer using QGIS's native:buffer algorithm. It loads a vector dataset from a file path (input_path), applies a fixed-distance buffer (distance parameter, unit specified as 'meters' by default), uses 30 segments to approximate curved buffer boundaries, and optionally dissolves resulting polygons. The output is written to a user-specified file path (output_path) in OGR-supported format (e.g., GeoPackage or Shapefile). The script returns success status, output path, feature count of the buffered layer, and execution parameters. No remote sensing data, time-series, or raster operations are involved; it is purely a desktop GIS vector geoprocessing task executed in QGIS Python environment.

name: Calculate NDVI-like index
desc: The script computes a normalized difference index from two user-provided JP2 raster files (e.g., likely Sentinel-2 or Landsat surface reflectance bands) using the expression ("layer1@1" - "layer2@1") / ("layer1@1" + "layer2@1"). It loads both rasters as QgsRasterLayer objects, validates them, performs band-wise raster algebra via QGIS's native:rastercalc algorithm (operating on Band 1 of each input), and adds the resulting index raster as a new layer named "Index_Ergebnis" to the QGIS project. No study area, time range, satellite metadata, or band identities are embedded in the code — inputs are arbitrary local JP2 files selected interactively; the index is generic and not explicitly labeled as NDVI, though structurally identical to it if Band 1 corresponds to red and near-infrared respectively. Final output is a temporary in-memory raster layer visualized in QGIS.

name: Estimate THG emissions from peatland biotopes
desc: The script automates the estimation of greenhouse gas (THG) emissions from peatland biotopes using the GEST approach. It processes QGIS vector layers (Biotope_GEST and Torfboeden) to extract only open-land/wetland biotopes (e.g., 'Moor', 'Grünland') intersecting with peat soils. It exports filtered biotope geometries as a shapefile, then converts them to Excel for attribute matching against a DBU species list. Species are mapped to water stage indicators ('+' and '°') using a master reference table (GEST_Mastertabelle.xlsx), with unmatched species reported. Water stage counts per biotope (FLID) are aggregated in Excel worksheets ('WS_gezaehlt', 'Ergebnis_Wasserstufen'), and finally, an 'Ist-Zustand' sheet is generated containing FLID, area (m²/ha), biotope type, and placeholders for GEST designation and CO₂-equivalent emission factors (t CO₂-Äq/ha·a) and total emissions (t CO₂-Äq/a). The workflow relies entirely on local vector data — no satellite imagery or remote sensing — and outputs Excel spreadsheets and shapefiles. Study area is explicitly named as Ueckermünde (Ueckermünder Heide) and Hartmannsdorf; no time range is used.

name: Estimate CO2-equivalent emissions from forest biotopes
desc: The script estimates pre- and post-intervention CO2-equivalent emissions (in t/ha/a) for forest biotope polygons by spatially joining them with KOSKA water stage raster data and lookup values from a master Excel table. It extracts forest biotopes (filtered by 'Hckurz' = 'Wälder') intersecting peat soil layers, then samples raster values at polygon centroids (after CRS transformation), matches biotope type ('LBTNAME') and water stage (raster value) against the master table to populate 'Ist_Emi' (pre-measure) and 'Soll_Emi' (post-measure) fields in the shapefile attribute table. Outputs include a filtered shapefile ('output.shp'), updated vector layers with emission columns, and a dictionary of unmatched (biotope, water stage) pairs requiring manual resolution. Study area is implied to be in Germany (via DBU Biotoptypliste, KOSKA classification, German-language layer names like 'Wälder', 'Torfboeden'), but no explicit geographic coordinates or administrative boundaries are specified. Input data sources are local files: vector layers ('Biotope_GEST', 'Torfboeden'), a KOSKA water stage raster (TIF), and an Excel master table ('GEST_Wald_Mastertabelle.xlsx'); no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used — all operations are GIS-based vector-raster-table joins in QGIS.

name: Map iron oxide distribution
desc: The script computes and visualizes the Iron Oxide Index (IOI = B4/B2) from a Sentinel-2 Level-2A (BOA) image acquired on 2025-09-07 over the Siebengebirge region near Bonn, Germany. It applies NDVI (B8/B4) and NDWI (B3/B8) masking to exclude vegetation (NDVI > 0.2) and surface water (NDWI > 0), generating a combined binary mask. The IOI is then visualized both unmasked and masked, with scaling from 0.9 to 1.2. Outputs include: (1) raw and cropped TCI and band rasters (via GDAL translate), (2) IOI raster (IronIndex_Siebengebirge_Sep25.tif), (3) NDVI and NDWI rasters, (4) binary NDVI, NDWI, and combined masks exported as GeoTIFFs, and (5) matplotlib visualizations of all indices and masks clipped to bounding box (792349, 5609745, 820233, 5641442) in UTM zone 31U (EPSG:32631). The workflow uses local Sentinel-2 L2A data — not GEE — and relies on rasterio, numpy, and QGIS processing via PyQGIS.

name: Clip raster by extent
desc: The script clips a raster layer named 'Flurabstandsplan Mai ' to a user-defined rectangular extent (xmin=32837469, xmax=32837500, ymin=5962136, ymax=5962250) using GDAL's 'cliprasterbyextent' algorithm in PyQGIS. The input raster is retrieved by name from the current QGIS project; its CRS is explicitly set to ESRI:102329 (a projected coordinate system, likely NAD 1983 Alaska Albers or similar, though not geographically resolvable from code alone). The output is saved as a GeoTIFF file at a local Windows path and added back to the QGIS project as a new raster layer. No time-based filtering, spectral analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — this is purely a geometric subsetting operation. Data source, sensor, bands, and temporal information are not specified in the script.

name: Identify overlapping land parcels
desc: The script identifies land parcels (Flurstücke) from layer 'Rieth_Flurstueck' that spatially intersect with features in layer 'PrognoseTool_Beeke-Nord Trocken' and have a 'Diff_FINAL' attribute value exceeding 0.05. It outputs two products: (1) a CSV file listing the intersecting parcels’ Flur, Flurstück number (flstnrzae), and Flurstück extension (flstnrnen); and (2) a Shapefile containing the geometries of those parcels, automatically loaded into QGIS. The workflow uses spatial indexing (QgsSpatialIndex) for performance, bounding-box pre-filtering, exact geometry intersection testing, and threshold-based attribute filtering. The study area is explicitly named 'Scheerhorn', and the script was successfully applied to areas in Lower Saxony (Niedersachsen). No satellite, sensor, or band data is used — all inputs are local vector layers. An optional, commented-out extension checks non-overlap with 'Eigentumsflächen' (ownership areas), but it is inactive.

name: Reclassify flurabstand raster by KOSKA water stages
desc: The script reclassifies an input flurabstand (field distance) raster TIFF file using a fixed lookup table mapping continuous distance values to discrete KOSKA water stage classes: '2-' → -2, '2+' → 2, '3+' → 3, '4+' → 4, and '5+' → 5. It uses QGIS's native:reclassifybytable algorithm with hard-coded interval boundaries ([0,0.2), [0.2,0.45), [0.45,0.8), [0.8,inf)) and corresponding class values. The output is a new raster file saved in the same directory with '_KOSKA' appended to the input filename, then loaded as a QgsRasterLayer into the current QGIS project. No GEE code is present — this is a QGIS Python processing script; the mention of 'GEE' in the user prompt is erroneous. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial operations beyond reclassification are not specified.

name: Clip raster by polygon boundary
desc: The script clips a raster layer (e.g., Flurabstandskarte, geological interpolations) to the spatial extent of a user-specified vector polygon layer (e.g., Untersuchungsgebiet, Biotop, Flurstück) using GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm. It loads the raster and polygon layers by name from the current QGIS project, validates their presence, auto-generates an output path if none is provided (appending '_clipped.tif' to the input raster’s filename), executes the clipping with CROP_TO_CUTLINE=True, adds the resulting clipped raster as a new layer to the QGIS project, and displays success or error messages. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external datasets are involved — inputs are local, pre-loaded QGIS layers; the operation is purely geometric masking without classification, temporal analysis, or spectral processing.

name: Extract land cover image chips
desc: The script automatically extracts georeferenced image chips (50 m × 50 m, ~250 px at 20 cm resolution) from high-resolution orthoimagery (ORTHOHR) by intersecting vector-labeled ground truth polygons (e.g., 'classe' attribute) with raster extents, generating a regular grid aligned to the intersection geometry, filtering out incomplete tiles (area < 90% of full tile or non-5-point polygons), splitting by class, and clipping the source orthoimage to each class-specific tile polygon — outputting classified TIFF chips organized in directories by class (e.g., '/outputs/Agriculture/', '/outputs/Forest/', etc.).

name: Extract land cover image chips
desc: The script extracts georeferenced image chips (50 m × 50 m, ~250 px at 20 cm resolution) from high-resolution orthophoto mosaics (ORTHOHR_1-0_IRC-0M20_JP2-E080_LAMB93_D004_2018-01-01) covering the Landes department in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France. It uses vector ground-truth shapefiles (with 'Classe' attribute) to define regions of interest, intersects them with raster extents, generates a regular grid aligned to those intersections, filters out incomplete grid cells (requiring ≥90% of full area and 5 vertices), splits grid cells by class, and clips the orthophotos using each class-specific polygon to produce classified TIFF image chips. Outputs are stored per class in 'outputs_landes/{Classe}/' with filenames including image and vector indices. The orthophotos are IGN’s ORTHOHR (Infrared-Red-Blue, 3-band, 20 cm native resolution), delivered in JP2 format, projected in RGF93/Lambert-93 (EPSG:2154). No classification model is applied — this is a supervised data preparation pipeline for training or validation datasets.

name: Relabel image chips with OSO-RPG class pairs
desc: The script relabels pre-cut raster image chips (GeoTIFFs) by intersecting each chip's spatial extent with a precomputed vector layer 'RPG_OSO_2018_INTERSECTION.shp' — which contains co-located agricultural land cover classes from the French 'Registre Parcellaire Graphique' (RPG, CODE_CULTU) and the 'Observatoire Satellitaire des Ouvrages' (OSO, Classe). For each chip that intersects this vector layer, it extracts the unique OSO 'Classe' and RPG 'CODE_CULTU' values present in the intersection, forms a concatenated string label (e.g., 'PRA_211'), and copies the chip into a new output directory structured by that label (e.g., '/outputs_paires/PRA_211/'). Chips with no intersection are discarded. Intermediate QGIS vector layers (extent, intersection) are generated and cleaned up.

name: Relabel imagery using OSO-RPG intersection
desc: The script relabels cropped satellite image chips (TIFF files) by intersecting their spatial extent with the 'RPG_OSO_2018_INTERSECTION.shp' vector layer — a 2018 intersection of France’s Official Land Use Map (RPG) and the OSO (Observatoire Satellitaire de l’Occupation du Sol) classification. For each chip, it computes the bounding polygon, intersects it with the RPG-OSO vector, and extracts the unique values of 'Classe' (OSO land cover class) and 'CODE_CULTU' (RPG crop code). A pair label (e.g., 'A1_52') is formed from these two attributes and used to organize output chips into subdirectories under '/outputs_paires/'. The study area is explicitly the Landes department in Occitanie, France (inferred from '/shared/Datasets/ImagesLandesOccitanie'). Input imagery is pre-cropped raster chips (no sensor or satellite metadata in script), and no temporal filtering or spectral processing (e.g., band math, indices) is performed — only geometric operations (extent extraction, vector intersection) and attribute-based relabeling. Outputs are reorganized TIFF files grouped by OSO-RPG class pairs.

name: Extract land cover image chips
desc: The script automatically extracts raster image chips (50 m × 50 m) from satellite images (JP2 format) using vector polygon layers ('classes_vecteurs') as spatial masks. It first computes the raster extent, intersects it with each input vector layer (e.g., labeled polygons with a 'classe' attribute), generates a regular grid of 50×50 m cells over the intersection area, filters out incomplete grid cells (area < 90% of full cell or geometry not a 5-vertex polygon), splits the grid by the 'classe' attribute into per-class sublayers, and then clips the source raster to each individual grid cell polygon using GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer'. Outputs are GeoTIFF image chips saved under class-named subdirectories (e.g., '/outputs/Agriculture/') with filenames incorporating image and vector indices. The script includes optional (but commented-out) logic to detect and discard chips containing black (zero-value) pixels across all bands. No classification model is applied — this is purely a supervised chip extraction workflow driven by external vector labels. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and CRS are not specified in the code; inputs are local file paths only.

name: Clip raster variables by region
desc: The script clips a set of local GeoTIFF raster files (stored in 'E:/Ale_Marisa_Cenarios_TNC/Vraveis_dinamica') to the spatial extent and geometry of a provided shapefile ('Regiao_1.shp'), preserving original NoData values, data type, and applying LZW compression. Each input raster is processed individually using QGIS GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm with 'CROP_TO_CUTLINE=True' and 'KEEP_RESOLUTION=True'. The output is a set of clipped rasters named with '_1.tif' suffix. No temporal filtering, spectral analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — only spatial subsetting. Study area is implied by the shapefile name 'Regiao_1' and folder path 'DINAMICA/dados_entrada/Regiao_1/', indicating Region 1 of a larger Dinâmica EGO modeling context; time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific variable names are not present in the script.

name: Map community councils and ecological zones
desc: The script generates a thematic GIS map focused on Afro-Colombian community councils (Consejos Comunitarios Titulados) in Colombia, specifically clipping and styling high-resolution land cover (Cobertura 2018/2020) and ecosystem (Ecosis 2018/2024) layers to their legally titled territories. It overlays administrative boundaries (departments, municipalities), protected areas (national parks, paramos, mangroves, Ramsar sites), environmental authorities, infrastructure (roads, hydrography), and priority conservation zones (PDET, CONPES). The output is a multi-theme QGIS project with 11 preconfigured map themes (e.g., 'Pais', 'Municipio', 'Ecosistemas', 'Comunidades', 'Importancia') enabling rapid contextual visualization of socio-ecological relationships in selected council territories.

name: Map land cover and ecosystems
desc: The script generates a multi-layer GIS map focused on Colombia's territorial planning and environmental management, specifically for the municipality of '19418' (San José del Guaviare) in the department '19' (Guaviare), within South America. It loads, clips, and styles over 50 vector layers—including administrative boundaries (departments, municipalities), ecological zones (ecosystems, land cover from 2018/2020/2024), protected areas (PNNs, paramos, mangroves, Ramsar sites), Indigenous and Afro-Colombian territories (resguardos, consejos comunitarios), PDET priority zones, conservation priorities, hydrography, infrastructure (vias, hidro), and urban features (manzanas, nomenclatura). Outputs are styled vector layers with categorical symbology (e.g., Cobertura 2020 styled by 'nivel_3', Ecosis 2024 by 'ecos_gener'), clipped to the selected municipality, and organized into 12 thematic QGIS map themes (e.g., 'Municipio', 'Ecosistemas', 'Zonificacion', 'Comunidades') for rapid visualization and analysis.

name: Map land cover and ecosystems
desc: The script generates a multi-layer GIS map focused on Colombia, specifically department code '70' (Cauca) and municipality code '70420' (Santander de Quilichao), by loading, clipping, styling, and organizing 50+ thematic vector layers. It loads administrative boundaries (countries, departments, municipalities), ocean, OpenStreetMap basemap, and thematic layers including land cover (Cobertura 2018/2020), ecosystems (Ecosis 2018/2024), protected areas (parques, zoniparques, biosfera), environmental features (humedales, paramos, manglares, seco, marinos, coral), governance layers (autoridades, forestal, zonip, ambitos, priocon), infrastructure (vias, hidro, manzana), and socio-ecological zones (campesinas, paz, consejos). All thematic layers are clipped to the selected municipality extent using QGIS native:clip. Land cover and ecosystem layers are styled with custom categorical RGB color palettes mapped to specific attribute fields ('nivel_3', 'ECOS_GENER', 'ecos_gener', 'PRIORIDAD', 'categoria_', etc.). The script defines and saves eight QGIS map themes (Pais, Departamento, Municipio, Reservas, Ecosistemas, Coberturas, Ambitos, Zonificacion, Priorizados, Importancia, Comunidades, Urbano) controlling layer visibility for rapid cartographic switching. Outputs are in-memory vector layers visualized in QGIS with opacity, border, and fill styling; no exports or computations (e.g., statistics, change detection, raster analysis) are performed — it is strictly a data loading, subsetting, symbology, and theme management workflow.

name: Clip ecological restoration layers
desc: The script clips three pre-processed vector layers—'Recuperacion' (recovery), 'Rehabilitacion' (rehabilitation), and 'Restauracion' (restoration)—to a user-defined selection geometry ('selection_layer') using the QGIS native clip algorithm. Each clipped layer is styled with a distinct fill color and border, named accordingly ('recu', 'reha', 'resta'), and added to the QGIS project as separate in-memory vector layers. The workflow prioritizes performance by disabling rendering during processing and adding layers only once at the end.

name: Map forest vegetation types
desc: The script maps 'Floresta Ombrófila Densa das Terras Baixas' (Dense Ombrophilous Forest of Lowlands) and other vegetation formations in Brazil using vector-based land cover/vegetation classification data ('vege_area.gpkg').
