It loads administrative boundaries (countries, states, intermediate regions, immediate regions, municipalities) for Latin America & Caribbean — specifically filtering for Brazil (CD_UF='26') and the municipality of Recife (CD_MUN='2607604'). The workflow includes clipping the vegetation layer to the selected municipality, applying three distinct QML-styled symbologies (vege_fito.qml, vege_legenda.qml, vege_legenda2.qml) to generate three thematic visualizations: one focused on phytogeographic classification ('fito'), and two on legend-based categories ('legenda', 'legenda2'). Outputs are three styled vector layers ('Coberturaf', 'coberturasl', 'coberturasl2') added to the QGIS project, plus WKT geometry export of the selected municipality. No raster processing, time-series analysis, or satellite-derived indices are performed; all operations are vector-based spatial selection, clipping, and styling.

name: Fix land cover geometry errors
desc: The script applies QGIS's native 'fixgeometries' algorithm to repair topological errors (e.g., self-intersections, gaps, overlaps, invalid rings) in three vector layers: (1) Colombia’s 2020 national land cover map (administrative and environmental boundary versions), (2) Colombia’s 2024 Continental, Coastal, and Marine Ecosystems map (100K scale), and (3) Brazil’s vegetation area layer. All outputs are saved as GeoPackage (.gpkg) files with corrected geometries, preserving original attributes and enabling downstream GIS analysis and integration.

name: Clip PDET territorial boundaries
desc: The script performs a vector clipping operation in QGIS to intersect the 'Ambitos_Territoriales_PDET' layer (PDET Territorial Boundaries) with a selected municipalities layer ('municipios_seleccionadosp.shp'), producing a geopackage ('Ambitos2.gpkg') containing only the portions of PDET boundaries overlapping the selected municipalities. It then applies a categorized symbology based on the 'categoria_' field using predefined RGB colors for three categories: 'AEIA', 'Frontera Agrícola', and 'Franja Estabilización'. The study area is Colombia, as indicated by the file paths containing 'Zonificacion Colombia' and layer names referencing 'PDET' (Plan de Desarrollo con Enfoque Territorial), a national Colombian policy framework. No satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or raster analysis is involved — this is a purely vector-based GIS workflow using local shapefile/GPKG data. Outputs include a clipped vector layer saved to disk and styled in the QGIS project.

name: Apply categorized symbology to vegetation cover layers
desc: The script loads vector layers (GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON) from a local directory '/Volumes/Disco J/Mapas/Ecosistemas y comunidades/Coberturas Vegetales/Coberturas_por_Consejo', optionally reprojects them to EPSG:3116 (Colombia), and applies a consistent categorized fill symbology based on the 'nivel_3' attribute field using a predefined dictionary of 58 land-cover class names and RGB color values. It then zooms the QGIS canvas to the combined extent of loaded layers. No remote sensing data, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — this is purely a local GIS layer loading and styling automation script for pre-existing vector datasets.

name: Apply standardized land cover symbology
desc: The script applies a predefined categorical color scheme to polygon vector layers representing land cover classes (e.g., '1.1.1. Tejido urbano continuo', '3.1.5. Plantación forestal') loaded from local geospatial files (GPKG, SHP, GeoJSON) in QGIS. It first removes existing layers matching the name pattern 'Coberturas', then loads all compatible vector files from a specified local directory ('/Volumes/Disco J/Mapas/Ecosistemas y comunidades/Coberturas Vegetales/Coberturas_por_Municipio'), optionally reprojects them to EPSG:9377 (Colombia), validates presence of the 'nivel_3' classification field, and applies a fixed RGB color mapping to each unique value. The styling is saved as default layer style and rendered in the QGIS canvas. No remote sensing imagery, cloud processing, or classification is performed — only local vector loading and deterministic cartographic styling.

name: Classify ecosystem types

name: Calculate road-school proximity overlap

name: Identify fynbos habitat suitability
desc: The script identifies spatially explicit suitable habitats for a rare fynbos plant species in the Cape Peninsula and surrounding region by integrating topographic (slope, aspect) and climatic (annual rainfall) constraints. name: Compute shortest and fastest road network paths
desc: The script computes three network analysis outputs using QGIS Processing algorithms on a road network vector layer: (1) Euclidean shortest path between two coordinate points (ignoring speed), (2) service area (reachable roads) within 250 m of input points, and (3) fastest path considering per-segment speed limits (using 'speed' field) and a default speed of 50 km/h. name: Identify north-facing low-slope terrain

It synthesizes these into a final 'best_areas.tif' raster where pixel value = 1 if either (slope ≤ 2°) OR (slope ≤ 5° AND aspect朝北), otherwise 0 — representing optimal terrain for applications like solar farm siting or ecological restoration requiring gentle, north-exposed slopes. name: Extract slope range mask

name: Generate hillshade from DEM

name: Generate hillshade from DEM

name: Filter ground points from DEM

name: Filter ground points from DEM

name: Generate terrain relief map

name: Generate terrain relief map

name: Extract east-facing slope aspect

name: Define urban scope and constraints
desc: The script supports urban renewable energy planning by enabling users to manually digitize and save geographic layers as 'scope' (study area boundaries) or 'constraints' (policy/technical restrictions) within QGIS. Outputs include shapefiles for scope boundaries and scored constraint layers, integrated into QGIS layer tree groups ('Scope', 'Policy', 'Technical'). No satellite imagery or automated classification is used — all geospatial operations are vector-based (clipping, attribute editing) and driven by interactive QGIS workflows. The study area is implicitly defined by the user-loaded city shapefile in '/Processing scripts/Shapefile conversion/City/', and no time-series or remote sensing analysis is performed.

name: Generate local district heating networks
desc: The script generates local district heating (LDH) network configurations by spatially clustering buildings within user-defined proximity thresholds (e.g., 5 km), buffering candidate points derived from opportunity areas, resolving overlapping buffers, computing centroids as network nodes, and intersecting with building layers to assign supply status based on cumulative heat demand versus network capacity. It calculates energy yield (MWh/yr), input energy (MWh/yr), COP-adjusted generation, and heat loss, then outputs two QGIS memory layers: (1) 'Local district heating networks' (point layer of network centroids styled with SVG markers and proximity-based boundary rings), and (2) 'Buildings within heating network' (polygon layer of intersected buildings with a binary 'Supply' field indicating whether each building is supplied, styled via QML). Results are inserted into the 'Additional information' layer group, top-aligned in layer order, and summarized in a formatted HTML report in the dockwidget's text browser. No satellite or Earth observation data is used; all inputs are local vector layers (e.g., 'Opportunities', 'building' layers) loaded from the QGIS project. The workflow relies entirely on QGIS native processing algorithms ('qgis:randompointsinsidepolygons'), geometric operations (buffering, intersection, distance calculation), and attribute-based energy accounting — no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or cloud-based GEE computation occurs.

name: Estimate wind energy potential
desc: The script estimates wind energy generation potential for urban deployment by calculating power density and total energy yield from hypothetical wind turbines placed within user-defined opportunity areas. It uses user-input parameters (wind speed, turbine efficiency, rotor diameter, spacing) to compute theoretical power (W) and annual energy yield (kWh or MWh), converts output to dwelling equivalents, generates spatially distributed turbine point layers with buffer-based spacing enforcement, applies SVG-based visual styling, and appends formatted summary statistics to a QGIS text browser. The workflow operates entirely on local vector layers (specifically a layer named 'Opportunities') loaded in the QGIS project — no remote sensing or Earth Engine data is accessed, processed, or exported. All calculations are deterministic physics-based (Betz-limited power equation), not derived from satellite-derived wind datasets or time-series analysis. Inputs are purely parametric; no geospatial raster or time-series data sources are used.

name: Convert DXF to GPKG

Outputs include a multi-layer GeoPackage file and associated QML style files.

name: Rasterize GeoPackage vector layers
desc: The script converts all vector layers from a GeoPackage file into a single georeferenced TIFF raster using QGIS's 'qgis:rasterize' algorithm. It loads each layer from the GeoPackage, computes their combined extent, and rasterizes them with specified parameters including extent buffer, pixel resolution (0.1 map units per pixel), tile size (20480), and transparent background. The output is a single TIFF file in the specified EPSG coordinate reference system.

name: Reproject edge PNGs to WGS84

Input paths are constructed dynamically per survey date under 'edge_pngs_n_pgws', and outputs are written to 'wgs_84_tifs_from_pngs'. The script is invoked via command line with '-d' specifying date(s), and includes error handling for invalid layers.

name: Merge shapefiles by filename

Outputs include merged/copied shapefiles in the specified output folder and a detailed HTML report summarizing success, copy, skip, invalid, and failure cases with file paths and reasons.

name: Reproject vector layers to EPSG:4326
desc: The script reprojects all non-memory vector layers in the currently open QGIS project to EPSG:4326, overwriting their original files on disk while preserving layer name, style, and custom properties. It uses QGIS native processing algorithm 'native:reprojectlayer', sets the project CRS to EPSG:4326, removes old layers, and adds the reprojected versions back into the project. The project file is then saved to persist changes.

name: Calculate bike trip shortest paths
desc: The script computes shortest network-based paths between bike share station pairs using QGIS's native shortest path algorithm. It reads trip records (with start/end station IDs), matches them to station point geometries, and routes each trip along a provided transportation network layer. The output is a memory vector layer of LineString features representing the calculated paths, each attributed with trip ID and station IDs. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code; all inputs (trips_layer, stations_layer, network_layer) are assumed to be pre-loaded QGIS layers with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata.

name: Merge ArcGrid raster datasets

If no such directories exist, it attempts to unzip .zip files (assumed to contain ArcGrid rasters) and then locates 'grd'-prefixed subdirectories within the extracted content. It uses QGIS's gdal:merge algorithm to combine all identified ArcGrid rasters into a single GeoTIFF file named 'merged_raster.tif' saved to the target_path directory. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis (e.g., classification, indices, masking) is involved — the operation is purely format-agnostic raster mosaicking of locally stored ArcGrid data. Input data sources are local filesystem paths only; no remote Earth Engine assets, satellite imagery, bands, sensors, or temporal filtering are used.

name: Calculate urban and rural RSU indicators
desc: The script calculates spatially aggregated, area-weighted indicators for Residential Statistical Units (RSUs) within 0.2°×0.2° grid cells across European countries, stratified by Urban and Rural zone types defined via GHS-SMOD (Urban: SMOD=30; Rural: SMOD=11–13). It filters cells intersecting European countries (Western, Northern, Southern, Eastern Europe) using administrative boundaries from 'world-administrative-boundaries.geojson', selects cells containing ≥5 pixels of the target zone type, samples up to 25 cells per country, loads precomputed LCZ and RSU indicator data (from OSM-derived datasets organized by bounding box), filters RSUs by LCZ class (e.g., Urban LCZs 1–105, Rural LCZs 101–107), and computes weighted fractions (e.g., building, vegetation, undefined), area-weighted average building height, and Sky View Factor (SVF). Outputs include: (1) CSV files with per-cell indicator values per country, (2) GeoPackage (.fgb) or GeoJSON files containing country-level median indicator values with geometry, and (3) boxplot PNG figures per indicator and zone type. The study area is explicitly Europe; data sources are local file paths (no GEE assets); no time range is specified; all operations are vector-based (zonal statistics, spatial intersection, sampling) using QGIS Processing and GeoPandas — no Earth Engine API calls are present.

name: Identify reservoir dam locations
desc: The script automatically identifies potential dam locations for artificial reservoirs by analyzing a Digital Terrain Model (DTM) to compute upslope catchment areas, iteratively testing barrier elevations (zs) to achieve a target reservoir volume (30,000 m³, ±5,000 m³ tolerance). It uses SAGA GIS hydrological tools (Fill & Sink, Catchment Area, Channel Network) within QGIS/PyQGIS to derive flow networks, places candidate closure points at regular intervals (50 m) along stream centerlines, computes inundated area and volume for each candidate via raster algebra and differencing against the filled DTM, and outputs a point vector layer ('Sez_Chiusura') with attributes: elevation (Q), dam crest elevation (zs), reservoir surface area ('Area Bac'), stored volume ('Volume Bac'), and dam height ('HS'). Final outputs include classified symbology and labels for HS values on the point layer.

name: Sample spatial data using spacing or decimation
desc: The script performs geometric sampling of vector spatial data (points or lines) using either a decimation method (for point geometry, requiring DTM and geology layers) or a spacing method (for line geometry). It reads input vector layers (SPATIAL_DATA, GEOLOGY) and a raster DTM, converts them to GeoDataFrames and GDAL datasets, then applies domain-specific sampling logic from external SamplerDecimator or SamplerSpacing classes. Output is a point vector layer with attributes ID, X, Y, Z (elevated if DTM-derived), and featureId. No remote sensing imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived indices are used; all operations are deterministic geometric resampling based on user-specified decimation integer or spacing distance (in map units). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and sensor information are not present in the code.

name: Sort stratigraphic units
desc: The script generates a stratigraphically ordered column (a ranked list of geological unit names) using one of several map2loop sorting algorithms—e.g., Age-based, NetworkX topological, Observation projections—applied to geology polygons, contacts lines, structural point data, and optionally a DTM. Inputs include user-specified field mappings (e.g., UNITNAME, MIN_AGE, MAX_AGE, GROUP, DIP, DIPDIR), and outputs are: (1) a QGIS vector feature sink containing a two-field table (order integer, unit_name string) with units sorted by inferred stratigraphic position; and (2) a JSON file listing the ordered unit names. The script does not perform remote sensing analysis, time-series processing, or satellite-derived calculations—it operates solely on local vector/raster layers provided by the user in QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Clip vector layers by Tokyo mesh extent
desc: The script clips multiple vector layers from a QGIS project file (500m_mesh.qgz) to a predefined rectangular extent corresponding to a subset of Tokyo’s 500m mesh grid. It uses GDAL’s `clipvectorbyextent` algorithm to extract features intersecting the bounding box (139.708694789, 35.642186746, 139.770192591, 35.695803397) in JGD2000 / Japan Plane Rectangular CS VIII (EPSG:4612). Input layers include '東京都500mメッシュ別将来推計人口' (Tokyo 500m mesh-based future population estimates) and '東京都バス停' (Tokyo bus stops), both sourced from MLIT’s KSJ GML dataset (http://nlftp.mlit.go.jp/ksj/gml/datalist/KsjTmplt-mesh500h30.html). Outputs are: (1) a clipped GeoPackage (`output.gpkg`) containing all input vector layers appended sequentially; (2) a new QGIS project (`output.qgz`) with layer data sources updated to point to the clipped GeoPackage; and (3) an auxiliary clipping polygon layer (`clip.gpkg`) added to the project. No raster, time-series, or classification is performed — only geometric clipping and datasource relinking.

name: Clip population mesh layers
desc: The script clips vector layers (specifically Tokyo 500m mesh-based future population estimates and Tokyo bus stops) to a user-defined rectangular extent (139.7087°E–139.7702°E, 35.6422°N–35.6958°N) using QGIS Processing's native:clip algorithm. It saves the clipped results into a single GeoPackage file (output.gpkg), updates the project’s layer data sources to point to this new GeoPackage, and appends the clipping polygon as a layer. Input data originates from MLIT’s Kansoku Shisetsu Jōhō (National Land Numerical Information — 500m mesh future population estimates and bus stop shapefiles). No temporal filtering, classification, or spectral analysis is performed; the operation is purely geometric clipping of pre-existing vector layers. Output products: clipped GeoPackage (output.gpkg), updated QGIS project (output.qgz), and auxiliary clipping polygon layer (clip.gpkg).

name: Compute weighted risk map
desc: The script computes a spatially explicit, normalized, and weighted overlay risk map by integrating multiple user-provided geospatial risk factor layers (vector or raster) within a defined study area. Each factor is processed through proximity conversion (if vector), min-max normalization to [0,1], optional inversion for inverse-risk correlation ('Lower values = Higher Risk'), and then combined via weighted linear combination. The final output is a clipped raster risk map (0–1 scale) named '{project_name}_RiskMap_Clipped.tif', loaded into the QGIS project.

name: Compute weighted risk overlay map
desc: The script computes a spatially explicit, normalized, and weighted risk map by integrating user-provided risk factor layers (vector or raster) within a defined study area. Each factor is processed through proximity analysis (if vector), normalization to [0,1], optional inversion for inverse correlation ('Lower values = Higher Risk'), and then combined via weighted linear combination. The final output is a clipped raster risk map (GeoTIFF) named '{project_name}_RiskMap_Clipped.tif', loaded into the QGIS project. No specific study area name, time range, satellite data, or external datasets are referenced in the code — all inputs are provided at runtime as QGIS layers (QgsVectorLayer or QgsRasterLayer), with no hardcoded paths, dates, or Earth Engine assets. The resolution, weights, and correlations are user-specified parameters. Output is purely a static, single-date, deterministic weighted overlay — not time-series, not cloud-masked, not sensor-derived.

name: Acquire service supply locations
desc: The script acquires point-of-interest (POI) data for service supply (e.g., hospitals, banks, schools, fuel stations, retail) by querying OpenStreetMap’s Overpass API using predefined or custom OSM tags. It extracts nodes and ways within the bounding box of a user-provided QGIS vector layer (study area), transforms coordinates to the study area’s CRS, constructs a memory-based QgsVectorLayer with attributes 'osm_id', 'name', 'type', and 'tags', and returns it as 'Supply_POIs'. If no POIs are found, it generates 15 random test points inside the study area extent for demonstration. No clipping is performed in practice due to a commented-out step and fallback logic; the output is always an unclipped memory layer. Data sources: OpenStreetMap Overpass API (no satellite/sensor/bands). Time range: not specified. Spatial location: not specified — study area is fully dynamic and provided at runtime as a QgsVectorLayer with no hardcoded geometry or place name.

name: Acquire service supply locations
desc: The script retrieves point-of-interest (POI) locations for predefined service categories (e.g., healthcare, banking, retail, education, fuel stations) from OpenStreetMap via the Overpass API. It uses the study area boundary layer’s extent to construct a WGS84 bounding box, issues an Overpass query filtering by OSM key-value tags (e.g., 'amenity'='hospital'), and parses returned nodes and ways into point geometries (using 'center' for ways). Features are transformed to the study area’s CRS, attributed with OSM ID, name, element type, and full tags JSON. If no real POIs are found, it generates 15 random test points within the study area extent for demonstration. The output is a valid QgsVectorLayer named 'Supply_POIs' containing these points — no clipping is applied due to a commented-out step and fallback logic; no geopackage export is performed. No time range, satellite data, or spectral analysis is involved.

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation. It takes a QgsVectorLayer of service points, applies a quartic kernel with a user-defined radius (in meters), and generates a raster layer with raw density values at a specified cell size. The analysis is clipped to the extent of a provided study area boundary vector layer. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or external datasets are used—the input is purely vector-based POIs and administrative/area boundaries; all operations are local GIS processing via QGIS's heatmap algorithm ('qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation').

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation. It uses QGIS's 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm with a quartic kernel (KERNEL=0), raw density output (OUTPUT_VALUE=0), and no weighting field (WEIGHT_FIELD=None). Input parameters include user-provided service POIs (QgsVectorLayer), analysis radius in meters, output cell size in meters, and a study area boundary layer to constrain the extent. The output is a QgsRasterLayer representing supply density (e.g., services per unit area), validated for validity before return. No time dimension, satellite data, or spectral bands are involved; inputs are purely vector-based geospatial features within a user-defined study area. All parameters (radius, cell_size, study_area_layer) are runtime arguments — no hardcoded study area name, time range, or external datasets are present in the code.

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity raster surface using kernel density estimation. It takes an input vector layer of service locations (supply_pois), applies a quartic kernel with a user-defined radius (in meters), and generates a raster with specified cell size (in meters) clipped to the extent of a provided study area boundary layer. The output is a QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_Density' representing raw density (counts per unit area). No time dimension, satellite data, or spectral bands are involved; inputs are purely vector-based GIS layers (points and polygon). Study area geometry is derived dynamically from the extent of study_area_layer; no projection handling or resampling logic is shown. Output is written to a temporary GeoTIFF file.

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation. It takes a QgsVectorLayer of service POIs, a user-defined analysis radius (in meters), output cell size (in meters), and a study area boundary layer to constrain the output extent. The workflow validates input layers, extracts the study area's extent, runs QGIS's 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm with a quartic kernel (KERNEL=0), no weighting field, raw density output, and writes the result to a temporary GeoTIFF. The output is a QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_Density', representing spatially continuous supply intensity (e.g., services per unit area). No satellite imagery, time-series, or spectral bands are involved; inputs are purely vector-based POIs and polygon boundaries. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using QGIS kernel density estimation. It validates the input POI layer, computes feature count, extracts extent from a study area boundary layer, and runs the 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm with user-specified radius and cell size, using a quartic kernel and raw density output. The result is loaded as a QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_Density'. No classification, temporal filtering, or satellite-derived inputs are involved.

name: Generate service supply density surface
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a rasterized supply density surface using kernel density estimation (quartic kernel) with a user-defined radius and cell size. It uses the QGIS 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm to produce a continuous intensity surface clipped to the study area extent (derived from 'study_area_layer'). The output is a styled QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_DensityRaster', visualized with a custom pseudo-color ramp (Red → Orange → Yellow → Green) representing increasing supply intensity. Input POIs are assumed to originate from an OSM query (per error message), but no specific dataset ID, time stamp, or satellite/sensor is involved — this is purely vector-to-raster geoprocessing. No classification, temporal analysis, or remote sensing bands are used.

name: Calculate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) locations into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation. It uses QGIS's 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm with a quartic kernel, a user-defined radius (scaled by 2 for visual spread), and cell size, constrained to the extent of a provided study area vector layer. Input POIs are validated for count and CRS; output is a styled raster layer named 'Supply_DensityRaster' with a red-to-green color ramp (red = low supply, green = high supply) applied via QgsSingleBandPseudoColorRenderer. No satellite or temporal data is involved — inputs are vector-based service locations (e.g., hospitals, clinics) and a study boundary polygon. The script does not perform clipping, relies on extent-based rasterization, and outputs only a local in-memory QgsRasterLayer object for QGIS visualization.

name: Estimate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) vector data into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation. It buffers the POI extent by a user-defined visual radius (2× input radius), clips to the study area boundary, and generates a raster heatmap with quartic kernel, raw density output, and cell size specified by the user. The output is a styled QgsRasterLayer named 'Supply_DensityRaster', visualized with a red-to-green color ramp (red = low supply, green = high supply) based on actual density value statistics. Input POIs are assumed to originate from an OSM query (explicitly referenced in error message), but no specific OSM tags, time filtering, or validation of temporal provenance is performed. Study area geometry and CRS are used for extent definition and clipping; no reprojection is applied — CRS mismatch warnings are not handled. No time dimension is involved; all operations are spatial only.

name: Calculate service supply density
desc: The script converts service point-of-interest (POI) locations into a continuous supply intensity surface using kernel density estimation. It uses the study area layer's extent (not buffered POI extent) to constrain the analysis, applies a quartic kernel with a visual radius set to 2× the input radius for color spread, and outputs a raster where pixel values represent raw density (counts per unit area). The output raster is styled with a red-to-green color ramp (Red=low supply, Green=high supply) to visualize spatial variation in service accessibility. Input POIs are assumed to originate from an OSM query (as indicated by the error message), but no specific OSM tags, time filters, or geometry constraints are applied in the code. The script validates input layer validity and feature count, logs debug information about CRS and extents, and skips clipping to preserve alignment with the study area extent. No temporal filtering, classification, or satellite-derived inputs are involved — the analysis is purely vector-to-raster geoprocessing on user-provided POIs.

name: Identify suitable land for afforestation
desc: The script identifies areas in Cascais municipality suitable for afforestation by integrating land use (COS2018), soil productivity (Carta de Solos + ProdS.csv), road proximity buffers (RedeViaria + ProtRV.csv), and main watercourses (LAgua). It performs geometric cleaning, spatial clipping, attribute-based filtering (e.g., 'Florestas', 'Matos', 'SAF'), table joins, buffer generation using road protection distances, difference operations to exclude road-adjacent zones, dissolution, single-part conversion, and intersection with streams. Final output is a GeoPackage layer ('final.gpkg') containing only polygons >300,000 m² that meet all suitability criteria.

name: Generate directed water network
desc: The script processes a GeoJSON layer of simplified waterlines to construct a directed graph representation suitable for hydrological or transport network modeling. It first computes the azimuth (angle) of each line segment, reorients segments so all are oriented consistently (to the right), removes zero-length segments, and subdivides long segments by interpolating additional vertices at regular intervals (determined by MAX_DIST_NODES, sourced from an external Python module find_dmax). Then, it constructs a directed network by: (1) creating parallel offset edges (3 units perpendicular to original direction) with reversed orientation and adjusted angle; (2) adding cross edges between original and offset vertices to enable bidirectional traversal and topological connectivity; and (3) handling simple two-vertex segments by adding reverse-direction duplicates. Finally, it explodes all lines into individual segments (using QGIS 'native:explodelines') to produce atomic directed edges. Input is a local GeoJSON file ('waterways_simplified.geojson'); output is a modified GeoJSON ('final_network.geojson') plus an exploded version. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or temporal filtering is involved — the entire workflow operates on static vector geometry in QGIS Python environment.

name: Construct directed water network graph
desc: The script constructs a directed graph representation of a waterway network for Delft, Netherlands, by processing an input GeoJSON of simplified waterlines. It first adds intermediate nodes to segments longer than 150 m via linear interpolation, computes and stores the azimuth (angle) of each segment in degrees, and orients all segments consistently (flipping zero-length or negatively oriented segments). Then it generates a directed network by: (1) creating parallel offset edges (3 m offset perpendicular to segment direction) with reversed orientation and adjusted angle; (2) adding cross-edges between original and offset vertices to enable bidirectional traversal and topological connectivity; and (3) duplicating two-node segments as reverse-direction edges. Finally, it explodes all resulting multiline features into individual line segments. The output is a fully exploded, topologically enriched, directed edge layer saved as 'delft_final_network_exploded_d150.geojson'. Study area is explicitly Delft; no time-dependent data or remote sensing inputs are used — input is static vector geometry only.

name: Construct directed water network
desc: The script constructs a directed graph representation of waterways in Groningen, Netherlands, by processing a GeoJSON line layer of simplified waterlines. It first adds an 'angle' attribute representing the azimuth of each segment's initial bearing, reverses segments with negative azimuth to standardize orientation, and subdivides segments longer than 150 meters by inserting equally spaced vertices. Then it generates a directed network by creating parallel offset edges (3 m perpendicular displacement), reversed duplicate edges, and cross-connecting edges between original and offset vertices — effectively building a bidirectional, topologically enriched graph suitable for flow or routing analysis. The final output is an exploded version (individual line segments) saved as 'groningen_final_network_exploded_d150.geojson'. Study area is explicitly 'Groningen'; no time dimension is involved; input is static vector data (GeoJSON), not satellite imagery.

name: Extract river network upstream downstream points
desc: The script extracts upstream (last vertex), downstream (first vertex), and next-to-downstream (second vertex) points from a D8 stream network vector layer clipped to a geographic domain; it then samples upstream accumulation values from a flow accumulation raster at these points, producing five shapefiles: clipped stream network, upstream points (domain and full), downstream points, next-to-downstream points, and their corresponding accumulation-sampled versions — all intended as spatial inputs for LISFLOOD-FP and mizuRoute hydrological modeling.

name: Extract upstream downstream river network points
desc: The script processes a precomputed river network vector layer (strn_network_*.shp) to extract specific topological vertices—namely the upstream endpoint (vertex index -1), the downstream endpoint (implied via 'downfile' used later), and the next-to-downstream vertex (index 1)—then samples upstream catchment accumulation values (from acc_downsample_*.tif) at those points. It outputs five shapefiles: (1) upstream endpoints with accumulated flow values, (2) next-to-downstream vertices with accumulation values, (3) downstream endpoints with accumulation values, (4) all line vertices for general use, and (5) the original stream network. These outputs feed into LISFLOOD and mizuRoute modeling to derive bankfull discharge along the river network.

name: Generate Curve Number layer
desc: The script generates a Curve Number (CN) raster layer for a user-provided Area of Interest (AOI) within the contiguous United States (CONUS), using NLCD 2021 Land Cover and Impervious Surface rasters and SSURGO soil vector data. It downloads NLCD data via WMS/WCS from www.mrlc.gov (EPSG:5070 projection, buffered extent), reprojects AOI to EPSG:5070, retrieves SSURGO soils via POST/WFS requests (with geometry fixing and XY swapping correction), processes soils to extract single Hydrologic Soil Group (HSG) codes (optionally removing '/D' for drained soils), polygonizes NLCD land cover, joins land cover and HSG attributes using a lookup table (default or custom CSV with 'grid_code' and 'cn'), and computes CN values by concatenating NLCD class codes and HSG codes (e.g., '11_A') to index into the lookup. Outputs include optional NLCD Land Cover and Impervious rasters, SSURGO-derived soils vector, and final CN raster — all reprojected back to the AOI’s original CRS. Time range is fixed to NLCD 2021; spatial scope is explicitly limited to CONUS; no satellite imagery is used — only preprocessed, publicly served geospatial datasets.

name: Validate cadastral quality rules
desc: The script validates cadastral data against a set of predefined LADM-COL (Latin American and Caribbean Land Administration Model) quality rules using spatial and logical consistency checks. It connects to a geodatabase (GeoPackage or PostgreSQL/PostGIS), executes selected rules (e.g., '1001': boundary points must not overlap; '3001': parcels must not overlap; '4005': cadastral ID must be 30 numeric characters), applies a geometric tolerance (1 mm), and generates two outputs: (1) a GeoPackage containing error layers (e.g., overlapping polygons, unclosed lines, attribute violations), and (2) a PDF report summarizing rule execution status, errors, and metadata. The study area is not defined by remote sensing — it operates on vector cadastral data stored locally at '/docs/geodata/gpkgs/pruebas/test_quality_rules_tolerance.gpkg'. No satellite, sensor, or time-series data is involved; the workflow is purely GIS-based database validation using QGIS Processing, Model Baker, and the Asistente LADM-COL plugin.

name: Convert DXF line features to polygon boundaries
desc: The script processes a directory of DXF files (imported as OGR vector layers with LineStringZ geometry), filters features where the 'Layer' attribute equals 'LIMIT' or 'LIMITS', saves the selected line features as temporary layers, converts those lines to polygons using QGIS's linestopolygons algorithm, merges all resulting polygon layers into a single GeoPackage file ('limits_Agg.gpkg'), and adds the merged layer to the QGIS project. Files failing geometry type checks (non-LineString/LineStringZ) or polygon conversion are logged in 'err_layers'. The output is a unified polygon layer representing boundary delineations extracted from CAD source files.

name: Generate raster value boxplot
desc: The script allows the user to interactively select a loaded raster layer in QGIS and optionally define a spatial extent using either the current map canvas extent or a selected feature from an active vector layer. It then clips the raster to that extent, converts the clipped raster pixels to point features with attribute values, samples up to 1000 pixel values (with user confirmation for larger datasets), and generates a matplotlib boxplot visualizing the statistical distribution (min, Q1, median, Q3, max, outliers) of the raster values within the defined area.

name: Manage invasive species data
desc: The script loads and processes two non-remote-sensing geospatial datasets: (1) CAOP2022 administrative boundaries (Cont_Conc_CAOP2022.shp) — a Portuguese national administrative shapefile — which is re-encoded to UTF-8 and exported as 'CAOP_UTF8.shp'; and (2) STOPvespa 2023 point locations of Asian hornet (Vespula velutina) sightings from ICNF, loaded from a CSV ('STOPVespa_2023_simplified.csv') using delimited text with lat/long coordinates (EPSG:4326). The workflow creates a new QGIS project ('stopvespa.qgz'), adds both layers, fixes encoding for attribute integrity, and saves the project. No satellite, raster, or time-series analysis is performed; all operations are vector-layer management and project setup for invasive species monitoring in Portugal.

name: Export CAOP administrative boundaries
desc: The script exports the 'Cont_Conc_CAOP2022' vector layer — a Portuguese administrative boundary dataset (Concelhos, i.e., municipalities) from the CAOP 2022 official cartography — from an open QGIS project to two separate ESRI Shapefile outputs ('CAOP_1.shp' and 'CAOP_2.shp') in UTF-8 encoding. It corrects the layer's character encoding if not already UTF-8, accesses the layer by name within the current QgsProject, and uses two distinct GEE-adjacent (but actually QGIS Python API) export methods: QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3 and processing.run('native:savefeatures'). No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed; the task is purely data export and encoding normalization. Study area is Portugal (inferred from CAOP — Carta Administrativa Oficial de Portugal); time range is 2022 (per filename 'CAOP2022'); no satellite, sensor, or band usage — this is a vector boundary dataset, not remotely sensed imagery.

name: Crop Sentinel-2 raster to Alcoutim municipality
desc: The script loads a Sentinel-2 Level-2A (surface reflectance) GeoTIFF (S2A-T29SNB-B2348-2021-8-22.tif), clips it spatially to the Alcoutim municipality boundary extracted from the official Portuguese CAOP 2022 administrative vector dataset (Cont_Conc_CAOP2022.shp), sets nodata value to 0 for all four bands (B2, B3, B4, B8), removes intermediate layers, and saves the final clipped raster as a GeoTIFF named 'S2SR-B2348_alcoutim.tif' in the output_subfolder. The workflow uses QGIS Python Console (PyQGIS) with native and GDAL processing algorithms — no GEE (Google Earth Engine) API calls are present; this is a local QGIS geoprocessing script, not a GEE script.

name: Compute Curve Number for Land Use
desc: The script computes the Curve Number (CN2) for hydrological runoff modeling by intersecting land use/land cover data (ZABAGED and LPIS) with soil hydrologic group (HSG) data, applying a lookup table (CN_table.csv), and calculating runoff depth using user-defined rainfall depth or return periods. Key steps include WFS-based download of Czech cadastral (ZABAGED) and agricultural parcel (LPIS) layers, merging and styling them, clipping soil data to the area of interest, performing vector intersection, joining CN values from CSV, and computing runoff via the SCS-CN method. Outputs are GeoPackage layers at each processing stage: merged land use, clipped soil, intersected layer, CN-assigned layer, and final runoff layer.

name: Compute Integrated Quality Metric for rivers
desc: The script computes the Integrated Quality Metric (IQM) for river segments by integrating nine ecological and anthropogenic pressure indices (A1–A4, F1–F5) derived from vector and raster inputs. It begins with D8 flow direction computation from a DEM and stream network, filters infrastructure points near rivers, then sequentially calculates: A1–A3 (morphological/structural integrity indices using dams, structures, and reference width points), A4 (longitudinal continuity index), F1–F5 (anthropogenic pressure indices incorporating roads, land use, riparian buffer adequacy, and transect-based width assessment). Finally, it synthesizes all nine indices into a single 'Score IQM' field using the formula 1 − (sum of indices)/38, outputting a vector layer (line or polygon) where each feature carries the final IQM score.

name: Extract and snap stream outlets
desc: The script extracts outlet points by interpolating a point near the downstream end of each stream segment (at 90% of length for short streams or 30 m from end for long streams), rasterizes the stream network using the input DEM as base, then snaps the interpolated points to the nearest stream pixel within 40 m using the Jenson Snap Pour Points algorithm; outputs a vector point layer of snapped outlets aligned to the stream raster.

name: Compute river width naturalness index
desc: The script computes the 'Indice F4' — a quantitative indicator of naturalness in river width variability along stream centerlines. It processes vector line features representing a river network ('RivNet'), generates evenly spaced points along each segment (using 'native:pointsalonglines' with spacing = segment length / 100), then queries nearest width values from an external point layer ('ptref_widths') using 'overlay_nearest'. It calculates the percentage of adjacent width-change rates (normalized by segment division distance and expressed per km) falling outside user-defined thresholds (LTHRESH=0, UTHRESH=0.2 by default, but configurable via 'thresh' parameter), and maps that percentage to a 4-class ordinal score (0–3). The output is a vector layer identical to the input 'RivNet' but with an added integer field 'Indice F4' per feature. No satellite imagery, raster processing, or temporal analysis is performed; all operations are vector-based and static. Study area, time range, coordinate reference system, and data provenance are not specified in the code.

name: Reproject and package GIS layers
desc: The script processes all vector layers loaded in the current QGIS project: (1) appends geometry-type–specific suffixes (_point, _line, _polygon, _no_Geometry) to layer names; (2) reassigns their CRS to MSK-64 (custom user CRS USER:100026, corresponding to Moscow System of Coordinates 1964, tailored for Leningrad region); (3) fixes geometries using QGIS 'native:fixgeometries'; (4) exports each layer individually as a GeoPackage (.gpkg); (5) merges all exported GeoPackages into a single consolidated GeoPackage (_Merged_Package.gpkg) using 'native:package'; (6) converts that merged GeoPackage into a File Geodatabase (.gdb) named Package_YYYY_MM_DD.gdb using GDAL's convertformat. All outputs are saved in the user-specified directory (D:\wrk_genplan\Data_2023).

name: Clip vector data by administrative regions
desc: The script performs spatial clipping of vector layers (e.g., buildings, greenery) using an administrative boundary layer (e.g., districts or islands), producing one output file per region — named with a '_data' postfix — in GeoPackage format. It first splits the boundary layer by a unique name field (e.g., 'Name'), then iteratively clips all loaded vector layers against each boundary part, filters out empty results, merges non-empty clipped layers per region, and cleans up intermediate files.

name: Import and geocode supermarket locations
desc: The script imports supermarket location data from user-provided template files (CSV, Excel, or Shapefile), performs address geocoding (via Nominatim) for non-Shapefile inputs to assign coordinates, validates required fields, transforms coordinates to the specified EPSG projection, and writes the resulting markets into a QGIS project database as Supermarket objects. It supports truncating existing markets and updating administrative unit codes (AGS). No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is involved; all operations are vector-based GIS workflows within QGIS using local file I/O and external geocoding.

name: Classify Local Climate Zones
desc: The script classifies vector grid cells into Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classes (1–10, A–G) using morphological parameters (e.g., building_surface_fraction, impervious_frac, anthro_heat) derived from local urban morphology data. It applies a v3.0 advanced classification workflow: (1) computes Normalized Root Mean Square Percentage Error (RMSEP) against LCZ parameter ranges, (2) applies adaptive thresholding based on parameter coverage (max 10 parameters), (3) outputs confidence scores (0.0–1.0), (4) corrects classifications using ESA WorldCover (via zonal statistics on raster land use layer) and CORINE Land Cover (via spatial join to vector polygons, specifically targeting industrial class 121 → LCZ 8 or 10 based on anthropogenic heat >100 W/m²), and (5) applies spatial smoothing via 3×3 majority filtering for low-confidence cells (<0.3). Outputs include updated vector attributes: 'lcz_class', 'lcz_rmsep_norm', 'lcz_confidence', 'lcz_esa_fix', 'lcz_corine_fix', 'lcz_vulnerability', and 'lcz_matches'. No explicit satellite imagery processing occurs — inputs are precomputed morphological and ancillary land cover rasters/vector layers. Study area and time range are not specified in the code.

name: Classify LCZ districts
desc: The script performs district-based LCZ (Local Climate Zone) classification using a Random Forest model trained on a knowledge base of urban morphology parameters. It first identifies urban 'seeds' (cells with Building Surface Fraction ≥10%), then applies multidimensional clustering (HDBSCAN-like, using spatial position, roughness height, and building fraction with weighted scaling) to group cells into coherent urban districts. Each district is assigned an LCZ class (e.g., 'C1', 'C2') via RF prediction on mean morphometric parameters (e.g., sky_view_factor, roughness_height, building_frac). Natural areas (non-district cells) are classified individually. Outputs include: (1) updated input vector layer with 'lcz_class', 'lcz_confidence', and 'lcz_score' attributes; (2) a separate GeoPackage layer 'distretti_lcz.gpkg' containing MultiPolygon district hulls annotated with cluster_id, lcz_id, and confidence; and (3) QGIS MessageLog diagnostics including feature importance ranking. The study area, time range, satellite data, and explicit geographic extent are not specified — the script operates purely on precomputed vector attributes (e.g., 'building_frac', 'roughness_height', 'svf') from an internal project directory's knowledge base and input vector layer.

name: Classify LCZ districts semantically
desc: The script performs semantic, rule-based Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classification of urban and natural districts using morphological parameters (e.g., building fraction, roughness height, sky view factor, impervious/pervious fractions, albedo, aspect ratio, terrain roughness, admittance, anthropogenic heat, industry heat) derived from precomputed grid cells. It clusters input features into context-aware districts—urban districts via building geometry clustering (using a local buildings layer), and natural districts via canopy/SVF-based spatial clustering—and applies expert rules including ESA WorldCover land use authoritative overrides (classes 20, 30, 40, 60, 80 → LCZ C/D/F/G), morphological parameter audits against standardized LCZ archetype ranges (10 parameters per class), contextual scoring with ESA reinforcement bonuses and penalties, and LCZ 1 vs 10 disambiguation using industry_heat/anthro_heat ratio. Outputs include: (1) updated input vector layer with fields lcz_class, lcz_score, lcz_confidence, lcz_ambiguity, lcz_matches, lcz_rmsep, lcz_vulnerability, lcz_esa_fix; (2) a separate district-level vector layer (GPKG) containing aggregated geometries, assigned LCZ IDs, scores, and textual explanations; and (3) QGIS log messages detailing clustering counts, ESA integration, and per-district diagnostics. Data sources are not satellite-derived in this script — all inputs are precomputed morphological metrics and ancillary layers (buildings, ESA WorldCover) assumed to be locally available in the project’s unified data directory.

name: Generate spatial grid layer
desc: The script creates a regular polygonal vector grid (square cells) aligned to the extent of an existing QGIS layer named 'rgb', using a user-specified cell size in map units. It saves the grid as a GeoPackage file ('grid.gpkg') in the same directory as the 'rgb' layer source and adds it to the QGIS project. The task is purely geometric — no remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or spectral processing is performed. Input is a local vector or raster layer named 'rgb' (name only; no metadata or CRS assumptions beyond project CRS), and output is a static, non-temporal, non-thematic vector grid layer. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Vectorize building mask raster
desc: The script converts a raster layer named 'mask' into a vector polygon layer stored in a GeoPackage file with suffix '_buildings.gpkg', then removes polygons where the attribute 'value' equals 0. The resulting vector layer is named 'buildings' and added to the same layer group as the source raster in QGIS. No explicit study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial inputs are used — the input raster 'mask' is assumed to already exist in the QGIS project, with no metadata or provenance specified in the script. All operations are local GIS processing (GDAL polygonize + attribute-based filtering) within QGIS Desktop using PyQGIS.

name: Calculate median distance to buildings
desc: The script computes a distance raster from a binary 'mask' raster (interpreted as building footprints) using GDAL's proximity algorithm, then calculates the median distance value within each polygon of a 'grid' vector layer and writes it into a new 'median_dist' attribute. The output is a modified vector layer with per-polygon median Euclidean distances to the nearest building pixel. No satellite imagery, time series, or classification is involved; inputs are local QGIS layers named 'mask' (raster) and 'grid' (vector), with no explicit geographic extent, temporal range, or external data sources specified in the code.

name: Compute median distance to mask features
desc: The script computes a Euclidean distance raster from a binary 'mask' vector layer (interpreted as presence/absence geometry), then calculates the median pixel value of that distance raster within each polygon feature of a 'grid' vector layer, storing the result in a new attribute 'median_dist'. The output is a vector layer ('grid') updated with a numeric field representing the median distance from each grid cell's interior to the nearest mask feature. No satellite imagery, time-series, or classification is involved — inputs are local QGIS vector layers named 'mask' and 'grid'; operations are purely GIS-based proximity analysis using GDAL's proximity algorithm and raster sampling within vector geometries.

name: Compute median DSM within grid zones
desc: The script computes the median value of a Digital Surface Model (DSM) raster, masked by a binary mask layer, within each polygon feature of a grid vector layer. The workflow includes: (1) retrieving three local QGIS layers named 'dsm', 'mask', and 'grid'; (2) multiplying the DSM raster (band 1) with the mask raster (band 1) using GDAL Raster Calculator to produce a masked DSM; (3) computing zonal statistics (median only) of the masked DSM over the grid polygons using QGIS Zonal Statistics; (4) replacing null median values in the resulting 'med_median' attribute field of the grid layer with 0. No external remote sensing data sources, time-series, or cloud-based processing are involved — all inputs are preloaded local layers in the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and coordinate reference system are not specified.

name: Clip topographic vector layers
desc: The script clips all vector layers within the QGIS layer group named 'Topografi 10' using a shapefile mask located at '//TP-Share/G/Documents/GIS/Danderyd/Surveying/18276/mask.shp'. It preserves original layer styles by saving and reapplying .qml files, saves clipped outputs as GeoPackage files in '//TP-Share/G/Documents/GIS/Danderyd/Surveying/18276/clip/', and organizes the clipped layers under a new QGIS layer tree group named 'clippedGroup'. The original clipped layers are removed from the source group. The study area is explicitly tied to Danderyd (a municipality in Stockholm County, Sweden), and no satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or classification/analysis methods are involved — this is a pure vector geoprocessing workflow using QGIS native clipping.

name: Tile raster for machine learning
desc: The script exports raster tiles (PNG and/or GeoTIFF) and optional binary masks (PNG) from a user-provided input raster layer, using a regular grid with configurable tile size and overlap. Tiles are named using Deepness-convention coordinates (tile_img_{x}_{y}.png), and optionally placed in a timestamped subdirectory. Mask generation is performed via vector-to-raster conversion of an optional input vector layer. Extent rounding to the input raster’s pixel grid is applied either via Deepness integration (deepness.processing.extent_utils.round_extent_to_rlayer_grid) or a fallback identity operation. The workflow is designed for preparing training data for deep learning models — no classification, modeling, or inference is performed; only data partitioning and export. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code — it operates on arbitrary QGIS raster layers provided at runtime.

name: Clean road network topology
desc: The script performs topological cleaning of a vector road layer using GRASS GIS v.clean tools within QGIS. It applies two sequential v.clean operations: first with tool=0 (snap) to resolve small gaps and overlaps, then with tool=6 (break) to split lines at intersections. Errors from the second clean are joined to the cleaned layer, and features without errors (i.e., 'e_fid IS NULL') are filtered into a new memory layer. The final cleaned road network is saved as a Shapefile, added to the QGIS project, and logged with feature count statistics and processing time.

name: Generate Voronoi polygons for road network centroids
desc: The script processes an input vector layer (typically OSM-derived road or linear infrastructure data) to generate Voronoi tessellations representing spatial influence zones around road segments. It first cleans the geometry (deletes holes, removes null geometries, converts multipart to singlepart), renumbers duplicate 'osm_id' attributes to ensure uniqueness, computes centroids of the cleaned single-part features, constructs a buffer around those centroids (distance scaled to CRS units), generates Voronoi polygons from the centroids, indexes the Voronoi layer, clips the Voronoi polygons to the buffer extent, and saves the clipped Voronoi polygons as a Shapefile. It also saves the intermediate centroid layer and logs processing metadata including timing and output paths.

name: Refactor MPA subregion attributes
desc: The script refactors a vector layer of Marine Protected Area (MPA) subregion information for 2018, renaming and re-typing specific fields to prepare standardized output for downstream R analysis. Key operations include field mapping: 'ess_unique_id' → integer; 'subreg2018' → text (3-char); 'clipped_to_2018_boundary_by_feature_areakm2' → double precision (area in km²); 'MPA_NETWOR' → text (network designation); 'original_areakm2' → double precision. No spatial or temporal filtering, reprojection, or classification is performed — only attribute restructuring. The input is a pre-existing vector layer named 'MPA subregion information 2018'; the output is a new vector layer 'ess_output_for_R_2018' with renamed and typed fields. Study area, satellite data, imagery, bands, and geospatial operations beyond field refactoring are not specified.

name: Refactor MPA subregion fields for R
desc: The script refactors a vector layer of MPA (Marine Protected Area) subregion information for 2025, renaming and re-typing specific fields to prepare the data for downstream R analysis. It uses QGIS's 'native:refactorfields' algorithm to map input fields — 'ess_unique_id', 'subreg2025', 'clipped_to_2025_boundary_by_feature_areakm2', 'MPA_NETWOR', and 'original_areakm2' — to standardized output field names and types (integer, text, double precision). The output is a new vector layer ('ess_output_for_R_2025') with five explicitly defined fields, preserving geometry and attribute structure for statistical modeling in R.

name: Compute river-viewshed visibility
desc: The script computes viewsheds (visibility analysis) from river observation points (midpoints along river segments) over a digital surface model (DSM), using SAGA GIS's visibility algorithm. It first clips the DSM to polygon boundaries corresponding to each river segment, then performs point-based visibility analysis using observer heights stored in the 'vheight' attribute (adjusted by +15 m to account for river elevation at −15 m), and outputs binary visibility rasters per river segment. The workflow includes progress tracking, NoData validation, and geopackage-based batch processing of river segments.

name: Compute proximity distance ranges
desc: The script computes the minimum Euclidean distance from each polygon (e.g., administrative units, land parcels, or buildings) to the nearest input point feature (e.g., service facilities, infrastructure nodes), generating a vector layer where each polygon is attributed with its shortest distance (in meters) to any point. It performs spatial join, geometry centroid extraction, distance calculation, group-wise minimum aggregation, and thematic rendering using graduated symbology based on distance ranges. Output is a styled vector layer named 'Distance ranges in meters' added to the QGIS project layer tree with feature count enabled.

name: Clip and merge cadastral features by department
desc: The script loads PostGIS vector layers from a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database (schema 'bdtopo_tmp') containing French topographic data, specifically the 'lieuditnonhabite' (uninhabited place names) layer partitioned per department (e.g., '_d051', '_d075', etc.). For each department code in [51,75,77,91,92,93,94], it selects the corresponding department boundary from the 'departement' layer (using 'code_insee' attribute), clips the respective 'lieuditnonhabite' partition to that boundary using geometry intersection, stores clipped features in an in-memory point layer, removes the original partitioned layer, then merges all clipped layers into a single unified vector layer ('OUTPUT' from 'native:mergevectorlayers'). The final merged layer is added to the QGIS project. The script explicitly notes manual database import is still required for the merged result. Study area is Île-de-France and adjacent departments (51,75,77,91,92,93,94); data source is BD TOPO® (French national topographic database); no satellite, sensor, or temporal data involved — purely vector-based spatial clipping and merging of administrative and cadastral features.

name: Attribute burnt areas with FSID
desc: The script adds standardized NAFI (Northern Australia Fire Information) metadata attributes to an input vector layer of dissolved burnt area polygons. It populates fields including Fire Scar ID (FSID), mapping period (start date only), month (current month), region name (from a predefined enum list NTRRP_REGIONS), upload date (current date), current status ('yes'), and user-provided comments. The output is a vector feature sink containing the original geometries augmented with these attributes.

name: Dissolve burnt area polygons
desc: The script dissolves adjacent or overlapping polygon features representing burnt areas into single, non-overlapping polygons. It first applies geometry validation and correction using QGIS's 'native:fixgeometries' algorithm, then performs a dissolve operation with no attribute field specified (i.e., merges all input polygons into one or more contiguous geometries based on spatial contiguity). The input is a user-provided vector layer of burnt areas; no raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, or classification logic is involved. The output is a vector feature sink containing the dissolved polygon geometry. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified — this is a pure vector topology operation in QGIS Processing, not a Google Earth Engine (GEE) script despite the prompt’s mischaracterization.

name: Download current burnt areas mapping
desc: The script downloads and extracts a ZIP file containing current burnt area mapping data for a selected NTRRP region. The data is sourced from a predefined URL pattern (e.g., 'bfnt_{region.lower()}_current_sr3577.zip') hosted at getNtrrpDataUrl(), and extracted into a region-specific subdirectory under the user-specified WorkingDirectory. The output is the filesystem path to that extracted directory ('CurrentMappingDirectory'). No geospatial processing, classification, or analysis is performed in the script — it is purely a data retrieval and unpacking workflow. Study area is defined by NTRRP_REGIONS (a list of Australian fire management regions, though exact names are not shown in code); time range is not specified; satellite/sensor/bands are not involved — this is vector or raster mapping data delivered as a pre-processed archive. Final product is an unzipped local directory containing the mapping dataset.

name: Download NAFI segmentation data
desc: The script downloads and unzips precomputed NAFI (Northern Territory Fire and Weather) segmentation data for a selected NTRRP region (e.g., 'Kakadu', 'Arnhem', 'Kimberley') from a remote URL. It uses QGIS Processing's native file downloader to fetch a region-specific ZIP archive (e.g., 'kakadu/kakadu.zip') hosted at a base URL obtained via getNtrrpDataUrl(), then extracts the contents into a user-specified local directory. No geospatial processing, classification, or analysis is performed — the script is purely a data retrieval and filesystem deployment utility. The output is a local folder containing unpacked segmentation data (raster or vector files, format not specified in code), with no explicit mention of study period, satellite imagery, bands, or geospatial operations beyond filesystem copy. The NTRRP_REGIONS list implies Australian northern tropical regions, but exact boundaries, time range, sensor origin, or data generation methodology are not specified in the script.

name: Rasterise burnt areas by FSID
desc: The script converts a vector layer of burnt areas (polygons attributed with an FSID field) into a raster map at 10m resolution, then merges it with an existing regional raster mapping layer; the output is a single merged raster where burnt areas are encoded by their FSID values and background/overlap is handled via GDAL merge with NODATA=0, followed by application of a color table for visualization.

name: Upload burnt areas
desc: The script prepares and uploads attributed burnt area vector data and a corresponding rasterised burnt area map to the NTRRP (Northern Territory Remote Sensing Program) / NAFI (Northern Australian Fire Information) system. It saves the input vector layer ('AttributedBurntAreas') as a Shapefile, copies the input raster layer ('RasterisedBurntAreas') as a GeoTIFF, packages both into a region-specific ZIP archive (e.g., 'bfnt_darwin_current_sr3577.zip'), and invokes an external Python upload script to submit the archive to a predefined NTRRP upload URL. The workflow is triggered per NTRRP region (e.g., 'Darwin'), uses EPSG:3577 (GDA94 / Australian Albers) projection (inferred from filename 'sr3577'), and relies on QGIS Processing algorithms for I/O. No satellite imagery processing, classification, or temporal analysis occurs in this script — it is purely a data packaging and upload utility. Study area is defined by user-provided vector and raster layers; time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations are not specified in the script.

name: Crop raster layer to extent
desc: The script crops a user-selected QGIS raster layer (e.g., SAR or optical TIF) to a user-defined geographic extent drawn interactively on the map canvas or provided in batch mode. It computes the corresponding pixel-aligned bounding box using GDAL geotransform and GCP_TPS transformation, optionally grows the pixel window to meet a minimum size (100×100 pixels), executes gdal:translate with -srcwin for lossless subsetting, builds overviews, preserves ICEYE-specific metadata (e.g., 'ICEYE_PROPERTIES'), and adds the resulting clipped GeoTIFF as a new raster layer named with '_CROP_' suffix and SHA-1 hash of the extent. A temporary vector mask layer is displayed during cropping and removed upon completion.

name: Generate SAR video frames from SLC
desc: The script generates a multiband GeoTIFF raster where each band represents a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) frame extracted from a cropped Single Look Complex (SLC) product. It reads complex-valued SLC data, applies FFT along the azimuth direction to isolate time-resolved frames, writes magnitude-only frames (|complex|) into sequential bands, preserves georeferencing and ICEYE-specific metadata (e.g., acquisition times, SAR resolution, observation direction), and builds overviews. Input is an active QGIS raster layer assumed to be an ICEYE SLC product; cropping is performed interactively or in batch via user-defined extents. Outputs include a new multiband raster layer added to the QGIS project with per-band temporal properties applied, and associated temporary files (cropped SLC, final video TIFF). No external GEE assets are used — this is a QGIS plugin workflow operating on local or loaded SLC rasters; satellite, orbit, and acquisition metadata are parsed from embedded ICEYE_PROPERTIES metadata, not hardcoded or fetched from Earth Engine.

name: Extract tent structures in IDP camps
desc: The script identifies tented structures within IDP (Internally Displaced Persons) camps using RGB satellite imagery and sample bare-ground points. It computes soil brightness index (BI) to characterize bare areas, derives spectral ratios (r = R/(R+G+B), g = G/(R+G+B)), constructs fuzzy features f1 (mean absolute deviation of r and g from their respective band values) and f3 (positive part of green minus min(red, blue)), normalizes and thresholds them using Otsu’s method, segments built-up-like pixels, excludes bare areas via inversion and masking, applies binary morphological opening to clean noise, and finally polygonizes the resulting binary mask to output vector polygons representing tented structures — requiring post-processing (e.g., rectanglify, differencing against known camp boundaries) for operational use.

name: Identify unpaid hunting licenses by monte intersection
desc: The script identifies hunting zones (manchas) scheduled for hunting within the next 7 days that intersect with municipal forest parcels (MUP montes) not yet licensed—by spatially joining mancha polygons with MUP monte polygons, calculating intersection area ratios, and cross-referencing against an Excel list of paid monte identifiers (Etiqueta column). Outputs include console-printed warnings (e.g., 'X% of mancha Coto Y is in MUP Z that has not paid') and populates two Python lists: listadecotosaestudiar (matriculation IDs of affected hunting zones) and listademontesaestudiar (Etiqueta IDs of non-paying montes). No persistent GIS layers are added; all processing is in-memory using QGIS Python API (QgsVectorLayer, processing.run, geometry.intersects()).

name: Convert points to polygons
desc: The script converts a selected QGIS vector point layer into a polygon layer by first creating a line path from the points (ordered by a user-selected attribute field), then converting that line to a closed polygon. It computes and adds a 'hectarea' field with area in hectares, applies red outline symbology with transparent fill, and labels each polygon with its area rounded to two decimals (e.g., '12.34 ha.'). Input points must be selected (or all used if none selected), and the ordering field determines path sequence — critical for meaningful polygon topology.

name: Export cadastral map tiles
desc: The script exports georeferenced PNG map tiles (2000×2000 px) and corresponding world files (.pgw) for cadastral and topographic vector layers sourced from a PostGIS database. Each tile corresponds to the bounding box of a feature in the 'zone_name' layer (schema 'temporary', table 'zone_name'), rendered at scale 1:1250 in EPSG:2154 (RGF93/Lambert-93). Layers include feuille (map sheets), parcelle (land parcels), batiment (buildings), localisant (location bounding boxes), coursdeau (rivers), zone_name (zones of interest), annotationriviere/rue/commune (text annotations), and toponymeriviere/rue (toponyms). Styling is applied via QML files per layer and theme (e.g., 'Agriculture', 'Atmosphere'). The background color is configurable via CSV control file. No raster or satellite data is used — all inputs are vector layers from PostGIS.

name: Select parcel-intersecting grid squares
desc: The script generates a regular grid of fixed-size squares (6620×6620 units) aligned to the extent of the 'feuille' layer in a PostGIS database, filters those squares that spatially intersect with features from the 'parcelle' layer (land parcels), then randomly selects N=160 of them. Outputs include: (1) a full grid shapefile ('full_grid.shp'), (2) a selected subset shapefile ('selected_areas.shp'), and (3) a CSV export of the selected grid features’ attributes (area_id, style, bounding coordinates). All operations occur within QGIS using PyQGIS API; no Earth Engine (GEE) code is present — the prompt incorrectly states 'GEE script', but the code is purely QGIS Python (PyQGIS) interacting with PostGIS layers and memory vector layers. Study area is implicitly defined by the extent of the 'feuille' layer loaded from schema 'travail' table 'feuille'; CRS is set to EPSG:2154 (RGF93 / Lambert-93, France). No satellite, sensor, bands, time series, or GEE assets are used.

name: Estimate treatment gain surface
desc: The script implements a geostatistical workflow to estimate and compare two agricultural treatment surfaces (T1 = control, T2 = experimental) over a study area using ordinary kriging. It partitions field-measured point data by treatment (T1/T2), performs 80/20 train/test splits, builds kriging models (with user-selected semivariogram: linear/exponential/gaussian/spherical) on the 80% training subsets to predict full-area rasters, computes prediction errors on the 20% test subsets, then applies a second round of kriging (using linear model only) on those errors to generate error-correction surfaces. Finally, it sums each treatment’s prediction raster with its corresponding error-correction raster, clips both to the study area polygon, and computes the Gain raster as T2 − T1 — representing spatially explicit estimated gain (e.g., yield increase, nutrient response) of T2 over T1 in original measurement units. Outputs include three rasters (T1, T2, Gain) and HTML statistics for Gain.

name: Map treatment gain surfaces
desc: The script performs geostatistical modeling (ordinary kriging) on point-based field measurements of an agricultural variable (e.g., yield, nutrient content, soil property) stratified by treatment labels (T1–T5), to generate spatially continuous raster surfaces for each treatment across a user-defined study area. It implements a two-step kriging approach: first estimating the variable surface using 80% of points per treatment, then computing prediction errors on the remaining 20%, followed by kriging those errors and adding them back (i.e., error-correction or ‘kriging with external drift’-inspired refinement). Finally, it computes pairwise ‘gain’ rasters (differences between treatment surfaces) based on a user-selected reference treatment, and outputs statistics (HTML reports) summarizing each gain surface’s distribution (mean, std, min/max, etc.). All outputs are clipped to the study area polygon and resampled to a user-specified pixel size.

name: Polygonize reclassified raster classes
desc: The script converts reclassified raster files (with DN values 1–3 mapped to predicted class IDs 228–230) into vector polygon shapefiles. It loads each .tif raster from a local directory, runs GDAL polygonize to convert pixel clusters into polygons, adds a 'predicted' integer field populated via a hardcoded DN-to-class lookup table {1→228, 2→229, 3→230}, and removes polygons where DN=0. Outputs are ESRI Shapefiles (.shp) saved in a specified local folder. No remote sensing data loading, time-series processing, or GEE server-side computation occurs — this is a local QGIS/GDAL-based post-processing workflow operating on pre-existing, locally stored rasters. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not referenced in the code and cannot be inferred from the script.

name: Create station buffer zones
desc: The script creates point and polygon vector layers representing train stations and their 1.5 km and 3 km circular buffers in the Apeldoorn region of the Netherlands. It uses hard-coded RD New (EPSG:28992) coordinates for 12 specific stations (e.g., 'Apeldoorn', 'Zutphen', 'Deventer'), generates memory-based QgsVectorLayer objects, saves them as ESRI Shapefiles to a local filesystem path, and loads them into the QGIS project under a '2. Station Analysis' layer group with subgroups by radius. It then performs spatial clipping (using 'native:clip') of four existing project layers — 'Mixed Use Index 2024', 'Floor Space Index 2024', 'Building Age Average', and 'Urbanity Index' — against each buffer layer, saving clipped outputs to disk and adding them to the corresponding radius subgroup. The study area is explicitly the Apeldoorn region; no satellite, sensor, or temporal data are used — all inputs are vector layers already loaded in QGIS. Outputs include: (1) a point layer 'Apeldoorn Stations.shp'; (2) two polygon buffer layers ('station_buffers_1km.shp', 'station_buffers_3km.shp'); and (3) eight clipped indicator layers (two per radius, one per indicator).

name: Fetch forest and terrain raster and vector data
desc: The script fetches geospatial raster (DEM, flow direction D8, CHM, DTW) and vector (forest stand attributes, ecological zones) datasets from Finnish national web services (Metsakeskus, Rajapinnat.metsaan.fi, Paituli/CSC, Avoin.metsakeskus.fi, Paikkatieto.ymparisto.fi) using WMS, WCS, WFS, and ESRI REST Image/Feature Server protocols. It clips or subsets these remote services to the extent of a local vector layer ('valuma_alueet' from 'ReTreeT.gpkg'), validates data presence via pixel value checks (e.g., max > 1.0 for rasters), and saves outputs as local GeoTIFF or GeoJSON files. The workflow includes bounding box derivation, CRS-aware parameter generation (bboxSR, imageSR, srsname, outSR), format-specific request construction (e.g., 'exportImage?' for ESRI ImageServer, 'GetCoverage' for WCS 2.0.0, 'getMap' for WMS, 'getFeature' for WFS), and GDAL/rasterio-based validation and visualization. No time-series analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — the core task is on-demand data acquisition and local persistence.

name: Calculate ecological retention tree value
desc: The script calculates an integrated environmental value ('env_value') for forest grid cells to support ecological retention tree selection. It computes four components: (1) biodiversity index ('biod') using Simpson's diversity index from stem counts of pine, deciduous, and spruce; (2) nitrogen/phosphorus retention potential ('pRetent') derived from euc_1 (likely a soil or vegetation index) and normalized DTW_1 (depth-to-water); (3) decay tree potential ('dtree') using species-specific polynomial models parameterized by fertility class and biogeoclass ('PaajakoNro'), applied either globally per grid or per tree via 'diameter' and 'treespecies'; and (4) normalized depth-to-water ('DTW_1n'). These are weighted equally and summed into 'env_value'. The final output is a binary 'reTree' selection identifying top-ranked grid cells (by 'HS_1', likely a hotspot score from hsAnalysis) for retention within cutting areas ('leimikko' = 1), exported as a GeoPackage layer. Input data is local vector data from 'data_example\ReTreeT.gpkg' — no satellite imagery or time-series analysis is used; all operations are attribute-based GIS processing in QGIS Python API (QgsVectorLayer). Study area and time range are not specified in the code.

name: Generate riparian buffer zone
