It performs CRS alignment (with optional reprojection), geometry validation and repair (using QGIS 'fix geometries'), and then invokes an external R-based tool (FHAST) via command-line to execute the overlap analysis. The output is generated by the external FHAST application (not shown in this script), likely including spatial statistics, area measurements, or clipped/intersected vector layers representing the overlapping region.

name: Run FHAST hydro-ecological simulation
desc: The script runs the FHAST (Fish Habitat Simulation Tool) model, a hydro-ecological simulation framework that integrates environmental forcing (daily flow/velocity/depth rasters), fish population and parameter files, habitat and interaction parameters, spatial inputs (grid top point, grid centerline, cover, canopy, tree growth, AOI, wildcard), and optional raster folders to simulate fish habitat suitability and dynamics. It constructs a configuration file (config.txt) from user-specified QGIS layer groups (e.g., 'Environmental Input File', 'Fish Population File', 'Grid Centerline'), validates input presence, derives paths via QgsLayerTreeGroup.findLayers() and QgsProviderRegistry.decodeUri(), handles optional layers (e.g., Tree Growth, Wildcard, Canopy, AOI — including intersection for multi-AOI), writes metadata to notes.txt, and executes an external R-based FHAST executable (Rscript.exe run_fhast.R) with a preview flag. Outputs include a timestamped output folder containing config.txt, notes.txt, optionally joint_aoi.shp, and FHAST-generated simulation results (not defined in this script but implied by the external tool). No satellite data, cloud masking, spectral indices, or GEE-specific geospatial operations are used — this is a QGIS plugin orchestrating local file-based model execution.

name: Identify subway stations near high-capacity roads
desc: The script identifies subway stations located within a 500-meter buffer of road segments with 8 or more lanes. It reads two local vector datasets: 'road_link2.shp' (containing road attributes including 'LANES') and 'subway_station.shp' (point locations of subway stations), both assumed to be in EPSG:5186 (Korea 2000 / Unified CS). It performs attribute-based selection (LANES >= 8), geometric buffering (500 m, 8 segments per quarter circle), spatial containment query (station geometry within buffer polygon), and exports the selected stations to 'Result.shp'. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, or classification model is used — all operations are static vector GIS workflows. Study area is implied to be South Korea (via CRS EPSG:5186 and Korean-language comments), but no explicit administrative boundaries or extent are defined in code. Data sources are local shapefiles; no satellite, sensor, or band information is present.

name: Identify subway stations near high-capacity roads
desc: The script identifies subway stations located within 500-meter buffers of road segments with 8 or more lanes, using PostgreSQL-sourced vector layers for roads and subway stations. It performs a spatial selection (within) between buffered road geometries and station geometries, then exports the selected stations to a Shapefile (Result2.shp). The study area is implicitly South Korea (EPSG:5186 — Korean Engineering Coordinate System), confirmed by CRS usage and layer names ('road_link2', 'subway_station') in a local PostGIS database. No satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or explicit geographic name (e.g., Seoul) is specified in the code; all inputs are static vector layers from a local DB. Outputs include a memory-based buffer layer, a selected subset of subway stations, and a saved Shapefile.

name: Generate CRS-aligned test polygons
desc: The script generates a GeoPackage file containing six identical polygon features (e.g., 'Parque Areiao', 'Setor Bueno') spatially located around Goiania, GO, Brazil — each layer reprojected into one of eight distinct EPSG coordinate reference systems (4326, 4674, 31982, 31983, 3857, 5880, 32722, 29192). All polygons are originally defined in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) coordinates and transformed using QGIS's QgsCoordinateTransform to target CRSs. The output is a single GeoPackage ('test_layers.gpkg') with eight vector layers (one per CRS), each named 'goiania_epsgXXXX', containing identical geometry, attribute fields ('id', 'name', 'crs'), and metadata. The purpose is explicit: CRS reprojection testing in QGIS Layer Grid View — verifying visual alignment of identically located features across different projections. No remote sensing data, time-series, classification, or analysis is performed; this is purely synthetic geospatial data generation for cartographic/coordinate system validation. Study area: Goiania-GO (center at -49.2648, -16.6869); time range: not specified; satellite/sensor/bands: not applicable.

name: Import iNaturalist species observations
desc: The script imports species occurrence records from the iNaturalist API based on a user-defined circular area (center coordinates and radius), applying filters for user, taxon, date range (or exact date or seasonal months), and quality grade. It retrieves observation metadata (ID, date, scientific name, vernacular name, coordinates, place guess, taxon ID/rank, URLs, observer info, quality grade, positional accuracy) and associated photo URLs. The output consists of two linked GeoPackage layers: (1) a point layer (EPSG:4236) containing the filtered observations with selected attributes, and (2) a non-spatial photos table linked via 'inat_id', configured with relation widgets and image viewers. All data is saved to the QGIS project’s directory, with styling and symbology deferred to Script 2. No satellite, remote sensing, or Earth observation data is used — the source is exclusively the iNaturalist REST API.

name: Identify short polygon segments
desc: The script performs geometric validation on a polygon layer named 'Single parts' (EPSG:32643) to detect and extract line segments shorter than 1.11 meters — likely indicating digitization errors, slivers, or topological artifacts. It iterates over all polygon rings, computes Euclidean length of each vertex-to-vertex segment, flags those < 1.11 m with console messages, and stores them as LineString features in a new memory layer 'Lines from segments' with attribute 'Length'. A second workflow identifies inter-feature distances < 1.11 m between polygon centroids (via pointOnSurface) within a 500 m radius using spatial indexing, storing shortest qualifying distances as lines in 'Shortest distances'. A third workflow merges selected polygons via geometry.combine(), and a fourth simplifies selected polygon geometries using QgsGeometry.simplify(tolerance=0.01). All operations are QGIS Python API-based, no Earth Engine (GEE) code is present — the prompt’s reference to 'GEE script' is erroneous; this is pure QGIS PyQGIS scripting. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and external datasets are not involved — input is a local vector layer only. Output layers are added to the QGIS project for visual inspection and manual correction.

name: Geocode addresses to points
desc: The script performs address geocoding using the VWorld Korean geocoding API (vworld.kr) to convert input addresses (from CSV or Excel files) into geographic point coordinates (x, y) in the current QGIS canvas CRS. It first attempts road-type geocoding; if that fails, it falls back to parcel-type geocoding. Results include successfully geocoded points (with x/y), success/failure status, and error messages. Output is a memory vector layer of type Point, with original table columns preserved plus an added '비고' (note) column indicating success or failure reason. No remote sensing, satellite data, time-series, or classification is involved — purely client-side geocoding via HTTP requests to VWorld's REST API.

name: Generate buffer circles around points
desc: The script converts a QGIS point vector layer into a polygon layer of circular buffers (radius = 10 units) centered on each input point, using EPSG:2177 (PUWG 2000 zone 6) as the coordinate reference system. It validates that the selected layer is point-based, reprojects it to EPSG:2177, constructs 36-segment approximated circles via trigonometric computation, stores them in an in-memory polygon layer, and exports the result to a DXF file named 'exported_points.dxf' in the user's home directory. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite imagery is involved — the entire workflow operates purely on local vector geometry within QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Create monoplotting project
desc: The script creates a QGIS geopackage (GPKG) project for monoplotting oblique images, initializing multiple vector layers (region, cameras, GCPs, image/ground control points, and line features) with predefined schemas and attributes. It reads a JSON mesh bounding box file to define the region polygon, then writes all layers into a single GPKG file. The workflow is triggered via a QGIS plugin dialog, and no Earth observation data processing (e.g., satellite imagery analysis, time-series, classification, or spectral computation) occurs — it is purely a GIS project scaffolding tool for photogrammetric monoplotting setup.

name: Regenerate emission calculation reference outputs
desc: The script regenerates 16 reference output files used for testing emission calculations: 14 GeoPackage (.gpkg) vector layers (each containing a QgsVectorLayer named 'output') and 2 CSV tables. These outputs are derived from emission calculations performed by the OpenALAQS plugin using local project databases (AIRPORT_A.alaqs, ANP.alaqs) and corresponding inventory files (AIRPORT_A_out.alaqs, ANP_out.alaqs). The vector layers represent spatially aggregated emissions (by pollutant and/or source type) for two study areas — AIRPORT_A (Rotterdam, NL) and ANP — with geometries corrected per updated UTM-origin and spatial.py fixes (Grid3D origin fix + B1–B10 improvements). The CSVs contain tabular emissions summaries: one 'by aggregation' and one 'by grid cell'. No satellite, remote sensing, or external geospatial raster data is used; all inputs are local SQLite-based .alaqs database files and internal QGIS vector processing.

name: Regenerate emission vector layers
desc: The script regenerates 14 GeoPackage (.gpkg) vector-layer fixtures used in automated testing of emission calculations. It drives the OpenAlaqsResultsAnalysis dialog programmatically — loading precomputed ALAQS inventory databases (e.g., AIRPORT_A.alaqs, ANP.alaqs), selecting specific pollutants (CO, PM10, NOx, HC, SOx, CO2) and optional source types (MovementSource, AreaSource, etc.), and invoking the 'EmissionsQGISVectorLayerOutputModule' to produce vector layers. Outputs are single-layer GeoPackages written to fixed paths under tests/data/AIRPORT_A/ and tests/data/ANP/, all explicitly reprojected to EPSG:3857. The script does not perform emission calculation itself — it consumes precomputed .alaqs inventory files and produces corresponding spatialized output layers matching the test’s expected structure and CRS. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is involved; inputs are local SQLite-based inventory databases generated offline by the OpenALAQS modeling framework.

name: Identify cloud-free satellite imagery
desc: The script identifies usable PlanetScope satellite imagery (PSScene) over user-defined AOIs that meet cloud-cover, coverage, and confidence thresholds. It queries Planet's API for scenes within a specified date range and spatial area, applies UDM2.1-based masking (cloud, shadow, haze, snow) or scene-level cloud metadata, filters by max_clouds (%), min_cover (%), confidence (%), satellite generation (e.g., PS2), and time frame (days). Outputs include: (1) a GeoJSON of usable tile footprints with properties (order ID, AOI ID, clouds %, confidence %); (2) optionally, a GeoJSON of AOIs with no usable imagery; (3) WMTS/XYZ tile service URLs for previewing selected scenes; and (4) a QGIS project (.qgz) embedding WMTS layers and filtered vector footprints per AOI. Input is a vector file (e.g., shapefile) defining AOIs; reprojection to EPSG:4326 is performed internally. No GEE Earth Engine assets or client-side geospatial processing (e.g., NDVI, classification) occur — all analysis is API-driven metadata/mask evaluation via planetcoveragefinder.

name: Recover archived DQE reports
desc: The script recovers and regenerates archived DQE (Dossier Qualité Énergétique) reports from PostgreSQL JSONB data stored in the `dqe.dqejson` table. It retrieves metadata (SRO, project type, name, version, timestamp, user), previews SQL result rows (e.g., 'designation', 'quantite', 'unite') with a styled HTML report watermarked 'ARCHIVÉ', and supports regeneration of Excel files and QGIS vector layers. The workflow relies entirely on database-stored JSONB records — no remote sensing or raster processing is performed. Data sources are internal: PostgreSQL schema `dqe`, table `dqejson`, and functions like `dqe.dqe_recover`. Outputs include: (1) interactive HTML preview in QTextBrowser, (2) time-stamped Excel (.xlsx) with ordered SQL results, and (3) QGIS vector layers loaded from dynamically created PostgreSQL schemas (e.g., `dqe_recover_<sro>_<timestamp>`). No satellite, sensor, bands, or geospatial analysis (e.g., classification, indices, masking) is involved — this is a database-driven archival recovery UI module.

name: Convert layer to different CRS
desc: The script converts a QGIS vector layer from its original Coordinate Reference System (CRS) to a user-specified target CRS, writing new ESRI Shapefile components (.shp, .shx, .dbf), generating a .prj file from a bundled resource, removing the QGIS-specific .qpj file, and optionally copying auxiliary files (.qml, .sld, .lyr, .xml metadata). It then loads the converted layer into the QGIS map canvas if requested. The operation is purely geospatial reprojection — no raster analysis, time-series, classification, or remote sensing processing occurs. All inputs and outputs are local vector files; no cloud-based GEE assets or satellite data are involved.

name: Paint stratigraphic order on geology polygons
desc: The script applies stratigraphic ordering (0 = youngest) or cumulative thickness values to geology polygon features based on a user-provided stratigraphic unit sequence. It reads a QGIS vector layer (geology polygons), matches unit names from a field (e.g., 'UNITNAME') against the stratigraphic order list obtained via `data_manager.get_stratigraphic_unit_names()`, and writes integer `strat_order` values to a new or existing field. Optionally, it duplicates the input layer into a memory layer, populates the `strat_order` field by geometry matching, and applies a graduated color ramp renderer using QGIS’s default style color ramps. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or external Earth observation datasets are used; all operations are vector-based GIS attribute assignment and styling within QGIS. The output is a styled vector layer in the QGIS map canvas, optionally with a new `strat_order` attribute, and no exports to disk are performed in this widget (debug export is conditional and internal). Study area, time range, satellite data, and coordinate reference system are not specified in the script — it operates generically on any loaded polygon layer.

name: Sample geological contact points
desc: The script configures and runs spatial sampling algorithms (Decimator and Spacing) on user-provided vector layers in QGIS to subsample or space geological contact points. It requires a point-based spatial data layer (e.g., observed geological contacts), optionally a DTM (raster) and geology polygon layer (for contextual constraints). The Decimator reduces point density by decimation; the Spacing algorithm enforces minimum inter-point distance. Outputs are new QGIS memory vector layers containing sampled point features (with X, Y, and optionally Z coordinates and attributes), added to the current QGIS project. Debug export includes CSV of sampled contacts. No remote sensing imagery, cloud processing, or Earth Engine server-side computation is performed — this is a desktop QGIS plugin widget interfacing with the map2loop Python API (sample_contacts). Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not involved or specified.

name: Add output rasters to group
desc: The script loads all valid GDAL-supported raster files from a user-specified local folder into the QGIS project, registers them in the temporary layer store, schedules them for loading on completion, and applies a custom post-processor that moves each loaded raster layer into a newly created or existing layer tree group named 'group1'. No geospatial analysis, classification, time-series processing, or remote sensing computation is performed — the script is purely a QGIS Processing algorithm for automated layer organization. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations are not specified because the script operates exclusively on local raster files with no Earth Engine (GEE) code, no imagery collection filtering, no band math, no temporal or spatial constraints, and no reference to any remote dataset or geographic extent.

name: Style raster layers with pseudocolor
desc: The script applies a single-band pseudocolor renderer to multiple GDAL-supported raster files loaded from a user-specified local folder. It computes band statistics (min/max) for Band 1, creates a linear gradient color ramp from blue (0,0,255) to red (255,0,0), and assigns a QgsSingleBandPseudoColorRenderer to each valid raster layer. The styled rasters are added to the QGIS project’s temporary layer store and registered for post-processing on load completion. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing computation is performed — the script is purely for visualization styling. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification methods, and exported products beyond styled layers in QGIS are not specified.

name: Map waterpoint proximity within paddocks
desc: The script computes Euclidean distance rasters from water points to all locations within each individual paddock polygon, producing clipped proximity rasters (in meters) where pixel values represent the shortest distance to the nearest water point inside that paddock; outputs are temporary raster layers named and clipped per paddock (e.g., 'PaddockA_waters_proximity'), with no permanent layer added to the project but processed via GDAL rasterize → proximity → clip workflow.

name: Transform paddock geometry to GDA94
desc: The script transforms the geometry of a vector layer named 'Mt_Sanford_Paddocks' from EPSG:28352 (GDA94 / MGA zone 52) to EPSG:4283 (GDA94 geographic), performs unary union on all features, applies coordinate transformation using QgsCoordinateTransform, validates the resulting geometry, and writes the transformed, merged polygon to a new in-memory vector layer named 'All paddocks' added to the QGIS project.

name: Manage GDAL/OGR metadata keys
desc: The script implements a metadata key management system for GDAL and OGR geospatial objects, enabling reading, writing, validation, and type-aware handling of metadata items across domains like ENVI, default, and XML. It supports domain-specific parsing (e.g., ENVI band names, wavelength, acquisition_time), immutable domains (IMAGE_STRUCTURE, SUBDATASETS), CRS handling via QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem, classification schemes via EnMAP-Box ClassificationScheme, and list-length constraints (e.g., 'nb' for number of bands). Key classes include MDKeyDomainString (for string/list metadata), MDKeyCoordinateReferenceSystem (for projection WKT ↔ CRS), MDKeyDescription (for object descriptions), and MDKeyClassification (for raster class definitions).

name: Rasterize class fractions from vector
desc: The script rasterizes a categorized vector layer into class-wise fractional rasters at a target grid resolution. It first creates a temporary 10× finer-resolution grid, rasterizes the vector categories onto that fine grid using nearest-neighbor burning (no majority voting), then aggregates pixel counts per class via spatial binning (rebinSum) to compute percentage-based class fractions at the original grid resolution. Output is a multi-band raster where each band corresponds to one category, storing integer percentages (0–100), with NoData=255, band names set to category names, colors preserved, and scale factor 0.01 (to interpret values as percentages). The process ensures percent-level accuracy by oversampling before aggregation. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are used — inputs are user-provided categorized vector and raster grid layers; all operations are vector-to-raster conversion and statistical aggregation.

name: Import Sentinel-2 L2A surface reflectance
desc: The script imports a Sentinel-2 Level-2A (atmospherically corrected) product by parsing its MTD_MSIL2A.xml metadata file, extracts selected spectral bands (e.g., B1–B12), resamples all bands to the finest common pixel size (10 m), stacks them into a single VRT raster, scales pixel values to 0–10000 range, and embeds wavelength metadata (in nanometers) and band descriptions. The output is a georeferenced, multi-band VRT file with ENVI-compliant spectral metadata, ready for spectral analysis or downstream processing in EnMAP-Box. No classification, time-series, or spatial aggregation is performed — only data import, band selection, resampling, and metadata annotation.

name: Rasterize categorized vector layer
desc: The script rasterizes a categorized vector layer (e.g., land cover or land use polygons with category names and colors) into a categorized raster layer aligned to a user-specified grid. It supports two resampling modes: (1) simple nearest-neighbor burn (fast, less accurate), or (2) a two-step majority voting approach — first burning at 10× finer resolution, then aggregating via mode resampling and masking low-coverage pixels using a configurable minimum coverage threshold (e.g., ≥50%). The output raster preserves original category IDs (1..n), names, and hex colors from the input vector’s categorized renderer, and is saved with a paletted renderer. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external imagery is involved — input is purely vector + grid raster; no temporal or spectral analysis occurs.

name: Rasterize vector layer
desc: Converts vector geometries (points, lines and polygons) into a raster grid using a user-specified target grid. The script supports burning fixed values, attribute-based values, or feature IDs; pre-initializing the output raster; enabling ALL_TOUCHED mode for inclusive pixel coverage; and adding values instead of overwriting. It handles CRS reprojection of the input vector to match the grid, creates temporary layers as needed (e.g., for FID-based burning), and invokes GDAL's rasterize algorithm with configurable data type, extent, resolution, and options. Outputs a single GeoTIFF raster file aligned to the provided grid. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic analysis is involved — this is a pure vector-to-raster geoprocessing utility.

name: Translate raster layer
desc: The script performs format conversion and geospatial preprocessing of raster layers, including band subsetting (by index or spectral matching via center wavelength), spatial clipping (by extent or pixel window), resampling (with configurable algorithms), data scaling/offset application, no-data value handling, data type conversion, metadata copying (GDAL and spectral ENVI domain), style transfer, and optional ENVI header generation. It uses GDAL Translate or Warp depending on CRS alignment and resampling requirements, and supports exclusion of bad bands using BBL metadata. The output is a processed GeoTIFF (or other GDAL-supported format) raster layer with user-specified properties.

name: Perform VRT band math calculation
desc: The script creates a single-band VRT raster layer using GDAL's VRT DerivedRasterBand with a user-defined Python pixel function. It reads selected input bands from a source raster, embeds custom NumPy-based arithmetic code into the VRT XML structure, sets output data type, no-data value, band name, and buffer radius for spatial operations, then writes the final VRT file with proper metadata and band configuration. The output is a VRT file that dynamically computes pixel values on-the-fly using the provided code.

name: Extract WFS vector layers
desc: The script extracts vector layers from French national geospatial web services (IGN Geoportail WFS) by querying specified thematic categories (e.g., 'orthohisto') and user-selected layer names. It constructs a bounding box around a user-provided coordinate pair (longitude, latitude), adjusts the bbox for geographic CRS using Earth radius correction, creates an extended clipping polygon (saved as Emprise_etendue.shp), and downloads requested layers as shapefile-zip archives. Outputs include downloaded and unzipped shapefiles (one per selected layer) and the clipping polygon, all saved to a user-specified output directory. Data sources are IGN WFS endpoints (e.g., https://wxs.ign.fr/orthohisto/geoportail/wfs?), not satellite or Earth observation imagery; no time-series analysis, classification, or spectral processing is performed.

name: Extract utility networks by spatial clipping
desc: The script extracts vector-based utility network layers (e.g., water, gas, electricity, telecom) from a local shapefile-based database ('Base_de_donnees_QGIS\Reseaux') using a user-provided project boundary polygon. It first extends the boundary by a user-defined buffer radius (in meters or degrees, with automatic geographic coordinate adjustment), reprojects both the boundary and network layers to a target CRS (EPSG_cible), performs vector clipping (qgis:clip), and exports each clipped network as a new shapefile named '<original_name>_decoupe.shp' in the results folder. It also generates a Mensura import script ('cmd_import.cmd') listing 'impshp' commands for all clipped shapefiles. The workflow assumes input networks are in the same source CRS (EPSG_source) as the project boundary and validates single-polygon input, rejecting multi-part or non-shapefile boundaries. No remote sensing, satellite, or raster data is used — all inputs and outputs are local vector files.

name: Quantify infrastructure assets by parcel
desc: The script performs spatial clipping of all vector layers (e.g., roads, buildings, utilities) in the QGIS project against two reference layers: (1) a project boundary ('emprise') and (2) a parcel layer. It computes total area, total length, and feature count per clipped layer, then disaggregates these metrics per parcel — optionally joined with external CSV attribute data (e.g., parcel ownership, land use codes). Outputs are two CSV files: 'Recap.csv' (aggregate metrics per layer within the emprise) and 'Recap_parcelle.csv' (per-parcel breakdown including linked CSV fields), both formatted with comma decimal separators for Excel compatibility. The workflow uses QGIS native processing algorithms ('qgis:clip'), QgsDistanceArea for geometric measurements, and robust validation of layer names, field existence, and CSV structure.

name: Extract cadastral parcel boundaries
desc: The script extracts cadastral parcel boundaries from the French national Geoportail WFS service (IGN) for a user-defined geographic area. It takes user-specified coordinates (longitude, latitude), an EPSG code, and an added radius (in meters) to define an extended bounding box. It constructs a memory polygon layer representing this extended extent, then queries the IGN WFS endpoint 'https://wxs.ign.fr/parcellaire/geoportail/wfs' for the layer 'CADASTRALPARCELS.PARCELLAIRE_EXPRESS:parcelle'. The downloaded shapefile ZIP is extracted, clipped to the user-defined extent, and saved as a clipped shapefile ('parcelle_decoupe.shp') in the output directory. An intermediate 'Emprise_etendue.shp' (extended extent polygon) is also exported. The script operates entirely within QGIS using PyQGIS and external HTTP requests — no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, satellite data, or time-series analysis are involved. All geospatial operations are vector-based (WFS query, bbox filtering, clipping). The study area is defined solely by user input coordinates and radius; no fixed region is hardcoded.

name: Extract feasibility study cartographic data
desc: The script extracts geospatial thematic maps for feasibility studies of a user-defined site in France. It constructs an extended bounding box around user-provided (longitude, latitude) coordinates using a configurable radius (in meters), transforms coordinates across CRS (EPSG:4326, EPSG:3857, and user-specified EPSG), and exports vector and raster layers for 11 thematic domains: Topographie, Geologie, Cavites, Pollution, Inondations, Inondations par sumersion marine, Remontee des nappes, Coulees de boue, Zones humides, Natura2000, ZNIEFF. It also downloads and saves IGN topographic plans (via ExtractionPlanIGN), orthophotos (ExtractionPlanOrtho), and general plans (ExtractionPlan), then compiles all extracted images into a Word document (.docx). All outputs are saved to user-specified local directories as shapefiles, GeoTIFFs, PNGs/JPEGs (implied by image export logic), and a final report. Data sources are internal French national services (e.g., IGN, BRGM, ONF, OFB) accessed via proprietary QGIS-based extraction functions — no GEE Earth Engine assets or satellite imagery are used; the script runs entirely in QGIS/Python with external HTTP requests and local file I/O. The study area is defined solely by user input (no fixed region).

name: Manage metadata key values
desc: The script defines a metadata key management system for GDAL/OGR geospatial objects, enabling reading, writing, validation, and type-conversion of metadata items across domains (e.g., ENVI, default, XML). It supports domain-specific behavior (e.g., immutable ENVI fields like 'bands', 'data_type'), type-aware value parsing (int, float, datetime64, QDate), list-length constraints (e.g., 'nb' for number of bands), CRS handling via QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem, and classification scheme integration via EnMAP-Box's ClassificationScheme. Key classes include MDKeyDomainString (for string/list metadata), MDKeyCoordinateReferenceSystem (for projection WKT), MDKeyDescription (for object descriptions), and MDKeyClassification (for band-level class definitions).

name: Build 3D spectral cube visualization
desc: The script builds a 3D isometric cube visualization from a spectral raster layer by generating two output rasters: (1) a 'cube face' raster created via GDAL Translate with modified geotransform to simulate spectral band offset along x/y directions, and (2) a 'cube side' raster constructed by stacking bands with spatial offsets (dx, dy) into a single-band array using NumPy, preserving no-data values and CRS. Inputs include raster layer, spectral scale (unused in logic), and integer pixel offsets dx/dy for isometric tilt. Outputs are VRT and GeoTIFF files representing orthogonal face and slanted side views of the spectral data cube.

name: Perform VRT band math calculation
desc: The script creates a single-band VRT raster layer using GDAL's VRT DerivedRasterBand with a user-defined Python pixel function. It reads selected input bands from a source raster, embeds custom NumPy-based arithmetic code into the VRT's PixelFunctionCode section, sets output data type, no-data value, band name, and buffer radius for spatial operations, and writes the final VRT file with proper metadata and scaling disabled. The workflow includes GDAL Translate to initialize the VRT structure, manual XML editing to inject pixel function logic and source definitions, and post-processing via RasterWriter to set no-data, band name, scale, and offset.

name: Remove vector layer features
desc: The script implements a QGIS vector layer action that allows users to delete selected or individual features from a memory-based point vector layer. It creates a test vector layer with fields 'fString', 'fInt', and 'fDouble', populates it with 5 point features, configures the attribute table to show an action button ('Remove this feature'), and attaches a GenericPython QgsAction that executes Python code to delete features (either selected ones or the current feature via [$id]). The action uses QGIS expression syntax ([% @layer_name %], [% @layer_id %], [% $id %]) and operates entirely within the QGIS GUI environment using QgsProject, QgsVectorLayer, and QgsActionManager. No remote sensing data, geospatial analysis, classification, or export occurs — the output is purely interactive feature deletion in a local QGIS session.

name: Subset EnMAP L2A spectral bands
desc: The script processes EnMAP Level-2A (L2A) hyperspectral data to generate wavelength-subsetted spectral rasters (SPECTRAL_IMAGE.vrt) using a curated list of 'good' wavelengths excluding 'bad' ones, as defined in external text files. It imports raw L2A products via ImportEnmapL2AAlgorithm, aligns and subsets bands to the user-defined spectral grid using TranslateRasterAlgorithm with a synthetic VRT template, warps ancillary quicklook (QL) products and spectral rasters to a custom tiling scheme (grid2.geojson), mosaics per-date products, and cuts them into tiles matching the scheme’s geometry. Outputs include tile-aligned GeoTIFFs under rootCube (e.g., ENMAPL2A_YYYYMMDD_SPECTRAL_IMAGE.TIF), warped QL rasters (e.g., QL_VNIR.TIF), and copied METADATA.XML files per tile. The study area is implicitly defined by the tiling scheme and scene bounding polygons derived from EnMAP XML metadata; no classification, modeling, or thematic analysis is performed — only spectral subsetting, georeferencing, tiling, and metadata preservation.

name: Sample spectral image values
desc: The script samples pixel values from the 'SPECTRAL_IMAGE.TIF' raster file(s) located within tile subdirectories of 'D:\data\EnFireMap\cube', using point locations from 'lib_points.shp'. It first spatially subsets the tiling scheme (grid2.geojson) to intersect with the extent of the points layer, then for each selected tile, identifies the SPECTRAL_IMAGE.TIF file, spatially subsets the points to the tile's bounding box, saves the subset as a GeoPackage, and runs EnMAPProcessingAlgorithm's SampleRasterValuesAlgorithm to extract raster values at those points—exporting results as GeoJSON files (e.g., 'SPECTRAL_IMAGE.TIF.geojson') per tile. The study area is implicitly defined by the tiling scheme and point layer; no temporal filtering, classification, or modeling is performed—the task is strictly raster value sampling for ground truth or validation purposes. Data sources are local filesystem paths (not GEE assets), satellite/sensor/bands are not specified in code.

name: Simulate irrigation water demand
desc: The script implements a SQLite-based database driver for the IdrAgra hydrological model, designed to manage and simulate water demand in irrigation districts. It defines and initializes spatial vector layers (e.g., weather stations, groundwater wells, control points, links, nodes, soil/land-use/irrigation/distribution maps) and non-spatial time-series tables (e.g., ws_tmax, ws_ptot, stp_irr, cp_irrig_mm) to store meteorological, soil, crop, irrigation, and simulation output data. Key methods include table creation via SQL DDL, import of CSV/numpy/vector data with type inference and unit conversion, time-series statistics (min/max/mean/percentiles), network flow tracing (upstream source routing), and spatial attribute mapping between QGIS layers. The workflow supports setting up a geopackage-compatible SQLite database with CRS metadata, managing constraints, and enabling runtime querying of temporal and spatial model inputs/outputs — all tailored for irrigation water balance modeling. No satellite or remote sensing processing occurs; the script is purely a local database management layer for a deterministic agro-hydrological model. Study area, time range, and satellite data sources are not specified in the code.

name: Extract irrigation network and reservoirs
desc: The script converts IdrAgra model output variables (specifically 'ret' for river network and 'reserv' for reservoirs) from a MATLAB (.mat) file into QGIS vector layers. For 'ret', it constructs polyline features from x/y coordinate arrays, assigning attributes like codice (code), ord_calc (calculated order), ramoValle (downstream branch), areamonte_km2 (upstream area), and others; for 'reserv', it creates point features from XYdam coordinates with attributes including zmax (maximum elevation), dampix (pixel ID), bacino (basin code), inlets, outlet, and hydraulic laws. The output is either an in-memory QgsVectorLayer or a saved ESRI Shapefile, with CRS inferred from the input model's GEOREF['crs'][1] (e.g., EPSG code). The script explicitly processes data from 'gisdata_CECINA_2014.mat', indicating the CECINA study area and 2014 reference year, but no time-series analysis or satellite-derived inputs are used — all inputs are hydrological model outputs stored in MATLAB format. No remote sensing imagery, cloud masking, spectral indices, or classification methods are present.

name: Summarize geospatial data
desc: The script implements a QGIS-based pivot table widget for interactive summarization of vector layer attributes and tabular data. It supports drag-and-drop field assignment to Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters; aggregation (sum, average, count, min, max, median, unique, variance, stddev); filtering (global search and per-column regex filters); row/column header expansion; numeric type inference; geometry-derived metrics (length/area); and export to CSV, Excel (with native Excel pivot creation on Windows), and GeoPackage. It does not perform remote sensing analysis, image processing, or time-series modeling — it is a local, desktop GIS data summarization and reporting tool operating on loaded QGIS vector layers or imported spreadsheets. No satellite imagery, spectral bands, cloud masking, NDVI, or geospatial ML classification is involved. All operations are applied to attribute tables or in-memory DataFrames.

name: Join cross-sections to grid cells
desc: The script spatially joins FLO-2D user-defined cross-section lines (user_xsections) to a computational grid (grid) by identifying which grid cell polygons contain the start and end points of each cross-section line. It creates a new memory vector layer of LineString geometry with attributes 'name', 'LB_grid' (left bank grid cell fid), and 'RB_grid' (right bank grid cell fid), then exports it as a shapefile. The study area is Lake Havasu, implied by the file path 'LAKE_HAVASU_FLO2D'; the input data are local vector layers from a GeoPackage (not satellite or remote sensing data); no time dimension is involved; geospatial operations include point-in-polygon intersection via buffered bounding box optimization, feature iteration, and attribute assignment. Output is a shapefile at 'SHP' directory containing joined cross-section geometries with grid cell identifiers.

name: Export point features by day
desc: The script exports a QGIS vector point layer, filtered by unique values in a 'day' attribute field, into separate KML files—one per distinct day value. It verifies the presence of the 'day' field, collects non-null unique day values (e.g., '2023-05-12', '2023-05-13'), sanitizes day strings for filename safety, creates memory-based temporary layers containing only points matching each day, and exports each to KML using QGIS's native:savefeatures algorithm. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing is performed; the workflow is purely attribute-driven feature filtering and file export. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, or sensor usage are not involved—the input is a local QGIS vector layer with no embedded temporal or spectral metadata specified in the code.

name: Generate paired random points
desc: The script generates exactly two spatially constrained random points per polygon segment (from the active QGIS vector layer), ensuring the Euclidean distance between them falls within a user-defined range (400–600 meters) in the layer's native CRS. It uses QGIS geometry operations (QgsGeometry.contains, QgsDistanceArea.measureLine) to validate point containment within polygons and distance compliance. No remote sensing data, time-series, or classification is involved — it is a deterministic stochastic point-sampling procedure applied directly to vector polygon geometries. Outputs are a new in-memory QGIS point vector layer named "Random_Points_Seed88" with all generated points, added to the current QGIS project. The study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified because the script operates purely on local vector input without external geospatial datasets or temporal logic.

name: Clip raster by country boundary
desc: The script clips a global or regional raster dataset (NATURAL_EARTH_RASTER) to individual country boundaries defined in a vector shapefile (NATURAL_EARTH_VECTOR). It iterates over all features in the vector layer, extracts the country name from the fourth attribute (index 3), selects each country by expression on the 'NAME' field, saves the selected geometry as a separate shapefile, and then uses GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm to mask the input raster to that country’s extent. Outputs include one clipped raster per country (saved as PNG) and optionally one vector layer per country loaded into the QGIS project under a 'Countries' group. The study area is implicitly global (Natural Earth data), time range is not applicable (static cartographic datasets), and no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — inputs are generic georeferenced raster and vector files. All paths (e.g., 'path_to_TIF_file/TIF_file.TIF', 'path_to_shape_with_country_borders/country_borders_file_name.shp') are placeholders; no real dataset identifiers, dates, coordinates, or sensors are specified in the code.

name: Clip raster and compute zonal histogram
desc: The script clips a user-provided input raster to the geometry of a vector polygon layer (mask), then computes a zonal histogram of the clipped raster values within each polygon feature. The output is a vector polygon layer enriched with histogram bin count attributes (prefixed 'HISTO_') for the raster's first band, enabling per-polygon distribution analysis of pixel values (e.g., land cover class frequencies, reflectance distributions, or index value bins).

name: Import standard land value polygons
desc: The script imports a CSV file containing standard land value data for Münster, Germany, with geometry in WKT format, creates a memory vector layer with fields for standard_land_value (double), type (string), and district (string), assigns CRS EPSG:25832 (ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N), populates features from the CSV rows, and exports the result as a Shapefile named 'final_standard_land_value_muenster.shp'. The final layer is added to the QGIS project. The study area is explicitly Münster (city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany); no time-dependent analysis or remote sensing is performed — this is a static vector data import and reformatting workflow. Data source is local CSV; no satellite, sensor, bands, or temporal filtering involved.

name: Detect crop row gaps using spectral indices
desc: The script detects gaps in crop rows by first clipping a multispectral raster to a polygon mask, computing vegetation indices (NDI, ExG, TGI, NDVI) via band-wise normalization and raster algebra, binarizing the index output using adaptive thresholding and morphological operations, extracting plant centroid points from contours, and then counting detected plants within buffered line segments (e.g., crop rows) to compute gap-related metrics — specifically 'POCT' (plant count per row segment) and 'MEZV' (gap ratio: observed count / expected count, expressed as %) — written back to the input line vector layer's attribute table. Outputs include a classified binary raster, a point layer of all detected plant centroids, a filtered point layer of plants within row buffers, and updated line attributes quantifying row continuity.

name: Convert forest inventory data
desc: The script converts Japanese forest inventory data from structured documents (DOCX code tables) and Excel spreadsheets (forest簿 XLSX) into geospatial vector layers, using an associated shapefile of forest planning maps as the spatial reference. It parses categorical code tables to interpret attribute meanings, reads forest inventory records row-by-row, joins them with spatial features (e.g., forest compartments or plots) from the shapefile, and optionally exports the result as a GeoPackage layer. The output includes a QGIS vector layer added to the project map canvas and a textual summary; no satellite imagery, remote sensing analysis, or time-series processing is performed — all inputs are local desktop files with no Earth Engine server-side computation.

name: Import Civil 3D pipe networks and surfaces
desc: The script imports LandXML files (v1.2 schema) containing Civil 3D engineering data — specifically PipeNetworks (Struct and Pipe elements) and Surfaces (P vertices and F triangular faces) — into QGIS as vector layers (points for structures, lines for pipes) or mesh layers (2DM format for surfaces). For PipeNetworks, it parses geometry (x,y coordinates from Center tags, line endpoints from refStart/refEnd), attributes (name, desc, elevRim, slope, diameter, invert elevations), resolves topology via cross-referencing, handles update vs. create modes for existing QGIS layers (JUNCTIONS and PIPES), applies standardized field schemas via QEsg_01Campos, adds C3D-specific fields (e.g., TIPO, Descript, CCM, CCJ, Coletor, Trecho), assigns QML styles ('c3d_struct.qml', 'c3d_pipe.qml'), and adds layers to the project. For Surfaces, it converts LandXML triangulated irregular network (TIN) data into a 2DM mesh file (MESH2D format with E3T elements and ND nodes), loads it as a QgsMeshLayer with the current map CRS, and zooms to it. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is involved; input is local XML files selected via QFileDialog; outputs are in-memory or saved 2DM mesh files and QGIS vector/mesh layers. Study area, time range, satellite data, and bands are not specified.

name: Generate elevation profile from line geometry
desc: The script validates the behavior of QgsLayoutItemElevationProfile in QGIS atlas mode for line-based atlas pages. It loads a coverage layer (line atlas pages) and a z-enabled track layer (from GeoPackage) to render an elevation profile tied to each atlas feature’s geometry. It compares two approaches: (A) native atlas-driven QgsLayoutItemElevationProfile (which fails or behaves unexpectedly in this context), and (C) a workaround using QgsProfilePlotRenderer to generate a static profile image and embed it as a picture in a layout. Key inputs include a specific activity ID ('17248394490'), a source GeoPackage containing activity_tracks and atlas_profile_samples tables, and a coverage GeoPackage with line geometries and extent metadata (center_x_3857, center_y_3857, extent_width_m, extent_height_m). The script computes max distance from atlas_profile_samples for axis scaling, renders three outputs: (1) FINAL-A-layout-item-atlas-driven.png — failed/incorrect atlas-driven profile; (2) FINAL-B-renderer-profile-image.png — correct profile image generated via QgsProfilePlotRenderer; (3) FINAL-C-composite-renderer-profile.{png,pdf} — layout combining map and pre-rendered profile image. All operations occur in EPSG:3857; no satellite, optical, or time-series data is used — only vector layers with Z values and atlas metadata. Study area and time range are not specified.

name: Render elevation profile chart
desc: The script renders a topographic elevation profile chart using QgsProfilePlotRenderer from a vector layer representing z-values (e.g., elevation or depth) along a defined curve geometry extracted from an atlas coverage layer. It loads a specific activity track (filtered by 'source_activity_id' = '17248394490') and a corresponding z-track layer (likely containing elevation or bathymetric values), generates a profile image (800×200 px) covering the full curve length and computed z-range, saves it as PNG, then embeds it into a QGIS print layout alongside a map view of the track segment (centered at EPSG:3857 coordinates cx_val/cy_val with extent width/height in meters). Final outputs are a PNG layout image and a PDF report titled 'Morning Nordic Ski — Native QgsProfilePlotRenderer'. The study area is implicitly defined by the GPKG layers (line-atlas-coverage-17248394490.gpkg and source GPKG), but no geographic name, satellite data, or time-series analysis is present — this is a static vector-based profile rendering workflow using local geopackage data.

name: Digitize geological map units
desc: The script digitizes raster-based geological maps into vector polygons using unsupervised clustering (K-means equivalent) on pixel colors. It accepts a user-provided raster layer (geological map scan or image) and an optional polygon/line layer defining the study area boundary. Key workflow steps include: (1) validating input layers; (2) applying median smoothing (configurable odd-kernel size) to suppress noise/text; (3) performing color-space clustering (K-means on RGB values) to identify dominant geological unit colors; (4) converting clustered raster to vector polygons; (5) sieving small polygons (pixel threshold) to remove artifacts; and (6) generating a categorized QGIS vector layer with cluster-ID- and hex-color-coded symbology. Outputs include a memory-based QgsVectorLayer with MultiPolygon geometry, 'cluster_id' and 'hex_color' attributes, automatically rendered with fill symbols matching extracted colors, and added to the QGIS project. No satellite imagery, time series, or spectral indices are used — inputs are arbitrary local raster layers (e.g., scanned paper maps), and no external GEE server-side computation occurs (all processing is client-side via QGIS + scikit-learn/OpenCV equivalents in DigitizerEngine, not shown here but implied by clustering/smoothing/sieving logic). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and CRS are all derived from the user’s loaded QGIS layers — none are hardcoded or inferred from the script.

name: Query seismic borehole data by location
desc: The script performs a spatial query of borehole seismic data (e.g., Amax_gal_, Tg__sec_,超越概率) from a Microsoft Access database (.mdb) based on user-provided latitude/longitude and radius. It computes geodesic distances using geopy.distance to filter boreholes within the specified radius, displays results in a Qt table with fixed column headers and centered alignment, and visualizes the query buffer as a polygon layer in QGIS (reprojected from EPSG:4326 to project CRS, saved as temporary Shapefile with SLD styling). The buffer layer is inserted at position 2 in the layer tree and the map canvas extent is set to the buffer’s bounding box.

name: Perform principal component analysis
desc: The script performs Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on a multiband raster input using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) from scipy.linalg. It supports optional standard scaling (unit variance per band), selection of components by count or cumulative variance threshold (e.g., 90–100%), and outputs a transformed raster containing PCA scores (projected data). Key outputs include: (1) a multiband GeoTIFF raster with bands labeled by explained variance percentage; (2) comprehensive PCA diagnostics logged in QGIS processing window and embedded as JSON metadata (singular values, eigenvectors, loadings, variance explained, cumsum variance, band means, and optionally band stds); and (3) an optional HTML plot (if Plotly is available) visualizing fraction and cumulative fraction of variance explained per component. Input is a local GDAL-readable raster layer (e.g., GeoTIFF), with no assumptions about satellite origin — it is agnostic to sensor, acquisition date, or geographic location. All operations are pixel-wise, memory-aware (with nodata masking and chunking via GDAL ReadAsArray), and use standard linear algebra conventions matching sklearn.decomposition.PCA.

name: Apply statistical raster filters
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin framework for applying SciPy-based raster filtering operations (e.g., median, minimum, rank, morphological, edge detection, blur, enhancement) to local GDAL raster files. It supports 2D per-band and 3D data-cube processing, configurable windowing with margin handling, border modes (reflect, constant, wrap, etc.), footprint/structure definition, origin control, no-data masking and filling, dtype conversion, band statistics computation, and output metadata preservation (projection, geotransform, nodata). The core workflow reads input rasters via GDAL, applies SciPy ndimage or custom functions in sliding windows (with optional wrapping), handles no-data values per band, writes results to GeoTIFF output, and optionally computes and embeds band statistics. No remote sensing data ingestion, cloud processing, time-series analysis, or satellite-specific logic is present — it operates exclusively on local raster layers provided by the user in QGIS.

name: Transform building footprint geometry
desc: The script applies an affine transformation (scaling by factor 2 in x and y, rotating 30° counter-clockwise around z-axis, no translation) to a local shapefile of building footprints for Penn State University. It loads the input vector layer from 'D:/Case_Studies/Data/Penn_State_Buildings.shp', executes QGIS's native:affinetransform algorithm with specified parameters, saves the transformed vector layer to a dynamically named .shp file in a QGIS plugin workspace directory, and adds the result as a new map layer in the current QGIS project. No remote sensing data, time-series, or raster operations are involved; the input is a static, local vector dataset with no explicit CRS metadata or georeferencing context provided in the code.

name: Apply affine transformation to buildings
desc: The script applies an affine geometric transformation (scaling by factor 2.0 in x and y, rotating z-axis by 30°) to a local vector layer of building footprints ('Penn_State_Buildings.shp') using GRASS GIS v.transform within QGIS. It reads the input shapefile from a fixed Windows path, generates a uniquely named output shapefile in a plugin-specific workspace directory, and loads the transformed layer into the current QGIS project. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations are performed; the operation is purely vector-based geometric reprojection/transformation. Study area is implied by input filename but not georeferenced in code; coordinate reference system is not specified or handled. Output is a transformed QgsVectorLayer added to the map canvas.

name: Optimize wind turbine platform height
desc: The script optimizes the elevation of a wind turbine crane pad platform to minimize earthwork (cut/fill) volumes. It imports a DXF file containing the crane pad outline (assumed in EPSG:25832, i.e., UTM zone 32N, Germany), downloads high-resolution (1m) digital elevation model (DEM) data from the German hoehendaten.de API (which serves official DGM1 and DGM5 datasets), tests platform heights in a user-defined range (e.g., 300–310 m ü.NN) at configurable steps, computes earthwork volumes using slope-constrained earthwork modeling (45° default slope angle), generates terrain cross-section profiles spaced every 10 m with overhang and vertical exaggeration, produces an HTML report with maps, volume summaries, and PNG profile plots, and saves outputs to a GeoPackage including the optimized platform polygon, profile lines, and a copy of the DEM TIFF. The study area is implicitly constrained by the input DXF geometry and the hoehendaten.de service coverage (Germany). No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used — the primary geospatial data source is a national-scale, ground-survey-derived DEM.

name: Model takeoff climb surface
desc: The script implements ICAO Doc 8168 Annex 10 — TOFPA AOC Type A surface modeling for aviation obstacle clearance analysis. It constructs a 3D polygonal takeoff climb surface (Z-aware) from user-specified runway and threshold layers, using geometric projection along azimuth to generate diverging width and linearly increasing elevation based on fixed ICAO constants (12.5% divergence ratio, 1.2% climb gradient, 10 km standard length). Outputs include: (1) a styled grey semi-transparent PolygonZ layer ('RWY_TOFPA_AOC_TypeA') representing the 3D surface; (2) a red reference line layer ('reference_line') perpendicular to the takeoff path at the start point; (3) optional contour lines ('RWY_TOFPA_Contours') at user-defined elevation intervals, styled with labels; (4) optional obstacle analysis layers (critical/safe/buffer/shadowed/visible) derived from intersection and shadow analysis against an input obstacles layer; and (5) optional KMZ (for Google Earth) and AIXM 5.1.1 (for aviation data exchange) exports. All geometry is CRS-aware, uses QGIS memory layers, and relies exclusively on vector inputs (runway polyline, threshold point, obstacles points/polygons) — no raster or satellite data is used. Study area, time range, and satellite sources are not specified, as this is a vector-based, site-specific airport engineering tool.

name: Geocode place name to location
desc: The script performs forward geocoding: it takes a user-entered place name (e.g., city, address) as input, queries the OpenStreetMap Nominatim API via the OsmGeoCoder class, and returns matching geographic coordinates (WGS84 lat/lon). It then transforms those coordinates to the current QGIS project's CRS, centers the map canvas on the result, and saves the location as a point feature in a memory vector layer named 'Pencarian Lokasi' with an 'address' attribute. Labels are enabled on the layer for display. No remote sensing, time-series, or Earth observation analysis is performed — this is purely a GIS utility for interactive location search and visualization within QGIS.

name: Generate drift corridor polygons
desc: The script generates directional drift corridor polygons for maritime or aerial route legs, categorized by compass direction (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW), using pre-collected input data (depth and height thresholds) and a separate generator class (DriftCorridorGenerator). It creates one QGIS memory vector layer per leg, styled with semi-transparent fill colors mapped to each of the 8 cardinal/intercardinal directions. The output layers are polygon geometries (WKT-based, EPSG:4326) with attributes 'direction', 'angle', and 'leg_index'. No satellite, sensor, band, time range, or explicit study area is referenced in this script — all geospatial inputs are assumed pre-loaded and abstracted away in the generator; the script itself performs only client-side QGIS layer construction and styling. Data sources, temporal extent, and geographic location are not specified in this module.

name: Mark coordinates as point features
desc: The script creates a QGIS memory vector layer named 'Marked_Locations' containing point geometries derived from longitude/latitude values in a user-provided CSV file. Each point is attributed with 'name', 'longitude', and 'latitude'. The layer is added to the current QGIS project and optionally exported as a shapefile ('marked_locations.shp'). No geospatial analysis, classification, time-series processing, or remote sensing operations are performed — the script is purely for importing and visualizing static coordinate locations. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, bands, classification methods, and raster operations are all not specified.

name: Generate raster tiles from WMS vector service
desc: The script enables generation of raster tiles (e.g., PNG tiles at multiple zoom levels) from a published WMS vector offering — i.e., a vector-based WMS service that serves vector data (e.g., GML/GeoJSON) but is rasterized on-the-fly. It does so via a dedicated wizard (TileRasterCreationWizard) triggered when the offering type is ConfigurationType.WMS_VECTOR. The workflow includes reading the WMS capabilities, configuring tiling parameters (zoom range, CRS, format), and initiating a QGIS processing task to produce tiled raster output. No classification, time-series analysis, or satellite-derived indices are performed; the core operation is service-driven raster tile publishing. Outputs include raster tile sets (e.g., in XYZ structure) stored as a new 'stored data' entity in the GeoPlateforme platform, referenced by an emitted stored_data_id signal. All geospatial operations are delegated to QGIS backend tools and external processing algorithms — no GEE (Google Earth Engine) code is present in this script.

name: Generate spatial grid layer
desc: The script creates a regular polygonal vector grid (square cells) aligned to the extent of an existing QGIS layer named 'rgb', using a user-specified cell size in map units. It saves the grid as a GeoPackage file ('grid.gpkg') in the same directory as the 'rgb' layer source and adds it to the QGIS project. The task is purely geometric — no remote sensing data, time-series, classification, or analysis is performed; it relies solely on the spatial extent and CRS of the local 'rgb' vector or raster layer. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified — the script operates entirely within QGIS desktop using native processing algorithms and local layer metadata.

name: Vectorize building mask raster
desc: The script converts a raster layer named 'mask' into a vector polygon layer (GeoPackage), filters out polygons where the raster value equals zero, and adds the resulting vector layer named 'buildings' to the same layer group as the source raster in QGIS. The output is a GeoPackage file with filename derived from the input raster path plus '_buildings.gpkg', containing only non-zero-value polygons. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are referenced — the input is a local raster layer already loaded in QGIS with name 'mask' and type RasterLayer; all operations are local GIS processing steps (polygonization and attribute-based feature deletion).

name: Calculate median distance to buildings
desc: The script computes a distance raster from a binary 'mask' raster (interpreted as building presence) using GDAL's proximity algorithm, then calculates the median distance value within each polygon of a 'grid' vector layer and writes it into a new 'median_dist' attribute. The output is a modified vector layer with per-polygon median Euclidean distances to the nearest building pixel. No satellite imagery, time-series, or external datasets are loaded or processed—the inputs are local QGIS layers named 'mask' (raster) and 'grid' (vector), with no explicit geographic extent, temporal range, or sensor information specified in the code.

name: Compute median distance to mask features
desc: The script computes a Euclidean distance raster from a binary vector mask layer ('mask'), then calculates the median pixel value of that distance raster within each polygon feature of a grid vector layer ('grid'). The result is a new attribute 'median_dist' added to the grid layer, representing the median distance from each grid cell's interior area to the nearest location in the mask. No satellite imagery or time-series analysis is performed; inputs are local QGIS vector and raster layers loaded from the current project. The study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code — it operates purely on user-provided layers named 'mask' and 'grid' within the QGIS project environment.

name: Compute median elevation per grid cell
desc: The script computes the median elevation value within each polygon of a vector grid layer, using a DSM (Digital Surface Model) raster masked by a binary mask layer. It first multiplies the DSM and mask rasters (pixel-wise) to retain only DSM values where mask = 1 (null or 0 areas become 0 or NoData), then performs zonal statistics (median only) over the grid polygons, and finally replaces any resulting null median values in the grid’s attribute table with 0. The output is the modified grid vector layer with a new field 'med_median' containing the median masked elevation per cell.

name: Draw horizontal scale bar
desc: The script draws a double-sided horizontal scale bar for aeronautical charts, consisting of two parallel rails (metres above, feet below) with major/minor tick marks and labeled numeric values and unit headers ('METRES', 'FEET'). It creates two vector layers — one for tick/spine lines and one for labels — grouped under 'Horizontal Scale'. The bar is placed relative to a user-selected guide line or explicit basepoint/angle in the current QGIS map canvas, projected in the map's CRS. No remote sensing data, classification, or time-series analysis is performed; it is a cartographic drafting tool operating purely on geometric construction using QGIS vector geometry methods (e.g., QgsPoint.project(), QgsGeometry.fromPolyline). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not involved — all outputs are synthetic vector features.

name: Generate vertical scale chart
desc: The script generates a cartographic vertical scale (1:10,000 by default) composed of two parallel linear rails (left for feet, right for meters), tick marks at specified intervals (0–300 ft every 50 ft; 0–100 m every 25 m), mid-step small ticks, secondary rails, and labeled text elements (numeric values, 'FEET', 'METERS', 'VERTICAL SCALE', and scale ratio). It derives geometry from a user-selected guide line (baseline) in QGIS — extracting its start/end points to compute azimuth and project perpendicular offset lines — then constructs memory vector layers ('Vertical Scale - Lines' and 'carto-vertical-scale-label') with styled features. Outputs are added to the QGIS project under a group named 'Vertical Scale'. No remote sensing data, raster processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed; it is purely a vector-based cartographic drafting tool operating on map canvas CRS and units.

name: Map earthquake loss estimation
desc: The script generates a QGIS print layout map visualizing earthquake-related geospatial data for rapid notification. It loads vector layers from TAB files (Epicenter.TAB, Evt1Fault.TAB, Evt1GbsTownLoss.TAB, Evt1GmDmnd.TAB, ScenarioData.TAB) and administrative geometry files (AdmTown.TAB, AdmTract.TAB), joins town-level loss tables to town geometry, overlays epicenter and fault layers, and renders them over an OpenStreetMap basemap (XYZ tile). Key metadata (time, location, magnitude, depth, response level) is extracted from ScenarioData.TAB and displayed in layout labels. The output is a JPG image exported at user-specified DPI, uploaded to Imgur, and sent via LINE Notify to a predefined recipient. The study area is implicitly Taiwan (EPSG:3826 = TWD97, used for AdmTown/AdmTract; SmsEpicX/SmsEpicY in decimal degrees; TELES system context). No satellite, sensor, or band-based analysis is performed — all inputs are tabular/vector GIS files and OSM raster tiles.

name: Extract flood extents from image
desc: The script extracts purple-colored regions (interpreted as flood extents) from a local PNG image file (imagename.png) using RGB color thresholding with tolerance-based matching against a target purple color (160,32,240). It converts the binary mask into vector polygons via contour detection (skimage.measure.find_contours), applies geometric scaling and translation to approximate UTM coordinates for Glenorchy, Tasmania (using GDA94 / MGA zone 55, EPSG:28355), filters polygons by minimum area (10 units²), validates geometry, and adds the resulting polygons as a temporary memory vector layer in QGIS. The study area is implicitly Glenorchy, Tasmania; no satellite, sensor, or temporal data are used — input is a static, locally stored raster image with no embedded georeferencing. Output is a QGIS vector layer of polygon features representing interpreted flood extents.

name: Manage fire incident response
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for real-time fire incident management in Münster, Germany. It enables firefighters to capture new fire events by selecting street and house number from preloaded vector layers, automatically assigns the nearest available fire station based on Euclidean distance (not network routing), calculates shortest-path routes using the 'edges_muenster' road network layer, updates vehicle availability at stations, records fire attributes (type, casualties, vehicles deployed, status), and supports post-incident status change (to 'geloescht'), route deletion, and PDF report generation. The system operates entirely on local vector GIS data — no satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is used. All operations are interactive, event-driven, and rely on QGIS native processing tools (e.g., 'native:shortestpathpointtopoint') and vector layer attribute editing. Study area is explicitly Münster (layer names: 'Strassen', 'Hausnummern', 'edges_muenster', 'Notrufmeldestellen'); no temporal filtering or date-based analysis is performed.

name: Convert shapefile to geopackage
desc: The script converts an input ESRI Shapefile (Acuifero.shp) located at 'C:\Workspace_PyQt\PythonPyQT\LibroCoobook\0_data\Acuifero.shp' into a GeoPackage file named 'my_new_file.gpkg' at 'C:\Workspace_PyQt\PythonPyQT\LibroCoobook\0_package\', creating the GeoPackage if it does not exist. It uses QGIS Python API (QgsVectorLayer and QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3) to read the source vector layer and write it with a new layer name 'Acuifero_temp' and UTF-8 encoding. No reprojection, filtering, attribute modification, or geometric transformation is performed — only format conversion. The study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification, or analysis methods are not involved; this is a pure vector format migration task.

name: Convert and export CAD layers
desc: The script converts DWG files to DXF using ODAFileConverter.exe, then imports the DXF into QGIS as a vector layer; for each DXF 'LAYER' (e.g., entities grouped by layer name), it exports separate vector files in KML, ESRI Shapefile, GeoJSON, and DXF formats—all reprojected to EPSG:32718 (UTM zone 18S), organized per layer, and finally compressed into timestamped ZIP archives. The workflow operates on local filesystem paths under 'C:\Workspace_PyQt\PythonPyQT\LibroCoobook', with no geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing involved—only format conversion, CRS-preserving vector export, and file packaging. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geoprocessing (e.g., clipping, masking, NDVI) are absent.

name: Convert DXF layers to GeoPackage
desc: The script converts AutoCAD DXF files into geospatial vector formats, specifically exporting each DXF layer (e.g., 'WALL', 'DOOR') as individual ESRI Shapefiles in the '0_package' subdirectory. It parses DXF entities (POINT, LINE, LWPOLYLINE) using ezdxf, constructs Shapely geometries (Point, LineString, Polygon), and writes them via GeoPandas to shapefiles with CRS EPSG:32718. The workflow includes layer enumeration, entity-type-specific geometry extraction, attribute preservation (e.g., layer name, color, linetype), and validation of layer visibility/lock status. No GEE (Google Earth Engine) API calls, satellite data, or remote sensing operations are present — this is a local desktop GIS preprocessing script using QGIS Python bindings and geopandas. The CRS EPSG:32718 (UTM zone 18S) suggests a focus on southern Chile or similar region, but no explicit study area is defined in code; coordinates are assumed native to the DXF and reprojected without source CRS inference. Output files are saved under 'LibroCoobook/0_package/{layer_name}.shp'.

name: Convert CAD layers to GeoPackage
desc: The script converts DWG/DXF CAD files (e.g., from '0_data' folder) into GeoPackage format by loading them as OGR vector layers in QGIS, enumerating their internal sub-layers (e.g., 'entities'), reprojecting each sub-layer to EPSG:4326, and exporting them individually as named layers into a single GeoPackage file (e.g., '0_temp/prueba.gpkg'). It uses QgsVectorLayer with CAD: URI syntax, QgsVectorFileWriter with CreateOrOverwriteLayer options, and handles sub-layer iteration via dataProvider().subLayers(). The output is a multi-layer GeoPackage containing all CAD sub-layers as vector features.

name: Import DWG boundary layer
desc: The script imports vector layers from a DWG file (specifically 'LIMITE_DEPARTAMENTAL_WGS84.dwg') into QGIS, reprojects them to EPSG:4326 if specified, and exports each sublayer as a named table into a GeoPackage file ('archivo.gpkg'). It uses the OGR DXF driver (not native DWG; note: GDAL's 'DXF' driver is used erroneously for DWG in the code, and actual DWG support in GDAL is limited/unsupported — this is a critical flaw in the script). The workflow includes validation of input file existence, layer loading via QgsVectorLayer with OGR provider, CRS assignment, sublayer enumeration via dataProvider().subLayers(), and per-sublayer export using QgsVectorFileWriter to GeoPackage. No raster data, satellite imagery, time-series, or classification is involved. The output is a GeoPackage containing vector geometry tables derived from the DWG entities, with layer names preserved from the DWG sublayers. Study area is implied by filename 'LIMITE_DEPARTAMENTAL_WGS84.dwg' — indicating a national administrative department boundary in WGS84, but no specific country or department is named in the code.

name: Map image location coordinates
desc: The script creates a QGIS point vector layer from GPS metadata (latitude, longitude, altitude, filename) stored in a JSON file. It loads the JSON, validates required fields, constructs a memory-based point layer in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), applies red-point styling, and optionally reprojects to UTM Zone 10N (EPSG:32610) for distance-aware analysis. The output is a temporary QGIS vector layer added to the current project — no satellite imagery, classification, or time-series analysis is performed; the only geospatial operation is coordinate transformation of point geometries. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and spectral bands are not involved — the input is purely tabular GPS records. The JSON path 'D:\241107_PetersonP6\Altum_image_locations.json' implies field-collected drone or ground-based imagery (Altum is a multispectral sensor by MicaSense), but the script itself does not access or process any raster or spectral data.

name: Plot camera positions from EO files
desc: The script reads Exterior Orientation (EO) CSV files containing camera position data (x, y, z in UTM Zone 10N) and timestamps, then creates a single QGIS memory vector layer of point features representing all camera locations. Each point is styled as a blue dot (size 2) and attributed with filename, altitude (z), timestamp, and source file name. The layer is added to the current QGIS project. No geospatial analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — only ingestion, parsing, geometry creation, and visualization. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not involved; input is tabular EO metadata, not remote sensing imagery. Output is strictly a QGIS vector layer for visual inspection of sensor platform positions.

name: Rebuild electrical infrastructure layers
desc: The script rebuilds four QGIS vector layers ('fixtures', 'switches', 'panels', 'runs') as memory-based GeoJSON files with enforced geometry types (Point or LineString), standardized field schemas, and a seeded dummy feature ('SEED') to ensure layer validity and consistency. It writes each layer to a GeoJSON file in '/home/jantman/GIT/house-electrical/data/', then reloads them into the QGIS project. The process ensures correct WKB geometry type, required attribute fields, CRS alignment (EPSG:4326 fallback), and immediate usability for manual digitizing of residential electrical systems. No remote sensing, time-series, or geospatial analysis is performed — this is purely a GIS data scaffolding and initialization workflow for a local house electrical mapping project.

name: Create Zone d'activite ou d'interet
desc: The script creates Zone d'Activité ou d'Intérêt (ZAI) features in QGIS based on signalement (report) geometries and linked croquis (sketch) layers. It either converts linear croquis into closed polygons, or generates a 5m×5m fictive square when no valid croquis is found or when the resulting area is below 25 m². Attributes including nature, nature_detaillee, acquisition methods, and toponymie are copied from the signalement or croquis. A GNSS XML file is generated for each created polygon. The ZAI fictif flag is set to '1' or 'Faux' depending on whether the geometry is synthetic.

name: Simulate snake game in GIS
desc: The script implements a Snake-style arcade game inside QGIS using vector layers for the play area, snake body, and food items. It dynamically creates memory-based polygon layers with customizable dimensions and styling (via QML files), sets up keyboard shortcuts for directional controls (Arrow keys, P for pause), manages layer grouping and rendering, and integrates with QGIS canvas navigation (zooming to active layer). The game logic is delegated to an external module (viper_game.ViperMain), but this script handles all GIS-specific setup: geometry creation (axis-aligned rectangle play area), CRS handling, layer styling fallbacks (solid colors if QML missing), shortcut validation, and layer lifecycle management (optional removal on game end). No remote sensing data, time-series, or geospatial analysis is performed; it is purely a vector-based interactive game UI within QGIS.

name: Measure vector layer FPS performance
desc: The script measures the average frames-per-second (FPS) achievable when updating geometries of memory-based QgsVectorLayer features in QGIS Desktop (via PyQGIS), for varying numbers of features (1 to 100,000). It isolates the cost of geometry updates (via `changeGeometryValues`) and initial feature creation time, using synthetic point geometries (all at 'POINT (1 1)') and fixed temporal attributes (start: 2023-06-01T00:00:00, end: 2023-06-01T23:00:00). The output is a dictionary mapping feature count to (average FPS, feature creation time in seconds), plus matplotlib plots of FPS and creation time vs. object count. No geospatial analysis, classification, or real-world data processing occurs — this is a synthetic benchmark for QGIS vector temporal rendering performance.

name: Benchmark trajectory geometry update methods
desc: The script benchmarks three geometry update methods (WKB, WKT, and PointXY) for rendering moving vessel trajectories from MobilityDB-stored tgeompoint data in QGIS. It fetches MMSI identifiers, temporal extents, and clipped tgeompoint trajectories for up to 25 time steps; constructs a memory-based QgsVectorLayer with temporal properties; and measures per-frame performance metrics—including value_at_timestamp computation, geometry assignment, and layer commit—across 25 animation frames.
