Outputs include printed timing statistics (FPS, on_new_frame avg, value_at_timestamp avg, geometry update avg) and serialized profiling records (fps_record, ts_record, qgis_overhead) for QGIS task-level analysis. The study uses real AIS-derived vessel trajectories stored in a local MobilityDB instance under table 'PyMEOS_demo' with SRID 4326, no satellite or remote sensing data involved.

name: Export geospatial layers to HIP format
desc: The script exports vector layers (points, lines, polygons, networks) to a proprietary HIP format used for HD mapping workflows, applying coordinate transformations (UTM offset), geometry conversions (e.g., polygons → linestrings → vertices), vertex extraction, field cleanup (dropping empty or redundant fields like vertex_index), and metadata enrichment (e.g., curvature/gradient averaging for Orbis road data). It supports multiple export modes: 'Export Points to Hip', 'Export Lines to Hip', 'Export Polygons to Hip', 'Export Polygons with Holes', 'Export NetworkZ to Hip', and 'Export PDF for Illustrator'. Inputs are user-selected QGIS vector layers; outputs are new QGIS layers named with '_Hip' suffix, saved in the project directory as GeoJSON or memory layers. The workflow is driven by a GUI dialog (fHIP_Dialog) that reads configuration from b9QGISdata.ini, including location-specific UTM offsets and extent layer preferences. Data sources include TomTom HD Map Vector Tiles (via orbis-layer API), TomTom Hillshade tiles (via map/1/tile/hill/main), Overture Maps (via overturemaps CLI), and local OSM/Orbis/MNR/Genesis datasets referenced in imported submodules — but no Earth Engine (GEE) satellite imagery or time-series analysis is present despite the prompt's 'GEE script' mischaracterization: this is a QGIS Python plugin script, not a Google Earth Engine script.

name: Export vector layers to HIP format
desc: The script exports QGIS vector layers (points, lines, polygons, networks) to a custom HIP (High-Definition Map Integration Platform) format, applying reprojection to WGS84, coordinate offset correction (based on location-specific UTM offsets), geometry normalization (e.g., Force Right-Hand Rule for polygons), decomposition (multi-to-single parts, polygon-to-lines, vertex extraction), field management (dropping empty or auxiliary fields like 'vertex_index', 'angle'), and attribute enrichment (e.g., 'CurvatureAvg', 'GradientAvg', 'HoleRings', 'LatLon'). It supports HD map ingestion via TomTom Orbis vector tiles, hillshade raster tiling from TomTom Maps API, Overture geospatial data download, and domain-specific preprocessing for Move Portal traffic, MNR speed profiles, OSM trees, and building part/footprint separation. Outputs include GeoJSON files (e.g., 'overture_building.geojson', 'hd_name_zoom12.geojson'), PNG hillshade composites, and QGIS memory layers named with '_Hip' suffix.

name: Extract TIFF center coordinate
desc: The script computes the geographic center (longitude, latitude) of a local GeoTIFF file by loading it as a raster layer in QGIS, calculating its geometric centroid in the native CRS, and transforming that point to WGS84 (EPSG:4326). It does not perform any remote sensing analysis, classification, time-series processing, or Earth Engine operations — it is purely a local geospatial utility for coordinate extraction. The input is a single static TIFF file (Ia.tif) located at '../../data/geology/ia/Ia.tif'; no satellite imagery, time dimension, or dynamic data sources are involved. Output is a pair of floating-point longitude and latitude values printed to stdout.

name: Compare raster value pairs
desc: The script extracts 1000 random valid (non-NoData) sample points from a.tif (dn.tif), retrieves their geographic coordinates (WGS 84), and then queries the corresponding pixel values from b.tif (dnn.tif) at those same locations. It outputs a structured list of tuples containing (longitude, latitude, value_a, value_b), prints summary statistics (valid vs. invalid b.tif matches), and exports all results to a CSV file with columns: 序号,经度,纬度,a_value,b_value. The script operates entirely within QGIS Python environment (3.40.15), uses QgsRasterLayer and QgsRasterDataProvider for I/O, handles on-the-fly coordinate transformations if source CRS differs from EPSG:4326, and performs strict NoData-aware sampling — no time-series, no classification, no modeling — only spatially aligned pointwise comparison of two static local GeoTIFF files. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; paths indicate local filesystem data (e.g., '../../data/geology/ia/dn.tif', 'E:\code\python\地质\计算结果\dnn.tif'), and domain context ('geology', 'ia' likely meaning 'index analysis' or 'interpretation analysis') suggests geological index raster comparison, but no explicit geologic variable names or units are present.

name: Convert PGA contours to Ia raster
desc: The script converts earthquake agency-provided KML-formatted PGA (Peak Ground Acceleration) contour files into GeoTIFF raster files of Arias Intensity (Ia), using multiple interpolation methods (QGIS IDW/TIN, scipy RBF-based IDW approximation, or pykrige Ordinary Kriging). It parses KML Placemarks with names like '0.01g', converts PGA from g to m/s² using gravity = 9.8 m/s², computes Ia via the empirical formula log₁₀(Ia) = 0.797 + 1.837 × log₁₀(PGA), determines UTM projection automatically based on longitude center (e.g., EPSG:32648 for central longitude 103°E), transforms coordinates in batches to avoid memory overflow, samples contour points at configurable intervals (default 5), removes duplicate points (rounded to 0.01 m), builds a regular UTM-aligned grid with 10-pixel buffer, and outputs Ia.tif (mandatory) and optionally PGA.tif. The study area is implicitly constrained to mainland China (73°E–135°E), as confirmed by UTM zone logic, projection selection comments, and example longitude 103°. No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — input is vector KML; output is interpolated georeferenced rasters.

name: Convert PGA contours to Ia raster
desc: The script converts earthquake agency-provided KML-formatted PGA (Peak Ground Acceleration) isoline files into georeferenced Ia (Arias Intensity) GeoTIFF rasters. It parses KML Placemarks containing PGA values (e.g., '0.02g'), converts them to physical acceleration (m/s²), computes Ia using the empirical log-linear relationship log₁₀(Ia) = 0.797 + 1.837·log₁₀(PGA), reprojects coordinates to an automatically selected UTM zone (EPSG:326xx), samples and deduplicates contour points, then applies QGIS Processing IDW or TIN interpolation to generate a continuous Ia.tif surface; optionally outputs a polygon-based PGA.tif raster via OGR vector-to-raster conversion.

name: Compute zonal statistics for grounded ice units
desc: The script computes zonal statistics (mean and standard deviation) of multiple geophysical raster datasets — including Bouguer gravity anomaly (ANTGG 10 km), Dziadek et al. (2021) magnetic compilation (250 m), ICESat-2 grounded-ice dmdt, PISM basal drag coefficient (beta), and Kirsty’s classified gravity/magnetic upward continuation rasters — over vector polygons representing grounded ice units (filtered by attribute 'groundediceNAME' = 'Grounded') from a pre-processed ASE (Amundsen Sea Embayment) magnetic vector dataset. The output is a GeoJSON file containing the original polygon geometry plus new attribute columns prefixed by 'grav_zones_', 'mag_zones_', 'bouger_', 'Dziadek_', 'dmdt_', and 'beta_', each storing mean and std dev values per zone.

name: Create vector layer
desc: The script creates a new QGIS vector layer (point, line, polygon, or multi-geometry type) with user-defined attributes (fields), coordinate reference system (CRS), and output format (Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, or temporary memory layer). It validates field names, enforces Shapefile naming constraints (10-character limit), scans for existing GeoPackage files in selected folders, supports custom CRS selection via QGIS dialog, and optionally adds the resulting layer to the QGIS project and starts editing mode. No remote sensing, time-series, or Earth Engine (GEE) processing is performed — this is a pure QGIS desktop plugin UI and logic for layer initialization.

name: Export infrastructure layers to RATF format
desc: The script exports QGIS vector layers to RATF-compliant Shapefile format following MRNF (Ministère des Ressources naturelles et des Forêts du Québec) standards. It performs attribute mapping from source layers to predefined RATF layer schemas (e.g., 'SUP_NON_TRAITEE', 'CHEMIN'), applies MTM NAD83 reprojection (EPSG:32180 + zone), optionally simplifies geometries using a fixed tolerance (GEOMETRY_PARAMS['tolerance_simplify']), computes derived attributes (e.g., 'SUP_HA' = area/10000, 'LONG_M' = length), and packages outputs as named Shapefiles (e.g., 'SUP_NON_TRAITEE_01_12345_UA01_R25_B01.shp') and optionally a ZIP archive. The study area is implicitly Quebec, Canada — confirmed by use of MTM (Modified Transverse Mercator) projection zones (MTM_ZONES), references to 'MRNF', 'Québec central', and French/English bilingual UI targeting Quebec forestry regulation compliance. Data sources are local QGIS vector layers (no satellite or remote sensing data used); no time-series analysis or temporal filtering is performed — fiscal year is only used for filename generation (e.g., 'R25' for 2024–2025).

name: Convert points to tracklines
desc: The script converts a set of georeferenced point features (from a GeoPackage layer named 'EN711_EN736_points') into ordered, grouped line features (tracklines) using QGIS's 'pointstopath' algorithm. Input points are sorted by the 'fid' field and grouped by the 'EN711' field — indicating each group corresponds to a distinct survey leg or transect identified by the 'EN711' attribute (likely a cruise or leg ID). The output is a GeoPackage file ('ENEN711_EN736_lines.gpkg') containing polyline features representing ship or platform tracklines. No satellite imagery, remote sensing calculations, classification, or temporal filtering is performed; the workflow is purely vector-based geometric reconstruction from sequential point observations. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Fuse connected line features by class and probability
desc: The script performs topological fusion of line features in a QGIS vector layer named 'DET_PRE', grouping connected (touching) line segments that share identical values of 'CLASSE_XY' (e.g., 'A', 'B', 'C') and 'PROB' (e.g., 'PROFONDEUR'), then outputs a new memory vector layer 'DET_PRE_Fusionnée' with merged geometries (via QgsGeometry.unaryUnion), updated attributes including auto-numbered 'NUMERO', Cartesian length ('Shape_Leng'), and duplicated 'CLASSE_Z'/'CLASSE_3D' fields; it enforces strict data validation: no null 'PROB' for classes 'B'/'C', no null/empty 'OBS' within connected groups, and consistency between 'OBS' containing 'PROFONDEUR' and 'PROB' equaling 'PROFONDEUR'. The input layer is assumed to be pre-processed (e.g., derived from detection algorithms), but the script itself contains no remote sensing data loading, cloud masking, spectral index calculation, or time-series analysis — it is purely a vector topology and attribute validation/fusion workflow operating on an existing local QGIS layer. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not referenced or inferred from the code.

name: Connect density-deficient points
desc: The script processes a user-selected set of point features from a QGIS layer named 'DET' (assumed to represent locations of under-density or sparsely sampled points) and constructs a sequential polyline connecting them in proximity order, starting from an extreme point (min-x or min-y) and ending at its counterpart (max-x or max-y). It computes inter-point Euclidean distances and turning angles between consecutive segments to classify each line segment as 'droite' (straight) or 'courbe' (curved) based on angle thresholds (>5°), and assigns color (blue/red) based on both distance and style thresholds (e.g., distance ≥25 m for straight, ≥2 m for curved). The output is a memory-based QGIS LineString layer with attributes 'distance' (rounded to 3 decimals) and 'style', rendered via rule-based symbology and labeled with distance values. No remote sensing data, time-series, or external geospatial datasets are loaded or processed — all operations are vector geometry-based within QGIS desktop using selected point features. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Compare DEM elevation differences
desc: The script compares two user-provided DEM rasters (Existing DEM and Proposed DEM) by computing their pixel-wise arithmetic difference (Proposed − Existing) over their spatial overlap extent. It resamples both rasters to a common resolution (minimum pixel size), aligns them to the overlapping bounding box, reads aligned arrays via GDAL, computes the difference raster, writes it as a GeoTIFF, and calculates cut/fill volumes in cubic yards using cell area and sign-based summation of negative/positive differences. Volume results are reported via QGIS feedback messages.

name: Build street network graph
desc: The script builds a topological node-edge graph from a user-selected QGIS LineString layer representing street segments. It snaps line endpoints within a tolerance (0.5 m) to detect shared nodes, classifies nodes by edge count (dead_end, bend, t_junction, crossroads, complex), computes edge bearings (clockwise from north), calculates edge lengths, and prints a detailed console summary. It then creates and adds a new QGIS point layer ('SF_nodes') visualizing nodes with categorized symbology by type. The graph object is stored globally as 'sf_graph' for subsequent scripts. No remote sensing data, time series, or external geospatial datasets are used — input is strictly the active vector layer in QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Model street intersection geometry
desc: The script generates vector layers representing geometric constructs used in the StreetForm India intersection design solver: (1) sweep circles centered at junctions (for debugging), (2) discrete hit points on those circles (indicating edge-side contact locations), (3) fillet arcs (corner rounding curves between road edges), and (4) conflict zone polygons (filled intersection areas derived from swept geometry). It consumes precomputed results stored in builtins.sf_results — which contain node positions, sweep radii, sweep points with edge IDs and clockwise angles, fillet arc point sequences, and conflict zone vertex coordinates — and renders them as styled QGIS memory layers. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, or classification is performed; all outputs are deterministic geometric constructions derived from input graph topology and design parameters. Study area is implied to be India (per script header 'StreetForm India'), but no specific cities, roads, or source geodata are referenced in the code. The script assumes an active QGIS layer for CRS inference and operates purely on coordinate pairs (nx, ny) and lists of [x,y] points.

name: Model municipal connectivity matrices
desc: The script computes and visualizes three spatial connectivity matrices for Brazilian municipalities: (a) Queen contiguity (polygon adjacency/touching), (b) 1-Nearest Neighbor (1-NN) among municipal centroids, and (c) distance-band connectivity (edges within a threshold equal to the maximum nearest-neighbor distance among centroids). It uses a vector layer named 'lisa_populacao_municipios' representing municipal polygons, extracts their centroids, computes pairwise spatial relationships using robust geometric operations (intersects/touches for queen, geodesic distance for NN and band), styles and layers the results in a 3-panel A4 landscape layout, and exports a high-resolution PNG figure. The study area is implied to be Brazil (via CRS EPSG:4674 — SIRGAS 2000, used nationally), and the layer name 'SE_Municipios_2022' appears in a comment referencing ellipsoid suitability, confirming the source is the 2022 Brazilian municipal boundaries dataset. No satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved — input is purely vector-based administrative geometry.

name: Build Queen contiguity graph
desc: The script constructs a Queen contiguity graph from a given polygon vector layer, where adjacency is defined by shared edges or vertices (including topological touch). It computes centroids for each polygon and creates line features connecting centroids of adjacent polygons. The output includes two in-memory vector layers: one for centroid points and one for adjacency edges (lines), styled and rendered in a print layout. A high-resolution PNG figure (300 DPI) is exported showing the graph overlaid on polygon outlines, with title 'Matriz de conectividade: Contiguidade queen (a)'. The script operates entirely within QGIS using PyQGIS, with no remote sensing data ingestion, no time-series analysis, and no raster processing — it is purely vector-based spatial topology and cartographic export. Study area and data source are not embedded in the script but depend on the loaded QGIS project; the example layer name 'lisa_populacao_municipios' suggests Brazilian municipal boundaries, but no CRS, extent, or attribute schema is hardcoded.

name: Validate point location against road buffers and administrative boundaries
desc: The script validates the positional accuracy of survey points (e.g., road signage or infrastructure markers) loaded from a CSV file by checking three criteria: (1) whether each point falls within a 50-meter buffer around a reference road centerline layer, (2) whether the 'cod_strada' (road code) attribute matches between the point and its corresponding buffered road segment, and (3) whether the point lies within an administrative boundary (comune), then populates a 'comune' field in the validated point layer. Outputs include a validated shapefile ('validated.shp'), a CSV export with XYZ geometry ('validated.csv'), and intermediate layers (buffer, selected features) for visual QA/QC in QGIS.

name: Validate signal point locations
desc: The script validates the spatial correctness of point features ('segnali', i.e., road signals or markers) against three criteria: (1) geometric inclusion within a 50-meter buffer around road centerlines ('routes.shp'), (2) attribute correspondence of 'cod_strada' (road code) between points and corresponding buffered road segments, and (3) assignment of administrative municipality ('comune') from 'limiti_comunali.shp' based on spatial containment. The study area is Piacenza province in northern Italy, inferred from file paths ('CS_Piacenza', 'limiti_comunali.shp') and CRS EPSG:25832 (ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N, used in Italy). Input data are local vector files: 'segnali.gpkg' (points), 'route.shp' (line roads), and 'limiti_comunali.shp' (polygons); no satellite, aerial, or time-series data are used. Outputs include: (a) a filtered point layer 'validated.shp' containing only points satisfying all criteria, (b) a CSV export 'validated.csv' with XYZ geometry and updated 'comune' field, and (c) intermediate layers ('buffer.shp', 'qfield.shp') for visualization and QA/QC in QGIS. The workflow is entirely vector-based, using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS) operations: buffering, attribute-based selection, spatial join via 'selectbylocation', field population, and vector format conversion.

name: Assess street address parity
desc: The script analyzes the spatial consistency of address numbering parity (odd/even) on left and right sides of street segments. It takes two vector layers—street centerlines and address points—and for each address, identifies the nearest street segment, determines which side of the street the address lies on (left/right) using geometric orientation and cross-product logic, then computes whether all addresses on each side are odd, even, or mixed ('both'). Outputs include a new QGIS line layer with added 'PARITY_L' and 'PARITY_R' string attributes, styled rule-based (red for 'both', green for consistent parity), and added to the QGIS project. No external remote sensing data is used; inputs are local vector layers loaded in QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Map earthquake events
desc: The script retrieves earthquake event data from the USGS FDSN Web Service API for a 10-year period (starting Jan 1 of 10 years ago to present) within the spatial extent of the Dominican Republic ('DOM') administrative boundary. It parses CSV-formatted seismic event records (with fields: id, time, depth, mag), converts them to point geometries using longitude/latitude, and loads them as a QGIS memory vector layer named 'events'. The output is a point layer visualized in QGIS alongside a simplified global country boundaries layer subset to DOM; no satellite imagery, remote sensing processing, classification, or export occurs — only API-driven vector feature ingestion and display.

name: Calculate flow accumulation
desc: The script calculates flow accumulation using the D-Infinity (DINF) method from a digital elevation model (DEM) input raster. It reads the DEM via GDAL, computes flow accumulation using the external function calculate_flow_accumulation_dinf from hydrologytools, writes the resulting float32 raster to a GeoTIFF output with matching geotransform and projection, and sets NoData value to -9999. The algorithm is implemented as a QGIS Processing tool with parameters for DEM input and flow accumulation output raster.

name: Calculate LS factor for erosion modeling
desc: The script calculates the LS factor (slope-length factor) from a digital elevation model (DEM) using the Desmet & Govers method. It reads the DEM raster, computes the LS factor via the external `ls_factor` function from `hydrologytools`, and writes the result as a GeoTIFF raster with matching geotransform, projection, and NoData value (-9999). Inputs are strictly a single DEM raster layer; outputs are a single LS factor raster layer.

name: Calculate slope from DEM
desc: The script calculates slope from a digital elevation model (DEM) using the Tarbaton (1997) D-infinity flow routing method implemented in the external module 'd_inf2'. It reads the input DEM raster via QGIS Processing parameters, applies the slope calculation function, writes the resulting slope raster to a GeoTIFF output file with matching geotransform, projection, and NoData value (-9999), and returns the output path. The algorithm is registered as a QGIS Processing tool under the 'Hydrology' group.

name: Generate parcel and beacon geometries from survey text
desc: The script converts tabular survey data (CSV) containing parcel IDs, beacon numbers, XY coordinates or bearing-distance measurements into geospatial vector features: (1) polygonal parcels derived from sequential beacon points, (2) point beacons with attributes (beacon_num, x, y, date_created), and (3) offset road centerlines. It performs spatial joins to assign LGA and block administrative codes to parcels using preloaded PostgreSQL layers (ogun_admin___lgas, land_registration___blocks), validates geometry integrity, applies coordinate transformations (e.g., EPSG:26391 → EPSG:26331), and outputs feature lists and metadata for QGIS layer insertion.

name: Run FME workspace transformation
desc: The script provides a QGIS Processing algorithm that enables users to select an input vector layer, configure and execute an FME workspace (.fmw) via command line, using GeoJSON as the intermediate data format. It automatically exports the input layer to a temporary GeoJSON file, injects --SourceDataset_GEOJSON and --DestDataset_GEOJSON parameters into the FME command (or substitutes them if already present), executes the FME process via subprocess.run(), loads the resulting GeoJSON output as a QgsVectorLayer, and writes features to the designated output sink. The algorithm returns both the output vector layer (for chaining in models) and the full FME stdout log as text. No remote sensing, time-series, or satellite-based analysis is performed — it is a geoprocessing orchestration tool bridging QGIS and FME. All operations are generic and dataset-agnostic; no study area, time range, or sensor-specific logic is embedded.

name: Run FME workspace transformation
desc: The script executes an FME (Feature Manipulation Engine) workspace (.fmw file) using a user-selected or configured command line, with QGIS vector layers as input and output. It exports the input layer to GeoJSON, injects `--SourceDataset_GEOJSON` and `--DestDataset_GEOJSON` parameters into the FME command (either by substitution or appending), runs the FME process via `subprocess.run`, loads the resulting GeoJSON output as a QGIS vector layer, and writes features to the designated output sink. The script does not perform geospatial analysis natively — it acts as a bridge between QGIS and external FME workflows. Key UI components include directory/FMW browsing, parameter table editing, path management, and command generation. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification logic is embedded in the script — all are delegated to the external FME workspace. Outputs are: (1) a QGIS vector layer sink (`OUTPUT_LAYER`) for chaining in Processing models, and (2) the raw FME stdout log (`OUTPUT_TEXT`).

name: Run FME workspace transformation
desc: The script executes an FME (Feature Manipulation Engine) workspace (.fmw file) from within QGIS, using a selected vector layer as input and producing a new vector layer as output. It exports the input layer to GeoJSON, injects it as a source dataset via --SourceDataset_GEOJSON, specifies a destination GeoJSON output path via --DestDataset_GEOJSON, and runs the FME command line. The output is a QgsVectorLayer loaded from the generated GeoJSON, written to the specified output sink. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or Earth observation processing is performed — the core functionality is GIS workflow orchestration via external FME execution. All parameters (including user-defined parameters parsed from the FMW header comments) are dynamically assembled into the command string. The script includes UI components for browsing FMW files, editing parameters, managing paths, and viewing logs — but no spatial analysis, classification, or time-series logic is embedded in the GEE-like sense; this is a QGIS Processing Algorithm wrapper for FME, not a Google Earth Engine script. Study area, time range, sensors, bands, and satellite data sources are not applicable — inputs/outputs are arbitrary vector layers defined by the user-selected FME workspace and QGIS layer.

name: Convert road centerlines to polygons
desc: The script takes a vector line layer named 'ARRUAMENTO_MA_LNH' (Portuguese for 'Road Network_MA_LNH'), first repairs invalid geometries using QGIS's fixgeometries algorithm, then polygonizes the corrected lines — effectively converting linear road features into polygonal representations (e.g., for road surface area modeling, buffer-free pavement delineation, or topological closure). The output is a new in-memory polygon layer 'POLIGONOS_DAS_LINHAS' added to the QGIS project.

name: Generate urban block polygons
desc: The script converts a vector line layer named 'ARRUAMENTO_MA' (Portuguese for 'street network') into polygon features representing urban blocks (quadras) using QGIS's 'linestopolygons' algorithm. It retrieves the layer by name from the current QGIS project, runs the polygonization process on all features (not selected-only), stores the result in a memory layer named 'Quadras_Geradas', and adds it to the map. No remote sensing data, time-series processing, classification, or satellite imagery is involved — this is a pure vector geometry operation on an existing local vector layer. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Build municipality centroid index
desc: The script builds a GeoPackage point layer containing one centroid feature per Swedish municipality, derived from the bounding boxes of Lantmäteriet’s ‘Belägenhetsadresser’ STAC collection items. It fetches paginated STAC features via authenticated HTTP GET requests to https://api.lantmateriet.se/stac-vektor/v1/collections/belagenhetsadresser/items, extracts the EPSG:3006 bounding box (proj:bbox), computes the centroid geometry, and populates attributes including municipality name (title), county code (lanskod), file size, timestamps, and direct download URL (href). The output is a single-layer GeoPackage (C:/temp/belagenhetsadresser_index.gpkg) named 'kommun_centroid', loaded into the QGIS project with clickable download links — no raster, classification, or time-series analysis is performed. Study area is Sweden; CRS is explicitly EPSG:3006 (SWEREF99 TM); no satellite, sensor, or band usage occurs.

name: Extract Markhöjdmodell 1m tile footprints
desc: The script queries Lantmäteriet’s STAC API for the 'Markhöjdmodell 1m' (MHM 1m) elevation dataset and extracts polygon footprints of all raster tiles whose bounding boxes intersect a user-defined area in EPSG:3006 (SWEREF 99 TM). It transforms the input bounding box to EPSG:4326 for STAC search, retrieves tile metadata (including bbox and asset href), reprojects each tile’s footprint polygon back to EPSG:3006, and writes them to a GeoPackage with attributes: id, collection, datetime, and data asset URL. The output is a vector layer of tile extent polygons — not elevation values or derived products — intended for spatial indexing, download planning, or coverage assessment. Study area is implicitly Skåne+ (per example bbox), no time filtering is applied beyond STAC item ‘datetime’ properties (which are retained but not constrained), and no classification, modeling, or raster analysis is performed.

name: Split place names by county code
desc: The script downloads Sweden's national gazetteer (ortnamn) data from Lantmäteriet’s STAC API, extracts the GPKG archive, loads it into QGIS, groups vector features by the 'lanskod' (county code) attribute, and exports one GeoPackage file per Swedish county (e.g., 'ortnamn_lan_01_stockholms_lan.gpkg'). The study area is Sweden; the data source is Lantmäteriet’s official orthotoponymy dataset; no time range is specified in the script (the data is static administrative gazetteer data); geospatial operations include attribute-based feature grouping and per-county vector file export; outputs are 25 county-specific GPKG files stored locally under C:\temp\ortnamn_lan.

name: Extract orthophoto tile footprints
desc: The script queries Lantmäteriet’s STAC API for orthophoto ('bild') imagery metadata within a user-defined bounding box in SWEREF 99 TM (EPSG:3006), transforms the bounding box to WGS84, authenticates via OAuth2 using provided consumer credentials, fetches STAC items (features) with pagination, parses tile IDs to extract acquisition year, ground resolution (in meters), and campaign code, constructs polygon geometries from each item’s 'bbox' property (not raster data), and exports all metadata—including id, datetime, download URL, parsed year, resolution, and campaign—as a GeoPackage layer of footprints (polygons) in EPSG:4326. The study area is explicitly set to Skåne (example bbox_3006 = (337500, 6127500, 487500, 6265000)), and no image processing, classification, or spectral analysis is performed — only metadata harvesting and vector footprint generation. Output is a single GeoPackage file containing one vector layer of rectangular footprints.

name: Generate kommun bounding boxes
desc: The script fetches municipality ('kommun') metadata from Lantmäteriet's Nationella Geodataplattform (NGP) Detaljplan (v2) API, extracts the spatial bounding box (bbox) for each kommun, constructs a polygon feature per kommun in SWEREF 99 TM (EPSG:3006), assigns the kommun ID as an attribute, and saves the result as a GeoPackage file. The study area is all Swedish municipalities covered by the NGP Detaljplan v2 dataset; no temporal filtering is applied — the API returns static administrative extents. Data source is Lantmäteriet’s REST API (no satellite, sensor, or bands involved). Output is a vector GeoPackage layer named 'NGP_detaljplanekommuner.gpkg' containing polygon features with 'id' attribute.

name: Download spatial regulation features
desc: The script downloads planbestämmelser (spatial regulatory features) from Lantmäteriet’s Nationella Geodataplattform (NGP) for selected Swedish municipalities. It fetches GeoJSON-formatted feature collections via NGP’s REST API (v2 /detaljplan endpoint), reconstructs geometries manually from coordinate arrays (Point, LineString, Polygon, MultiPolygon) to ensure QGIS/Windows compatibility, and writes them to individual GeoPackage files (EPSG:3006) per municipality. Each output feature includes attributes: id, title, typ, kategori, beteckning, namn, status, lagakraft (date of legal force), plan_url (link to the full detaljplan PDF), and geomtyp. The script targets only active municipal boundaries loaded from a local layer named 'NGP_detaljplanekommuner.gpkg', with fallback to all Skåne County municipalities (ID prefix '12'). No classification, modeling, or temporal analysis is performed — it is a data acquisition and format-conversion pipeline.

name: Generate atlas map sheets
desc: The script generates a memory vector layer named 'map_sheets' containing rectangular polygons (280 m × 180 m) spaced along a user-selected polyline route, with each rectangle oriented perpendicular to the local route direction. It computes the mathematical azimuth (east=0°, CCW) at each sheet center, stores center coordinates (x,y) and azimuth ('azi') as attributes, and outputs the layer for use as a QGIS Atlas coverage layer. Rotation for layout maps is deferred to the QGIS expression '(180 - "azi") % 360'. No remote sensing data, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — the script is purely geometric and cartographic, operating on vector geometry only. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not involved or specified.

name: Extract HPP river sub-segments
desc: The script calculates hydropower plant (HPP) load on rivers by matching water abstraction and discharge points using a shared numeric code field ('N_Jrar' for abstraction, 'N_Jrher' for discharge). It identifies the nearest river segment for each abstraction and discharge point; if they fall on the same river feature, it extracts the sub-segment between the two projected points using `curveSubstring`. If they fall on different river features, it computes their intersection (typically a confluence point), then extracts two sub-segments: (1) from abstraction point to confluence along the abstraction river, and (2) from confluence to discharge point along the discharge river — but only if the abstraction catchment flows into the discharge catchment (validated via `select_catchment_features_by_id` using the 'RCode' field). Outputs include a red-styled memory vector layer 'HPP Load Segments' containing all extracted line sub-segments, and a derived 'RiversCoverage' layer showing per-river coverage percentage (length of overlapping HPP segments divided by total river length), styled with a blue/red graduated renderer (<40% vs ≥40%). All operations are performed client-side in QGIS using native QgsGeometry methods (`lineLocatePoint`, `curveSubstring`, `intersection`, `unaryUnion`) and spatial indexing; no GEE server-side computation occurs. The script relies entirely on user-provided local vector layers (rivers, abstraction points, discharge points, catchments) with no embedded remote sensing data or time-series logic.

name: Calculate water stress metrics
desc: The script calculates three Water Stress (WS) metrics—WS Surface, WS Groundwater, and WS Total—for a user-selected point in QGIS, based on spatial intersection and attribute aggregation from five local vector layers: water bodies (for natural/ecological flow), catchments (for spatial union), water abstraction (for abstraction volumes), water discharge (for discharge volumes), and groundwater bodies (for usable groundwater). It identifies the nearest water body to the clicked point, finds the catchment intersecting that water body, selects hierarchical catchment features by RCode prefix logic, unions them into a single geometry, then intersects this union with the other thematic layers to sum their quantitative attributes (e.g., 'abs_m3_yr', 'Tm3_y', 'GW_Usable', 'W_av', 'W_ef'). Results are displayed in a formatted message box and visualized as a new memory layer symbolized by WS_Total using a custom graduated renderer with line-pattern fills and outline. All operations are performed client-side in QGIS using PyQGIS; no Earth Engine (GEE) server-side computation occurs—the script is purely desktop GIS logic. Study area, time range, satellite data, and coordinate bounds are not specified.

name: Geocode cadastral parcels
desc: The script geocodes Italian cadastral parcels (particelle) by matching user-provided province, municipality, sheet (foglio), and comma-separated parcel numbers against local GML files (_map.gml for sheet boundaries and _ple.gml for parcel geometries). It performs spatial intersection to retrieve only those parcels falling within the specified sheet, validates column names case-insensitively (e.g., 'foglio', 'particella', 'label'), handles suffixes like '_1'/_2', and loads the resulting intersected geometries as a new in-memory QGIS vector layer with preserved attributes. The study area is explicitly limited to Sardegna (Sardinia, Italy), with data organized hierarchically in local filesystem directories under 'Sardegna/{province}/{municipality}/'. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used; all inputs are static, locally stored GML files from the Italian Revenue Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate) cadastral dataset. Outputs are QGIS vector layers named e.g., 'Cagliari - F. 18 - P. 123, 456', with geometry type inferred (Polygon/MultiPolygon) and CRS taken from the GML source or defaulted to EPSG:3003 (Monte Mario / Italy zone 1).

name: Filter land cover class A
desc: The script filters out vector features where the attribute 'CLASSE' equals 'A' from a local ESRI Shapefile named 'recalage.shp'. It loads the shapefile using QGIS Python bindings (QgsVectorLayer), applies an attribute-based filter to retain only features with CLASSE ≠ 'A', then overwrites the same shapefile on disk with the cleaned feature set using QgsVectorFileWriter. No geospatial operations (e.g., reprojection, geometry editing, raster analysis), time-series processing, satellite data, or classification methods are performed. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified — the script operates solely on pre-existing local vector data with no external GEE or remote sensing logic.

name: Extract streamlines from elevation and flow direction grids
desc: The script executes the external 'grd2stream' command-line tool to compute streamline trajectories (flow paths) starting from a user-selected map coordinate, using two input raster grids: one interpreted as elevation or potential surface and the other as flow direction or vector field components. It reads the resulting ASCII output (streamline.txt), parses metadata headers (# @N, # @T, # @D) and point records (x y z [v_x v_y] [time]), and loads them as a QGIS memory point vector layer with attributes. The workflow is entirely local—no GEE server-side computation occurs; Google Earth Engine is not used at all. All data sources are local GDAL-readable rasters (e.g., GMT, NetCDF, GeoTIFF) selected by the user in QGIS; no satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or fixed study area is specified in the code. The output is a point layer named 'Streamline' visualized in QGIS.

name: Connect transmission towers with lines
desc: The script connects point features representing electrical transmission towers (named 'TORRES_CNO') into a sequential polyline layer ('VLT_CNO') by iteratively linking each tower to the nearest unconnected tower, starting from a prioritized initial tower ('Pórtico Inicial', 'Torre 1', or 'Torre 1A'). It constructs line features with attributes including a generated span ID ('VAO-XXX'), source tower ID ('IDBDITTF'), target tower ID ('IDBITTT'), and line type ('LT_CNO'). The output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer of LineString geometries added to the QGIS project. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or geoprocessing beyond vector geometry operations (distance calculation, polyline creation) is used — the entire workflow operates on pre-existing vector point features in the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Create square buffer zones
desc: The script creates square (axis-aligned bounding box) buffers of 500 m around point features from the 'delta_state' layer, stores them as a temporary in-memory vector layer named 'square_buffer', then dissolves overlapping buffers into disjoint polygonal regions. The workflow is purely vector-based, using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS); it does not involve raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, classification, or statistical analysis. Input points are read from an existing project layer; buffer geometry is derived via .buffer(500, -1) followed by .boundingBox() to enforce square shape (i.e., axis-aligned envelope of circular buffer), and final output is a dissolved memory layer added to the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Calculate shortest road route
desc: The script calculates the shortest driving route between two user-specified geographic points (origin and destination) within a user-defined location (e.g., city or administrative area), using OpenStreetMap-derived road network data. It fetches a street network graph via OSMnx's `graph_from_place`, identifies nearest network nodes to input coordinates, computes the optimal path using the A* algorithm with Euclidean distance heuristic, constructs a LineString geometry from node coordinates, converts it to a QgsVectorLayer, and adds it as a temporary memory layer in QGIS. The study area is dynamically defined by user text input (e.g., 'São Paulo'), no fixed time range applies, data source is OpenStreetMap (not satellite-based), and outputs are purely vector-based route geometries visualized in QGIS. No satellite imagery, remote sensing bands, temporal filtering, classification, or raster operations are involved.

name: Import road network and marker data
desc: The script imports vector-based road edge (line) and marker (point) data from QGIS layers into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database using temporary tables and a custom PL/pgSQL function road_graph.import_data_from_template_tables. It validates required attribute fields (e.g., 'road_code', 'edge_order', 'abscissa'), reprojects inputs to EPSG:2154 (RGF93 / Lambert-93), loads them into temporary tables, invokes the database function to transform and persist the data into production schema tables (e.g., roads, edges, nodes, markers), and returns a structured JSON summary of import counts and status. Outputs include an integer status code (0=error, 1=success) and a localized human-readable message with import statistics.

name: Manage entrance point attributes
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin tool for managing vector point layers representing building or site entrances. It supports creating new entrance layers (in memory, Shapefile, or PostGIS), loading existing compatible layers, assigning unique IDs, setting thematic attributes (category, subcategory, access level), and applying a predefined QML style. Key operations include layer validation (checking for required fields: E_ID, E_Category, E_SubCat, E_Level), feature attribute updates on creation or selection, and dynamic connection/disconnection of layer signals (featureAdded, selectionChanged, featureDeleted) to synchronize UI controls (list widgets) with layer edits. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, raster processing, or geospatial modeling is performed; all operations are vector-based GIS editing workflows within QGIS Desktop. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not involved or specified.

name: Extract building frontage lines
desc: The script creates and manages a vector layer of building frontage lines (line segments representing building perimeters or facade edges) from polygon building layers. It supports generating frontages by exploding building polygon boundaries into constituent line segments, assigning attributes (F_ID, F_Group, F_Type, F_Length), updating IDs and lengths automatically, applying thematic styling, and optionally pushing attribute data from building layers to frontage features via spatial intersection. Outputs include an editable QGIS vector layer (memory, Shapefile, or PostGIS), styled with QML, and interactive UI controls for attribute editing and visualization. The script operates entirely within QGIS Desktop as a plugin and does not use remote sensing imagery, cloud platforms, or time-series analysis — it is purely vector-based GIS processing with no satellite, sensor, or temporal components specified.

name: Create land use classification layer
desc: The script creates a new vector polygon layer for land use classification (LU) with attributes organized by floor level (Ground, Lower, Upper), including categorical codes (e.g., GF_Cat, LF_SubCat), descriptive fields (e.g., GF_Descrip), and quantitative fields (LU_ID, Floors, Area). It supports initialization from an existing building polygon layer (copying geometry and optionally linking via 'build_id'), or creation as an empty memory layer. Outputs include a styled QGIS vector layer (with thematic QML), optionally exported to Shapefile or PostGIS, and integrated into the QGIS project with editing enabled. The tool does not perform remote sensing analysis, classification, or raster processing — it is purely a vector-based land use attribute management and layer generation tool within QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis methods are not involved or specified.

name: Aggregate vector features by attribute
desc: The script computes centroids of spatially aggregated vector features based on user-defined attribute expressions (e.g., field values or custom QGIS expressions). It supports one- or two-level hierarchical aggregation: first grouping features by Expression 1 (e.g., unique values of a field or a filter expression), then optionally subdividing each group using Expression 2. For each resulting subset, it collects geometries, computes their centroid (via QgsGeometry.collectGeometry().centroid()), and writes a point feature with attributes storing the original expression string and count of contributing features. Outputs include a memory-based point layer named '<input_layer_name>_centroids', labeled with the expression string, added to the QGIS map canvas with white-buffered Arial labels; no raster, time-series, or external export (e.g., CSV, GeoTIFF) is performed. The script operates entirely within QGIS desktop using native PyQGIS geometry and attribute handling — no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, no remote sensing data, no cloud processing, and no temporal filtering are present. All operations are local, synchronous, and vector-only.

name: Aggregate vector layer centroids
desc: The script computes centroids of spatially aggregated features from a user-selected QGIS vector layer, based on one or two attribute-based filtering expressions (either field-value equality or custom expressions). It iteratively groups features by unique values in the first field (or expression result), computes the centroid of each group’s geometry collection, and stores the centroid as a new point feature in a memory layer. If a second expression/field is provided, it further subdivides each first-level group and computes nested centroids. Outputs include a labeled point vector layer named '<input_layer_name>_centroids' added to the QGIS map canvas, with labeling driven by the 'Selection' field and automatic extent zoom. No remote sensing data, time series, or raster operations are involved — this is purely a vector aggregation and centroid computation tool operating entirely within QGIS using PyQGIS APIs. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Compute attribute-based centroids
desc: The script computes the geometric centroid of all features in a user-selected vector layer that share the same attribute value (or match a QGIS expression filter). It iterates over unique values of a selected field (or evaluates a single expression), collects geometries matching each value, computes their collective centroid using QgsGeometry.collectGeometry().centroid(), and outputs a new memory point layer containing one point per attribute group with attributes: the original field value (or expression string), count of features, and percentage of total features. Labels are automatically enabled on the output layer using the attribute field for display. The script operates entirely within QGIS desktop using native PyQGIS geometry operations—no remote sensing data, time-series, or Earth Engine API calls are involved.

name: Place military symbol markers
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for interactive placement of military symbols (e.g., units, statuses, sizes) as point features on a map canvas. It captures user-clicked map coordinates, reprojects them to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), creates a memory vector layer named 'MilitarySym-V Symbols' if none exists, and adds a feature with attributes including symbol_id, symbol_name, unit_name, size, status, and svg_path. The layer is styled using a rule-based renderer from SymbolManager. No remote sensing data processing, time-series analysis, or automated classification occurs — it is purely a GIS digitizing/annotation tool for military symbology.

name: Extract road networks by region
desc: The script clips OpenStreetMap (OSM) road vector layers for Scotland, Wales, and England to 10 km grid cells (e.g., 'TQ67') covering Great Britain, reprojects them from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:27700 (British National Grid), writes each clipped layer as a GeoPackage per grid cell (with suffixes '_s', '_w', '_e'), then merges the three regional road layers into a single GeoPackage per grid cell. The study area is explicitly GB (via OS grid naming like 'TQ67' and paths containing 'UK Data/OSM Paths'), and the workflow relies entirely on pre-downloaded OSM shapefiles — no satellite, sensor, or time-series data is involved. Outputs are georeferenced GeoPackage files containing road geometries clipped to OS 10 km grid tiles.

name: Convert building mask to vector boundary
desc: The script converts a raster mask representing building areas (loaded from a local GeoTIFF file 'ras.tif') into a polygonized vector shapefile ('shp_2.shp') using GDAL's Polygonize operation. It reads the input raster as a NumPy array (via PIL), preserves its original georeferencing (geotransform and projection), writes it temporarily as a GeoTIFF, then raster-to-vector converts non-zero pixel values (retaining only DN ≠ 0 features after filtering out DN = 0), and optionally loads the resulting shapefile into QGIS. The workflow is purely post-classification raster-to-vector conversion — no satellite data processing, no time-series analysis, no classification logic, and no cloud masking or spectral index computation occurs in this script. Input raster origin, spatial extent, and coordinate reference system are inherited from 'ras.tif', but neither the raster’s provenance (e.g., source satellite, acquisition date, preprocessing method) nor its thematic meaning beyond 'building mask' is specified in the code.

name: Extract ODK survey geometry
desc: The script extracts, transforms, and loads geospatial survey data from ODK/KoboToolbox REST APIs into QGIS vector layers (GeoPackage, Shapefile) or CSV. It supports point, line (geotrace), polygon (geoshape), and their repeated/multi-geometry variants (e.g., repeat geotrace → MultiLineString). Key workflow steps include: (1) authenticating and fetching JSON-formatted ODK submission data via HTTP GET; (2) parsing nested/irregular JSON structures to infer consistent field names (keysList) and row-aligned data (dataList); (3) detecting geometry type (Point/LineString/Polygon/MultiPoint/MultiLineString/MultiPolygon) by inspecting coordinate string patterns (e.g., semicolon-separated coordinates, first=last for polygons) or dictionary keys (e.g., 'segment/geotrace'); (4) constructing QgsGeometry objects using QgsPointXY, QgsGeometry.fromPolylineXY, etc., with coordinate order corrected (lat/long → long/lat); (5) writing features with all attributes (string-cast for compatibility) to vector files or updating existing layers in-place. No study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is involved — data source is exclusively ODK/KoboToolbox API endpoints (e.g., 'https://kc.kobotoolbox.org/api/v1/data/648039', 'https://api.whonghub.org/api/v1/data/11139.json'), as hardcoded in comments and used in connectionStatus(). Outputs are local vector files (.gpkg, .shp) or CSV, optionally loaded into QGIS map canvas.

name: Join origin-destination point relations
desc: The script processes paired origin (O) and destination (D) point layers for 15 zones (i=2 to 16), performing spatial union to link O and D geometries, assigning a unique integer ID per feature, converting multipart geometries to single parts, and joining these IDs twice—first to the OD relation table on 'ID_POINT' = 'Ruta', then again on 'ID_NEAR' = 'Ruta'—to propagate the generated point IDs into a final enriched relation table (Relations_i.gpkg). The output is a set of 15 geopackage layers containing OD pairs augmented with unified spatial IDs for downstream network or accessibility analysis.

name: Convert KML to CSV coordinates
desc: The script converts a KML file containing point features into a CSV file with columns 'Name', 'Latitude', and 'Longitude'. It does so by loading the KML as a QGIS vector layer, exporting it to an intermediate shapefile (to ensure editable attribute access), reloading the shapefile, and iterating over features to extract the 'Name' attribute and geometry coordinates (x = longitude, y = latitude). The output is a plain CSV file with one row per feature.

name: Generate QGIS maps from geospatial vector files
desc: The script generates QGIS project files (.qgz) and static PNG map images from input .gpkg and .geojson vector files. It applies geometry-type-specific styling (points for cities/castles/museums with categorized symbols and labels; polygons with semi-transparent black fill and gray stroke; lines with 2-pixel gray stroke), sets the project CRS to EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator), calculates a combined extent across all layers (with 10% padding), and exports a white-background PNG at fixed resolution (2568×2232 px). The output includes two distinct map configurations: 'Westerwald PTV' (filtered to layers containing keywords 'base', 'railway', 'datawrapper', 'limes', or 'national') and 'Westerwald Regions' (all input layers). No raster analysis, time-series processing, or satellite-derived metrics are performed — all operations are vector-based cartographic rendering and project packaging. Study area is Westerwald (explicitly named in output filenames and main usage example); no time range, satellite data, or classification/analysis methods are present.

name: Configure watershed land parcel and line layers
desc: The script configures a QGIS plugin for the CAUSERIE serious game, loading pre-defined watershed data (parcel and linear feature layers) from GeoPackage files, creating editable vector layers with derived attribute fields (e.g., type_middle, type_top, type_bottom for lines; type_parcel mirroring origin), applying named QGIS styles, adding labeling to parcels, and launching an interactive dock widget for gameplay. It supports both loading existing watersheds (e.g., 'brenne', 'sologne') from bundled geopackages under serious_game_data_folder and launching a watershed creation dialog for new areas. All operations are desktop GIS-based — no remote sensing imagery or cloud processing is involved; inputs are local vector geopackages, outputs are styled, edited, and labeled QgsVectorLayer instances in the QGIS project, plus a memory layer for legend rendering. Study area, time range, satellite data, and bands are not specified.

name: Identify altitude and slope-based environmental restrictions
desc: The script processes a Digital Elevation Model (DEM/DTM) to generate three vector polygon layers: (1) Areas above 1800 m elevation (APP per Brazilian Forest Code), (2) Areas with slope >45° (APP), and (3) Areas with slope between 25° and 45° (restricted use). It reprojects the input DEM to a user-specified projected CRS (e.g., UTM), computes slope in degrees using GDAL’s slope algorithm, applies binary thresholding via LFTools to isolate elevation and slope classes, and converts each resulting binary raster to vector polygons containing only pixels with DN = 1.

name: Train species distribution model
desc: The script downloads canonical SDM example datasets (Bradypus variegatus and Ariolimax) — including occurrence points (e.g., bradypus.csv, ariolimax-ca.gpkg) and environmental rasters (e.g., bioclimatic variables bio1–bio17.grd/.tif, biome.grd/.tif, or CA surface temperature/cloud cover rasters) — and loads them into QGIS as raster layers and a vector presence layer. It supports optional post-download raster transformations (reprojection, resampling, extent shift) to demonstrate QMaxent’s raster harmonization workflow. The final output is a fully loaded QGIS project with ready-to-use layers for training a Maxent model; no geospatial analysis, classification, or export is performed by the script itself — it is purely a data provisioning and setup utility. Study area: South America (Bradypus) and California (Ariolimax). Time range: not specified. Data sources: CRAN dismo package (hosted on GitHub) and elapid’s research data hosting — both are static, archival example datasets with no temporal dimension. Satellite/sensor/bands: not applicable — all rasters are derived climatic or remote-sensing-derived gridded products (e.g., WorldClim bioclim), not raw satellite imagery; no satellite, sensor, or band metadata is referenced or used in the code.

name: Extract geodatabase layer metadata
desc: The script extracts metadata (abstract, keywords, contacts, rights, licenses, history) from each vector layer in an ESRI File Geodatabase (All_studies_JornadaGDB.gdb), filters layers that contain at least one non-empty metadata field, exports each qualifying layer as a shapefile with its associated QGIS metadata file (.qmd), then moves only the .qmd files to a dedicated output directory. The study area is implicitly the Jornada Experimental Range (via 'Jornada' in gdb_name and path), but no spatial analysis, classification, time-series processing, or remote sensing operations are performed — it is purely a metadata harvesting and packaging workflow using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS). Data sources are local vector layers from a File Geodatabase; no satellite, sensor, bands, or temporal filtering are involved.

name: Create check dams vector layer
desc: The script creates an empty GeoPackage vector layer with polygon geometry and a single 'fid' integer attribute field, configured for check dams mapping. It uses QGIS PyQGIS APIs to instantiate a memory-based QgsVectorLayer with CRS from the current project, adds the fid field via the data provider, writes the layer to a user-specified .gpkg file using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3, and adds the resulting OGR layer to the QGIS project. The dialog enforces GeoPackage format selection and enables export only when a valid file path is provided.

name: Create terracing vector layer
desc: The script creates an empty GeoPackage vector layer with polygon geometry and a single 'fid' integer attribute field, intended for manual digitization of terracing features in QGIS. It does not perform any geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing; it only initializes and exports a blank vector layer structure. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial operations are involved — the tool is purely a QGIS UI-driven layer scaffolding utility.

name: Create land use classification layer
desc: The script creates an empty QGIS vector layer (GeoPackage) with a 'land use value' integer field pre-configured with a ValueMap editor widget that maps human-readable land use class names to numeric codes. The mapping is selected from one of four predefined land cover classification systems: globcover, esa_worldcover, vito, or corine. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing is performed — the script only scaffolds the attribute structure and UI-driven legend mapping for manual digitization in QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial operations are not involved; the output is purely a schema-initialized vector file with no geometry or classified data.

name: Create reservoir vector layer
desc: The script creates an empty vector layer with predefined reservoir-specific attribute fields (e.g., Lake_name, Depth_avg, ResMaxVolume, ResTargetFullFrac) and saves it as a GeoPackage file. It uses QGIS PyQGIS APIs to instantiate a memory-based polygon layer with the project's CRS, adds 12 typed fields via QgsField and QMetaType, writes the layer to the user-specified .gpkg path using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3, and loads the resulting layer into the QGIS project. The dialog enforces GeoPackage output format and enables export only when a valid file path is selected.

name: Convert KML to DXF with text preservation
desc: The script converts a user-selected QGIS vector layer (imported from KML) into a DXF file, preserving textual attributes by extracting point geometries (original points, or centroids of lines/polygons) and embedding the selected text field as an attribute in a new memory layer. It does not perform remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing; it is a GIS vector format conversion tool with geometry simplification (centroid extraction) and attribute retention. The output is a single DXF file written to user-specified disk location, with no raster outputs, visualizations, or statistical summaries. Study area, time range, satellite data, sensors, and bands are not involved — this is a desktop GIS file conversion plugin for QGIS.

name: Align orthophoto rasters to common GSD
desc: The script aligns input GeoTIFF orthophotos (e.g., 'TOF_2_26_to_51_Merge_fix_fixx.tiff') to a user-specified ground sampling distance (GSD) — here 5 cm — by resampling and regridding using GDAL Warp. It checks alignment via geotransform origin and pixel size conformity to the target GSD, skips already-aligned rasters, applies bilinear resampling, enforces consistent extent bounds aligned to GSD grid, saves outputs in a specified folder (e.g., 'D:\Ban_ortho\Aligned_chunks'), optionally saves alignment metrics (execution time, pixel count, GSD) to CSV, and can load results into QGIS. The study area is implied by file paths ('Ban_ortho'), and no satellite/sensor/bands are involved — inputs are pre-processed orthophotos, not raw satellite imagery. No classification, modeling, or spectral analysis occurs; only geometric alignment and reprojection/resampling operations.

name: Generate parallel line grid
desc: The script generates a set of parallel, rotated, buffered, and clipped line segments (as QgsGeometry LineString or MultiLineString) covering the extent of a single input polygon layer. It constructs an infinite grid of equally spaced lines oriented at a user-defined angle (converted from clockwise-from-North to counter-clockwise-from-East), anchored to a fixed coordinate (600000, 5390000), then buffers the input polygon, clips the lines to the buffered polygon, removes line segments shorter than a threshold, merges adjacent line segments across small gaps (≤ merge_gaps meters) by collapsing intermediate endpoints, and finally decomposes any remaining MultiLineString geometries into individual LineString geometries. The output is a list of QgsGeometry objects (all LineString), suitable for vector export or further GIS processing — no raster, classification, time-series, or satellite-derived analysis is performed. Input data source is a local Shapefile (e.g., 'test_2_ab_lake_poly_UTM.shp'), and all operations are purely geometric (buffer, intersection, length filtering, point distance merging) using QGIS Python API (QgsGeometry). No remote sensing data, bands, temporal filtering, or machine learning is involved.

name: Generate swath rectangles from line features
desc: The script generates rectangular buffer polygons (swaths) centered on input line features, where each rectangle is oriented parallel to the line segment connecting its start and end points, with a user-specified width. It transforms input line geometries to a target CRS (EPSG:32617), computes the azimuth angle between the first and last vertex of each line, then constructs a closed 4-vertex polygon perpendicular to that direction. The output is a Shapefile containing these rectangles, styled via a copied QML file. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived metrics are used — the script is purely vector geometric processing. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Assign grid flight line names to survey lines
desc: The script processes a vector shapefile of linear survey lines (e.g., geophysical or airborne survey lines), rotates them to a common orientation (horizontal) using the angle of the first line, partitions the rotated lines into parallel strips spaced at 245 units (likely meters), assigns hierarchical alphanumeric identifiers (e.g., 'T00101', 'T00102') based on strip order and intra-strip position, and outputs a new shapefile with a 'Grid_Fltln' attribute field containing these identifiers. It also optionally generates a matplotlib plot visualizing the rotated lines, strip boundaries, and assigned names. The input is a local ESRI Shapefile at 'I:\CONTRACT_Senoa\Ram\SHP\tof5_mag_tie_split_more_ext.shp'; no satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used — this is purely a vector geometry processing and naming workflow for survey line management.

name: Filter flight lines by orientation
desc: The script filters line features from an input shapefile to retain only those aligned approximately with a user-specified flight line orientation (defined relative to north, clockwise). It calculates the compass angle of each two-point line segment, normalizes it to [0°, 180°), and retains segments whose angle falls within ±5° of a derived target angle (flight_line_angle = -flight_line_angle_cwN + 90) or within [170°, 180°]. The output is a new shapefile containing only the filtered line features, preserving original attributes and geometry. Input is a local ESRI Shapefile (split_more_ext_flt_lines.shp); no remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite imagery is used — this is purely vector geometry processing in QGIS/PyQGIS. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Compute IECH mean and scenario delta metrics
desc: The script computes the mean of IECH (Índice de Estrés Hídrico en Cultivos) values across years 2015–2024 for NUTS3 administrative units in Spain (implied by 'IECH' — a Spanish national agricultural drought stress index), then casts scenario fields (S0/S1 2026–2030 projections and their delta) to numeric type, enriches the NUTS3 vector layer with these derived attributes, exports the enriched layer as GeoPackage, and generates standardized A4 landscape PDF/PNG map layouts (with legend, scale bar, title) for visual reporting of IECH mean and Δ(S1−S0). Outputs include: (1) enriched GeoPackage layer 'nuts3_iech_enriched.gpkg', (2) two QGIS print layouts (PDF + PNG) showing spatial patterns of IECH mean 2015–2024 and scenario delta 2026–2030, (3) a QGIS project file, and (4) a JSON report with metadata, field detection log, and export paths.

name: Reproject point layer to EPSG:3763
desc: The script performs a minimal QGIS-based geoprocessing test (micro-run) that creates an in-memory vector layer with 3 hardcoded points approximating Lisbon, Évora, and Beja in Portugal (WGS84/EPSG:4326), reprojects it to EPSG:3763 (a Portuguese national coordinate system), and writes both the original and reprojected layers to a GeoPackage file named '__debug_micro_run.gpkg'. It does not use remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or modeling. The workflow is purely coordinate transformation validation using QGIS Processing's 'native:reprojectlayer' algorithm. No study area boundaries, temporal range, satellite data, or thematic analysis is performed — only geometry reprojection and I/O testing. All inputs are synthetic and hardcoded; outputs are local GPKG files.

name: Reproject point geometries
desc: The script initializes PyQGIS and Processing, creates a memory vector layer with 3 hardcoded WGS84 points (EPSG:4326), reprojects them to EPSG:3763 using QgsCoordinateTransform (not Processing algorithms), and writes both layers to a GeoPackage file at a fixed path under GATA_ROOT. The workflow is explicitly labeled 'MICRO-RUN' — a fast, minimal test bypassing native Processing algorithms — and outputs two layers: 'micro_pts' (original) and 'micro_pts_3763' (reprojected).

name: Reproject point geometries
desc: The script creates three in-memory point features in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), reprojects them to EPSG:3763 (Portuguese National Grid, PT-TM06) using QgsCoordinateTransform (not Processing algorithms), and writes both layers to a GeoPackage file. The output is a single GPKG file containing two vector layers: 'micro_pts' (WGS84) and 'micro_pts_3763' (PT-TM06). No analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed; the task is purely coordinate system conversion of synthetic test points. Study area is implicitly Portugal (due to EPSG:3763 usage), but no real-world data sources, time range, satellite imagery, or thematic analysis is involved.

name: Exclude features by attribute and geometry
desc: The script performs feature exclusion from a source vector layer based on matching records in a comparison vector layer, using both attribute join fields (with case-sensitive/insensitive options) and optional geometry comparison (using 'Intersects' or 'Contains' spatial relations with user-defined buffer tolerance). It generates an interactive table of candidate features to delete, with geometry status classification ('Equal' or 'Different'), supports backup creation (ZIP for file-based layers or shapefile for memory/database layers), CSV export of selected features, temporary layer creation with geometry-status-based styling (green/red), and deletion confirmation workflow. All operations occur within QGIS using native QgsVectorLayer, QgsSpatialIndex, and QgsGeometry methods — no external or remote data sources, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis are involved.

name: Filter unpaid property tax records
desc: The script loads a CSV file containing property-level tax compliance data with geographic coordinates (Latitude/Longitude in EPSG:4326), filters rows where the 'Tax_Compliance' field equals 'False', saves the filtered point features to a GeoPackage file ('unpaid_properties.gpkg'), and loads that layer into the QGIS project. The input CSV is explicitly named 'tax_compliance.csv', and the output layer is named 'Unpaid_Tax'. No geospatial analysis, modeling, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed — only attribute-based filtering and vector file I/O. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations beyond coordinate-based point loading are not specified.

name: Assess RTRWH site suitability
desc: The script performs comprehensive GIS-based assessment of Rainwater Tank and Recharge (RTRWH) site suitability using QGIS, GDAL, Shapely, and rasterio. It processes user-provided site coordinates (e.g., Delhi: 28.6139°N, 77.2090°E), optional roof polygon geometry, and local geospatial data files (DEM, soil vector, land use vector, rainfall raster). Key workflow steps include: (1) dynamic UTM coordinate system selection and transformation; (2) roof geometry construction and morphometric analysis (area, perimeter, rectangularity, aspect ratio); (3) DEM-based elevation, slope, and aspect extraction using gdal.DEMProcessing; (4) soil attribute querying from OGR vector layer and infiltration rate calculation from clay/sand/organic matter percentages; (5) contributing area estimation (simplified circular buffer); (6) runoff coefficient and time-of-concentration estimation using empirical formulas; (7) multi-factor spatial suitability scoring (topographic, soil, distance-based); (8) optimal tank/recharge location placement via geometric reasoning on roof polygon; (9) excavation condition assessment and equipment recommendations; and (10) generation of visualizations (site overview map, suitability factor bar chart). Outputs include a structured JSON report (gis_analysis_results.json), visualizations (PNG maps/charts), and design recommendations — all saved to /app/output. No satellite or cloud-based Earth Engine assets are used; all data sources are local file paths (e.g., dem_path, soil_data_path), and no GEE-specific APIs (ee.Image, ee.FeatureCollection, etc.) appear in the code.

name: Detect shipwreck locations
desc: The script detects potential shipwrecks in raster bathymetric or sidescan sonar imagery by applying deep learning models (UNet, HRNet, BASNet) to segmented chunks. It loads a QGIS raster layer, crops it to a user-specified extent (parsed from a string containing coordinates and CRS), converts chunks to NumPy arrays for inference, runs model-specific post-processing (including thresholding, contour extraction, small-object removal, and transparency-aware merging), and outputs a final GeoTIFF mask of shipwreck candidates plus a CSV file listing point locations derived from contours. Input data is assumed to be high-resolution georeferenced raster (e.g., multibeam bathymetry or acoustic backscatter), but no satellite/sensor metadata, time range, or explicit study area is embedded in the code — all geospatial inputs are provided at runtime via QGIS layer and extent string. Outputs retain georeferencing, nodata handling, and metadata from the source raster.

name: Detect individual tree crowns
desc: The script detects individual tree crowns in high-resolution RGB aerial or satellite imagery by slicing the input raster into tiles, sending each tile to an external DeepForest tree detection API (running at http://10.125.93.137:5000/), transforming bounding box coordinates from pixel space to map coordinates using the source layer’s extent and CRS, resolving overlapping detections across tile boundaries via geometric overlap and area-based suppression, and exporting the final non-overlapping tree polygons as a GeoJSON file with CRS metadata. Input is a local QGIS raster layer (e.g., orthophoto) — no satellite collection is loaded or processed within GEE; the script runs entirely in QGIS as a Processing plugin and does not execute any Earth Engine (GEE) code. The script uses only Bands 1–3 (assumed RGB) from the input raster, reads them via GDAL, stacks them into a 3-channel numpy array, and saves as JPEG for API submission. No time-series analysis, cloud masking, spectral index calculation, or GEE-specific operations occur — all geospatial logic is coordinate transformation and polygon deduplication. Study area, time range, and satellite/sensor are not specified in the script; it is sensor-agnostic and location-agnostic, relying solely on the user-provided QGIS raster layer.

name: Reclassify DEM into elevation bands
desc: The script reclassifies a user-provided digital elevation model (DEM) raster into discrete elevation bands, assigning integer class values (1, 2, 3, ...) to each band. It supports default bands (0–100 m, 100–200 m, ..., 4000+ m) or custom comma- or semicolon-separated ranges (e.g., '0-100, 100-200, 1000+'). The output is a GeoTIFF raster of type UInt16 with nodata pixels set to 0, preserving input geotransform and projection. No external GEE server-side computation is used — all processing occurs locally via GDAL and NumPy within QGIS Processing Framework. Input DEM source, time range, study area, satellite, sensor, or bands are not specified in the code; it is a generic raster reclassification tool operating on any local or QGIS-loaded DEM layer.

name: Load Environmental GeoPortal data
desc: The script loads geospatial vector data from Japan's Ministry of the Environment (MOE) Environmental GeoPortal — an ArcGIS FeatureServer-based portal — into QGIS. It dynamically resolves the first layer URL from a dataset-specific base URL (e.g., with prefecture substitution), optionally applies user-specified CRS, reprojects features during export if needed, saves output as a local vector file (e.g., GeoPackage, Shapefile) or adds it directly as an ArcGIS REST layer, and applies bundled or auto-generated QML styling. The study area is constrained to Japanese prefectures (via PREFECTURES dict), and all datasets originate from MOE’s official geoportal (https://geoportal.env.go.jp/). No satellite imagery, raster processing, time-series analysis, or classification is performed — only vector feature ingestion, CRS handling, and style management. Data sources are exclusively ArcGIS FeatureServer endpoints; no Earth observation satellites, sensors, or spectral bands are involved.

name: Generate AGOpenGPS section file
desc: The script converts a QGIS vector layer representing field boundaries and weed patches into an AGOpenGPS-compatible Sections.txt file. It generates two nested grid layers (small and large quadrats) within the field boundary, computes the area *outside* weed polygons (i.e., already-applied sections), extracts grid cells fully contained in that applied area, performs geometric difference to avoid double-counting overlapping grids, merges all valid section polygons (large-grid cells, small-grid-only cells, and boundary-aligned cells), and exports them as a WGS84-referenced polygon layer plus a text file where each section is written as a 5-line block: number of vertices (always '5'), RGB color string, then four local-meter coordinates (Easting,Northing,0) ordered as [0,3,1,2] — corresponding to lower-left, lower-right, upper-left, upper-right — all relative to a base origin (StartFix) read from AGOpenGPS Fields.txt. The coordinate conversion uses latitude-dependent meters-per-degree approximations for local planar projection.

name: Compute flow accumulation
desc: The script computes flow accumulation from a pre-existing flow direction raster.
