It reads a GDAL-supported raster layer (assumed to contain flow direction values in degrees, encoded as floating-point angles), applies a custom angular flow routing logic to distribute flow from each cell to its eight neighboring cells based on directional proximity and upstream accumulation counts, and outputs a flow accumulation raster where each cell value represents the total number of upstream cells contributing flow (weighted by angular distance within 45° sectors). The algorithm iteratively resolves accumulation values using a custom 'ACM' (angular contribution model) function until convergence or 10,000 iterations. Input is a single-band raster (user-specified band); output is a GeoTIFF with same geotransform and projection. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external GEE assets are used — this is a local GDAL/Numpy-based raster processing algorithm operating on an arbitrary user-provided flow direction input.

name: Compute flow accumulation from flow direction
desc: The script computes flow accumulation raster from an input flow direction (FD) raster using a custom angular flow direction encoding (0–360°). It implements a recursive, neighbor-weighted accumulation algorithm where flow is distributed across eight neighboring cells based on the angular difference between the local flow direction and each neighbor's direction, using fractional weights derived from 45° sector thresholds. The output is a GeoTIFF file containing the accumulated flow values (floating-point), with nodata handled as -1.0 in FD and -0.5 in FA; no external GEE assets, time-series, or cloud masking are involved — it is a pure local raster processing algorithm applied to a single user-provided FD raster. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor information are not specified — the script reads a generic GDAL-raster layer (e.g., from QGIS) with no embedded temporal or mission metadata.

name: Calculate flow accumulation area
desc: The script computes flow accumulation area (not cell count) from a directional flow raster (flow direction), where each cell's value represents the total upstream contributing area in square units. It identifies 'flow initiation cells' (no inflow from any of 8 neighbors) and assigns them an initial value equal to the raster's cell area (dx * dy). Flow accumulation is computed using weighted contributions from neighboring cells based on angular flow direction intervals (45° sectors), with fractional weights applied for diagonal/edge flows. The final output is a raster where each cell contains the accumulated upstream surface area (m² or other ground units depending on input projection), written as a GeoTIFF with preserved geotransform and projection. Input is a user-provided flow direction raster (in degrees, likely from D8 or Rho8 algorithm), no study area, time range, or satellite data are involved—this is a pure GIS hydrological raster processing algorithm implemented in QGIS Python Processing Framework using GDAL and NumPy.

name: Calculate flow accumulation area
desc: The script computes flow accumulation area from a flow direction (FD) raster input, where each cell's value represents the downslope flow direction in degrees (0–360°). It identifies 'flow initiation cells' (no upstream inflow), then iteratively accumulates contributing upstream area using weighted fractional flow routing across the eight neighboring cells—each directional segment is partitioned into 45° bins (e.g., east = 135°–225°, north = 225°–315°, etc.), and inflow contributions are linearly interpolated within each bin. Crucially, it adds +1 to each cell’s accumulated count (representing the cell itself), then multiplies the final integer-like accumulation count by the total raster area (Xsize × Ysize × dx × dy) — *not* per-cell area — to produce output values in absolute area units (e.g., m² if dx/dy are in meters). The output is a single-band GeoTIFF with same geotransform and projection as input. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial context is embedded in the code; it is a generic, local, non-temporal, raster-only QGIS processing algorithm operating on user-provided FD rasters.

name: Compute flow direction and slope
desc: The script computes two raster outputs from a digital elevation model (DEM): (1) a slope raster (OUTPUT_S) in degrees, and (2) a flow direction raster (OUTPUT_D) in compass degrees (0°=North, 90°=East, etc.), using the D-infinity (D∞) algorithm with optional sink resolution. It reads a user-provided raster layer via GDAL, extracts a specified band, computes cell-wise slope magnitude and steepest downslope azimuth by evaluating eight directional neighbor pairs (e.g., east→north, north→west), applies trigonometric slope decomposition with diagonal distance correction (dxy = √(dx²+dy²)), handles edge cases and NoData, identifies sinks and flats via local neighborhood analysis (Around/Flag functions), resolves sinks by flooding to the nearest outlet using iterative minimum-elevation propagation, and writes both outputs as GeoTIFFs with preserved geotransform and projection. No external GEE server-side assets or time-series operations are used — all processing is local GDAL/Numpy-based within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Compute flow direction and slope
desc: The script computes two raster outputs from a digital elevation model (DEM): (1) slope magnitude (in degrees) and (2) flow direction (in degrees, following D-infinity and D8 conventions, with flat/sink handling). It reads the input DEM via GDAL, performs neighborhood-based elevation gradient analysis using 3×3 window logic, implements D-infinity slope/azimuth derivation for steepest flow path per cell, handles flat areas and sinks via iterative depression filling and D8 routing to nearest non-flat neighbor, and writes both outputs as GeoTIFFs with preserved geotransform and projection. No external GEE assets or cloud-based Earth Engine operations are used — this is a local GDAL/Numpy-based QGIS Processing algorithm. Input source, spatial extent, time, satellite, or study area are not specified in the code.

name: Compute flow direction and slope
desc: The script computes two hydrological raster products from a digital elevation model (DEM): (1) a slope raster (OUTPUT_S) in degrees, and (2) a flow direction raster (OUTPUT_D) in compass degrees (0–360°), using the D-infinity (D∞) algorithm with flat and sink resolution via BFS-based routing. It reads a local GeoTIFF DEM layer via GDAL, handles edge cases and NoData implicitly via array bounds checking and NaN propagation, applies D∞ slope/angle calculations per cell using 8 neighbor pairs and diagonal distances, classifies cells as D∞-flowing (0), flat (1), or sink (2), then resolves flat and sink areas by identifying contributing zones and computing flow paths using breadth-first search (Maze/BFS) and D8-derived direction assignment. Outputs are two GeoTIFF files preserving input geotransform and projection. No external GEE assets, time-series, or cloud-based imagery are used — all processing is local GDAL/Numpy-based within QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Compute flow direction and slope
desc: The script computes two raster outputs from a digital elevation model (DEM): (1) a slope raster (in degrees) and (2) a flow direction raster (in compass degrees: 0–360°, with values like 0, 45, 90, ..., 315 for D-infinity-derived 8-directional flow, plus -1 for undefined/flat/sink cells). It implements a custom D-infinity (D∞) flow routing algorithm with explicit handling of flat areas and sinks via iterative depression filling and breadth-first search (BFS)-guided flow path assignment. The workflow includes flagging cells as 'D∞', 'Flat', or 'Sink'; computing directional slope components (east-north, north-east, etc.) using GDAL-derived geotransform cell sizes; resolving flow directions via arctangent and quadrant logic; and propagating flow across flat/sink regions using maze-solving BFS and reverse path tracing. Input is a generic GDAL-readable raster layer (e.g., DEM), with no satellite or time metadata embedded — it operates purely on local raster geometry and elevation values. All operations are pixel-wise or neighborhood-based (3×3 windows), with no external time-series or multi-temporal logic.

name: Compute D-infinity flow direction and slope
desc: The script implements the D-infinity (D∞) flow routing algorithm to compute two raster outputs from a single input digital elevation model (DEM): (1) a slope raster (in degrees), and (2) a flow direction raster (in degrees, referenced to north, using the D∞ angular convention where directions range 0–360° or -1 for flat/no-flow). It reads the input DEM via GDAL, computes local slope magnitude and flow direction for each cell by evaluating eight triangular facets (NE, NE, NW, WN, WS, SW, SE, ES) using 3×3 neighborhood elevation differences, accounts for pixel geometry (dx, dy, dxy, dtan), handles edge cells and no-data conditions (< -999), and writes both outputs as GeoTIFFs with preserved geotransform and projection. No external GEE server-side computation is performed—the entire workflow runs locally in QGIS using GDAL/NumPy; the script is a QGIS Processing Algorithm, not a Google Earth Engine script despite the prompt's mischaracterization.

name: Search French toponymic place names
desc: The script performs text-based searches (simple, consonant-skeleton, or regex) against six French geolocated toponymic databases: IGN BD TOPO toponyms (points), IGN BD TOPO odonyms (lines), FANTOIR road names (points), SANDRE hydronyms (points), FANTOIR communes (points), and Cassini historical communes (points). All results are returned as GeoJSON-like JSON responses, converted into temporary QGIS vector layers (point or line) in EPSG:4326. The study area is explicitly France (inferred from all data sources: IGN, FANTOIR, SANDRE, Cassini-EHESS — all nationally scoped French official/historical databases). No time filtering is applied; no satellite, sensor, or spectral data is used — this is a pure geocoded gazetteer lookup. Outputs are in-memory vector layers added to the QGIS project with descriptive names and feature counts reported in feedback.

name: None
desc: This script is a QGIS plugin dialog for configuring and monitoring remote Earth Engine-based worker jobs (e.g., cloud-processed geospatial analyses). It does not contain or implement any GEE client-side JavaScript or Python code for satellite data processing, classification, modeling, or visualization. Instead, it provides a GUI to select inputs (raster/vector files or QGIS layers), configure compute resources, submit jobs to a backend service (via JobSession and _client), and handle post-run actions (download outputs, add them as QGIS layers). The script defines UI components (file pickers, log viewers, outputs tree), manages job state transitions, handles file I/O and layer loading logic for local disk files only, and integrates with a cloud client abstraction (_client) — but no Earth Engine API calls, image collections, reducers, band math, time-series analysis, or spatial operations are present in this file. All geospatial logic resides externally in the worker definitions and backend services, which are not included here.

name: Build anthropogenic influence mask
desc: The script applies user-defined distance thresholds (e.g., 1000 m for roads, 2000 m for large built-up) to precomputed raster distance surfaces — specifically 'Distance surface — roads', 'Distance surface — built-up (small)', 'Distance surface — built-up (large)', and 'Distance surface — agriculture' — and combines them via pixel-wise maximum into a single binary anthropogenic mask raster (1 = influenced, 0 = not influenced). The workflow reads GDAL rasters, performs threshold-based boolean masking (arr <= threshold), aggregates influences using np.maximum, and writes a compressed GeoTIFF with matching geotransform and projection. No distance computation occurs here — it relies entirely on cached inputs. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the script; all inputs are user-provided local or QGIS-loaded rasters with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata.

name: Identify primary forest candidates
desc: The script implements a three-tier decision logic to generate a binary raster 'pre_connectivity_forest.tif' identifying primary forest candidate areas. Tier 1 selects forest pixels (input binary forest raster) outside anthropogenic influence (using an anthropogenic mask from Tool 3b). Tier 2 selects forest pixels inside anthropogenic zones that occur on steep slopes (≥ user-defined threshold in degrees), either using a pre-computed slope raster or computing slope from a DEM input. Tier 3 selects forest pixels inside anthropogenic zones, on gentle slopes (< threshold), and overlapping protected areas (binary PA raster). The tiers are combined via logical OR (using np.maximum). All operations are pixel-wise raster algebra on co-registered input rasters. Inputs include user-provided binary rasters (forest, anthropogenic mask, protected areas), optional DEM or slope raster, and a configurable slope threshold. No classification model, time-series analysis, or spectral band processing is performed — the script is purely rule-based raster masking and combination. Study area, time range, satellite data sources, and geographic extent are not specified in the code; it is a generic GIS processing algorithm designed for arbitrary regional inputs compatible with QGIS ≥ 3.38.

name: Reconstruct 3D building geometry
desc: The script converts LiDAR point cloud data and 2D building footprint vector data into 3D building representations using the geoflow (geof.exe) tool. It processes each feature (building) individually by selecting it via SQL query on a user-specified attribute field (e.g., building ID), then executes geoflow with parameters including input point cloud folder, reconstruct JSON configuration, footprint layer name from a GeoPackage, output CRS (OGR/EPSG), output GeoPackage for results, CityJSON (.json), and OBJ (.obj) files per building. Inputs are local filesystem paths (not GEE assets); no Earth Engine server-side computation occurs — this is a QGIS plugin wrapper for external CLI geoprocessing. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified because the script operates on local LiDAR and vector data, not remote sensing imagery.

name: Extract LiDAR file metadata and boundaries
desc: The script processes a folder of .laz or .las files using PDAL to extract metadata including CRS (EPSG code), encoding type (laz/ las), COPC flag, and boundary geometry (Polygon or MultiPolygon) from the 'boundary_json' field in PDAL's JSON output. It validates axis order (Easting/Northing vs Northing/Easting) to correctly construct QgsGeometry objects, enforces CRS consistency across all files (only files matching the first file’s EPSG are retained), and writes the aggregated metadata + geometries to a single GeoPackage layer with fields: filename, epsg, encoding, copc. The output is a vector GeoPackage containing one polygon feature per valid LiDAR file, all sharing the same CRS.

name: Calculate street-level green view index
desc: The script calculates the Green View Index (GVI) for each input point by analyzing Google Street View (GSV) panoramic images associated with those points. It processes JPG images from a local folder, applies vegetation pixel detection using either Li et al. (2015) — based on green-red and green-blue spectral differences — or Dong et al. (2018) — based on HSV hue thresholds (75–170), followed by brightness filtering (RGB sum > 520) and spatial smoothing (11×11 modal filter). For each point, it aggregates GVI across all corresponding GSV images (e.g., multiple headings/pitches), outputs a CSV file (Points_GVIs.csv), and produces a joined vector layer linking original point geometries to their mean GVI value. Optionally, binary green mask images (_GVI.jpg) are saved.

name: Generate sample points along roads
desc: The script generates spatially distributed sample points for Green View Index (GVI) assessment: (1) if only an Area of Interest (AOI) polygon is provided, it creates random points inside the AOI using 'qgis:randompointsinsidepolygons'; (2) if only a road network line layer is provided, it places points along the lines using 'qgis:randompointsalongline'; (3) if both AOI and road network are provided, it first clips the road network to the AOI boundary using 'qgis:clip', then generates points along the clipped roads. All outputs are reprojected to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), converted from multipart to singlepart geometry, and assigned a sequential integer ID field 'random_point_id'. Minimum distance (in meters) takes precedence over point count to ensure spatial separation.

name: Detect oil palm tree canopy
desc: The script detects oil palm tree canopy locations in high-resolution raster imagery using a deep learning model (RetinaNet with ResNet101 backbone) trained specifically for small-object detection. It applies sliding-window inference (500×500 px windows, 470 px step) over the input GDAL raster, normalizes multispectral bands using 2nd–98th percentile scaling per band, performs inference, aggregates bounding boxes and scores, applies non-maximum suppression (IoU=0.3), and outputs vector geometries—either point (centroid), bounding box (polygon), or circle (diameter = bbox width)—with confidence scores as attributes. Input raster CRS is preserved; no explicit cloud masking, temporal filtering, or spectral index computation (e.g., NDVI) is performed. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor metadata, and training data provenance are not specified in the code.

name: Derive least cost zones
desc: The script computes least-cost zones from a cumulative cost raster and a traceback raster using a custom network propagation algorithm. It reads both rasters via GDAL, applies nodata masking (including thresholding by maximum accumulated cost), reindexes traceback values to align with NumPy array indexing conventions, computes parent-child neighbor relationships, and iteratively propagates peak identifiers across the cost surface until convergence. The output is a raster where each cell is assigned the ID of its ultimate peak (source) location, or -999 for masked/no-data cells. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are used—the inputs are user-provided local raster files (e.g., 'Cumulative cost raster', 'Traceback raster'), and the algorithm operates purely on their pixel values and spatial adjacency. All operations are deterministic, CPU-based, and rely on GDAL, NumPy, and a custom Python module ('doNetworks').

name: Optimize vehicle routing and scheduling
desc: The script implements a QGIS Processing algorithm that constructs a Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) input JSON from user-provided vehicle, pickup, and delivery point layers; sends it to either a local VROOM Express server or the OpenRouteService (ORS) optimization API; parses the returned solution; and generates three output layers: (1) line features representing optimized routes with attributes including cost, duration, distance, and violations; (2) point features representing all route steps (start, pickup, delivery, end, breaks) with arrival times, service durations, loads, and waiting times; and (3) a summary table with aggregate metrics (e.g., number of routes, unassigned tasks, total delivery/pickup amounts, setup/service/duration/waiting_time/distance, violations, and computing times). It handles time windows, capacities, skills, priorities, break constraints, and optional depot start/end conditions.

name: Distribute digital sketch maps
desc: The script generates and distributes satellite-based sketch maps (croquis) for individual control points (pontos de controle) using a QGIS atlas layout. It loads a pre-designed template ('croqui.qpt'), applies a point layer style, sets map scale based on user input (default 1:500), exports one image per point using the 'native:atlaslayouttoimage' algorithm with the satellite image and point layer overlaid, then organizes the exported images into a folder structure matching the input control point directory. The final output is a set of georeferenced (but GEOREFERENCE=False in params) raster images named by the 'cod_ponto' attribute, placed in subfolders corresponding to each point’s identifier. No classification, time-series analysis, or spectral computation is performed; the satellite image is used as-is. Study area, time range, sensor/band usage, and satellite identity are not specified in the code — only a generic 'imagem_de_satelite' raster layer is accepted as input.

name: Distribute aerial imagery by administrative scale
desc: The script generates and organizes georeferenced aerial imagery exports (satellite, municipal, and state scale) for control points using QGIS Atlas functionality. It applies predefined QML styles to input vector layers (points, municipalities, states, country), sets map scales per administrative level (1:1,000 for satellite, 1:25,000 for municipality, 1:2,000,000 for state), exports atlas pages as images into structured subfolders (satelite/, municipio/, estado/), then distributes those images into pre-existing control point folder structures using a custom handler class. Outputs are organized image sets per control point, with no raster analysis or time-series processing performed.

name: Generate topographic raster tiles
desc: The script automates the creation of a regular grid over a merged digital elevation model (DEM), clips the DEM to each grid cell to produce individual georeferenced GeoTIFF tiles (e.g., tile_01_01.tif), and outputs a vector grid layer (print_grid.shp); it does not perform DEM-to-STL conversion itself but prepares inputs for external 3D printing via the DEMto3D QGIS plugin using specified physical dimensions, spacing, base height, and vertical exaggeration.

name: Create topographic raster tiles
desc: The script creates a regular grid of rectangular vector polygons covering the extent of an input DEM raster, then clips the raster to each grid cell to produce individual georeferenced GeoTIFF tiles. The input raster is named 'merged_full_area.tif' and appears to be a merged digital elevation model (DEM); no classification, modeling, or time-series analysis is performed. All operations are spatial partitioning and clipping using QGIS native and GDAL algorithms. The study area is implied by the file path but not explicitly named; the output tiles are saved in '/home/x/repos/future-relief/data/processed/tiles' with naming convention 'tile_XX_YY.tif'. No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or spectral analysis is involved — this is purely a static, single-scene raster tiling workflow for downstream 3D printing (via DEMto3D plugin).

name: Create fixed-size DEM tiles
desc: The script creates a regular grid of ROWS × COLS (5 × 6 = 30) non-overlapping rectangular tiles by splitting a single pre-processed raster file (merged_full_area.tif) into smaller georeferenced GeoTIFFs. It loads the raster in QGIS, computes its extent and CRS, generates a vector grid layer using qgis:creategrid with equal horizontal/vertical spacing derived from extent dimensions, then clips the input raster to each grid cell’s bounding box using gdal:cliprasterbyextent. Outputs are individual .tif files named tile_RR_CC.tif (e.g., tile_01_01.tif), stored in a local filesystem directory. No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or modeling is performed — it is purely a deterministic tiling workflow for a static, locally stored DEM. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the script; the input is a generic processed raster with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata.

name: Create topographic raster tiles
desc: The script creates a regular grid of rectangular raster tiles from a single input DEM (Digital Elevation Model) raster file named 'merged_full_area.tif'. It first loads the raster in QGIS to extract its extent and CRS, then generates a vector grid layer with ROWS × COLS cells (5 × 6 = 30 tiles) aligned to that extent. For each grid cell, it uses gdalwarp to clip the original raster to the cell’s bounding box (with a 1-meter buffer), exporting each as a compressed GeoTIFF (LZW) named tile_RR_CC.tif (e.g., tile_01_01.tif). The output is a set of georeferenced, non-overlapping, equal-area (in map units) DEM tiles suitable for downstream 3D printing (as indicated by the comment 'Next: Convert each tile to STL using DEMto3D'). No classification, modeling, temporal analysis, or spectral processing is performed — only spatial partitioning via clipping. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified; the input is a local pre-processed raster file.

name: Tile DEM raster by grid
desc: The script divides a pre-processed digital elevation model (DEM) raster ('merged_full_area.tif') into a fixed ROWS × COLS regular grid (5×6) using QGIS vector grid generation, then clips the raster to each grid cell’s bounding box using GDAL or native QGIS clipping algorithms, producing individual GeoTIFF tiles (e.g., 'tile_01_01.tif') with preserved georeferencing and pixel values. Outputs are spatially contiguous, non-overlapping raster tiles suitable for downstream processing, visualization, or tiling workflows (e.g., web mapping or model input).

name: Estimate property tax value
desc: The script estimates Property Tax (PBB) for land parcels in Indonesia using administrative boundaries, land parcel geometries, building footprints, and land value zone (ZNT) polygons. It performs spatial intersection (clipping and overlay) to assign administrative attributes (e.g., region name, tariff rate, existing PBB) and ZNT values to each land parcel; computes parcel area, building footprint area (via intersection with buildings), and optionally applies building level multipliers; calculates land tax (area × ZNT value), building tax (building area × NJOP_BG × level), and total PBB (tariff × sum of land + building tax). Outputs include: (1) a shapefile of land parcels enriched with tax-related attributes (luas_persil, luas_bangunan, pajak_bumi, pajak_bangunan, PBB), and (2) an HTML report with summary statistics, per-region PBB comparison table (existing vs. estimated), and a doughnut chart visualizing regional PBB distribution. All geospatial operations are performed client-side using GeoPandas overlays (not GEE server-side); no Earth Engine assets or remote sensing data are loaded or processed — the script is purely vector-based GIS analysis within QGIS/Python.

name: Convert DEM to curvature-slope map
desc: The script converts an input digital elevation model (DEM) raster layer into a CS (Curvature and Slope) topographical map in GeoTIFF format. It applies Gaussian filtering (configurable size/sigma), computes slope and curvature (with configurable filter size), scales each component (height, slope, curvature) to user-defined min/max ranges, and composites them into a multi-band output. Processing supports full-scene or preview mode (central ~5% subset). The workflow uses GDAL for I/O and chunked parallel processing via multiprocessing; no Earth Engine server-side operations are present — it is a QGIS Processing Algorithm wrapper around a local Python library (csmap.py). Input is a generic raster DEM layer (no satellite-derived constraints specified); output is a single GeoTIFF file with unspecified band count (likely 3-band: height-scaled, slope-scaled, curvature-scaled). Study area, time range, satellite data sources, and sensor details are not specified — the algorithm is sensor-agnostic and operates on arbitrary local DEM rasters.

name: Compute average elevation
desc: The script computes the mean elevation value (in meters) over the currently visible map canvas extent using the 'srtm' raster layer loaded in the QGIS project. It creates a temporary memory vector layer representing the canvas extent as a polygon, then runs QGIS's 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' algorithm to calculate the mean statistic (STATISTICS=[2]) of band 1 of the 'srtm' raster. The result is displayed as an info message in the QGIS message bar (e.g., 'Average Elevation in Extent 423.17m'). No outputs are saved to disk; the operation is ephemeral and interactive. The SRTM source is not specified in the script — only its layer name 'srtm' is referenced — and no time range, geographic coordinates, or satellite metadata are present in the code.

name: Calculate zonal elevation statistics
desc: The script computes the mean elevation (statistic ID 2) from an SRTM digital elevation model raster ('srtm.tif') within polygon boundaries defined by a seismic zones vector layer ('seismic_zones.shp'). It first repairs invalid geometries in the input vector using QGIS's 'native:fixgeometries' algorithm, then performs zonal statistics using 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' with prefix 'elevation_' and only the mean statistic. The output is a vector layer (loaded into QGIS session) with a new attribute field 'elevation_mean' containing the mean elevation value for each seismic zone polygon. No time-series analysis, cloud masking, classification, or export to file is performed; all operations are local file-based and executed via QGIS Processing Toolbox in PyQGIS context. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified — inputs are local shapefile and GeoTIFF files with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata.

name: Extract zoning classification values
desc: The script extracts unique categorical values from the 'zoning' attribute field of a vector layer ('sf.gpkg|layername=zoning') loaded from a local GeoPackage file. It uses QGIS's 'qgis:listuniquevalues' processing algorithm to enumerate distinct strings in the 'zoning' column. No spatial filtering, temporal filtering, raster analysis, or classification modeling is performed — the task is purely tabular attribute enumeration. The output is a Python list of unique strings (e.g., 'residential', 'commercial', etc.), printed to stdout and intended for inspection or downstream use (e.g., defining class labels). The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations are not applicable because the input is a static, local vector dataset with no temporal component or remote sensing derivation.

name: Compute elevation statistics for seismic zones
desc: The script computes the mean elevation (zonal statistic) from an SRTM digital elevation model raster for each polygon in a seismic hazard zone vector layer. It first fixes invalid geometries in the input vector layer ('seismic_zones.shp'), then performs zonal statistics (mean only, statistic code 2) using the 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' QGIS algorithm, and saves the result—including a new 'elevation_mean' attribute—to a GeoPackage file named 'seismic_zones_with_elevation.gpkg'.

name: Fetch vehicle location data
desc: The script fetches real-time or historical vehicle location data from the Open Bus Stride API using a time window (start time + duration in minutes) and optional spatial bounding box. It transforms geometries from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to Israel Grid (EPSG:2039), maps API response fields to a typed QGIS point layer with attributes including timestamps, coordinates, velocity, bearing, distances, and GTFS identifiers (e.g., siri_line_ref, siri_ride_id). If enabled, it optionally enriches the output with GTFS route data via a downstream processing algorithm ('openbusstride:enrichwithroutes'). The output is a vector point layer in EPSG:2039, not a raster or satellite-derived product. Study area is implicitly Israel (via CRS EPSG:2039 and API domain 'Open Bus Stride', an Israeli public transport data initiative); time range is user-specified at runtime and not hardcoded; data source is the Stride REST API, not satellite/remote sensing data.

name: Detect burned area severity
desc: The script computes the differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) from pre- and post-fire NIR and SWIR raster layers to identify burned areas. It calculates NBR for both time periods using the formula (NIR − SWIR)/(NIR + SWIR), then computes dNBR as a binary mask where (NBR_before − NBR_after) ≥ user-defined threshold (default 0.1); this binary raster is polygonized and filtered to retain only pixels classified as burned (DN = 1), outputting a vector layer of fire scar polygons.

name: Classify directional slope polygons
desc: The script computes directional slope (along a user-specified azimuth) and perpendicular slope from an input DEM raster. It filters pixels where the absolute perpendicular slope falls within a user-defined range [min,max], then classifies the directional slope into discrete angular bins (e.g., ±2.5° → 5° bins). These classified pixels are polygonized, optionally simplified, filtered by minimum area (in map units²), and vertex-thinned to enforce a minimum spacing (derived from a 'definition distance' parameter, e.g., 6 m → ~3 m min vertex separation). The final output is a vector layer of polygons, each attributed with its binned directional slope value (in degrees), representing contiguous terrain facets oriented toward the specified azimuth and satisfying the perpendicular slope constraint.

name: Compute Global Moran's I
desc: The script computes Global Moran's I statistic to assess spatial autocorrelation of a user-specified numeric variable in a vector layer (point or polygon). It constructs spatial weights using one of four methods—Queen contiguity, Rook contiguity, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), or Distance Band—and calculates Moran’s I, expected I, z-score, and p-value. It generates a Moran scatterplot (Z vs. spatial lag of Z) as a PNG output, and returns a detailed textual summary including pattern interpretation (clustered/dispersed/random), statistical significance at user-selected confidence level (90%/95%/99%), descriptive statistics, and lay explanations. Input is a QGIS vector layer; no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or raster data is used—the analysis is purely vector-based and static. All geospatial operations are performed via GeoPandas and libpysal on local geometry (centroids used for polygons when needed for KNN/Distance Band).

name: Detect spatial clusters and outliers
desc: The script computes Local Moran's I statistic to classify each feature in an input vector layer (point or polygon) into spatial cluster/outlier categories: High-High (HH), Low-Low (LL), High-Low (HL), Low-High (LH), or Insignificant, based on a user-specified numeric variable and spatial weights matrix. It supports four spatial weighting methods: Queen contiguity, Rook contiguity, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Distance Band. Outputs include: (1) a new vector layer with 'Cluster' attribute and categorized symbology applied (red for HH, blue for LL, orange for HL, green for LH, grey for Insignificant); (2) a CSV file containing Local Moran's I values ('LMI'), quadrant classifications ('LMQ'), pseudo p-values ('LMP'), and 'Cluster' labels; and (3) a detailed log message with descriptive statistics, cluster counts, example identifiers per cluster, and interpretation. The script operates entirely on user-provided vector data — no remote sensing imagery or time-series processing is involved; all geospatial operations are performed via GeoPandas and libpysal on the loaded vector geometry and attributes. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified in the code.

name: Track built-up area centroid shift
desc: The script calculates the spatial centroid (mean X,Y coordinates) of pixels labeled with a user-specified built-up value (e.g., 1) in each input land cover raster layer, ordered chronologically from oldest to newest. It outputs: (1) a point vector layer containing one point per raster, with attributes 'Layer_Name', 'X', and 'Y'; and (2) if ≥2 points exist, an auxiliary line vector layer connecting consecutive centroids, with attributes 'Connection', 'Azimuth' (0–360°, measured clockwise from north), 'Distance' (Euclidean, in CRS units), and 'Direction' (cardinal quadrant). All inputs must share the same CRS; no reprojection is performed. The script uses rasterio to read rasters, NumPy to compute row/column means of matching pixels, and affine transforms to convert pixel indices to map coordinates. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic extent is embedded in the code — it is purely a generic post-processing tool for externally generated land cover rasters.

name: Generate contour lines from DEM
desc: The script generates elevation contour lines from digital elevation models (DEMs) sourced either from INPE TOPODATA (Brazil-only, ~30 m resolution, covering lat -34°S to 6°N and lon -75°W to -34.5°W) or Copernicus GLO-30 (global, 30 m resolution, hosted on AWS S3). It downloads required raster tiles based on the user-defined extent (EPSG:4326), clips them to the area of interest using a temporary shapefile, merges them into a single GeoTIFF ('merged.tif'), optionally applies terrain-smoothing using TPI-based weighted blending of Gaussian-blurred DEMs (3×3, 7×7, or 13×13 kernels), then runs gdal.ContourGenerate to produce vector contour lines at user-specified intervals (e.g., 10 m). Output includes a styled QGIS vector layer with rule-based symbology (master/normal contours), elevation labels masked on master contours, and an optional hillshade overlay raster rendered via QML. No time-series analysis is performed — the DEMs are static, non-temporal products.

name: Convert AGS file to spatial database
desc: The script parses an AGS (Association of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Specialists) format text file — a standardized geotechnical data exchange format — and converts each GROUP (e.g., LOCA, SAMP, TEST) into separate vector layers in a GeoPackage or SpatiaLite database. It detects numeric vs. text fields per group, creates spatial geometry for the LOCA group using coordinate fields in priority order (LOCA_NATE/LOCA_NATN → LOCA_LOCX/LOCA_LOCY → LOCA_LAT/LOCA_LON), reprojects LAT/LON from EPSG:4326 to user-specified CRS, writes all groups as layers, applies a QML style to the LOCA layer, registers the output database in QGIS Browser, and adds custom SVG symbol paths. Input is a plain-text AGS4 file; output is a multi-layer geodatabase with non-spatial attribute tables and one spatial point layer (LOCA).

name: Extract DSM height statistics
desc: The script extracts height statistics (mean, maximum, minimum) from a Digital Surface Model (DSM) raster for circular buffers (radius in meters) centered on input point features. It reads the DSM using GDAL, clips a region around each point using gdal.Translate with a bounding box, loads the clipped raster into a NumPy array, computes summary statistics, and writes them to a tab-delimited text file alongside the point ID. The script operates entirely locally using QGIS Processing framework inputs—no GEE server-side computation occurs; it uses GDAL and NumPy for raster I/O and statistics. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified because the DSM is provided as a local raster layer (QgsProcessingParameterRasterLayer), with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata in the code.

name: Merge TIFF images
desc: The script merges multiple GeoTIFF files from a specified input folder into a single output GeoTIFF. It optionally reprojects all inputs to EPSG:4326 prior to merging, builds an intermediate VRT (Virtual Dataset), applies bilinear resampling during warping, and allows user control over output data type (e.g., Float32) and whether to retain the temporary VRT file. No classification, time-series analysis, spectral index computation, or satellite-specific processing is performed — it is a pure raster mosaicking/stacking utility operating on pre-existing local TIFF files. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code; inputs are generic filesystem-based TIFFs with no embedded temporal or mission metadata handling.

name: Perform RBF interpolation
desc: The script performs advanced Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation on point vector data to generate a georeferenced output raster. It supports seven RBF functions (thin_plate, multiquadric, inverse_multiquadric, gaussian, linear, cubic, quintic), adjustable smoothing, local interpolation with neighbor limits and search radius, and multiple extrapolation methods (none/constant/nearest/linear). Input is a QGIS point vector layer with a numeric field; output is a GeoTIFF raster with configurable cell size and extent, properly georeferenced and added to the QGIS project. No satellite, time-series, or external Earth observation data is used — all inputs are user-provided vector points and parameters. The workflow includes point geometry extraction, NaN/inf filtering, grid generation, call to external `interpolate_rbf_advanced` function (in `rbf_utils`), GDAL-based GeoTIFF export with projection and geotransform, and optional NoData handling. Study area, time range, sensor, bands, and satellite are not specified — this is a generic GIS interpolation algorithm for arbitrary point datasets.

name: Register target image to reference
desc: The script performs image-image registration in the frequency domain using log-polar / Fourier cross-correlation (Reddy & Chatterji) to estimate a similarity transform (scale, rotation, translation) between one band of a reference and target image. It applies the estimated transform to all bands of the target image. When chunksize is specified, it processes the image in blocks, estimates transforms per block, warps each block, and mosaics them via gdal.Warp. Outputs include a georeferenced warped GeoTIFF file with '_warp' suffix and temporary block files that are cleaned up.

name: Assess road-based sampling bias
desc: The script evaluates spatial sampling bias in Neolithic archaeological site distributions relative to modern road networks in Croatia. It performs two core analyses: (A) point-based statistical comparison (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Vargha-Delaney A effect size) between real sites ('neolitik_svi_odredeni') and truly random points ('nasumicni_lokaliteti_umjetno_generirani') for road length within 1 km and 2 km buffers; and (B) grid-based correlation analysis (Pearson and Spearman) between road density and site density per grid cell. It further conducts partial correlation (C) controlling for wet soil percentage (Gleysol + Fluvisol) derived from a WRB soil raster ('tipovi_tla'), and generates road-biased random points ('random_ceste_biased') for diagnostic comparison. Outputs are console-printed statistical summaries with interpretations, including effect sizes, p-values, and mechanistic interpretations (e.g., 'sampling bias moguć', 'sampling bias je dominantan'). No rasters or vectors are exported — all results are textual diagnostics for GIS-assisted archaeological inference.

name: Calculate river density and Strahler order proximity
desc: The script computes three hydrological proximity metrics for eight point layers (e.g., archaeological sites, random points) relative to a vector river network ('tekucice') in QGIS: (1) precomputed Euclidean distance to nearest river (exported as CSV with 'fid' and 'dist_rijeka'); (2) river density (km/km²) within 1000 m and 2000 m circular buffers around each point, derived via 'qgis:sumlinelengths' on buffered polygons intersecting the river layer; (3) Strahler stream order of the nearest river segment, extracted from the 'STRAHLER' attribute of the closest river feature using spatial indexing and nearest-neighbor search. Background statistics are also exported: total river length and study area (derived from raster extent or river bounding box) for regional density, and Strahler-order-wise length distribution (km and %) across the entire river network. All outputs are saved as UTF-8 CSV files in predefined local directories (e.g., 'gustoca_rijeka_/csv_output/', 'strahler_/csv_output/'). The script explicitly uses two river layers — 'tekucice' (primary) and 'tekucice_copy' (corrected) — and a reference raster 'nadmorska_visina' (elevation) only for bounding box area estimation. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or satellite-derived data is used; all inputs are local vector/raster layers loaded from the QGIS project. Study area is not georeferenced in code but implied by layer contents.

name: Calculate relative elevation prominence
desc: The script computes 'relative prominence' for point features (archaeological sites and random points) as the difference between the mean elevation within an inner circular buffer (radius x) and the mean elevation within an outer annular buffer (radii x to y), using a digital elevation model named 'nadmorska visina' (Croatian for 'elevation above sea level'). It processes multiple vector point layers (e.g., 'neolitik_c_starcevacka', 'kontinuirana_naselja') against this raster, adds new attributes (e.g., 'rel_100_250m', 'inner_100m', 'outer_100_250m') directly to each input layer in QGIS, and exports per-layer, per-radius-combination CSV files containing feature IDs and computed relative prominence values. The study area is implicitly Croatian (evidenced by Croatian language comments, layer names like 'neolitik_c_starcevacka', and output path on 'C:\Users\Martin\Desktop'), but no explicit coordinate system or bounding box is defined in the script — CRS is inherited from input layers. No satellite, sensor, or band information is present; the elevation raster is a local QGIS layer with no GEE asset references.

name: Quantify soil type area around settlements
desc: For each settlement point, the script computes the area (in km²) occupied by each WRB soil type (e.g., Luvisols, Chernozems) within circular buffers of 100 m, 250 m, 500 m, and 1000 m radius. It does so by performing zonal histogram analysis on a categorical soil raster layer, converting pixel counts to area using raster resolution, and appending results as new numeric attributes (e.g., `tlo_100_Luvisol`) to the settlements vector layer.

name: Model outdoor thermal comfort
desc: The script models outdoor thermal comfort using the SOLWEIG (Solar and Longwave Environmental Irradiance Geometry) model to compute mean radiant temperature (Tmrt) across a tiled, buffered, and debuffered raster domain. It processes high-resolution digital surface models (bDSM, cDSM, DEM), wall parameters (aspect, height), land cover, precomputed sky view factors (SVF), and meteorological forcing data (a text file with hourly weather for 'Metro_Boston'). The workflow includes: (1) tiling the input rasters with buffer pixels; (2) clipping SVF rasters and packaging them into per-tile ZIP archives; (3) running SOLWEIG in parallel worker processes with isolated QGIS/UMEP environments; (4) debuffering the resulting Tmrt rasters to restore correct global georeferencing; and (5) merging debuffered Tmrt outputs by time-step (e.g., 'Tmrt_2023_208_0900D.tif') into final mosaicked GeoTIFFs. The study area is Boston (inferred from paths and meteo file path), and outputs are multi-temporal Tmrt rasters (e.g., day-of-year 208 at 09:00, 13:00, 17:00 local time) in EPSG:26986 (NAD83 / Massachusetts Mainland), saved to '/storage/scratch1/2/glin71/SOLWEIG/output/boston_old_met_data'. Input rasters are sourced from local filesystem paths — not GEE assets — and include lidar-derived DSMs, cleaned vegetation DSM, merged 1-m DEM, wall geometry rasters, land cover, and precomputed SVFs. No satellite, sensor, or band information is present; all data are locally stored geospatial rasters.

name: Detect duplicate water network nodes
desc: The script identifies geometrically duplicated node features in a PostgreSQL database's water utility network schema. It connects to a specified PostgreSQL connection, validates the existence of a given schema, and executes one of two database functions—ass_noeud_doublon() for wastewater (ASS) or aep_noeud_doublon() for drinking water (AEP)—which are assumed to return point geometries representing duplicate nodes (e.g., spatially coincident or topologically redundant infrastructure nodes). The output is a QGIS vector point layer loaded into the project, containing all detected duplicates with their original geometry and attributes. No remote sensing, time-series, or raster processing is involved; the analysis is purely relational/spatial SQL-based within PostGIS. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified.

name: Identify missing water network nodes
desc: The script retrieves missing nodes (points) from a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database for water distribution (AEP) or wastewater (ASS) networks by calling schema-specific SQL functions (ass_noeud_manquant() or aep_noeud_manquant()). It validates the target schema existence, constructs a dynamic PostgreSQL URI to execute the function as a subquery, loads the result as a QgsVectorLayer of point geometries, and writes the features to a user-specified vector point sink. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations beyond SQL-based spatial query are not specified — this is a database-driven GIS processing algorithm with no remote sensing or temporal analysis components.

name: Identify orphaned water network nodes
desc: The script retrieves orphaned nodes (points with no connected edges) from a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database containing water infrastructure data. It connects to a specified schema and executes one of two database functions—ass_noeud_orphelin() for wastewater/sewer networks or aep_noeud_orphelin() for drinking water networks—both returning point geometries representing disconnected nodes. The output is a QGIS vector point layer loaded into the project, with no raster processing, remote sensing, or temporal analysis involved. All operations are SQL-based spatial queries executed server-side; the script acts as a thin QGIS Processing wrapper over pre-defined PostGIS functions. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified in the code.

name: Filter vector layer features
desc: The script enables interactive SQL-like filtering of vector layers in QGIS using attribute-based conditions (e.g., 'field = value', 'field > threshold'). It supports three output modes: (1) selecting features in the current layer using QgsVectorLayer.selectByExpression(), (2) creating a new temporary vector layer via 'native:extractbyexpression' processing algorithm, or (3) applying a subset string (definition query) to filter the layer’s visible features. The script dynamically populates field-value dropdowns based on field type (string, numeric, date/datetime), including unique string values and statistical quantiles (min, 25th, 50th, 75th, max) for numeric fields. No remote sensing imagery, time-series analysis, or Earth Engine server-side computation is performed — all operations are client-side within QGIS using local vector layers. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial modeling methods are not involved or specified.

name: Build RS-Minerve hydrological model layers
desc: The script builds input layers for the RS-Minerve hydrological modeling software by processing user-provided GIS layers in QGIS. It takes three mandatory input layers: (1) a vector layer of watershed polygons (expected to have 'GRIDCODE' and later 'iWatershed' attributes), (2) a vector layer of stream centerlines (line geometry), and (3) a raster digital elevation model (DEM). Key workflow steps include: computing watershed polygon areas using QgsDistanceArea; removing duplicate or fragmented watersheds based on GRIDCODE and area; converting watersheds to lines; intersecting streams with watersheds and watershed lines to identify junctions; buffering junctions and performing spatial joins to validate topological consistency (e.g., no stream crossing >2 watersheds, no junction touching >2 watersheds or >1 stream); building hierarchical catchment–junction–stream connectivity dictionaries; generating new standardized output layers — 'rs_junctions' (point layer with iJunction and iStreamDownstream), 'rs_streams' (line layer with iStream, iJunctionDownstream, length, slope, n, width, zone), and 'rs_watersheds' (polygon layer with iWatershed, iJunctionDownstream, area, zone); computing reach slopes via zonal statistics on a large (200-unit) junction buffer applied to the input DEM; and simplifying stream networks by merging short reaches below a user-defined minimum distance threshold. Outputs are memory-based QgsVectorLayer objects added to the QGIS project. No remote sensing data is loaded or processed — all inputs are local QGIS map layers selected by the user via GUI comboboxes. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified.

name: Extract building and address features
desc: The script processes INSPIRE-compliant GML files containing building and building part geometries, and address/thoroughfare data for the municipality of Barcelona (BCN). It merges multiple GML layers, filters features intersecting the Barcelona municipal boundary (bcn_municipalities.geojson), computes geometry attributes (area, perimeter), generates centroids for spatial joins, and performs successive spatial joins with administrative boundaries (Barcelona districts 'barcelonaciutat_barris', census tracts 'bcn_census_tracts', and postal codes 'bcn_postal_codes') to attach hierarchical location identifiers. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage of filtered and geometry-enhanced buildings (08900_buildings_geom.gpkg), (2) a centroid GeoJSON joined with district/census/postal attributes (08900_buildings_geom_centroid_ba_ct_pc.geojson), (3) a GeoPackage of filtered building parts with centroids (08900_building_part_geom_centroid.geojson), and (4) a GeoJSON of filtered and geometry-enhanced addresses (08900_address_geom.geojson). All operations are performed in EPSG:4326; no time-series or satellite imagery is used — inputs are static vector datasets.

name: Download and process LiDAR-derived DTM tiles
desc: The script fetches National LiDAR Programme Digital Terrain Model (DTM) tiles from the UK's Environment Agency WFS service and Agrimetrics API based on a user-selected vector polygon layer's extent and year. It downloads ZIP-packaged GeoTIFFs, unzips them, merges multiple tiles into a single raster, optionally clips the merged raster to the input polygon boundary, and loads the final clipped or merged GeoTIFF as a valid QGIS raster layer for visualization and analysis.

name: Download and merge DTM tiles
desc: The script fetches Digital Terrain Model (DTM) files from the Welsh Government LiDAR Tile Catalogue (2020–2023) via a WFS endpoint using the bounding box of a user-selected QGIS vector polygon layer in EPSG:27700. It downloads HTTP-linked DTM GeoTIFFs for a selected year, merges them into a single raster using GDAL merge, and optionally clips the merged raster to the input polygon boundary using GDAL cliprasterbymasklayer. The final output is loaded as a valid QgsRasterLayer into the QGIS project. Study area is implicitly constrained to Wales (via datamap.gov.wales domain and EPSG:27700 — British National Grid), time range is 2020–2023 per catalogue name, and data source is airborne LiDAR-derived DTM (no satellite/sensor — ground-based active remote sensing).

name: Quantify flower fraction in Zinnia acerosa
desc: The script quantifies spectral vegetation and floral indices—including NDVI, PRI, ARI, CRI, EVI, FLI, REIP, mNDVI, mSR, and Flower Fraction—using hyperspectral reflectance data from the EMIT L2A RFL product (2023) for the plant species Zinnia acerosa. It processes NetCDF files containing calibrated surface reflectance across ~285–1640 nm (with wavelength sampling used to extract bands at specific nanometers), aligns them spatially to GPS-derived field locations from a CSV (decimalLatitude/decimalLongitude), and computes per-location raster layers georeferenced using a fixed 0.00054° pixel size. Key methods include band selection by nearest-wavelength matching, index computation via string-evaluated formulas (e.g., '(r500 - r_background) / (r_leaf - r_background)' for Flower_Fraction), linear spectral unmixing using synthetic endmembers (flower/leaf/soil at 500/700 nm), and RGB compositing (650/550/450 nm). Outputs are GeoTIFFs per index and coordinate, styled with index-specific pseudocolor ramps in QGIS, plus georeferenced TIFF and NetCDF-derived RGB layers. The study area is implicitly defined by the CSV coordinates and EMIT overpass geometry; no explicit region name is given beyond the species and file paths.

name: Georeference TIFF to CSV coordinates
desc: The script georeferences a single EMIT L2A reflectance GeoTIFF file (EMIT_L2A_RFL_001_20230224T181000_2305512_020.tiff) to multiple geographic locations defined by unique latitude/longitude points extracted from a QGIS CSV vector layer named "Zinnia_acerosa_DC_A_Gray_OpenFlowers". For each coordinate, it computes a custom geotransform assuming a fixed pixel size (0.00054°), centers the raster extent on that coordinate, assigns WGS84 projection, writes a new georeferenced GeoTIFF per coordinate, and loads each as a raster layer into the QGIS project. The study area is not spatially bounded — it is point-based and driven entirely by the CSV’s decimalLatitude/decimalLongitude fields. No temporal filtering or spectral analysis is performed; the input TIFF is copied and re-georeferenced without resampling or band processing. Outputs are individual GeoTIFF files (e.g., "georeferenced_tiff_coord_0.tif") and corresponding QGIS raster layers.

name: Dissolve polygons by attribute
desc: The script performs vector polygon dissolution based on user-selected attribute field(s) from a QGIS vector layer. It supports two modes: (1) dissolve only selected features using QGIS native:dissolve processing algorithm, and (2) dissolve all features using geopandas.dissolve (with optional explode for disjoint geometries). Input is a local vector source (e.g., Shapefile path retrieved via layer.source()), and output is a new Shapefile written to user-specified path with enforced '.shp' extension. No remote sensing imagery, GEE server-side computation, or Earth Engine assets are used — this is a desktop QGIS plugin dialog for vector geometry aggregation. The script includes progress feedback, error handling for non-polygon layers, file cleanup on cancel, and optional auto-loading of result into QGIS project. All operations are client-side; no time-series, raster, or satellite data involved.

name: Calculate road network accessibility isochrones
desc: The script calculates travel-time isochrones (e.g., 5-, 10-, 15-minute access polygons) from user-specified origin points using the OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) routing engine. It retrieves point coordinates either via interactive canvas clicking or from a selected QGIS point layer, sends batched 'table' and 'locate' API requests to an OSRM server (URL configured externally), interpolates travel times over a snapped road-network grid using scipy's griddata, generates contour polygons at user-defined time intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes up to a max time), converts Matplotlib contour paths to QgsGeometry MultiPolygon features, renders them with graduated symbology by time interval, and adds both the isochrone polygons and origin point layers to the QGIS project. The output includes styled vector layers named 'isochrone_osrm_N' and 'isochrone_center_N', with opacity 0.25 and color-coded time bands; no satellite, in-situ, or archival geospatial datasets are loaded or processed — all spatial analysis is performed client-side via external OSRM HTTP API calls. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/bands are not specified because the script is a QGIS plugin frontend for real-time routing, not a GEE (Google Earth Engine) script.

name: Calculate batch origin-destination routes
desc: The script calculates pairwise point-to-point road network routes using the OSRM (OpenStreetMap Routing Machine) API. It supports two input modes: (1) QGIS point vector layers for origin and destination, with on-the-fly reprojection to EPSG:4236 if needed; (2) CSV files with coordinate columns specified by user-selected fields. It validates coordinate formats via regex, constructs OSRM route URLs with 'overview=full&steps=false&alternatives=false', decodes polyline geometries using 'decode_geom', and creates a memory-based Linestring layer with attributes 'id', 'total_time_min', and 'distance_m'. Outputs are saved as ESRI Shapefile (if path provided) and/or added to the QGIS canvas as 'routes_osrm{N}' layers. The script enforces rate limits (e.g., blocks >20 requests to routing.openstreetmap.de) and includes UI-driven functionality for field/layer swapping, CSV loading, output path selection, and route clearing.

name: Compute road route geometry
desc: The script computes point-to-point or multi-point road routes using the OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) API. It constructs HTTP requests with origin, destination, and optional intermediate coordinates (in WGS84 decimal degrees), sends them to an OSRM server (base URL configured externally), and parses the JSON response containing encoded polyline geometries, durations, distances, and turn-by-turn instructions. Key workflow steps include: (1) capturing or parsing coordinate strings from QGIS map canvas clicks or text fields; (2) validating coordinate format and length; (3) building a compliant OSRM /route query URL with parameters like overview=full, alternatives=true/false, and steps=true/false; (4) decoding Polyline-encoded geometries into QgsGeometry line features; (5) creating three memory vector layers — a route layer (Linestring, with time/distance attributes), an origin/destination/intermediate markers layer (Point, with role-based rule rendering), and an instruction layer (Point, with maneuver attributes like type, bearing, exit, street name, distance, duration); (6) styling and adding all layers to the QGIS project with proper z-ordering (markers on top of routes, instructions on top of markers). Outputs are visualized in the QGIS map canvas as interactive vector layers — no satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is involved. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified because the script is a client-side routing interface, not a geospatial analysis script.

name: Solve traveling salesman routing problem
desc: The script solves the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for a user-selected point layer using the OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) routing engine. It constructs a TSP query by extracting coordinates from the input point layer, sends an HTTP request to an OSRM instance (URL and optional API key configured externally), parses the JSON response containing optimized trip geometry, duration, distance, and maneuver instructions, then visualizes three output layers in QGIS: (1) a linestring layer representing the optimal TSP route(s) with attributes for total time (minutes) and distance (meters); (2) a point layer showing ordered waypoints labeled with sequence numbers (TSP_nb); and (3) an optional instruction point layer with step-by-step navigation maneuvers (location, type, modifier, exit, street name, length, time). No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis beyond coordinate-based routing is involved — all operations are vector geometry construction and QGIS layer rendering driven by external OSRM web service responses.

name: Export OSM infrastructure as DXF
desc: The script downloads OpenStreetMap (OSM) vector data (specifically 'way' elements representing linear features like roads, paths, and boundaries) for the current QGIS map canvas extent using the Overpass API. It processes only ways (not nodes or relations), constructs LineString geometries from node coordinates, assigns a 'type' attribute based on OSM tags (prioritizing 'highway', then 'leisure', 'landuse', 'building', 'amenity'), reprojects the resulting layer from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to the appropriate UTM zone (dynamically computed from the extent's central longitude), and exports it as a DXF file with attributes mapped to DXF layer names. The exported DXF is then loaded back into QGIS. No time-based filtering, classification, or satellite-derived data is involved; the source is purely crowd-sourced OSM vector data.

name: Classify soil texture
desc: The script classifies soil texture using user-provided sand and clay raster layers (loaded from QGIS map canvas) and a user-selected triangular texture classification schema file (.dat). It reads sand and clay pixel values, maps each (sand, clay) coordinate pair into a USDA or similar soil texture triangle defined by polygonal rules in the schema, assigns a numeric texture class code (e.g., 'SAND', 'CLAY', 'LOAM'), and outputs: (1) a classified GeoTIFF raster with Byte data type and -9999 NoData; (2) an optional vectorized shapefile with attribute fields 'code' and 'label_txt' derived from the schema’s legend; and (3) a CSV file ('_ternaryPlot.csv') containing per-pixel CLAY,SAND,SILT triplets for ternary plotting. The script operates entirely on local raster files — no GEE server-side computation is performed; it is a QGIS desktop plugin with GDAL/Numpy-based local raster processing. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code — inputs are arbitrary local rasters selected by the user via QGIS layer list.

name: Interpolate aerial image time series
desc: The script performs linear temporal interpolation between two user-provided georeferenced aerial RGB images (aerial_image_ini and aerial_image_end) over a user-defined area of interest (vector polygon or polyline). It crops both images to the area, resamples them to identical dimensions, then generates intermediate daily RGB rasters for all dates in the user-specified date range using weighted averaging based on temporal distance. Outputs are GeoTIFFs named with YYYYMMDD format (e.g., '20220803_interpolation.tiff'), loaded into QGIS under an 'Output' layer group. No satellite imagery, cloud masking, spectral indices, or classification is used — only local raster I/O, GDAL-based cropping/resampling, and pixel-wise linear interpolation. Study area, sensor, bands, and satellite are not specified; inputs are arbitrary local raster files.

name: Assess harvest accessibility distance
desc: The script computes two key accessibility distances for forest harvesting operations: (1) d1 — the straight-line distance from each grid point (p1) inside an operation polygon to the nearest forest road, and (2) d2 — the shortest network distance along the road layer from the snapped road point (p2) to the nearest landing point. It aggregates per-grid-point d1 and minimum d2 values, then outputs an HTML report with summary statistics (mean d1, mean d2, count of unreachable points), and optionally loads intermediate layers (p1 grid, p2 snapped points, routes) in debug mode.

name: Generate contour lines from elevation data
desc: The script generates vector contour line layers from either (1) an input raster elevation layer using GDAL's contour algorithm, or (2) a point vector layer with an elevation attribute by first interpolating a raster surface (via TIN or IDW) and then extracting contours. Outputs include a styled vector layer added to the QGIS project and optionally exported to Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML, or DXF format, with attributes including elevation ('ELEV'), interval-based classification (e.g., major vs. minor contours), and configurable Z-factor scaling.

name: Calculate line segment azimuth and bearing
desc: The script computes geometric attributes—azimut (forward angle from north), rumbo (compass quadrant bearing), segment length, and cumulative length—for each straight-line segment of polyline features in a QGIS vector layer. It processes vertices of input line geometries, uses QgsDistanceArea with WGS84 ellipsoid for geodesic distance and angular calculations, formats angles in decimal degrees or DMS per user selection, and outputs results as point features (at segment midpoints) with attribute fields including coordinates, lengths, and formatted/unformatted azimuth/bearing values. Outputs include optional temporary or saved vector layers (Shapefile/GeoPackage), a plain-text summary report, and export options to CSV, Excel (.xlsx), and PDF. No remote sensing data, time-series, or raster processing is involved—the analysis is purely vector-based and coordinate-geometry-driven on user-provided local GIS layers.

name: Calculate polygon geometric properties
desc: The script performs topographic/geometric calculations on user-provided polygon vector layers in QGIS, including internal/external angles, azimuth, bearing, vertex-to-vertex distances, cumulative distances, area, and perimeter. It processes each polygon’s vertices sequentially, computes angular and linear measurements using planar (Cartesian) distance for local calculations and ellipsoidal (WGS84) measurement for area/perimeter, formats angular outputs in degrees decimal, DMS, or radians, converts area to m²/ha/km², and generates a structured textual report. Outputs include a point layer with vertex-level attributes, optional temporary or file-based vector output (Shapefile/GeoPackage), and exportable reports in TXT, CSV, Excel (.xlsx), or PDF formats. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or satellite data is used — input is strictly local vector polygon layers loaded in QGIS; all operations are deterministic geometric computations on static geometry.

name: Calculate travel time to hospitals
desc: The script computes the shortest travel time (in minutes) from a user-specified departure point to each hospital in a point layer, using a road network vector layer. It first builds spatial indexes on both the road network and hospitals for efficiency, then computes the fastest path from the departure point to every hospital using Dijkstra’s algorithm (via QGIS's 'shortestpathpointtolayer' with 'fastest strategy'). It calculates travel time assuming a constant speed of 80 km/h, converts path length to minutes with rounding, sorts paths by ascending time, ranks hospitals by accessibility (1 = fastest), selects only the top-ranked (fastest) route, and outputs two layers: (1) all hospital routes with calculated 'temps_minutes' and 'Classement' fields, and (2) the single fastest route geometry as a separate feature sink.

name: Plan bus transit routes
desc: The script performs multimodal public transport routing in Shanghai, China, using QGIS-integrated Python to build a graph-based representation of the bus network from two vector layers: '上海市公交线路' (bus lines) and '上海市公交_点' (bus stops). It clusters stops by geographic location (Lng/Lat) to identify physical stop locations, constructs directed edges between consecutive stops on each line-direction combination, estimates travel time using Euclidean (or haversine) distance and a fixed average bus speed (20 km/h), and applies a Dijkstra shortest-path algorithm with transfer penalty (15 min) to compute optimal routes between user-specified origin/destination coordinates. The outputs include a human-readable step-by-step route description (with transfers, lines, directions, and intermediate stops) and a visualized polyline layer ('规划路径') drawn on the QGIS map canvas showing the sequence of stop-to-stop segments. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are local vector layers loaded in QGIS. Study area is explicitly Shanghai (via layer names in Chinese), and no temporal filtering or time-series analysis is performed.

name: Search and locate addresses
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for searching and geolocating German street addresses from local CSV files containing house number, street name, postal code, and geographic coordinates (RW = Easting, NW = Northing in EPSG:4647). It loads address data into an SQLite database, performs text-based fuzzy matching on formatted address strings, filters optionally by current map canvas extent, displays results in a table, and allows zooming to selected addresses. Optionally, it saves selected addresses as point features in a memory layer with SVG markers and labeling. The script does not use remote sensing or Earth Engine imagery; all data is local tabular input. Study area is implicitly Germany (evidenced by ADV ZSHH standard reference, German field names like 'HNR', 'STN', 'PLZ', CRS EPSG:4647 — DHDN / 3-degree Gauss-Kruger zone 3), but no specific region or city is named. Time range is not applicable. Outputs include interactive table results, map canvas navigation, and optional vector point layer(s) in the QGIS project.

name: Export slippy map tiles
desc: The script exports raster map layers from QGIS as either GeoTIFF or MBTiles format. It computes tile bounds in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) using slippy-tile math, renders map images at specified zoom levels and tile sizes via QgsMapRendererParallelJob, applies optional padding, and writes georeferenced GeoTIFFs (with GDAL) or SQLite-based MBTiles databases containing PNG-encoded tiles with TMS-compliant y-coordinates. Inputs include a user-selected QGIS layer, bounding box (as min/max lat/lon), zoom range, tile size, and output path; no satellite imagery processing, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — it is purely a cartographic export utility.

name: Export agricultural field boundaries
desc: The script processes QGIS vector line layers representing agricultural field boundaries (e.g., harvest lines) and exports them in multiple standardized agro-automation formats: John Deere GEN4 (MasterData.xml + AdaptiveCurve .gjson), John Deere GS3_2630 (SpatialCatalog + setup.fds), Trimble PTX AgData (.agf), and Trimble PTX AgGPS (WGS84 Shapefile). It performs geometry simplification (Douglas-Peucker–style vertex reduction with min/max spacing and deviation tolerance), attribute classification (client, farm, field/talhão, line type: 'Curva', 'AB', or 'Limite'), and intelligent block splitting when output exceeds 2.5 MB — allowing drag-and-drop reorganization of fields into named blocks ('Parte', 'Bloco', or 'Gleba') before export. All operations are client-side within QGIS; no Earth Engine server-side computation, imagery, or time-series analysis is involved. Input is strictly local shapefiles (LineString geometry only); outputs are filesystem ZIP archives or structured directories containing vendor-specific XML, JSON, FDS, AGF, and SHP files.

name: Convert CSV addresses to point layers
desc: The script converts user-provided CSV files containing geographic coordinates (latitude/longitude) or address strings into QGIS vector point layers. When latitude/longitude fields are present and geocoding is disabled, it directly builds a memory layer with geometries from those coordinates (EPSG:4326). When an address field is selected and geocoding is enabled, it performs synchronous or asynchronous geocoding using one of six configurable providers (Nominatim, Google, Mapbox, OpenCage, HERE, Yahoo Japan), appending geocoding result metadata (e.g., 'lat', 'lng', 'formatted_address', 'status') as attributes. Outputs include a QgsVectorLayer added to the QGIS project, with success/failure feedback via the message bar; no remote Earth observation data, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis is involved — all operations are local CSV parsing, coordinate conversion, and API-based geocoding.

name: Segment tree crowns using watershed
desc: The script performs individual tree crown segmentation on LiDAR-derived or point cloud raster data (LAS/LAZ format) using a watershed algorithm. It takes an active LAS/LAZ layer in QGIS, applies Gaussian smoothing, detects local maxima (LM) as treetop candidates based on user-defined minimum height and minimum distance thresholds, and then segments crowns via watershed transform. The workflow is entirely local (no GEE server-side computation), implemented in Python using the external `watershed_backend` module. Inputs are file-based LAS/LAZ point clouds; no satellite, aerial imagery, or time-series data is used. Outputs are two in-memory QGIS vector layers: (1) red-labeled treetop points (LM layer), and (2) color-categorized crown centroid points with `tree_id`, both georeferenced to the input layer’s CRS. Metrics reported include number of input points and segmented trees. No raster outputs, exports, or time-series analysis are performed.

name: Model geomagnetic field component
desc: The script processes a user-selected vector layer (polygon) representing a region of interest to compute and visualize a geomagnetic field component (e.g., 'X', 'Y', 'Z', or 'F') using spherical harmonic modeling. It exports the result as a NetCDF raster file containing gridded magnetic field values at a specified altitude, based on the IGRF or equivalent model parameters (l_min, l_max), grid resolution, and visualization settings. The output is loaded as a QGIS raster layer. No satellite imagery, time-series filtering, or Earth observation bands are involved — the core computation is external (via process_script2.py), likely invoking a geomagnetic field calculator (e.g., NOAA's MagPy, IGRF-13/14 C code, or custom SH implementation). Input geometry is converted to GeoJSON; no explicit study area, time range, or remote sensing data sources appear in this plugin script.

name: Browse Databricks database catalogs
desc: The script implements a QGIS Browser Panel provider that enables users to browse Databricks SQL warehouse connections, recursively listing catalogs → schemas → tables → columns. It detects geometry-capable tables (with GEOMETRY/GEOGRAPHY columns) using system.information_schema, displays appropriate icons, and provides context-menu actions to add vector layers (first 1000 features, all features, or live viewport-based layers) or view table data via SQL queries. Outputs include expandable hierarchical browser items, memory-based QgsVectorLayer instances with proper field typing and WKT geometry parsing, and metadata-stored layers for refresh functionality. No remote geospatial analysis, modeling, or satellite data processing occurs — it is purely a database connectivity and browsing interface.

name: Solve Chinese Postman route
desc: The script solves the Chinese Postman Problem (CPP) on a user-selected vector line layer (e.g., road network) in QGIS. It converts selected line features into a NetworkX graph, identifies the largest connected component, computes the minimal-length Eulerian supergraph by duplicating necessary edges (i.e., finding shortest paths between odd-degree nodes), and outputs a single continuous polyline layer representing the optimal closed-route traversal that covers every input edge at least once. Key outputs include: (1) a memory-based QgsVectorLayer showing the full traversed path with arrow-marked directional rendering; (2) quantitative metrics — total input road length, total CPP path length, and duplicate (retraversed) length — all reported in km; and (3) a sampled list of node coordinates (every 10th node, with x/y swapped for lat/lon order). The script performs no remote sensing, no time-series analysis, and no satellite data ingestion — it operates purely on local vector geometry using QGIS and NetworkX. Study area, time range, satellite data, and external datasets are not involved or specified.

name: Geocode administrative units and addresses
