desc: The script performs geocoding and reverse-geocoding of Spanish administrative units (comunidades autónomas, provincias, municipios), postal codes, and address-like features (e.g., streets, portals, POIs) using the CartoCiudad geocoder API (https://www.cartociudad.es/geocoder/api/geocoder). It loads hierarchical administrative filter lists from GitHub-hosted CSV files (e.g., cartociudad.comunidad_autonoma.csv), applies client-side filtering (e.g., province dependent on selected comunidad), constructs parameterized API requests with filters (e.g., &comunidad_autonoma_filter=), retrieves candidate locations as JSON, displays them in a QTableWidget, and on selection, fetches precise WKT geometries via /find endpoint. It then creates memory vector layers per result (Point/LineString/Polygon) grouped by type (e.g., 'Viales', 'Municipios'), applies QGIS QML styles from local filesystem paths, adds attributes from the JSON response, and zooms the map canvas to the geometry’s bounding box after reprojection to the project CRS. The study area is explicitly Spain (via CartoCiudad — official Spanish national geocoding service), data sources are static CSVs from IDEESpain’s GitHub and live CartoCiudad REST API, no satellite/sensor/bands involved, and outputs are interactive QGIS vector layers with symbology and attribute tables.

name: Generate atlas grid layer
desc: The script generates a regular polygonal grid layer aligned to a user-specified paper size, orientation, scale, and input vector layer extent. It projects the input layer to an appropriate UTM CRS, computes a bounding box with 10 m offset, then creates non-overlapping rectangular grid cells (in target projected CRS) that intersect the transformed input features. Only cells intersecting the input geometry are retained. The output is a memory vector layer with attributes 'grid' (e.g., 'A1', 'B2') and 'serial' (1-based index), styled with semi-transparent aqua fill, navy outline, and bold white-buffered numeric labels. No satellite or remote sensing data is used — it is a pure GIS cartographic grid generation tool for QGIS Atlas map series setup.

name: Assess landslide susceptibility
desc: The script performs regional landslide susceptibility assessment using the First Order Reliability Method (FORM) with the Hasofer–Lind–Rackwitz-Fiessler (HLRF) iterative algorithm. It processes user-provided raster inputs representing geotechnical and seismic parameters — including friction angle (φ), cohesion (c), unit weight of soil (suw), depth (D), slope angle, and seismic PGA source layer — to compute four output rasters: (1) probability of failure (Pf), (2) reliability index (β), (3) factor of safety (FOS), and (4) pseudo-static seismic coefficient (k). The workflow includes raster loading via GDAL, statistical normalization (mean-fill for NaN/outliers when enabled), angular unit conversion (degrees → radians), seismic attenuation modeling (distance-based PGA/Sa estimation using empirical GMPE-like equations), equivalent normal transformation (EqvN) for non-normal distributions (Normal, Lognormal, Extvalue1, Exponential, Gamma, Weibull), and pixel-wise HLRF iteration to solve the limit state function g(x)=FOS−1=0 in standard normal space. Outputs are saved as GeoTIFFs aligned to the slope raster’s georeferencing. No explicit satellite data sources, time range, or geographic location are embedded in the code; all inputs are local file paths selected interactively via QGIS file widgets.

name: Convert coordinate reference systems
desc: The script converts vector layer geometries between WGS84, GCJ02, and BD09 geographic coordinate systems. It supports point, line, and polygon geometries, preserves all original attributes, and outputs either a new file (Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML, MapInfo, or DXF) or a temporary memory layer. Conversion is performed using mathematical transformations (e.g., wgs2gcj, gcj2bd) via the imported Transform utility class; no projection or datum transformation via QGIS CRS engine is used — only algorithmic coordinate shifts specific to Chinese geodetic standards. Input is any loaded QGIS vector layer; output is a new vector layer with transformed coordinates and identical schema. No remote sensing data, time series, or spatial analysis beyond coordinate arithmetic is involved.

name: Download hydrological station data
desc: The script downloads and processes hydrological time-series data (streamflow and rainfall) from Brazil's National Water Agency (ANA) Hidroweb API. It filters stations by spatial intersection with a user-provided polygon layer (e.g., watershed or buffer), optionally applies a buffer, and uses the HidroInventario service to obtain station metadata (code, latitude, longitude, station type). For selected stations matching user criteria (rain only, flow only, or both), it retrieves monthly historical series via the HidroSerieHistorica web service, parses XML responses, reconstructs daily values per month (e.g., 'Vazao01'–'Vazao31', 'Chuva01'–'Chuva31'), and exports CSV files containing date, coordinates, consistency level, and observed values. It also creates QGIS memory vector layers for each station with point geometry and attribute tables containing time-series records. The study area is implicitly defined by the user’s input polygon and station inventory; no fixed geographic extent is hardcoded. Data sources are exclusively ANA’s telemetric web services — no satellite, remote sensing, or Earth observation data is used.

name: Extract airport by name
desc: The script extracts airport features from a local Shapefile (ne_10m_airports.shp) using a SQL-like expression to filter for airports whose 'name' field contains the substring 'Congonhas'. It uses QGIS Processing's 'native:extractbyexpression' algorithm to perform attribute-based feature selection. The output is a new Shapefile (congonhas.shp) containing only the matching airport feature(s). No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, raster operations, or satellite imagery is involved; the input is a static vector dataset. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial modeling methods are not specified — the operation is purely vector attribute filtering in a local GIS workflow.

name: Process GTFS transit data
desc: The script processes GTFS (General Transit Feed Specification) data to correct calendar inconsistencies by renaming 'calendar_dates.txt' to 'calendar.txt' and repackaging into a corrected 'gtfs_corrigido.zip'. It also ingests demand point data (CSV with X/Y coordinates), converts it to a GeoPackage layer named 'dados_demanda', and appends a derived 'shape_id' field constructed from 'LINHA', 'SUBLINHA', and 'PC' attributes (e.g., 'I' or 'V'). The workflow is triggered via QGIS plugin UI buttons, operates on local file paths selected by the user, and applies attribute-based filtering (e.g., 'shape_id' matching) to subset layers. No satellite, remote sensing, or Earth Engine (GEE) code is present — this is purely a QGIS desktop plugin for transit and demand data preprocessing.

name: Snap points to line geometry
desc: The script snaps point geometries to a reference line layer using QGIS's native 'snapgeometries' algorithm with a tolerance of 200 map units and behavior mode 1 (snap start/end vertices). It retrieves layer paths and names from the current QGIS project, identifies specific layers by name ('pontos_1502 — pontos_1502_pc_2' for points and 'pontos_1502 — linha_1502' for line), and runs the snapping operation producing a temporary output. The commented-out section suggests an alternative manual implementation using closestSegmentWithContext for point-to-line projection within 5 map units, but it is not executed.

name: Load cadastre parcel data
desc: The script connects to a PostgreSQL database hosting a 'cadastre' table containing cadastral parcel records with attributes including commune, lieudit, proprio, pres_sol, pres_bati, nbr_parc, surface, and surfaceCompte. It enables interactive filtering via UI comboboxes and text fields (e.g., ILIKE-based string matching on commune/lieudit/proprio, and numeric comparisons on nbr_parc/surface/surfaceCompte), creates a temporary filtered table in the database, and loads it as a QGIS vector layer named 'cadastre' with geometry column 'geom'. The workflow is entirely database-driven — no remote sensing, satellite imagery, or Earth Engine (GEE) processing occurs. All operations are local to the QGIS plugin interface and PostgreSQL backend. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not present or referenced.

name: Transform coordinates between formats
desc: The script transforms geographic coordinates between decimal degrees, degree-minute-second (DMS), and UTM representations, using user-specified source and target UTM zones. It validates input formats, performs coordinate transformations via QgsCoordinateTransform, and optionally creates a labeled point feature in QGIS at the transformed location. Outputs include formatted UTM coordinates (X,Y) displayed in a QLineEdit, and — if enabled — a new point feature in an existing or newly created memory vector layer with optional naming and labeling. No remote sensing data, time-series, or Earth observation analysis is involved; all operations are local, deterministic coordinate conversions within the QGIS desktop environment.

name: Create grid patches from selected tiles
desc: The script creates regular grid patches (vector polygon layers) from user-selected features in an active vector layer. It reads the bounding box of each selected feature, computes horizontal and vertical spacing based on a user-specified number of tiles (n_tiles), and uses QGIS's native:creategrid algorithm to generate a square grid covering that extent. The resulting grids are added as new vector layers named 'grid_<attribute_value>', styled with customizable outline color and width, and optionally saved to a user-defined directory. No remote sensing data, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — the workflow is purely vector-based geometric partitioning using QGIS processing tools.

name: Route transit networks between locations
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for transit routing that geocodes user-provided start and end location names (e.g., bus stops or train stations) using Nominatim, retrieves real-time multimodal transit routes (bus/train) via the Google Maps Directions API (transit mode), and visualizes the resulting route geometries, start/end points, and associated infrastructure (bus stops, train stations) as temporary vector layers in QGIS. It also populates UI dropdowns with point names from existing project layers named 'Buses' and 'Trains'. The script does not process satellite or Earth observation data; it relies entirely on external geocoding and routing APIs and local vector layers. No study area, time range, satellite data, or EO-derived analysis is performed — it is a GIS client-side routing interface.

name: Generate stratified random sample points
desc: The script generates stratified random reference sample points for ground truth collection and accuracy assessment of a classified raster. It detects classes and pixel counts from the input classified raster layer (via QGIS layer source), computes recommended sample size using confidence level, expected accuracy, and margin of error parameters, allocates samples per class using proportional or equal allocation strategies, optionally restricts sampling to user-drawn Areas of Interest (AOIs: rectangles, circles, polygons) on the map canvas, applies minimum distance constraints, and exports the resulting points as a GeoPackage or Shapefile vector layer. The output includes a temporary in-memory point layer in QGIS with attributes (point_id, map_class, map_label, ground_truth, notes), visualized via rubber bands for AOIs, and warnings/messages for allocation issues. No satellite imagery processing occurs — the script operates entirely on an existing local or QGIS-loaded classified raster; data sources, study area, time range, and satellite/sensor/bands are not specified in the code.

name: Geolocate digital images
desc: The script extracts GPS coordinates from EXIF metadata of JPEG/JPG images in a user-specified local folder and creates a QGIS memory vector layer (Point, EPSG:4326) with one feature per geotagged image, storing the filename as an attribute. It also adds an OpenStreetMap XYZ basemap for visual context. The output is a point layer named 'Imágenes geolocalizadas' loaded into the QGIS project, with no remote Earth Engine (GEE) computation involved — this is a pure desktop QGIS plugin using exifread for local EXIF parsing.

name: Generate atmospheric temperature contours
desc: The script generates contour vector layers from GPV (Grid Point Value) raster data of the Japan Meteorological Agency's Mesoscale Model (MSM). It parses layer names to extract forecast time, pressure level (e.g., 'Lsurf' for surface or 'L-pall' for pressure levels), and meteorological element (e.g., '1000hPa気圧面気温' — 1000 hPa temperature). For each selected element, it identifies relevant raster bands using hardcoded band offsets and step intervals (e.g., every 92 bands for pressure-level data), then runs GDAL contouring with element-specific intervals (e.g., 3 hPa for temperature). Outputs are temporally enabled vector contour layers named with forecast validity time, labeled conditionally (e.g., only every 6°C for temperature), styled in gray, and added to QGIS. The script exclusively supports MSM model output rasters named in a strict underscore-delimited convention (e.g., containing '_MSM_', '_Lsurf_', '_L-pall_', and forecast hour 'FH' at position [9]), and does not perform any remote sensing processing, classification, or Earth Engine computation — it is a QGIS plugin frontend for local raster contouring.

name: Construct points in local orthogonal coordinate system
desc: The script implements an interactive QGIS plugin that allows users to define a local orthogonal coordinate system on a map canvas by selecting two points: an origin and a second point defining the Y-axis direction. It then computes and visualizes new points based on user-entered X (orthogonal) and Y (axis-aligned) offsets relative to that local system. Computed points are stored, displayed in a dockable dialog with coordinates, and optionally exported as a memory vector layer containing attributes: ID, X-offset, Y-offset, and resulting map coordinates (Easting/Northing). No remote sensing data, time-series, or external geospatial analysis is performed — all operations are geometric transformations (rotation, translation) applied client-side using QgsPointXY and Euclidean vector math within the current QGIS project CRS. The study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified because the plugin operates purely on interactive user clicks and does not load or process any raster or time-dependent datasets.

name: Calculate COVID infection percentage
desc: The script computes the percentage of COVID-infected population per administrative polygon in the 'Tamaulipas' vector layer. It first calculates the total sum of the 'covid' field across all features, then adds a new field 'por_cov' containing (covid * 100) / total. Finally, it applies a quantile-based graduated thematic map using the 'YlOrRd' color ramp and saves both the updated shapefile ('Tamaulipas_v2.shp') and its styled QML file for visualization.

name: Calculate COVID-19 percentage index
desc: The script computes a normalized percentage index ('por_cov') for a field named 'covid' in each vector layer loaded in the QGIS project. It first calculates the total sum of the 'covid' field across all features, then adds a new floating-point field 'por_cov' containing (covid * 100) / total_sum. It saves the result as a new shapefile (e.g., 'layername_v2.shp'), applies a quantile-based graduated symbology using the 'YlOrRd' color ramp to the 'por_cov' field with 5 classes, and exports the style as a .qml file. The script operates on all currently loaded vector layers in the QGIS project without filtering by geometry, time, or attribute — no satellite data, raster operations, or external geospatial analysis is performed. Input data source, study area, time range, and coordinate reference system are not specified in the code.

name: Reclassify urban typology classes
desc: The script reclassifies categorical attribute values in a QGIS vector layer (e.g., land use or building class codes) into standardized urban typology names and IDs using a preloaded database dictionary ('db_dict'). It reads a user-selected polygon vector layer, identifies unique values in a chosen attribute field, maps each old class to a new typology name (from 'db_dict["Types"]["nameOrigin"]') and its corresponding integer ID (via pandas DataFrame index lookup), then adds two new fields — 'TypolName' (string) and 'TypolID' (integer) — to the layer. The reclassified layer is saved as a shapefile and added to the QGIS project. No remote sensing imagery, cloud masking, spectral indices, or time-series analysis is performed; all operations are vector-based attribute reclassification using local QGIS API and pandas data structures. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band usage are not involved or specified.

name: Load Mapillary coverage tiles
desc: The script loads vector tile (MVT) layers from Mapillary's public VTP (Vector Tile Protocol) services to display street-level imagery coverage (image and sequence layers) in QGIS. It downloads cached MVT tiles at Web Mercator zoom levels (0–14) for the current map canvas extent, applies optional year-based filtering on 'captured_at' timestamps (2012–current year), and styles layers using local QML files. Outputs are two in-memory QgsVectorLayer instances named 'Mapillary image' and 'Mapillary sequence', added to the QGIS project; no raster, satellite, or Earth observation data is used.

name: Extract land surface temperature
desc: The script prepares input data for an LUHI (Local Urban Heat Island) analysis by ingesting and organizing geospatial rasters including Landsat 9 LST (Land Surface Temperature), DEM, land cover (DWV1), soil texture, canopy height, hydrologic soil group, and LCZ (Local Climate Zone) layers. It extracts EPSG from the Landsat filename to auto-generate standardized output filenames (e.g., 'LST_32632.tif'), reorganizes input files into 'Data' and 'Results' subfolders, sets the calculation extent by reprojecting the Landsat raster’s bounding box to EPSG:4326, and collects user-defined field names for attribute mapping. The final output is a parameter dictionary passed to ExtractionDuFichierCsvPourOutilIa — an algorithm that converts these rasters into a CSV table for downstream IA (AI/ML) tool use. No time-series or temporal aggregation is performed; the Landsat 9 image is treated as a single static snapshot. Study area is inferred from folder naming ('city' extracted from parent directory name, e.g., 'Paris_2023_32632'), but no explicit city or region is hardcoded. Data sources are all local file paths (not GEE asset IDs), so satellite metadata is derived only from filename conventions (e.g., 'LST_32632.tif') and UI labels ('Image LandSat 9').

name: Extract vector layer vertices
desc: The script extracts vertex points from an input vector layer (test.geojson) using QGIS's native processing algorithm 'native:extractvertices', producing a new GeoJSON file (vertices.geojson) containing point geometries at each vertex of the original features. It then loads and visualizes the resulting point layer using geopandas (static plot and interactive folium-based explore map). No remote sensing, time-series, or classification is performed; the workflow is purely vector geometry processing within a local QGIS/conda environment. Input data path './data/test.geojson' and output './data/vertices.geojson' are local filesystem paths; no study area, time range, satellite, or sensor information is present or implied.

name: Classify land cover in Uzbekistan
desc: The script classifies land cover across Uzbekistan using machine learning models trained on satellite-derived features. It loads training data (CSV) exported from Google Earth Engine, trains Random Forest and Gradient Boosting classifiers, saves the best-performing model, applies it to a local raster composite (e.g., *composite*.tif), performs tile-wise classification to manage memory, applies QGIS-based majority filtering for noise reduction, and generates per-class area statistics (in km² and %) based on pixel counts and approximate geospatial area conversion. The study area is explicitly Uzbekistan; the input raster composite is assumed to be a multi-band surface reflectance or index stack (band names inferred as 'B1'–'Bn' from code logic); training labels use 'layer_id' corresponding to LAND_COVER_CLASSES defined externally; outputs include a classified GeoTIFF, post-processed GeoTIFF, confusion matrix plots, model .joblib files with metadata, and CSV classification statistics. No GEE execution occurs in this script — it is strictly a local QGIS/scikit-learn post-processing and classification pipeline that depends on prior GEE-generated training data and imagery.

name: Extract OpenStreetMap tile patches
desc: The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) raster tiles as 256×256 PNG images over user-defined geographic areas, subdivided into non-overlapping or overlapped patches aligned to Sentinel-2 tile boundaries. It uses QGIS layout-based export (not GEE) to render OSM XYZ tiles (https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png) at zoom level 17 (internally adjusted via tile_size scaling factor of /8 * 1.5). The workflow includes: (1) computing initial extent from input lat/lon and zoom using Web Mercator (EPSG:3857); (2) transforming extents between CRSs (e.g., EPSG:3857 ↔ EPSG:32630); (3) tiling a Sentinel-2 UTM tile (e.g., 'T30TVK') into patches based on an example patch extent; (4) exporting OSM imagery for each patch using QgsLayoutExporter with cropToContents=True and fixed QSize(256,256). Outputs include georeferenced PNG files (e.g., 'patch_T30TVK_000_000_OSM.png') and numpy .npz files storing bounding box coordinates (min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y) per patch. No Sentinel-2 spectral data is actually loaded or processed in the provided code — only OSM imagery is exported; the B4+B3+B2+B8 mention in the description is aspirational/unimplemented. Study area is constrained to cities listed in available_cities_IDs (e.g., 'Madrid', 'Paris'), with concrete coordinates for 'Mostoles' (ul_coords = (40.3379,-3.8894), br_coords = (40.3055,-3.8351)) and tile geometry derived from provide_inner_tile_coords().

name: Extract OpenStreetMap patches for urban areas
desc: The script extracts georeferenced 256×256 PNG patches of OpenStreetMap (OSM) basemap imagery and co-located Sentinel-2 spectral band composites (B4, B3, B2, B8) over user-defined geographic regions. It operates by subdividing a Sentinel-2 tile’s spatial extent into regular or overlapped grid patches (based on a user-provided example patch extent in EPSG:3857), then exporting OSM tiles via QGIS layout export at zoom level ~14–17 (adjusted via tile_size scaling factor /8 * 1.5). For each patch, it exports an OSM RGB image and — via `layoutbased_extract_raster_portion` — extracts corresponding Sentinel-2 JP2 band files (B4/B3/B2/B8) using QGIS layout-based raster clipping. The workflow is explicitly tied to predefined cities (‘Paris’, ‘Madrid’, ‘Toulouse’, ‘Poitiers’) and uses Sentinel-2 tile IDs (e.g., ‘T30TVK’) and file paths pointing to local JP2 assets. Outputs include: (1) PNG files named as ‘patch_{tile_id}_{x:03}_{y:03}_OSM.png’, (2) NumPy `.npz` files storing the bounding box extents of all generated patches (e.g., ‘np_extent_T30TVK_EPSG_3857.npz’), and (3) implicitly, co-registered Sentinel-2 band patches (though the band extraction function lacks explicit band selection logic and assumes full JP2 file input). The study area is limited to urban subregions within these four European cities; no temporal filtering or time-series analysis is performed — only static snapshot extraction. Data sources are local Sentinel-2 JP2 files and remote OSM XYZ tiles.

name: Extract OpenStreetMap and Sentinel-2 tile patches
desc: The script extracts georeferenced 256×256 PNG image patches from OpenStreetMap (OSM) and Sentinel-2 spectral bands (B4, B3, B2, B8) over user-defined geographic regions. It operates by subdividing a user-specified area (defined by two corner coordinates) into tiles aligned with the OSM tiling scheme at a given zoom level (e.g., zoom=14 or 17), then exports co-located OSM visual tiles and corresponding Sentinel-2 band patches. The workflow uses QGIS layout-based export to render raster layers (OSM XYZ tiles and local Sentinel-2 JP2 files) within precisely bounded QgsRectangle extents. Outputs include: (1) OSM PNG patches named as 'patch_{tile_id}_{x:03}_{y:03}_OSM.png'; (2) corresponding Sentinel-2 band patches (not fully implemented in exported function calls but explicitly referenced in description and filename patterns); (3) NumPy .npz files storing extent coordinates ('np_extent_{tile_id}_...') for reproducibility; and (4) intermediate CRS-transformed rectangles. The study area is implicitly defined by coordinate inputs (e.g., Mostoles: ul_coords=(40.3379,-3.8894), br_coords=(40.3055,-3.8351)) and Sentinel-2 tile IDs (e.g., 'T30TVK'), with data sourced from local filesystem paths (e.g., 'C:/DATASETs/UC2Training/Sentinel2/{tile_id}/'). No cloud masking, time-series analysis, classification, or spectral index computation is performed — only geometric tiling, CRS transformation, and layout-driven raster cropping.

name: Import CSV TXT as point layer
desc: The script provides a QGIS dialog to load delimited text files (CSV/TXT) by specifying delimiter, longitude/latitude column names, and CRS; it previews the first 10 rows of selected coordinate columns and imports the file as a QGIS vector layer (delimitedtext provider), then immediately exports it as a Shapefile (.shp) with the same base name. No GEE (Google Earth Engine) code is present — this is purely a QGIS Python plugin UI/dialog for local file ingestion and projection-aware vector layer creation. All operations occur client-side using pandas and QgsVectorLayer URI construction; no remote sensing data, cloud processing, image analysis, or Earth Engine API calls are involved.

name: Compute rover-based viewshed visibility
desc: The script computes terrain-based visibility (viewshed) from Mars rover camera viewpoints using orbital digital elevation models (DEMs). It parses PDS3/PDS4 labels to extract camera geometry (azimuth, elevation, FOV), retrieves rover position and orientation from interpolated CSV trajectory files, creates viewpoint vector layers with observation parameters (offset height, azimuth bounds, vertical angle bounds), runs the QGIS Viewshed Analysis plugin to generate binary raster viewsheds (0=not visible, 1=visible), applies a semi-transparent red color ramp for visualization, and saves all intermediate layers (CSV points, viewpoints, viewshed rasters) and updates the QGIS project. Outputs are per-image viewshed rasters aligned with Mars surface topography.

name: Generate site boundary and key areas map
desc: The script generates a live interactive web map (Leaflet) from an ODM (OpenDroneMap) orthophoto, using its spatial extent to automatically derive a site boundary polygon and partition the area into four labeled key zones (Northwest Construction, Northeast Storage, Southwest Access, Southeast Staging). It processes local raster files (odm_orthophoto.tif and dsm.tif) stored in the project's '01_Raw_Data' directory, extracts their georeferenced extent via GDAL, creates a GeoPackage ('NH1_layers.gpkg') containing two vector layers (site_boundary and key_areas), exports both layers to GeoJSON, and bundles them with a self-contained HTML/JavaScript Leaflet map that loads satellite and OSM basemaps, displays styled polygons with popups, and includes a legend and scale bar. The study area is implicitly named 'NH1', and all outputs are written to structured subdirectories under the input project_dir. No remote Earth observation satellite data or time-series analysis is used — inputs are static drone-derived rasters.

name: Map fire scar extent
desc: The script maps fire scar extent by applying a pre-trained U-Net deep learning model to paired pre-fire and post-fire multispectral raster inputs. It loads QGIS raster layers (assumed to be pre-processed satellite imagery), extracts pixel values across 8 bands—including Blue (B1), NIR (B4), SWIR2 (B6), NDVI (B7), and NBR (B8)—performs inference, thresholds the output logits at ≥0 to generate binary burn scar masks, writes georeferenced GeoTIFFs with matching CRS/extent/geotransform from the pre-fire layer, applies nodata masking from input, and adds styled pseudocolor raster layers to QGIS. The study area is explicitly constrained to Biobío and Valparaíso regions in Chile (stated in warning message). Model variants ('AS' and '128') correspond to different input patch sizes and architectures; outputs are named as 'FireScar_{fire_id}_{datatype}.tif' and stored under 'results/{datatype}/'. No raw Earth Engine (GEE) server-side code is present—the script runs locally in QGIS using PyTorch and GDAL, consuming user-provided local or QGIS-loaded rasters.

name: Generate vertical section scale
desc: The script generates a memory-based point vector layer representing a vertical cross-section line at a user-specified X coordinate, with points spaced at regular Y-intervals between user-defined Y min and Y max values. Each point is labeled with its Y-coordinate as 'Depth'. The output includes styled point features (red cross markers) with black Arial labels, added to the QGIS project. No remote sensing data, imagery, or Earth Engine server-side computation is used — all operations are local QGIS PyQt UI and in-memory vector layer creation. Study area, time range, satellite data, and external geospatial inputs are not involved.

name: Apply vertical exaggeration to vector and raster layers
desc: The script applies a user-specified vertical exaggeration factor to the y-coordinate (northing/elevation axis) of vector geometries (points, lines, polygons) and adjusts the geotransform of raster layers to stretch the vertical (Y) dimension proportionally — preserving X-dimension and pixel values. It processes all layers within a selected QGIS layer group, creates a new output group with transformed layers, clones symbology and labeling for vectors, and reloads rasters with updated georeferencing. No terrain analysis, interpolation, or DEM derivation is performed; it is purely a geometric/georeferencing transformation. Study area, time range, satellite data, and classification methods are not involved — the script operates on already-loaded local QGIS layers without referencing any Earth Engine (GEE) assets, imagery, or temporal filtering.

name: Threshold NDVI GNDVI SAVI classification
desc: The script performs threshold-based binary classification of vegetation indices (NDVI, GNDVI, SAVI) on input GeoTIFF rasters to generate polarized (vegetated/non-vegetated) rasters, then clips them to vector boundaries and converts the resulting rasters into polygonized shapefiles (e.g., 'polygonized-NDVI.shp'). It uses fixed thresholds (0.60) applied to index calculations derived from specific spectral bands (e.g., NDVI uses band 5 and band 7), implying Sentinel-2 or Landsat-like multispectral data. The workflow is driven by a JSON configuration file listing raster paths and corresponding vector boundary files. No cloud masking, temporal compositing, or radiometric calibration is performed; inputs are assumed preprocessed. Study area, time range, satellite metadata, and sensor calibration are not specified in the code — only band numbers (1, 4, 5, 7) and output naming conventions are used. Final outputs are clipped, thresholded, and vectorized shapefiles per index type.

name: Visualize hurricane wind field and track
desc: The script generates a static PNG/JPEG layout map from a QGIS project that overlays a hurricane wind field raster (PNG) and a hurricane track vector layer (CSV) onto a base map. The hurricane wind field is styled using a categorized QML style ('hurricane_cat_raster.qml'), and the track is styled with a line-based QML ('hurricane_track.qml'). The layout extent is automatically set to the bounding box of the non-base-map layer (i.e., raster or track), reprojected from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857). Legend items are customized: the raster layer is renamed to "[HurricaneName] [Year] Wind Field" and its legend node order is fixed to indices [2–7]; the track layer is renamed to "[HurricaneName] [Year] Track" (if forecasts excluded) and its legend node order set to [0]; the base map layer is removed from the legend. The final output is a cropped, timestamped JPEG file (e.g., 'larry2021_100x100_2023-10-05T142000Z.jpeg') saved in the data directory. Input data paths are derived from a hurricane file base string (e.g., 'LARRY_2021_100x100'), implying hurricane name, year, and spatial resolution — but no geospatial processing (e.g., reprojection, resampling, classification) is performed in this script; it is purely cartographic export using precomputed raster and vector assets. Study area and time range are not specified in the code — only hurricane metadata (name/year/resolution) is parsed from the input string.

name: Generate elevation contour lines
desc: The script generates vector contour line features from a raster digital elevation model (DEM), using GDAL's contour algorithm. It takes an input DEM raster layer and a user-specified contour interval, then produces a vector line layer where each line is attributed with an 'ELEV' field representing its elevation value. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification methods are involved — it is a pure raster-to-vector geoprocessing operation on arbitrary DEM input. All parameters (e.g., 'input_dem', 'contour_interval') are user-provided at runtime; no hardcoded paths, dates, regions, or sensors appear in the code.

name: Flatten DEM surface to plane
desc: The script flattens a user-provided DEM raster by replacing elevation values within each input polygon with elevations interpolated from a least-squares-fitted plane through the DEM-sampled vertices of that polygon. It reads the input DEM via GDAL, samples z-values at polygon vertices using geographic-to-pixel coordinate conversion, fits a planar surface (z = ax + by + c) to those (x,y,z) points, then overwrites all DEM pixels whose centers lie inside the polygon with values from that plane. The output is a modified GeoTIFF written to output_path. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial APIs are involved — inputs are local file paths and a QGIS vector layer; processing is purely geometric and algebraic.

name: Smooth DEM surface harmonically
desc: The script smooths a user-provided input DEM raster (e.g., '/path/to/input_DEM.tif') within polygon boundaries defined in QGIS by solving Laplace's equation via harmonic interpolation — either using a direct sparse linear system solver (scipy) or iterative Gauss-Seidel relaxation. It preserves original elevation values on the polygon boundary (Dirichlet boundary conditions) to ensure seamless, continuous transitions with surrounding terrain, eliminating artificial seams or elevation jumps. The output is a modified DEM raster written to 'output_path' (e.g., '/path/to/output_DEM.tif'), where only pixels strictly interior to each polygon feature are updated; all other pixels retain their original values. No remote sensing data ingestion, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived processing occurs — inputs are local GeoTIFF and QGIS vector layers only.

name: Generate park overview map
desc: The script generates a static cartographic layout (QGIS Print Layout) for a park overview map, using vector layers ('sl_landmass' and 'park_boundary') loaded from a Spatialite database. It sets project CRS, styles polygon/line layers with predefined colors and outline properties, calculates page size based on the 'SL Landmass' layer extent and configured scale, creates a full-extent map item, and exports the layout to SVG or PNG. The output is a georeferenced (but non-geospatially interactive) raster or vector graphic of the park boundary overlaid on landmass, saved to a user-specified file path. No time-series, remote sensing analysis, classification, or dynamic geoprocessing is performed — it is a GIS cartographic publishing workflow. Study area is implied by database table contents but not specified in code; data sources are local Spatialite tables; no satellite, sensor, or band usage occurs.

name: Fuse ASC DEM tiles
desc: The script copies selected ASCII (.asc) digital elevation model (DEM) files listed in a CSV file from a source directory to a destination directory, then merges them into a single GeoTIFF using GDAL's VRT and Warp functionality. The output is a fused, LZW-compressed GeoTIFF raster named 'grenoble_fusionne.tif'. The script explicitly references 'grenoble' in the output filename, indicating the study area is Grenoble, France. No satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or classification methods are involved — it is a purely local file-based raster fusion workflow operating on pre-existing ASC DEM tiles. Inputs are user-specified: a CSV listing tile names (e.g., 'NOM_DALLE'), source folder of ASC files, and destination paths; outputs are the fused GeoTIFF and optional QGIS layer loading.

name: Regress raster against RGB imagery
desc: The script performs Colour Pattern Regression (CPR), a calibration and validation workflow that regresses a target raster (e.g., hydrological or biophysical variable) against an RGB satellite image using linear spectral unmixing with red, green, and blue coefficients. It uses two spatially constrained areas — a calibration area (for coefficient optimization via grid search) and an interest area (for extrapolation and statistical assessment). The workflow includes GDAL-based raster cropping, resampling, and band-wise linear combination (R×cr + G×cg + B×cb), followed by pixel-wise computation of three performance metrics: NNSE (Normalized Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency), KGE (Kling–Gupta Efficiency), and PBIAS (Percent Bias). Outputs include: (1) optimized RGB coefficients; (2) three metric rasters (nnse.tif, kge.tif, pbias.tif) visualized with custom discrete color ramps in QGIS; (3) a summary table showing the percentage of pixels falling into four qualitative performance classes ('Very good' to 'Unsatisfactory') for each metric; and (4) a normalized RGB-derived output raster (rbg_interest_area.tif). All inputs are local file paths (no GEE server-side assets), and no satellite metadata, temporal filtering, or cloud masking is performed — data provenance and acquisition date are not specified in the code.

name: Classify forest degradation zones
desc: The script classifies forest degradation zones using the Forest Cover Degradation (FCD) framework integrated with machine learning land cover classification. It processes satellite imagery (Landsat, Sentinel, or Planet, per config['I_satellite']) over a user-defined AOI to generate: (1) cloudless mosaicked images; (2) spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI, MSAVI2, MTVI2, VARI); (3) FCD1_1 and FCD2_1 degradation layers derived from PCA-enhanced spectral-temporal analysis; (4) Hansen Global Forest Change tree loss year and 2000 forest extent; (5) FCD-based zone classification (e.g., HighForestDense) and ML-based land cover classification (RF/SVM/GBM/CART) using OBIA-segmented features; (6) final integrated 'Final_zone_ML' layer combining ML land cover with Hansen loss and FCD zoning logic; (7) slope classes (from SRTM GL1) and FAO HWSD2 soil type overlays; and (8) exported GeoJSON training/validation points and KML zone polygons. The study area, time range, and satellite source are fully driven by external JSON configuration ('balaban_conf.json'), with no hardcoded AOI or dates in the script.

name: Download VIIRS nighttime light annual composites
desc: The script downloads VIIRS Nighttime Lights annual composites (avg_rad band) from the Earth Engine dataset 'NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMSLCFG' for user-selected years (2014–2025), clips them to the bounding box of an input polygon layer (reprojected to EPSG:4326), computes the annual mean image, exports it as a GeoTIFF via Earth Engine's getDownloadURL, extracts and renames the TIFF to 'VIIRS_YYYY.tif', repackages it into a ZIP archive with the same name, and loads the resulting GeoTIFF as a raster layer in QGIS. The study area is defined dynamically by the input vector polygon’s extent; no fixed geographic region is hardcoded. The time range per year is full calendar year (e.g., 'YYYY-01-01' to 'YYYY-12-31'). Outputs are individual zipped GeoTIFFs (VIIRS_YYYY.zip containing VIIRS_YYYY.tif) saved to a user-specified folder.

name: Map conflict-related strike events
desc: The script generates a QGIS-based static map visualizing geolocated military strike events in Iran and Israel during a specified 2026 time window. It loads administrative boundaries (ADM0–ADM2) from GeoBoundaries for IRN and ISR, reads ISW (Institute for the Study of War) storymap event data from a CSV containing longitude/latitude and event_family fields, filters events to those classified as 'iran_axis_retaliatory_strike' or 'us_israel_combined_force_strike' within the date range and spatial extent, and renders them as distinct point symbols ('Iran-axis strikes' in red tones, 'US/Israeli strikes' in orange tones). Basemap is Esri World Terrain Base (XYZ tile service). The output includes a QGIS project (.qgz), a GeoPackage (.gpkg) storing all vector layers, and a high-resolution PNG export (600 DPI) of the final layout featuring grid lines, scale bar, north arrow, legend, city labels, and styled administrative boundaries. Study area is defined by unioned ADM0 geometries of Iran and Israel with 0.25° padding. No satellite imagery, spectral analysis, or classification algorithms are used — this is a cartographic visualization workflow using vector point and boundary data.

name: Screen conflict events for NTL relevance and building proximity
desc: The script screens geolocated conflict events (from ISW storymap) for spatial containment within Iran and Israel administrative boundaries (ADM0–ADM2) using OSM-derived GeoBoundaries datasets, reuses prior LLM-based NTL applicability labels and 5km building intersection results, and performs buffer-based clustering (5km/10km) of downstream-qualified events. The study area is limited to Iran (IRN) and Israel (ISR), time range is 2026-02-27 to 2026-04-21, inputs include CSV event tables and GeoJSON administrative geometries, geospatial operations are QGIS-native spatial joins and centroid-based Euclidean buffering in Web Mercator, and outputs include screened event CSVs, cluster summary tables, membership mappings, and a JSON summary with counts and top cluster statistics. No satellite, sensor, or spectral band processing occurs — this is a vector-based GIS screening pipeline.

name: Estimate clear-cut timing and area per sub-parcel
desc: The script processes forest management geospatial data (NVG parcels, silviculture, and harvesting records) to estimate clear-cut timing at the sub-parcel (sub-talhão) level by integrating ground-based harvest dates with satellite-derived NDVI time series. It generates: (1) chronologically sorted activity tables per parcel; (2) merged parcel-level attributes including first/last harvest dates, number of cuts, area, and S2 image count; (3) sub-parcel-level tables with estimated clear-cut dates (from NDVI drop analysis), date-of-biggest-drop, S2 coverage metrics (empty/non-empty cells), and sub-parcel area; (4) visualized QGIS layers with temporal color-coding (e.g., 'estimated_date' or 'drop_date'); (5) statistical summaries on cut timing distribution, cloud impact on NDVI detection, month-grouped S2 data quality, and alignment between field-reported and satellite-inferred cuts; and (6) CCD-ready shapefiles for Change Detection analysis with start/end windows and filtered break dates.

name: Export hydroobject selection view
desc: The script exports the SQLite database view 'hydroobj_sel_export_damo' — containing hydrographic features with hydraulic and morphological attributes (e.g., streefpeil, waterbreedte_BGT, WS_BODEMHOOGTE, geselecteerde_hydraulische_diepte) — into a GeoPackage file. It loads the view as a QGIS spatialite vector layer via a dynamic SQL SELECT URI, validates the layer, maps and enforces specific field types (e.g., double-precision numeric fields with defined precisions, integer and string fields), copies features into a memory layer with that exact schema, and writes the result to a user-selected .gpkg file. The CRS is preserved from the source layer (inferred as EPSG:28992 based on the commented-out crs=EPSG:28992 hint), and the output includes geometry and 20+ explicitly declared attributes. No remote sensing, time-series, or classification logic is present — this is a database-to-GeoPackage schema-aware export workflow for Dutch hydrological infrastructure data.

name: Convert multipoint to convex hull
desc: The script converts a vector layer containing multipoint geometries into convex hull polygons (minimum bounding geometry of type 'convex hull') by first decomposing multipoint features into single-point features, then computing the minimum bounding geometry for each group of points. It outputs a polygon vector layer where each polygon represents the convex hull enclosing all points belonging to the original multipoint feature.

name: Assign cadastral parcels to legal acts
desc: The script implements a GIS-based cadastral parcel assignment workflow within a QGIS desktop application. It enables users to select parcels from a spatial layer (loaded from SHP files in ZIP archives), preview them in a map canvas (EPSG:31259, BMN M34), and assign them to legal acts ('Akt') via a dialog that captures shared attributes (e.g., AWB status, legal basis, annotations). The core data model includes BGst (parcels), BGstEz (survey editions), BGstVersion (geometry + metadata per edition), BGstEigentuemer (owners), BGstNutzung (land uses), and BGstZuordnung (assignment links). Data ingestion involves parsing CSV files (Grundstuecke_V2.csv, Eigentuemer.csv) and SHP geometries from ZIP archives, transforming coordinates to EPSG:31259, and upserting records into a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database with conflict resolution based on KG_EZ and KG_GST identifiers and 'datenstand' timestamps. Outputs include updated database tables, synchronized QGIS vector layers, and UI feedback (import time label, selection highlighting, footer counters). Study area is implicitly Austria (BMN M34 CRS, 'KG' = Katastralgemeinde, 'EZ' = Einmessungszahl, 'BEV' = Bundesamt für Eich- und Vermessungswesen). Time range is not specified in the code logic; import timestamps are parsed from CSV headers but no global temporal filtering or analysis is performed.

name: Process Ukrainian cadastral XML files
desc: The script processes Ukrainian cadastral exchange XML files (UkrainianCadastralExchangeFile schema) to extract, validate, visualize, and generate geospatial documentation including cadastral plans and boundary agreements. It parses XML structure (e.g., PointInfo, ParcelMetricInfo, AdjacentUnits), reconstructs parcel geometries from polyline definitions (ULID-referenced lines), synchronizes QGIS vector layers (e.g., 'Ділянка', 'Вузли', 'Суміжники') with XML content, applies layer-specific QML styles, creates memory layers for derived features (e.g., 'Вузли ділянки', 'Вузли суміжників'), computes map scale for layout generation using parcel extent and PARCEL_MARGIN_FACTOR, and produces printable cartographic layouts (via PlanLayoutCreator) and legal documents (e.g., BoundaryAgreementCreator, DocumentGenerator). All operations are localized for Ukraine, rely on SK-63 CRS templates, and target cadastral parcel management workflows — not remote sensing or time-series analysis.

name: Create GeoPackage layer with field aliases
desc: The script creates an in-memory QGIS vector layer with predefined fields (name, age, is_active) and human-readable aliases, saves it to a GeoPackage file (forms.gpkg), reloads it into the project, and persists both the layer and its field aliases as the default style within the GeoPackage. It explicitly targets QGIS project integration and metadata usability—not geospatial analysis, modeling, or remote sensing. The study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification methods, and analytical outputs are not present or implied; this is purely a GIS data structuring and styling automation workflow.

name: Convert file geodatabase layers to GeoPackage
desc: The script converts vector layers from an ESRI File Geodatabase (Tax Parcel Data Management.gdb) to a GeoPackage (Tax Parcel Data Management2.gpkg), iterating over all feature classes in the GDB, loading each as a QgsVectorLayer using OGR URI syntax, and writing it to the target GeoPackage using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3 with layer creation/overwrite capability. The output is a GeoPackage containing all original GDB feature classes as separate layers.

name: Convert FileGeodatabase to GeoPackage
desc: The script converts one or more vector layers from an Esri FileGeodatabase (FGDB) into a single GeoPackage (.gpkg) file. It first creates an empty GeoPackage with a predefined point layer schema (id: Integer, name: String), then iterates over all layers in the input FGDB (named 'Cemetery Data Management.gdb'), validates each layer, inspects geometry type and field definitions, and writes each layer individually into the same GeoPackage using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3 with CreateOrOverwriteLayer behavior. The output is a multi-layer GeoPackage containing all feature classes from the source FGDB, preserving original names, geometries, and attributes. No reprojection, filtering, transformation, or analysis is performed — only format conversion and packaging. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis are not involved.

name: Manage biotope editing transactions
desc: The script implements a transactional workflow for managing biotope features in a QGIS plugin, enabling users to lock selected biotope features from a PostGIS layer, copy them into an editable memory layer, modify them, and then merge changes back to the original PostGIS layer with conflict-aware updates (attribute and geometry comparison), inserts, and unlocks. It also supports canceling edits and deleting biotopes with history logging. Key methods include transfer_from_biotop_to_edit, transfer_from_edit_to_biotop, cancel_edit, delete_selected_biotope, and merge_source_to_target_layer, all relying on database transactions, locking mechanisms, and precise geometry/attribute comparison logic.

name: Calculate point buffer area
desc: The script calculates the total geometric area (in square meters) of fixed-distance buffers applied to a single synthetic point feature located at coordinates (42, 42) in EPSG:27700 (British National Grid). It creates a memory vector layer with one point, applies QGIS's 'qgis:fixeddistancebuffer' algorithm using a user-specified buffer distance and 100 segmentation segments, then iterates over the resulting polygon features to sum their planar areas. No real-world geospatial dataset is used — the input point is hardcoded and artificial. The output is a scalar numeric value ('total_area') representing the summed buffer area, exported via HDF5 and assigned to a global variable for QGIS Processing integration. All operations occur client-side within QGIS using PyQGIS and Processing Toolbox algorithms; no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, imagery, or cloud computing are involved — despite the prompt's mischaracterization as a 'GEE script'. The mention of 'GEE' in the user instruction is erroneous: this is purely a QGIS Processing Python script with zero Google Earth Engine code.

name: Execute SQL layer query
desc: The script executes a user-defined SQL query against a PostgreSQL or SpatiaLite vector database layer in QGIS, creates a new temporary vector layer from the query result, optionally applies a QML style (either from a local file or from a 'layer_styles' table in the database), highlights the original geometry on the map canvas during execution, and adds the resulting layer to the QGIS map registry. It performs error handling, feature existence checks, CRS transformation for highlighting, and status messaging via the QGIS message bar. The script is designed as a QGIS action plugin and does not perform any remote sensing, raster analysis, or Earth Engine operations — it is purely a desktop GIS database layer querying utility.

name: Query Landsat imagery by municipality
desc: The script queries a PostgreSQL/SpatiaLite database to retrieve Landsat catalog records (image ID, path/row, acquisition date, orbit, point, geometry) that spatially intersect a specified Brazilian municipality (geocoded as '1304104', corresponding to Manaus, Amazonas). It uses an SQL JOIN with the 'municipio_ibge' administrative boundary layer and applies MbrIntersects and ST_Intersects for spatial filtering. The output is a QGIS vector layer named 'landsat_muni_1304104' containing matching Landsat scenes, styled using either a local QML file or a database-stored QML style, and added to the QGIS map canvas with a temporary red highlight polygon around the input municipality geometry. No Earth Engine (GEE) processing occurs — this is purely a QGIS Python plugin-style database query and layer loading workflow.

name: Geocode Estonian addresses
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for geocoding and reverse geocoding using the Estonian national InADS (Inaadress) gazetteer service. It sends HTTP requests to http://inaadress.maaamet.ee/inaadress/gazetteer with address queries (e.g., street names, ADS OID, ADR ID) or coordinate pairs (x/y in EPSG:3301), parses JSON responses containing address features, and adds resulting points as a memory vector layer in QGIS with attributes like 'aadresstekst', 'viitepunkt_x', 'viitepunkt_y', 'boundingbox', etc. The layer is labeled with 'aadresstekst' and uses CRS EPSG:3301 (Estonia TM). The plugin supports forward geocoding (text → point) and reverse geocoding (map click → address), with configurable query types (EHAK, TANAV, EHITISHOONE, etc.) and result limits. Study area is explicitly Estonia; no time-series or temporal filtering is performed — all operations are static, real-time API calls to a national address database.

name: Simplify vector geometry
desc: The script simplifies the geometries of input vector features using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm with a user-defined tolerance. It iterates over each feature, computes vertex count before and after simplification, replaces original geometries with simplified ones, and writes results to a new in-memory memory layer with CRS EPSG:2180. The output includes the simplified vector layer and a log message reporting total vertex reduction.

name: Model flood hazard by terrain classification
desc: The script models flood hazard at the RW (Rukun Warga, neighborhood-level administrative unit) scale in Jakarta, Indonesia, using a digital elevation model (DEM) raster ('jkt_erase.tif') and administrative boundary data ('boundary.shp'). It first splits the RW boundary shapefile into individual RW-level shapefiles; then masks the DEM to each RW polygon using GDAL's gdalwarp with -cutline; reclassifies each masked DEM raster into 4 hazard classes (1–4, where 4 = non-hazard/NoData) based on slope-derived thresholds—using either fixed intervals (if DEM range ≤5 m) or standard deviation–adjusted intervals; polygonizes each reclassified raster; and finally merges all RW-level hazard polygons into a single 'hazard.shp', excluding class 4 (null/no-hazard areas). The final output is a vector hazard map with attribute 'KELAS' indicating hazard level per polygon. No time-series or temporal analysis is performed; inputs are static geospatial datasets. Study area is explicitly Jakarta (via 'jkt_erase.tif', 'riverdki_polygon.shp', and 'DKI' in variable name), and outputs are stored in local Windows paths under 'JakSAFE' and 'PEMODELAN RW BANJIR QGIS'.

name: Label contour lines with elevation values
desc: The script generates labeled contour points and optionally clipped contour lines from input vector contour data. It computes label rotation based on contour segment geometry, identifies index contours (e.g., every 25 m), applies hierarchical labeling logic using configurable buffer distances (start_buffer, buffer_increment) to avoid label collisions, and supports smoothing (via GRASS v.generalize) and label orientation inversion. Inputs are two vector layers: contours (with an elevation field, default 'elev') and label guide lines (e.g., linear features guiding label placement). Outputs are: (1) a point layer ('output_labels') containing labeled elevation points with 'elev', 'index', 'rot' (rotation angle), and 'label' (1/0 flag indicating whether to display the label); and (2) a line layer ('output_contours') — either the original contours or a clipped version where segments near labels are removed to improve cartographic clarity. No raster or satellite data is used; all operations are vector-based GIS processing in QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the script.

name: Apply angular constraint to line features
desc: The script applies an angular constraint to vector line features by rotating intersecting line segments to align with one of eight canonical orientations (multiples of π/4, i.e., 0°, 45°, 90°, ..., 180°) relative to a reference line — specifically the longest input line. It iteratively identifies topologically connected lines (via geometry intersection), rotates them around shared endpoints to enforce discrete angular alignment, and updates geometries in-place using spatial indexing for efficiency. The output is a modified vector layer where all lines conform to constrained angles, intended for cartographic generalization or network regularization. No raster data, time series, satellite imagery, or external geospatial datasets are used; input is purely a user-provided QGIS vector layer of arbitrary LineString geometry. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified.

name: Compute time-series raster statistics
desc: The script computes per-pixel temporal statistics (min, max, mean, standard deviation) across all bands of a multi-temporal raster layer. It reads the input raster band-by-band, processes each row (line) of pixels to compute statistics either ignoring nodata values (if Use_nodata is True and nodata value is specified) or including all values, then writes min/max to one output GeoTIFF and mean/std to another, both with two bands and LZW compression. Outputs are suffixed '_minmax' and '_float' respectively.

name: Project points onto nearest line
desc: The script computes the closest projected point from each selected input point feature onto the nearest selected line feature, calculates Euclidean distance between original and projected points, and outputs a new memory vector layer of projected points with attributes including distance, original and projected coordinates, and midpoint coordinates. It uses a spatial index for efficient nearest-line lookup, then iterates over line segments to find the true orthogonal projection (or nearest endpoint if projection falls outside segment bounds). The workflow is purely vector-based, relying on QgsSpatialIndex, QgsGeometry.asPolyline(), and custom geometric functions (magnitude, intersect_point_to_line); no raster, time-series, or satellite data is involved. Input layers are user-provided QGIS vector layers (points and lines), with selection-based processing only. Output layer name is dynamically generated as 'Projected_ Points_From_[input_point_layer_name]'.

name: Generate air tasking order
desc: The script generates an Air Tasking Order (ATO) package for airborne snow and ice surveys, including: (1) a formatted text file (.txt) listing priority flight lines with remarks, survey metadata, and operational requirements; (2) KML files (_Priority_1_Lines.kml, etc.) visualizing flight lines with extruded 3D geometry, start/end markers, and rich attribute schemas (e.g., LENGTH, RIVER_BASI, RFC, LAT_MIDPNT, LON_MIDPNT, Remarks); (3) CSV exports of flight line attributes; (4) ESRI Shapefile exports of prioritized subsets; and (5) a georeferenced PNG map image generated from a QGIS print layout ('airborne_survey.qpt') showing flight lines overlaid on boundaries, airports, and master flight lines. The workflow validates input line IDs against a master flight line shapefile, computes spatial extents to auto-zoom the map, and applies QGIS layer styles (e.g., 'pri_style.qml'). All outputs are saved in a survey-named subfolder under the user-specified Save_Air_Tasking_Order_To directory. The script operates entirely within QGIS Desktop (PyQt4, QgsVectorLayer, QgsComposition), using local vector data — no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, imagery, or cloud processing occur.

name: Generate assimilation point dataset
desc: The script generates a merged point dataset for data assimilation by combining existing assimilation points (ssm1054_md_based_*.shp) with newly derived buffer-zone sampling points. It first buffers a process region (e.g., 'West') by ~1,000 meters (using 0.009 decimal degrees ≈ 1 km at mid-latitudes), computes the symmetrical difference to extract only the buffer ring (excluding interior), rasterizes that ring at 0.008333333° resolution (~927 m), converts the raster to vector points, deletes every 5th point to subsample, assigns sequential POINTID, merges with original assim points, and adds XY coordinate fields (POINT_X, POINT_Y, X, Y). The final output is a shapefile (e.g., 'ssm1054_md_based_YYYYMMDDHH_YYYYMMDDHH_US.shp') stored in 'C:/Users/shawn.carter/Documents/Assim/point_data_shape_new'. The study area is implicitly continental US (final_region='US', RAST_EXT='-130.516666667,-62.25,24.1,58.2333333333'), and time is defined by Start_Date and End_Date parameters (e.g., '2023010100'). No satellite, sensor, or band-based analysis occurs — all operations are vector/raster geoprocessing on pre-existing shapefiles; the 'ssm1054' prefix suggests Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) or similar soil moisture product, but no GEE image collection or remote sensing computation is present in the script.

name: Find shortest path in raster
desc: The script computes the shortest path between two user-specified points (start and end) on a raster layer using the A* graph search algorithm. It reads a selected raster band, applies a threshold-based cost model where pixels with values >= user-defined 'max_value' are treated as impassable (infinite cost), and all others as traversable (unit cost). The path is computed in pixel coordinates, converted back to CRS coordinates, and visualized as a colored memory vector line layer in QGIS. Outputs include: (1) a temporary line vector layer added to the QGIS project, (2) logged path length (in map units), step count, and computation duration, and (3) GUI label update showing path length. No remote sensing data is loaded or processed — input is any local raster layer accessible via QGIS (e.g., DEM, slope, cost surface), with no fixed study area, time range, or satellite source specified in the code.

name: Draw joined boundary feature
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin that enables interactive selection of a feature (e.g., an outlet/exutoire) from one vector layer and automatically selects and draws the corresponding feature(s) from a second vector layer (e.g., watershed/bassin versant) based on attribute join (e.g., matching 'ID_BNBD' in exutoire layer to 'IDENTIF' in BV layer). It dynamically populates two combo boxes with loaded vector layers, monitors selection changes on the 'exutoire' layer, extracts attributes (notably 'ID_BNBD' and 'SUPERFICIE'), uses that ID to query and select matching features in the 'bassin versant' layer via QgsFeatureRequest with filter expression, then creates and adds a new temporary memory vector layer ('Polygon?crs=epsg:2154') containing the joined geometry(ies) with 50% transparency. The study area, time range, satellite data, and remote sensing operations are not specified — this is a desktop GIS vector join/drawing tool, not a GEE cloud script. Data sources are local or QGIS-loaded vector layers only; no Earth Engine assets, imagery, or time-series analysis are involved.

name: Import LAS point cloud to PostgreSQL
desc: The script imports one or more LAS/LAZ point cloud files into a PostgreSQL database with the PointCloud extension enabled, using PDAL's writers.pgpointcloud pipeline. It validates and executes the PDAL pipeline, then creates a vector layer (QgsVectorLayer) representing the spatial extent (bounding box polygon) of each imported LAS file as a feature in a QgsFeatureSink output. The output is a single vector layer containing one polygon per input LAS file, derived from the LAS header's min/max X/Y coordinates. No raster, classification, or time-series analysis is performed; the workflow is purely data ingestion and metadata-driven spatial footprint generation.

name: Export cities layer to CSV
desc: The script exports the currently active vector layer in QGIS (assumed to represent cities) to a CSV file with WKT geometry, then reloads it as a delimited text layer using LONGITUDE and LATITUDE fields for point geometry. It immediately removes the reloaded layer from the TOC. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed; the workflow is purely format conversion and temporary layer handling within QGIS Desktop. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Compute concave hull geometry
desc: The script computes a concave hull polygon from an input point layer using an alpha-shape algorithm based on Delaunay triangulation. It first generates Delaunay triangles, calculates the maximum edge length across all triangles, removes triangles containing any edge longer than alpha × max_edge_length, dissolves the remaining triangles into a single polygonal geometry, and optionally removes interior rings (holes) or splits multipart output into singleparts. The output is a vector polygon layer representing the concave hull envelope of the input points.

name: Calculate hypsometric curves
desc: The script computes hypsometric curves for polygon features (e.g., watersheds, basins, or administrative units) overlaid on a digital elevation model (DEM). It extracts elevation values within each feature’s geometry, bins them into user-defined elevation intervals (step), and accumulates area (either absolute in m² or percentage of total feature area) cumulatively from lowest to highest elevation. The output is one CSV file per input feature containing two columns: 'Area' (cumulative area or %) and 'Elevation' (upper bound of bin), written to a user-specified output directory. The workflow includes raster clipping via vector masking, GDAL-based rasterization, NumPy masked array operations for NODATA and geometry masking, and cumulative histogram calculation. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or sensor information is embedded — the script is generic and operates on user-provided local raster (DEM) and vector (boundary) layers loaded via QGIS Processing Framework; all geospatial operations are performed using GDAL/OGR and NumPy, not GEE's cloud API.

name: Generate points along line
desc: The script converts vector line features into a set of point features, where each point corresponds to the centroid of a raster pixel intersected by the line segment. It uses GDAL and QGIS geometry operations to map line vertices to raster pixel coordinates, then applies a modified Bresenham’s line algorithm (via buildLine) to traverse all pixels crossed by each line segment, converting each traversed (row, col) pixel index back to map coordinates using the raster’s geotransform. The output is a point vector layer with attributes 'id', 'line_id', and 'point_id', preserving topological association between input lines and generated points. Input data sources are a user-provided raster layer and a vector line layer; no time-series, classification, or spectral analysis is performed — it is purely geometric sampling of raster grid cells along lines. Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Generate pixel centroid points inside polygons
desc: The script converts raster pixel centroids that fall within input polygon geometries into point vector features. It reads a raster layer to obtain geotransform parameters, computes bounding box-aligned pixel indices for each polygon, iterates over those pixels, converts each pixel center to map coordinates, and tests containment using QgsGeometryEngine. Output is a point vector layer with fields 'id', 'poly_id', and 'point_id', where each point represents the geographic center of a raster cell fully or partially inside a polygon. No classification, time-series, or spectral analysis is performed; the operation is purely geometric and raster-to-vector conversion. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate road network service area
desc: The script computes service areas from a line-based transport network (e.g., roads) and point-based start locations (e.g., facilities or origins), using graph-based shortest-path or fastest-path analysis. It builds a directed graph from the input line layer, snaps start points to the network, runs Dijkstra’s algorithm to find all vertices reachable within a user-defined travel cost (distance or time), and outputs: (1) boundary nodes (points) representing reachable vertices and interpolated edge endpoints at the travel-cost limit, optionally including upper/lower bound points; and (2) service-area lines (polylines) tracing traversed network segments up to the cost threshold. The script uses QGIS native network analysis classes (QgsVectorLayerDirector, QgsGraphBuilder, QgsGraphAnalyzer) and does not involve remote sensing, time-series, or Earth observation data — it is purely vector network analysis operating on user-provided layers with no embedded study area, time range, satellite, or sensor logic.

name: Calculate network service area
desc: The script computes the service area reachable from a user-specified start point along a vector line network (e.g., roads or trails), using either shortest distance or fastest travel time as the cost metric. It constructs a graph from the input line layer, accounts for directionality (forward/backward/both) and optional speed fields, performs Dijkstra’s algorithm to find all vertices within a given travel cost threshold, and outputs: (1) boundary nodes (points) representing reachable vertices and interpolated edge endpoints at the travel-cost limit; (2) lines representing traversed network segments fully or partially within the cost threshold; and (3) optional upper/lower bound points marking the transition between reachable and unreachable segments. No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or environmental variables are involved — this is a pure vector-based network analysis routine operating on local CRS geometry with no remote sensing data.

name: Calculate shortest path layer to point
desc: The script computes the shortest or fastest path from each start point in a vector point layer to a single user-specified end point, using a line network layer (e.g., roads or rivers) as the graph. It constructs a network graph with configurable directionality (forward/backward/both) and cost strategy (distance or speed-based), snaps start and end points to the network, runs Dijkstra’s algorithm for each start point, and outputs a line feature class where each feature is the optimal path geometry, along with attributes: original start point attributes, string representations of start and end coordinates, and the computed cost (distance in meters or time in seconds). No study area, time range, satellite data, or remote sensing operations are involved — it is purely vector-based GIS network analysis operating on local CRS-aligned input layers. All parameters (e.g., tolerance, speed field, direction field) are user-configurable via QGIS Processing Framework; no hardcoded region, date, or sensor logic exists.

name: Calculate shortest path from point to layer
desc: The script computes the shortest or fastest path(s) from a user-specified start point to each point feature in an input point layer, using a vector line network layer (e.g., roads, rivers, or trails). It builds a graph from the network with optional directionality (forward/backward/both) and speed-based costing, snaps start and end points to the network within a topology tolerance, runs Dijkstra's algorithm to compute paths, and outputs a line feature sink where each feature represents a shortest/fastest path geometry between the start point and one end point, with attributes including start point coordinates, end point coordinates, and travel cost (distance in meters or time in seconds). The output includes topological line geometries and attribute fields 'start', 'end', and 'cost'. No remote sensing data, time series, or satellite-derived inputs are used — all inputs are local vector layers provided by the user.

name: Calculate shortest path between points
desc: The script computes the shortest or fastest path between two user-specified points on a vector line network layer (e.g., roads, trails, rivers) using QGIS's built-in graph-based routing algorithms. It constructs a network graph from the input line layer with optional directionality and speed attributes, snaps start/end points to the nearest network vertices, runs Dijkstra’s algorithm to find the optimal path, and outputs a single-line feature representing the path geometry along with its travel cost (distance in meters or time in hours). No satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or Earth observation data is used; the analysis is purely vector-network-based and relies entirely on the provided line layer and user-defined parameters. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations beyond graph building and Dijkstra traversal are not specified.

name: Summarize household disaster risk indicators
desc: The script computes spatial summaries of Participatory Disaster Risk Assessment (PDRA) household survey indicators across administrative or geographic boundaries. It performs four types of aggregations per selected indicator field: (1) total household count per boundary unit, (2) count of households where the indicator value is >0, (3) percentage of households with indicator >0, and (4) sum of affected persons (using 'Household members' fields) where the indicator is >0. All operations are performed using QGIS processing algorithms ('qgis:joinbylocationsummary', 'qgis:joinattributestable') on vector layers — no raster or satellite data is used. Inputs are user-selected vector layers: a household point/polygon layer containing PDRA indicator fields (e.g., 'Food security', 'Shelter quality'), and a boundary polygon layer (e.g., barangays, municipalities). Outputs are new memory-based polygon layers named e.g., 'HH_Layer_Name (Food security - Households Affected)', styled with categorized or ranged symbology and labeled with computed values. The analysis is driven by a CSV-based indicator taxonomy ('pdra-household-indicators.csv') that defines categories (e.g., 'Agriculture', 'Health') but excludes computed risk levels. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified — this is a purely vector-based, non-remote-sensing desktop GIS tool for post-survey spatial aggregation.

name: Compute household risk exposure
desc: The script computes participatory disaster risk assessment (PDRA) summary risk metrics for household survey data spatially joined to administrative or geographic boundary layers. It calculates: (1) total number of households per boundary unit; (2) counts of households categorized as 'LOW', 'MEDIUM', or 'HIGH' risk for a selected PDRA indicator (e.g., flood, landslide); and (3) percentage-based risk composition (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH %) per boundary unit by joining and processing intermediate outputs. All outputs are memory-based vector layers in QGIS with categorized symbology and formatted labels. The analysis relies on pre-collected household-level PDRA survey data (CSV-sourced indicators) and user-provided vector layers — no remote sensing imagery, satellite data, or time-series processing is used. Study area, time range, satellite sensors, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Extract polygon centroid
desc: The script extracts centroid points from input polygon features in a shapefile (sample_data.shp), assigns original attribute values (e.g., 'code') and coordinates (x, y) to each centroid, writes the result to an in-memory point layer, commits edits, adds it to the QGIS layer registry, and exports the centroids to a CSV file with XYZ geometry (i.e., longitude, latitude, and null Z). The input is a local shapefile at 'Sample_Data/sample_data.shp'; no remote geospatial data, satellite imagery, time-series filtering, or classification is performed. All operations are vector-based geometric transformations within QGIS using PyQGIS API — specifically QgsGeometry.centroid(), QgsVectorLayer, and QgsVectorFileWriter. No study area, time range, satellite data, or sensor information is involved.

name: Plot GeoRSS flood events
desc: The script parses GeoRSS feeds to extract flood-related entries containing georeferenced coordinates, averages polygon vertices when needed, and creates a QGIS memory vector layer of point features representing flood events. It filters entries by title prefix 'Flood' or 'flood', extracts event type, location, publication date, and coordinates, then adds the resulting points to the QGIS project map canvas. Outputs include a memory-based point layer named 'flood' in EPSG:4326 and a QMessageBox showing feature count.

name: Rasterize seasonal polygon attribute
desc: The script converts vector polygon shapefiles (each representing a species' range with a 'SEASONAL' attribute) into raster TIFF files. It uses GDAL's rasterize algorithm to burn the 'SEASONAL' field values into a global raster grid (−180° to 180° longitude, −90° to 90° latitude) at 0.1° × 0.1° spatial resolution. Input shapefiles are sourced from a local Windows directory path containing IUCN-related mitogenomic species polygons; no geospatial filtering, reprojection, or temporal logic is applied. The output is a set of GeoTIFFs (one per .shp), each named by replacing '.shp' with '.tif' and preserving the input subdirectory structure under a 'Rasters' folder. No satellite imagery, time-series, classification, or modeling is performed — only attribute-preserving vector-to-raster conversion.

name: Optimize emergency responder locations
