desc: The script performs a Maximum Coverage Location Problem (MCLP) optimization to determine optimal placements of emergency responders (e.g., fire or ambulance units) within the 'KERR' local area of Vancouver, Canada. It uses vector GIS layers — including a local area boundary ('local_area_boundary.shp'), block outlines ('block_outlines.shp'), and public streets ('public_streets.shp') — all in NAD83 CRS. Workflow steps include: (1) isolating the 'KERR' sub-area using the 'MAPID' attribute; (2) generating a 250 m resolution point grid covering the area; (3) extracting roads intersecting the area and densifying them into road points; (4) computing a response service area radius (≈0.347 km) based on responder speed (5 KPH), buffer time (180 s), and target response time (300 s); (5) building polygonal response areas around road points using Euclidean distance (not network-based); (6) computing partial coverage of demand-weighted block polygons by these response areas; (7) solving an integer linear program (via PuLP/GLPK) to select minimum number of response areas covering ≥80% of total demand; and (8) exporting the selected response areas as a shapefile. Outputs include cropped shapefiles for the local area, blocks, grid, roads, road points, response areas, and the final optimized model result ('KERR_model_output_15.shp'). No satellite, raster, or temporal data is used — all inputs are static, pre-processed vector datasets.

name: Optimize service area coverage
desc: The script performs a Maximum Coverage Location Problem (MCLP) optimization to select a subset of candidate service areas (buffered grid points) that maximizes coverage of demand points within a defined study area (Kerrisdale, Vancouver). It reads a polygon layer (kerrisdale_map.shp) to define the spatial extent, generates a regular point grid at 300-unit spacing (assumed meters, though CRS not verified), filters points to lie inside the polygon, creates circular service areas (0.01-degree buffer, ~1.1 km at mid-latitudes), computes binary coverage between demand points (grid points with 'demand' attribute) and service areas, solves the MCLP using PuLP/GLPK to select optimal service areas, and outputs a SQL-like selection query and percentage coverage metric. Inputs include local shapefiles: kerrisdale_map.shp (study boundary), points_2.shp (demand points), zones.shp (predefined service areas — used in initial run_example but overridden later), and tl_2018_us_county.shp (unused in final execution). No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used; all operations are vector-based GIS analysis in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS). Final outputs are three shapefiles: county_049_grid.shp (filtered point grid), county_049_sas.shp (buffered service areas), and a console-reported selection query for visualization.

name: Synthesize synthetic population locations
desc: The script synthesizes a synthetic individual-level population dataset by disaggregating census block-level demographic data (race and age group counts) into spatially explicit points. It reads Ohio census block data (from 'Data/ohio_census_sample.csv'), maps each block ID to its corresponding polygon in a shapefile ('shp_files/ohio_census_blocks_nad83_17.shp'), computes race and age group probability distributions per block using multinomial sampling, generates synthetic persons with 'race' and 'age' attributes, assigns each person a random location uniformly sampled within their block’s geometry (using QGIS point-in-polygon containment testing), and exports the full set of individuals as a point shapefile ('/Users/andrewlaird/PycharmProjects/Van_Mapping_test/Data/pop_layer.shp'). The study area is Ohio; no satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is involved — it is purely a GIS-based spatial microsimulation using administrative boundary and tabular census data. Output includes a point vector layer with attributes: subpop (block ID), id (synthetic person ID), race, and age.

name: Compute shortest path to nearest hospital
desc: The script computes the shortest travel distance (in km) from a fixed origin point (73.02217460971042, 19.04214447607201 — near Mumbai, India) to hospitals in a local CSV dataset ('Hospital_final.csv'), filtered by user-selected specialty and type. It uses QGIS's native 'shortestpathpointtopoint' algorithm on a local road network vector layer ('hosp_road.shp') with Euclidean (unweighted) or default speed-based routing (DEFAULT_SPEED=50 km/h). The output includes: (1) a KML file of the optimal route, (2) visualized map canvas showing source (yellow), destination (red), and route (blue), and (3) printed distance (km) and hospital name. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used; all inputs are static local vector files (CSV points, SHP roads) and an ArcGIS Online basemap raster. Study area is implicitly Mumbai Metropolitan Region (based on origin coordinates and road layer naming), but no temporal dimension, sensor, bands, or Earth observation data are involved.

name: Convert multipart polygons to single parts
desc: The script converts multipart vector geometries in a shapefile (dissolve_0.shp) into single-part geometries, producing a new shapefile (single_part.shp). It uses QGIS's native 'multiparttosingleparts' algorithm via the Processing framework in a standalone Python application. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or geospatial modeling is performed. The input and output are local vector files; the workflow is purely geometric decomposition with no reference to study area, temporal extent, spectral bands, or environmental variables.

name: Clip POI with buildings layer
desc: The script performs a vector clipping operation: it uses the 'native:clip' QGIS processing algorithm to clip a point-of-interest (POI) layer (poi_osm_r.shp) using a buildings polygon layer (buildings_1.shp), producing a new clipped shapefile (cliped.shp) containing only the POIs that fall within the building footprints. The input layers are local filesystem shapefiles; no remote sensing imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations are performed. All paths are hardcoded Windows file paths under the user 'achituv'; the script runs in standalone QGIS Python mode without GEE integration — despite the prompt mentioning 'GEE script', the code contains zero Earth Engine (ee.*) calls, imports, or dependencies. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and geospatial analysis methods beyond vector overlay are not present or specified.

name: Calculate distance from points to nearest hub
desc: The script computes the Euclidean distance from each feature in an input point layer ('cliped.shp') to its nearest hub in a separate hubs point layer ('points_along.shp'), generating line features connecting each input point to its nearest hub and storing the distance in an attribute field ('vis_id'). It uses QGIS's native HubDistanceLines algorithm, sets the project CRS to match the input layer, and writes the output as a shapefile ('line_to_points.shp').

name: Extract POI within buildings
desc: The script performs a spatial intersection (extract by location) between a point-of-interest (POI) layer (poi_osm_r.shp) and a buildings layer (buildings_1.shp), retaining only those POI features that intersect (predicate = [2], i.e., 'contain' or 'within' — per QGIS native predicate code 2 mapping to 'contains' geometry predicate in context of point-in-polygon) the building geometries. The output is a new shapefile (extracted.shp) containing the subset of POIs located inside buildings. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or spectral processing is involved; it is a vector-based geometric selection operation using local shapefiles. Study area is implied by file paths but not explicitly named; data sources are local OSM-derived and building footprint shapefiles. Final product is a clipped vector layer of POIs confined to building footprints.

name: Compute line intersection points
desc: The script computes geometric intersections between two vector line layers: 'line_to_points.shp' (input lines) and 'poly_as_lines.shp' (boundary or feature lines derived from polygons), using QGIS's native 'lineintersections' algorithm. The output is a point layer ('off_pnts.shp') containing vertices at all crossing locations between the input and intersect lines. No raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, or classification is involved; the workflow is purely vector-based geometric processing within a local filesystem context. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Map POI-building-road intersections
desc: The script processes vector GIS layers to integrate points of interest (POIs) with building footprints and road networks: (1) clips POIs to building extents, (2) extracts POIs intersecting buildings, (3) generates evenly spaced points along highway geometries (every 10 meters), (4) assigns sequential integer IDs ('vis_id') to those points, (5) computes shortest line connections from clipped/extracted POIs to the highway points, (6) converts building polygons to boundary lines, (7) computes intersection points between the POI-to-highway lines and building boundaries, (8) merges three point layers — extracted POIs, pre-existing mean-close points, and off-building intersection points — and (9) removes duplicate geometries. The final output is a cleaned, unified point layer ('final.shp') representing spatially refined POI locations relative to buildings and road infrastructure, intended for visibility or accessibility analysis.

name: Merge vector point layers
desc: The script merges three local shapefile layers (mean_close_coor.shp, extracted.shp, and off_pnts.shp) into a single output shapefile (merge.shp) using QGIS's native merge vector layers algorithm. All layers are loaded as QgsVectorLayer objects with provider 'ogr', reprojected to EPSG:3857 during merging. The workflow is purely vector-based, involving no raster data, remote sensing, time-series analysis, or classification. Input layers originate from the 'visibilitysyntax' QGIS plugin test directory, suggesting they are synthetic or derived point geometries related to visibility analysis (e.g., observer points, target points, offset points). No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis beyond coordinate reprojection and layer concatenation is performed. Output is a merged point shapefile in Web Mercator projection.

name: Extract features by distance threshold
desc: The script performs a vector attribute-based filtering operation on a shapefile named 'distance_matrix.shp', selecting only features where the 'Distance' field has a value less than 10 (using operator code 4, which corresponds to '<' in QGIS native algorithms). The output is a new shapefile 'extracted.shp' containing the subset of features meeting this condition. No raster data, satellite imagery, time series, or geospatial modeling (e.g., classification, regression, index calculation) is involved — it is a purely vector attribute query. Input and output paths are hardcoded to local Windows filesystem locations under a QGIS plugin directory named 'visibilitysyntax\test\mean_close_point'; the context suggests this is part of a visibility or proximity analysis workflow, but the script itself executes only the extraction step. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Upload and annotate intersection points
desc: The script loads a local shapefile of road intersections ('intersections.shp'), verifies the presence of a 'vis_id' field, adds it if missing, and populates it with sequential integer IDs (0, 1, 2, ...) for each feature. It performs no geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations — only vector layer ingestion, schema modification, and attribute population in QGIS via PyQGIS in a standalone context. No satellite data, imagery, time series, or Earth Engine (GEE) functionality is used; the script is purely desktop GIS preprocessing for visibility or network analysis inputs. All paths are local (e.g., 'C:/Users/achituv/AppData/.../intersections.shp'), and no outputs are exported or visualized beyond in-memory layer creation.

name: Compute mean coordinates of points
desc: The script computes the centroid (mean coordinate) of a set of input point features from a local Shapefile ('cleaned.shp'), using QGIS's native 'meancoordinates' algorithm. It reads a vector layer with an identifier field 'InputID', calculates the arithmetic mean of X and Y coordinates across all features (or per group if UID is used for grouping), and writes the result to a new Shapefile ('mean_close_coor.shp'). No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, raster operations, or satellite imagery is involved — the workflow is purely vector-based geometric aggregation. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified, as the script operates solely on static local vector data.

name: Convert multipart polygons to single parts
desc: The script converts multipart vector geometries in a shapefile to single-part geometries using QGIS's native 'multiparttosingleparts' algorithm. It reads an input shapefile ('extracted.shp') and writes the result to a new shapefile ('single_part.shp'). No remote sensing data, classification, time-series analysis, or raster operations are involved; the workflow is purely vector geometry decomposition. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods beyond geometry splitting are not specified.

name: Dissolve highway network by group
desc: The script dissolves a vector layer of highways (highways_1.shp) by the 'group' attribute using QGIS's native:dissolve algorithm, producing a dissolved output saved as dissolve_0.shp. It uses QgsVectorLayer to load input data, QgsProcessingFeedback for execution context, and processing.run() with explicit parameters {'INPUT': network, 'FIELD': 'group', 'OUTPUT': junc_loc_0}. The workflow is standalone QGIS Python scripting, not involving raster analysis, remote sensing, or time-series operations.

name: Extract raster and vector attributes to points
desc: The script extracts attribute values from selected raster bands and vector layer fields (point and polygon) to a target point layer. It supports extracting point-layer fields (copying existing attributes), polygon-layer fields (via spatial intersection within a small buffer around each point), and raster-band values (via pixel sampling at point locations). The output is a new vector layer (Shapefile, CSV, or GeoPackage) containing the original point geometries plus the extracted attributes as new fields. All operations are performed client-side in QGIS using native QgsVectorLayer/QgsRasterLayer APIs; no Google Earth Engine (GEE) server-side computation occurs — despite the user prompt mentioning 'GEE', the script contains zero GEE code (no ee.Initialize, no ee.ImageCollection, no .map(), no Export, etc.). The script performs CRS validation, field name uniqueness checks, and handles multi-point geometries. Study area, time range, satellite data, and specific sensors are not specified because the script operates on locally loaded QGIS layers without referencing any remote or time-series datasets.

name: Analyze animal movement temperature correlation
desc: The script analyzes correlation between air temperature and animal (bird) activity patterns in North Rhine-Westphalia. It loads a user-provided bird tracking shapefile (point geometry with timestamps and individual IDs), preprocesses it by joining with external air temperature data (source not embedded but implied via preprocessing module), filters by bird ID and season, computes daily travelled distance per bird, and generates three visual outputs: (1) bar charts of average distance per temperature bin, (2) monthly average distance statistics, and (3) scatter plots of distance vs. temperature with linear fitting. All outputs are dynamically rendered as PNGs in QGIS plugin dialogs. The study area is explicitly named as 'North Rhine-Westphalia'; no satellite or Earth observation imagery is used — temperature data is assumed external/tabular (e.g., weather station or gridded model output), and bird data is vector-based GPS tracking. No image classification, spectral indices, or cloud masking occurs; geospatial operations are limited to vector filtering, temporal aggregation, and distance calculation on point sequences.

name: Generate concave hulls from points
desc: The script computes concave (α-shape) or convex hulls from an input point vector layer. It groups points by an optional key field (e.g., CLUSTER_ID), computes Delaunay triangulations for each group, filters triangles based on circumscribed radius threshold (alpha ∈ [0,1]), and dissolves the retained triangles into polygonal hulls. The output is a vector polygon layer where each feature represents a hull — either one per group (if key field provided) or a single hull (if no key). No raster data, satellite imagery, time series, or external geospatial datasets are used; input is purely a local QGIS vector layer. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Map gun crime density by ward
desc: The script maps and compares gun-related crime density across electoral wards in a specific city (inferred from dataset names: 'Ward_from_2012.shp', 'Crime_Incidents_in_2017.shp', 'Shot_Spotter_Gun_Shots.shp') by performing spatial joins between point-based crime/shot-spotter incidents and polygon-based wards, then computing normalized rates (per 10,000 people) using ward-level population data ('POP_2011_2'). The outputs are two joined shapefiles ('crime_wards.shp', 'Shot_Spotter_Gun_wards.shp') loaded into QGIS and printed summary statistics per ward. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or spectral analysis is used; all inputs are local vector files (shapefiles) with no explicit study area name, satellite, sensor, or bands involved.

name: Add multi-format layers to QGIS
desc: The script adds vector layers to QGIS from local shapefiles (.shp) and Excel files (.xls/.xlsx) by converting tabular point data (with X/Y fields) into point shapefiles. It reads coordinate columns (user-specified xField and yField), infers field types (string/double), creates a new ESRI Shapefile in the user-defined target directory using the CRS and encoding of an existing '시군구' (Si-gun-gu, i.e., county-level administrative) layer, populates it with features derived from Excel rows, and adds the resulting layers to the QGIS project. No remote sensing, time-series, or Earth Engine (GEE) processing occurs—the script is purely a QGIS desktop plugin for local file ingestion and conversion. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis methods are not involved.

name: Convert KML to Shapefile
desc: The script converts one or more user-selected KML files into ESRI Shapefile format, reprojecting them to EPSG:5186 (Korea 2000 / Central Belt), and adds the resulting vector layers to the QGIS project. It performs no geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing; it is a pure file format conversion and import utility. The script operates entirely within QGIS desktop using PyQGIS APIs, with no Earth Engine (GEE) code present — despite the prompt's framing. All operations are local, interactive, and triggered via GUI buttons. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic analysis is involved.

name: Reproject layer coordinate system
desc: The script reprojects a selected QGIS vector or raster layer from its current CRS to a user-specified target CRS (e.g., EPSG codes or custom Korean datum transformations using +towgs84 parameters). It uses QGIS Processing algorithms: 'native:reprojectlayer' for vectors and 'gdal:warpreproject' for rasters. The output is a new saved file (Shapefile for vectors, GeoTIFF for rasters) in the target CRS, which is then added to the QGIS project and zoomed to its extent. No remote sensing imagery, time-series, or classification is involved — it is purely a geospatial coordinate system translation tool.

name: Tag grid replacements manually
desc: The script performs a manual visual inspection and tagging workflow for candidate grid replacements in urban infrastructure planning. It loads pre-processed administrative boundary grids (e.g., 'fin_grid.shp') for cities in Guangdong Province, merges them by MCELL (a grid cell identifier), overlays Google Satellite tiles via TileLayerPlugin, and iteratively selects candidate grids (from 'candidate' Excel sheet) matching GRID_CHANGE values. For each candidate GRID_ID, it zooms to the selected feature on the merged grid layer and prompts the user via QInputDialog to assign a binary tag (1 = should be replaced, 0 = should not). Tagged decisions are appended to a summary DataFrame ('Grid_replacement.csv'), and selected grids (where tag == 1) are exported as shapefiles ('selected_grid2_*.shp'). The study area is explicitly Guangdong Province; input data includes Excel files ('testing.xlsx' with sheets 'change' and 'candidate', and 'map_file.xlsx'), local shapefiles ('fin_grid.shp'), and no Earth Engine assets — this is a QGIS Python plugin/script, not a GEE script. All geoprocessing (clip, union, count unique points) uses QGIS Processing Toolbox algorithms; coordinate transformations include WGS84 ↔ GCJ-02 ↔ BD-09 for Chinese location bias correction. Output products: CSV of tagged replacements and per-MCELL shapefiles of selected grids.

name: Convert KML to SHP
desc: The script converts KML files representing urban blocks (BAU blocks) into Shapefile format, performing vector geoprocessing including coordinate reference system assignment (EPSG:4030), geometry cleaning (v.clean), null geometry removal, dissolving by 'block_id', validity checking, and merging of multiple input layers. Input KMLs are sourced from 'C:\Users\base7005\Documents\BAUblocks2018\test\', and outputs include a cleaned, dissolved, validated shapefile 'output.shp' at 'C:\Users\base7005\Documents\BAUblocks2018\result\'. The workflow is explicitly intended for 'Amin' and targets residential/urban block delineation in Chinese cities (evidenced by Excel tracking list 'CCE_2018W2UE_TrackingList.xlsx' with columns 'citycode' and 'AD_CODE', and path references to 'Liaoning'). No satellite imagery, raster analysis, or time-series processing is performed — it is purely vector data conversion and topology harmonization.

name: Count POI within urban grids
desc: The script counts unique points of interest (POIs) within merged grid cells that are intersected by a new urban boundary layer ('inbound_UTM.shp')—assigning value 1 to grids inside the urban boundary and 0 outside. It processes shapefile-based vector data (grids, urban boundaries, and POI point layers) using QGIS geoprocessing algorithms including clip, union, dissolve, count unique points in polygon, merge, remove null geometries, field calculation (area in km²), and spatial join. Input POI data originates from text files (poi_path) converted to point layers; grid layers are pre-projected UTM shapefiles per administrative district (e.g., '重庆市' — Chongqing Municipality), identified by AD_CODE. Outputs include saved shapefiles (e.g., merged_grids.shp, area-calculated layers) added to QGIS interface, with attribute fields such as 'NUMPOINTS', 'Resident', 'area', and 'new_id'. No raster or satellite imagery is used; all operations are vector-based topological and attribute aggregations.

name: Classify government POIs by administrative level
desc: The script processes point-of-interest (POI) data for cities in Jiangsu Province, China, to classify government and management institutions (L2='government and management institutions') according to administrative hierarchy levels (111, 112, 121, 122, 123, 210, 220) derived from a local administrative boundary and name-matching CSV ('Citylist.csv'). It cleans both POI names and administrative unit names (removing suffixes like '市', '区', '镇', '街道', etc.), constructs combined names ('NameCmb'), and performs case-insensitive substring matching to assign administrative levels. Outputs include: (1) filtered infrastructure POI CSVs per level (e.g., '_111.csv'), (2) styled QGIS vector layers with Webdings font markers color-coded per level, and (3) exported ESRI Shapefiles (e.g., '320211_111.shp') in WGS84/EGM96 (EPSG:4030) CRS. The study area is Jiangsu Province; input POI files are named using Chinese city/district names and AD_Code (e.g., '无锡市_滨湖区_320211.txt'); CRS is explicitly set to EPSG:4030 (a geodetic CRS, not projected). No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is performed — all inputs are static tabular/spatial CSVs with X/Y coordinates.

name: Tag grid cells with infrastructure presence
desc: The script processes administrative grid polygons (by AD_code) and infrastructure point data (loaded from CSV with X/Y coordinates in CRS 4030) for counties in Jilin Province, China. It buffers infrastructure points by 0.0135 decimal degrees, dissolves the buffers, and computes intersection area between each grid cell and the dissolved infrastructure buffer. For each grid cell, it interactively prompts the user via QInputDialog to tag it (1 = yes, 0 = no) based on visual assessment of overlap area; when no infrastructure points exist, tagging is done without spatial intersection. Outputs include a per-county shapefile 'selected_grid_<AD_code>.shp' containing only tagged grids, and a consolidated CSV 'selection_check_RD2.csv' with grid_id, AD_code, and tag columns. All operations occur within QGIS Python environment using processing algorithms (clip, union, dissolve, selectbyattribute) and QgsGeometryAnalyzer. No satellite imagery or Earth Engine API calls are used — this is a desktop QGIS geoprocessing workflow, not a GEE script.

name: Carve out non-residential grid cells
desc: The script processes administrative grid polygons (fin_grid.shp or resident_grid.shp) to generate fin_base.shp — a refined residential grid layer by removing areas identified as non-residential. Key steps include: (1) subtracting built-up area boundaries (BatchX_city_d.shp) from the input grid using difference operations; (2) removing null geometries; (3) for cities marked in ccecities0911.xlsx with 'fin' = 0, further carving out: (a) grid IDs listed in GRID_nonresidential.xlsx (e.g., based on AD_CODE and GRID_ID), (b) big rivers (big_rivers.shp), and (c) target_NoPeople1.shp (farmland/forest polygons); (4) converting multipart geometries to singleparts; (5) calculating area (in km²) and filtering out grids with area < 0.01 km². The study area is explicitly Jiangsu Province (path contains '江苏省'), with processing applied per county-level AD_CODE (e.g., 320102, 320104). Input data sources are local shapefiles only — no satellite, sensor, or band usage. CRS is set to EPSG:4030 (Beijing 1954 / 3-degree Gauss-Kruger zone 37). Output is fin_base.shp — a cleaned, area-filtered, single-part polygon layer of residential grid cells.

name: Correct surface elevation model
desc: The script performs surface correction by computing elevation residuals (deltas) between input point measurements and an existing raster surface, interpolating those deltas into a delta surface (using a custom 'creategridwithfaults' algorithm that incorporates fault lines as constraints), adding the delta surface to the original surface to produce a corrected raster, and generating a quality control vector layer with post-correction residuals. The workflow is evidence-based: Step 1 extracts point-wise residuals (inputField − raster value); Step 2 interpolates residuals using faults as barriers; Step 3 adds the delta raster to the input raster via QgsRasterCalculator; Step 4 re-samples the corrected surface at original points to compute new residuals for QC. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific sensor/bands are referenced — inputs are generic local raster/vector files (e.g., 'INPUT_RASTER', 'INPUT_LAYER', 'INPUT_FAULT'), and the algorithm is purely geometric/interpolative, not remote sensing–based.

name: Determine UTM zone for CRS selection
desc: The script determines the appropriate UTM zone (31, 32, or 33) for a user-selected QGIS vector layer by computing its geographic centroid and checking containment within polygon features from a local UTM zones shapefile (utmzones.shp). It then prints the corresponding ETRS89-based UTM EPSG code (25831, 25832, or 25833) — all of which are valid for Europe. The workflow involves reprojection of the active layer to EPSG:25832 (ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N), extraction of its extent, calculation of the centroid point, and spatial lookup against the UTM zone polygons. No satellite data, time series, classification, or export occurs; the output is purely console text indicating the recommended CRS. Study area is not specified; time range is not applicable; data sources are local vector files only.

name: Manage PostGIS subtypes and domains
desc: The script is a QGIS plugin that manages database subtypes and domains in PostGIS. It connects to PostgreSQL/PostGIS databases configured in QGIS, initializes the 'data_manager' extension (if superuser), retrieves database schemata and layers/tables, populates a tree widget with spatial and non-spatial tables, and supports automatic loading of related tables (via QgsRelation) and joined tables (via QgsVectorLayerJoinInfo). It also configures ValueMap editor widgets for foreign-key fields using lookup tables. The plugin does not perform geospatial analysis, remote sensing processing, or Earth Engine operations — it is purely a database schema and layer management tool for QGIS. All functionality is local to the user’s QGIS desktop environment and relies on existing PostGIS connections; no external satellite, sensor, or time-series data is accessed or processed.

name: Reproject layer to UTM zone 47N
desc: The script reprojects the currently active QGIS vector layer from its original CRS to EPSG:32647 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N) and saves it as a new Shapefile at 'D:/test_chengeCRS.shp'. It achieves this by creating a new QgsVectorLayer instance from the source URI (delimited text), defining the target CRS using QgsCoordinateReferenceSystem(32647), and writing the layer using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormat with explicit CRS override and 'ESRI Shapefile' format.

name: Interpolate rainfall data
desc: The script retrieves real-time rainfall observations from Thailand's Meteorological Department (TMD) API (http://data.tmd.go.th/api/WeatherToday/V1/?type=json), converts the JSON response into a CSV file containing station-level attributes (Province, StationNameTh, Latitude, Longitude, Date, Rainfall), imports it as a point vector layer in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), reprojects to UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), and performs Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation with power coefficient 2 to generate a continuous rainfall surface raster (GeoTIFF). The interpolation extent and resolution are user-defined — either using the active layer’s bounding box or a default extent — and the output raster is added to the QGIS map canvas. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is performed; data is strictly near-real-time (single-date) ground observations from Thai weather stations.

name: Calculate building statistics for census units
desc: The script computes six building-related metrics—average building size (AvgSize), building density (BD), building coverage ratio (BCR), building proximity (ProxMean), and building contiguity (ContRatio)—for three administrative and spatial units: input census tracts (CT), dissemination blocks (DB), and a generated 1 km² regular grid aligned to the CT extent. It loads vector shapefiles of building footprints, census tracts, and dissemination blocks; validates geometries; clips buildings to the CT extent; generates a grid; computes nearest-neighbor edge distances between buildings using the NNJoin QGIS plugin; and performs spatial joins and field calculations to derive per-unit statistics. Final outputs are three shapefiles (CT_Stats.shp, DB_Stats.shp, GRID_Stats.shp) containing all computed metrics as attributes, ready for visualization and analysis in QGIS.

name: Find amenities near reference entity
desc: The script queries OpenStreetMap (OSM) via the Overpass API to locate points of interest (amenities) within a user-specified distance of a selected reference entity (e.g., a named building or facility) in a given administrative area (e.g., a municipality). It uses OSM's 'amenity' key for both the target resources and the reference object. The workflow includes: (1) selecting a location (admin_level=8, e.g., a Spanish municipality), (2) searching OSM taginfo API for amenity values matching user input, (3) querying Overpass for nodes with those amenities in the area, (4) selecting a reference entity by name from the resulting nodes, (5) generating a geographic buffer (in meters) around that entity’s coordinates (WGS84 → ETRS89/UTM31N → WGS84), and (6) identifying and visualizing all target-amenity nodes intersecting the buffer as a QGIS memory vector layer. Outputs are point features with OSM tags, rendered as a temporary QGIS layer with auto-zoom. Data sources are exclusively OSM — no satellite, aerial, or temporal data is used; no time range is involved. Study area is defined dynamically by user-input place name (e.g., 'Barcelona'), not hardcoded coordinates or fixed region.

name: Map worker distribution by service centre
desc: The script generates an A0-sized multi-panel PDF layout showing spatial distributions of workers across 40 service centres in Western Sydney, Australia. Each panel includes: (1) a graduated symbology map of SA1-level job counts within the service area, overlaid on base layers (roads, ocean, MUA, open space, and centre points); (2) a centre name and type label; (3) a pie chart image (pre-generated, file-based) for sectoral composition; (4) an HTML table summarizing job sector counts and totals using colour-coded rows; and (5) a compact legend. The analysis is driven by PostgreSQL-sourced tabular data (jobs_centres_clean.csv and database query results), vector geometries from a GeoPackage (basemaps.gpkg), and CRS EPSG:28356 (GDA94 / MGA zone 56). No satellite or remote sensing data is used — all inputs are vector GIS layers and relational database tables. Study area is explicitly Western Sydney (including 'Western Sydney Airport and Badgerys Creek Aerotropolis').

name: Download and package provincial OSM shapefiles
desc: The script downloads the latest OpenStreetMap (OSM) shapefile archive for a selected Dutch province from Geofabrik's Europe/Netherlands server, extracts all .shp files, reclassifies them by geometry type (point/line/polygon) via WKB type codes (1/5/6), writes them to renamed shapefiles in a temporary directory, then packages all into a single GeoPackage (.gpkg) file named after the province. It additionally attempts to apply QML/SLD styling from a local 'styling/' subdirectory using layer style metadata stored in the GeoPackage's 'layer_styles' table. The study area is limited to one of the twelve provinces of the Netherlands, specified at runtime via the 'provincie' parameter. No satellite, sensor, or time-series data is used; the source is static vector data from OSM.

name: Buffer autobahn infrastructure layers
desc: The script loads two vector layers—'Environment' and 'Autobahn'—from user-selected local files, then generates three concentric buffer zones (20 m, 100 m, and 300 m) around the Autobahn layer using QGIS’s native buffer algorithm. Each buffer is added as a new named vector layer ('Autobahn 20', 'Autobahn 100', 'Autobahn 300') in the QGIS project. No spatial or attribute analysis beyond buffering is performed; the output consists solely of buffered polygon layers representing proximity zones around road infrastructure.

name: Model autobahn buffer impact zones
desc: The script models cumulative buffer zones around an Autobahn (motorway) vector layer to delineate multi-tiered impact areas: a 20 m buffer (Autobahn 20), then successive 100 m and 200 m expansions (yielding Autobahn 100 and Autobahn 300), followed by union operations to merge overlapping buffers into non-redundant inner and full impact area polygons. The final output is a single 'Impact Area' vector layer representing the cumulative spatial extent of all three buffer distances, intended for infrastructure-related environmental or planning impact assessment.

name: Create Autobahn buffer layer
desc: The script loads two vector layers—'Environment' and 'Autobahn'—from user-selected local files using QGIS Python bindings, then generates a 20-meter buffer around the Autobahn layer using the QGIS 'qgis:buffer' algorithm with default geometric parameters (5 segments, round end caps, no dissolve). The buffered layer is added to the QGIS project as 'Autobahn 20'. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or export beyond in-session layer addition is performed. All inputs are local vector files; no study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis beyond buffering is specified or implied.

name: Generate elevation hillshade
desc: The script generates a hillshade raster from a local DEM file (dem.asc) using GDAL's hillshade algorithm. It loads the DEM as a QGIS raster layer, runs the 'gdal:hillshade' processing algorithm with azimuth=315.0°, altitude=45.0°, z_factor=1.0, and scale=1.0, writes the output to 'hillshade.tif', then loads and adds that resulting hillshade raster layer to the QGIS project. The input DEM source, spatial extent, coordinate reference system, and temporal attributes are not specified in the script; it operates solely on a local ASCII grid file with no time dimension or satellite/sensor metadata. All parameters and paths are hardcoded; no remote sensing imagery, cloud masking, classification, or time-series analysis is performed.

name: Join population attributes to census tracts
desc: The script joins population data from a CSV file to a US Census tract shapefile (California, 2013) using the GEOID field. It performs two join operations: one via QgsVectorLayerJoinInfo (memory-cached layer join) and another via the QGIS 'qgis:joinattributestable' processing algorithm. The output is a joined vector layer where each census tract polygon carries associated population attributes (e.g., from 'ca_tracts_pop.csv'), enabling spatial visualization and analysis of demographic data. Study area is California (inferred from filepath 'tl_2013_06_tract.shp' — FIPS 06 = California, and CSV name 'ca_tracts_pop.csv'); time range is not specified in the script but the TIGER/Line shapefile is from 2013; no satellite, sensor, or band usage — purely vector attribute joining with local GIS files.

name: Join populated places to countries
desc: The script performs a spatial join-by-location between two vector layers: 'ne_110m_populated_places.shp' (populated places) and 'ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp' (country boundaries), using the 'contains' predicate (index 5 in QGIS predicate list, corresponding to 'geometries intersect' — though commonly used for point-in-polygon joins here). It appends the 'SOVEREIGNT' (sovereignty name) attribute from the countries layer to each populated place feature. The output is a new shapefile ('joinloc.shp') containing all original point features with an added 'SOVEREIGNT' field indicating the country in which each place is located. Study area is global (Natural Earth 110m and 10m cultural datasets); time range is not applicable (static administrative/vector data); data sources are open vector datasets, not satellite-derived; no temporal filtering, cloud masking, spectral analysis, or classification is performed. The operation is purely geometric attribute transfer via spatial containment.

name: Buffer Autobahn network
desc: The script loads two vector layers—'Environment' and 'Autobahn'—from user-selected local files using QGIS's file dialog. It then creates a 20-meter buffer around the 'Autobahn' layer using QGIS's native buffer algorithm with default parameters (5 segments, round end caps, miter limit 2, no dissolve), storing the result in memory and adding it to the project as 'Autobahn 20'. The workflow is purely vector-based geometric processing with no raster or temporal analysis.

name: Reproject satellite image raster
desc: The script reprojects a local GeoTIFF raster file (SatImage.tif) from source CRS EPSG:4326 (WGS84 geographic) to target CRS EPSG:3722 (a Korean coordinate system, specifically the Korea 2000 / Central Belt projected coordinate system). It uses GDAL's warp algorithm via QGIS Processing with nearest neighbor resampling (implied by RESAMPLING=None and documented behavior of gdal:warpreproject when unspecified — defaults to nearest neighbor), sets NODATA=0, preserves original resolution (TARGET_RESOLUTION=None), and outputs a new GeoTIFF at /home/abhishek/out.tif. No study area, time range, satellite, sensor, or bands are specified — the input is a generic local raster file with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata visible in the script. The operation is purely geometric reprojection; no classification, analysis, or spectral processing is performed.

name: Identify bicycle station blind spots
desc: The script supports public bicycle station siting by identifying coverage blind spots through spatial analysis of road network, administrative zones, and existing bicycle station locations in Suzhou. It loads vector layers (administrative boundaries '区域.shp', bicycle stations '自行车站点_utf8.geojson', and road network '路网_utf8.geojson'), performs attribute-based selection (e.g., filtering road segments by 'ad_code'='320583' and 'link_flag'=21), builds spatial indices for proximity queries, computes geometric properties (perimeter/area) on polygon layers (e.g., '区域'), applies symbology changes to road layers, and saves updated QGIS projects. No classification, modeling, or time-series analysis is performed — the workflow is GIS project setup, layer management, spatial querying, and cartographic styling for urban infrastructure planning. Study area: Suzhou (explicitly in file paths and 'ad_code'=320583, which corresponds to Kunshan City, Jiangsu Province, under Suzhou Prefecture-level City). Data sources are local vector files (no satellite/remote sensing data); one raster ('大众点评_荆门_密度_3857_new.tif') is loaded but not used in any analysis — it appears unrelated to the core task and originates from Jingmen (a different city), suggesting auxiliary or exploratory use. Final outputs include modified QGIS project files ('test.qgz') and a newly created point shapefile ('Johny.shp').

name: Identify shortest path and reachable area
desc: The script performs network analysis on a road network vector layer (路网_utf8.geojson) to compute the shortest path between two geographic points (e.g., (120.6, 31.3) → (120.53, 31.27)) and determine the set of graph vertices reachable within a 200-meter network distance from a start point (e.g., (120.56646, 31.28188)). It uses QGIS’s QgsVectorLayerDirector and QgsGraphBuilder to construct a weighted graph with directional road attributes (field index 11 encoding direction as '2'/'3'/'1'), applies Dijkstra’s algorithm via QgsGraphAnalyzer.dijkstra(), reconstructs the optimal path as a GeoJSON LineString, and generates a reachable-area polygon by collecting boundary vertices where accumulated cost ≤ 200 m. Outputs include two GeoJSON files: '最短路.geojson' (shortest path line) and '可达区域.geojson' (polygon approximating 200-m network buffer), both saved to a local file path in Suzhou, Jiangsu. Study area is explicitly named '苏州公安-公共自行车' (Suzhou Public Security — Public Bicycle), confirming urban transportation planning context for bicycle station blind-spot identification. No satellite, sensor, or time-series data is used; all inputs are static vector layers in GCJ-02 and WGS84 (EPSG:4326) CRS.

name: Identify local summit points
desc: The script identifies local summit (peak) points within user-defined buffer zones around input point features, using a digital elevation model (DEM). It resolves conflicts where multiple buffers overlap and a single summit falls within more than one buffer by iteratively refining the search area: for conflicting summits, it computes the minimal distance from the summit to the original source points, creates smaller dual-point buffers at that distance, re-runs summit detection in those refined areas, and merges the new, non-conflicting summits into the final output layer. The final output is a vector layer of unique, non-duplicated summit points, each associated with its nearest input point (via the provided or auto-generated ID field), along with intermediate files saved to a user-specified folder.

name: Extract summit points from DEM
desc: The script identifies local elevation maxima (summit points) within each polygon of an input area layer by performing zonal statistics to compute the maximum elevation per polygon, then raster sampling of the clipped DEM to locate all pixel centers matching that maximum value. It outputs a point vector layer containing one or more summit points per polygon, preserving original attributes (except the temporary '_max' field), and saves intermediate clipped rasters and polygon subsets in a user-specified folder.

name: Clip mosaic raster by polygon grid
desc: The script clips a single orthorectified aerial photo mosaic raster (Nomedaaerofoto_Mosaico_Recorte.tif) into individual tile rasters using a vector grid layer (Nomedaaerofoto_Mosaico_Quadricula.shp), where each tile is named according to the 'indice' attribute value of its corresponding polygon. It performs attribute-based vector subsetting (extracting one polygon at a time) followed by GDAL-based raster clipping with nodata=250.0, preserving resolution and cropping strictly to the cutline. Outputs are georeferenced GeoTIFF tiles (e.g., Nomedaaerofoto_1.tif, Nomedaaerofoto_2.tif) aligned to the grid, suitable for tiled distribution or per-tile processing.

name: Clip raster by vector features
desc: The script clips a single raster file (aerofoto.tif) to the geometry of each individual feature in a vector layer (quad2.shp), using the 'indice' attribute value as an identifier for naming output clipped rasters. Each clip is performed with GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm, applying a mask, setting nodata to 250.0, preserving resolution, and cropping strictly to the cutline. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified — the input raster is a local GeoTIFF ('aerofoto.tif'), likely an aerial photograph, and the vector layer contains polygon features indexed by 'indice'. No temporal filtering, spectral analysis, or classification is performed; the workflow is purely geometric raster clipping per vector feature.

name: Clip raster by vector polygon
desc: The script clips a single raster file ('aerofoto.tif') to the geometry of each feature in a vector layer ('quad2.shp'), using the 'indice' attribute to name and isolate individual clipped rasters (e.g., 'cliped_1.tif', 'cliped_2.tif'). It iterates over vector features, applies a SQL subset string to select one feature at a time, then executes GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm with mask-based cropping, nodata value set to 250.0, resolution preserved, and no alpha band. The input raster is a local GeoTIFF ('aerofoto.tif'), interpreted as an aerial photograph; the vector layer contains polygon features (likely quadrants or tiles) with an 'indice' field. No temporal filtering, classification, or spectral analysis is performed — only spatial subsetting. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Clip raster by vector mask
desc: The script clips the raster file 'AestheticMax.tif' to the spatial extent defined by the vector layer 'TestVectorExtent.shp' using GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm. It applies nodata value -9999, preserves input resolution, and outputs a georeferenced GeoTIFF at '/Users/ep9k/Desktop/output_clip.tif'. No time-series analysis, classification, or spectral computation is performed; the operation is purely geometric masking and cropping. The study area is implicitly defined by the vector mask and raster input paths but no geographic context (e.g., region name, coordinates) is encoded in the code. Data sources are local files — not GEE assets — so satellite, sensor, and band information are not applicable. The output is a static, clipped raster product for downstream use in QGIS or other GIS software.

name: Reclassify aesthetic suitability raster
desc: The script applies a conditional reclassification to the input raster 'AestheticMax.tif', where pixel values equal to 255 are set to 0, and all other values are preserved unchanged. This is implemented using GDAL's raster calculator with the formula '(A != 255) * A', operating on Band 1 of the input raster. The output is written to '/Users/ep9k/Desktop/reclassoutput.tif' and loaded into QGIS. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis methods (e.g., classification algorithms, masking, compositing) are present in the script — it is a simple per-pixel arithmetic reclassification of a pre-existing local GeoTIFF file. The input raster path suggests it originates from a local desktop workflow ('Key-LogEcovaluator'), but no metadata, source provenance, spatial extent, or temporal information is embedded in the code.

name: Buffer features by attribute search
desc: The script selects vector features from an input layer where a user-specified field contains a substring matching a given search key (e.g., 'C'), then generates a dissolved buffer polygon around those selected features using a user-defined distance. The output is a single multipart polygon feature class representing the buffered area.

name: Join census tract attributes
desc: The script joins a CSV-based U.S. Census dataset (ACS_12_5YR_S1901_with_ann.csv) to a shapefile of census tracts (hancock_tracts.shp) using the GEOid2 field from the CSV and GEOID field from the shapefile. It performs an attribute join in QGIS via QgsVectorJoinInfo, caches the join in memory, then writes the joined layer to a new Shapefile (joined.shp). The output is a vector layer with 142 fields (vs original 12), confirming successful attribute enrichment of spatial census tracts with demographic/economic census data.

name: Convert shapefile to KML
desc: The script converts a local ESRI Shapefile (hancock.shp) into KML and GeoJSON formats using QGIS Python bindings (QgsVectorLayer and QgsVectorFileWriter). It reprojects the input vector layer from its native CRS to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) during export. The study area is implied by the file path '/qgis_data/hancock/hancock.shp', referencing Hancock County — a known U.S. county, but no explicit geometry, time range, satellite data, or analysis operations are present. The outputs are two files: 'hancock.kml' and 'hancock.geojson', both containing the vector boundary data in standardized geospatial interchange formats.

name: Compute least cost path
desc: The script computes a least cost path between two user-defined points (start-point.shp and end-point.shp) over a digital elevation model (dem.asc), using QGIS Processing Toolbox algorithms. It first calculates an accumulated cost raster via GRASS 'r.cost.points' using the DEM as the cost surface, then merges the start and end point layers, and finally applies SAGA's 'leastcostpaths' algorithm using the cost raster and DEM to derive a vector line representing the optimal path. The outputs include a cost raster (cost.tif), a merged point layer (merge.shp), a least cost path vector layer (path.shp), and a profile points layer (profilePts.shp). All inputs are local file-based rasters/vector files with no cloud-based or satellite-derived data; the study area is defined implicitly by the extent of dem.asc, but no geographic identity (e.g., region name, coordinate reference system details, or projection info) is specified in the script. Time range is not applicable as the inputs are static, non-temporal GIS files.

name: Visualize geotagged photo locations
desc: The script extracts GPS coordinates from EXIF metadata of JPEG images stored in a local directory (/qgis_data/photos/), converts DMS-formatted GPS tags to decimal degrees, and creates a QGIS memory vector layer of points (EPSG:4326) with photo file paths as attributes. It adds an OpenUrl action to each feature for clicking to open the photo. The script runs entirely in QGIS Python environment (not GEE), uses PIL and ExifTags for EXIF parsing, and relies on QgsVectorLayer, QgsGeometry, and QgsMapLayerRegistry for GIS layer creation and display. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or Earth Engine API calls are used; it is a local desktop GIS workflow for photo geolocation mapping. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified because the script does not perform remote sensing analysis.

name: Rectangularize building footprints
desc: The script processes vector-based building footprint polygons from a local Shapefile (irregular.shp) to generate more rectangular approximations by geometric transformation. It identifies the top-right vertex of each input polygon, computes slopes and intercepts of adjacent edges, derives perpendicular lines, and calculates intersection points to construct a 5-point rectangle-like polygon aligned with the dominant edge orientation. The output is a new in-memory QgsVectorLayer named 'Rectangles' containing these adjusted polygons, added to the QGIS map layer registry alongside the original footprints. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; input is purely vector geometry from a local file path '/qgis_data/shapes/irregular.shp'. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods beyond deterministic Euclidean geometry are not specified.

name: Dissolve features with sum aggregation
desc: The script performs a vector-based dissolve operation on an input vector layer using a specified categorical field (dissolve_field), while simultaneously aggregating (summing) numeric values from a selected field (sum_field) across dissolved groups. It first computes the sum per unique value of the dissolve field by iterating over all source features, then runs QGIS's native:dissolve algorithm to merge geometries, and finally constructs output features with the dissolved geometry and the precomputed summed attribute. The output is a new vector layer with two fields: the original dissolve field (as string) and a new field named 'SUM_' + sum_field (as double), containing the aggregated sums. No raster data, time-series, or remote sensing calculations are involved; the script operates purely on vector attribute and geometry logic within QGIS Processing Framework. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and sensor information are not specified.

name: Convert attribute table to raster style
desc: The script reads a vector attribute table (e.g., DBF) containing pixel value–class mappings and associated color definitions (RGB, HSV, hex, or random), then generates and applies a QgsColorRampShader-based pseudocolor renderer to a raster layer in QGIS. It optionally reclassifies the input raster into a new GeoTIFF using the value mapping and applies the same style to the output. The workflow includes field extraction, color ramp construction, shader creation, renderer assignment, and optional raster reclassification and TOC insertion. No remote sensing analysis, time-series processing, or geospatial modeling is performed — it is strictly a QGIS desktop plugin for visual styling and categorical reclassification based on tabular metadata. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor information are not involved or referenced in the code.

name: Map COVID-19 mortality rates by US state
desc: The script maps and visualizes state-level COVID-19 mortality rates across the contiguous United States using joined administrative boundaries (TIGER/2017 US states) and daily Johns Hopkins CSSE COVID-19 US reports. It filters out non-contiguous territories (Alaska, Hawaii, PR, Guam, etc.), computes a graduated color symbology for mortality rate (Data_Mortality_Rate), applies labeling for deaths, generates a print layout with legend and map extent matching the layer’s bounding box, and exports a PNG image titled 'Geographic_distribution_Number_deaths.png'. The analysis is purely vector-based (no raster or satellite data), relying on CSV-derived attributes joined to polygon geometry; no classification algorithm or modeling is performed—only cartographic rendering and statistical aggregation (top/bottom 5 rankings, pie chart of active cases). Data sources are static shapefiles and GitHub-hosted CSVs; no time-series analysis or temporal filtering beyond selecting a single date (2 days prior to execution) is conducted.

name: Compute minimal bounding circle
desc: The script computes the minimal bounding circle (smallest enclosing circle) for each convex hull geometry derived from 'districtes' and 'barris' layers in a GeoPackage. It uses a computational geometry algorithm that tests all point pairs and triples on the convex hull to find the optimal center and radius. For each feature, it renders a square 200x200 pixel PNG image cropped to the circle's extent, masks it to a circular shape using QPainter.drawEllipse, saves it with a .png extension, and generates a corresponding world file (.pgw) containing georeferencing parameters (pixel scale and top-left corner coordinates). Output filenames are based on feature names (e.g., 'Les Corts_districtes.png').

name: Generate circular map captures
desc: The script generates circular PNG map captures centered on the minimal bounding circle of each district or neighborhood geometry from 'districtes' and 'barris' layers in 'Dades\Zones.gpkg'. It computes the minimal enclosing circle for each feature's convex hull, sets a QgsMapSettings extent to that circle, renders the map image, masks it to a circular shape using QPainter, saves the PNG with a .pgw world file for georeferencing, and outputs metadata including center coordinates and radius for each zone.

name: Generate random point layer
desc: The script creates a memory-based QGIS vector layer of n randomly generated point features in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), each assigned a unique integer ID and placed at random integer coordinates (x,y) within the range [1,50] for both axes. No geospatial analysis, classification, remote sensing processing, or external data ingestion is performed. The output is a QgsVectorLayer object added to the current QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, classification methods, and derived products are all not specified.

name: Join GLF footprints with classification attributes
desc: The script joins Souness GLF (Glacial Landform) footprint polygons (from an intersected shapefile with 'context9') with tabular attributes from a CSV file containing Gauss-classified raster attribute table (RAT) data. The join is performed on the 'DN' field in the vector layer and 'FID' field in the CSV, using QGIS's 'qgis:joinattributestable' algorithm. Inputs are 6-band raster-derived vector polygons (filename pattern '*6band*vectorpolygons_isectCtx9.shp') and corresponding ASCII RAT CSV files ('*6band*ASCII_RAT_GaussClass_noNDR.csv'). Outputs are new shapefiles named with '_joined' suffix, retaining original geometry and appending CSV attributes. The study area is implied by the local filesystem path and naming conventions (e.g., 'SounessCatalog3_backup', 'rsgis_02sqkm'), consistent with planetary geomorphology mapping of glacial landforms—likely Mars, given 'Souness' refers to the published Souness et al. (2012, 2016) catalogs of Martian glacial landforms. No satellite imagery processing occurs in this script; it is purely vector–tabular attribute joining. Data sources are local disk files—not GEE assets—so no GEE image collections, dates, or sensors are involved.

name: Intersect DEM-derived segments with glacial landform contexts
desc: The script intersects vector polygons derived from RSGISlib segmentation of a DEM layerstack with five pre-defined Souness Glacial Landform (GLF) shapefiles: (1) GLF head locations, (2) 5 km buffers around GLF heads, (3) GLF extent polygons, (4) GLF context polygons, and (5) GLF context9 polygons (likely a refined or expanded context class). All inputs are in Mars 2000 Equidistant Cylindrical projection (lat_ts=40). The output consists of four new shapefiles per input segment polygon file — one for each intersection type — written to the same directory as the source *6band*vectorpolygons.shp files under names like '_isectHead.shp', '_isectHead5km.shp', '_isectCtx.shp', and '_isectCtx9.shp'. The study area is implicitly Mars (via coordinate system '+proj=eqc +lat_ts=40 +a=3396190 +b=3376200' and dataset names 'SounessROI...' referencing Martian glacial landforms), and the workflow uses QGIS geoprocessing ('qgis:extractbylocation') within a Python/GEE-adjacent local GIS environment (though not Google Earth Engine itself — this is a QGIS/PyQGIS script mistakenly labeled as GEE). No satellite, sensor, or band information is present; the primary raster input (DEM layerstack) is not specified in the script beyond being segmented by RSGISlib. Time range is not specified.

name: Classify land cover with CNN-supervised learning
desc: The script performs a two-stage supervised classification of a local RGB image: first using a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to generate tile-level class predictions (50×50 pixel tiles), then refining the result using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) trained on CNN-predicted class labels and median-filtered RGB pixel values. Input is a local georeferenced RGB image (e.g., aerial or satellite-derived mosaic), optionally validated against a ground-truth class raster. The CNN model is loaded from a user-specified .h5 file trained externally (via TrainCNN.py), and class mapping is guided by a CSV key ('LocalClass' → 'HierarchClass'). Outputs are two georeferenced GeoTIFF rasters: (1) 'CLASS_CNN_' + input filename — the CNN tile-based classification map; (2) 'CLASS_CSC_' + input filename — the final pixel-wise CNN-Supervised Classification (CSC) map, produced by the MLP trained on CNN-labeled pixels. Both outputs are automatically loaded into QGIS. Validation reports (classification report and confusion matrix) are printed if a ClassFile is provided.

name: Dissolve vector and clip raster
desc: The script dissolves input vector features (e.g., administrative or land parcel boundaries) into a single multipart geometry, then uses that dissolved geometry as a mask to clip an input raster dataset. The output is a clipped raster matching the spatial extent and shape of the dissolved vector layer. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or classification method is involved — it is a pure geoprocessing workflow using QGIS native and GDAL algorithms. Input vector and raster layers are selected interactively via the plugin dialog; no hard-coded datasets, temporal filters, or spectral operations are present.

name: Identify upstream watershed area
desc: The script identifies the upstream watershed area for a user-selected point along a river network. It uses vector-based spatial operations: (1) a user clicks on a river polyline layer to select a location; (2) the script extracts the downstream and upstream endpoints of the clicked river segment’s multiline geometry; (3) it recursively traverses upstream by spatially intersecting adjacent river segments with watershed polygons (using OGR spatial filters and geometry intersection); (4) all watershed polygon FIDs intersecting the upstream flow path are collected into a list; (5) the corresponding watershed polygons are selected in QGIS. The output is a QGIS vector selection of upstream contributing catchments, which can be saved as a Shapefile. No raster data, satellite imagery, or temporal analysis is used — the workflow is purely vector GIS-based and relies entirely on pre-existing local shapefiles (river centerlines and watershed boundaries). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and coordinate reference system are not specified in the code; CRS handling is delegated to user input in the save dialog.

name: Load AVP project infrastructure layers
desc: The script loads and caches seven vector layers (Cofopri, Comunidades Campesinas, Predio Matriz, Predio Rural, Sitios Arqueologicos, Sunarp Lima PSAD56, Sunarp Lima WGS84) and one raster layer (Anillo Vial) from a GeoServer WFS/WMS endpoint (http://200.121.128.102:8080/geoserver/avp/ows and /geoserver/ddp/wms). It downloads WFS features as local GeoJSON files in the plugin's /data/ directory, verifies layer existence before loading, sets project CRS to EPSG:4326, and adds layers to the QGIS project. The Anillo Vial layer is loaded directly as a WMS raster. Layer loading is gated by internet connectivity checks and user login state.

name: Convert polygon WKT text to georeferenced shapefile
desc: The script converts delimited text files (.txt) containing WKT geometry strings into ESRI Shapefile format, reprojects them to EPSG:4326, adds attribute fields (NOMBRE, CURP, POLIGONO, AREA, PERIMETRO), computes area and perimeter using QGIS geometry functions, populates metadata derived from filename parsing (e.g., CURP extraction, polygon number), and cleans up intermediate layers. Input files are assumed to be in a local Windows directory (F:\), with no Earth Engine (GEE) server-side processing — this is purely a QGIS desktop Python automation script using PyQGIS. No satellite imagery, remote sensing analysis, or GEE-specific operations occur; all geospatial operations are vector-based (WKT parsing, reprojection, field calculation) and executed locally via QgsVectorLayer and QgsVectorFileWriter. Study area, time range, satellite data, and GEE assets are absent — the script operates on pre-existing tabular vector data.

name: Delineate watershed drainage basins
desc: The script delineates drainage basins (watersheds) for seven hydrometric stations (A029, B008, B003, B002, C001, C002, E001) located in the Nechako region of British Columbia, Canada. It uses a precomputed flow direction raster (Flow_Direction.tif) as input to GRASS GIS's r.water.outlet tool to derive basin rasters for each station, using manually identified outlet coordinates (lat/long) that must fall within stream-channel grid cells (as verified against a separate stream channel raster). Each basin raster is then vectorized into a polygon shapefile using GDAL's polygonize tool. The study area is explicitly named 'Nechako database' in file paths; outputs are GeoTIFF rasters and ESRI Shapefiles stored in 'C:/Users/margo/Desktop/Nechako database/GIS/Outputs/'. No satellite, sensor, or band information is present — all inputs are local, pre-processed raster files (flow direction and stream channel), and no time-series or imagery processing occurs. The workflow is purely hydrological terrain analysis based on digital elevation-derived hydrography.

name: Detect land surface change
desc: The script performs multi-algorithm raster-based change detection between two temporally distinct, user-selected raster layers with active temporal properties in QGIS. It buffers the input vector extent by 10 map units, exports the buffered geometry to a temporary shapefile, and invokes one of seven pre-implemented change detection methods (PCA, EVI, NDVI, NGRDI, Euclidean Norm, Correlation Norm, Cosine Norm) — each implemented in external Python modules (e.g., LittoDynChangeDetectorPca) — to compute a change raster from the two input rasters over the buffered ROI. The output is a single-band change raster (e.g., 'pca_changes.tif') saved to a temporary location and loaded as a QgsRasterLayer into the QGIS project. Input rasters are assumed to be georeferenced, co-registered, and compatible in projection and resolution (no reprojection or resampling logic is present). No cloud masking, atmospheric correction, band selection, or spectral index computation is performed inside this script — those operations are delegated to the external detector classes. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the script; all inputs are selected interactively via QGIS GUI widgets. The script does not export final products outside the QGIS session.

name: Binarize grayscale raster
desc: The script performs Otsu's automatic thresholding on a user-specified band of an input raster layer to produce a binary (0/1) output raster. It reads the raster band as a NumPy array, computes the Otsu threshold using skimage.filters.threshold_otsu, applies pixel-wise comparison (arr < th), and optionally fills holes in the binary mask using scipy.ndimage.binary_fill_holes. The output is a GTiff raster with Int32 data type, same geotransform and projection as input, and nodata value set to -9999. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic context is embedded in the code — it is a generic, local, band-agnostic raster processing algorithm operating on any loaded QGIS raster layer.

name: Generate 10km grid mesh
desc: The script generates a 10,000 m × 10,000 m fishnet (regular grid) covering the administrative boundary of Chongqing Municipality, projected in EPSG:2381 (CGCS2000 / 3-degree Gauss-Kruger zone 37), using QGIS native processing algorithm 'native:creategrid'. Input is a GeoJSON file named '重庆市.geojson'; output is saved as '重庆10000x10000渔网测试.geojson'. No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or thematic modeling is performed — the task is purely geometric mesh generation for spatial partitioning or sampling design. Study area is explicitly Chongqing; projection and spacing are specified; no temporal component, cloud masking, spectral indices, or machine learning methods are involved.

name: Assess crop damage area
desc: The script assesses agricultural crop damage extent using a precomputed DVDI (Dual-polarization Damage Detection Index) raster derived from Sentinel-1 SLC imagery. It applies a two-stage thresholding workflow: (1) reclassifies pixels exceeding a user-defined dB difference threshold (e.g., −3 dB) into preliminary damaged/non-damaged classes; (2) applies morphological shrink-and-expand filtering to remove noise and fill holes; (3) converts the filtered raster to vector polygons; (4) computes polygon areas and filters out features smaller than a user-specified area threshold (e.g., 10,000 m²); and (5) rasterizes the final filtered polygons to produce a cleaned damage map. The output includes a final binary damage raster (FinalRaster.tif), a vector layer of validated damage polygons (FinalVector.shp), and a QMessageBox reporting the total estimated damaged area in map units.

name: Detect crop damage area
desc: The script detects and quantifies agricultural crop damage by computing the pixel-wise backscatter difference (in dB) between pre-event and post-event Sentinel-1 SLC (Single Look Complex) SAR images. It applies raster differencing, boundary-constrained clipping, mosaic integration across multiple image frames (e.g., different acquisition geometries or tiles), threshold-based reclassification to isolate significant change, morphological shrink-and-expand filtering to remove noise and fill gaps, vectorization, area-based attribute filtering (removing polygons smaller than user-defined area threshold), and final rasterization. The output is a cleaned, georeferenced binary damage raster and a vector layer of validated damaged polygons, accompanied by a total estimated damaged area (in map units) reported via GUI message.

name: Measure river bank and flood line distances
desc: The script computes perpendicular distances from a reference line (chainage line) to both river banks and a flood line, generating a CSV with three distance metrics per perpendicular: (1) from reference line to left river bank, (2) to right river bank, and (3) to flood line. It achieves this by first densifying the reference line with XY coordinates, generating perpendicular line segments at each vertex, intersecting those segments with input river bank and flood line vector layers, extracting geometry of intersection points, and finally computing planar (ellipsoidal WGS84) distances from each reference point to its three intersection points. Outputs include shapefiles for perpendiculars and intersections, a coordinate CSV, and the final summary CSV with line-numbered distance measurements.

name: Generate hillshade and slope maps
desc: The script reprojects a vector layer of Brazilian states ('Estados Brasil lim_unidade_federacao_a') to EPSG:102033, then loads a local SRTM-derived raster ('BR_SRTM.tif') and applies two GDAL/QGIS geoprocessing algorithms: 'qgis:hillshade' (with azimuth=300°, vertical angle=40°, z-factor=111120) and 'gdal:slope' (band=1, scale=111120, not computing edges, Zevenbergen=False). The outputs are visualized hillshade and slope rasters loaded into the QGIS canvas. No classification, time-series, or statistical analysis is performed; the core task is terrain derivative generation from a pre-existing DEM. Study area is implicitly Brazil (via 'Estados Brasil' layer and 'BR_SRTM' filename), but no explicit spatial extent or CRS for the raster is defined in the script — it is loaded as-is. All operations are desktop GIS (QGIS Python API), not GEE — despite the prompt stating 'You are a professional GEE developer', the script contains zero Earth Engine (ee.*) code and instead uses PyQGIS (QgsProject, iface, processing).

name: Calculate NDVI from Landsat 8 bands
desc: The script loads a pre-processed, cut Landsat 8 surface reflectance raster (L8_20180901_cortado.tif) for the PARNASO area, applies contrast enhancement and band-based RGB visualization (red=band 4, green=band 1), then computes NDVI using band 4 (NIR) and band 1 (blue) via GDAL Raster Calculator with formula '(A-B)/(A+B)'. The resulting NDVI raster is loaded, assigned a custom interpolated color ramp (red → yellow → green) based on its min/mean/max statistics, and rendered as a pseudo-color layer. Histograms for both the original RGB raster and the NDVI layer are generated and saved as PNG files. The study area is explicitly named 'PARNASO', the acquisition date is 2018-09-01, and the sensor bands used for NDVI are band 4 (NIR) and band 1 (blue) — indicating non-standard NDVI computation (typically NIR/red); however, the script logic and band indexing (0-based or 1-based?) is ambiguous, but the code explicitly uses BAND_A=4 and BAND_B=1 in the raster calculator call. Final outputs: (1) enhanced RGB visualization of the input raster, (2) NDVI raster file (NDVI.tif), (3) styled NDVI layer in QGIS, (4) two histogram images (HistogramaRGB.png, HistogramaNDVI.png).

name: Map civilian violence events
desc: The script loads a CSV file containing geolocated ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data) records from November 2020 in the USA, filters out Alaska and Hawaii, selects only 'Violence against civilians' events, creates a new vector layer from those selected features, exports it as GeoJSON, and visualizes it first as red point symbols then as a heatmap using the Magma color ramp. The study area is the conterminous United States; the time range is explicitly tied to the filename 'USA_2020_Nov21.csv', indicating data collected through November 21, 2020. No satellite, sensor, or band-based analysis is performed — the input is purely tabular point data with longitude/latitude coordinates. Outputs include a filtered and exported GeoJSON layer and two symbology renderings (point and heatmap) in QGIS.

name: Generate terrain analysis products
desc: The script automates a comprehensive terrain analysis workflow using locally stored DEMs (in meters) to produce: (1) a mosaicked and resampled DEM (displayed with cumulative count cut symbology); (2) a hillshade raster (stretched between 2nd and 98th percentiles); (3) a vertical-unit-converted DEM (meters → feet); (4) base and index contour vector layers (in feet); (5) slope-as-percent raster and its classified/vectorized equivalents; (6) aspect raster (with rainbow gradient) and its classified/vectorized equivalents; (7) a filled DEM for hydrologic analysis; and (8) a Strahler-order-classified vector channel network. All outputs are saved to a project-local 'Script-Outputs' folder and added to the QGIS map canvas with domain-appropriate symbology.

name: Create polygon vector layer
desc: The script programmatically constructs a memory-based QgsVectorLayer of type 'Polygon' with two manually defined polygon geometries using QgsPointXY coordinates, adds them via the data provider, updates layer extents, adds the layer to the current QGIS project, and exports it to a Shapefile ('test.shf'). No geospatial analysis, remote sensing data, time-series processing, classification, or external datasets are involved — it is purely vector geometry creation and I/O. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, classification methods, and analytical outputs are all not specified.

name: Generate county-level buffer zones
desc: The script processes a point dataset (Test.txt) containing longitude and latitude coordinates to create three concentric variable-distance buffers (64Distance, 50Distance, 34Distance) around each point. It then computes ring-shaped difference layers (64kt−50kt, 50kt−34kt) and clips each buffer or ring to U.S. county boundaries (cb_2015_us_county_5m.shp), producing three clipped polygon outputs: one for the full 64-knot buffer area, one for the 50–64 knot annulus, and one for the 34–50 knot annulus. The study area is explicitly limited to U.S. counties; the input point data appears related to tropical cyclone wind radii (given field names '64Distance', '50Distance', '34Distance' — standard Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind radii thresholds in nautical miles), suggesting hazard exposure mapping. No satellite, temporal, or spectral analysis is performed; all operations are vector-based GIS workflows in QGIS via PyQGIS. Outputs are shapefiles: temp_clip1.shp, temp_clip2.shp, temp_clip3.shp.

name: Generate Roman milestone points
desc: The script processes the 'Appia Antica' line layer to generate evenly spaced point features (miliaria) along it at 1480-meter intervals, starting 1480 meters from the beginning of each line segment. It then assigns sequential 'miliarium' identifiers per line group using an auto-increment field. The original intermediate 'miliaria' layer is removed after final output creation. The workflow uses QGIS native processing algorithms 'pointsalonglines' and 'addautoincrementalfield', operating entirely within memory layers.

name: Adjust platform elevation for road access
desc: The script adjusts the elevation (z-value) of polygonal platform features to ensure minimal vertical difference with adjacent road segments, enabling feasible internal ramp access; it computes optimal platform elevation based on perimeter-to-ramp-length ratio and ramp gradient (1:GRAD), then generates two outputs: (1) a Z-enabled polygon layer 'Platform_adjusted' with updated 'platz' elevation values, and (2) a point layer 'Access_adjusted' containing interpolated access points along intersecting road segments, each assigned an access elevation ('accz') and linked attributes (platid, lid, wid, etc.).
