The workflow includes boundary extraction, buffering, intersection with road centerlines (Segmentz), multipart-to-singlepart conversion, line substring trimming, z-value validation, per-platform minimum-elevation-difference selection, and geometry-aware interpolation of access points at 10% or 90% along the intersecting segment depending on which endpoint yields smaller elevation difference.

name: Generate platform access points
desc: The script computes 3D access points between railway/platform polygons and adjacent road centerline segments, using platform elevation (platz), road segment z-values (sz, ez), perimeter-derived maximum ramp length constraints, and user-defined gradient (1:GRAD) and perimeter-to-ramp-length ratio (RATIO). It outputs a point layer (Access) with interpolated 3D geometries at calculated access elevations (accz), plus an optional Inaccessible platform layer for platforms failing ramp feasibility. Input layers are pre-styled with QML files (Node_z.qml, Segment_simple.qml, Inaccessible.qml, Platform_access.qml), and visibility of non-input layers is optionally toggled off.

name: Extend platform polygons to road center lines
desc: The script generates polygonized platform geometries extended to road center lines by buffering road nodes, merging with road segments and platform lines, polygonizing the combined line network, filtering out small polygons (area > 200 m²), computing mean elevation from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) via zonal statistics, adjusting the platform elevation downward by 0.4% (via expression `"_mean" * .996`), adding fields for adjusted platform elevation (`platz`) and raw mean DEM value (`meanz`), and assigning the adjusted elevation as Z-values to the output 3D polygon layer; the output is styled using a QML file (`Platform_rdm_z_downcen.qml`) and loaded into the QGIS project.

name: Compute linear-polygon intersection count
desc: The script computes the total number of geometric intersection points between input vector layers of mixed geometry types (linear and polygon). It merges all input layers into a single layer, then calculates pairwise intersections between line and polygon geometries — specifically extracting point geometries where lines cross polygon boundaries or interiors. The output is a point vector layer containing one point per detected intersection, along with a summary dictionary reporting the input layer names and the total count. No raster data, time-series, remote sensing indices, or classification is involved; the analysis is purely vector-based topological computation using QGIS processing core geometry operations (e.g., QgsGeometry.intersection()). Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and sensor information are not specified — this is a generic GIS vector topology tool operating on user-provided local or loaded vector layers in QGIS.

name: Buffer boxes and classify cables by capacity and connection count
desc: The script performs two main geoprocessing tasks: (1) creates a dissolved buffer polygon layer around input vector features (e.g., utility boxes) using a user-specified distance; (2) filters a preloaded 'cables' vector layer (from a local Shapefile) to select only cable segments where 'capacite' > user-defined threshold AND 'mode_pose' equals user-specified string (e.g., 'AERIEN'), then saves the selection and applies a graduated symbology renderer based on the 'nb_prises' attribute (number of outlets/connections), with four classes (Faible, Moyen_1, Moyen_2, Eleve) mapped to green/yellow/orange/red colors. Outputs are two vector layers: buffered polygons and filtered+styled cables.

name: Generate elevation contour lines
desc: The script loads a local ASCII DEM raster file (dem.asc) into QGIS and runs the GDAL 'contour' algorithm to generate vector contour lines at 50-meter elevation intervals. The output is a shapefile (/Users/georg/GIS/contours.shp) containing polyline features with an 'Elv' attribute storing elevation values. No remote sensing data, time-series, cloud masking, classification, or satellite-derived processing is involved — it is a deterministic, single-band, static topographic vectorization workflow using a pre-existing DEM. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Generate hillshade from DEM
desc: The script generates a hillshade raster from a local ASCII DEM file (dem.asc) using GDAL's hillshade algorithm in QGIS Processing. Input is a single-band raster with no temporal component; parameters include azimuth=315°, altitude=45°, z-factor=1.0, and scale=1.0. The output is saved as a GeoTIFF (hillshade.tif). No study area, time range, satellite, sensor, or bands are involved — the input is a static, locally stored digital elevation model. All geospatial operations are deterministic raster terrain rendering, not classification or time-series analysis.

name: Resample raster resolution
desc: The script resamples a local GeoTIFF raster file (/Users/georg/Downloads/SatImage/SatImage.tif) to coarser spatial resolution by doubling the original pixel size (using rasterUnitsPerPixelX() * 2), reprojects it to its native CRS (retrieved via crs().postgisSrid()), and exports the result as /Users/georg/GIS/resampled.tif. It uses GDAL's 'warpreproject' algorithm (equivalent to gdalwarp) with nearest-neighbor resampling (RESAMPLING: 0). No classification, time-series analysis, spectral index calculation, or thematic mapping is performed. Input CRS, extent, and resolution are derived dynamically from the source layer; no external GEE ImageCollection, satellite data, bands, or temporal filtering is involved — this is a local QGIS Python processing script, not a Google Earth Engine script. The script runs entirely outside GEE using PyQGIS and GDAL.

name: Calculate vegetation quality index
desc: The script computes a composite Vegetation Quality Index (VQI) by integrating four ecological indicator layers derived from ESA CCI Land Cover and MaxNDVI Plant Cover composites: (1) Plant Cover Score (normalized and reclassified NDVI-based plant cover), (2) Erosion Protection Index (reclassified land cover classes mapped to erosion resistance levels), (3) Fire Risk Score (reclassified land cover classes mapped to fire susceptibility), and (4) Drought Resistance Score (reclassified land cover classes mapped to drought resilience). Each indicator is rescaled to a 1.0–2.0 continuous score via table-based reclassification; the final VQI is the geometric mean (fourth root of the product) of these four scores, producing a single raster representing integrated vegetation functional quality.

name: Compute Vegetation Quality Index
desc: The script computes a Vegetation Quality Index (VQI) raster by geometrically averaging four input thematic rasters: fire risk, drought resistance, vegetation cover, and erosion protection. All inputs are reprojected to match a reference raster’s CRS, extent, and cell size. The VQI is calculated per pixel as the fourth root of the product (FR × DR × VC × EP), with nodata handling using masked arrays and QGIS’s default float32 nodata value (-3.4028230607370965e+38). Outputs include a single-band GeoTIFF raster with georeferencing and projection inherited from the reference raster. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is specified in the code; all inputs are user-provided local raster files (TIFF format), and no remote sensing imagery or time-series processing is involved.

name: Aggregate administrative area by mesh
desc: The script performs spatial aggregation of administrative boundary polygons (INPUT) to mesh polygons (meshlayer) using area-proportional apportionment. It first computes the area of each administrative polygon, then unions it with the mesh layer to generate intersecting polygons. For each intersecting polygon, it calculates its area and the ratio of that area to the original administrative polygon's area. Using this ratio, it apportions (scales) a user-specified numeric field (aggrefield, e.g., population or area) from the administrative layer to the intersecting polygons. Finally, it aggregates (sums) the apportioned values by mesh ID (meshid field) and joins the aggregated results back to the original mesh layer, producing an output vector layer where each mesh polygon has an attribute (e.g., 'snum') representing the total apportioned value within that mesh.

name: Aggregate population to mesh units
desc: The script performs areal interpolation of population (or other attribute) values from an input 'population × administrative boundary' polygon layer to a target mesh (grid) layer. It does so by computing the geometric intersection (via union) between the two layers, calculating the area ratio of each intersected polygon relative to its original administrative-population polygon, scaling the population value proportionally by that ratio, and then aggregating (summing) the scaled values per mesh ID. The final output is a mesh layer with one attribute — 'snum' — representing the estimated total population (or other proportional quantity) assigned to each mesh unit.

name: Aggregate CSV addresses to mesh polygons
desc: The script reads a CSV file containing address records, spatially joins them to an administrative address layer (e.g., postal or block-level polygons), then aggregates the count of addresses per mesh polygon (e.g., Japanese 500-m or 1-km mesh) using geometric intersection. When aggregated counts fall below a user-defined minimum sample size (e.g., <3), it optionally applies iterative mesh subdivision (up to maxdivide levels) — either uniformly (equal partitioning) or unevenly (preserving parent mesh IDs and excluding problematic subdivisions) — until all mesh units meet the threshold or maximum iterations are reached. Outputs a vector layer (GeoPackage or other format) with mesh polygons attributed by aggregated count ('snum'), optionally reprojected to a specified CRS.

name: Aggregate population by mesh
desc: The script performs spatial disaggregation and aggregation of population data using administrative boundaries, census-based population mesh layers, and CSV-sourced address-level point data (e.g., survey samples or facility counts). It first joins CSV addresses to administrative polygons, then unions them with high-resolution population mesh (e.g., Japanese 1-km mesh), computes proportional population allocation ratios (pv / oppv), applies those ratios to scale sample counts (snum) into estimated mesh-level population values (pvsum), and finally aggregates these estimates into user-provided target mesh polygons (e.g., 500-m or municipal meshes). It supports iterative mesh subdivision (up to maxdivide times) and optional uneven division to ensure all output mesh units meet a minimum sample count threshold (limit_sample), retaining under-threshold parent meshes unchanged while subdividing others — producing a final vector layer with mesh IDs and aggregated population-like values (snum-adjusted pvsum).

name: Aggregate CSV addresses by administrative polygons
desc: The script reads a CSV file containing address records, joins them to a polygon vector layer (e.g., administrative boundaries) based on a shared address field, computes counts per polygon (implicitly via join + optional aggregation — though the current logic lacks explicit count aggregation and instead relies on downstream use of joined attributes; however, the plugin name 'Stat_CSVAddressPolygon' and description 'CSV住所別集計(行政界別)' confirm its purpose is statistical aggregation of CSV address occurrences per administrative polygon), and outputs a georeferenced vector layer (e.g., GeoPackage or other format) with joined attributes — including a 'snum' field initialized/updated to 0 where null, suggesting it is intended to hold summary counts. The workflow includes CSV parsing (with encoding selection), spatial join, packaging, NULL handling in SpatiaLite, and optional reprojection.

name: Aggregate addresses by CSV counts
desc: The script reads a user-provided CSV file, counts occurrences per unique value in a specified address field, joins those counts to a polygon vector layer (e.g., administrative or address polygons), fills null count values with zero, and exports the joined, updated layer as a GeoJSON file. The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms: CSV-to-stat table conversion, attribute table join (on address field), GeoPackage packaging, SpatiaLite SQL update to set NULL counts to 0, and GDAL format conversion to GeoJSON. No remote sensing data, imagery, or time-series analysis is involved; all inputs are local vector/CSV files. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Allocate mesh population to administrative boundaries
desc: The script performs a spatial disaggregation of population from statistical mesh polygons to administrative boundary polygons using area-proportional allocation. It first computes the area of each population mesh polygon, then unions the mesh layer with an administrative boundary layer (e.g., address/ward polygons), computes the area of each resulting intersection polygon, and calculates a proportional population value (dpop) for each intersection as: (intersection_area / original_mesh_area) × mesh_population. Finally, it aggregates these allocated population values by administrative unit (grouping on the specified address field) and joins the summed results back to the original administrative layer, producing an output vector layer with population estimates per administrative unit.

name: Generate Voronoi polygons from category points
desc: The script reads a GeoPackage file (nc_result.gpkg) containing point features with a 'category' attribute, computes Voronoi polygons covering the extent of the input points (with zero buffer), then dissolves the resulting polygons by the 'category' field to produce aggregated, non-overlapping polygon regions representing spatial dominance zones per category. The final output is a dissolved GeoPackage (nc_vor_poly_dissolve.gpkg) where each feature corresponds to a merged Voronoi region for a unique category value.

name: Color-code soil nutrient fields
desc: The script generates a QGIS project containing a vector layer of field polygons (imported from a user-provided GeoJSON file), applies thematic color-coding based on soil variables (e.g., 'P index', 'pH'), adds labeled maps with scalebar and north arrow, inserts a data table showing UI-friendly attribute fields (e.g., 'name', 'Area (ha)' or 'Area (ac)'), and exports a custom layout to PDF. It uses EPSG:32629 (UTM zone 29N) for projection, overlays ESRI World Imagery as a basemap, and organizes outputs in a structured QGIS project (.qgs) with embedded styling, labeling, and layout elements. The study area is not defined by the script itself — it is fully driven by the input GeoJSON geometry and CRS transformation logic; no fixed region, time range, or satellite data is used.

name: Color-code soil polygon layers
desc: The script generates a QGIS project (.qgs) containing a vector layer loaded from an input GeoJSON file (field polygons), applies thematic color rendering based on user-specified attributes (e.g., 'index', 'pH', or arbitrary numeric fields), adds labeled map layouts with scalebar, north arrow, farm name, and attribute tables, and optionally exports the layout to PDF. It uses EPSG:32629 (UTM zone 29N) as the project CRS, overlays ESRI World Imagery via XYZ tile layer, and performs coordinate transformation of layer extents for map framing. The study area is not specified in the code; no temporal analysis or satellite-derived data processing occurs — all inputs are static vector geometries and attributes from the provided JSON file.

name: Generate field layout map
desc: The script generates a QGIS project (.qgs) containing a vector layer of agricultural fields (from input GeoJSON), styled polygons (with optional color-coding by attribute), labeled features, a full-page A1 landscape layout with a main map, optional inset maps, an attribute table showing specified fields (e.g., 'name', 'referenceArea_ha'), scale bar, north arrow, farm name label, color coding legend, and optional PDF export. It uses EPSG:32629 (UTM zone 29N) CRS and adds an ESRI World Imagery WMS basemap. The workflow includes layer creation, geometry reprojection, symbology assignment (default white outline/no fill or graduated/colored by user-specified field), labeling, layout item placement, and project persistence. Study area is not specified in the code; no time-series analysis or temporal filtering is performed — input is static GeoJSON. Data sources are limited to the user-provided JSON file and the external WMS tile layer.

name: Rasterize landslide susceptibility factors
desc: The script prepares geospatial inputs for landslide susceptibility analysis by rasterizing discrete conditioning factors (UGS, SubunidadesGeomorf, CoberturaUso, CambioCobertura) from vector shapefiles using field-based encoding and GDAL rasterization; extracts and harmonizes landslide and rockfall occurrences from point/polygon vector layers; converts polygons to points (centroids or pixel-centroids); merges overlapping point sources; splits landslides into success/validation subsets (user-defined %); exports all outputs as GeoTIFFs and shapefiles to /Pre_Proceso/, /Resultados/, /Amenaza/, and validation curve directories. Inputs include user-specified local shapefiles and rasters; no satellite or cloud-based Earth Engine assets are used — this is a QGIS Python Processing script, not a GEE (Google Earth Engine) script. The workflow assumes planar CRS, requires matching attribute field names across point/polygon MM layers, and generates lookup CSVs (e.g., DF_Raster_UGS.csv) mapping original codes to integer raster values. Study area boundary is optionally provided as a polygon shapefile.

name: Characterize landslide susceptibility for rockfall
desc: The script characterizes susceptibility to rockfall-type mass movements using three geospatial conditioners: (1) slope (reclassified to binary 0/1 based on user-defined threshold, default ≥45°), (2) geomorphic subunits (reclassified via lookup table from 'GeoformasIndicativasProcesoTipoCaida.csv' using first 3 characters of acronyms, assigning values 0/1/2), and (3) surficial geological units (UGS, reclassified to values 0/2/5 based on rock hardness: 'Rb'=soft=5, 'Ri'=intermediate=2, else=hard/soils=0). These rasters are summed, then reclassified into final susceptibility classes (Baja/Media/Alta) for both initiation zones and deposition zones. Deposition zones are integrated by rasterizing input polygon layers ('Zona_Deposito', 'Caida_poligonos') and overwriting the summed susceptibility raster with value 4 (later remapped to 'Alta'). Outputs include: (i) pre-processed CSVs ('DF_RasterCaida_SubunidadesGeoform.csv', 'DF_Raster_UGS.csv'), (ii) intermediate rasters ('Suscep_Caida_Pendiente.tif', 'Suscep_Caida_SubunidadesGeomorf.tif', 'Suscep_Caida_UGS.tif', 'Susceptibilidad_Caida_Pre.tif', 'Susceptibilidad_Caida_Pre_Ajustada.tif'), and (iii) final classified raster 'Susceptibilidad_Caida.tif' visualized with custom color ramp (green=low, yellow=medium, orange=high). The study area is implied to be in Colombia (author’s institutional email: @uis.edu.co — Universidad Industrial de Santander), but no explicit geographic coordinates or named region (e.g., department, basin) is specified in the code. Input data sources are local files only (no GEE asset IDs or satellite imagery), including user-provided .tif (slope), .shp (deposition zones), and .csv (geoform indicators); no satellite, sensor, or band information is present.

name: Identify landslide trigger mechanisms
desc: The script identifies the dominant triggering mechanism (earthquake vs. rainfall) for historical mass movements in an unspecified study area, using spatiotemporal proximity analysis. Key inputs include: (1) a vector layer of mass movements (Mov_Masa.shp) with date (Fecha_MM) and type (Tipo_MM) attributes; (2) seismic point data (Sismos.shp) with magnitude (Magnitud_Sismo), unit (Unidad_Sismo), and date (Fecha_Sismo); and (3) pluviometric station data (Estaciones.shp) with station codes (Codigo_Estacion). It performs magnitude unit conversion to Mw using multiple empirical formulas (Scordilis, Grunthal, etc.), filters earthquakes ≥5.0 Mw, then matches mass movements to earthquakes occurring within a user-defined temporal window (dias, e.g., 30 days) and spatial distance (<50 km). Remaining movements are assigned 'Lluvia' (rainfall) as trigger. Outputs include: (1) CSV files classifying each mass movement by trigger ('Sismo' or 'Lluvia'); (2) spatially separated vector layers (Mov_Masa_Sismos.shp, Mov_Masa_Lluvias.shp); (3) rasterized Voronoi polygons for rainfall hazard zoning (Poligonos_Voronoi.tif); (4) sampled susceptibility rasters (Susceptibilidad_Deslizamientos.tif, optionally Susceptibilidad_Caida.tif and Susceptibilidad_Flujos.tif) attached to mass movement points; and (5) intermediate geoprocessing outputs (clustered movements, centroids, buffers, clipped polygons). The workflow relies entirely on local vector/raster files — no Earth Engine server-side assets or satellite imagery — and uses QGIS processing algorithms (e.g., native:kmeansclustering, qgis:voronoipolygons, gdal:rasterize).

name: Load municipality boundary layer
desc: The script creates an in-memory QGIS vector layer for municipal boundaries, configures red fill with blue border styling and bold blue labels using the 'clave' attribute, then fetches GeoJSON municipal geometry data from a local HTTP API (http://192.168.0.25:8080) based on the current QGIS project's SRID setting, transforms geometries to that CRS, adds features to the memory layer, and zooms the map canvas to the bounding box of the last loaded geometry.

name: Load administrative boundaries layer
desc: The script loads and displays vector layers representing administrative boundaries—specifically French communes (from 'administratif_commune.shp') and departments (from PostGIS table 'administratif_departement' in schema 'formation'). It performs no geospatial analysis, classification, or time-series processing; the core workflow consists of loading vector layers via QGIS Python API (iface.addVectorLayer or QgsProject.instance().addMapLayer), validating layer integrity, inspecting metadata (CRS, extent, feature count, geometry type), and exporting layers to Shapefile format using QgsVectorFileWriter. The study area is implicitly France (based on layer names 'administratif_commune' and 'administratif_departement', standard French administrative nomenclature), and no satellite, sensor, bands, or temporal data are involved. Outputs include in-session QGIS map layers and two exported Shapefiles: 'export_communes.shp' and 'export_departements.shp'.

name: Filter fire detection events
desc: The script loads a MySQL database table named 'firecard' containing fire detection records, filters them by date range (date_fire_detect_from to date_fire_detect_to) and attribute ft (likely fire type or flag), then converts the filtered query result into a virtual vector layer. It subsequently creates a point layer from that virtual layer using X and Y fields (indexed at 18 and 17 respectively) and reprojects to EPSG:4326. The final output is a reprojected point layer added to the QGIS project for visualization or further analysis. No satellite imagery, cloud masking, classification, or geospatial modeling is performed — only SQL-based filtering and vector geometry reconstruction from tabular coordinates. Study area, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Interpolate atmospheric temperature values
desc: The script performs Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation on point-based CSV data containing latitude/longitude and time-series columnar measurements (e.g., temperature-like variables), using coordinates 'LON'/'LAT' in EPSG:4326. For each column from index 4 onward (skipping first 4 metadata columns), it generates a raster surface at 0.01° resolution over a fixed bounding box (120.8799,14.3239,121.1660,14.8050), converts raster pixels to points, adds X/Y fields, and exports each as a separate CSV file named after the source column (with leading zero for columns <12). The workflow is purely geostatistical interpolation of ground station observations — no satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are tabular point measurements.

name: Locate diamond ore deposits
desc: The script scans Minecraft Anvil region (.mca) files to identify coordinates of blocks matching TRACKED_ORES (specifically 'minecraft:diamond_ore' by default) using NBT parsing and palette-based BlockStates decoding. It decodes block state arrays from chunk sections—applying legacy unstream() for DataVersion < 2529 and nether_unstream() for ≥2529 (1.16 Nether Update format)—then maps indices to world coordinates (x,y,z) via bit-masking logic in index_to_coordinates(). It creates a QGIS memory vector layer of Point features with attributes: type (block name), x, y, z. The output is a temporary QGIS layer visualizing ore locations in 3D world space. Study area is implicit: a single Minecraft region file (32×32 chunks = 512×512 m horizontal extent); time range is not applicable; data source is local .mca file parsed via overviewernbt; no satellite/sensor/bands involved.

name: Calculate route overlap length
desc: The script computes the geometric overlap between two linear vector layers ('route1' and 'route2'), clips the portion of 'route1' that intersects 'route2', dissolves the resulting overlapping line segments into a single multipart feature, calculates the total length of the dissolved overlap in kilometers, and appends three attributes to the dissolved layer: 'overlap_km' (total overlap length), 'ov_prc_r1' (overlap as percentage of 'route1' total length), and 'ov_prc_r2' (overlap as percentage of 'route2' total length). The final output is a dissolved line layer with these computed metrics stored as attributes.

name: Construct topologically consistent geological map polygons
desc: A polygonal layer with guaranteed topological consistency (no overlaps, holes, or duplicated geometries), generated from input line boundaries and attributed via spatial join with indicator points; the output is suitable for geological mapping applications.

name: Discretize raster by percentiles
desc: The script performs unsupervised discretization of a single-band input raster into 4 ordinal classes (0–3) using quartile thresholds (0th, 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles) computed from the full raster band array. It reads the input raster via GDAL, computes percentiles on flattened pixel values, applies np.digitize to assign integer class labels, and writes the result to a new Byte-typed raster with identical georeferencing (spatial reference and geotransform). No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial context is referenced — the algorithm is purely local, raster-agnostic, and format-driven (GDAL-based), operating solely on the provided raster layer's pixel values. Output is a classified raster file (e.g., .tif) with discrete integer values representing quartile-based intensity bins.

name: Generate suburb-based freight zone maps
desc: The script processes a user-provided suburb/locality shapefile and a text file defining administrative or functional zones (e.g., freight zones), each listing constituent suburbs. It performs spelling correction of suburb names using a custom letter-overlap heuristic (80% character match), harmonizes zone assignments to the suburb layer via attribute joining, splits the layer into per-zone suburb and dissolved boundary shapefiles, and programmatically generates georeferenced, labeled, and styled PDF map layouts (with legend, scalebar, north arrow, title) for each zone — all within QGIS Desktop (not GEE). The output consists of: (1) a modified suburb layer with 'Zone' attribute; (2) individual shapefiles per zone (suburbs + dissolved boundaries); and (3) publication-ready PDF (and PNG) maps per zone.

name: Attach layer fields by nearest neighbors
desc: The script performs a nearest-neighbor spatial join between two vector layers: it computes the Euclidean distance from each feature in the 'Initial layer' to its nearest feature in the 'Layer to link', and appends two new attributes to the output layer — the distance (in source CRS units) and the 'id' field value of the nearest neighbor from the attached layer. The workflow uses centroid geometry for point-based distance computation, handles on-the-fly reprojection when input layers have mismatched CRSs, and relies on scipy's cKDTree for efficient nearest-neighbor search. No raster data, time-series, or satellite imagery is involved; all inputs and outputs are vector features (any geometry type). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Generate perpendicular buffer polygons
desc: The script generates polygon buffers along an input line vector layer by constructing perpendicular line segments at each vertex midpoint, then assembling them into closed polygons. It simplifies the input line to its vertices, computes perpendicular offsets of fixed radius (‘Radius’ parameter) at each segment midpoint, groups consecutive perpendiculars into chunks of fixed length (‘Length’ parameter), and constructs individual polygons from concatenated forward and reverse edge points. Output is a new vector layer of polygons with attributes including ID, centroid coordinates in source CRS, and reprojected (to WGS84/4326) longitude/latitude of the centroid. No raster data, time-series, or satellite imagery is involved — it is purely vector geometric processing within QGIS Processing Framework using GDAL/OGR and NumPy.

name: Smooth coastline geometry
desc: The script simplifies vector line geometries (e.g., coastlines or contours) by applying subsampling and Gaussian filtering to reduce vertex count and suppress high-frequency geometric noise. It reads input vector features, extracts all vertices as coordinate arrays, reparameterizes the line by cumulative Euclidean distance, resamples at a user-defined spacing ('Submuestreo'), applies 1D Gaussian smoothing ('Gaussiano') independently to x and y coordinates, and reconstructs a new smoothed LineString. The output is a single simplified vector line feature with identical CRS and geometry type as input, attributed only with an integer 'id'. No satellite, raster, or temporal data is involved; the algorithm operates purely on vector geometry in Cartesian coordinate space.

name: Compute building morphology parameters
desc: The script computes a suite of geometric and morphological parameters for building polygons, including centroid coordinates (x, y), area, perimeter, shape index (perimeter/(4*sqrt(area))), detour (convex hull perimeter), detour index (perimeter/convex hull perimeter), range (diameter of minimal enclosing circle), range index (normalized compactness ratio), bounding box width and height (lengh is a typo for length), vertex count (pnt_count), exchange (area of intersection between building and its inscribed circle), exchange_index (exchange/area), and perimeter_index (building perimeter / inscribed circle perimeter). It first reprojects the input building layer to a user-specified CRS (default EPSG:5931), then refactors fields to compute all metrics as new attributes, and finally exports the enriched feature layer to an Excel or ODS spreadsheet.

name: Compute building morphology parameters
desc: The script processes OpenStreetMap (OSM) building polygon data for a specific remote community (Arviat, Nunavut) to compute 16 geometric and morphological metrics—including area, perimeter, shape index, detour index, range, range_index, width, length (note: 'lengh' is a typo), point count, exchange area/ratio, and perimeter index—then exports the enriched attribute table to an Excel or ODS spreadsheet. Input CRS is configurable (default EPSG:5931), and the workflow includes OSM file parsing, reprojection, field refactoring with geometry-based expressions, and spreadsheet export.

name: Map ROV seafloor substrate units
desc: The script processes ROV navigation and annotation data to generate spatially explicit, substrate-classified wedge buffers representing the camera viewshed at each annotated seafloor location; it then dissolves overlapping wedges by substrate type to produce a final polygon shapefile of CMECS-compliant substrate mapping units, symbolized with standardized QML styling for visualization in QGIS.

name: Map ecosystem services value
desc: The script maps and visualizes monetary ecosystem services (ES) values per hectare for Timor-Leste, derived from a regional CSV table joined to biome polygons. It produces a multi-panel A4 landscape layout map showing total and disaggregated (Cultural, Regulating, Provisioning) ES values using Jenks natural breaks classification and gradient color ramps. The output includes a main map with protected areas (WDPA), background basemap (CartoDB Positron), graticule, legend, north arrow, BIOPAMA logo, and metadata text box; exported as a 300 DPI PNG file named 'map_es_val_reg.png'. Study area is Timor-Leste; time reference is 2020 USD/ha (from ESVD 2020); data sources include regional_mainESvalue.csv (biome-level ES valuations), timorBiomes.gpkg (biome polygons), WDPA_WDOECM_TLS_shp-polygons.gpkg (protected areas), and Copernicus Hotspot LCCS 2016 land cover (used only for extent setting, not analysis). No satellite imagery or remote sensing processing is performed — all operations are vector-based attribute joins, symbology rendering, and print layout composition in QGIS.

name: Map ecosystem services value
desc: The script maps and visualizes ecosystem services (ES) monetary values per biome in Timor-Leste, using a precomputed CSV table of biome-level ES values (Cultural, Regulating, Provisioning, Total) joined to a vector layer of biomes ('timorBiomes.gpkg'). It produces a QGIS print layout with a main map showing total ES value (Jenks classification, 5 classes, gradient from #ffffcc to #564135), plus inset maps for each ES category (Cultural, Regulating, Provisioning), all overlaid on CartoDB Positron basemap and WDPA protected areas. The layout includes graticule (1° intervals, EPSG:4326), legend, north arrow, BIOPAMA logo, and metadata text. Final output is a PNG export ('map_es_val.png') at 150 DPI to './RAMPAO/sompa_maps/'. Study area is Timor-Leste; time range is not specified in the script; data sources include UNEP-WCMC, Copernicus Hotspot land cover 2016, Conservation International, and ESVD 2020 — but no satellite imagery or Earth Engine code is present: this is a pure QGIS desktop workflow loading local vector/raster layers and CSV.

name: Add XY coordinates to point layer
desc: The script processes shapefiles in a local input directory (C:/input) and, for each point-type vector layer, runs the SAGA GIS 'addcoordinatestopoints' QGIS processing algorithm to append X and Y coordinate fields to the attribute table. The output is a new shapefile saved in C:/output with '_withcoordinatesadded.shp' appended to the original filename. The script filters input layers by geometry type (only QgsWkbTypes.Point), skips non-point layers with a printed message, and handles exceptions during processing. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or GEE-specific functionality is present—the entire workflow is local desktop GIS using QGIS Python bindings and SAGA algorithms. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods beyond coordinate addition are not specified.

name: Compute longest inscribed line
desc: The script computes, for each input point feature, the longest straight-line segment that can be inscribed within the intersecting polygon(s) from a polygon layer. It does so by projecting diametrically opposed rays (180° apart) from each point at azimuth intervals (controlled by 'azimuthsteps'), intersecting those rays with the polygon geometry, extracting all resulting line segments, and selecting the longest one per point. The output is a memory-based vector layer ('Longest_line') containing one LineString feature per input point — the longest line fully contained in the intersecting polygon and passing through that point. No remote sensing data, time-series, or spectral analysis is involved; the workflow is purely vector-based geometric computation using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), with no GEE (Google Earth Engine) code present — despite the prompt's mischaracterization as a 'GEE script'. The script operates entirely within QGIS Desktop via PyQGIS, using spatial indexing, geometry projection, intersection, multipart-to-singlepart conversion, and length evaluation.

name: Snap line endpoints to nearest points
desc: The script modifies the geometry of line features by snapping their start and end vertices to the nearest point features within a specified tolerance (10000 CRS units). It first ensures input points are single-part geometries, builds a spatial index for efficient nearest-neighbor search, then iterates over each line feature’s parts and vertices. Only start and end vertices of each part are considered; if a point lies within the tolerance, that vertex is moved to the coordinates of the nearest point. The output is an in-place edit of the 'lines' vector layer — no new layers or exports are created, and no classification, raster analysis, time-series, or thematic modeling occurs. All operations are purely geometric and topological, performed within QGIS using PyQGIS APIs. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and thematic indicators are not involved — this is a vector GIS editing workflow, not a remote sensing analysis.

name: Fix vector geometry for habitat and infrastructure layers
desc: The script validates and repairs invalid geometries in six input vector layers (frog habitat, administrative region, hydrology, major roads, vegetation, and planning zones) using QGIS processing algorithms ('qgis:checkvalidity' and 'native:fixgeometries'), then exports corrected versions as ESRI Shapefiles to a '_FIXED_DATA' directory. It operates within a QGIS Python environment (not GEE), loading a pre-existing QGIS project, initializing QGIS application and Processing framework, and iterating over layer definitions to ensure topological correctness prior to downstream GIS analysis or modeling.

name: Quantify existing frog habitat vegetation composition
desc: The script analyzes the spatial overlap between existing frog habitat and vegetation cover to quantify the proportional area of each major vegetation type (using NVIS 6.0 classification) within the frog habitat boundary. It also computes the proportional area of hydrological features (e.g., water bodies) within the same frog habitat extent. Key outputs are two CSV files: 'vegetation_existing_habitat.csv' (containing MVS_NAME, total area, percent coverage, and aggregated NVIS_IDs) and 'hydro_existing_habitat.csv' (containing FTYPE_CODE, total area, and percent coverage), both derived from vector-based geometric operations (clip, dissolve, area calculation, aggregation) in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Identify suitable frog habitat areas
desc: The script conducts spatial suitability analysis for Growling Grass Frog (Litoria raniformis) habitat within the 'SOUTHERN METROPOLITAN' administrative region of Victoria, Australia. It integrates vector layers — administrative boundaries, hydrology (watercourses and lakes), planning zones (FARMING, GREEN WEDGE, CONSERVATION, etc.), and vegetation (NVIS-coded), joined with a national vegetation classification lookup table (NVIS6_0_LUT_AUST_FLAT.csv). Key steps include: (1) selecting the 'SOUTHERN METROPOLITAN' study area; (2) filtering hydrology to 'watercourse_area_river' and 'wb_lake' features, applying a 100 m outward buffer, and retaining only water bodies ≥4500 m²; (3) filtering planning zones using keyword matching ('WEDGE', 'FARMING', 'CONSERVATION', etc.) and applying a 50 m inward buffer; (4) intersecting buffered hydrology and zones to define candidate site cores; (5) intersecting those cores with vegetation polygons joined to NVIS vegetation names; (6) dissolving and splitting into single-part candidate regions; and (7) selecting only those regions containing 'Temperate tussock grasslands' (as specified in input), while generating per-region CSV files summarizing vegetation composition (area and % by MVS_NAME). Outputs are: (a) a vector layer of selected suitable habitat polygons (with OBJECTID-based naming), and (b) a folder of CSV files (e.g., 'vegetation_stats_area_1.csv') containing vegetation type-area statistics for each selected region.

name: Render DEM with elevation-based color ramp and multi-interval contours
desc: The script processes a local DEM raster to generate: (1) a pseudo-color rendered DEM layer using a 5-step interpolated color ramp based on elevation quartiles (blue → green → yellow → orange → red), (2) two contour vector layers — one at 400 m interval (darker, semi-transparent black lines) and another at 100 m interval (lighter, more transparent black lines), (3) a hillshade raster (azimuth 300°, Z-factor 1) for terrain visualization, and (4) an OSM-derived point layer of natural peaks (‘natural=peak’) clipped to the DEM extent, styled as black crosses. All layers are added to the QGIS project in overlay order: hillshade (bottom), DEM, fine contours (100 m), coarse contours (400 m), and peaks (top).

name: Plot points and lines by azimuth and distance
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for interactive geodetic plotting: users input an initial coordinate (X/Y or longitude/latitude), then iteratively specify azimuth (bearing) and distance to generate new points along that direction. It supports both point-only and point+line workflows, dynamically creating memory vector layers for points and polylines, populating attribute tables with IDs, coordinates (for points), or lengths (for lines), and transforming coordinates between user-selected CRS and a fixed reference CRS (EPSG:32749 — WGS 84 / UTM zone 49S). The plugin includes CRS-aware UI labeling (e.g., 'Bujur/Lintang' for geographic CRS), validation (e.g., latitude < 90°, distance < ~30,864 km to avoid antipodal ambiguity), and real-time map canvas zoom-to-layer. No remote sensing data, time-series, or classification is involved — it is purely a coordinate geometry and vector feature generation tool.

name: Track ground parrot movement distance
desc: The script computes annual centroid (mean coordinate) locations of Ground Parrot occurrence records (2000–2019) within the East Gippsland study area, then calculates Euclidean distances between consecutive annual centroids to quantify inter-annual movement magnitude — specifically, the straight-line distance (in meters) between the mean location of records in year t and year t+1. Outputs are individual shapefiles (e.g., Mean_dist_2000_2001.shp) containing distance attributes, enabling analysis of temporal movement patterns relative to fire history and habitat (wet heathland).

name: Analyze ground parrot movement distance
desc: The script analyzes Ground Parrot (Pezoporus wallicus) species movement patterns between consecutive years from 2000 to 2019 by computing Euclidean distances between annual mean centroid coordinates of occurrence records. It uses pre-fire ground parrot point records (with STARTDATE field), clips them to the East Gippsland study area (EPSG:7855 → EPSG:3111), extracts year integers from STARTDATE, filters out records before 2000 and null years, splits the layer by YEAR, computes mean coordinates per year (one point per year), then calculates inter-annual distances using QGIS distance matrix (nearest neighbor, single-source-to-single-target). Outputs are individual shapefiles containing distance attributes (e.g., Mean_dist_2000_2001.shp), visualized as vector layers in QGIS. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are local vector shapefiles: east_gippsland.shp (study boundary), pre_fire_gp.shp (occurrence points), hist_fire.shp, post_fire_gp.shp, and heath.shp (wet heathland habitat). The CRS transformation note confirms use of GDA2020 MGA Zone 55 (EPSG:7855) source data, reprojected to EPSG:3111 (VICGRID94) for analysis.

name: Generate watershed superpixel segments
desc: The script performs superpixel segmentation on an input raster using the Watershed algorithm from scikit-image. It reads a multi-band or single-band raster via GDAL, normalizes pixel values using exposure.rescale_intensity, computes a gradient image (using sobel + rgb2gray for multi-band; sobel alone for single-band), and applies the watershed transform with user-defined markers and compactness parameters. The output is a single-band integer raster where each pixel value represents a unique superpixel segment ID. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic coordinates are referenced in the code — it is a generic, file-based, desktop GIS processing algorithm for QGIS, operating entirely on locally provided raster files without any Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, cloud imagery, or spatiotemporal metadata.

name: Generate superpixel segments
desc: The script applies the Felzenszwalb superpixel segmentation algorithm to a user-provided input raster to produce a labeled segment raster where each pixel is assigned an integer ID corresponding to its superpixel region. It reads the input raster via GDAL, stacks all bands into a multichannel NumPy array, normalizes intensity values to [0.0, 1.0] using skimage.exposure.rescale_intensity, and applies felzenszwalb() with configurable scale, sigma, and min_size parameters. The output is a single-band GeoTIFF raster with the same georeferencing (projection, transform) as the input, containing integer segment labels. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is embedded in the code — it is a generic, local, file-based image segmentation tool for QGIS Processing Toolbox.

name: Generate Felzenszwalb superpixel segments
desc: The script applies the Felzenszwalb superpixel segmentation algorithm to a user-provided multiband raster input. It reads the raster using GDAL, stacks its bands into a NumPy array, normalizes pixel values using skimage.exposure.rescale_intensity, and computes superpixels via skimage.segmentation.felzenszwalb with configurable scale, sigma, and min_size parameters. The resulting integer-labeled segment map is written to a GeoTIFF output raster preserving geotransform and projection from the input. No classification or thematic labeling is performed—only geometric segmentation.

name: Generate superpixel segments
desc: The script implements the QuickShift superpixel segmentation algorithm on an input raster layer to produce a segmented output raster where each pixel is assigned a segment ID. It reads the input raster using GDAL, stacks all bands into a 3D NumPy array (height × width × bands), normalizes intensity values using scikit-image's rescale_intensity, applies the quickshift() function with user-specified kernel_size, max_dist, and ratio parameters, and writes the resulting integer-valued segment ID array to a GeoTIFF output raster preserving georeferencing (geotransform and projection). No classification or thematic labeling is performed — only unsupervised spatial grouping (superpixels). Input raster source, study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not specified in the code; the algorithm operates generically on any multiband raster provided via QGIS Processing interface.

name: Generate superpixel segments
desc: The script applies the SLIC (Simple Linear Iterative Clustering) superpixel segmentation algorithm to an input raster layer to produce a labeled raster where each pixel is assigned a segment ID. It reads the input raster using GDAL, stacks all bands into a numpy array, normalizes intensity values using skimage.exposure.rescale_intensity, and runs slic() with user-configurable parameters (number of segments, compactness, sigma, start label). The output is a single-band raster of integer segment labels, georeferenced and projected identically to the input. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic region is referenced in the code — it is a generic, local, file-based image processing algorithm operating on any provided GeoTIFF or GDAL-readable raster. Input bands are read wholesale without selection or transformation; multiband handling is automatic but no band-specific logic (e.g., NDVI, indices) is implemented. All operations occur client-side within QGIS Processing Framework using scikit-image and GDAL.

name: Watershed superpixel segmentation
desc: The script performs watershed-based superpixel segmentation on an input raster using scikit-image's watershed algorithm. It reads a user-provided raster (any number of bands), normalizes pixel intensities, computes a Sobel gradient image (grayscale conversion applied for multi-band inputs), and applies watershed segmentation with user-defined markers and compactness parameters. The output is a single-band integer raster where each pixel value represents a unique segment ID. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial metadata (e.g., projection handling beyond copying from input) is embedded in the logic — it is a generic, local, band-agnostic image segmentation tool operating purely on the provided raster file’s pixel values and geotransform/CRS metadata. Input raster source is read via QGIS’s QgsRasterLayer and GDAL; no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, collections, or remote sensing-specific preprocessing (e.g., cloud masking, atmospheric correction, spectral index computation) are present — despite the prompt mentioning 'GEE script', the code is purely a QGIS Processing plugin written in Python using GDAL and scikit-image.

name: Calculate hospital accessibility matrix
desc: The script computes origin-destination (OD) travel time and distance matrices between municipalities (nodes) within each mesoregion of Minas Gerais, Brazil, using the ORS Tools plugin in QGIS. It selects only municipalities with SUS-funded ICU beds ('UTI_SUS' is not null) as destinations, performs a many-to-many road network matrix calculation (via OpenRouteService), constructs virtual line layers representing OD flows, saves them as GeoPackage layers, and aggregates results per origin municipality to identify the fastest travel time (min(DURATION_H)) — producing optimized accessibility metrics for healthcare infrastructure planning.

name: Calculate hospital accessibility matrix
desc: The script calculates origin-destination travel time and distance matrices between municipalities with hospitals equipped with UTI (Intensive Care Units) in Minas Gerais, Brazil. It iterates over a vector layer of municipalities (identified by 'CD_GEOCMI'), selects only those with UTI_SUS attribute populated, uses ORS Tools to compute road-network-based matrices (duration in hours and distance in km), constructs virtual line layers representing origin-destination flows, saves them as GeoPackage layers, and aggregates results per origin municipality to identify fastest routes. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage layer 'PROVISORIO' storing raw OD matrices; (2) virtual 'FLUXO' layers visualizing flow lines; (3) saved GeoPackage files named 'FLUXO_<region>.gpkg'; and (4) aggregated result layers 'RESULTADOS_<region>.gpkg' containing minimum duration per origin ID.

name: Calculate hospital accessibility matrix
desc: The script computes an origin-destination (OD) distance and travel time matrix between municipalities with hospitals equipped with UTI-SUS in the Jequitinhonha region of Minas Gerais, Brazil. It loads a GeoPackage layer named after the region ('JEQUITINHONHA'), selects only points where 'UTI_SUS' is not null, runs ORS Tools' matrix_from_layers algorithm using the same layer for origins and destinations, creates a virtual line layer ('FLUXO') joining origin and destination geometries with duration and distance attributes, saves it as a GeoPackage, then executes an SQL GROUP BY query to compute the minimum travel time ('fastest') per origin ID. Outputs include a renamed matrix layer, a virtual flux layer, a saved FLUXO GeoPackage, and a final aggregated result GeoPackage with fastest travel times per origin.

name: Join census tract attributes
desc: The script joins a CSV file containing U.S. Census ACS data to a shapefile of census tracts (Hancock County) using a common identifier field (GEOid2 in CSV and GEOID in shapefile). It uses QGIS's QgsVectorJoinInfo to perform the join in memory, then writes the joined layer to a new Shapefile. The output is a shapefile with 142 fields (original 12 + 130 from CSV), confirming successful attribute table join.

name: Convert shapefile to KML
desc: The script converts a local ESRI Shapefile (hancock.shp) into KML and GeoJSON formats using QGIS Python bindings (QgsVectorLayer and QgsVectorFileWriter). It reprojects the input vector layer from its native CRS to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) during export. The study area is implied by the file path '/qgis_data/hancock/hancock.shp', referencing Hancock County — a known U.S. county, but no explicit geometry, time range, satellite data, or analysis operations are present. The outputs are two files: 'hancock.kml' and 'hancock.geojson', both containing the vector boundary data in standardized geospatial interchange formats.

name: Compute least cost path
desc: The script computes a least cost path between two user-defined points (start-point.shp and end-point.shp) over a digital elevation model (dem.asc), using QGIS Processing Toolbox algorithms. It first calculates an accumulated cost raster via GRASS 'r.cost.points' using the DEM as the cost surface, then merges the start and end point layers, and finally applies SAGA's 'leastcostpaths' algorithm using the cost raster and DEM to derive a vector line representing the optimal path. The outputs include a cost raster (cost.tif), a merged point layer (merge.shp), a least cost path vector layer (path.shp), and profile points (profilePts.shp). All inputs are local file-based rasters/vector files with no cloud or time-series processing; the DEM is assumed to be projected (per comment), but its origin, resolution, or acquisition details are not specified. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not present in the script.

name: Geolocate photos on map
desc: The script extracts GPS coordinates from EXIF metadata of JPEG images stored in a local directory (/qgis_data/photos/), converts DMS-formatted GPS tags to decimal degrees, and creates a QGIS memory vector layer of point features representing photo locations. Each point is attributed with the full file path. The layer is added to the QGIS map canvas and configured with an OpenUrl action to launch the photo when clicking its feature. No remote GEE data or satellite imagery is used; all operations are local file-based EXIF parsing and QGIS vector layer construction. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified.

name: Rectangularize building footprints
desc: The script processes vector-based building footprint polygons from a local Shapefile (irregular.shp) to generate more rectangular approximations by geometric transformation. It identifies the top-right vertex of each input polygon, computes slopes and intercepts of adjacent edges, derives perpendicular lines, and calculates intersection points to construct a 5-point rectangle-like polygon aligned to the dominant edge orientation. The output is a new in-memory QGIS vector layer named 'Rectangles' containing these adjusted polygons, alongside the original irregular footprints. No remote sensing imagery, GEE assets, or time-series analysis is involved—the workflow is purely vector geometry manipulation using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), with no Earth Engine code executed. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and GEE-specific operations are not present or referenced.

name: Identify habitat conversion patches
desc: The script identifies patches of land that transitioned from a specific land cover class (value 2) in time series 's3' (earlier period) to the same class (value 2) in 's5' (later period), but only where the later raster has value 2 *and* the earlier raster does *not* — i.e., newly emerged patches of class 2. It achieves this by: (1) binarizing s3 and s5 to 1 (where ==2) / 0 (else); (2) computing agg_s5_s3 = (A==1)*(A−B), which yields 1 only where s5==2 AND s3≠2; (3) nulling 0 values; (4) clumping contiguous 1-pixels into unique patch IDs; and (5) outputting a vector layer ('new_patches.shp') with 'patch_id' attributes for each newly emerged class-2 patch. The final output is a polygonized map of newly formed patches of land cover class 2, enabling spatial analysis of habitat emergence or expansion.

name: Compute slope from DEM
desc: The script computes slope rasters from pre-generated Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) in GeoTIFF format, using GDAL's slope algorithm. It first assigns the EPSG:26918 (NAD83 / UTM zone 18N) coordinate reference system to each input DEM (though the DEMs are already reprojected per the comment 'Run after CloudCompare has created DEMs' and path 'reprojected/laz_utm_...'), then runs gdal:slope with default parameters (vertical units matching horizontal, no edge computation, Zevenbergen=False) to generate slope-in-degree GeoTIFFs. Output files are named 'slope_<basename>_utm.tif' and saved to a dedicated slope directory per batch group (e.g., '1600-2199').

name: Map population density by administrative region
desc: The script generates a series of A4-sized, portrait-oriented PDF map layouts — one per administrative region (okres) in the Czech Republic — each showing: (1) a choropleth map of municipalities (obce) colored by population density (persons/km²), calculated from OB01 (population count) and geometry area; (2) clipped road and river networks; (3) labeled city points using NAZOB_ENG names; (4) graduated legend for density (5 equal-interval classes), auxiliary legend for linear/point layers, scalebar in km, and region name title. All temporary layers are cleaned after export.

name: Calculate population density and generate adaptive buffers
desc: The script reads point-based population data (name, population count, latitude/longitude) from a text file, creates a point shapefile (MidTerm.shp) in EPSG:32638, computes population density as Population/100 (a unitless proxy, not per-area density), adds a 'Density' field to the layer, then generates buffer zones around all points—1200 m for Density < 1200, 2000 m for 1200 < Density < 2000, and 3000 m otherwise—writing the final buffer polygon to Buff.shp and loading it into QGIS. Critically, the buffer operation is misapplied: it repeatedly overwrites the same output file using the *entire input shapefile* (path) as INPUT in every iteration, rather than buffering individual features; thus only the last buffer (based on the final feature’s Density) persists, and no spatially varying buffer per point is achieved.

name: Calculate river segment length
desc: The script calculates the geometric length (in meters and kilometers) of line features in a local shapefile ('Rivers.shp') using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS) within the QGIS environment. It adds two new fields — 'length' (meters) and 'lengthKM' (kilometers) — to the layer’s attribute table by evaluating the $length geometry expression and dividing it by 1000. Then, it selects features where lengthKM is simultaneously less than 55 AND greater than 155 — a logically impossible condition (always false), resulting in no features being selected; consequently, the output shapefile 'NewRivers.shp' will be empty or contain zero features. The script performs no remote sensing, no time-series analysis, no satellite data ingestion, and no geoprocessing beyond field calculation and faulty attribute-based selection. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Classify rivers by length for buffer distance assignment
desc: The script processes a local shapefile of rivers (Rivers.shp) to compute and store each river segment's length in meters and kilometers, then classifies segments into three categories (Code = 1, 2, or 3) based on length thresholds (<75 km, 75–150 km, >150 km). It then applies a *single* dissolve-enabled buffer operation per Code class — but critically, the loop over features rewrites the same output file (Rivers_Diss.shp) three times with different buffer distances (1000 m, 2000 m, 3000 m), meaning only the last executed buffer (Code = 3) persists. The final output is a dissolved buffer polygon layer derived from the entire input river network, buffered at 3000 m — not stratified buffers. The script uses QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), not Google Earth Engine (GEE); the prompt’s reference to 'GEE developer' is erroneous — no GEE code (e.g., ee.Image, ee.FeatureCollection, ee.Reducer) appears anywhere. All operations are vector-based (length calculation, field addition, conditional classification, buffering, dissolve) on a local shapefile. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial data sources are not specified.

name: Plan drilling sequence along vessel route
desc: The script generates a drilling program by assigning sequential drill site numbers (Seq) to input point sites based on their nearest proximity to vertices extracted from a vessel route line layer. It optionally integrates TOPAS sub-bottom profiler trackline proximity (within 15 m) and overlays geological or seabed feature classifications (e.g., 'Feature' from polygon layer) via spatial join. Coordinates are transformed from UTM zone 33S (EPSG:32733) to WGS84 and formatted in degrees-minutes (DM) notation for 'WGS Lat' and 'WGS Lon'. Bathymetry, sediment thickness, Easting/Northing, Sample_ID, and Topas/Feature attributes are retained or joined. The final output is a point layer sorted by sequence number with cumulative distance between consecutive drill points calculated along the route order.

name: Clip multispectral and elevation rasters by vector mask
desc: The script clips co-located multispectral (red, blue, green, nir, red_edge) and elevation (dsm, dtm) raster tiles to the spatial extent of individual GeoPackage vector masks, producing masked, cropped GeoTIFFs per band per vector file. It first validates that each vector layer is fully contained within the raster’s extent, then executes GDAL-based raster clipping with cutline cropping, organizing outputs into subdirectories named after each vector file.

name: Load and export administrative boundaries
desc: The script loads vector layers representing French administrative boundaries (communes and départements) from a local Shapefile and a PostGIS database, validates them, adds them to the QGIS project, retrieves metadata (extent, CRS, feature count, etc.), and exports them as new Shapefiles. The study area is implied to be France (from layer names 'administratif_commune' and 'administratif_departement' and typical French administrative nomenclature), with no temporal component. Data sources are local filesystem (Shapefile) and PostGIS database; no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved. Outputs include in-session vector layers in QGIS and two exported Shapefiles: 'export_communes.shp' and 'export_departements.shp'.

name: Split polygon with line
desc: The script constructs a memory-based point layer (7 points labeled A–Z), a polygon layer (defined by 5 vertices), and a line layer (vertical segment connecting points A and B) — all in EPSG:21037. It then executes the QGIS 'native:splitwithlines' geoprocessing algorithm to split the input polygon using the line geometry, producing a new multipart polygon layer. The resulting layer is added to the QGIS project, its area field is populated using $area expression (planar area in CRS units), and a 'name' field is set to 'splitted'. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or external datasets are involved — this is purely vector geometry manipulation within QGIS Python API.

name: Dissolve adjacent polygons by area and adjacency
desc: The script dissolves small input polygons (smaller than a user-defined area threshold in map units) into adjacent larger polygons, using one of three adjacency-based merging criteria: (1) merge into the largest adjacent polygon, (2) merge into the smallest adjacent polygon, or (3) merge along the longest shared boundary. It first converts multipart geometries to singleparts, fixes invalid geometries, calculates area (in square map units), selects polygons below the threshold, and applies QGIS’s 'Eliminate Selected Polygons' algorithm with the chosen dissolve mode. The output is a vector layer of dissolved polygons with an updated 'Area_m2' attribute field.

name: Segment image into homogeneous regions
desc: The script performs Felzenszwalb’s efficient graph-based image segmentation on a user-provided input raster to produce spatially contiguous, spectrally homogeneous segments. It outputs (1) a segmented raster where each pixel is assigned a unique segment ID, and (2) a polygon vector layer derived from that raster. Optionally, it computes zonal statistics (e.g., mean, std dev, min/max) of the original raster bands within each segment polygon and writes them as attributes; it further attempts to rasterize those statistics into a multiband output raster (though this part is logically flawed and non-functional in practice due to temporary file handling and GDAL Translate misuse). The core workflow is: read raster → apply skimage.felzenszwalb segmentation → write segment IDs to GeoTIFF → polygonize → optionally compute and embed band-wise zonal statistics into vector attributes and attempt multiband raster reconstruction.

name: Perform quickshift image segmentation
desc: The script performs unsupervised image segmentation on an input raster using the scikit-image `quickshift` algorithm in color-(x,y) space. It accepts user-defined parameters (ratio, kernel_size, max_dist, sigma) to control clustering behavior. The workflow includes: (1) reading the input raster via GDAL and converting to double-precision NumPy array; (2) applying `quickshift` segmentation to generate integer-labeled segment IDs; (3) writing the segment ID raster to a GeoTIFF output with preserved georeferencing; (4) polygonizing the segment raster into a vector layer (with 'DN' field); and optionally (5) computing zonal statistics (e.g., mean, std dev, min/max per band) of the original raster within each segment, deleting fid/DN fields, and rasterizing those statistics into a multiband output raster (via GDAL rasterize + buildvirtualraster). No satellite data ingestion, cloud masking, temporal filtering, or geographic constraints are performed — the script is purely local, raster-in/raster-out/vector-out, operating on arbitrary user-provided rasters. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Perform SLIC image segmentation
desc: The script performs superpixel segmentation using the SLIC (Simple Linear Iterative Clustering) algorithm on an input raster. It reads the raster via GDAL/skimage, applies SLIC with user-defined n_segments, compactness, and sigma parameters, writes the resulting segment labels to an output GeoTIFF raster, then polygonizes that raster into a vector layer. Optionally, it computes zonal statistics (e.g., mean, std dev, min/max per band) of the original raster within each segment polygon, deletes fid/DN fields, and attempts to rasterize those statistics back into a multiband output raster. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic context is embedded in the code — it is a generic, local, file-based QGIS processing algorithm operating on user-provided raster layers without remote sensing metadata handling or Earth Engine API calls.

name: Watershed-based image segmentation
desc: The script performs watershed segmentation on a user-provided input raster using skimage's watershed algorithm with Sobel gradient and user-defined markers and compactness. It outputs (1) a segmented raster where each pixel is assigned a segment ID, and (2) a polygonized vector layer representing the segmented regions. Optionally, it computes zonal statistics (e.g., mean, std dev, min/max per band) of the original raster within each segment, deletes fid/DN fields, and attempts to rasterize those statistics into a multiband output raster — though this part contains critical path/logic flaws (e.g., writing to 'band*.tif' in working directory without context management, hard-coded temporary file names, missing CRS propagation, and overwriting the original out_raster). No satellite data ingestion, cloud masking, time-series analysis, or georeferenced statistical modeling occurs; the workflow is purely local, raster-in–raster-out segmentation with optional QGIS zonal stats. All inputs are provided by the user via QGIS Processing interface; no hardcoded study area, time range, or sensor-specific bands are present in the code.

name: Calculate road route distance
desc: The script calculates the shortest road-based travel distance and route between two user-specified points (start and end) in EPSG:25832 (ETRS89/UTM zone 32N), transforms them to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), sends a request to the OpenRouteService (ORS) API for driving-car or foot-walking routing, retrieves the GeoJSON response, saves it as a .geojson file, visualizes the route and endpoints in QGIS (green line, green start point, red end point), and generates a two-page PDF print layout containing a main map, two inset maps (start/end), street names list ('über'), and total distance in meters and kilometers. The CRS is hard-coded to EPSG:25832, indicating operation in Germany (North Rhine-Westphalia, where Kreis Unna is located), and the ORS API key is embedded. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used — all geoprocessing is vector-based and API-driven.

name: Extract wind speed area polygons
desc: The script processes GeoTIFF raster files representing wind speed classes (5–10 m/s) by state abbreviation, polygonizes each raster to generate vector layers, filters out non-wind-area features (retaining only DN = 1 pixels), computes geometry area, appends state abbreviation, computed area (in map units), and wind speed (inferred from filename substring: '5', '6', ..., '10'), then deletes the original 'DN' field. Outputs are cleaned, attributed shapefiles per wind speed class per US state, stored in state-name-named subfolders. The study area is the conterminous United States (implied by US state abbreviation mapping), and inputs are pre-generated wind speed rasters — no GEE image collection or satellite data is loaded or processed within this script; it is a local GDAL/QGIS-based post-processing workflow for raster-to-vector conversion and attribution.

name: Classify roads by functional class
desc: The script filters OpenStreetMap (OSM) road vector data for California (specifically the 'socal-latest-free.shp' dataset) to separate roads into 'Major_Roads' and 'Minor_Roads' shapefiles based on the OSM 'fclass' attribute. It explicitly includes 'motorway', 'trunk', 'primary', 'secondary', 'tertiary', 'living_street', 'residential', and their '_link' variants in the Major class, and all other fclass values in the Minor class. The workflow reads a local .shp file, iterates features, evaluates 'fclass', writes matching features to two new ESRI Shapefile outputs, and loads them into QGIS. Study area is Southern California (inferred from 'socal-latest-free.shp'); no time range is used (static OSM vector data); data source is local OSM-derived shapefile; no satellite, sensor, or bands involved.

name: Polygonize wind transmission raster data
desc: The script processes GeoTIFF raster files containing wind transmission suitability data (e.g., speed classes 5–10) for Connecticut, converting them to vector polygons using GDAL's polygonize algorithm. It filters out non-relevant features (where DN ≠ 1), adds attributes including State_Abbr ('CT'), computed area, and inferred wind speed class (from filename), then removes the 'DN' field. Outputs are shapefiles named with state name and input raster basename, stored in a state-specific subfolder.

name: Vectorize wind transmission raster areas
desc: The script converts GeoTIFF raster files (representing wind transmission suitability or related binary classification) into vector polygon layers for the U.S. state of Missouri (MO). It performs raster-to-vector conversion using GDAL's polygonize algorithm on Band 1, filters resulting polygons to retain only those with DN = 1 (discarding background/no-data polygons), appends a 'State_Abbr' attribute (set to 'MO'), calculates and stores polygon area in square meters, and deletes the original 'DN' field. Input rasters are sourced from a local folder path containing state-wise wind transmission data; no remote sensing imagery, time-series processing, or cloud masking is involved — all operations are local desktop GIS (QGIS Processing + PyQGIS). The final outputs are cleaned, attributed shapefiles (.shp) per input raster, stored in a subfolder 'Vectorized'. Study area is explicitly MO; time range, satellite/sensor, and spectral bands are not present or applicable since inputs are pre-processed local rasters, not Earth Engine assets.

name: Buffer centroid and clip to original geometry
desc: The script creates a buffer of specified size around the centroid of each input polygon feature, then clips that buffer to the original polygon geometry. It enforces projected CRS, validates buffer size ≥100, converts multipart geometries to singleparts, computes clipped buffered geometries, adds an area expression field ($area), and applies a Jenks-classified graduated color renderer (grayscale to red) with 5 classes. No remote sensing data, imagery, or temporal analysis is involved — it is a pure vector geometric processing algorithm operating on user-provided polygon layers in QGIS Processing Framework.

name: Extract building footprint and attributes
desc: The script imports an IFC4 file to extract georeferenced building footprints, construction year, occupancy type, building name, above/below-ground floor counts and heights, and net floor area per space. It computes building standard based on construction year, generates a shapefile (zone.shp) with polygon geometry and attribute fields (Name, floors_ag, floors_bg, height_ag, height_bg), and creates a DBF table (typology.dbf) containing building typology metadata (NAME, STANDARD, YEAR, 1ST_USE, etc.). Georeferencing uses IFC site coordinates (RefLatitude/RefLongitude/RefElevation) and applies UTM zone selection (EPSG:32632 or 32633) based on longitude, followed by coordinate transformation using TrueNorth direction and origin shift. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is involved — input is purely vector-based BIM (IFC) data.

name: Compute hydraulic average slope
desc: The script computes the hydraulic average slope (HSA) of a principal river channel (astaprincipale) using a digital terrain model (DTM). It generates contour lines at a user-defined interval, filters out closed contours and those intersecting the river, splits the river line at contour intersections, calculates elevation at the midpoint of each segment via raster sampling, assigns segment IDs by descending elevation order, computes segment lengths and cumulative lengths, and finally derives two hydraulic slope metrics: 'if_med-i' (hydraulic mean slope, inverse-weighted by sqrt(slope)) and 'if_med-g' (geometric mean slope, weighted by length²/interval), outputting them as aggregated scalar values in a vector feature sink.

name: Calculate centrality-based network metric
desc: The script computes a normalized centrality metric (Cc) from input closeness values using a 6-tier exponential scaling based on standard deviations from the mean. It rasterizes the Cc values, then derives two polygon outputs: 'centreCc' (polygons where Cc ≤ 4, representing high-centrality core zones) and 'meanCc' (polygons where Cc ≤ 8, representing broader medium-to-high centrality zones), both simplified to single largest polygons with holes removed. The workflow involves field calculation, rasterization, conditional raster algebra, polygonization, area-based feature extraction, and hole removal — all targeting spatial representation of network centrality for transport or utility infrastructure analysis.

name: Clean vector network layer
desc: The script performs topological cleaning of an input vector network layer using GRASS GIS v.clean with tools 'break' (tool=0) and 'snap' (tool=6), targeting all geometry types (point, line, boundary, centroid, area, island, face). It applies a minimum area threshold of 0.0001 map units and default snapping tolerance (-1, i.e., auto-determined), outputs a cleaned vector layer, and optionally logs verbose feedback. No raster data, time series, satellite imagery, or classification is involved — the workflow is purely vector geometry repair and topology enforcement. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Correct layer geometry using network topology
desc: The script performs topological cross-layer correction by first building a network graph from merged clean layers using GRASS v.net, buffering the network to define proximity zones, subtracting those buffered zones from an input 'Clean Layer n' to isolate non-overlapping features, decomposing multipart geometries, snapping the resulting geometries to the network layer for alignment, and finally removing the 'fid' field to produce a cleaned, topologically consistent output layer. It is explicitly intended for layers other than 'clean layer 0' and assumes input vector layers are pre-cleaned but require geometric harmonization across layers via shared network structure.

name: Calculate degree centrality for network
desc: The script computes graph-theoretic degree centrality for a vector network layer ('Corrected Network') using GRASS GIS v.net.centrality, then derives a normalized centrality index 'Cd' as the ratio of each node's degree to the minimum degree in the network. The output is a vector feature sink ('Cd') containing the original geometry plus two new attributes: 'degree' (integer, from v.net.centrality) and 'Cd' (real, computed via field calculator). No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial inputs beyond the input vector layer are referenced or implied in the code; all operations are topological/graph-based on the provided vector network.

name: Assess flood and sea level rise suitability
desc: The script performs a vector-based Land Suitability Analysis for post-disaster housing relocation in Boston, Massachusetts. It uses three primary input layers: FEMA Flood Hazard Zones (100- and 500-year), NOAA Sea Level Rise projections, and Boston Zoning polygons.
