The workflow includes calculating polygon areas, intersecting zoning parcels with flood/sea-level-rise layers, computing percentage overlap, mapping flood zone categories (e.g., 'B' → '500-year'), assigning categorical scores (0–4) based on risk thresholds (e.g., 0 if overlap ≤50%, else 0; high scores indicate low risk), handling NaNs by imputing maximum+1 scores, summing individual scores (flood zone, future development, sea level rise) into a total suitability score, joining scores back to the Boston zoning layer, and exporting CSVs and geopackages. Final outputs include scored CSV files (e.g., 'total_scores.csv'), joined geopackage ('total_scores.gpkg'), and PNG visualizations (e.g., 'total_scores.png') color-ramped by total score using the 'YlOrRd' palette. All operations are performed using PyQGIS (QGIS 3.x) in a standalone Python environment; no satellite imagery or raster analysis is used — only vector overlay and attribute manipulation.

name: Delineate polygonal features from persistent line segments
desc: The script processes a local shapefile of persistent linear features (e.g., field boundaries, roads, or geomorphic lineaments) to generate non-overlapping, topologically consistent polygons by iteratively dissolving lines by 'id', polygonizing each dissolved group, dissolving resulting polygons (to merge adjacent ones per group), and then detecting and classifying spatial relationships (intersection, containment) among the final polygon groups. The output is a merged vector layer of all generated polygons, with intermediate layers added to QGIS for inspection and optional cleanup.

name: Compute persistent diagram from point features
desc: The script computes a persistent homology diagram (0-dimensional, i.e., connected components) from input vector point geometries extracted from QGIS layers named in `layer_names` (e.g., "barrier_exp"). It processes geometries (points, lines, polygons) to generate a list of coordinate-based points with identifiers, then applies threshold-based clustering via Euclidean distance to infer topological persistence. The key output is a persistent diagram (`diagram_per`) containing birth/death radii for connected components; the script selects the `count_object`-th largest death radius as a threshold (`porog`) to perform hierarchical clustering, then draws clustered points and inter-point connection lines into dedicated QGIS vector layers (`persistent_points`, `persistent_lines`). Finally, it dissolves the `persistent_lines` layer by 'id' attribute. No satellite imagery, raster processing, or time-series analysis occurs — all operations are vector-based geometric and topological in QGIS Python API context.

name: Dissolve and polygonize line segments
desc: The script processes a local shapefile of linear features ('persistent_lines.shp'), dissolves them by 'id', then iteratively selects each dissolved feature, polygonizes it to form closed polygons, dissolves each resulting polygon set (to merge overlapping or adjacent polygons), and finally merges all individual polygon layers. It also detects topological relationships (intersection, containment) between the resulting polygon sets using area comparisons after geometry validation and area calculation. The final output is a merged vector layer of all processed polygons, with intermediate layers cleaned up if 'delet' is True.

name: Compute persistent diagram from vector features
desc: The script computes a persistent homology diagram (0-dimensional) from point, line, and polygon vector features loaded from QGIS layers named 'кладбище 1', 'кладбище 2', 'кладбище 3' (Russian for 'cemetery 1/2/3'). It extracts vertex coordinates from geometries (points, polylines, polygons), constructs a point cloud, computes a persistence diagram using an external module (my_import.persistent_diagram), selects a persistence threshold based on the count_object parameter to isolate topological components (e.g., connected components), connects points within that threshold, assigns group IDs, draws resulting points and lines in QGIS layers 'persistent_points' and 'persistent_lines', then performs geometric post-processing: dissolving lines, polygonizing line networks, dissolving individual polygons, detecting spatial relationships (intersection, containment) among resulting polygons, and merging all final polygons into a single output layer. The workflow is purely vector-based and topological — no raster or satellite data is used; inputs are local QGIS vector layers with no georeferencing metadata visible in code. Study area is implied by layer names ('cemetery') but no coordinate system, CRS, or projection is specified or enforced.

name: Calculate image complexity metrics
desc: The script computes spatial complexity metrics (He, He/Hmax, SDL, LMC) for each band of an input raster using a custom convolution-based function 'convolucao' from the external module 'entropia'. It processes every raster band independently, applies a sliding window (user-defined kernel size = JANELA − 2), and writes each result as a separate GeoTIFF file (e.g., '_B1.tif', '_B2.tif') preserving georeferencing (geotransform and projection). The input raster is read via GDAL; no cloud masking, temporal filtering, or classification is performed. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and band semantics are not specified in the code — only generic raster I/O and entropy-derived texture metrics are implemented. Output files are band-wise complexity rasters.

name: Generate pedestrian navigation path polygons
desc: The script generates a pedestrian navigation route from the last GPS point in a MySQL database to a specified destination address (e.g., '울산광역시 남구 남산로68번길 13'), transforms coordinates between EPSG:4326 and EPSG:5181, buffers each route segment into 20-meter-wide rectangular polygons aligned with the local coordinate system, inserts them into a MySQL table (gps_waypoint_data), and visualizes them in QGIS as blue (unvisited) and red (_Polygons, visited) memory layers alongside a dynamic polyline tracing real-time GPS movement. It uses SK Telecom’s TMAP Geocoding and Pedestrian Routing APIs for address resolution and pathfinding, and processes GPS data stored in a MySQL table (gps_data) where latitude/longitude are stored in DMS format and converted to decimal degrees before reprojection. The study area is implicitly centered on Ulsan Metropolitan City, South Korea, based on the hardcoded destination address and coordinate system (EPSG:5181 — Korean 2000 / East Sea Belt). No satellite, remote sensing, or Earth Engine assets are used; all geospatial operations are client-side via pyproj and QGIS Python API.

name: Compare DEM elevation differences
desc: The script compares two user-provided DEM rasters (a test DEM and a reference DEM) by computing their pixel-wise difference, optionally adjusting for geoid height. It computes slope from the reference DEM using GDAL's Zevenbergen method (as percent), then stratifies the elevation differences by slope classes (user-defined number of quantile-based bins). For each slope class, it calculates statistics including mean, std, RMSE, median, NMAD, LE68, LE90, min, and max of the elevation residuals. Results are visualized in a custom matplotlib bar/point plot showing central tendency and dispersion metrics per slope bin. Outputs include: (1) a difference raster (tif), (2) a slope raster (tif), and (3) an interactive histogram-style plot with labeled statistical indicators. No explicit study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic coordinates are embedded — inputs are arbitrary local GeoTIFF files selected via QGIS file dialogs.

name: Select features by spatial and attribute filters
desc: The script selects vector features from a source shapefile layer ('nombre_capa.shp') using two filters: (1) a spatial filter restricting features to those intersecting the bounding box (extent) of a second shapefile ('nombre_capa2.shp'), and (2) an attribute filter applying a user-defined SQL expression via QgsExpression. The selected features are written to a new shapefile ('nombre_capa_seleccion.shp') preserving the original CRS and encoding. No raster data, time-series, classification models, or satellite-derived metrics are involved; the workflow is purely vector-based GIS subsetting. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and specific analysis methods are not specified.

name: Generate polygon buffer layers
desc: The script generates multiple buffered vector layers (as ESRI Shapefiles) from input shapefiles, applying circular buffers at distances of 100 m, 200 m, 300 m, 400 m, and 500 m. Each output layer retains the original attribute schema (copied from input fields) and appends a sequential integer ID field. The buffers are computed using QGIS’s native geometry.buffer() method with a negative segment count (-1), indicating default segmentation. Input shapefiles are read from a local Windows directory ('C:\ruta\'), and outputs are written to a subdirectory 'RESULTADOS\' under the same path. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or georeferenced raster operations are involved — this is purely a local vector geoprocessing workflow. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate site slope and aspect
desc: The script calculates slope and aspect from a LiDAR-derived DEM (2m statewide VRT) for a user-selected vector layer in QGIS. It buffers the input layer, clips and reprojects the DEM using gdalwarp, computes slope and aspect rasters using gdaldem, extracts mean statistics from those rasters, converts aspect mean to a compass direction, measures the input layer's area using QgsDistanceArea, and queries a Tasmanian government WMS service to retrieve the 1:25k geology map sheet name covering the canvas extent. Outputs are concatenated into a text report displayed in a QGIS dialog.

name: Optimize utility network layout
desc: The script computes a Steiner minimum tree to optimize the layout of linear infrastructure (e.g., fiber, power, or water lines) across a design area, using a cost-weighted grid derived from topographic land cover and private land constraints. It begins by generating a regular square grid aligned to the bounding box of the 'design_area' layer (in EPSG:27700), assigns row/column indices, spatially joins surface-type and per-meter construction costs from the 'Topographicarea' layer (using a CSV cost lookup table), identifies terminal connection points from the 'connection_point' layer, constructs directional non-overlapping arcs between adjacent grid cells (with searchCrit=1), calculates arc costs as length-weighted sums of intersected topographic features, applies a 10× penalty for arcs crossing privately designated wayleaves ('Land_Registry_Cadastral_Parcels' with 'private'='y'), builds a NetworkX weighted graph, computes an approximate Steiner tree over terminal nodes using networkx.algorithms.approximation.steiner_tree, and exports the resulting minimal-cost subgraph as two QGIS layers: 'steiner_point' (nodes) and 'steiner_arc' (edges). All operations are performed within QGIS using PyQGIS; no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls are present — the script is mischaracterized as 'GEE' in the prompt but is purely desktop QGIS/PyQGIS. Data sources are local vector layers (e.g., OS Open UPRN, Land Registry parcels) and a user-provided CSV cost sheet; no satellite, sensor, or temporal data is used. The CRS is explicitly EPSG:27700 (OSGB 1936 / British National Grid), indicating a UK study area.

name: Calculate land cover percentage around points
desc: The script performs site catchment analysis by buffering each input point by a user-defined radius, intersecting the buffer with polygon features from a land use/land cover layer, and computing the area (and percentage) of each polygon type (identified by a user-specified ID field) within each buffer. It outputs a memory vector layer with point geometry, sample ID, polygon class ID, absolute intersection area, and relative area percentage, then exports this as a CSV table. No remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite imagery is used — inputs are purely local vector layers (point and polygon), with no explicit study area, time range, sensor, or satellite references. All parameters (paths, field names, radius) are placeholder strings requiring user substitution.

name: Compute NDVI statistics by administrative units
desc: The script computes zonal statistics (count, sum, mean) of NDVI raster values over two vector layers: Dutch municipalities ('gemeenten') and neighborhoods ('buurten'). It uses QGIS's native zonal statistics algorithm to aggregate NDVI pixel values within each polygon, outputting CSV files containing per-polygon NDVI summary metrics (e.g., mean NDVI per municipality and per buurt). No temporal aggregation or modeling is performed — only spatial summarization of a static NDVI raster layer.

name: Compute tasseled cap greenness
desc: The script computes zonal statistics (count, sum, mean) of the second band of a precomputed 'Nederland_tasseledcap' raster dataset over two administrative vector layers: 'buurten' (neighborhoods) and 'gemeenten' (municipalities), exporting tabular results to CSV files. The output values represent aggregated tasseled cap greenness (TCG) metrics per administrative unit. The study area is the Netherlands (inferred from 'Nederland_tasseledcap' and 'buurten'/'gemeenten' — standard Dutch administrative units); the raster is precomputed (no time filtering or image collection processing occurs in the script); no satellite, sensor, or band logic is executed here — only extraction of band 2 from an existing tasseled cap stack; the workflow uses QGIS's native zonal statistics algorithm with prefix '_' and statistics [count, sum, mean].

name: Verify hydrographic flow direction and elevation consistency
desc: The script verifies the correct flow direction of hydrographic polyline features (e.g., rivers, channels) by analyzing Z-values (elevation) along vertices to detect inflexions violating monotonic descent or ascent; checks for endorheic basins by testing whether flow lines terminate without intersecting boundary or downstream layers; validates that polygonal surfaces at rest (e.g., lakes, reservoirs) maintain constant Z-values; and ensures intersection points (e.g., confluences, boundaries) have consistent elevation between layers. It uses PostgreSQL/PostGIS vector layers accessed via QGIS Python bindings, spatial indexing for efficient intersection queries, and outputs CSV error reports listing layer name, feature ID, error type (e.g., 'Error - Previous vertex inflexion', 'Error - Endorheic'), height values, height differences, and XY coordinates. Input data includes a consignment boundary shapefile (args.rem), database connection parameters, and a JSON configuration specifying layer groups for flow analysis ('flujo'), continuity checks ('continuidad'), endorheic validation ('endorreicas'), and constant-height polygons ('altura_area'). No satellite, raster, or time-series data is used — all operations are vector-based, geometry-driven, and elevation-aware (Z-enabled geometries). Study area and time range are not specified.

name: Clean language boundary dataset
desc: The script processes the 'langa.shp' language boundary dataset downloaded from worldgeodatasets.com to produce a cleaned, standardized vector layer ('wldsout') with: (1) fixed geometries to ensure topological validity; (2) an auto-incremented integer ID field ('GID'); (3) a computed integer field ('length') containing the character count of the 'NAME_PROP' attribute; (4) a filtered subset retaining only features where 'NAME_PROP' has fewer than 11 characters; (5) a new string field ('lnm') copying 'NAME_PROP' for those filtered features; and (6) removal of 16 redundant or non-essential attribute fields (e.g., ISO codes, population, family classifications), resulting in a minimal, ready-to-use language boundary layer optimized for cartographic or spatial join applications.

name: Reproject agricultural suitability raster
desc: The script reprojects and assigns a permanent projection to a local raster file ('hdr.adf') representing agricultural suitability, sourced from the University of Wisconsin–Madison's SAGE database (https://sage.nelson.wisc.edu/?incdataset=Suitability%20for%20Agriculture). It performs two GDAL-based geoprocessing steps: (1) warp/reprojection from an unknown source CRS to EPSG:4326 using nearest-neighbor resampling, and (2) extraction and writing of a .prj file for the output raster. The input path indicates local storage on a Windows machine ('C:/Users/felip/Documents/UdeSA/Maestría/Herramientas computacionales/Clase 4/Input/suit/hdr.adf'), and the output is a user-specified GeoTIFF raster ('Suitout'). No classification, time-series analysis, masking, or band computation is performed; the workflow is purely coordinate system standardization and metadata finalization. Study area, time range, satellite, sensor, and bands are not applicable — this is a static, non-remote-sensing raster dataset with no temporal or spectral attributes.

name: Compute national mean population density
desc: The script computes the mean population density (popd) for each country in 1800, 1900, and 2000 using zonal statistics over administrative boundaries. It starts with Natural Earth’s global country polygons (ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp), repairs geometries, drops all non-geographic attribute columns, then sequentially joins mean raster values from three HYDE 3.0 population density rasters (1800AD, 1900AD, and 2000AD) — plus an auxiliary land quality raster — via zonal statistics. The final output is a vector layer (country polygons) enriched with four new numeric fields: _mean (land quality), pop1800_mean, pop1900_mean, and pop2020_mean (note: despite filename 'popd_2000AD.asc', the column prefix is 'pop2020'), and saves the result as a CSV table ('raster_stats.csv').

name: Count languages per country
desc: The script counts the number of language polygons (from the 'langa.shp' dataset, derived from WLMS model1 output) intersecting each sovereign country polygon (from Natural Earth 10m Admin 0 Countries). It performs geometry repair on both inputs, computes their spatial intersection, and aggregates counts per country (using the 'ADMIN' field) to generate a CSV file ('languages_by_country.csv') listing each country name and its associated language count. The study area is global (inferred from use of Natural Earth's worldwide country dataset), no time dimension is involved, and all inputs are static vector shapefiles — no satellite, sensor, or band information is present. Data sources are local shapefiles: 'clean.shp' (WLMS-derived language areas), 'ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp' (Natural Earth), and 'langa.shp' (referenced in comment but not directly loaded; 'clean.shp' is its processed equivalent).

name: Calculate country centroid distance to coastline
desc: The script computes the Euclidean distance from the geographic centroid of each sovereign country to the nearest point on the global coastline. It imports and repairs country boundary and coastline vector datasets (Natural Earth 10m), generates country centroids, adds coordinate fields (latitude/longitude), performs a nearest-neighbor spatial join using GRASS v.distance to compute distances, corrects indexing artifacts, joins attributes to associate centroids with their nearest coastal segments, extracts vertex coordinates of the nearest coastal points, and outputs cleaned point layers containing centroid coordinates, nearest-coast coordinates, and the computed distance value for each country.

name: Calculate country area
desc: The script computes the area (in km²) of sovereign countries using a Natural Earth vector dataset (10m Admin 0 Countries). It drops >200 non-essential attribute fields, reprojects the geometry from WGS84 to ESRI:54034 (Equal-Area Cylindrical), fixes invalid geometries, then calculates planar area using $geometry.area() and converts to km² via division by 1,000,000. The final output is a vector layer with a new 'km2area' float field; a CSV export is attempted but overwritten by QgsProcessing.TEMPORARY_OUTPUT, so only the 'Areas_out' feature sink is functionally produced. Study area is global (all countries); no time dimension; data source is static vector (no satellite/sensor/bands).

name: Compute agricultural suitability by county
desc: The script computes the mean agricultural suitability value (from a raster dataset 'suit/hdr.adf') for each U.S. county (from 'USA_adm2.shp'), after reprojecting the raster to WGS84, simplifying the county vector layer by dropping non-essential fields and adding a unique integer ID, then performing zonal statistics (mean) and exporting the results—including all original county attributes plus the computed mean suitability value—to a CSV file ('counties_agrisuit.csv').

name: Clean language boundary geometry
desc: The script processes a shapefile of language boundaries (langa.shp) by fixing invalid geometries, adding a unique auto-incrementing GID field, copying the 'NAME_PROP' attribute into a new shorter-named field 'lnm', and dropping all other attributes except 'GID', 'ID', and 'lnm', resulting in a simplified, topologically clean vector layer (wlds_cleaned.shp) suitable for cartographic or spatial analysis workflows.

name: Reproject land suitability raster
desc: The script reprojects a local ArcInfo Binary Grid raster file (suit/hdr.adf) — representing land suitability — from its native (unspecified) coordinate reference system to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) using GDAL's warp operation, then generates a corresponding .prj projection file. The input path indicates the data originates from a local directory on a macOS system ('/Users/magibbons/Desktop/Herramientas/Clase5/input'), and the output is saved as 'landquality.tif' in a subdirectory. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification logic is present — this is a pure geospatial reprojection and projection metadata extraction workflow. All parameters (e.g., resampling method, nodata) are set to defaults or None; the CRS is explicitly set to EPSG:4326. The script runs standalone outside QGIS GUI using QGIS Processing via PyQGIS.

name: Compute population density zonal statistics
desc: The script computes mean zonal statistics (specifically mean values, STAT=2) of four raster datasets—land quality, and three historical population density rasters (1500 AD, 1990 AD, 2000 AD)—for each country polygon from the Natural Earth admin-0 countries dataset. It fixes geometries, retains only 'ADMIN' and 'ISO_A3' attributes, then appends prefixed mean statistics (e.g., 'pd15_', 'pd19_', 'pd20_', 'lqua_') directly to the vector layer’s attribute table via QGIS zonal statistics. Finally, it exports the enriched country-level attribute table—including original country names, ISO-A3 codes, and computed mean raster values—as a CSV file ('country_level_zs.csv').

name: Count languages per country
desc: The script computes the number of distinct languages (from the World Language Dataset, 'wlds_cleaned.shp') intersecting each sovereign country (from Natural Earth 'ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp'). It performs geometry validation on both inputs, computes spatial intersection between language polygons and country boundaries, then aggregates counts per country ('ADMIN' field) using QGIS's 'Statistics by Categories' tool. The output is a CSV file ('nlangs_country.csv') listing each country name and the count of languages occurring within its territory. Study area is global (Natural Earth admin-0 countries + global WLD), time range not applicable (static vector data), data sources are local shapefiles with no satellite/sensor/band involvement.

name: Calculate country area in square kilometers
desc: The script computes the area (in km²) of each country polygon from the Natural Earth 10m administrative boundaries dataset. It first drops unnecessary attribute fields, reprojects the vector layer to World Cylindrical Equal Area (ESRI:54034) for accurate area measurement, fixes invalid geometries, then calculates a new field 'km2area' using the $geometry area expression divided by 1,000,000 to convert m² to km², and exports the result as a CSV file containing country names (ADMIN), admin codes (ne_10m_adm), ISO_A3 codes, and computed areas.

name: Generate equal-area polygon grid
desc: The script takes an input vector layer of polygons (e.g., administrative or planning units) and subdivides each polygon into an n×n grid of smaller, equal-area rectangular sub-polygons. It uses bilinear interpolation over the four corner points of the input polygon’s outer ring to compute interior grid vertices, then constructs quadrilateral sub-polygons from those vertices. The output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer containing one feature per sub-rectangle, with attributes inherited from the input layer plus a hierarchical 'GridID' (e.g., 'A.1', 'A.2') and a numeric 'id'. No raster data, time-series, or remote sensing analysis is performed; the operation is purely geometric and vector-based. Input CRS is assumed to be EPSG:22391 (a projected coordinate system), and the script explicitly avoids file I/O by using a scratch memory layer. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not involved or specified.

name: Extract annual and monthly raster statistics by vector partition
desc: The script partitions a vector layer by a categorical attribute (cut_param), filters partitions based on the sum of a numeric field (value_param) exceeding a threshold (min_value), then extracts mean pixel values from an annual raster layer and twelve monthly raster layers (grouped under a QGIS layer group) for each qualifying partition. It outputs a point shapefile where each feature represents either (a) an annual summary (MONTH = 0, ANNUAL_DATA populated, MONTHLY_DATA = NULL) or (b) a monthly summary (MONTH = 1–12, MONTHLY_DATA populated, ANNUAL_DATA = NULL), with geometry artificially placed at (cut_id, month) — not georeferenced — and attributes including cut ID, total summed value, month index, annual mean, and monthly mean.

name: Dissolve and filter land parcels by attribute sum
desc: The script processes a vector layer (e.g., administrative or land parcel polygons) by first filtering features using an attribute-value condition (FILTER_PARAM = FILTER_VALUE), then grouping remaining features by a categorical field (ITER_PARAM), dissolving each group into a single polygon, computing the summed value of a numeric attribute (COMPARE_PARAM) per group, and retaining only those dissolved polygons where the sum meets or exceeds a threshold (MIN_VALUE). It outputs two shapefiles: (1) a merged layer containing all dissolved groups (_total_dissolved), and (2) a merged layer containing only those dissolved groups satisfying the threshold condition (_value_dissolved). Both outputs are saved as ESRI Shapefiles with EPSG:25830 CRS and added to the QGIS project.

name: Calculate MPRI vegetation index
desc: The script processes a user-provided raster (e.g., multispectral satellite image) and vector mask layers from the QGIS map canvas. For each vector layer, it clips the raster to the vector geometry, computes the MPRI (Modified Pigment Ratio Index) as (Green − Red) / (Green + Red) using bands 1 (Red) and 2 (Green), applies histogram-based classification into 5 vegetation abundance classes (None → Much), renders the MPRI raster with a custom color ramp, generates a 5×5 unit grid clipped to the vector boundary, computes zonal mean MPRI per grid cell, and applies Jenks natural breaks classification with NDVI color ramp to symbolize the resulting grid polygons ('Zona de Manejo') by MPRI mean value. Outputs include: (1) clipped raster ('Recortado*.tif'), (2) MPRI raster ('MPRI*.tif'), (3) classified MPRI raster layer with legend, (4) clipped grid vector layer ('MPRI_Zona de manejo*.shp'), and (5) graduated symbology applied to that vector layer based on MPRI mean.

name: Classify NDVI vegetation zones
desc: The script computes NDVI from multi-band raster layers (assumed to be satellite imagery with at least 4 bands, where Band 4 = NIR and Band 2 = Red), applies Jenks natural breaks classification to partition NDVI values into 5 ecologically interpreted vegetation density classes (e.g., 'Nenhuma Vegetação' to 'Muita Vegetação'), crops both original RGB rasters and NDVI rasters to input vector boundaries, generates a fishnet grid aligned to each vector’s extent, clips the grid to the vector, computes zonal NDVI means per grid cell, removes null-statistics cells, dissolves adjacent grid cells by NDVI class, merges the five dissolved class layers into a single classified vector layer ('Zona NDVI mesclado'), calculates area (ha) per polygon, and applies a graduated symbology using Jenks classification and the 'Prisma' color ramp — producing a thematic vector map of spatially explicit, management-ready NDVI-based vegetation density zones.

name: Identify designated conservation sites near boundary
desc: The script identifies designated conservation and protected area features (AW, LNR, NNR, Ramsar, SAC, SINC, SPA, SSSI) within 2000 meters of a user-provided site boundary (site_boundary.shp), computes the shortest line from each site to the boundary, reverses the line direction, calculates the bearing and compass direction (N, NE, E, etc.) from the site to the boundary, extracts endpoint coordinates for labeling, applies layer-specific symbology, adds styled layers to the QGIS map, prints counts per designation type, and exports each result as a CSV containing geometry, bearing, direction, and endpoint coordinates.

name: Detect forest change
desc: The script performs forest change detection using two user-provided Landsat 8 raster layers (‘Before’ and ‘After’). It computes NDVI using Band 5 (NIR) and Band 4 (Red) from each input image via QgsRasterCalculator, then reclassifies each NDVI raster into forest/non-forest using a fixed threshold-based reclassification table (values mapped to classes 1 and 2; no dynamic thresholding or training data). Change is derived as the pixel-wise difference (After − Before) of the two reclassified rasters, producing a single-band integer raster with values interpreted as: −1 = Forest Loss, 0 = No change, 1 = Forest Gain (per hardcoded color ramp labels). The output is a styled paletted raster layer added to QGIS with predefined colors and legend labels. No study area, time range, or geographic extent is specified in the code — inputs are generic raster layers supplied by the user at runtime. Data sources are not embedded in the script; only band indices (4 and 5) are hard-coded, confirming Landsat 8 OLI spectral assignment.

name: Calculate hard-tie bearings relative to True North
desc: The script calculates expected hard-ties (distance and compass bearing relative to True North) from a single user-selected reference point to all features in a specified vector layer, using ellipsoidal distance and CRS-aware True North correction. It computes the grid-to-true north convergence angle at each target feature location via coordinate transformation and meridional shift, then adjusts the grid bearing accordingly. Outputs are polyline features representing each hard-tie, with attributes including 'From', 'To', and a formatted description (e.g., '124.35 m @ 42.7 deg from RPID_001'). No satellite, raster, or temporal data is involved — all operations are vector-based and rely solely on QGIS project CRS, selected vector layers, and their geometry/attribute fields. Study area, time range, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Generate weed polygon shapefiles
desc: The script processes user-provided GeoTIFF raster files (presumed to be classified or thresholded outputs, e.g., binary weed/non-weed masks) to generate vector polygon shapefiles per image using GDAL's polygonize algorithm. It removes soil polygons (where 'id' = 0), computes area and perimeter attributes for each polygon, joins tabular CSV data (by 'id') to the shapefile, and loads both rasters and resulting shapefiles into the QGIS project. Input rasters are assumed to be georeferenced in EPSG:32633 (UTM zone 33N). The workflow is fully file-path-driven via user-selected text files listing raw rasters, classified TIFFs, and a target directory; no satellite imagery processing (e.g., band math, cloud masking, NDVI) occurs in this script — it operates on pre-generated classified rasters. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Order vertices of multipart line
desc: The script processes a user-provided QGIS vector layer named 'line' to resolve unordered vertex sequences in multipart line geometries. It first decomposes multiparts into single parts, snaps line endpoints within 10 map units to ensure topological continuity, dissolves the snapped lines (re-aggregating by geometry), merges collinear and coincident lines into continuous polylines, and finally extracts ordered vertices — producing a point layer where each feature corresponds to a vertex in topologically correct sequence along reconstructed lines.

name: Project points onto line and compute scale factor
desc: The script computes orthogonal projections of input point features onto a given line feature, reorders the line's vertices by inserting the projected points in correct sequence along the line (based on distance from preceding vertex), splits the resulting enhanced line into segments at each projected point location, and calculates segment lengths and a scale factor defined as 1000 divided by each segment's length. The outputs are two new vector layers added to the QGIS map canvas: (1) a single 'new_line' polyline geometry containing the original line vertices plus inserted projected points in correct topological order, and (2) a 'segments' layer containing individual LineString features for each sub-segment between consecutive projected points (including endpoints), each with attributes 'length' (in CRS units) and 'scale_f' (1000/length). All operations are performed client-side in QGIS using PyQGIS; no remote sensing data, time-series, or external geospatial web services are involved — inputs are local vector layers named 'points' and 'lines' loaded in the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

name: Validate point location against road buffers
desc: The script validates the spatial correctness of point features (e.g., roadside markers or infrastructure assets) loaded from a CSV file by checking whether each point falls within a 50-meter buffer around a reference road network layer; it further cross-validates attribute correspondence (via 'cod_strada' field matching between points and road/buffer layers), filters points that satisfy both geometric inclusion and attribute alignment, appends administrative municipality names ('nome' from polygon layer) to validated points via spatial join, and exports the final validated and enriched point set as both a Shapefile and a CSV with XYZ geometry coordinates.

name: Plot points and lines by azimuth and distance
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for interactive geodetic point and line plotting based on user-input Cartesian coordinates (x, y), azimuth (in degrees), and distance (in meters). It validates the input coordinate system (requiring a projected CRS, not geographic), checks whether the input point lies within the valid bounds of the selected projection, creates a memory vector layer for plotted points ('Plot Titik'), and optionally draws straight-line segments ('Plot Garis') from the previous point to the newly computed point using QgsPoint.project(). The output consists of dynamically updated in-memory vector layers visible in QGIS, with automatic zoom-to-layer. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, or classification is involved — it is purely a coordinate geometry and cartographic drafting tool operating entirely client-side within QGIS using PyQGIS APIs.

name: Calculate total and European population
desc: The script calculates the total global population (sum of 'POP_EST' field) and the population of European countries (filtered by 'CONTINENT' == 'Europe') from a local Natural Earth shapefile of world countries. It performs vector attribute extraction, conditional filtering, summation, and creates new in-memory point layers with random geographic distributions. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, or Earth Engine operations are used—the entire workflow runs in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS) using local vector data. Study area is global; outputs are printed numeric sums and a new in-memory point layer with 50 random features.

name: Correct terrain polygon geometry
desc: The script performs topological correction of a vector polygon layer (e.g., cadastral or terrain parcels) by snapping geometries to themselves within a 0.2-meter tolerance and then fixing invalid geometries (e.g., self-intersections, ring errors); it updates the original editable layer in-place by matching features via 't_id' attribute and replacing their geometries with the corrected versions — no new layer is saved, and editing is rolled back without committing, implying the correction is applied directly to the source layer's geometry storage.

name: Calculate protected area coverage percentage
desc: The script computes the proportion of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) covered by Protected Areas, disaggregated by ecosystem type. It does so by: (1) intersecting KBA polygons with Protected Areas boundaries to identify overlapping regions; (2) performing zonal statistics on an input ecosystem map raster to sum pixel counts per protected area polygon; (3) intersecting the overlap result with the zonally summarized protected areas to link ecosystem-specific pixel sums to KBA-PA overlaps; (4) calculating geometric area (in m²) and pixel-based area (pixel size × count) for each intersected feature; and (5) deriving two percentages per KBA: (a) percentage of KBA area covered by protected areas (‘Area_meter’-based), and (b) percentage of KBA area covered by protected areas *weighted by ecosystem type* (i.e., pixel-count × pixel-area / KBA geometric area), reported as mean values in a log file. Outputs include a vector layer with attributes ‘Area’, ‘PixArea’, ‘OvN_sum’, and ‘Percentage’, plus a text/HTML log containing summary statistics.

name: Compute slope from DEM
desc: The script computes slope rasters from pre-generated DEM GeoTIFF files. It first assigns the CRS EPSG:32129 (NAD83 / Pennsylvania South) to each input DEM using 'gdal:assignprojection', then runs 'gdal:slope' to generate slope rasters in degrees. Input DEMs are located in a Windows filesystem path containing 'pennsylvania_michaux' and 'laz_utm_0-597', indicating they were derived from LiDAR point clouds processed via CloudCompare and reprojected to UTM. The outputs are slope GeoTIFFs written to a dedicated output directory, named with the prefix 'slope_' followed by the original DEM filename stem (e.g., 'slope_laz_utm_0-597_...tif'). No classification, time-series analysis, or satellite imagery is involved — only deterministic raster geoprocessing on locally stored DEMs.

name: Simplify vector geometry
desc: The script processes each loaded QGIS vector layer by (1) calculating and adding a new 'AREA' attribute using the $area expression (in layer's CRS units), then (2) simplifying the geometries using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm (METHOD=2) with tolerance 0.006 (unitless, interpreted in layer's CRS), saving the simplified result as a Shapefile (.shp) and also exporting the original (unsimplified but area-annotated) layer to CSV with WKT geometry and comma-separated fields. The simplified Shapefiles are added back to the QGIS project.

name: Reproject shapefiles to target CRS
desc: The script reprojects all shapefiles (.shp) in the same directory as a user-selected input shapefile to match that input layer's coordinate reference system (CRS). It identifies mismatched CRS layers, appends a user-defined suffix to output filenames (e.g., 'input.shp' → 'input_reprojected.shp'), runs QGIS's native:reprojectlayer algorithm on each, and clears the QGIS project upon completion. No raster data, time-series, or remote sensing is involved; it is a pure vector CRS alignment workflow operating entirely on local filesystem shapefiles. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified — this is a desktop GIS batch reprojection utility, not an Earth Engine (GEE) script.

name: Calculate slope and drainage density
desc: The script computes slope from input DEM rasters (e.g., '.tif' files in '/Users/61410/SIS/VM/') using QGIS's native:slope algorithm; then derives drainage density via SAGA's 'channelnetworkanddrainagebasins' tool using the same DEM and a pre-existing 'drainrast.sdat' raster; combines slope and drainage density into a weighted sum raster ('weighted.tif') using fixed coefficients (0.4 for drainage, 0.6 for slope); clips the weighted raster to buffered vector features (e.g., 'PRIORITY_RIVERS.shp', 'VLR_POINT.shp'); calculates and filters priority rivers by attribute 'PRIORTYRVR' containing 'Y'; and programmatically creates a new landfill point feature at hardcoded UTM coordinates (747930, 5724503) in EPSG:28354 — all executed in QGIS Desktop via PyQGIS, not Google Earth Engine. The script does not use GEE APIs, imagery, or cloud processing — it is a local QGIS geoprocessing workflow. Study area CRS (EPSG:28354) indicates Australian Map Grid zone 54, but no explicit geographic extent or place name is given beyond file paths and coordinate values. Final outputs include: slope rasters (with '_slope' suffix), buffered shapefiles (with '_buff' suffix), 'drainrast.sdat', 'weighted.tif', 'clip.tif', 'newlandfill.shp', and symbolized visual layers in QGIS.

name: Estimate lavaka erosion volume
desc: The script reconstructs the pre-erosion topographic surface for each lavaka (a type of gully landform common in Madagascar) by interpolating elevation values from random points sampled within user-defined pre-erosion surface polygons; it then computes the volumetric difference between this reconstructed surface and the current DEM (SRTM or TanDEM-X), producing clipped, lavaka-specific elevation-difference rasters and summary statistics (e.g., unique value reports) used to quantify eroded volume per lavaka.

name: Clip deforestation vector by point locations
desc: The script loads a Landsat 8 Level 1 T1 scene (LC08_L1TP_227063_20180721) and a deforestation vector layer (2017_deforestationA.shp), then creates a memory point layer from four manually defined longitude/latitude coordinates. It adds this point layer to the QGIS project and performs a vector clip operation — using the point layer as the clipping mask (OVERLAY) on the deforestation vector (INPUT) — producing a clipped output shapefile. Subsequently, it rasterizes the original (unclipped) deforestation vector into a georeferenced TIFF using a fixed UTM zone 21N extent and resolution, assigning burn value 1; this raster is intended for alignment with the Landsat scene. The workflow is thus focused on spatial subsetting (via clipping) and raster conversion of deforestation features relative to discrete field points, not spectral analysis or classification.

name: Classify field into quantiles
desc: The script classifies a numeric attribute field of a vector polygon layer into user-specified quantile-based classes (e.g., quartiles, deciles) by computing percentile thresholds and assigning integer class labels to each feature. It modifies the input vector layer in-place by adding a new integer field (user-named) containing the quantile class ID (1 to n). No new file is exported; changes are committed directly to the source layer and trigger a project-wide layer reload. The script uses only local vector data — no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or external raster inputs — and performs purely statistical (percentile-based) discretization on a single attribute. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial operations beyond vector attribute editing are not specified.

name: Clean points by raster kernel value
desc: The script cleans a point vector layer (e.g., landslide inventory or field observations) by filtering points based on local maximum slope values within a user-defined square kernel (buffer radius in pixels) extracted from a co-registered slope raster. It first crops the slope raster to the input extent, converts input points to a binary raster mask aligned with the slope raster’s geotransform, applies a scipy.ndimage.generic_filter with np.nanmax over the slope raster using the kernel size, multiplies the filtered slope raster with the point mask to retain only slope maxima coincident with points, then thresholds the result against a user-specified minimum acceptable slope value. Points falling within raster cells where the kernel-maximized slope meets or exceeds the threshold are retained; others are discarded. The output is a new point vector layer containing only the retained points. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific sensor/bands are referenced — inputs are generic local file paths (e.g., 'Slope' raster and 'Inventory' vector), and all geospatial operations are performed via GDAL, NumPy, and OGR outside GEE’s cloud environment. The script runs as a QGIS Processing Algorithm, not a Google Earth Engine script — despite the prompt’s mischaracterization — and uses no GEE API calls, assets, or ee.* objects.

name: Count points per raster grid cell
desc: The script converts a vector point layer into a raster where each pixel value represents the count of input points falling within that pixel, using an existing raster layer's geometry (extent, resolution, projection) as the template. It reads the input raster to extract geotransform, projection, and dimensions; reads the point layer via QgsVectorLayer; filters points to those within a user-specified extent; maps point coordinates to pixel indices using the raster’s geotransform; and accumulates counts per cell. Output is a single-band GeoTIFF with NoData = -9999, preserving the input raster’s spatial reference, pixel size, and origin. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic classification is embedded — it is a generic geometric aggregation tool operating on arbitrary local vector/raster inputs.

name: Convert polygon grid to raster
desc: The script converts an input vector polygon layer (interpreted as a grid) into a regular raster grid with user-defined pixel width (w) and height (h). It computes the extent of the input polygon layer, calculates raster dimensions (cols, rows) based on the extent and pixel size, initializes a float32 raster array filled with -10 (later set to -9999 as NoData), and writes it to a GeoTIFF output with correct geotransform (origin, pixel width/height) and projection (inherited from input layer's WKT CRS). No spatial analysis, classification, or attribute computation is performed — only geometric gridding. The study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and any thematic analysis are not involved; this is a pure vector-to-raster discretization utility. Input is a static polygon layer (e.g., fishnet or administrative grid), no temporal or remote sensing data is loaded or processed.

name: Sample landslide training points
desc: The script performs spatially constrained random sampling of landslide point data within a user-defined polygon mask, ensuring no pixel contains both training and validation points. It rasterizes the input landslide points into a grid with specified pixel width/height, clips the raster to the polygon boundary, then partitions the landslide locations into two disjoint sets (training and validation) based on a user-defined percentage, guaranteeing spatial independence at the pixel level. Outputs are two ESRI Shapefile layers: one containing the sampled training points and another containing the remaining (1-sample) validation points.

name: Calculate kernel statistics around points
desc: The script computes spatial kernel statistics (real value, max, min, std, sum, average, range) from a raster layer centered on input point features, using a user-defined circular buffer radius in pixels. It reads a raster (e.g., slope or terrain metric), clips/aligns it to a contour polygon extent, identifies raster cell indices corresponding to each point location, applies scipy.ndimage.generic_filter with square kernels (size = 2×radius+1) to compute local statistics, and exports results as a shapefile where each point is attributed with all seven statistics. The workflow uses GDAL for raster I/O, NumPy for array operations, and QgsVectorFileWriter for vector output. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or sensor metadata is embedded — inputs are generic local file paths (e.g., 'Slope', 'Inventory', 'poly') provided by the QGIS user at runtime. Output is an ESRI Shapefile with Point geometry and fields: id, real, max, min, std, sum, average, range.

name: Fit Decision Tree susceptibility model
desc: The script fits a Decision Tree (DT) classifier to spatial polygon vector data containing covariates (independent variables) and a binary dependent variable (0 = absence, >0 = presence) — interpreted as landslide susceptibility modeling. It supports either pure fitting (test percentage = 0) or k-fold–style cross-validation (user-specified test percentage). Key workflow steps: (1) load vector layer and extract selected covariate fields + dependent field; (2) binarize the dependent field (values >0 → 1); (3) split data into train/test subsets; (4) standardize covariates and train DT with entropy criterion; (5) compute susceptibility index (SI) as predicted class probability (P(y=1)); (6) export train and/or test results as GeoPackage layers; (7) generate ROC curves (AUC scores) and save figures (PNG/PDF) in user-specified output folder. No satellite, raster, or time-series processing occurs — input is purely vector-based. Study area, time range, sensor, bands, and explicit geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Fit decision tree susceptibility model
desc: The script performs k-fold cross-validated Decision Tree (DT) classification to compute a Susceptibility Index (SI) for landslide or hazard occurrence using polygon vector covariates. It reads a user-provided polygon layer containing independent variables (e.g., topographic, land cover, or environmental covariates) and one dependent variable field (named via 'fieldlsd', where values > 0 indicate presence/occurrence and 0 indicates absence). The workflow includes: (1) loading the vector layer into a pandas DataFrame; (2) standardizing independent variables; (3) applying StratifiedKFold (if k > 1) or full-fit (if k = 1) DT with entropy criterion; (4) computing class-probability predictions (P(y=1)) as SI; (5) saving the SI-augmented polygons to a GeoPackage output file; (6) generating a multi-fold ROC curve plot (fig02.pdf) with per-fold AUC scores in an output folder; and (7) auto-loading the test/output layer into QGIS. No raster data, satellite imagery, or temporal filtering is used — all inputs are static vector features. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Fit logistic regression susceptibility model
desc: The script fits a logistic regression (LR) model to predict landslide susceptibility using user-provided polygon vector covariates and a binary dependent variable field (0 = absence, >0 = presence). It supports both pure fitting (test percentage = 0) and cross-validation (user-specified test percentage), outputs trained/test GeoPackage vector layers with predicted Susceptibility Index (SI) values, and generates ROC curve visualizations (PNG/PDF) in an output folder. The workflow includes: (1) loading and preprocessing the input vector layer (converting geometry to WKT, encoding dependent variable as binary, dropping NaNs); (2) splitting data into train/test sets; (3) standardizing covariates and fitting LR; (4) computing SI probabilities; (5) saving results to GeoPackage with correct field typing (Int for 'ID'/'y', Double for covariates); and (6) generating AUC-annotated ROC plots — success (train) and prediction (test) curves when cross-validating, or single complete-dataset ROC when fitting only. No satellite, raster, or time-series processing occurs; all inputs are static vector features. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified.

name: Fit logistic regression susceptibility
desc: The script performs logistic regression (LR) modeling for landslide susceptibility assessment using k-fold cross-validation. It reads a vector layer of covariates (e.g., topographic, land cover, geological factors) and a binary dependent variable field (0 = absence, >0 = presence of landslides). It standardizes predictors, fits LogisticRegression from scikit-learn, computes predicted susceptibility indices (SI) per test fold, saves coefficients to 'r_coeffs.csv', exports the full dataset (with added 'SI' and 'y' fields) as a GeoPackage, and generates a multi-fold ROC curve plot ('fig02.pdf') showing AUC per fold. No remote sensing imagery or time-series processing is performed — input is static polygon vector data with pre-extracted covariate values. Study area, time range, satellite data, and specific covariate names are not specified in the code.

name: Fit Random Forest susceptibility model
desc: The script fits a Random Forest (RF) classifier to predict landslide susceptibility using user-provided polygon vector covariates and a binary dependent variable field (0 = absence, >0 = presence). It supports either pure fitting (test percentage = 0) or k-fold–style cross-validation (by splitting the input layer into train/test subsets based on user-specified percentage). Key workflow steps include: (1) loading the input vector layer and extracting specified independent fields plus geometry; (2) binarizing the dependent variable field (≥1 → 1, 0 → 0); (3) standardizing features and training an RF classifier (10 trees, entropy criterion, random_state=0); (4) computing susceptibility index (SI) as predicted class probability for presence; (5) exporting train and test results as GeoPackage layers; and (6) generating ROC curves — a single AUC plot for fitting mode, or dual-success/prediction ROC plots with AUC values for cross-validation mode — saved as PNG/PDF in the user-specified output folder. No remote sensing imagery, satellite data, or time-series processing is involved; all inputs are static vector layers. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Model landslide susceptibility
desc: The script performs Random Forest (RF) classification to model landslide susceptibility using vector-based covariates and a binary dependent variable (0 = absence, >0 = presence). It supports both single-fit (k=1) and k-fold cross-validation (k>1) using StratifiedKFold. Input is a polygon vector layer with user-specified independent fields and one dependent field (‘fieldlsd’). The workflow loads the vector data into a pandas DataFrame, standardizes features via StandardScaler, trains an RF classifier (10 trees, entropy criterion), computes prediction probabilities for test folds, and assigns susceptibility index (SI) values to each feature. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage file containing the input polygons augmented with ‘SI’ (susceptibility index) and ‘y’ (binary label); (2) a PDF ROC curve figure (fig02.pdf) showing per-fold AUCs in the specified output folder; (3) the test/output layer automatically loaded into QGIS as a temporary layer named 'test'. No satellite or raster data is used — all inputs and operations are vector-based and statistical. Study area, time range, satellite data, and explicit geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Fit SVM susceptibility model
desc: The script applies Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification to a vector layer of covariates and a binary landslide presence/absence label field to compute a Susceptibility Index (SI). It supports either pure model fitting (testN=0) or train-test cross-validation (testN>0). Key workflow steps: (1) load vector layer and extract specified covariate fields and dependent variable field (‘fieldlsd’), binarizing it (>0 → 1, else 0); (2) standardize covariates using StandardScaler; (3) train SVC with linear kernel and probability output; (4) compute SI as predicted class probability for presence; (5) export training and/or test results as GeoPackage layers; (6) generate ROC curves — single AUC plot for fitting mode, dual (success/prediction) AUC plots for CV mode — saved as PNG/PDF in user-specified folder. No satellite or raster data is loaded or processed; all inputs are vector-based (polygon features with attribute covariates). Study area, time range, sensor, bands, and explicit geographic location are not specified in the code.

name: Fit SVM susceptibility model
desc: The script performs Support Vector Machine (SVM) modeling for landslide susceptibility assessment using vector polygon input data containing covariates and a binary dependent variable (0 = absence, >0 = presence). It implements k-fold cross-validation (StratifiedKFold) with user-specified k (≥1), standardizes covariates via StandardScaler, trains an SVC classifier with linear kernel and probability estimates, and computes pixel-level susceptibility index (SI) values. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage file ('Output test/fit') containing the input polygons augmented with 'SI' (susceptibility index) and 'y' (binary label) fields; (2) a folder ('Outputs folder destination') containing a PDF ROC curve figure (fig02.pdf) showing per-fold AUC scores; and (3) automatic loading of the output layer into QGIS as a temporary map layer named 'test'. No raster inputs, satellite data, or time-series processing are used — all operations are vector-based and statistical. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and explicit geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate landslide susceptibility
desc: The script applies the Weight of Evidence (WoE) statistical method to calculate landslide susceptibility index (SI) from polygon-based covariate and landslide presence/absence data. It supports both fitting-only (test percentage = 0) and cross-validation (test percentage > 0) modes. Key workflow steps include: (1) loading a vector layer of covariates (e.g., slope classes, lithology, land use), (2) extracting user-selected independent variables (categorical fields) and one dependent variable field (binary: 0 = absence, >0 = presence of landslides), (3) splitting data into train/test sets if cross-validation is enabled, (4) computing WoE values (W+, W−, Wf) per class per covariate and replacing original class labels with WoE scores, (5) summing WoE scores across covariates to derive Susceptibility Index (SI), and (6) exporting train/test vector layers (GeoPackage), WoE calculation table (CSV-like TXT), and ROC diagnostic plots (PNG/PDF). Outputs include: (a) GeoPackage files for training (mandatory) and test (if testN > 0) datasets with SI and all WoE-transformed fields; (b) a text file listing covariate name, class, Npx1–Npx4 counts, and W+, W−, Wf values; (c) ROC curves and AUC metrics saved in an output folder — 'fig01.png' for fitting-only mode, 'fig02.pdf' for cross-validation mode showing both success (training) and prediction (test) performance. No satellite imagery or raster processing is performed — input is purely vector (polygon) GIS data. Study area, time range, and specific data sources are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate landslide susceptibility index
desc: The script applies Weight of Evidence (WoE) modeling to calculate a Susceptibility Index (SI) for landslide occurrence using polygon vector covariates and a binary dependent variable field (0 = absence, >0 = presence). It supports both single-fit (k=1) and k-fold cross-validated WoE estimation (StratifiedKFold), where covariate classes are replaced by WoE values (W⁺, W⁻, Wf) computed per class from training folds. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage vector layer containing the SI values per feature (test/fitted), (2) a folder with ROC curves (fig02.pdf) aggregating AUC scores across all k folds, and (3) per-fold WoE weight tables (e.g., 'W0.txt') listing Npx1–Npx4 counts and computed W⁺, W⁻, Wf per covariate-class combination. Input data is purely vector-based — no raster or satellite-derived inputs are loaded, processed, or referenced; the script operates entirely on attribute columns of a user-provided polygon layer. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and explicit geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate landslide susceptibility index
desc: The script implements Frequency Ratio (FR) modeling to compute a Susceptibility Index (SI) for landslide occurrence using polygon vector covariates. It loads a user-provided polygon layer containing independent variables (e.g., land cover, slope classes) and a dependent variable field indicating landslide presence (values > 0) or absence (value = 0). The workflow includes: (1) splitting the input data into training and test sets based on a user-defined percentage; (2) computing FR weights per class per covariate as Wf = (Npx1/Npx2)/(Npx3/Npx4), where Npx1 = landslides in class i, Npx2 = total pixels in class i, Npx3 = total landslides, Npx4 = total pixels; (3) replacing original covariate class values with their FR weights; (4) summing weighted covariates to obtain SI per polygon; (5) generating ROC curves and AUC scores for model evaluation — success rate (training set) and prediction rate (test set); (6) exporting trained/test polygons with SI and weights to GeoPackage files, and saving FR weight tables (.txt) and ROC plots (.png/.pdf) to an output folder. No satellite imagery, raster processing, or temporal filtering is performed — all inputs are static vector layers. Study area, time range, and specific covariate semantics are not specified in the code.

name: Fit Frequency Ratio susceptibility model
desc: The script implements Frequency Ratio (FR) modeling for landslide susceptibility assessment using k-fold cross-validation. It takes a vector polygon layer of covariates (e.g., slope classes, lithology, land use) and a dependent variable field indicating presence (≥1) or absence (0) of landslides. For each covariate class, it computes the FR weight Wf = (Npx1/Npx2)/(Npx3/Npx4), where Npx1 = number of landslide pixels in class i, Npx2 = total pixels in class i, Npx3 = total landslide pixels, Npx4 = total pixels. The Susceptibility Index (SI) is the sum of FR weights across all covariate fields per feature. Outputs include: (1) a GeoPackage vector layer containing input features with added 'SI' (susceptibility index) and 'y' (binary label) fields; (2) a CSV text file listing all computed FR weights per covariate class with counts (Npx1–Npx4); (3) a PDF ROC curve figure showing AUC per fold in cross-validation; and (4) an output folder containing the ROC plot. The script operates entirely on vector attribute data — no raster inputs, satellite imagery, or time-series processing are used. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Classify landslide susceptibility labels
desc: The script labels each polygon feature in an input vector layer as True Positive (0), True Negative (1), False Positive (2), or False Negative (3) based on a user-specified index field (e.g., susceptibility index) and a dependent variable field encoding presence (≥1) or absence (0) of landslides. It computes a percentile-based cutoff (e.g., 50th percentile) on the index field, classifies features above cutoff as 'positive', compares against observed landslide presence/absence, and assigns tptnfpfn codes accordingly. Input is a pre-processed vector layer (e.g., covariates-classed polygons) with geometry, index values, and landslide labels; no remote sensing data is loaded or processed within this script — all operations are tabular/spatial attribute-based. Output is a GeoPackage file containing the original attributes plus the new 'tptnfpfn' integer field. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor details are not specified in the code.

name: Extract OSM infrastructure features
desc: The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) features within a user-defined bounding box using the Overpass API, parses the XML/JSON response into QgsVectorLayer objects grouped by thematic categories (e.g., 'voidGreyAreas', 'volumeBuildings', 'networkStreet'), applies coordinate transformations (EPSG:4326 ↔ projected CRS), buffers specific layers (e.g., 'voidGreyAreas'), and saves results as GeoPackage layers grouped in QGIS layer tree. Outputs include geopackage files (one per group, e.g., 'infrastructure.gpkg') with named layers (e.g., 'voidGreyAreas', 'networkPTStops'), and optional in-session QGIS layer visualization. The study area is defined by CONFIG.bbox_M (a QgsRectangle), and the projected CRS is read from CONFIG.projectedCrs. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used — the sole data source is OSM via Overpass API.

name: Join urban lot polygons with point-based annotations and rent data
desc: The script performs a spatial join between urban polygon layers (e.g., 'TG_HU', 'TG_MZ_URB', 'TG_LT_URB') and corresponding point layers (e.g., 'ANN_HU', 'ANN_TG_MZ_URB', 'ANN_TG_LT_URB') using centroid containment to transfer text annotations ('Text_' field); then constructs a concatenated annotation field ('idrentas') across multiple joined layers via QGIS expression; finally joins the resulting polygon layer ('TG_LT_URB_join') with an external CSV ('rentas') on matching ID fields ('idrentas' ↔ 'ID_LOTE_URB') to produce a final geopackage ('TG_LOTE_FINAL.gpkg') containing both geometric attributes and socioeconomic rent information for urban lots.

name: Manage cadastral editing projects
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for controlled download, editing, and commit of the Spanish National Topographic Base (BTN) geospatial database. It enables users to select a municipality (e.g., via province–municipality hierarchy), download project-specific working tables (e.g., btn0508s_ed for buildings, btn0201l_cur_niv for contour lines) and spatial queries (e.g., query_btn0605l_carretera for roads intersecting the municipality) from a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database into QGIS layers. It enforces concurrency control by checking for existing working tables per user/project/table, applies predefined QML styles from the layer_styles table, orders layers in a fixed visual hierarchy, and performs validation (e.g., list-value checks on edificios fields, contour intersection detection). On upload, it detects inserts, updates, and deletes by comparing working tables in the 'proyectos' schema against source tables in the 'public' schema using geometry-aware spatial joins (ST_Intersects with ST_Centroid or direct geometry), resolves conflicts via interactive UI, logs edits, and commits changes back to the main database. Outputs include edited QGIS map layers, conflict reports, log entries in log_apps, and updated flag metadata in both public and proyectos tables.

name: Extract unique vector geometry points
desc: The script processes a QGIS vector layer to extract all unique coordinate points from its geometries (e.g., vertices of lines, polygons, or points), deduplicating them spatially. It either writes these points to a new Shapefile ('allpoints.shp') in the same directory as the input layer (processAlgorithm), or appends only the *new* points — those not already present in an existing point layer — to that layer (processAlgorithm2). The output is a point layer with attributes 'layername' (source layer name) and optionally 'pointname'. No raster data, time series, satellite imagery, classification, or geospatial modeling is involved; it is purely vector geometry decomposition and set-based point deduplication. Input source is a local Shapefile path (/home/alex/coding/1-1.shp), CRS is preserved from input, and no projection transformation beyond QGIS’s native context is applied. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and thematic analysis methods are not applicable.

name: Reproject future climate and land cover rasters
desc: The script reprojects two sets of raster datasets to EPSG:4326 with 0.01° resolution: (1) ensemble bioclimatic rasters for the future climate scenario 'ssp585_2071_2100' (8-GCM ensemble, BioClim variables), stored under '/Users/huangliting/Desktop/kissing_bugs_stats/future_reprojection/ssp585_2071_2100/'; and (2) seven land-cover class rasters (water, forest, grassland, barren, cropland, urban, permanent_snow_ice) extracted from a multi-band global LULC dataset under SSP1-RCP26 for 2025, reprojected and stored under '/Users/huangliting/Desktop/kissing_bugs_stats/future_reprojection/global_SSP1_RCP26_2025/'. No classification or modeling is performed—the script is purely geoprocessing: band extraction, reprojection, and resampling using QGIS GDAL warp and raster calculator.

name: Map species presence cells
desc: The script processes species occurrence point data (latitude/longitude CSV files) and overlays them onto a fixed-resolution geographic grid (0.05° and 0.5° grids). For each species in sp_rare_name_list, it (1) loads presence points and grid vector layers; (2) identifies grid cells intersecting ≥1 presence point (‘presence cells’) via spatial selection-by-location (predicates: intersect, contain, overlap, within); (3) assigns value 1 to a 'count' attribute for those cells; (4) exports the annotated grid as a CSV with presence/non-presence flags per cell; and (5) repeats the process using buffered presence points (0.5° diameter buffer) to derive ‘buffered presence’ cells (attribute 'b_05'). Outputs are species-specific CSV files listing grid cell IDs and binary presence/buffer-coverage indicators — intended for downstream statistical modeling (e.g., species distribution modeling or ensemble machine learning). No raster or satellite data is used; all inputs are vector-based point and polygon layers.

name: Extract climate variable means
desc: The script extracts mean zonal statistics for raster climate variables (e.g., from AdaptWest and Guangzhao Chen et al. datasets) over a fixed 0.05-degree grid (grid_005d.shp) covering an unspecified geographic area. It processes two sets of future climate rasters: (1) 'ssp585_2071_2100' (2071–2100, SSP5-8.5 scenario), and (2) 'global_SSP5_RCP85_2085' (2085, global SSP5/RCP8.5). For each raster, it runs QGIS's native zonal statistics (mean only) using vector grid cells as zones, then incrementally merges results into a single CSV per climate dataset — one column per raster variable, keyed by 'id'. The final outputs are two CSV files ('5km.csv') containing gridded mean values of climate variables (e.g., bioclimatic, temperature, precipitation layers), with no satellite imagery, classification, or modeling performed — only aggregation. No study area name, coordinate bounds, or sensor/band information is embedded in the code; all inputs are local GeoTIFFs with no metadata parsing.

name: Calculate parcel-level spectral band medians
desc: The script computes median values for the first 13 bands of each multiband GeoTIFF satellite image (excluding QA bands) over polygonal agricultural parcels. It loads a vector layer of parcels (e.g., 'belgium_extract.shp'), iterates over all .tif files in a specified satellite imagery directory, validates each as multiband, and applies QgsZonalStatistics to compute per-parcel median reflectance per band. Output is saved as a CSV with columns: [parcel_id, satellite_date, band1_int, ..., band13_int], where values are scaled from float (0–1) to int (0–10,000). The script explicitly handles Sentinel-2-like band count (13 bands, skipping QA10/QA20/QA60), implies use of surface reflectance data, and targets agricultural land parcels — evidenced by input path example 'data/parcels/belgium_extract.shp' and exclusion of QA bands typical of Sentinel-2 L2A. No classification, modeling, or temporal aggregation (e.g., NDVI, phenology) is performed — only zonal median extraction. Study area is Belgium (explicitly named in CLI example), time range is inferred from filenames (YYYYMMDD format), and no cloud masking or radiometric correction is applied in code.

name: Support missing person search
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin (Patrac) for supporting search-and-rescue operations for missing persons. It manages search unit configurations (handlers, searchers, drones, etc.), terrain friction modeling, distance estimation models (LSOM, Hill, UK), sector geometry validation and repair, email notification setup, user status management (on-duty, waiting, etc.), and integration with external servers (e.g., SAROPS, HSCR API) for real-time coordination. Key geospatial operations include vector geometry fixing (via QGIS native:fixgeometries), area calculation of search sectors, and configuration-driven travel time estimation across land cover classes using CSV-defined friction and unit-specific traversal times. The study area is explicitly Czech Republic administrative regions (kraje), referenced via two-letter codes (e.g., 'US', 'ST', 'KA', 'KH') corresponding to Czech regions (e.g., Ústí nad Labem, Středočeský, Karlovarský, Královéhradecký). Data sources are local filesystem-based (e.g., shapefiles at D:/patracdata/kraje/XX/vektor/ZABAGED/line_x/) and include precomputed stats.db files from a remote server (gisak.vsb.cz/patrac/). No satellite, sensor, or spectral band processing occurs in this script — it is purely a desktop GIS coordination tool with no Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing logic despite the prompt’s mischaracterization.

name: Visualize freight network tonnage by state
desc: The script loads and visualizes U.S. Freight Analysis Framework (FAF5) geospatial layers for regions, highway network links, and 2022 truck freight tonnage assignments. It filters layers to California and Nevada ('CA', 'NV'), joins tonnage data (from CSV) to highway links via 'ID', applies a categorized renderer to FAF5 regions by 'FAF_Zone_D', and applies a Jenks-classified graduated line width renderer to network links proportional to 'TOT Tons_22 All'. Outputs are styled vector layers in QGIS: colored FAF5 zones, filtered network links, and links scaled by 2022 total truck tonnage. Study area is limited to CA/NV; time range is explicitly 2022 (from filename 'FAF5_2022_Highway_Assignment_Results'); data sources are local shapefiles and a CSV — no satellite, sensor, or band usage.

name: Optimize retention tree selection
desc: The script computes and selects individual retention trees (säästöpuut) for ecological conservation within forest stands (leimikko), using a multi-criteria environmental valuation model. It integrates CHM-derived tree detection, forest stand attributes (e.g., species composition, stem counts, mean diameters/heights), biogeoclimatic grid data, protected area overlays, DTW (depth-to-water), Euclidean distance to watercourses, phosphorus retention capacity, biodiversity indices, and decay tree potential. Final output is a vector layer of optimized retention tree locations (points or small polygons), styled with QML, and accompanied by a PNG environmental factor contribution graph (Ympäristötekijät.png).

name: Mosaic LiDAR DEM tiles
desc: The script reads a CSV list of tile identifiers, constructs full file paths to individual GeoTIFF DEM files (e.g., 'DEM_CC11_2016_1000_0839.tif') located in a source folder, builds a GDAL Virtual Raster (VRT) from the list, then translates it into a single merged GeoTIFF mosaic ('merged.tif'), and loads the result as a QGIS raster layer named 'LiDAR DEM'. The workflow is designed for on-disk tile assembly—not cloud-based or GEE-native—using QGIS Processing Toolbox GDAL algorithms ('gdal:buildvirtualraster' and 'gdal:translate').

name: Sum night lights by country
desc: The script computes the sum of stable nighttime lights values (1–63, with background noise set to 0 and no-cloud areas coded as 255) across 21 annual DMSP-OLS stable lights raster files (1992–2013) for each country polygon in the TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3 shapefile. It uses QGIS’s SAGA 'rasterstatisticsforpolygons' algorithm with METHOD=0 (sum only) and no other statistics (mean, min, max, etc. disabled). The input rasters are NOAA/NCEI DMSP-OLS 'avg_vis' stable lights products, manually loaded from local file paths. Output is a vector layer attribute table where each country feature contains a summed pixel value across all years (i.e., per-polygon sum over time and space), then exported as a CSV with ISO-aligned geometry (via 'GEOMETRY=AS_XYZ') for merging with external datasets. Study area is global (all countries in TM_WORLD_BORDERS-0.3), time range is 1992–2013, and no spatial subsetting or reprojection is performed in the script.

name: Join and bin freight network links by tonnage
desc: The script joins FAF5 highway assignment flow data (total truck tons by commodity for 2022) to the FAF5 network links shapefile using the 'ID' field, then applies Jenks natural breaks classification to bin the joined tonnage values into 5 intervals. It outputs a full joined shapefile ('network_links_all.shp') and five binned shapefiles segmented by tonnage ranges. Styling is applied via graduated renderer with line width proportional to tonnage, and bin edges are extracted programmatically from the renderer.

name: Calculate green space percentage per neighbourhood
desc: The script calculates the percentage of green space area within each neighbourhood polygon in Toronto by intersecting green space and neighbourhood vector layers, reprojecting to UTM 17N (EPSG:6660) for metric-area accuracy, dissolving intersections by neighbourhood ID, computing neighbourhood total area (Area_NB) and intersected green space area (Area_GS), joining results back to the neighbourhood layer, and deriving PCT_GS = (Area_GS / Area_NB) × 100. It then symbolizes the result using graduated colours and exports a publication-ready PDF layout with map, legend, scale bar, north arrow, and inset photo of a Toronto park.

name: Standardize attribute structure to KUGI
desc: The script standardizes the attribute table of a user-selected vector layer to comply with the Indonesian National Spatial Data Infrastructure (KUGI) standard. It retrieves KUGI feature catalog metadata (categories, feature types, and attribute structures) via REST API calls to https://kugi.ina-sdi.or.id:8080/kugiapi/. It dynamically populates UI comboboxes with KUGI categories and feature types filtered by geometry type (point/line/polygon), then maps existing field names and types to KUGI-specified attribute names and value types (e.g., 'String', 'Integer', 'Date').
