It generates sampling points inside each building polygon at a user-defined density, samples the underlying raster’s three bands (assumed R/G/B), computes Euclidean distances between each sampled RGB and each legend entry, filters distances below a threshold, aggregates statistics (counts, proportions, min/avg distances) per building and legend category via SQL virtual joins, and outputs a final vector layer where each building is assigned a dominant category based on maximum proportional representation of sub-threshold distances — effectively performing supervised pixel-based spectral classification using discrete RGB legend anchors without ML, directly in QGIS via PyQGIS processing and virtual layers.

name: Sample raster values at points
desc: The script creates a set of random sampling points inside negatively buffered input polygons (i.e., points constrained to interior regions away from polygon edges), then extracts pixel values from an input raster at those point locations. The output is a point vector layer where each feature contains geometry and raster band values prefixed with 'band_', enabling spatially referenced in-situ sampling for validation, training, or statistical analysis.

name: Convert OSM waterbody JSON to vector layers
desc: The script converts OpenStreetMap (OSM) JSON export data into QGIS vector layers: linear waterbodies (Streams, Canals, Rivers) as LineString features in a GeoPackage, and areal waterbodies (Lakes, Ponds, Reservoirs) as Polygon features in a separate GeoPackage. It parses OSM 'node' and 'way' elements from the input JSON, maps them to domain-specific Python classes (e.g., Stream.fromOSMWay, Lake.fromOSMWay), and constructs QgsFeature objects with attributes NAME, TYPE, and geometric properties (LENGTH for lines, AREA for polygons). No remote sensing, time-series, or GEE server-side computation is performed — this is a client-side, OSM-to-GIS vector conversion tool operating entirely within QGIS using PyQt5 and QGIS Python API.

name: Create airport point layer
desc: The script reads a plain-text file 'airports.txt' containing comma-separated airport attributes (name, IATA code, latitude, longitude), parses each line, and creates a QGIS memory point vector layer with those attributes. It uses QgsGeometry.fromPointXY with longitude/latitude order (note: coordinate order is swapped in the call, but the input is standard lat/lon; the code incorrectly passes longitude first, implying WGS84 x,y order). The layer is added to the current QGIS project and exported as a shapefile 'airports.shp' in the same directory as the script. No geoprocessing, classification, or analysis is performed—only data ingestion and vector layer creation.

name: Buffer and merge vector layers
desc: The script performs geoprocessing on two user-provided shapefiles: it creates distance-based buffers around each input layer (with user-specified distances), merges the resulting buffered layers into a single vector layer, and optionally dissolves the merged features into a single multipart geometry; outputs are saved as Shapefile (.shp) layers — buffer1.shp, buffer2.shp, merge.shp, and optionally final_mit_dissolve.shp — and added to the QGIS project map canvas.

name: Clip LAI raster by county boundaries
desc: The script clips MODIS-derived Leaf Area Index (LAI) rasters — one per year from 2000 to 2022 — to individual county boundary layers loaded in the current QGIS project. It uses GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm to spatially subset each annual LAI GeoTIFF using vector layers named with the prefix 'County_' (e.g., 'County_Alameda'). The output is a set of clipped rasters named as '{county_name}_LAI_{year}.tif', saved to 'D:/thesis_data/lai_2000_2022/LAI_county_clipped/'. The input LAI files are pre-processed, locally stored GeoTIFFs (not raw GEE assets), and no temporal aggregation, statistical analysis, or classification is performed — only geometric clipping. Study area is implicitly defined by the loaded county layers and input rasters; time range is 2000–2022; satellite/sensor/bands are not specified in the script as it operates on precomputed LAI rasters.

name: Clip MODIS LAI raster data
desc: The script clips a time series of 23 pre-processed MODIS Leaf Area Index (LAI) rasters (2000–2022) to the North Carolina state boundary. It loads a local shapefile of North Carolina’s state and county boundaries as the mask, then applies GDAL-based raster clipping (gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer) to each annual LAI GeoTIFF. The output is a set of 23 clipped rasters saved in 'D:/thesis_data/lai_2000_2022/LAI_adjusted_Sclipped', each named with prefix 'clipped_' and retaining original year-based filenames. Input rasters are locally stored, pre-adjusted LAI products; no on-the-fly computation, classification, or temporal analysis (e.g., trend, anomaly) is performed — only spatial subsetting. CRS is preserved from input rasters, and nodata is set to -9999.

name: Clip NDVI raster by county boundaries
desc: The script clips precomputed annual NDVI rasters (2000–2022) — stored as local GeoTIFFs and labeled 'clipped_ndvi_adjusted_YYYY.tiff' — to individual county polygon layers loaded in the QGIS project (named 'County_X'). Each clip operation uses GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm with the county layer as mask, preserving the input CRS. The outputs are county-specific NDVI rasters saved to 'D:/thesis_data/ndvi_evi_2000_2022/NDVI/NDVI_county_clipped/_<county_name>_LAI_<year>.tif' (note: output path contains erroneous double underscore due to string formatting bug). The script does not perform any temporal analysis, classification, or statistical computation — only spatial subsetting. Study area is implied to be a region covered by both the MODIS-derived NDVI rasters and the 'County_' vector layers in the QGIS project; satellite/sensor/bands are not specified in the script, as inputs are already processed rasters. Time range is 2000–2022 (annual files).

name: Clip NDVI time series to state boundary
desc: The script clips a time series of pre-processed NDVI rasters (2000–2022) to the North Carolina state boundary using vector-based raster masking. The input rasters are locally stored GeoTIFFs named 'ndvi_adjusted_YYYY.tiff', indicating annual composite NDVI values; the clipping is performed via QGIS GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm with a nodata value of -9999 and CRS preservation. The output consists of 23 clipped GeoTIFF files saved in 'D:/thesis_data/ndvi_evi_2000_2022/NDVI/NDVI_adjusted_Sclipped/', each prefixed with 'clipped_' and retaining original filenames and projection. The study area is explicitly North Carolina (USA), confirmed by the shapefile path ('North_Carolina_State_and_County_Boundary_Polygons.shp') and layer name ('NC State Boundary'). No classification, temporal analysis, or statistical aggregation is performed — only geometric subsetting.

name: Generate Sentinel-2 RGB and geologic composites
desc: The script generates three virtual raster outputs for visual and geological interpretation: (1) a natural color composite (B04-red, B03-green, B02-blue) at native 10m resolution; (2) a geology-oriented false-color composite (B12-SWIR2, B04-red, B02-blue); and (3) a regolith-focused composite derived from band ratios — specifically B11/B12 (SWIR1/SWIR2), B8A/B12 (Narrow NIR/SWIR2), and resampled B8A/B03 (resampled 20m B8A divided by 10m B03) — all stacked as RGB bands. It performs resampling of B8A to 10m using GRASS r.resample and multiple GDAL raster calculator ratio operations before assembling composites via gdal:buildvirtualraster with separate bands and highest resolution.

name: Derive wind orientation field
desc: The script computes the orientation (direction) of a 2D vector field (velx, vely) representing surface motion or flow, transforms pixel coordinates from an orthographic projection centered at (-23.99218, -46.30013) — near Santos, Brazil — into WGS84 lat/lon, and exports the orientation (in degrees, normalized to [0, 360)) as a GeoTIFF raster named 'vector_field_santos.tif'. The input vector components (velx, vely) and spatial positions (posx, posy) are read from four external ASCII files ('extracted_posx.txt', 'extracted_posy.txt', 'extracted_velx.txt', 'extracted_vely.txt'), implying precomputed displacement or velocity data. The orthographic projection parameters and output filename ('santos') strongly indicate the study area is the Santos region in southeastern Brazil. No satellite imagery, time-series filtering, or classification is performed; the core geospatial operation is coordinate transformation + arctan2-based orientation derivation. Output is a single-band GeoTIFF with geographic extent inferred from transformed lat/lon bounds and affine geotransform.

name: Generate perpendicular transect lines
desc: The script generates a set of evenly spaced perpendicular line segments along input polyline features (e.g., rivers, roads, or survey lines). It computes the length of each input line, places perpendiculars at regular intervals (user-specified distance), and constructs symmetric segments of user-defined length oriented orthogonally to the local line direction. The output is a new memory vector layer of LineString geometries, each attributed with an integer ID and the accumulated distance along the original line where the perpendicular was placed. Labels are configured to display the 'distance' attribute, anchored near the end of each perpendicular line. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations are performed — this is purely a geometric vector processing workflow within QGIS using PyQGIS.

name: Generate urban activity spaces
desc: The script automates the creation of individualized urban activity spaces by modeling pedestrian or vehicular movement networks (via Steiner tree routing) from survey-derived origin/destination segments (e.g., home, work, school) along a road network. It buffers the resulting optimal routes to define activity zones, clips survey-referenced point data (e.g., trip attributes, land-use exposures) to those buffers, appends respondent IDs, exports per-respondent spatial and tabular outputs (shapefiles and CSVs), and computes aggregated statistics (averages and totals) — specifically for variable 'X3.7.03.1' — across all respondents, saving summary CSVs for totals and averages.

name: Process road distress data
desc: The script processes CSV files containing road distress measurements by joining them to a vector layer representing road sections (lines), using label and subsection ID fields for spatial attribution. It imports and optionally converts the split layer to GeoPackage format, then runs a custom 'process_distress_layer' algorithm for each CSV to produce joined output shapefiles (one per CSV). Unjoinable CSVs are reported separately. The workflow is folder-based, recursive over CSVs in the input directory, and outputs shapefiles in the specified output folder. No satellite, imagery, or temporal analysis is performed — inputs are purely tabular (CSV) and vector (line layer); no study area, time range, or sensor data is encoded in the script.

name: Join distress data to road sections
desc: The script performs a left attribute join between a 'split layer' (e.g., road segments or pavement sections) and a 'data layer' (e.g., pavement distress observations), using concatenated section and subsection identifiers (e.g., 'SectionID_SubsectionID') as the join key. It first computes a 'combined' field in both layers by concatenating user-specified label and subsection fields, then joins the split layer to the data layer on this combined field — ensuring all split features are retained (with nulls where no distress data exists). The output is a vector layer containing all attributes from both input layers, filtered to retain only the original field schemas of the inputs (via 'native:retainfields'), suitable for spatial distress mapping and reporting per road segment.

name: Join data to road network geometry
desc: The script joins a tabular data layer (e.g., maintenance records, traffic counts, or condition assessments) to a linear road network layer by matching section labels. It then computes the precise geometry of each data record as a subsection of the corresponding network line using start and end chainage values — either directly as distances along the line geometry or scaled by an optional length field — producing a new vector layer where features inherit both network topology and data attributes with dynamically derived linestrings.

name: Reposition raster image using ground control points
desc: The script repositions a raster image by applying four ground control points (GCPs) corresponding to the top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right corners of the input raster. It first reprojects the input raster to EPSG:27700 (OSGB 1936 / British National Grid) using GDAL translate, then applies GCP-based georeferencing with -gcp flags to assign real-world coordinates to pixel corners. The output is a georeferenced GeoTIFF with updated geotransform and projection metadata, preserving the original pixel values and dimensions. No resampling or warping is performed — only affine transformation via GCPs. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified, as the script operates generically on any user-provided raster layer without referencing temporal or spectral properties.

name: Calculate river sinuosity along reach
desc: The script computes sinuosity (reach length / straight-line distance) for sequential 5 km reaches along a river centerline geometry, stepping downstream by 500 m. It writes mid-reach station distances and corresponding sinuosity values to '/tmp/workfile.csv'. Additionally, it extracts and visualizes two points at 10 km and 20 km along the same river line as memory point layers, and includes a function to extract and visualize a sub-reach between two interpolated points as a new line layer. The input is a local shapefile of the river's thalweg ('asse_alveo_topino.shp'), located in the 'topino' subdirectory under 'frane_alveo_regione/pianure/elementi_morfo/'. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all operations are vector-based geometric computations on a QGIS QgsGeometry object. Output products are a CSV file with sinuosity metrics and temporary QGIS map layers for points and line segments.

name: Buffer and clip road networks
desc: The script performs a geoprocessing workflow to generate a service area buffer around point features (e.g., facilities or sensors), clip linear infrastructure (road/arruamento layers) to that buffer, dissolve the clipped roads, compute total length, count overlapping point features (e.g., traffic counts or monitoring points) within the buffer, and produce three renamed output layers: 'Area_Cobertura' (dissolved polygon buffer), 'Ruas_Atingidas' (dissolved clipped roads with length attribute), and 'Pontos_Sobrepostos' (polygon layer with point count per polygon). It computes and reports area (in km²), road length (in km), and point count; applies custom symbology (#ca9696 fill for buffer, #ff0000 line for clipped roads, #868686 for original roads); auto-zooms to the buffer extent; and saves a text report. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used — all inputs are local QGIS vector layers selected interactively by the user from the current project.

name: Manage geozone boundary features
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin for managing geospatial zones (GeoZone_Layer) by importing selected geometries from other vector layers, initializing mandatory attribute fields (e.g., 'localid', 'zonetype', 'datebegin', 'disease', 'countryf'), editing attributes interactively, and exporting selected features as a timestamped ESRI Shapefile bundle (including .shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, .cpg) zipped with metadata.json. It enforces data integrity via mandatory field validation, assigns operation types ('INSERT'/'UPDATE'), auto-generates UUIDs based on feature attributes and timestamp, applies an SLD style, and opens the export folder post-processing. No remote sensing analysis, satellite data, or GEE-specific functionality is present — this is a desktop GIS (QGIS) plugin for vector layer curation and metadata-driven export. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial analysis methods are not specified.

name: Clip raster by vector features
desc: The script clips a single local GeoTIFF raster (MergedLayer.tif) using individual polygon features from a local GeoPackage vector layer (vectorMask.gpkg), producing one clipped GeoTIFF per feature. Each output is saved with a unique filename incorporating the feature ID (e.g., clip_0.tif). The clipping is performed via QGIS Processing's gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer algorithm with CROP_TO_CUTLINE=True and KEEP_RESOLUTION=True, preserving original pixel resolution and extent to the mask geometry. No time-series analysis, spectral calculation, classification, or cloud masking is performed. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified — inputs are generic local files with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata discernible from the code.

name: Calculate polygon interior angles
desc: The script computes interior angles of a user-provided polygon by buffering its vertices (points), converting the buffered polygons to lines, and intersecting those lines with the original polygon to isolate angular line segments representing interior angles. The output is a vector layer ('Ângulos Internos') containing line features that geometrically correspond to the interior angles at each vertex of the input polygon.

name: Remove polygon vertex spikes
desc: The script processes vector polygon or multipolygon layers loaded in QGIS to detect and remove geometric spikes—sharp, narrow protrusions caused by digitization artifacts or noise—by computing interior angles at each vertex and filtering out vertices where the angle falls below a user-specified threshold (e.g., 10°). It operates entirely on client-side vector geometry using QgsGeometry and NumPy, with no raster or remote sensing data involved. The workflow includes: (1) selecting a polygon/multipolygon layer from the QGIS project; (2) prompting the user for an angle threshold; (3) iterating over each feature’s exterior ring coordinates; (4) calculating the angle formed by three consecutive vertices (prev–curr–next); (5) retaining only vertices where the computed angle ≥ threshold; (6) optionally adjusting the first vertex if it becomes degenerate after filtering; and (7) constructing a new cleaned polygon geometry. Outputs include a new in-memory vector layer named '<original_name>_unspiked', added to the QGIS project, and optionally exported to GeoPackage. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are referenced—the script is purely geometric preprocessing for vector topology cleanup.

name: Calculate polygon internal angles
desc: The script computes internal angles at polygon vertices by buffering vertex points, converting buffered polygons to lines, and intersecting those lines with the input polygon. The output is a line vector layer representing angular segments (portions of the buffered vertex circles clipped by the polygon boundary), symbolized in red and labeled with angle values rounded to two decimal places. No raster or satellite data is used; inputs are user-provided vector layers (polygon and point vertices). Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified — the algorithm is purely geometric and agnostic to location or temporal context.

name: Split parcels with river buffer
desc: The script splits polygon features representing land parcels ('Lotes') using a buffered representation of a river line layer ('Rio'). It first creates a 1.5-meter-wide rounded buffer around the river line, then uses that buffer geometry as a cutting line to divide the input parcel polygons. The output is a new vector layer ('Lotes Divididos') containing the subdivided parcel geometries where intersections with the buffered river occur — effectively partitioning parcels that straddle or adjoin the river corridor.

name: Plan drone flight lines
desc: The script computes optimal drone flight planning parameters—including lateral and frontal photo overlap distances—based on user-specified sensor geometry (dc, dl), focal length (f), flight altitude (H), and overlap percentages. It extracts the northernmost edge of the input polygon terrain layer, extends it to span the full west–east extent, generates parallel flight lines spaced by the calculated lateral spacing (deltaLat), unions them into a single continuous flight line geometry, and then places photo capture points along that line at intervals equal to the calculated frontal spacing (deltaFront). Outputs are two QGIS vector layers: (1) a red polyline layer 'LinhaVoo' representing the complete planned flight path, and (2) a blue point layer 'Pontos' with labeled IDs indicating individual photo locations along the flight line.

name: Visualize real-time point locations
desc: The script visualizes static and dynamically updated point features (e.g., moving assets or monitored sites) on a QGIS map canvas using a world base layer and CSV-sourced initial points. It reads latitude/longitude coordinates from 'selected_rows.csv', renders them as red points on an EPSG:4326 memory layer, and updates their positions in real time via ZeroMQ messages (formatted as 'id,long,lat') received on tcp://localhost:5555. The study area is implicitly global (world_map.shp), but the visualization is centered on the extent of the loaded shapefile. No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or geoprocessing is performed — only vector point rendering and geometry updates. Outputs include an interactive QGIS canvas showing a semi-transparent world map with animated/red point markers, refreshed upon each ZeroMQ message.

name: Quantify unwalled border length by corridor
desc: The script calculates the annual length (in meters and miles) of unwalled US-Mexico border segments by corridor (CORNO) from 1990 to 2021. It buffers pedestrian fencing/wall geometries (from Arizona) by 300 meters, clips them against corridor-aligned border line geometries using QGIS difference operation, computes remaining line lengths per corridor, and aggregates results into a yearly time-series DataFrame. Outputs include a GeoJSON of clipped border lines, a CSV ('empty_border_cor_year_1990.csv') with columns year, length (m), CORNO, and miles.

name: Buffer roads and remove building overlaps
desc: The script processes a road centerline vector layer by applying a 4-meter buffer (with round end caps and joins), dissolving the buffered polygons, converting multipart geometries to singleparts, adding a UID field starting from 888, then subtracting (via difference operation) building footprint polygons to produce a final road buffer layer where road buffers are clipped to exclude areas occupied by buildings. The output is saved as a shapefile (ICM_ROADS.shp) and loaded into QGIS.

name: Select optimal school site
desc: The script performs multi-criteria suitability analysis for school site selection using GIS-based rasterization and proximity modeling. It takes user-provided shapefiles representing criteria (e.g., roads, rivers, existing schools, land use), rasterizes them to a common extent and resolution (28.38985503875978 m) derived from a study area shapefile, then computes Euclidean distance (proximity) rasters for each criterion. The outputs are georeferenced GeoTIFF rasters: (1) binary rasters of input criteria (e.g., 'roads.tif'), and (2) corresponding proximity rasters (e.g., 'prox_roads.tif'). No classification, weighting, or final suitability map synthesis is implemented in the provided code — only preprocessing steps. Study area is defined by an input shapefile; no time-dependent data or satellite imagery is used. All operations are local GDAL/OGR-based, not GEE cloud processing.

name: Map TROPOMI acquisition time differences
desc: The script visualizes the temporal difference (in minutes) between collocated ground-based measurements and the closest TROPOMI satellite overpass time, using a precomputed GeoPackage containing point geometries with time-difference attributes. It applies a QGIS layer style to render these differences spatially, overlays them on a world basemap, and exports the result as a high-resolution PNG image via a predefined print layout template.

name: Assign projection to raster layer
desc: The script reprojects selected vector layers to a target CRS (EPSG:28355 — GDA94 / MGA Zone 55) using QGIS's native reprojection algorithm, and assigns the same CRS to selected raster layers (without resampling or georeferencing — i.e., only updates the CRS metadata) using GDAL's assignprojection tool. It outputs in-memory reprojected vector layers (with '_reprojected' suffix) and raster layers with assigned CRS (with '_assigned_crs' suffix), both added to the current QGIS project. No new files are written to disk; all outputs remain in memory.

name: Modify WKT geometry strings
desc: The script modifies a delimited text (CSV) feature layer by replacing invalid or placeholder WKT geometry strings — specifically '(EMPTY)' and '(0 0)' — with randomly generated POINT geometries that lie within a user-selected polygon boundary layer. It copies the original CSV file to a new location/name, parses the CSV, identifies the WKT column via user prompt, iteratively replaces each invalid WKT token with a valid random point inside the bounding polygon’s geometry (using rejection sampling), writes the updated CSV, and loads it back into QGIS as a valid delimited text layer with MULTIPOINT WKT interpretation (though replacement produces POINTs; the input layer type is MultiPoint, but output geometry is coerced via WKT string substitution). No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived metrics are involved — this is a local GIS data-cleaning and geometry-imputation workflow operating entirely on vector layers loaded in QGIS desktop.

name: Quantify fault overlap or separation distance
desc: The script computes the geometric relationship (overlap vs. separation) between two selected fault line features by constructing a quadrilateral buffer polygon from their transects, intersecting transect-derived lines with that polygon, measuring lengths and bearings of clipped segments, and statistically comparing mean bearing against mean fault strike to classify the interaction as 'Overlap' (O) or 'Separation' (S); outputs include clipped transect line layers labeled with depth, fault shorthand (e.g., 'CA_SF_O'), mean length, standard deviation, and a final polygon layer annotated with O/S ratio, average lengths, and total fault length.

name: Generate lidar tile polygons from DSM and DTM rasters
desc: The script generates a GeoPackage vector layer containing polygon footprints (tiles) representing the spatial extent of paired DSM (Digital Surface Model) and DTM (Digital Terrain Model) raster files from a LiDAR campaign. It processes raster files from two user-specified local folders (DSM and DTM), computes each raster’s geographic extent using its geotransform, creates WKT polygon geometries, matches DSM and DTM tiles by identical geometry (not filename), and writes attribute-rich features including resolution, filenames, directory paths, CRS (EPSG code), authority ('ENTE'), year ('ANNO'), and format. Output is a GeoPackage named 'tile_dsm_dtm.gpkg', optionally reprojected to a user-defined output CRS, and automatically loaded into QGIS. The script relies entirely on local GDAL-readable raster files (e.g., GeoTIFF) — no remote GEE assets are used; it is a QGIS plugin, not a Google Earth Engine script. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified because the script operates on arbitrary local LiDAR-derived rasters without embedded temporal or sensor metadata.

name: Execute SQL query on vector layers
desc: The script executes a user-defined SQL query over one or more input vector layers using QGIS's virtual layer provider. It constructs a QgsVirtualLayerDefinition by registering each input layer as 'input1', 'input2', etc., optionally writes transient memory layers to disk if not in the project, expands expressions in the SQL query, sets UID/geometry field/type/CRS metadata, creates a temporary virtual vector layer, validates it, and exports the resulting features to a feature sink (e.g., memory layer or file). No raster data, time-series analysis, remote sensing calculations, or machine learning is involved — it is purely a vector SQL execution engine within QGIS Processing framework.

name: Export vector layer to SpatiaLite
desc: Exports a vector layer to a SpatiaLite database file, creating a new table (or overwriting an existing one) with optional spatial index, geometry column customization, field name case conversion, string length constraint dropping, and single-part geometry enforcement. The script performs no remote sensing analysis, no time-series processing, no classification, and no visualization—it is a pure vector data export utility within QGIS Processing Framework targeting SpatiaLite databases.

name: Execute and load PostgreSQL SQL query
desc: Executes a user-provided SQL query against a configured PostgreSQL/PostGIS database connection and loads the resulting table (with geometry and ID fields) as a valid QGIS vector layer in the current project. The script resolves the database connection via QGIS provider metadata, constructs a QgsDataSourceUri with the SQL subquery as a virtual table, sets geometry and primary key field names, instantiates a QgsVectorLayer, validates it, and registers it in the processing context for automatic loading. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed — it is purely a database query execution and vector layer ingestion tool. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Calculate river bank erosion and accretion
desc: The script calculates spatially explicit river bank erosion and accretion between two user-provided vector shapefiles representing river centerlines or banks for two distinct time periods. It creates a 30m fishnet grid clipped to a user-defined study area polygon, overlays each year’s river geometry with the fishnet to compute intersecting areas, computes unchanged area via intersection of year-1 and year-2 overlays, then derives erosion (Year2_area − unchanged_area) and accretion (Year1_area − unchanged_area) per grid cell. Results are aggregated into 3 km stretches (grouping ~300 grids), and the top 30 stretches with highest erosion and accretion (in km²) are exported as separate shapefiles. Input data sources are user-provided local shapefiles — no satellite imagery, cloud masking, spectral indices, or GEE server-side processing is used; all operations are client-side using GeoPandas and Shapely. Study area, time periods, and river geometries are fully user-specified at runtime and not hardcoded.

name: Calculate land use enrichment factors
desc: The script computes pairwise enrichment factors between user-specified land use classes from a single input land use raster, then generates neighborhood maps for each class. It reads a local GeoTIFF land use classification raster (e.g., 'LandUse layer name'), extracts unique land use values, allows users to assign descriptive names to each value via a QGIS dialog table, and passes them to a Model class that performs spatial neighborhood analysis (e.g., calculating co-occurrence or proximity-based enrichment) and plots both enrichment factor matrices and neighborhood maps. Outputs include plotted figures (enrichment factor heatmaps and neighborhood maps) saved to a user-specified output directory. No remote sensing imagery processing, time-series analysis, or cloud-based GEE computation occurs — all operations are local (GDAL/Numpy-based) on a static raster. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Model flood inundation extent
desc: The script models flood inundation by integrating hydrographic features (rivers), digital elevation data (MNT), land cover (OCS), building footprints (BD_topo), and population layers to identify areas vulnerable to submersion. It clips all input layers to a user-defined study boundary ('couche_decoupe'), computes terrain-based statistics (median elevation for buildings/population, minimum elevation for land cover), buffers hydrographic lines by a user-specified terrestrial buffer distance, then extracts features where terrain-derived elevation values fall below a user-defined submersion height threshold — finally intersecting or clipping these vulnerable features with the buffered hydro network to produce spatially constrained flood-impacted outputs: a masked DEM ('MNT_final'), flooded population polygons ('pop_final'), flooded building polygons ('Bati_final'), and flooded land cover polygons ('ocs_final').

name: Map fire scar extent
desc: The script maps fire scars by applying a pre-trained U-Net deep learning model to paired pre-fire and post-fire georeferenced raster images. It loads rasters via QGIS (GDAL), extracts pixel data as numpy arrays, constructs input pairs using the custom `create_datasetAS` function, runs inference on the CPU (or GPU if available), generates binary prediction masks (1 = scar, 0 = non-scar), writes outputs as GeoTIFFs with georeferencing preserved from the pre-fire layer, and adds them to the QGIS project in grouped layers with pseudocolor rendering (Reds ramp) for visualization. Input rasters must be manually pre-cropped to the affected area and share identical extent, resolution, and naming convention (e.g., 'ImgPreF_CL-BI_ID74101_u350_19980330_clip.tif'). The model is downloaded on-demand from an S3 bucket if missing. No cloud masking, atmospheric correction, or band math (e.g., NDVI, dNBR) is performed — raw multiband inputs are fed directly to the neural network. Study area, satellite/sensor, and time range are not specified in the code; inputs are arbitrary local files selected interactively.

name: Map fire scar extent
desc: The script maps fire scar extent by applying a pre-trained U-Net deep learning model to paired pre-fire and post-fire georeferenced raster images. Input rasters must be manually selected by the user via file dialogs, conform to a strict naming convention (e.g., 'ImgPreF_CL-BI_ID74101_u350_19980330_clip.tif'), and be spatially aligned (same extent, resolution, CRS). The model processes multiband spectral inputs (exact bands not specified in code; inferred as ≥3 from dataset creation logic), computes pixel-wise binary burn/no-burn predictions, and writes output GeoTIFFs ('FireScar_*.tif') with nodata=0. Outputs are added to QGIS project in grouped layers (pre-fire, post-fire, and scar) with pseudocolor rendering (white→black gradient) applied automatically to scar rasters. No cloud masking, atmospheric correction, or spectral index computation is performed — raw raster data is fed directly to the model. Study area, time range, satellite, and bands are not encoded in the script logic and must be provided externally by the user.

name: Split vector layer by attribute
desc: The script performs attribute-based splitting of a QGIS vector layer: it filters the input layer by a user-specified field-value pair (e.g., 'type' = 'road'), retrieves all unique values in that field, then creates and exports separate vector layers (as Shapefile or GeoJSON) for each unique value. It applies subset string filtering on the original layer, constructs memory layers with matching geometry type and CRS, copies fields and features, and prompts the user to save each split layer. No remote sensing, raster, or time-series analysis is performed; the entire workflow operates client-side within QGIS using local vector data. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geospatial modeling methods are not involved or referenced.

name: Determine needed schools from population data
desc: The script calculates the number of additional schools required per administrative area (e.g., adm3_en level) by dividing population (from a PostgreSQL-sourced polygon layer) by a user-defined maximum students per school, then subtracting the count of existing schools (point layer) within each polygon. It generates a QGIS memory vector layer ('Needed Schools') with attributes: Location_Name, Expected_Schools, current_number_of_schools, Schools_that_are_supposed_to_be_built, and a formatted label string. The layer is added to the QGIS project with Arial 10pt labeling enabled. All geospatial operations (ST_Within, ST_Transform, ST_GeomFromText, ST_AsText) are performed server-side in PostgreSQL; no GEE (Google Earth Engine) code or API calls appear in the script — despite the prompt’s mischaracterization, this is a QGIS Python plugin dialog using psycopg2, not a GEE script. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and Earth Engine assets are not present or referenced.

name: Find shortest path to hospital
desc: The script connects to a local PostGIS database to retrieve hospital names and road numbers from two tables: 'hotosm_mwi_health_facilities_points_shp' (health facilities in Malawi) and 'roads1' (road network). It presents a QGIS dialog for the user to select one road number and one hospital name. It then copies all features from the 'roads1' layer to an output feature sink — no actual shortest-path routing (e.g., Dijkstra, A*) is implemented; the script merely exports the full road layer without spatial or network analysis. The study area is implicitly Malawi (from 'hotosm_mwi_' prefix in table name), but no geoprocessing, distance calculation, or path optimization occurs. Output is a vector layer identical to the input roads layer.

name: Create polygon from coordinates
desc: The script reads latitude and longitude coordinates from an Excel file and constructs a closed polygon geometry in EPSG:4326, then saves it as a shapefile and adds it to the QGIS project. It does not perform any Earth Engine (GEE) computation, satellite data processing, classification, or time-series analysis — it is purely a local GIS vector creation workflow using QGIS Python API (PyQGIS). The study area is defined solely by the input coordinates; no spatial filtering, projection transformation beyond WGS84, or attribute derivation is performed. Output is a single ESRI Shapefile containing one polygon feature with an 'id' field.

name: Extract public lighting infrastructure
desc: The script downloads a public lighting dataset from DATASUD (Marseille region), filters it spatially to the current QGIS canvas extent using a bounding box in WGS84, and exports the filtered point features (streetlights) as a GeoPackage. The input is a CSV file containing LATITUDE and LONGITUDE columns; it is converted to a GeoDataFrame with point geometries, then spatially joined with the canvas-derived bounding box. The study area is dynamically defined by the user’s QGIS map canvas extent. No time filtering or temporal analysis is performed; the dataset source has no explicit temporal metadata in the code. Output is a GPKG layer of public lighting assets intersecting the canvas extent.

name: Extract street lighting infrastructure
desc: The script extracts street lighting infrastructure (e.g., street lamps, street lights) from three distinct geospatial sources — Mapillary (via vector tile API for 'object--street-light' features), OpenStreetMap (via OSMnx using 'highway=street_lamp' tags), and DataSud (a CSV dataset of public lighting assets in Marseille with LATITUDE/LONGITUDE coordinates). It operates on the current QGIS canvas extent, reprojects it to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), computes bounding box coordinates (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax), and filters all retrieved features to intersect only that bounding box. Outputs are GeoPackage (.gpkg) or GeoJSON files: one for raw Mapillary/OSM/DataSud data (OUTPUT_INT used only for DataSud intermediate download), and one final filtered output layer (OUTPUT) containing only street lighting features within the user-defined map extent. No temporal filtering, classification, or modeling is performed — it is a spatial extraction and format conversion workflow.

name: Visualize PS-InSAR time-series displacement
desc: The script visualizes point-wise InSAR time-series displacement data from a CSV file containing latitude/longitude and time-series columns (e.g., dates as column headers), plots displacement over time for a single selected point, computes and displays velocity, residual height, standard deviation, and coherence, and applies a graduated color scheme to a vector layer based on the 'vel' attribute using 20 velocity bins. It also supports conversion of input CSV (with lat/lng columns) to a point shapefile and saving plots as PNG files.

name: Extract municipality-scale topographic rasters
desc: The script extracts municipality-scale digital elevation model (DEM) rasters by clipping the NASA SRTM NASADEM GeoTIFF to individual municipal boundaries from the 'BR_Municipios_2023.shp' shapefile. It loads a single static DEM raster ('srtm_nasadem.tif'), filters a national municipal boundary layer for three specific municipalities in Brazil — 'Torres', 'Mampituba', and 'Itati' — and performs vector-masked raster clipping (gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer) for each, producing three georeferenced GeoTIFF outputs named '<municipio>_recorte.tif'. The study area is explicitly limited to these three coastal municipalities in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. No temporal analysis is performed; the input DEM is a static, non-temporal product. Outputs are loaded as raster layers into QGIS and saved to disk.

name: Compute landscape metrics for class patches
desc: The script computes landscape-level metrics—including total surface area, total perimeter, and patch count—within a regular grid overlaying a user-specified land-cover class (e.g., class value '1') extracted from an input classified raster. It first isolates the target class via raster algebra, labels connected components (patches), vectorizes them, filters out background (patch_id = 0), fixes geometries, overlays a user-defined square grid (e.g., 300 m spacing), intersects grid cells with patches, calculates per-polygon area and perimeter, aggregates counts and sums per grid cell, and outputs a table where each row represents a grid cell with its aggregated metrics (id, bounding box coordinates, first/last patch ID, total surface, total perimeter, and patch count).

name: Convert GPS points to polygons
desc: The script converts a CSV file of GPS points (with longitude, latitude, and 'id' fields) into closed polygon geometries by first creating ordered paths per 'id' group, then joining attributes from an existing QGIS layer named 'xrf_data' (also keyed by 'id'), fixing geometries, and finally converting the resulting lines to polygons. The input CSV is located at 'C:\mapping_final\ch2_graduatedmap.csv', and the workflow relies entirely on vector processing in QGIS Processing Toolbox (not GEE), despite the prompt referencing 'GEE script'—no Earth Engine code is present; all operations are desktop QGIS Python processing algorithms. Study area, time range, satellite data, and Earth Engine-specific parameters are absent. The output is a temporary polygon layer derived from point sequencing and attribute joining.

name: Rasterize DEPTH2D vector layers
desc: The script converts user-selected vector layers containing a 'DEPTH2D' attribute into georeferenced rasters at 0.5 m resolution using GDAL's rasterize algorithm. It preserves the input layer's extent and coordinate reference system, saves outputs as GeoTIFFs in the same directory as the source vector files, inserts each raster layer directly above its corresponding vector layer in the QGIS layer tree, and applies a predefined QML style (depth_style.qml) for visualization. The script operates entirely on locally loaded vector layers in QGIS — no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or Earth Engine data is used; all inputs are user-provided shapefiles or similar vector sources with a 'DEPTH2D' field. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified because the script performs local GIS rasterization only.

name: Generate canopy height model from LiDAR point clouds
desc: The script processes .laz (LiDAR point cloud) files to generate a Digital Terrain Model (DTM/MNT) by filtering ground points (Classification = 2), a Digital Surface Model (DSM/MNS) using all points, fills NoData gaps in both rasters using interpolation, merges all individual MNT and MNS rasters into single seamless layers, and computes the normalized difference (MNS − MNT) to produce a Canopy Height Model (CHM), also referred to as MNV (Model of Normalized Vegetation). Outputs are three GeoTIFFs: 'mnt_fusionne.tif', 'mns_fusionne.tif', and 'mnv_fusionne.tif', each loaded as raster layers into the QGIS project.

name: Add Esri Standard basemap to QGIS project
desc: The script configures and adds an XYZ raster tile layer (Esri World Street Map) as a basemap in a QGIS project. It removes any pre-existing layer with the same name, constructs a WMS-compatible XYZ connection string with zoom range [0,19], validates the layer, and adds it to the project. It also transforms a vector layer named 'Districts' to EPSG:3857, sets its opacity to 40%, creates a red star-shaped marker at (-74.0, 4.6), and adds a page frame to a newly initialized print layout named 'DemoLayout'. No geospatial analysis, classification, modeling, or time-series processing is performed — the operations are purely cartographic and layer management tasks within QGIS Desktop using PyQGIS. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and analytical methods are not involved or specified.

name: Delimit cultural heritage buffer zones
desc: The script computes multi-ring buffer-based protection zones around cultural heritage assets ('Bienes') by generating 50 m and 200 m solid buffers, converting them to annular (ring-shaped) geometries by removing the original asset footprints, then intersecting these rings with land-use/land-cover categories (SueloUrbano, SueloUrbanizable, SueloRustico) to define legally relevant environmental envelopes. It synthesizes three distinct regulatory envelopes: (1) a 50 m urban envelope (overlaid on urban soil), (2) a 50 m urbanizable envelope, (3) a 200 m rustic envelope; merges and dissolves them by 'ID' to produce one polygon per heritage asset; adds a 150 m intermediate urbanizable ring (200 m minus 50 m); and finally unifies all components into a single multipart geometry layer 'EntornoDA' — representing the automatically derived statutory protection perimeter for each cultural heritage site.

name: Detect riparian vegetation change
desc: The script performs multi-temporal riparian vegetation change detection by separating drone-derived vector layers (2021 and 2023) into riparian and upland components, rasterizing them using a buffered valley bottom extent as spatial template, clipping constant rasters to each polygon subset, and combining them via a weighted raster algebra expression (e.g., +2 for 2021 riparian, +6 for 2023 riparian, −2/−6 for corresponding upland classes) to produce a single classified change raster ('veg_final.tif') encoding directional vegetation status shifts; outputs include the final raster and a histogram-based HTML report of pixel value frequencies.

name: Extract terrain elevation profiles
desc: The script extracts elevation profiles along two orthogonal transects (north-south and east-west) centered on a local DEM raster layer ('DEM.tif'). It loads the DEM as a QGIS raster layer, computes its spatial extent, constructs two memory vector lines bisecting the extent at its center (one meridional, one zonal), samples elevation values at 100 evenly spaced points along each line using QGIS raster identification, handles missing values via linear interpolation over valid elevations, computes cumulative distance arrays, and plots both profiles in a single matplotlib figure labeled 'Profil wysokościowy wzdłuż wybranych transektów' with axes 'Dystans [m]' and 'Wysokość [m]'. The study area is defined solely by the extent of the local file 'DEM.tif'; no satellite imagery, time-series, or external GEE assets are used — this is a desktop QGIS/Python workflow operating on a pre-existing local DEM. All operations are coordinate-reference-system-aware (EPSG:2180 specified for the output vector layer), but CRS handling for the DEM itself is implicit and not validated in the script.

name: Count nearby point features
desc: The script implements an interactive spatial query tool in QGIS that, upon clicking a map location, (1) retrieves and displays the WGS84 coordinates (lat/lon), (2) performs reverse geocoding via the French GeoPlatform API to return the nearest address (street name, INSEE code, city), (3) counts the number of point features from a user-selected vector layer that fall within a user-specified distance (in meters) buffer around the clicked point, (4) draws both the buffer (as a transparent black-outline polygon layer named 'Buffer' in EPSG:3857) and the clicked point (as a red point layer named 'Clicked_Point' in EPSG:3857) on the map canvas. The study area is not specified — it operates interactively over any loaded vector point layer in the current QGIS project; no satellite, raster, or time-series data is used. All operations are vector-based geometric intersections and coordinate transformations.

name: Count point features near clicked location
desc: The script enables interactive point-based spatial analysis in QGIS: upon clicking the map canvas, it (1) transforms the click coordinates to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), (2) performs reverse geocoding against the French BAN (Base Adresse Nationale) API to retrieve the nearest street address, (3) constructs a user-defined meter-radius buffer around the clicked point, (4) counts vector point features from user-selected QGIS project layers that intersect the buffer, and (5) visualizes the buffer as a temporary transparent polygon layer named 'buffers'. All operations occur client-side in QGIS using local project layers — no Earth Engine (GEE) imagery, time-series, or cloud-based geospatial processing is used. The script does not access Google Earth Engine at all; despite the prompt’s framing, this is a pure QGIS Python plugin with no GEE dependencies or code.

name: Convert CSV coordinates to path shapefile
desc: The script converts a CSV file containing latitude and longitude columns into a point shapefile (EPSG:4326), then connects those points in sequence (without closing the path) to generate a polyline (path) shapefile. It uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'native:createpointslayerfromtable' and 'native:pointstopath' — no spatial analysis, classification, or time-series operations are performed; the workflow is purely vector geometry generation from tabular coordinate data.

name: Convert GPS points to linear path
desc: The script converts a CSV file containing latitude and longitude columns into a point shapefile (EPSG:4326), then connects those points in sequence (without closing the path) to generate a polyline shapefile representing a trajectory or route. The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'native:createpointslayerfromtable' and 'native:pointstopath', with no spatial filtering, temporal analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations. Input CSV structure is inferred to contain 'Latitude' and 'Longitude' fields; output files are written to fixed local paths on Windows. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis beyond vector geometry generation is present — it is purely a tabular-to-vector conversion pipeline.

name: Count pipeline-road intersections
desc: The script counts the total number of geometric intersections between a single-line pipeline route vector layer and multiple road line vector layers (each loaded from individual shapefiles in a directory). It uses QGIS’s native 'intersection' processing algorithm to compute point or line intersections for each road layer, accumulates the feature counts across all road shapefiles, writes the cumulative count to a plain-text file (Roads.txt), and prints the final total. The study area is implied by the local file paths but not geographically specified; CRS is set to EPSG:4326 for all layers, but no reprojection or topology validation is performed. Input data sources are local ESRI Shapefiles — one pipeline route (A.shp) and multiple road network files (e.g., RoadLink/*.shp); no satellite, sensor, or spectral data is used. Output is a scalar integer count stored in a text file.

name: Calculate soil type intersection length
desc: The script computes the length of line features (e.g., roads, pipelines, or transects) from an input shapefile (A.shp) that intersect with polygon features in a soil overlay layer (DSMW.shp), then calculates the percentage of each line’s total length falling within each soil type (DOMSOI attribute). It outputs a shapefile of the geometric intersection and a CSV table listing each soil type, its intersected line length (in meters, projected CRS: EPSG:32630), and the percentage of the original line’s total length. The study uses vector layers only — no time-series, satellite imagery, or raster analysis. CRS mismatch is present (input forced to EPSG:32630, overlay to EPSG:4326), implying on-the-fly reprojection during intersection; however, the script does not validate or reproject overlay_layer to match input CRS before processing. Output paths are hardcoded to local Windows directories under 'F:/Internship at DTNEC/QGIS Pipeline/'. No study area name, time range, or satellite data is referenced.

name: Calculate soil type intersection length
desc: The script performs a vector intersection between an input line layer (e.g., roads, pipelines, or transects) and an overlay polygon layer containing soil type attributes (DOMSOI). It computes the length of each intersected line segment per soil type, calculates the percentage of total line length attributed to each soil type, and exports the results (soil type, intersected length, percentage) to a CSV file. The intersection is executed using QGIS's native:intersection algorithm; CRS handling explicitly sets the input layer to EPSG:32630 and overlay layer to EPSG:4326; output shapefile and CSV paths are hardcoded.

name: Calculate radar beam blockage by terrain
desc: The script computes terrain-induced radar beam blockage for the Phitsanulok radar (Thailand), using its real-world geometric configuration (azimuth angles from an original radar shapefile, elevation angle = 0.5°, radar height = 30 m above ground + 47 m ASL). It constructs a polygonal coverage layer ('poly_beamblock') representing contiguous radar bins along 360 azimuths up to 237 km range, with bin size = 1000 m. For each polygon, it calculates beam height above sea level using effective Earth radius (4/3 × 6374 km) and assigns DEM-derived terrain height (from 'DEM_for_PHS_radar.tif') via centroid sampling. Beam blockage is determined per azimuth: the first bin where beam height ≤ DEM height defines the blocking horizon distance; all subsequent bins at that azimuth are flagged as blocked (BeamBlock = 1); unblocked bins are set to 0. Outputs include a vector shapefile ('BeamBlockPhitsanulokRadar.shp') and a rasterized version ('BeamBlockPhitsanulokRadarRaster.tif') at 500 m resolution in UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), covering the radar’s full coverage extent. The study area is implicitly defined by the radar location (100.2179637°E, 16.7754090°N) and the DEM extent.

name: Model radar beam blockage
desc: The script computes terrain-induced radar beam blockage for Chiang Rai radar using real radar geometry (azimuth angles extracted from a reference shapefile of Chiang Rai radar scans), calculates effective beam polygons along each azimuth at range bins (500 m), estimates beam height above sea level using the 4/3 Earth radius model, extracts DEM elevation at polygon centroids, and determines beam blockage status (1=blocked, 0=unblocked) by comparing beam height to terrain height. Outputs include: (1) a memory polygon layer with attributes — elevAngle, radialAng, horizonDis (range in meters), size (beam width in km), heightASL (beam height m ASL), DEM_ASL (terrain height m ASL), BeamBlock (binary); (2) a saved shapefile 'BeamBlockChiangraiRadar.shp'; and (3) a rasterized version 'BeamBlockChiangraiRaster.tif' (500 m resolution, EPSG:32647) where pixel values encode blockage status. Study area is Chiang Rai radar coverage in northern Thailand; time range is not temporal — it is a static geometric/terrain analysis based on fixed radar parameters and a static DEM. Input data sources: radar scan shapefile ('rad_cri_utm201908041300.shp') providing real azimuth angles, and a local DEM GeoTIFF ('DEM_for_CRI_radar.tif'). No satellite or remote sensing imagery is used — all inputs are ground-based radar geometry and topographic data.

name: Validate radar precipitation against gauge measurements
desc: The script validates 15-minute rainfall estimates from radar imagery against in-situ rain gauge measurements in the Yom River basin, Thailand. It reads gauge station metadata (including WGS84 coordinates) and time-synchronized 15-minute gauge rainfall values from CSV files; transforms station coordinates from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647); samples radar raster values at each transformed gauge location using QgsRasterLayer.dataProvider().sample(); and writes paired gauge-radar rainfall values (station ID, gauge mm, radar mm) to a CSV file ('temp_val15min.csv') for statistical validation. The study area is the Yom River basin; the time is fixed to a single timestamp — 2018-07-17 at 18:00 (15-minute accumulation); data sources are local CSV files (gauge locations and 15-min rainfall) and a local GeoTIFF radar mosaic (path_rr); no satellite or sensor is involved — the radar data is ground-based (weather radar), not satellite-derived; geospatial operations include coordinate transformation and point sampling; output is a CSV table of collocated gauge-radar pairs.

name: Validate radar rainfall against gauge rainfall
desc: The script validates radar-derived rainfall against in-situ rain gauge measurements at 15-minute temporal resolution over the Yom River Basin in Thailand. It reads gauge station coordinates (from '1สถานีวัดฝนกรมอุตุลุ่มน้ำยม2018.csv'), transforms them from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), then spatially extracts radar rainfall values (from GeoTIFF files in 'z_temp/1outp_mosaic_temp/') at each gauge’s UTM location using QgsRasterLayer.dataProvider().sample(). Simultaneously, it reads co-temporal 15-minute gauge rainfall values from CSV files (in '1outp_gauge_temp/1gauge15min/'). For each matched radar–gauge timestamp and station, it pairs the gauge value (column index 2 of the CSV row) and extracted radar value into a tuple. The output is a CSV file ('validate_rr_rg_15min.csv') containing station ID, gauge rainfall (mm), and radar rainfall (mm) — intended for subsequent statistical validation (bias, MSE, RMSE). Study area is explicitly the Yom River Basin; time range is not specified in code but implied by filenames and context as 2018 (from gauge filename '1สถานีวัดฝนกรมอุตุลุ่มน้ำยม2018.csv') and likely aligned with radar mosaic files generated for that year; however, no explicit timestamps or date filtering logic appears in the script — only filename-based matching (e.g., '20200613' in comment is a script version date, not data date). Data sources are local raster (radar mosaics) and tabular (gauge logs); no GEE Earth Engine assets or satellite APIs are used — this is a PyQGIS desktop workflow, not a GEE script despite the prompt's mischaracterization.

name: Validate radar rainfall against gauge rainfall
desc: The script validates radar-derived rainfall estimates against in-situ rain gauge measurements for the Yom River Basin in Thailand. It processes co-located 24-hour accumulated rainfall files: radar mosaics (GeoTIFF) and gauge time series (CSV), both named by date (e.g., '20180613.csv'). For each matching date, it transforms gauge coordinates from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647), samples radar raster values at each gauge’s UTM location using QgsRasterLayer.dataProvider().sample(), extracts corresponding gauge rainfall values from CSV, and pairs them as (station_id, gauge_rainfall_mm, radar_rainfall_mm). The output is a CSV file ('validate_rr_rg_24h.csv') containing these paired observations for subsequent statistical validation (bias, MSE, RMSE). The study area is explicitly the Yom River Basin; time coverage is inferred from input filenames and comments referencing '2018' and '20200613' (a script version date, not data date); data sources are local raster (radar mosaic) and tabular (gauge) files — no GEE Earth Engine assets or satellite imagery are used; all geospatial operations occur in PyQGIS (coordinate transformation, point sampling), not GEE.

name: Encode image features with SAM
desc: The script computes image embeddings (features) from user-provided raster imagery using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) image encoder. It reads a raster layer (local or QGIS-loaded), optionally reprojects it to a UTM CRS if input is geographic, resamples to target resolution, clips to user-defined extent, selects up to 3 bands (defaulting to first 3), rescales pixel values to [0,255] using min-max statistics computed over the processing extent, and passes patches through SAM’s vision transformer encoder. Output consists of GeoTIFF files containing the encoded feature tensors (e.g., 256×64×64 for vit_l), one per patch, alongside CSV index files recording bounding boxes, CRS, resolution, and metadata. No classification, segmentation masks, or time-series analysis is performed — only feature extraction.

name: Aggregate MODIS fire detections by date
desc: The script processes a point-based MODIS fire detection dataset (delimited text) to filter high-confidence active fire observations (confidence > 70 and type == 2), then aggregates them by acquisition date ('acq_date') to compute per-date statistics: count of detections ('days_burning'), and mean values of FRP ('average_frp'), brightness ('average_brightness'), and bright_t31 ('average_bright_t31'). It subsequently buffers the aggregated points by 60 m, dissolves overlapping buffers, and selects only those original aggregated points whose geometries intersect the dissolved buffer extent — effectively retaining only points that are spatially clustered within 60 m of at least one other point in the same date-aggregated set. The final output is an edited memory vector layer containing clustered, date-aggregated fire events with derived metrics and reduced attribute schema.

name: Generate hypsometric curves
desc: The script computes elevation distribution statistics (hypsometric curves) for polygon features overlaid on a digital elevation model (DEM). It rasterizes each input polygon, extracts the underlying DEM values within that geometry, bins elevations at user-defined step intervals (e.g., 100 m), and accumulates area (or percentage) from lowest to highest elevation — producing cumulative area–elevation CSV files (one per feature) with columns 'Area' and 'Elevation'. The workflow uses GDAL/OGR for raster–vector interaction, NumPy for array masking and binning, and QGIS Processing Framework for parameter handling and progress feedback. Input data are a local DEM raster layer and a vector polygon layer (boundary layer); no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or satellite-derived products are involved. All operations are static, single-scene, and geometry-driven. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Generate points along line
desc: The script converts vector line features into a set of point features located at the centroids of raster pixels intersected by each line segment. It uses GDAL to read raster geotransform parameters, projects line vertices into pixel coordinates, and applies a modified Bresenham’s line algorithm (via buildLine) to traverse all raster cells crossed by each line segment. For each traversed pixel, it computes the corresponding map-coordinate centroid using pixelToMap and writes a point feature with attributes 'id', 'line_id', and 'point_id'. Input is a QGIS vector line layer and a raster layer; output is a point vector layer in the same CRS as the raster. No classification, time-series, or spectral analysis is performed — it is purely geometric sampling of lines onto a raster grid. Study area, time range, satellite data, and specific bands are not specified in the code.

name: Calculate terrain elevation differences
desc: The script computes elevation differences between gravimetric station points and surrounding terrain annuli (rings) extracted from DEMs, following Hammer’s (1936) method for terrain correction in gravity surveys. It partitions a radial ring (defined by inner_radius and outer_radius) into num_compartments equal angular sectors; for each sector, it samples all DEM pixels within the polygonal ring, computes absolute elevation differences relative to the station’s DEM height, and stores the mean difference per sector as a new attribute in the input point layer. Outputs include: (1) updated point layer with new numeric fields (e.g., '53_170_6.1') containing mean |Δh| per sector; (2) a new memory vector layer 'Rings_53_170' containing polygonal ring sectors with attributes 'Name', 'Particion', 'd_Height' (mean |Δh|), and 'n_pixels'; and (3) a CSV export of the updated point layer’s full attribute table. The study area is not specified in the code; inputs are user-provided UTM-projected point layer (gravimetric stations) and user-organized DEM raster layers under a QGIS layer group named 'DEMs'. No satellite or time-series data is used — only local raster DEMs loaded in QGIS. Geospatial operations include point-in-polygon containment checks, manual ring polygon generation via trigonometric coordinate sampling, raster pixel iteration over bounding boxes, and per-pixel DEM value extraction using QgsRasterDataProvider.identify().

name: Calculate building coverage percent
desc: The script computes the percentage of building area within each grid cell by intersecting building footprints with a polygon grid layer. It reprojects all vector layers from EPSG:4326 to EPSG:2180 (Poland national coordinate system), builds a spatial index on buildings for efficient intersection queries, and for each grid polygon calculates the total area of intersecting buildings. Only grid cells where building coverage exceeds 5% are retained in the output layer. The output is a memory-based QgsVectorLayer named per Config.GRID_ANALYSIS_LAYER_NAME, containing original grid attributes plus a 'building_percent' field, styled and added to the QGIS project. No satellite imagery or time-series data is used — input is static vector data (buildings and grid). Study area is implicitly Poland (EPSG:2180 is the Polish national CRS), but no explicit location name, time range, or remote sensing data sources appear in the code.

name: Clip raster by extent
desc: The script loads a local GeoTIFF raster file ('SR_50M_alaska_nad.tif') into QGIS as a QgsRasterLayer, retrieves its spatial extent, and then executes GDAL's 'cliprasterbyextent' algorithm to extract a subregion defined by a hardcoded bounding box (PROJWIN: [-6232946, 6363148, -735684.661767209, 9275122]). The clipped output is saved as 'PRACTICE_CLIPPED.tif' at a specified local path. No time-based operations, satellite data, classification, or analysis beyond geometric subsetting is performed. The study area is implicitly Alaska (from filename 'SR_50M_alaska_nad.tif'), but the clipping extent does not correspond to Alaska’s geographic coordinates — it appears to be in a projected coordinate system (likely Alaska Albers Equal Area Conic, EPSG:102006 or similar), and the PROJWIN values are manually supplied, not derived from the input raster’s extent. All operations are local-file-based; no GEE server-side processing occurs — this is a QGIS Python (PyQGIS) script, not a Google Earth Engine script.

name: Buffer input vector layer
desc: The script reprojects an active QGIS vector layer to EPSG:3857 and generates a dissolved buffer polygon layer with a fixed 300-unit (projected CRS units, i.e., meters) distance; the output is a single-feature (if DISSOLVE=True) in-memory polygon layer added to the QGIS project.

name: Generate random point layer
desc: The script creates a QGIS memory vector layer of n=50 randomly distributed Point features in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326), each with a unique integer 'id' attribute. Coordinates are uniformly sampled from the full global extent (longitude: -180 to 180, latitude: -90 to 90). No geospatial analysis, classification, remote sensing processing, or time-series operations are performed. The layer is added to the current QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, data sources, and analytical methods are all not specified — this is purely synthetic point creation for testing or scaffolding purposes.

name: Buffer municipal boundaries
desc: The script reprojects a municipal boundaries shapefile from its native CRS to EPSG:3857 and then generates a dissolved buffer of 300 meters around all municipalities. The output is a GeoPackage file containing the buffered, dissolved polygon geometry representing the buffered municipal zones.

name: Combine point layers by year
desc: The script combines point vector layers from three years (2020, 2023, 2024) — 'points2020', 'points2023', and 'points2024' — into a single memory-based point layer named 'combined_points'. It extracts specified attribute fields ('num2020', 'Name', 'num', and optionally 'name_2') as 'name' and 'second_name', transforms all geometries to EPSG:4326 (WGS84), records the original x/y coordinates in decimal degrees, and appends a 'year' attribute. No raster data, satellite imagery, classification, or modeling is performed; it is purely a vector layer aggregation and reprojection workflow. Study area, satellite data, bands, classification methods, and exported products beyond the in-session QGIS memory layer are not specified.

name: Construct field perimeter polygons
desc: The script constructs 24 closed polygon features representing agricultural field perimeters by spatially connecting pre-defined labeled point features (e.g., 'I1', 'I"2', 'II6k') from an existing QGIS vector layer named 'field_2_perimeter_points'. It uses exact string matching on the 'Point' attribute field to retrieve and order points, then builds polygons in sequence (with first point repeated to close), assigning each polygon a unique ID and name (e.g., 'I-1', 'IV-6'). The output is a new in-memory QGIS vector layer ('2field_2_polygon') in EPSG:4326, added to the current project. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived metrics are involved — the entire workflow is vector geometry construction based on static point labels. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Create perimeter polygons
desc: The script creates two in-memory polygon vector layers ('Polygon1' and 'Polygon2') in QGIS using predefined WGS84 (EPSG:4326) coordinates. It constructs closed polygon geometries from ordered lists of labeled points (e.g., 'Perim1'–'Perim16'), assigns integer IDs and string names as attributes, and adds the resulting layer to the QGIS project for visualization. No geospatial analysis, classification, remote sensing, or time-series processing is performed — the script is purely geometric layer construction. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and external data sources are absent; all coordinates are hardcoded and no Earth Engine (GEE) API calls, image collections, or server-side operations occur — despite the prompt referencing 'GEE script', the code is entirely QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), not Google Earth Engine.

name: Evaluate parcel geometric regularity
desc: The script evaluates the geometric regularity of cadastral parcels (land plots) based on multiple shape metrics: number of borders, right-angle count, border length uniformity, azimuth alignment of opposing borders, and circuit-to-area ratio. It computes derived attributes including plot area (ha), perimeter (m), internal angles, border azimuths, length ranges per border pair, and directional consistency. The final output is a classification field 'shape_evaluation' with integer scores (0=irregular, 1=moderately regular, 2=highly regular), assigned per parcel and written to a vector feature sink.

name: Assess spatial harmony of land use
desc: The script evaluates spatial harmony between cadastral parcels (dzialki ewidencyjne) and land use categories (uzyki gruntowe) by computing a binary 'eq_land_use' indicator per parcel. It achieves this by: (1) intersecting parcels with land use polygons; (2) converting parcel boundaries to lines, exploding them into segments, and computing centroids of those segments; (3) intersecting those centroids with the land use layer to assign land use types to boundary segments; (4) applying a rule-based compatibility matrix (e.g., 'Ls' [forest] is harmonious with 'Ł' [meadow], 'P' [pasture], etc.) to flag compatible adjacent land uses along parcel edges; (5) aggregating the minimum 'eq_land_use' value per parcel (so a single incompatible boundary segment yields eq_land_use = 0); and (6) joining the result back to the original parcel layer. Output is a polygon vector layer with an 'eq_land_use' field (0 or 1) indicating whether all land use transitions along the parcel’s boundary meet statutory compatibility criteria (as defined in Polish land use classification regulations).

name: Extract multispectral band means
desc: The script computes zonal mean values of five spectral bands (Blue, Green, NIR, Red, RedEdge) from co-located raster files over polygon features (field parcels) defined in a shapefile. It processes one raster folder per date (inferred from folder structure under 'CXZ-WN-2023'), applies QgsZonalStatistics to calculate per-polygon mean pixel values, merges results into a multiband.csv file per folder, and saves it alongside the rasters. The study area is the 'CXZ-WN' region (likely Chuxiong–Wenshan, Yunnan Province, China), with parcel-level vector data ('CXZ-WN-caijian.shp') and time-series multispectral rasters organized by date folder. No satellite or sensor metadata is present in the code; bands are assumed to follow standard multispectral naming but source (e.g., Sentinel-2, UAV, or PlanetScope) is not specified. Outputs are CSV tables containing id-indexed mean reflectance values for each band per date.

name: Clip raster by plot polygons
desc: The script clips a single UAV-acquired raster (Blue.tif) using a vector layer of plot polygons, producing one clipped GeoTIFF per polygon feature. The input raster is from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) survey at the CXZ-WN site (Changxiangzhen–Wen’an), with filename structure indicating acquisition on 2024-01-30. The vector layer ('plot.shp') defines spatial units for clipping; no classification, modeling, or spectral analysis is performed — only geometric raster masking. Outputs are individual GeoTIFFs named as '{parent_dir}-{raster_filename}-{fid_3digit}.tif' (e.g., 'CXZ-WN-2024-Blue-000.tif'), saved to a user-specified output folder. All operations occur locally using QGIS processing algorithms (gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer), not GEE — despite the prompt referencing 'GEE script', the code uses QGIS Python API and GDAL, with no Earth Engine calls, credentials, or ee.* imports.

name: Generate TIN mesh from point data
desc: The script generates a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN) mesh layer from user-selected vector point layers in QGIS. It supports using either the Z-dimension of 3D point geometries or a numeric attribute field (e.g., elevation, depth) as the height value. Input validation ensures the selected layer is a point layer; optional selection-based processing restricts mesh generation to only selected features. The output is a QgsMeshLayer (loaded as 'Malha_TIN') in MDAL-compatible format (.mesh), added to the QGIS project. No external GEE datasets or cloud processing is used — all operations are local QGIS vector-to-mesh workflows using the native 'tinmeshcreation' processing algorithm. Study area, time range, satellite data, and remote sensing bands are not involved — this is a desktop GIS meshing tool.

name: Convert polygons to lines
desc: The script converts polygon vector layers to line vector layers in QGIS, preserving or adding attributes (ID, length), applying user-specified styling (color, line thickness), optional reprojection, and optional labeling. It operates on user-selected vector layers within the current QGIS project, with no external remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, or raster processing involved. All inputs are local vector layers loaded in QGIS; outputs are new in-memory line layers added to the project, optionally replacing the original polygon layer if deletion is enabled. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geographic extent is specified — it is a generic GIS vector geometry conversion tool.

name: Rasterize mesh layer
desc: The script rasterizes a selected QgsMeshLayer using QGIS's native 'native:meshrasterize' processing algorithm. It takes the mesh layer's extent, user-specified pixel size, and first dataset group ([0]) with static time, then generates a GeoTIFF raster output. The output raster is loaded as a QgsRasterLayer into the QGIS project. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is involved — input is strictly a vector-based mesh layer (e.g., from TIN, FEFLOW, or TELEMAC models) stored in the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite sensors, and bands are not specified because the script operates purely on local, project-loaded mesh layers without external Earth observation data.

name: Export raster to KML/DXF
desc: The script exports selected QGIS raster layers to KMZ (KML + embedded images) or DXF format. For KMZ export, it reprojects rasters to WGS84, renders them as PNG, generates a legend image, creates a KML with GroundOverlay and ScreenOverlay using simplekml, and packages everything into a ZIP archive. For DXF export, it handles both regular raster layers (by exporting high-res TIFF → PNG → DXF with georeferenced image insertion) and map service layers (WMS/XYZ) by capturing the current canvas view as PNG and embedding it in DXF via ezdxf. Outputs include KMZ files containing KML, raster image, and legend image; and DXF files embedding georeferenced raster imagery.

name: Compute zonal statistics for seismic zones
desc: The script computes zonal statistics (mean, min, max) from an SRTM digital elevation model (srtm.tif) over fixed seismic zone polygons (seismic_zones.shp). It first repairs invalid geometries in the input vector layer using 'native:fixgeometries', then runs 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' to summarize raster values per polygon. The output is a vector layer with added fields prefixed by '_' containing the computed statistics.

name: Clip DEM by shoreline mask
