desc: The script clips a digital elevation model (SRTM) raster using a shoreline vector layer (shoreline.shp) to extract topographic data within the coastal zone, then generates a hillshade visualization from the clipped DEM. Input data sources are local files: 'srtm.tif' (SRTM elevation data) and 'shoreline.shp' (vector shoreline boundary). No cloud masking, temporal filtering, classification, or statistical analysis is performed; the workflow consists solely of two GDAL/QGIS geoprocessing operations — raster clipping by vector mask and hillshade generation. Outputs are an intermediate clipped DEM and a hillshade raster, both loaded into the QGIS session as temporary layers. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Generate forest stand maps
desc: The script generates forest stand maps (Bestandeskarte) from canopy height models (CHMs), specifically VHM 10m and VHM 150cm rasters, using a multi-stage geoprocessing workflow. It performs stand delineation via threshold-based height range classification (using relative min/max tolerance and correction parameters), simplification and elimination of small polygons, merging of similar neighboring stands based on hdom relative difference, clipping to a user-provided perimeter vector layer, calculation of dominant height (DG) from the high-resolution VHM 150cm, addition of coniferous proportion using an optional coniferous raster, attribution with biogeoclimatic variables (Vegetation Zone and Forest Site Category) via spatial join or default values, and final cleanup (field removal). Outputs include a GeoPackage vector layer 'TBk_Bestandeskarte.gpkg' containing stand polygons with attributes such as DG, coniferous proportion, VegZone_Code, ForestSite, and others; a timestamped output directory with intermediate files (e.g., tmp/ folder); and a QGIS project file generated by an external script. Input data sources are local raster files (TIFF) and vector layers — no Earth Engine assets or cloud-based satellite image collections are used; all processing occurs locally in QGIS using GDAL/rasterio-based functions (e.g., run_stand_classification, post_process) and QGIS Processing algorithms. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic coordinates are not specified in the code.

name: Detect forest stand change using canopy height
desc: The script calculates two change rasters from two versions (old and new) of the TBk forest stand mapping toolkit: (1) 'change_DG' — a raster encoding differences in dominant height (DG) layers via a base-10 digit concatenation formula '(A*10 + B) + 1', where A is TBkoldDGBestand and B is TBknewDGBestand, computed over their intersecting extent; (2) 'change_DG_hdom' — a refined change raster that flags stands where upper layer or hdom has changed (e.g., clearing) only in stands with old hdom >= hdom threshold (default 28 m), using a conditional formula involving rasterized hdom values from both Bestandesgrenzen vector layers and the initial DG change raster. The workflow uses GDAL raster calculator and rasterize operations within QGIS Processing, with no Earth Engine (GEE) code present — despite the prompt’s reference to 'GEE script', the provided code is purely QGIS Python Processing (QgsProcessingAlgorithm), and no GEE API calls, image collections, or ee.* objects appear. Study area, time range, satellite data, and explicit geospatial extents are not specified in the code; inputs are generic parameterized layers with no embedded metadata or paths indicating origin.

name: Clean forest stand map geometry
desc: The script cleans a forest stand map vector layer ('TBk Bestandeskarte') by (1) filtering out features with area_m2 < 100 m², (2) removing features where area_m2 is NULL (i.e., missing or invalid area calculation), (3) fixing invalid geometries using QGIS's 'Structure' method, (4) replacing the original 'ID' field with a new unique auto-incremented integer ID (sorted by the original 'ID' field), and (5) renaming the new field to 'ID'. The output is a cleaned vector layer ('TBk_Bestandeskarte_clean') with valid geometries, no null/zero-area polygons, and deduplicated, stable stand identifiers. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external imagery is used — input is a pre-existing vector layer of forest stands. All operations are vector-based GIS cleaning steps; no raster, remote sensing, or temporal analysis occurs.

name: Extract forest stand map perimeter
desc: The script extracts overlapping forest stand polygons and associated raster/vector layers from a TBk (Bestandeskarte) forest stand mapping project based on a user-provided perimeter geometry. It first intersects the main TBk stand map (.gpkg) with the perimeter using 'extract by location' (predicate: intersect). Then, for vector layers, it buffers the extracted stands by 0.0001 decimal degrees and extracts features fully within that buffer (predicate: within). For raster layers (e.g., DG, VHM, MG), it creates resolution-specific buffers around the extracted stands and clips rasters either by mask (default) or by extent (configurable per group). Outputs include: (1) a clipped TBk stand map .gpkg in the same relative path as input; (2) optionally copied TBk QGIS project file (.qgz); (3) clipped/copied rasters (DG, VHM_10m, VHM_150cm, VHM_detail, MG_10m, MG_10m_binary); (4) optional intermediate layers (.tif/.gpkg from bk_process folder); (5) optional local density vector layers (.gpkg); and (6) user-specified additional materials (.gpkg, .tif, or folders thereof). All outputs preserve the original folder structure and naming relative to the input TBk project root. The script is QGIS-based (not GEE-native) and uses QGIS Processing algorithms (e.g., native:extractbylocation, gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer, native:buffer); no Earth Engine (GEE) server-side computation occurs — this is a desktop GIS postprocessing tool. Study area, time range, satellite data, and coordinate reference system are not specified in the script.

name: Compute height deviation from stand dominant height
desc: The script computes a raster difference layer (diff_hdom_vhm) by subtracting a rasterized 'hdom' (height dominant) attribute — derived from the vector layer 'TBk: Bestandesgrenzen' (forest stand boundaries) — from the input VHM_10m (vegetation height model at 10 m resolution). It rasterizes the 'hdom' field using GDAL's rasterize tool with 10 m pixel size, then performs band-wise subtraction (VHM − hdom_raster) via GDAL raster calculator. Additionally, it converts the VHM_10m raster to a point layer (vhm_10m_points), where each pixel center becomes a point with its VHM value. The workflow is purely postprocessing: no time-series analysis, no classification, no cloud masking, and no sensor-specific radiometric processing. Input data sources are local/user-provided layers (no GEE asset IDs visible); the study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Classify local forest density zones
desc: The script computes local density classes within forest stand polygons (TBk stands) by applying focal statistics (circular moving windows of 7m and/or 14m radius) to a degree-of-cover (DG) raster layer, then reclassifying and polygonizing resulting smoothed DG values into user-defined density classes (e.g., '85–100%', '60–85%'). It filters, smooths (via minus/plus buffering), and intersects these density polygons with stands ≥1200 m²; calculates zonal statistics (mean DG, optional NH/mixture degree, and DG layers per height class: KS, US, MS, OS, UEB); and outputs two geopackages: (1) TBk_local_densities.gpkg containing density-class polygons with area, area_pct, and mean raster metrics per class; and (2) TBk_Bestandeskarte_local_densities.gpkg — the original stand map augmented with per-class summary metrics (e.g., z1_area, z1_dg, z2_nh) for all overlapping density zones.

name: Merge forest stand maps
desc: The script merges multiple TBk (Technisches Buch für die Forstwirtschaft / Technical Book for Forestry) forest stand map layers into a single vector layer. It renames the original 'ID' field to 'ID_pre_merge', adds a new 'ID_meta' field containing a unique prefix per input layer (alphabetical A, B, C… or numerical 1, 2, 3…), and constructs a new globally unique 'ID' field as '{prefix}_{ID_pre_merge}'. The merge order is deterministic: layers are sorted by descending YMAX (most northern first) and ascending XMIN (most western first) based on their bounding boxes (rounded to nearest km grid), ensuring consistent spatial ordering. No remote sensing imagery, classification, or time-series analysis is performed — the input layers are pre-existing vector stand maps. Study area, time range, satellite data, and sensor/band information are not specified in the script; it operates purely on user-provided QGIS vector layers.

name: Export forest stand map for WIS2
desc: The script exports a QGIS vector layer of forest stands (polygons) into a WIS2-compliant XML format. It processes attribute fields representing tree species proportions (p100–p800), dominant height (hdom), diameter at breast height (DG), area (area_m2), and forest site categories. It performs spatial join with an optional forest site layer, handles missing/NULL field values using defaults (e.g., '7a' for site category, 'NH' for tree species), enforces sum-to-100% normalization for species proportions, and writes structured XML with <Stand> elements containing standardized tags (ID, area, DG, hdom, p100–p800, siteCategory). The output filename follows the pattern 'wis2_stands_export_YYYYMMDD-HHMM.xml'. No satellite or raster data is used — input is purely vector-based (stand polygons and optional forest site polygons); no study area, time range, or remote sensing data sources are specified in the code.

name: Prepare VHM and MG rasters
desc: The script prepares two key raster inputs for forest stand mapping: (1) a detailed Vegetation Height Model (VHM) raster, optionally cropped to a polygon mask, converted to BYTE datatype, reclassified to min/max/NA values, and resampled to 10 m and 150 cm resolutions; and (2) a Forest Mixture Degree (MG) raster, aligned to the 10 m VHM extent, optionally rescaled (e.g., from WSL’s 0–10,000 range using factor 100), and optionally reclassified into a binary coniferous proportion layer (0–100) based on user-defined Laubholz (deciduous) and Nadelholz (coniferous) value thresholds. All outputs are GeoTIFFs with LZW compression and optional BIGTIFF support. The script is part of the TBk QGIS plugin developed by Berner Fachhochschule HAFL for forest stand map generation. No satellite or time-series processing occurs — inputs are pre-existing local GeoTIFF files; no study area, time range, or sensor metadata is embedded in the code.

name: Prepare VHM raster for forest stand mapping
desc: The script prepares a Vegetation Height Model (VHM) raster for use in the TBk forest stand mapping toolkit. It takes a detailed input VHM TIFF file and applies a sequence of geospatial preprocessing steps: (1) optional conversion to BYTE datatype with user-defined NA value (255), (2) optional cropping to a vector mask shapefile (either via GDAL's cliprasterbymasklayer or via rasterization + masking using QgsRasterCalculator), (3) reclassification of pixel values to a specified range (vMin=0, vMax=60 by default, clipping outliers), (4) aggregation/resampling to two output resolutions — 10 m (using 'max' resampling) and 1.5 m (150 cm) — both saved as compressed GeoTIFFs. Outputs are three rasters: 'vhm_detail.tif' (reclassified original resolution), 'vhm_10m.tif', and 'vhm_150cm.tif'. The script is part of a QGIS plugin (TBk) developed by Berner Fachhochschule HAFL for forest stand map generation; no satellite, sensor, or time-series data is involved — input is a precomputed VHM raster (source not specified in code).

name: Prepare VHM and forest mixture degree rasters
desc: The script prepares Vegetation Height Model (VHM) and optional Forest Mixture Degree (MG) rasters as inputs for the TBk 'Generate BK' algorithm. It performs: (1) optional BYTE conversion of VHM; (2) optional masking of VHM to a user-provided polygon mask; (3) optional reclassification of VHM values outside [vMin, vMax] to NoData (default 0–60 m); (4) resampling/aggregation of VHM to three resolutions — detail (input resolution), 10 m, and 150 cm — using maximum resampling (for height preservation); (5) alignment of output rasters using one of three methods: aligned to origin (0,0), aligned to MG input (if MG is provided and exactly 10 m resolution), or mask-driven random alignment; (6) optional rescaling of MG values (e.g., dividing by 100 for WSL’s 0–10,000 layer); (7) optional binary reclassification of MG into deciduous (0–50%) vs. coniferous (50–100%) classes. Outputs are five TIFF files: VHM_detail.tif, VHM_10m.tif, VHM_150cm.tif, MG_10m.tif, and optionally MG_10m_binary.tif — all placed in a user-specified output folder. The script uses GDAL-based QGIS processing algorithms (e.g., gdal:warpreproject, gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer, gdal:rastercalculator) and custom helper functions (PreProcessingHelper.reclassify_min_max, PreProcessingHelper.reclassify_mixture). No satellite, sensor, or time-series data is involved — inputs are local raster/vector files. Study area, time range, and coordinate reference system are not specified in the code but inferred from usage context (e.g., EPSG:2056 mentioned in help text implies Switzerland).

name: Optimize spatial join with singlepart conversion
desc: The script performs an optimized spatial join between two vector layers: it first ensures both layers have spatial indices (creating them if missing), converts the secondary 'attribute layer' from multipart to singlepart geometry, fixes geometries using the 'Structure' method, and then joins attributes from the singlepart, indexed attribute layer onto the primary layer using the 'largest overlap only' (one-to-one) method with intersection predicate. The output is the primary layer augmented with selected fields from the attribute layer, prefixed as specified (e.g., 'VegZone_'), preserving all original features including non-matching ones (DISCARD_NONMATCHING=False).

name: Apply convolution kernel to raster
desc: The script applies a user-defined convolution kernel (e.g., high-pass or Gaussian) to a local GeoTIFF raster file using GDAL's built-in convolution filter via gdal.Translate with the GDAL_CONVOLUTION_FILTER config option. It reads the input raster, applies the kernel (3×3 by default), writes the filtered output to a new GeoTIFF, and reports execution time and success status. The script operates entirely on pre-existing local raster files — no GEE server-side computation, no image collections, no cloud masking, no temporal filtering, and no geographic projection handling beyond what GDAL natively supports. Input/output paths, kernel values, and kernel size are hardcoded or passed as task parameters; no study area, time range, satellite data, or remote sensing metadata is involved. All operations are local CPU-based raster algebra using GDAL’s internal convolution engine.

name: Correct Landsat 7 SLC-off scan line gaps
desc: The script performs gap-filling correction on Landsat 7 Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+) Level-1 or higher raster images affected by the Scan Line Corrector (SLC) failure (SLC-off mode). It accepts a user-selected local GeoTIFF/IMG raster file (e.g., pre-processed Landsat 7 surface reflectance or top-of-atmosphere product), identifies nodata/gap pixels (typically using the band’s NoDataValue), and applies one of two geospatial raster interpolation methods: (1) Optimized Focal Mean — using SciPy’s convolution to compute spatially weighted mean over an odd-sized square window (3–51 px) only for gap pixels, or (2) Nearest Neighbor Diffusion — using GDAL’s FillNoData function with a user-defined maximum search distance (same numeric parameter as window size) to propagate valid pixel values into gaps. The output is a corrected GeoTIFF with identical georeferencing (projection, geotransform), dimensions, and band count as input; each band is processed independently; nodata is preserved or set to -9999.0; the corrected raster is automatically loaded as a new layer in QGIS. No specific study area, time range, or cloud masking is applied — the script operates purely on the provided local file without temporal or spatial filtering.

name: Detect aquatic plants using NDAI
desc: The script calculates the Normalized Difference Algae Index (NDAI) from Sentinel-2 imagery using bands B2 (blue), B3 (green), B4 (red), and B8 (narrow NIR) to detect aquatic vegetation in water bodies. It applies user-defined thresholding (e.g., 0.5–0.8) to filter NDAI values, produces a masked raster where only pixels within the NDAI range retain their value (others set to 0), and applies a dynamic GnBu color ramp symbology scaled to the thresholds. The output is a filtered, georeferenced GeoTIFF raster layer added to the QGIS project with pseudo-color rendering. No study area, time range, or specific water body is specified in the code — all inputs are user-provided via QGIS Processing interface; the algorithm operates on an arbitrary Sentinel-2 raster layer supplied by the user.

name: Map administrative districts
desc: The script generates individual district-level map images for all administrative districts (Kreise) in Hessen, Germany, using vector boundary data (KREIS_LA.shp), styled with unique categorical colors per district. It overlays OpenStreetMap (EPSG:3857) as a basemap and adds vector layers for highways (black lines) and waterlines (blue lines). For each district, it creates a dedicated QGIS print layout with a centered map extent buffered around the district’s geometry, title, scale bar (in km), compact legend showing only that district’s symbol, and north arrow. It also produces a final statewide composite map of all Hessen districts with highways and waterlines, including full legend, title, scale bar, and north arrow. All outputs are exported as PNG images; the QGIS project is saved as a .qgz file. The study area is explicitly Hessen (Germany), CRS is EPSG:25832 (ETRS89 / UTM zone 32N), and no satellite, sensor, or temporal data are used — all inputs are static vector/raster layers (OSM XYZ tiles, shapefiles, GeoPackages).

name: Extract tectonic segment geometries
desc: The script converts a MATLAB-generated CSV table containing coordinate pairs (x_1,y_1 and x_2,y_2) and structural attributes (e.g., strahler, angle, length, slope, ksn) into a GIS-ready line vector layer ('segments.shp'), then joins the original tabular attributes to the line features, producing 'segments_indx.shp' — a georeferenced shapefile of linear tectonic or fluvial segments with morphometric and structural indices for neotectonic analysis in the Dagua-Calima region.

name: Compute weighted generator centroids
desc: The script computes spatially weighted centroids of electricity generators by energy type, year, balancing authority, and state, using generator point locations and capacity data. It filters generators based on operational status across years (2018–2028), calculates capacity-weighted average coordinates for three groupings (total, balancing authority, and state), and outputs a GeoPackage layer with point features containing fields for energy_type, year, total_capacity, avg_x, avg_y, group_type, and group_name. Styling and labeling are applied in QGIS: points are colored by energy_type using predefined single_color values from energy_source_code, labeled with formatted 'energy_type year', and saved to '../hex.gpkg'. The input generator layer is explicitly required to be in EPSG:5070 and named 'Generator Points'; auxiliary layers 'States' and 'Balancing_Authorities' are loaded but not used in centroid computation—only their attribute fields ('Plant State', 'Balancing Authority Code') are read from the generator layer. No satellite, remote sensing, or raster data is involved; all operations are vector-based attribute filtering and geometric aggregation. Study area is implicitly continental US (inferred from use of EPSG:5070 — NAD83 / Conus Albers — and standard US energy infrastructure terminology like 'Balancing Authority' and 'Plant State').

name: Summarize generator capacity by status and energy source
desc: The script spatially aggregates electric power generator point features (with attributes including 'Status' and 'Nameplate Capacity (MW)') into a hexagonal grid layer ('Grid') using spatial join with summary statistics (count, range, sum). It filters generators by predefined operational statuses and energy source categories (e.g., 'Conventional Hydro', 'NUC'), creates separate GeoPackage layers per energy-source/status combination, applies consistent logarithmic graduated symbology scaled in MW/GW to the summed capacity field, and organizes outputs in a QGIS layer tree under 'Generators'. The study uses pre-loaded vector layers named 'Grid' and 'Generator Points' in EPSG:5070; no remote sensing imagery or time-series analysis is involved — all operations are vector-based spatial aggregation and cartographic rendering. Data sources are local QGIS vector layers, not satellite-derived.

name: Extract grid cells containing generator points
desc: The script creates a regular 40 km × 40 km grid in EPSG:5070 (Conus Albers) over a defined extent, loads generator point locations from a GeoPackage (current and planned electricity generators), reprojects those points to EPSG:5070, then spatially extracts only the grid cells that contain at least one generator point (using 'contains' predicate). The final output is a GeoPackage file (Grid.gpkg) containing the subset of grid cells intersecting generator locations, styled with transparent fill and light outline for cartographic display.

name: Aggregate battery capacity by subregion
desc: The script computes and maps battery energy storage capacity (MW) and battery fraction (%) aggregated by U.S. states and balancing authorities (BAs), using EIA generator-level data filtered for operational status and retirement year (<2026). It performs SQL-based spatial joins and aggregations in QGIS virtual layers, saves results to a GeoPackage (sums.gpkg), applies graduated color rendering (Jenks classification with inverted Greens ramp), and configures formatted labels (e.g., 'CA\n1245.7MW' or 'CA\n12.3%'). The output layers include five thematic GeoPackage layers: battery capacity by state, battery capacity by BA, battery fraction by state, battery fraction by BA, and bivariate BA-level capacity metrics (battery, renewable, hydro, peaker, total). Study area is the United States; no satellite, remote sensing, or time-series raster analysis is involved — all inputs are vector layers ('States', 'Generator Points', 'World Grid Subdivisions') loaded from the QGIS project. Data sources are internal tabular/spatial datasets with no explicit external URIs, timestamps, or sensor metadata.

name: Map generator capacity by grid cell
desc: The script maps electricity generator capacity (MW) to hexagonal grid cells (EPSG:5070) using point-based generator locations and attributes. It assigns each generator to the nearest grid cell, infers temporal validity intervals from operating/retirement years and months, merges overlapping or adjacent time intervals per cell–energy-source pair using event-based interval arithmetic, and outputs a temporal vector layer (GeoPackage) where each feature represents a grid cell, energy source, start/end date range, and associated capacity. The output layer is configured with QGIS temporal properties for animation over time. Input layers are named 'Grid' and 'Generator Points', both in EPSG:5070; capacity is sourced from the field 'Nameplate Capacity (MW)'; energy source classification is driven by user-defined filters in `energy_source_code`. No satellite, remote sensing, or raster data is used — all operations are vector-based spatial joins, attribute parsing, and temporal interval merging.

name: Calculate quadrat-level NDVI coverage
desc: The script computes zonal statistics (specifically mean NDVI or binary coverage above a user-defined threshold) for vector-defined quadrats over an input NDVI raster. It optionally clips the raster to a user-provided boundary layer and thresholds the NDVI to produce a binary (vegetated/non-vegetated) raster before computing the statistic. The output is a GeoJSON-based vector layer where each quadrat feature is enriched with the computed statistic (e.g., mean NDVI or fractional coverage > threshold) and its original geometry, added to the QGIS project as 'Quadrat Coverage'.

name: Cluster points using road network topology
desc: The script performs network-constrained clustering of point features (e.g., facilities, addresses, or sampling points) using an underlying road network layer. It constructs a NetworkX graph from line geometries (roads), maps input points to their nearest road nodes via cKDTree spatial search, computes shortest-path distance matrices on the graph, and applies AgglomerativeClustering (precomputed distance matrix) — either directly for ≤1000 points or in hybrid mode (KMeans pre-clustering + Agglomerative on road-node centroids) for larger datasets. The output is a memory vector layer (Point or Polygon, matching input geometry type) with a 'cluster' integer attribute, optionally saved as a Shapefile. No satellite, remote sensing, or temporal data is used; all inputs are local QGIS vector layers (point and line). Study area, time range, satellite data, and bands are not specified — the analysis is purely vector-based and location-agnostic.

name: Identify suitable landfill sites
desc: The script performs a Boolean logic-based multi-criteria suitability analysis for sanitary landfill siting in a defined geographic area. It processes vector and raster inputs—including infrastructure (roads, railways, airports), environmental constraints (water bodies, protected areas, hydrography), topography (slope), and land use/land cover—to derive three primary outputs: (1) 'LocaisAptosParaAterroSanitrio' — polygon layer of spatially contiguous, ≥3 ha areas satisfying all suitability criteria (e.g., slope 1–30°, non-protected, >200 m from water, >500 m from settlements, excluding unsuitable land cover classes); (2) 'LocaisInaptosParaAterroSanitrio' — complementary exclusion zones derived via symmetrical difference; and (3) 'AterrosSanitarios' — union-derived candidate site polygons, plus 'Multiparte' — centroids of apt areas for point-based prioritization, and a kernel density heatmap ('MapaDeCalorEstimativaDeDensidadeKernel') highlighting spatial clustering of viable sites.

name: Reproject layer to MeridianShift
desc: The script reprojects a user-selected QGIS vector layer from its native CRS (or first to WGS84 if needed) into a custom equal-area triangular projection (Wintri) centered on 135°E (MeridianShift), then validates and repairs invalid geometries, and exports the result as a Shapefile or GeoJSON. It does not perform spatial analysis, classification, or time-series processing; it is purely a coordinate transformation and geometry cleaning workflow. No study area, time range, satellite data, or thematic analysis is involved — only CRS reprojection and topological correction.

name: Decode OpenLR road location references
desc: The script decodes binary-encoded OpenLR location references into geometric line features aligned with a local road network (‘roads’ layer) stored in a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database. It uses the openlr and openlr-dereferencer Python libraries to interpret encoded locations, queries matching road segments by ID from the ‘roads’ vector layer, copies their geometries, and creates a new in-memory QGIS vector layer with attributes (ID, FRC, FOW, Length). The output includes a text summary of decoded line properties and a visualized layer of decoded road segments added to the QGIS map canvas. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, or satellite-derived metrics are involved; the core operation is geospatial dereferencing and database-backed feature retrieval. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Generate transit points along line
desc: The script generates a memory-based point vector layer along selected or all line features in the active QGIS layer, placing points at fixed metric intervals (user-specified in meters) and assigning each point two attributes: cumulative distance from the start of the line (in meters) and an estimated passage time (HH:MM:SS) calculated from a user-provided departure time (HH:MM) and average speed (km/h). It performs on-the-fly reprojection to EPSG:3857 for accurate planar distance measurement, interpolates points along the reprojected geometry, then transforms them back to the original CRS. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or temporal analysis is involved — it is purely a geometric and temporal interpolation tool for linear infrastructure (e.g., roads, pipelines, transit routes). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Model cellular coverage distance
desc: The script computes predicted coverage distances for candidate cell tower sites based on service level requirements, technology type (3G/4G), frequency band, antenna heights, and propagation models (COST-231 or Hata). It retrieves service levels from a 'Popn Density Cells' layer using 'Cell ID', selects appropriate propagation model and link budget parameters per technology and service tier, calculates maximum path loss, derives coverage distance in km, converts it to degrees for buffering in EPSG:4326, and generates polygon buffers around 'candidate_cell_sites_v8' points. Outputs include a new memory vector layer named 'Coverage Buffers' with attributes Cell_ID, tech, frequency, and Buffer_km, added to the QGIS project.

name: Derive slope and contour from elevation raster
desc: The script clips a global elevation raster (HYP_50M_SR.tif) to administrative boundaries (ne_110m_admin_1_states_provinces.shp), then computes slope (in degrees) and generates elevation contours at 100-unit intervals. Outputs include a clipped elevation GeoTIFF, a slope GeoTIFF, and a vector contour shapefile with 'ELEV' attribute; batch processing extends clipping across multiple input shapefiles, followed by statistical summary (min/max/mean/stddev) of each clipped raster.

name: Import HDF5 geophysical variable
desc: The script imports geophysical data from an HDF5 file and converts it either into a QGIS vector point layer (using latitude/longitude/value arrays) or a raster layer via GDAL rasterization. It reads user-selected datasets (e.g., 'latitude', 'longitude', and a main data variable like 'temperature' or 'precipitation') from arbitrary HDF5 files, filters out NaN and _FillValue entries, and constructs geometry accordingly. No fixed study area, time range, satellite, or sensor is embedded in the code — all inputs are user-selected at runtime via GUI. Outputs are ephemeral QGIS layers: either a memory-based point vector layer with attribute 'value', or a GeoTIFF raster generated from those points using gdal.Rasterize with user-defined pixel size and NoData value. The script does not perform analysis, modeling, classification, or temporal aggregation — only format conversion and spatial representation.

name: Identify maritime land parcels
desc: The script identifies whether a cadastral lot (from the 'LOTES_JP' layer) intersects with federally owned maritime lands ('TERRENOS_MARINHA') or accreted maritime lands ('ACRESCIDOS_MARINHA') in Brazil. It performs vector-based geometric intersection operations between the selected lot geometry and the two reference boundary layers, computes intersecting areas, classifies the lot's legal status (e.g., 'Totalmente dentro de Terreno de Marinha', 'Dentro de Terreno de Marinha e Acrescido de Marinha'), and generates temporary memory layers visualizing the intersections (purple for TM, pink for AM). Outputs include: (1) QGIS map layers showing intersection geometries with area attributes; (2) textual classification and area summaries (in m², formatted with comma decimal separator); (3) an HTML report containing a static map screenshot (at fixed scale 1:900), institutional header (SPU logo), and classification result. The study area is implicitly defined by the local file paths and layer names — specifically, the project file 'ExMapa.qgz' located at 'G:/TCC_14042025/MAPA_BESSA/', and layers named 'LOTES_JP', 'TERRENOS_MARINHA', and 'ACRESCIDOS_MARINHA'. No satellite, sensor, or spectral data is used; all inputs are local vector layers loaded from disk. Time range is not specified.

name: Convert polygon centroids to points
desc: The script converts polygon vector layers in QGIS into point layers by computing the centroid of each polygon feature. It allows users to select input vector layers from the current QGIS project, choose which attribute fields to retain (with optional renaming), and export the resulting point layer either as a GeoPackage (.gpkg) or ESRI Shapefile (.shp) to the user's Downloads folder. The output point geometry is derived solely from the input polygon geometry via QgsGeometry.centroid(), and attributes are copied verbatim (converted to string) from selected fields. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or external datasets are involved — it is a pure vector geometry transformation workflow within QGIS desktop.

name: Select points of interest within district boundary
desc: The script selects and retrieves attribute data for points of interest (POIs) located within the bounding box of the 'Accra Metro' district polygon in Ghana. It uses QGIS Python bindings (PyQGIS) to load two local shapefiles — one for administrative districts and one for POIs — performs a spatial filter via bounding box intersection (not full geometry containment), and outputs the attribute maps of matching POI features. The study area is Ghana, specifically the Accra Metro district; no satellite, sensor, bands, time range, or classification/analysis methods are involved — this is purely vector-based spatial subsetting using local file-based GIS data. Final output is a printed list of POI attributes and count.

name: Validate polygon geometry anomalies
desc: The script performs geometric validation of polygon vector layers in QGIS to detect and visualize topological and geometric anomalies including slivers (low area/perimeter ratio), overlapping polygons, vertices that are too close, duplicate vertices, and sharp angles below a user-defined threshold. It highlights anomalies using rubber bands on the map canvas and creates three memory vector layers (Error_Points, Error_Lines, Error_Polygon) storing point, line, and polygon geometries representing detected errors with attributes (feature ID, error type, length, area). The anomaly list is interactive: clicking an item zooms the map canvas to its bounding box. No remote sensing data, time-series, or external geospatial datasets are used — input is strictly local QGIS vector layers of polygon type. All operations are client-side geometric computations using QgsGeometry, QgsPointXY, and math-based angle calculation; no satellite imagery, raster processing, or temporal analysis occurs.

name: Join SHELDUS hazard data to US counties
desc: The script joins a CSV dataset (SHELDUS_combined.csv) containing natural hazard event records to a US county-level shapefile (tl_2024_us_county.shp) using a one-to-many spatial join on the FIPS code (5-digit county identifier). It first adds and populates a 'FIPS' field in the shapefile by concatenating STATEFP (2-digit) and COUNTYFP (3-digit) fields, then performs a relational join where each county polygon may be duplicated for every matching SHELDUS record (e.g., multiple hazard events per county). Outputs are a joined shapefile and GeoPackage, both in EPSG:4326, preserving original county geometry and appending all non-FIPS CSV columns as attributes. Study area is the contiguous United States (implied by tl_2024_us_county), time range of SHELDUS data is not specified in the script, and no satellite, sensor, or band processing occurs — this is purely vector attribute joining.

name: Join SHELDUS hazard data to US counties
desc: The script performs a one-to-many spatial join between a U.S. county-level shapefile (tl_2024_us_county.shp) and the SHELDUS (Spatial Hazard Events and Losses Database for the United States) CSV dataset, using the 5-digit FIPS code as the join key. It first adds and populates a 'FIPS' field in the shapefile by concatenating STATEFP (2-digit) and COUNTYFP (3-digit) fields. Then it joins all matching SHELDUS records (e.g., multiple hazard events per county) to the county geometries, preserving geometry and appending numeric damage/loss attributes (e.g., 'CropDmg', 'Fatal', 'PropDAdj') as double-precision fields. The output is a new shapefile and GeoPackage containing one feature per (county, hazard event) pair — i.e., exploded county-level hazard records with geospatial geometry. Study area is the entire contiguous United States (implied by tl_2024_us_county). Time range of SHELDUS data is not specified in the script. Data sources are non-remote-sensing: a Census TIGER/Line county boundary vector layer and a tabular hazard loss database; no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are used.

name: Save ArcGIS Feature Service layers
desc: The script saves vector layers from ArcGIS Feature Server web services (identified by data provider 'arcgisfeatureserver') as ESRI Shapefiles (.shp) in the QGIS project's './Layers/Basemap' directory, saves corresponding QGIS style files (.qml) in './Styles', and appends metadata—including timestamp, layer name, local file path, and source URL—to a log file '_data_sources_log.txt'. It also adds the saved shapefiles to a new or existing 'basemap' group in the QGIS layer tree and applies saved styles. The script explicitly supports only vector layers (not rasters), operates in the project’s current CRS (tested with EPSG:26917 but not restricted to it), and requires a saved QGIS project. No geospatial analysis, transformation, classification, or modeling is performed—only data export, logging, and layer management.

name: Generate road buffer zones
desc: The script generates polygonal buffer zones around line features representing roads in a user-selected QGIS vector layer. It uses QGIS's native 'buffer' algorithm with user-specified distance (in map units), 10 segmentation segments, and no dissolve. The output is a new in-memory or temporary vector layer added to the QGIS project map canvas. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, or external geospatial datasets are used — all inputs are local vector layers loaded in QGIS. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified because the script operates purely on desktop GIS vector geometry without temporal, spectral, or raster components.

name: Load REST service layers
taskType: Load Esri MapServer & FeatureServer layers into QGIS
desc: The script loads Esri REST API-based map and feature services (MapServer and FeatureServer endpoints) into QGIS as raster or vector layers. It supports three loading methods: native QGIS providers (arcgismapserver, arcgisfeatureserver), OGR GeoJSON queries with spatial filtering, and fallbacks to WMS and XYZ tile layers. Layer names are cleaned (trailing digits and underscores removed), and optional QML styles are applied from a local 'styles' folder. The output includes loaded layers in the QGIS project, with success/failure/no-data reporting per URL. No geospatial analysis, classification, or time-series processing is performed — only data ingestion and visualization setup.

name: Map wildfire incident locations
desc: The script fetches current wildfire incident point data from the NIFC WFIGS ArcGIS Feature Service (https://services3.arcgis.com/T4QMspbfLg3qTGWY/arcgis/rest/services/WFIGS_Incident_Locations_Current/FeatureServer/0), applies a rule-based symbology in QGIS based on 'IncidentTypeCategory' and binned 'IncidentSize' (five size classes: 0–1,999.9, 2,000–4,999.9, 5,000–6,999.9, 7,000–9,999.9, ≥10,000 acres), exports the styled layer to KML with custom PNG icons (colored circles scaled by size bin), injects missing <name> elements from 'IncidentName', assigns appropriate <styleUrl> per feature using category+size lookup, and packages the result as a KMZ containing doc.kml and icons/ directory. The study area is the contiguous United States (inferred from NIFC/WFIGS scope), and no temporal filtering is applied — it retrieves all current incidents via 'where=1=1'. Data source is an operational ArcGIS REST Feature Service; no satellite, sensor, or spectral bands are involved.

name: Map wildfire perimeters
desc: The script fetches current wildfire perimeter geometries and attributes from the NIFC WFIGS ArcGIS Feature Service (https://services3.arcgis.com/T4QMspbfLg3qTGWY/ArcGIS/rest/services/WFIGS_Interagency_Perimeters_Current/FeatureServer/0), applies symbology based on 'attr_IncidentTypeCategory' using the service's drawingInfo renderer, sets display names to 'attr_IncidentName', and exports a fully compliant, styled KML file (Current_NIFC_Incidents.kml) with shared <Style> definitions, proper <name> tags, ABGR-encoded colors, and cleaned inline styles. The study area is continental United States (inferred from NIFC/WFIGS scope), time range is real-time/current (no temporal filtering applied — '1=1' query), and no satellite, sensor, or band processing occurs — this is a vector feature ingestion, styling, and KML export workflow.

name: Analyze river flow trends and extremes
desc: The script performs time-series hydrological analysis on in-situ river flow measurements from CSV files containing station-based flow data (m³/s), dates, and geographic coordinates. It computes trend lines using linear regression, identifies maximum/minimum flow days, calculates annual total flow, seasonal max-flow timing, monthly average flow, Mann-Kendall trend significance, flood thresholds (90th percentile), and dry period statistics (20% of mean flow). Outputs include matplotlib plots for trend, annual sum, and monthly averages; tabular results (CSV/Excel); and geospatial vector layers (Shapefile/GeoPackage) with station-level metrics, rendered on QGIS map canvas. The study area is not specified in the code — no explicit region, basin, or coordinate bounds are defined; only generic station metadata (Latitude/Longitude) is used for mapping. Time range is user-selectable via GUI date widgets (default: 2014-10-01 to 2015-09-30). Data sources are local CSV files (no satellite, sensor, or band usage); all analysis is purely statistical on ground-based hydrometric time series.

name: Synchronize vector layers with REST API
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin that synchronizes local vector layers (Points, LineStrings, Polygons) with a remote REST API. It loads features from the API endpoint 'http://localhost/features' (GeoJSON format), creates or retrieves in-memory vector layers in QGIS with fields 'name', 'type', and 'id', and populates them with geometries and attributes. It also captures user edits (feature additions and deletions) in QGIS and propagates them to the API via POST (for new features) and DELETE (for removed features) requests. The plugin logs operations and handles errors but does not yet support attribute or geometry updates to the API. No satellite, sensor, time series, or geospatial analysis is performed — it is purely a bidirectional vector data synchronization tool for local GIS editing and remote persistence. Study area, time range, satellite data, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Assess playground accessibility
desc: The script assesses pedestrian accessibility to public playgrounds from a user-selected point on the map. It uses OpenStreetMap (OSM) Overpass API to query 'leisure=playground' features within a configurable buffer (100–1000 m) around the point, transforms coordinates between CRSs (EPSG:4326 ↔ project CRS), computes straight-line Euclidean distances in map units, and optionally retrieves walking routes via OSRM’s foot routing service. It generates QGIS vector layers (analysis point, buffer polygon, playground points, and optional walking route line), displays summary metrics (count, nearest straight-line distance, best walking distance, accessibility score), and exports a PDF report with map snapshot and textual results. No satellite, aerial, or time-series data is used; all inputs are vector-based OSM features and real-time routing. Study area is user-defined interactively via map click; no fixed region or temporal dimension is involved.

name: Map households near evacuation centers
desc: The script processes household location data (from a CSV with latitude/longitude) and evacuation center point features (filtered by specific DRRM-related subtype or SPECTYPE values) within a municipal boundary. It reprojects the household points to UTM Zone 51N (EPSG:32651), extracts evacuation centers matching designated emergency site criteria, buffers them by 1 km (dissolved), and identifies which households fall within those buffers. Outputs include: (1) a 1-km buffered polygon layer of evacuation centers, (2) the original household points layer, (3) the filtered evacuation center points layer, and (4) the subset of households spatially within the 1-km buffer — all styled with predefined QML files for visualization in QGIS.

name: Map households with PWD members
desc: The script maps household locations containing persons with disabilities (PWD) by converting a CSV file with latitude/longitude coordinates into a point layer, overlays it on a CityMun administrative boundary polygon layer, and applies predefined QGIS styling (CityMun_AdmBdry.qml and HH_with_PWD.qml) to both layers for visualization. It does not perform spatial analysis (e.g., aggregation, intersection, or counting), only data loading, geometry creation, and stylistic rendering within QGIS.

name: Map housing wall roof floor characteristics
desc: The script processes a CSV file containing household survey data with latitude/longitude coordinates and housing attributes (wall, roof, floor) to generate three georeferenced point layers—HC-CityMun-Wall, HC-CityMun-Roof, and HC-CityMun-Floor—each retaining core identifiers (unique_id, uuid, case_id) and the respective housing attribute. It joins these points with an administrative boundary layer (CityMun), applies QGIS layer styling (via .qml files), and outputs styled vector layers for visualization and spatial analysis of housing construction materials across municipal boundaries.

name: Map senior citizens living alone
desc: The script visualizes senior citizens living alone as point features derived from a CSV table containing latitude and longitude coordinates, overlaid on a city/municipality administrative boundary layer. It loads two input layers: (1) a CSV file ('input_f2_csv') with 'latitude' and 'longitude' fields used to generate points in EPSG:4326, and (2) a polygon vector layer ('input_citymun_boundary') representing city/municipality administrative boundaries. The workflow includes creating a points layer from the CSV, loading both layers into the QGIS project, and applying pre-defined QML style files ('4. CityMun_AdmBdry.qml' and '6. SC Living Alone.qml') for cartographic visualization. No geospatial analysis, classification, or temporal processing is performed — the script is purely for data loading and styling. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Filter municipalities by state
desc: The script loads a local Shapefile named 'municipios.shp', filters its features to retain only those where the attribute 'uf' equals 'MG' (Minas Gerais, Brazil), and exports the filtered vector layer to a GeoPackage file at 'C:\Users\Túlio\Documents\Processo - TerraLab\atividade-pratica-sprint-2-pyqgis\dados\results\municipiospr.gpkg'. The workflow is purely vector-based, involving no remote sensing imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or raster operations. It uses QGIS Python API (PyQGIS) within a desktop GIS context — not Google Earth Engine (GEE). The study area is implicitly Minas Gerais state in Brazil, inferred from the SQL subset string 'uf = \'MG\''. No satellite, sensor, bands, temporal filtering, or geospatial analysis beyond attribute-based subsetting is performed.

name: Extract cadastral parcel data
desc: The script performs a spatially partitioned extraction of cadastral data (parcels, interested parties, addresses) from a PostgreSQL database into per-parcel GeoPackage files, each containing clipped orthophoto rasters and associated vector layers (lc_terreno, lc_predio, lc_interesado, lc_direccion, lc_unidadconstruccion, lc_contacto, archivo). It splits an input vector layer by 'asignacion' attribute to generate individual geopackages, renames internal tables, adds triggers, updates fid fields, organizes outputs into numbered subfolders, and bundles supporting files (Excel templates, domain definitions, validation templates).

name: Extract raster pixel values within polygons
desc: The script extracts pixel values from two raster layers (e.g., drone and satellite imagery) within user-provided polygon boundaries, reprojects both rasters and the polygon to a common CRS, clips extracted point-based geodataframes to the polygon, and exports them as shapefiles and CSVs. It optionally performs spatial buffering and intersection analyses: (1) buffer point features by a user-defined radius (in meters/km/cm/mm/degrees) and extract overlapping raster-derived points; (2) buffer raster-derived points and intersect with the other raster’s points; (3) intersect the buffered point and buffered raster-derived layers for combined analysis. All outputs are saved to a user-specified directory as .shp and .csv files. No specific study area, time range, satellite data sources, or spectral indices (e.g., NDVI) are hardcoded — inputs are fully user-selected QGIS layers. The 'data_collection' function reads raster values per polygon geometry using rasterio.mask, computes row/col coordinates, converts to lat/lon via affine transform, and builds a GeoDataFrame of sampled points. The workflow is purely geometric sampling and spatial join — no classification, modeling, or temporal aggregation is performed.

name: Connect to PostGIS database
desc: The script connects to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database to load a vector layer named 'my_table' from the 'public' schema, applying a SQL query that filters features where 'active' = true and 'created_date' >= '2024-01-01', orders by 'name', and selects 'id', 'name', 'geometry', and WKT representation of geometry. It adds the resulting QgsVectorLayer to the QGIS project and logs success or failure. No geospatial analysis, classification, satellite data, or Earth observation processing is performed — it is purely a database connectivity and vector layer loading utility. Study area, satellite/sensor/bands, geospatial operations beyond SQL filtering, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Create vector layout test
desc: The script initializes QGIS programmatically, creates two in-memory vector layers (a polygon and a point), adds them to the QGIS project, displays them on a QgsMapCanvas with zoom-to-full-extent, and runs the Qt event loop for visualization. It does not perform any Earth observation analysis, remote sensing processing, classification, or time-series operations. The output is a GUI window showing a simple polygon (with vertices at (30,10), (40,20), (30,20), (30,10)) and a point at (10,20) in EPSG:4326 — no raster data, no satellite imagery, no temporal filtering, no export of maps or reports. All geometry is synthetic and coordinate values are arbitrary; no real-world study area, time range, or geospatial analysis is involved.

name: Map flood inundation extent
desc: The script generates static map layouts (PNG or PDF) showing flood inundation extent for multiple scenarios, distinguishing between 'connected' and 'disconnected' inundation polygons. It overlays these on a selected basemap (Bing Aerial, Google Satellite, or OpenStreetMap), adds bounding box overlays, grid lines, scale bars, north arrows, text attribution, and legends. Inputs are precomputed shapefiles (e.g., *_connectivity.shp, *_disconnected.shp) representing spatial flood extent; outputs are georeferenced, publication-ready map images named by scenario (e.g., 'scenario1_zoom_0.png'). The study area is defined by a bounding box in WGS84 coordinates and optionally refined per scenario using additional bounding boxes. No remote sensing processing occurs — all inputs are vector layers. The script uses QGIS Python API (PyQGIS) to automate cartographic composition, not Earth Engine — despite the user prompt referencing 'GEE', the code contains zero Google Earth Engine (ee.*) calls and instead relies entirely on QgsApplication, QgsVectorLayer, QgsPrintLayout, etc.

name: Downscale coarse raster with RF
desc: The script performs dasymetric downscaling of a user-provided coarse-resolution raster (e.g., VIIRS NTL, LST, or population) to a user-specified target resolution (e.g., 30 m) using Random Forest regression trained on high-resolution covariates (e.g., Sentinel indices, elevation, roads, built-up). It resamples both target and covariates to the target grid using appropriate resampling (bilinear for continuous, nearest-neighbor for categorical), applies spatial-block or random train/test splitting, trains an OOB-enabled Random Forest (200 trees), predicts pixel values across the full extent (optionally in memory-safe chunks), clips predictions to nonnegative values if requested, and outputs (1) the downscaled raster, (2) a CSV with R², RMSE, MAE, OOB score, and feature importances, and (3) a PNG with three panels: observed vs. predicted scatter plot, residual histogram, and horizontal bar chart of covariate importance. No specific study area, time range, or satellite data sources are embedded — all inputs are user-supplied raster layers; the script is generic and agnostic to geography, temporal extent, or sensor origin.

name: Integrate PKW vehicle data with administrative boundaries
desc: The script integrates tabular CSV data containing vehicle registration statistics (PKW) with Polish administrative boundary shapefiles (voivodeships, counties/powiaty, or communes/gminy) by matching TERYT codes. It reads a user-provided CSV file, auto-detects the administrative unit type (województwo/powiat/gmina) from column headers, normalizes and maps TERYT codes (e.g., converts województwo names to 2-digit TERYT codes using a built-in dictionary), identifies corresponding fields in PRG shapefiles (A01_Granice_wojewodztw.shp, A02_Granice_powiatow.shp, A03_Granice_gmin.shp), and joins CSV attributes (excluding name columns) to the geometry. Output is a new QGIS memory vector layer named 'Wybory_[unit_type]' with original boundary geometries plus appended CSV attributes, added to the current QGIS project. The script operates entirely within QGIS desktop using PyQt6 and QgsVectorLayer; no remote sensing, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, or cloud processing is involved.

name: Compute shortest path from point to zip codes
desc: The script computes the shortest or fastest path from a single starting point to multiple ZIP code centroid locations using a road network layer. It first calculates the mean coordinates of the starting point layer (in case of multipoint), converts them to a string coordinate field, extracts unique coordinates, then applies QGIS's native shortest path algorithm (point-to-layer mode) on a classified road network with configurable speed and topology tolerance. The resulting paths are reprojected to EPSG:4326, length-calculated in meters, and filtered to retain only specified fields (start, end, postcode, city, address, length), producing three outputs: raw shortest-path lines, length-annotated lines, and a final cleaned line layer with selected attributes.

name: Merge vector layers into GeoJSON
desc: The script automatically detects all vector layers (points, lines, polygons) in the current QGIS project, merges them into a single unified layer preserving geometries and attributes, and exports the result as a GeoJSON file to the user's Desktop; it employs three fallback methods (native merge tool with layer IDs, temporary memory layer export, and manual feature copying) to ensure robustness against CRS or layer object compatibility issues, and adds the combined layer to the QGIS map canvas.

name: Extract lot boundary segments
desc: The script processes a local shapefile of polygonal land parcels (lotes) and decomposes each parcel's exterior ring into individual line segments (edges). For each segment, it calculates Euclidean length and classifies its orientation relative to cardinal directions ('Frente', 'Fundo', 'Direita', 'Esquerda') using the azimuth angle derived from start-to-end coordinates in the layer's native CRS. The output is a new line shapefile containing one feature per boundary segment, with attributes: id_lote (inherited or auto-generated), comprimento (meters or map units), and posicao (orientation class). No remote sensing data, time-series, or GEE-specific operations are used — this is purely local vector geometry processing in QGIS/PyQGIS.

name: Classify lot boundary sides
desc: The script processes a polygonal shapefile of land parcels (lotes) and decomposes each parcel's exterior ring into line segments (sides). For each side, it computes length and classifies its positional role—'Frente' (front), 'Fundo' (back), 'Esquerda' (left), or 'Direita' (right)—based on y-coordinate ranking (for front/back) and segment orientation angle (for left/right). The output is a new LineString shapefile containing one feature per side, with attributes: id_lote (inherited or auto-generated), comprimento (Euclidean length), and posicao (classified side type). Input is a local ESRI Shapefile at D:/data/_____dados/consultorias/Larissa/amostra_lotes_shp.shp; no remote sensing, satellite, or temporal data is used. CRS is preserved from input. Output path is D:/data/_____dados/consultorias/Larissa/amostra_lotes_shp_laterais_v003.shp.

name: Generate lot boundary lines with geolink attribution
desc: The script processes a point layer representing sequential boundary vertices of land lots (e.g., 'Frente', 'Lateral Esquerda', etc.) to generate line segments connecting consecutive points, classifies each segment by its positional label (e.g., 'Frente', 'Lateral Direita') and length, then assigns a 'geolink' identifier from an overlapping polygon layer (presumably cadastral or parcel polygons) by computing the centroid of each complete lot (closed at 'Lateral Direita') and spatially joining to the nearest matching polygon. The output is a Shapefile ('laterais_com_geolink.shp') containing LineString features with attributes: 'direct' (original numeric code), 'posicao' (translated label), 'comprimento' (Euclidean length in map units), and 'geolink' (inherited from the matched polygon). No remote sensing data, time-series, or satellite imagery is used; inputs are local vector files on disk (shapefiles), and all operations are vector-based geometric processing within QGIS Python API.

name: Map lot boundary segments with geolink attribution
desc: The script processes a point layer representing sequential boundary vertices of land parcels (lots), grouped by directional codes ('1'=Frente, '2'=Lateral direita, '3'=Fundo, '4'=Lateral esquerda), to construct line segments between consecutive points. It identifies when a segment corresponds to a lateral side ('Lateral direita' or 'Lateral esquerda'), triggers closure of the current lot group, computes the centroid of all accumulated line geometries for that lot, spatially joins it to a polygon layer (presumably cadastral lots) using a spatial index and intersection test, and assigns the 'geolink' attribute from the matched polygon to all lines in that lot group. Duplicate line geometries are removed. The final output is a Shapefile of non-overlapping line segments with attributes: 'direct' (original code), 'posicao' (mapped label), 'comprimento' (Euclidean length), and 'geolink' (cadastral identifier). Input data sources are local Shapefiles on disk; no remote sensing or time-series data is used.

name: Generate lot boundary lines with geolink attribution
desc: The script processes point features representing lot boundaries (e.g., 'Frente', 'Lateral direita') and constructs line segments between consecutive points, classifying each segment's lateral position (e.g., 'Frente', 'LinhaApoio') using a rule-based logic on the 'direct' field. It associates each line segment group (closed lot) with a 'geolink' attribute by spatially intersecting the centroid of the segment polyline with polygon features from a separate shapefile. Outputs include a Shapefile of LineString features with attributes: 'direct' (transition label), 'posicao' (lateral classification), 'comprimento' (Euclidean length), and 'geolink' (inherited from intersecting polygon).

name: Generate lot boundary segments
desc: The script processes a point shapefile representing sequential vertices of lot boundaries, where each point has a 'direct' field indicating direction (1–5). It constructs line segments between consecutive points, maps numeric 'direct' values to positional labels (e.g., '1' → 'Frente'), computes segment length, and filters out segments labeled 'Fechamento' (code '5'). The output is a LineString shapefile containing oriented boundary segments with attributes 'direct', 'posicao', and 'comprimento', saved to disk and added to the QGIS project.

name: Extract lot boundary segments
desc: The script processes a point-based shapefile representing sequential vertices of land parcel boundaries, where each point is labeled with a 'direct' code indicating its position (e.g., '1'=Frente/Front, '2'=Lateral Esquerda/Left Side). It pairs consecutive points to construct line segments, assigns positional semantics and lengths, filters out closure points ('5'=Fechamento), and outputs a LineString shapefile containing these boundary segments with attributes: 'direct' (original code), 'posicao' (mapped string), 'comprimento' (Euclidean length), and 'medida' (duplicate of length). The script computes and prints total lengths per lateral type (Front, Left Side, Back, Right Side). It performs two sequential 'Join by Location Summary' operations in QGIS: first aggregating fire count ('N') and spatial average FRP ('S ave(frp)') using summary type 'count' (code 5), then aggregating day-of-month ('day') and monthly average FRP ('M ave(frp)') using summary type 'max' (code 6). Outputs are shapefiles named '<country>_persistence_10m.shp' (e.g., derived from filename stem before '_monthly_persistence.shp'), containing grid cells enriched with fire count, spatial avg FRP, max day, and monthly avg FRP. Input fire layers originate from 'monthly fire persistence' processing (likely MODIS or VIIRS active fire detections given 'frp' — Fire Radiative Power — and temporal aggregation), but satellite/sensor/bands are not specified in the script. Study area is country-level (implied by 'country_monthly_persistence_shp' directory and filename parsing), time range is monthly (9 pairs processed), and geometry is vector-based — no raster or satellite imagery processing occurs in this script.

name: Map fire persistence using spatial join
desc: The script performs a spatial join between monthly fire occurrence vector layers (containing attributes 'day', 'N', 'M ave(frp)', 'S ave(frp)') and a fixed 2 km grid vector layer, producing per-country monthly fire persistence shapefiles. Each output shapefile contains grid cells intersecting fire polygons, with fire attributes appended; the filename pattern indicates country-level processing (e.g., 'Brazil_persistence_2km.shp'). The study area is country-level but unspecified beyond path fragments; time range is not encoded in the script logic (no date filtering or temporal variables); data sources are local shapefiles only — no satellite, sensor, or band usage — implying pre-processed fire detections (likely from MODIS or VIIRS FRP products given 'ave(frp)' fields) and a static grid; no raster operations, classification, or time-series modeling occurs — only vector-based spatial overlay (predicate types 0–6 = 'intersects', 'contains', 'within', 'equals', 'touches', 'overlaps', 'crosses').

name: Aggregate fire detections to grid cells
desc: The script spatially joins fire detection points (from Himawari satellite data) to a set of pre-defined polygon grids over Indonesia, computing summary statistics (count and maximum of 'ave(frp)' and 'max(frp)') for each grid cell. It iterates over multiple grid shapefiles (distinguished by resolution in filename), performs a join-by-location with summary, and exports one gridded output shapefile per resolution containing fire count and FRP statistics.

name: Join drought indices to fire grids
desc: The script spatially joins monthly drought index values (TCI, VCI, VHI) from CSV point files to corresponding monthly fire grid vector layers (shapefiles), using a common 'id' field and spatial indexing for efficiency. It processes data for years 2012–2022 (inclusive), iterating over 12 months per year. The output is a set of shapefiles — one per month per year — stored in 'YYYY Monthly Subsets' subdirectories, each containing the original fire grid geometry augmented with drought index attributes. The study area is not specified in the code; input files are read from local filesystem paths (e.g., 'F:\WORK January 2023\monthlydroughtindices'), with no explicit geographic bounds, CRS handling limited to EPSG:4326 assignment during CSV layer loading, and no satellite, sensor, or band usage — all inputs are vector-based tabular/spatial data (CSV points and SHP grids).

name: Merge annual fire vector layers
desc: The script merges multiple yearly fire occurrence vector layers (shapefiles) for Vietnam spanning 2012–2023 into a single unified shapefile; it first merges all .shp files in the specified directory, converts any multipart geometries to singleparts (ensuring each fire event is a distinct feature), and exports the result as a consolidated ESRI Shapefile named 'vietnam_2012-2023.shp'.

name: Clip fire locations to country boundary
desc: The script merges archived and near-real-time (NRT) fire vector layers for Afghanistan (region 'SA') located in a local desktop directory ('Desktop/January 2022/FIRES/SA/afghanistan/'). It identifies shapefiles containing 'SV' (likely indicating fire source layers) and loads them as QgsVectorLayer; non-'SV' files are assumed to be country boundary layers. It builds a spatial index on the fire layer, then clips the fire points/polygons using QGIS's native:clip algorithm with the country boundary as overlay — producing a clipped fire dataset confined to Afghanistan’s administrative boundary. Inputs are local .shp files (no satellite or GEE data); no time range is parsed from filenames or metadata; outputs are written to a local shapefile ('afghanistan_fires.shp'), but the destination variable assignment is malformed (uses `country` — a QgsVectorLayer object — in filename formatting, and `countrygrid` is undefined). The workflow is purely vector-based GIS processing in QGIS Python API (PyQGIS), not Google Earth Engine.

name: Merge forest fire vector layers
desc: The script merges archived and near-real-time (NRT) forest fire vector layers (shapefiles) from a local directory. It first identifies all .shp files in the specified path, then iterates over NRT layers to modify attribute field index 10 to value '1' for all features. Finally, it runs QGIS's mergevectorlayers algorithm to combine all shapefiles into a single output layer with EPSG:4326 CRS. The output filename includes a country placeholder and '_fires.shp', indicating merged fire event data.

name: Summarize fire radiative power and fire count by grid
desc: The script spatially joins monthly fire shapefiles (containing FRP and FC attributes) to a static 30-arcminute grid layer using QGIS's 'join by location summary' tool. It computes summary statistics (mean and sum, as indicated by SUMMARIES=[5,6] corresponding to 'mean' and 'sum' in QGIS documentation) for the 'FRP' (Fire Radiative Power) and 'FC' (Fire Count) fields per grid cell. The output is a set of monthly shapefiles, one per input fire layer, each containing the original grid geometry plus new columns with aggregated FRP and FC values. The study area is implied by the file paths but not explicitly defined; the time range is tied to the '2020' directory and 'Monthly Fires' subdirectory; inputs are vector layers only — no satellite imagery or raster data is processed. No classification, modeling, or temporal analysis is performed — only spatial aggregation.

name: Clip and filter fire events by state and month
desc: The script processes a yearly HMS fire shapefile (e.g., hms_fire2012.shp) by clipping it to individual U.S. state boundaries and then filtering the clipped features by month using the 'YEARDAY' attribute (converted from YYYYDDD format). For each state and month, it exports a separate shapefile containing only fire events occurring in that state during that month. Outputs are ESRI Shapefiles organized in directories by state name and year (e.g., 'AL/2012/AL_2012_01_hms.shp').

name: Clip and filter fire events by state and month
desc: The script clips HMS (Hazard Mapping System) fire point data (from shapefiles named 'hms_fireYYYY.shp') to individual U.S. state boundaries and then filters the clipped fire points by month using the 'ACQ_DATE' attribute field. It exports one shapefile per state-month combination (e.g., 'AL_2012_01_hms.shp') containing only fire observations acquired between the first and last day of each month in 2012. The study area is the Southeast USA, inferred from the directory path 'Southeast USA Data Download' and the use of a 'seusa_'-prefixed input file pattern; the time range is explicitly limited to 2012 (curryear = '2012'), with monthly subsetting. Input data sources are local vector files — no satellite imagery, raster data, or GEE assets are used; all operations occur in QGIS via PyQGIS processing algorithms ('native:clip', attribute-based selection, and shapefile export). No classification, modeling, or spectral analysis is performed.

name: Count monthly forest fires in protected areas
desc: The script counts the number of forest fire points within polygon boundaries of peninsular countries (loaded from a local shapefile) for monthly fire datasets filtered to years 2019 and 2021. It uses QGIS's 'native:countpointsinpolygon' algorithm with 'VERSION' as weight field and outputs count results ('Fires') as new shapefiles in a dedicated 'Protected Monthly Fire Counts' directory. Input fire point layers are sourced from local filesystem paths matching 'Protected Monthly Fires/*.shp', and the country polygons are loaded from 'peninsular_countries.shp'.

name: Convert fire count shapefiles to CSV
desc: The script converts monthly forest fire count shapefiles (stored in 'Protected Monthly Fire Counts') into CSV format for years 2019 and 2021. It iterates over .shp files in that directory, extracts the year from the filename (positions -23 to -19), loads each as a QgsVectorLayer, and writes it to CSV using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV2 with driverName 'CSV'. Output CSV files are saved in a newly created 'Protected Monthly Fire Counts CSV' subdirectory.

name: Subset fire events by month
desc: The script subsets annual fire shapefiles into monthly subsets using date range filtering on the "ACQ_DATE" attribute. It iterates over each fire shapefile in a yearly directory (e.g., '2018'), constructs monthly date ranges (e.g., '2018-01-01' to '2018-01-31'), selects features within each range using QGIS expression-based selection, and exports each subset as a new ESRI Shapefile named with year and month (e.g., '2018_01.shp') into a dedicated '2018 Monthly Fires' subdirectory. Leap year handling adjusts February end date for years 2012, 2016, and 2020.

name: Sample fire locations with land cover
desc: The script samples vector fire point or polygon features (from shapefiles) using a raster land cover layer representing non-protected forest areas in the Iberian Peninsula. It performs raster-based attribute sampling—assigning land cover values from the raster to each fire feature—using QGIS's 'rastersampling' algorithm. The input raster is explicitly named 'LC_peninsular_non_protected_forest_areas.tif', indicating it is a land cover product covering the peninsular (i.e., mainland) part of the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal). The output is a set of new shapefiles (one per input fire layer), each containing an added attribute column prefixed 'SAMPLED' holding the sampled land cover value(s) at fire locations. No time filtering, cloud masking, classification, or satellite-derived processing occurs in this script—it is purely a GIS sampling operation on pre-existing raster and vector data. Study area: Iberian Peninsula (peninsular); Time range: not specified; Data sources: local raster file (no satellite/sensor/bands); Geospatial operations: raster sampling (point/polygon-to-raster value extraction); Final products: sampled shapefiles with appended land cover attributes.

name: Clip grid to country boundaries
desc: The script clips a global or regional 10-meter hexagonal grid layer (hc_grid10m.shp) to the extent of individual country boundary shapefiles. It iterates over all .shp files in the 'countries' directory, uses QGIS's native:clip algorithm to intersect each country polygon with the fixed grid layer, and saves the resulting clipped grid as a new shapefile per country (e.g., 'ALB_10m.shp') in the 'countries-10m' output folder. The input grid is explicitly named 'hc_grid10m.shp', suggesting a precomputed hexagonal tiling (likely H3 or similar), and the country shapefiles are sourced from a local Windows path — no satellite, sensor, temporal, or classification logic is present. All operations are vector-based geometric clipping; no raster data, time-series, bands, or thematic analysis is performed.

name: Filter forest fire locations

name: Count fire points per grid cell
desc: The script counts the number of fire locations (points) falling within each polygon of a spatial grid covering Afghanistan. It uses QGIS’s native 'countpointsinpolygon' algorithm on two local shapefiles: 'afghanistan_fires.shp' (fire point locations) and 'afghanistan_grid.shp' (polygon grid). The output is a memory-layer vector dataset where each polygon contains a new attribute field named 'Count' representing the number of fire points it contains. name: Sample burned area counts within administrative zones

The workflow uses QGIS processing algorithms within a Python environment (not GEE), relying on local raster and vector data—no Earth Engine code is present despite the prompt's reference to 'GEE script'.

name: Clip raster by state boundary
desc: The script clips a set of georeferenced raster files (GOES-derived rasters in EPSG:4326) to individual U.S. state boundaries using vector shapefiles. It iterates over each state shapefile and each raster, extracts the year from the raster filename (e.g., '2023_01_01_GOES...tif' → '2023'), extracts the state name from the shapefile stem (e.g., 'Texas_state.shp' → 'Texas'), and outputs a clipped GeoTIFF named '{statename}_{year}.tif'. The clipping is performed via QGIS GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm with CROP_TO_CUTLINE=True and KEEP_RESOLUTION=True, preserving original pixel resolution and extent within the mask geometry. Input rasters originate from GOES satellite imagery (inferred from directory name 'GOES-ANIMATIONS' and 'rasters_4326'), but no band, sensor, or processing details (e.g., ABI bands, channel, or derived product like brightness temperature or reflectance) are specified in the code. No classification, modeling, or temporal analysis is performed — only spatial subsetting.

name: Extract positive pixel values
desc: The script processes local GeoTIFF raster files stored in 'C:\Users\aeaturu\Desktop\brunei_test' by applying a raster calculator operation that creates binary masks where pixel values are greater than zero (i.e., '(A > 0)'). Each input raster is loaded as a QgsRasterLayer, and the output is saved as a new GeoTIFF file (e.g., 'filename_gt0.tif') in the 'output' subdirectory. name: Identify common valid pixels
desc: The script aligns 12 input GeoTIFF rasters to a common extent, projection, and resolution using GDAL warp (nearest neighbor resampling), then computes a binary mask where a pixel is marked valid (1) only if *all* 12 aligned rasters have values > 0 at that location. The output is a single-byte GeoTIFF raster representing the spatial intersection of valid (non-zero) pixels across all inputs. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification method is specified in the code — inputs are local file paths; the script performs purely geometric and logical raster alignment and masking. The output raster is loaded into QGIS as 'Common Valid Pixels'.

name: Extract raster centroid locations
desc: The script processes local Planet satellite .tif files to extract the geographic centroid of each raster's extent, parses acquisition date from the filename (first 8 characters interpreted as YYYYMMDD), and compiles all centroids into a single shapefile with attributes 'filename' and 'acq_date'. The study area is not specified in the code — input rasters are read from a local folder path (E:\Planet Data) with no geospatial filtering or region definition; time range is inferred solely from filenames and not constrained programmatically; data source is local Planet imagery (no GEE asset IDs used); geospatial operations include extent extraction, centroid calculation, and vector layer merging; final output is a shapefile (allplanetdata.shp) containing point features representing raster footprints.

name: Extract forest loss year pixels
desc: The script processes a single pre-aligned raster file (hansenAligned.tif) to generate 23 separate binary raster layers, one for each year from 1 to 23, where pixel value = 1 if the Hansen Global Forest Change loss year band (band 4) equals that year, and 0 otherwise. No study area, time range of original Hansen data, or spatial extent is specified in the script — only the local file path and band index are used. name: Count forest loss pixels by year
desc: The script processes a set of GeoTIFF raster files named by year (e.g., 'loss_2001.tif') located in a local directory, each representing annual forest loss pixel counts. It uses QGIS's native:rasterlayeruniquevaluesreport algorithm to extract the second unique value from Band 1 of each raster — interpreted as the count of non-zero (i.e., loss) pixels — and aggregates these counts per year into a dictionary. The output is a CSV file ('pixelvalues.csv') listing years and their corresponding loss pixel counts. No remote sensing data is loaded or processed via GEE; the script runs entirely in QGIS Desktop using local rasters. Study area, satellite/sensor, geospatial operations beyond pixel counting, and classification methods are not specified in the code.

name: Sample fire locations with forest mask
