name: Model road network traffic density
desc: The script models traffic flow density on a road network by computing shortest paths between origin and destination zone centroids, aggregating path overlaps to generate a density raster-like point layer, and weighting junction points based on density thresholds and time-of-day rules. It uses QGIS vector layers (origin/destination polygons, road lines, junction points) as inputs; performs centroid extraction and reprojection; applies k-means reduction to limit representative zones; computes pairwise shortest paths using QNEAT3; aggregates path geometry points to compute normalized density values; and outputs three GeoPackage layers: (1) OD route lines with route_id, (2) density-weighted points at 6-decimal precision grid locations, and (3) junctions with 'UsedByComm', 'Corridor_Weight', and 'CrossTraffic_Weight' fields. No satellite or remote sensing data is used — all inputs are local vector layers loaded from QGIS project. Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified.

name: Compute concave hull geometry
desc: The script computes a concave hull polygon from an input point layer using the alpha shapes algorithm. It performs Delaunay triangulation on the points, calculates edge lengths to identify and remove triangles with longest edges exceeding alpha × maximum edge length, dissolves the remaining triangles into a single (or multipart) polygon, optionally removes interior rings (holes), and optionally splits multipart geometries into singleparts. The output is a vector polygon layer representing the concave hull envelope of the input points. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are involved — the algorithm operates purely on user-provided vector point geometry.

name: Execute SQL on vector layers
desc: The script executes a user-provided SQL query against one or more input vector layers using QGIS's virtual layer provider. It constructs a QgsVirtualLayerDefinition by registering each input layer as 'input1', 'input2', etc., optionally writes memory layers to temporary disk files if not in the project, expands expressions in the SQL query, sets UID and geometry configuration (field, type, CRS), creates a valid QgsVectorLayer from the definition, and exports the resulting features to a feature sink. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, raster operations, or satellite imagery is involved — it is purely a vector SQL execution tool operating on arbitrary vector sources provided at runtime. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code.

name: Generate hypsometric curves
desc: The script computes hypsometric curves for polygon features intersecting a DEM raster. It extracts elevation values within each polygon, bins them into user-defined elevation intervals (step), calculates cumulative area (or percentage) for each bin, and exports CSV files containing cumulative area/percentage versus elevation. Input includes a DEM raster, a vector boundary layer of polygons, step size, and an output directory. The workflow involves raster clipping via vector masking, nodata handling, masked array computation, and cumulative histogram generation.

name: Export vector layer to SpatiaLite
desc: The script exports a QGIS vector layer (e.g., point, line, polygon) into a SpatiaLite database file (.sqlite), optionally overwriting an existing table, creating a spatial index, converting field names to lowercase, dropping string length constraints, forcing single-part geometries, and specifying geometry column name, primary key field, and encoding. It uses QgsVectorLayerExporter with spatialite provider and handles non-geometry tables by clearing the geometry column. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis is performed — this is a pure database export utility.

name: Generate points along lines
desc: The script converts vector line features into a set of point features located at raster pixel centroids intersected by the lines. It uses GDAL to read raster geotransform parameters, projects line geometries to the raster CRS, converts line segment endpoints to pixel coordinates, and applies a Bresenham-like line-drawing algorithm (in `buildLine`) to generate integer pixel coordinates along each line segment. For each traversed pixel, it computes the corresponding map coordinate using `raster.pixelToMap` and emits a point feature with attributes 'id', 'line_id', and 'point_id'. Input is a QGIS vector line layer and a raster layer; output is a point vector layer in the same CRS as the raster. No study area, time range, satellite data, or specific geographic location is referenced — the algorithm is purely geometric and coordinate-system dependent. The script operates within QGIS Processing framework and relies on GDAL and QgsGeometry APIs.

name: Execute and load PostgreSQL SQL query
desc: The script executes a user-provided SQL query against a configured PostgreSQL/PostGIS database connection and loads the resulting table (with geometry and ID fields) as a valid QGIS vector layer. It constructs a QgsDataSourceUri from the connection and SQL, wraps the SQL in a subquery, sets geometry and ID field names, creates a QgsVectorLayer, validates it, and registers it in the processing context for output. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing operations are performed — the task is purely database interaction and layer loading. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Generate autonomous spatial SQL queries
desc: The script discovers the complete PostGIS database schema (tables, columns, geometry types, unique values) from loaded QGIS vector layers, then uses an LLM to generate syntactically and semantically correct PostGIS SQL (e.g., CREATE TABLE AS SELECT...) based on natural language user requests. It executes the SQL against the connected PostGIS database, loads the resulting 'public.analysis_result' layer into QGIS with auto-styling, zooms to extent, and logs full execution feedback. The workflow is fully iterative and error-resilient: on SQL execution failure, it parses the PostgreSQL error, identifies the problematic column/table, feeds context back to the LLM for correction, and retries up to 5 times. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is performed — all operations are relational-spatial (PostGIS) over local database layers.

name: Draw H3 cell boundary
desc: The script draws one or more H3 geohash cells as polygon features in a temporary memory vector layer (EPSG:4326), styles them with semi-transparent cyan fill and white outline, adds the layer to the QGIS project, and zooms the map canvas to their combined extent (reprojected to the project's CRS). It validates input H3 indexes, computes their resolution and geographic boundaries using the h3 Python library (with fallback between v3/v4 APIs), and reports invalid IDs. No remote sensing data, time-series, or Earth observation analysis is performed — the task is purely geometric conversion and cartographic display of H3 indices.

name: Reprocess ABR polygon layers
desc: The script reprocesses cadastral or land parcel polygon layers based on an ABR (Built/Open) classification column. It performs spatial merging of built-up polygons into adjacent open parcels using geometric criteria (shared vertices ≥3, within containment, shared boundary length, overlap area), then dissolves the merged features by a generated PARCEL_ID_final to produce two final shapefile outputs: 'Parcel Area.shp' (dissolved merged parcels) and 'Built up Area.shp' (isolated built-up polygons). Input layers are QGIS vector layers (polygons) loaded from the current project; no remote sensing or raster data is used. The workflow includes folder structuring (by District/Mandal/Revenue Village/LGD Code), backup export of original layer and project, GPKG intermediate saves ('merged.gpkg', 'PARCEL_ID_final.gpkg', 'Built_only.gpkg'), and final visibility management in QGIS—showing only the two output shapefiles. All operations are purely vector-based (geometry union, dissolve, spatial indexing, attribute copying) and executed locally in QGIS using PyQGIS and processing algorithms. Study area is implicitly Andhra Pradesh, India, as evidenced by the hardcoded district list containing 27 districts including 'Alluri Sitarama Raju', 'YSR Kadapa', 'Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore', etc., all of which are administrative districts of Andhra Pradesh.

name: Generate concentric buffer rings
desc: The script generates a series of non-overlapping, geometrically precise concentric ring-shaped polygons (annuli) centered on input point features. Each ring has an exact width ('Shape Width') and exact spacing between successive rings ('Buffer Distance'), calculated as absolute distances from the original base points—not cumulatively—ensuring consistent geometry across iterations. Rings are constructed via buffered outer/inner circles (with configurable segment count, cap/join styles), followed by geometric difference and dissolution. The output is a single merged vector layer containing all rings as polygon geometries.

name: Create intersection-based circular buffer
desc: The script implements an interactive QGIS map tool that allows users to snap to vertices or edges of existing vector layers, compute curved intersections (e.g., at road or line feature crossings), and generate two memory vector layers: (1) a circular string (approximated as a 4-point circle using 90° intervals) representing a user-defined distance buffer centered on the snapped/intersection point, stored in a LineString memory layer with attributes 'distance', 'x', and 'y'; and (2) a point geometry at the same center location, stored in a Point memory layer. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, raster processing, or satellite-derived inputs are involved — the tool operates purely on vector geometry interaction within QGIS. All layers are created dynamically in memory with CRS matching the canvas, and no external datasets, imagery, or temporal filtering are used.

name: Ingest geotagged media metadata
desc: The script ingests image and video files from a user-selected local folder, extracts EXIF datetime (for images) or filesystem modification time (for videos), associates them with a fixed camera location from a QGIS vector layer ('camera_loc'), and appends records to a GeoPackage layer (either new or existing) derived from a template layer ('image_classification'). Each record stores the full file path in 'media_path', camera ID, local time (Pacific/Auckland), timezone, and geometry at the camera's known coordinates. Duplicates are skipped by checking existing 'media_path' values. The script operates entirely within QGIS desktop using PyQt and PIL — no remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or GEE cloud processing is involved; it is a local GIS metadata curation tool.

name: Detect parcel evolution by geometry
desc: The script performs a geometric change detection analysis between two agricultural parcel vector layers (T1 and T2) using QGIS processing tools. It harmonizes CRS, fixes geometries, computes a topological union to decompose overlapping and non-overlapping polygon areas, then calculates per-geometry surface area for each time step (surf_T1, surf_T2), absolute and relative change (var_abs, var_pct), and classifies each resulting geometry into one of five status categories: 'nouvelle' (new parcel at T2 only), 'disparue' (parcel present at T1 only), 'conservee' (area change < user-defined % threshold), 'augmente' (positive % change ≥ threshold), or 'diminuee' (negative % change ≥ threshold). Outputs include a GeoPackage or Shapefile vector layer with these attributes and an optional CSV export of the attribute table.

name: Export SHYFEM grid geometry
desc: The script exports vector line or polygon layers from QGIS to the SHYFEM .grd file format, a structured ASCII format used by the SHYFEM hydrodynamic model. It processes active vector layers (lines or polygons), extracts all vertices, deduplicates coincident points using coordinate tolerance based on CRS (8 decimals for geographic, 2 for projected), assigns sequential point IDs, and writes two sections: (1) point records with type '1' followed by ID, type, x, y; and (2) line/polygon connectivity records with type '3' followed by line ID, type, count, then a space-separated list of point IDs. For polygons, it auto-closes rings by appending the first point ID to the end if not already present. The import function reads .grd files, parses point and line definitions, reconstructs point and lineString vector layers in QGIS (grouped under 'SHYFEM_<basename>'), and zooms the canvas to their combined extent. No geospatial analysis, modeling, or time-series processing is performed — only geometric I/O conversion between QGIS vector layers and SHYFEM’s native grid definition format. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification, or analysis methods are not involved or referenced.

name: Export SHYFEM grid geometry
desc: The script converts QGIS vector layers (lines or polygons) into SHYFEM .grd format — a structured ASCII grid file used in hydrodynamic modeling. It extracts vertices, deduplicates coordinates with ID mapping, writes point records (type '1' lines), and connectivity records (type '3' for lines/polygons), enforcing column wrapping (≤132 chars) and CRS-aware coordinate precision (2 decimals for projected, 8 for geographic). It also imports SHYFEM .grd files by parsing type '1' (points), '2' (polygons), and '3' (lines) records, reconstructing QGIS point, line, and polygon layers with attribute preservation (point_id, line_id, polygon_id, node IDs, depth). The 'Save Modified Grid' function preserves original element connectivity while writing updated coordinates — critical for maintaining mesh topology in numerical simulations. No remote sensing data, time series, or classification is involved; the entire workflow operates on static vector geometry and mesh topology.

name: Identify disconnected poles and chambers
desc: The script performs spatial quality control on utility infrastructure layers: (1) it fixes geometries of the 'route' (line) layer to ensure topological validity; (2) it identifies 'poles' that are spatially disjoint (i.e., not intersecting or touching) the fixed routes, outputting them as a new layer named 'Diconnected_Poles'; (3) it first extracts chambers that *touch* the fixed routes, then identifies chambers that are *disjoint* from those touching chambers — effectively isolating chambers with no topological connection to the route network — and outputs them as 'Disconnected_Chambers'. All outputs are vector layers added to the QGIS project with descriptive names and printed status messages.

name: Generate geodesic flow map
desc: The script generates a geodesic flow map by computing great-circle routes between airport pairs using WGS84 ellipsoid geometry. It reads IATA-coded airport coordinates (latitude/longitude) from an Excel file and flight route records (origin/destination IATA codes) from another Excel file. For each valid origin–destination pair, it computes the geodesic distance using QgsDistanceArea with WGS84 ellipsoid, subdivides the geodesic line into segments (~50 km minimum), and assigns a flow value proportional to distance (flow = round(distance_km × 10)). Output layers include: (1) a memory-based LineString layer ('Jeodezik_Akimlar') with attributes Origin, Dest, Flow, and Dist_km; (2) a memory-based Point layer ('Havalimanlari') containing only actively used airports; both layers are styled (graduated line width by Flow, point labels by IATA) and exported as a single GeoJSON file ('akim_analizi.geojson') saved to the user's Documents folder. The map canvas is zoomed to the extent of the line layer. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used — all inputs are static tabular (Excel) and outputs are vector GIS layers.

name: Calculate raster statistics per polygon
desc: The script performs batch zonal statistics: for each input raster file (e.g., GeoTIFFs), it computes user-selected statistical metrics (e.g., mean, min, max, std, coverage_pct) for every polygon in a QGIS vector layer. It supports optional post-processing including custom algorithm integration (aggregated and pixel-level), multi-raster score calculation (weighted normalized indicators), and time-series analysis on polygon attributes. Outputs include an updated or new GeoPackage vector layer with appended statistic fields, plus optional exports to CSV, HTML, PDF, and JSON formats. No satellite imagery processing occurs — rasters are treated as opaque local files; CRS validation is performed via GDAL but no reprojection is applied. The study area, time range, satellite sensors, bands, and geographic location are not specified in the code — all inputs are generic file paths and user-provided layers.

name: Classify flood risk levels
desc: The script classifies continuous numeric field values (e.g., flood risk scores) from a user-selected vector layer into discrete, user-defined categories (e.g., 'Low', 'Medium', 'High') using one of four geostatistical classification methods: Equal Intervals, Quantiles, Natural Breaks (Jenks), or Custom Breaks. It operates entirely within QGIS via a PyQt widget, reads numeric attribute fields from the selected vector layer, computes class assignments using an external PostProcessingEngine (not shown in this script), appends a new string-type classification column (e.g., 'flood_risk_class') to a copied GeoPackage output, and adds the result to the QGIS project. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and raster inputs are not involved — this is a vector attribute classification tool with no embedded Earth Engine (GEE) code; the mention of 'GEE' in the user prompt is a mischaracterization — the script is purely QGIS/PyQt-based and uses local vector layers only.

name: Create composite risk score
desc: The script creates a composite score (e.g., Risk Score) by combining multiple numeric indicators (e.g., flood_mean, population, elevation) from a QGIS vector layer. It normalizes values (Min-Max, Z-Score, or None), applies user-defined importance weights (Very High/High/Medium/Low → 0.5/0.3/0.15/0.05), and computes either a Weighted Sum or Weighted Average. The output is a new GeoPackage file containing the original features plus a new column with the computed score value. No remote sensing imagery or Earth Engine assets are used — all data comes from local vector layer fields. The workflow is fully interactive within QGIS via a PyQt widget; no external geospatial processing backend (e.g., GEE) is invoked in this script.

name: Analyze hospital proximity to districts
desc: The script computes the Euclidean distance from the centroid of each administrative district polygon to the nearest hospital point feature in Lima Metropolitana, Peru. It classifies districts into five distance-based categories (<2 km, 2–5 km, 5–10 km, 10–20 km, >20 km), applies thematic symbology, generates a PDF map layout (A4 landscape) with title, legend, scale bar, and date, produces a textual report with statistics and top-3 nearest/farthest districts, exports results to GeoPackage with attributes 'dist_hospital' (km) and 'categoria', and creates a matplotlib bar chart of category distribution. The study area is explicitly named 'Distritos de Lima' and 'Hospitales'; input data comes from local GeoJSON files ('data/distritos.geojson', 'data/hospitales.geojson'); no satellite or remote sensing data is used — all operations are vector-based (centroid calculation, planar distance measurement using QgsDistanceArea with WGS84 ellipsoid, attribute assignment, categorization, and cartographic export).

name: Extract building footprints
desc: The script extracts building footprint vector features from a local shapefile (e.g., 'g.shp' for Shenzhen) using spatial filtering against a user-defined rectangular region of interest (ROI) specified in 'tmp/city_roi.json'. It loads the shapefile via QGIS Python API, constructs a polygon from WGS84 coordinates, transforms the ROI to the layer's CRS, performs intersection-based feature selection, converts selected QGIS features to a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame (preserving geometry and attributes), renames 'Height' → 'height', assigns sequential IDs, reprojects to EPSG:4326, and exports directly to GeoJSON ('tmp/tmp.geojson') — no intermediate Shapefile. Study area is defined per city (Shenzhen, Chongqing, Chengdu, Suzhou, Hangzhou, Hefei) via dictionary mapping; data source is local vector data, not satellite-derived. No classification, modeling, or time-series analysis is performed.

name: Calculate urban spatial pattern indicators
desc: The script computes nine quantitative urban morphological indicators from user-provided geospatial inputs: Building Coverage Ratio (BCR), Compactness Index (CI), Plaque Density (PD), Shape Index (SI), Edge Density (ED), Road Density (RD), Intersection Density (ID), Skyline Index (SLI), and Average Building Height (ABH). Inputs are local files — raster or vector — supplied via QGIS file widgets (e.g., building footprints, height data, road networks, optional analysis boundary). For vector inputs, the script rasterizes them using GDAL with user-specified resolution (default 10 m or 0.0001°), auto-detecting height fields in building vectors. Grid-based analyses (e.g., BCR, CI, PD, ED, ABH, SLI) use a user-defined physical grid size in meters (e.g., 500 m), which is dynamically converted to pixel count based on input raster resolution and coordinate system (geographic vs projected). Road and intersection density analyses accept missing boundaries and offer three fallback strategies: bounding box, convex hull, or buffered road network. Outputs include a GeoTIFF raster of the indicator map, optionally a CSV table with per-grid statistics, and optionally a PNG visualization (only for Shape Index). Styling is applied automatically using a reversed Spectral color ramp. No remote sensing imagery or GEE server-side processing is used — all operations are local (GDAL, OGR, NumPy-based core functions imported from `.core`).

name: Convert KML KMZ to vector formats
desc: The script converts input KML/KMZ files into user-specified vector geospatial formats (Shapefile, GeoPackage, or GeoJSON), reprojecting them to a user-selected CRS. It loads each KML/KMZ as a QgsVectorLayer using GDAL/OGR, validates layer integrity, writes the output using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV3 with UTF-8 encoding and target CRS, and adds successfully written layers to the QGIS project. No raster processing, temporal analysis, classification, or remote sensing computation is performed — it is purely a format and CRS translation utility for vector data.

name: Fuse multisensor optical bands
desc: The script performs sensor-specific band fusion: (1) For Landsat 8, it applies GDAL pansharpening to fuse 30 m multispectral bands B4 (Red), B5 (NIR), B6 (SWIR-1) with 15 m panchromatic band B8, producing a sharpened 15 m RGB-like composite; (2) For Landsat 5, CBERS-4A, and Sentinel-2, it builds virtual rasters stacking specified bands in defined spectral order (B3-B4-B5 for L5; B5-B4-B3 for CBERS-4A; B11-B8-B4 for S2) without sharpening, preserving native resolutions (30 m, ~64 m, and mixed 10/20 m respectively); all outputs are reprojected to a user-specified CRS (default EPSG:4674). The result is a single georeferenced, multi-band raster optimized for visual interpretation or downstream analysis.

name: Create point location marker
desc: The script creates a single-point vector layer in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) with a styled marker and label, representing a named geographic location (e.g., 'San Francisco' at latitude 37.7749, longitude -122.4194). It defines a memory-based QgsVectorLayer, adds one feature with geometry and attributes ('name', 'description'), applies a red circular marker symbol with black outline, and configures white-buffered black text labels using QgsPalLayerSettings. The layer is added to the QGIS project and the map canvas is zoomed to its extent. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or geoprocessing operations are performed — it is purely a static point visualization workflow. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Import CSV with geometry
desc: The script imports CSV files containing spatial data in various geometry formats (WKT, WKB, GeoJSON, XY coordinates) into QGIS as vector layers. It supports auto-detection of geometry format and column types, handles encoding/delimiter variability, validates geometries, optionally skips invalid rows, and outputs either a temporary memory layer or a saved file (GeoPackage, Shapefile, or GeoJSON). When enabled, it generates auxiliary report layers for null and invalid geometries. The script does not perform remote sensing analysis, time-series processing, or Earth observation modeling — it is a local GIS data ingestion tool operating entirely on user-provided CSV files. No study area, time range, satellite data, or geospatial analysis methods are involved; all inputs are local tabular files with embedded or coordinate-based geometry.

name: Add point coordinates to GIS layer
desc: The script is a QGIS plugin that enables users to input geographic coordinates in various formats (DD, DDM, DMS, EPSG:3794, EPSG:3857, UTM) and add them as point features to either a newly created scratch vector layer or an existing point vector layer in the QGIS project. It performs coordinate parsing, CRS validation, on-the-fly reprojection from input CRS to target layer CRS, and feature insertion. No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, or Earth observation processing is involved — it is purely a coordinate entry and vector editing tool. The study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial modeling methods are not specified because the script operates interactively on user-provided coordinates without referencing any external geospatial datasets, imagery, or temporal constraints.

name: Analyze masonry component dimensions
desc: The script performs quantitative analysis of architectural masonry components (e.g., stones, bricks, blocks) from vector polygon survey data. It computes oriented minimum bounding boxes (OMBBs) for each component to extract geometric attributes — width, height, angle, perimeter, and area — then calculates modular metrics relative to a user-defined module (e.g., Roman foot = 0.296 m), including integer modulo counts (width_modulo, height_modulo) and remainders (Δwidth_modulo, Δheight_modulo). It applies optional material-based filtering, separates components by 'intera'/'parziale' surface condition if the field exists, computes aggregate statistics (count, min/max/mean/stddev/range) on width, height, and area, and generates binned frequency distributions ('range' tables) for width and height using configurable step intervals. Outputs include: (1) oriented bounding box polygons with geometric fields; (2) enriched survey layer with all computed metrics and virtual modulo fields; (3) tabular aggregate statistics; (4) categorical count tables for width and height ranges.

name: Analyze dry-stone component dimensions
desc: The script performs quantitative analysis of dry-stone masonry components (e.g., stones, blocks) from vector polygon survey data. It computes oriented minimum bounding boxes (OMBB) for each component polygon to extract geometric metrics: width_bbox, height_bbox, angle_bbox, perimeter_bbox, and area_bbox. It then calculates modulo-based metrics (width_modulo, Δwidth_modulo, height_modulo, Δheight_modulo) using a user-defined module value (default 0.296 m, corresponding to the Roman/Attic foot). Statistics (count, min, max, mean, stddev, range) are aggregated over width, height, and area fields — restricted to 'intera' (full) components if the optional 'superficie' field is present, otherwise applied to all components. Outputs include: (1) OMBB polygons with geometric attributes; (2) enriched survey layer with bbox metrics and modulo fields; (3) tabular aggregate statistics; (4) categorical frequency distributions for width and height ranges (binned by user-specified step sizes). No remote sensing or raster data is used — input is strictly vector-based survey polygons. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

name: Analyze masonry component dimensions
desc: The script performs quantitative analysis of masonry components (e.g., bricks, stones) from vector polygon survey data ('layer rilievo'), without requiring a sample area layer. It computes oriented minimum bounding boxes (OMBBs) for each polygon, extracts geometric metrics (width, height, angle, perimeter, area of bbox), joins them back to the original survey layer, and calculates aggregate statistics (count, min, max, mean, stddev, range) — exclusively on 'intera' (full/complete) components when the 'superficie' field is present and populated. It further bins width and height measurements into user-defined step-based ranges (e.g., 0.004 m and 0.002 m) and generates frequency distribution tables per range. All operations are purely vector-based; no raster, satellite, or temporal data is involved. Inputs are local QGIS vector layers with mandatory fields: 'fid', 'tipo', 'area_componente', 'num_componente', and optionally 'superficie'; outputs include five vector layers: oriented bbox polygons, enriched survey polygons, a non-geometric statistics table, and two categorical count tables for width and height ranges.

name: Model landslide runout probability
desc: The script computes the probabilistic spatial extent of landslide runout impact by performing Monte Carlo simulations over friction coefficient uncertainty. For each realization, it generates a deterministic runout path from source cells (binary raster) using an alpha-angle criterion derived from local friction and slope, constrained by fan-angle spreading, maximum runout distance, and runout-to-source length ratio. The output is a raster of impact probability (0–1), where each pixel value equals the fraction of Monte Carlo iterations in which that pixel was traversed by at least one runout path.

name: Model deep seated landslide runout
desc: The script models the runout extent of deep-seated landslides using a probabilistic Monte Carlo approach or deterministic method, based on source locations (binary raster), DEM, friction raster, slope, and aspect. It computes runout distance along fan-shaped directions constrained by alpha angles (derived from friction and slope coefficients), a cone-fall-inspired directional propagation, maximum runout length (m), and maximum runout-to-source-distance ratio (3.5). Outputs a raster of impact probability (0–1) representing the frequency of pixel inundation across N Monte Carlo realizations.

name: Create cloud project and initialize QGIS workspace
taskType: Project creation and local QGIS workspace initialization
desc: The script creates a new cloud-based project via an API, then initializes a local QGIS project (.qgz) and a GeoPackage (.gpkg) file containing a dummy memory vector layer (Point geometry, EPSG:4326). It establishes a local directory structure under 'TopMapSync' with project-specific safe-name subfolders. No geospatial analysis, classification, or remote sensing processing is performed — the script is purely infrastructure setup for project onboarding. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, classification methods, and analytical outputs are not present or referenced in the code.

name: Detect water leak locations
desc: The script detects water leak locations along a user-provided road/highway line layer interpreted as a pipeline network. It generates synthetic sensor data (moisture, pressure, flow) along the network, trains a lightweight Random Forest classifier using moisture, pressure, flow, and a random noise feature to predict leak probability, evaluates model accuracy with confusion-matrix-based metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1), compares current moisture against a simulated 3-month historical baseline to flag anomalies, identifies high-confidence leak points with precise lat/lon coordinates, renders two QGIS layers — one showing all sensors (red for predicted leaks, green for normal) and another showing only critical leak locations as red point markers — and performs Dijkstra-inspired bypass route analysis by computing affected vs. safe road segments within a 50m buffer of detected leaks, reporting measured lengths in meters/km. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are synthetic or derived from the user’s vector layer. The study area is implicitly constrained to the extent of the loaded road layer, and no real-world geolocation, time-series satellite imagery, or external datasets are referenced.

name: Calculate time of concentration
desc: The script calculates time of concentration (TC) in minutes for subbasin polygons using four empirical hydrologic methods (Kirpich, FAA, SCS/NRCS, Kerby), based on subbasin length (ft) and slope (%). It requires user-provided vector subbasin layers (with a selected attribute field) and a raster DEM. Length is estimated from bounding box dimensions (converted from meters to feet), and slope is currently hardcoded to 2.0% (a placeholder pending implementation of flow-path-based slope calculation). Outputs include: (1) a shapefile (subbasins_tc.shp) with appended TC fields per method and summary statistics; (2) a detailed CSV (tc_calculations_detailed.csv) listing all TC values per subbasin and method; and (3) an interactive QTableWidget in the GUI displaying subbasin ID, length, slope, min/max/avg TC, and individual method results. The study area is not specified in the code logic; the default output path contains 'Crooked' (suggesting Crooked River or similar), but no explicit geographic definition or CRS-based spatial constraint is applied during calculation — the tool assumes input layers are pre-projected to EPSG:3361 (NAD83 / Michigan Oblique Mercator), and no satellite, sensor, or temporal data is used.

name: Clip raster by polygon mask
desc: The script performs batch clipping of raster layers using a user-selected vector polygon layer as the mask. It processes selected rasters (e.g., DEMs, orthophotos) in QGIS via GDAL's 'cliprasterbymasklayer' algorithm, preserving resolution and CRS. Output rasters are saved as GeoTIFFs in a user-specified directory and optionally organized into two thematic groups in the QGIS layer tree: 'DEM clip' (for layers with 'dem', 'dtm', or 'dsm' in their name) and 'Orthophoto clip' (all others), sorted by date extracted from filenames. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing is performed — only geometric clipping. Study area, time range, satellite data, and geographic extent are not defined in the script; it operates purely on locally loaded QGIS layers.

name: Identify earthquake occurrences in buffer zone
desc: The script selects features from an active QGIS vector layer, creates a buffer polygon around them (distance input via dialog), then clips earthquake point data (layerTerremoti) to that buffer. It filters earthquakes by user-specified year range (rangeInizio to rangeFine), writes the clipped and filtered points to a new shapefile ('terremotiRitag.shp'), adds an 'Anno' (Year) integer field, populates it with source attribute values, applies red circular symbology and year-based labeling, and adds both the buffer layer and clipped earthquake layer to the QGIS project. The script also displays a message box reporting the count of matched earthquakes.

name: Assess post-earthquake building reconstruction
desc: The script analyzes temporal relationships between earthquake events and subsequent building reconstruction within a buffer zone. It selects earthquake features (with attributes 'Io' intensity and 'Anno' year) from an active QGIS layer, computes a user-defined buffer (in km) around each selected earthquake point, clips building features (from 'Edifici.gpkg') that were constructed in the interval [earthquake year + 1, earthquake year + interval] to that buffer, and renders the clipped buildings with SVG symbols based on their 'Tipo' (type) attribute and a distance-to-epicenter / intensity ('IoNum') coefficient threshold (<9000). Outputs include: (1) a memory vector layer 'isosisme' showing earthquake buffers; (2) a shapefile 'LayerGIS/edificiRitag.shp' containing reconstructed buildings within the buffer and time window; (3) categorized symbology applied to 'edificiRitag.shp' using custom SVG icons per building type; (4) data-driven labels showing 'DataEd' (reconstruction year); and (5) a QMessageBox summarizing counts. Input data sources are local vector files: 'Edifici.gpkg' (buildings with 'Data_Edificio', 'Tipo', 'fid'), 'LayerGIS/edificiSel.shp' (intermediate selection layer), 'LayerGIS/edificiRitag.shp' (output clip layer), and icon SVGs under 'LayerGIS/icone/'. The study area, satellite/sensor/bands, and time range of input vector data are not specified in the script.

name: Identify earthquake occurrences in buffer zone
desc: The script selects features from an active QGIS vector layer (e.g., infrastructure or administrative boundaries), creates a buffer polygon layer around them based on user-input distance (km), clips the 'Terremoti' earthquake point layer (with 'Anno' attribute) to that buffer, filters earthquakes by user-specified temporal range (year-based), assigns the 'Anno' attribute to clipped features, visualizes results with red circular markers and year labels, and adds both the buffer and clipped earthquake layers to the QGIS project. Outputs include a clipped shapefile ('terremotiRitag.shp'), a styled buffer layer, and a QMessageBox reporting count of matched earthquakes.

name: Buffer and clip earthquake locations
desc: The script buffers selected features from an active QGIS vector layer using a user-specified distance (in km), creates a memory polygon layer for the buffer, styles it with a semi-transparent orange fill and dark red outline, then clips a preloaded earthquake point layer (terremoti) using that buffer. The clipped earthquake points are saved to 'LayerGIS/terrRit.shp', loaded as a new layer, styled with blue circular markers, and added to the QGIS project. Input layers include 'Edifici.gpkg', 'totaleepicentriterremotiinunareadi200kmdatoscanaliguria.gpkg', and two container shapefiles ('edContenitore.shp', 'terrContenitore.shp').

name: Identify post-earthquake building construction
desc: The script identifies buildings constructed within a user-specified time interval (e.g., 1–10 years) after selected earthquake events, using buffer zones around earthquake point features to spatially constrain the analysis. It loads two local vector layers: 'Edifici.gpkg' (buildings with 'Data Edificio' attribute) and a QGIS active layer containing earthquake points (with 'Anno' attribute). For each selected earthquake, it creates a buffer polygon (distance input by user), clips buildings intersecting that buffer, filters them by construction year ('Data Edificio') falling in [Anno, Anno + intervallo], and outputs a final clipped layer 'ritaglioFinale' of qualifying buildings. The output is added to the QGIS project as a new vector layer. No satellite or remote sensing data is used; all inputs are local vector files. Study area and time range of earthquakes/buildings are not specified in the code.

name: Convert CSV precipitation points to GeoPackage
desc: The script converts a CSV file containing point-based precipitation observations (with 'lon' and 'lat' columns) into a georeferenced vector layer in GeoPackage format. It loads the CSV using QGIS's delimited text driver with WGS84 (EPSG:4326) CRS, creates a temporary QgsVectorLayer of points, adds it to the QGIS project for visualization, and exports it to a GeoPackage file (GPKG_OUT) under the specified layer name (GPKG_LAYER). The input CSV is identified as MERGED_STD_OUT; no spatial filtering, temporal filtering, reprojection, or analysis is performed — only format conversion and CRS assignment. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor data, and classification/analysis methods are not specified.

name: Allocate demand points to pipe network
desc: The script allocates water or utility demand from building/house polygons to a pipe network by computing polygon centroids, snapping them to the nearest pipe segment, clustering snapped points within a user-defined threshold distance (default 50 m), generating aggregated demand points at cluster centroids, and creating reference lines linking original centroids to assigned demand points. Outputs include two vector layers: (1) 'House Load Points' — point layer with attribute 'NUM' indicating number of houses per cluster; and (2) 'Reference Lines' — line layer with attributes 'NUM_HOUSES' and 'DISTANCE_M'. The core logic is delegated to an external module ('allocation_logic.run_allocation') and operates entirely on user-provided local vector layers (no remote sensing data). All geospatial operations — centroid calculation, snapping, clustering, line generation — are performed using QGIS geometry engine (e.g., QgsGeometry, QgsSpatialIndex, QgsPointLocator) within memory layers or optionally saved as ESRI Shapefiles. No study area, time range, satellite data, or external geospatial datasets are referenced in the script.

name: Identify suitable slope zones
desc: The script identifies contiguous land areas within a user-defined slope range (5–8 degrees) and minimum area threshold (10,000 m²) inside a specified boundary (AOI), using contour-derived elevation data. It performs TIN interpolation of contour lines (with 'elev' attribute) to generate a 10m-resolution DEM, computes slope raster, applies a Boolean mask for the slope range, converts valid pixels to polygons, filters by area and spatial containment within the AOI, and outputs a final vector layer of qualifying terrain polygons suitable for infrastructure or development planning (e.g., ski resort trail alignment, solar farm siting).

name: Evaluate YOLO object detection
desc: The script evaluates a YOLO-style object detection model by computing precision, recall, and F1-score across confidence thresholds (0.0–1.0 in 0.02 steps) using intersection-over-union (IoU ≥ 0.3) matching between prediction and ground-truth vector geometries. It loads three OGR vector layers: predictions (with 'confidence' attribute), ground truth, and AOI; reprojects GT and AOI to match the predictions’ CRS; clips both GT and predictions to the union of AOI geometries; builds a spatial index for efficient candidate matching; computes pairwise IoUs only for intersecting bounding boxes; applies greedy matching (highest-confidence predictions first) to assign true positives; and outputs a CSV ('metrics.csv') and PNG plot ('f1_curve.png') showing the F1-precision-recall curve vs. confidence threshold. The best F1 score and corresponding confidence threshold are logged. No satellite imagery, time-series, or raster processing is involved — input is purely vector-based detection output.

name: Prepare YOLO object detection dataset
desc: The script prepares a YOLO-formatted object detection dataset from georeferenced raster tiles (.tif) and vector-labeled features (e.g., bounding boxes or oriented bounding boxes). It auto-detects ground sampling distance (GSD) across input tiles, resamples imagery to a target GSD (default ~6.0 cm), transforms vector geometries to match each tile’s CRS, converts geometries to YOLO format (AABB or OBB), applies optional small-object enhancement, splits samples into train/val sets (15% validation), and saves JPEG images + TXT labels in standard YOLO directory structure with dataset.yaml. Inputs are local filesystem paths: a directory of GeoTIFF tiles, a shapefile of labels, and an output directory; no cloud-based Earth Engine assets or remote collections are used — all operations are local GIS processing via rasterio, shapely, pyproj, and QGIS Python API. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Generate labeled image tiles
desc: The script generates georeferenced raster image tiles (GeoTIFF) for machine learning training: primary tiles containing at least one vector geometry intersection (with corresponding binary mask implicitly generated via rasterize), and background tiles sampled from areas without geometry overlap. Input is a user-provided shapefile of vector labels and a list of local GeoTIFF rasters (not GEE assets). It performs CRS-aware spatial intersection filtering, sliding-window tiling with configurable size and overlap, on-the-fly rasterization of vector geometries per tile to determine label presence, and JPEG-compressed GeoTIFF export. No time-series analysis, cloud masking, spectral index calculation, or classification model is present — only spatial tiling and label-aware sampling. Study area, time range, satellite sensors, and bands are not specified in the code; all inputs are local files with no embedded temporal or sensor metadata parsed.

name: Calculate trail shadow exposure
desc: The script calculates the proportion of a hiking trail that lies in shadow versus sunlit conditions at the time the hiker physically reaches each point, using high-resolution LiDAR-derived Digital Surface Model (MNS) from IGN France to model terrain occlusion and solar geometry. Key steps include: (1) densifying and temporally sampling the input trail vector layer based on departure time, hiking speed (optionally adjusted for slope), optional picnic break, and direction reversal; (2) downloading two-resolution MNS rasters (0.5 m high-res for shadow casting, 15 m low-res for broader context) and an MNT (Digital Terrain Model, 15 m) from IGN’s open geospatial services; (3) sampling elevation values along the trail from the MNT; (4) computing solar position (elevation and azimuth) for each trail point’s timestamp and location; (5) performing ray-casting or horizon-based shadow analysis using the high-res MNS to determine whether each point is shaded by surrounding topography/vegetation/structures; (6) generating a point layer with attributes including shadow status, solar angles, coordinates, elevation, and course; (7) exporting statistics (percent shady/sunny, time-in-shadow, total points) to CSV; and (8) styling output points categorically (gold for sun, blue for shadow) with directional arrowheads aligned to trail course. Study area is implicitly France (via IGN data access, Lambert-93 CRS usage, and French plugin name 'Marche À l’Ombre'), but no explicit region or bounding box is hardcoded. Data sources are exclusively French national geospatial products (IGN MNS/MNT), not satellite imagery.

name: Apply RGB band contrast enhancement
desc: The script applies histogram-based contrast enhancement (StretchToMinimumMaximum) to the red, green, and blue display bands of a single input GeoTIFF raster to improve visual interpretability. It computes global min/max pixel values across the three display bands (band 3 for red, band 2 for green, band 1 for blue), then applies identical stretch limits to all three bands’ contrast enhancements. The enhanced RGB rendering is written to a new GeoTIFF file (_rgb_render.tif). No classification, time-series analysis, or multi-image processing occurs — it is a single-raster, single-scene, display-oriented rendering operation. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and classification methods are not specified.

name: Apply RGB contrast enhancement
desc: The script reads a local GeoTIFF raster file (sourceRaster), configures its renderer to display red, green, and blue bands as bands 3, 2, and 1 respectively (i.e., B3→R, B2→G, B1→B — typical for near-infrared-red-green or false-color composites), computes global min/max statistics across those three bands, applies identical StretchToMinimumMaximum contrast enhancement to each band using the joint min (maximum of per-band mins) and joint max (minimum of per-band maxes), and exports a new rendered GeoTIFF (_rgb_render.tif) with enhanced RGB visualization. The script operates entirely on a single local raster file; no remote sensing time series, cloud masking, classification, or geospatial analysis is performed. All operations are QGIS-based raster rendering and export — no GEE code is present. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor metadata, and geographic location are not specified in the script.

name: Calculate map projection distortion
desc: The script computes Quasi-Tissot Indicatrices — point-based ellipses representing local map projection distortion — by numerically differentiating coordinate transformations between a user-defined ellipsoidal geographic CRS and the current QGIS project CRS. It calculates scale factors (h, k), area distortion (s), angular deformation (omega), semi-major/minor axes (a_ind, b_ind), and rotation angle for each indicatrix point. Outputs include a memory vector layer of points with ellipse symbology (data-defined width/height/angle), attribute table with distortion metrics, and optional graticule lines; all dynamically updated per project CRS change. No remote sensing imagery or time-series data is used — inputs are purely geometric: user-specified ellipsoid parameters (a, b), numerical delta, bounding box (lat/lon min/max), resolution steps, and QGIS project CRS. Study area, time range, satellite data, and external datasets are not involved.

name: Add Excel point layer
desc: The script imports point coordinates (X, Y, optionally Z) from an actively open Microsoft Excel workbook into QGIS as a memory vector layer. It reads only the first worksheet, infers numeric columns, validates coordinate values against the selected CRS (e.g., geographic bounds ±180/±90 or UTM zone constraints), and constructs QgsPoint or QgsPointZ geometries. The output is a QGIS vector layer named after the Excel file, added to the current project with all original table columns preserved as attributes and appropriate field types (Int, Double, or String inferred per column). No remote sensing data, time-series analysis, classification, or GEE cloud processing is involved — this is a local desktop GIS interoperability tool bridging Excel and QGIS via COM automation.

name: Generate TIN mesh from point data
desc: The script generates a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN) mesh layer from user-selected QGIS vector point layers. It supports two Z sources: (1) native geometry Z-dimension (if the point layer is 3D), or (2) a numeric attribute field selected via comboBoxZ. Input validation ensures only point layers are accepted, and optional selection filtering allows processing only selected features. The output is a QgsMeshLayer loaded into the QGIS project using the MDAL driver (format: .mesh), optionally saved to a user-specified file path. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, time series, or external geospatial datasets are used — all inputs are local QGIS vector layers. The workflow includes real-time preview rendering in a QGraphicsView, progress feedback, error handling, and UI state synchronization (e.g., enabling/disabling controls based on layer properties).

name: Convert polygons to lines
desc: The script converts polygon vector layers to line vector layers in QGIS, preserving or adding attributes (ID, length), applying user-specified styling (color, line thickness), optional reprojection, and optional labeling. It supports selection-based conversion, attribute field retention/removal, CRS selection, and automatic cleanup (deletion of source polygon layer). Outputs are in-memory QgsVectorLayer objects added to the QGIS project; no external exports or satellite data processing occurs. All operations are local desktop GIS workflows—no remote sensing, time-series, or Earth Engine (GEE) functionality is present despite the misleading prompt reference to 'GEE script'. The code is purely QGIS Python Plugin logic.

name: Rasterize mesh topography
desc: The script rasterizes a QGIS QgsMeshLayer into a georeferenced GeoTIFF raster layer using the native QGIS 'native:meshrasterize' processing algorithm. It validates the input mesh layer, checks for dataset groups, uses user-specified pixel size, preserves the input CRS and extent, and outputs either to a user-defined path or a temporary directory. The resulting raster is loaded as a QgsRasterLayer into the QGIS project. No external remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis is involved — the input is strictly a local mesh layer (e.g., TIN or unstructured grid) already loaded in the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified — all operations are desktop GIS-based and rely solely on the user-loaded mesh layer.

name: Offset OFC line features
desc: The script offsets optical fiber cable (OFC) line features by 1 meter left or right based on guidance points derived from start/end XY coordinates in a separate point or tabular layer. It validates that the OFC layer is a line geometry in EPSG:4326, and the offset_pt layer contains required fields 'start_X', 'start_Y', 'end_X', 'end_Y' (also in EPSG:4326). The offset direction is determined by computing the cross product sign between the first segment of each OFC line and the nearest centroid-derived guidance point after reprojection to EPSG:3857 for metric distance calculation. Output is a new ESRI Shapefile vector layer named 'OFC_1m_offset' with identical attributes and geometry type as input, containing offset curves. No satellite, remote sensing, or temporal data is involved — it is purely vector-based geometric processing within QGIS using GDAL/OGR and QgsGeometry.offsetCurve().

name: Assess point accuracy by multi-attribute clustering
desc: The script processes a user-selected QGIS point vector layer to generate a new memory layer of 'best-fit' centroid points derived from spatially clustered, multi-attribute-matched observations. It groups features by user-selected attribute fields (e.g., ID, name, timestamp), then within each group performs distance-based clustering (using a configurable radius in meters) to identify co-located measurements; for each cluster, it computes a weighted centroid (inverse-accuracy weighting) and mean accuracy. The output layer includes original attributes plus STATUS (categorized as 'Accurate' or 'Low Accuracy' relative to a user-defined threshold), SRC_LAT/SRC_LONG of the best-fit position, and OBS_COUNT. Symbology is applied using green/red categories based on the threshold. No external GEE image collections, time-series, or satellite data are used — all operations are vector-based and local to the loaded QGIS layer.

name: Filter GPS accuracy points
desc: The script analyzes a QGIS vector layer to identify features with GPS accuracy values below a user-defined threshold (default 2.0 meters). It reads the specified numeric field (e.g., 'GPS ACCURA'), validates and converts values to floats, computes descriptive statistics (min, max, mean), ranks features by ascending accuracy, selects the top-performing subset in QGIS, and optionally exports them as a new vector layer (Shapefile or memory layer). The script operates entirely on pre-collected vector point data — no remote sensing imagery, time-series, or raster processing is involved. Inputs are local GIS layers loaded in QGIS; no external satellite, sensor, or temporal data is accessed or processed.

name: Clean ODK GPS point accuracy
desc: The script cleans field-collected GPS point data (e.g., from ODK Collect) by filtering on positional accuracy, clustering spatially proximate points (optionally grouped by matching attributes), consolidating them via best-point or weighted-average methods, optionally aligning points to linear features (e.g., roads), and applying cluster-aware symbology. It outputs a new memory vector layer with fields STATUS (Accurate/Low Accuracy), OBS_COUNT (cluster size), CLUSTER_ID, and IS_NUCLEUS, visualized with rule-based coloring (nucleus vs. family members) or binary red/green status. Input is a QGIS point layer; no satellite or remote sensing data is used — all operations are vector-based geometric and attribute processing within QGIS.

name: Assess river segment forest cover suitability
desc: The script evaluates 4km river segments for habitat suitability based on contiguous deciduous forest cover within a 20m buffer; it generates two shapefiles — one containing all 4km segments (stepped every 50m) with attributes including segment ID, start/end distance along river, length, forest intersection length (m and km), and a 'YES/NO' suitability flag (≥1.9km forest required), and another containing only segments meeting the forest length criterion. The workflow includes buffering deciduous forest polygons, unary union of buffered geometries, dense sampling of river lines into overlapping 4km segments, geometric intersection to compute forest-covered length per segment (handling fragmented intersections via multipart decomposition and summation), and classification against the 1900m threshold.

name: Extract potential stream channels
desc: The script extracts potential stream channels (lits d'écoulements potentiels) from a LiDAR-derived hydrographic dataset (Hydro_LiDAR_02AE.gdb layer 'Ecoulements_02AE') by spatially clipping it to the area south of the Etchemin River using a predefined mask layer (STH_masque_lit_ecoul_pot_02AE.shp). The workflow loads the source vector layer, adapts the canvas extent to its CRS to avoid coordinate mismatch errors, filters features visible in the current map view, performs a vector difference operation (overlay subtraction) between the filtered stream channel layer and the mask, saves the result as a new shapefile (Hydro_LiDAR_02AE_decoupe.shp), and loads it into QGIS. The study area is explicitly defined as south of the Etchemin River in Quebec's administrative unit '02AE' (likely Chaudière-Appalaches or adjacent region); data source is provincial LiDAR-derived hydrography (MRNF, 2025); no time-series or temporal filtering is applied; output is a clipped vector layer of potential stream channels.

name: Route corridor generation
desc: The script performs geometric routing and corridor clipping for infrastructure planning. It takes a user-selected polygon layer (e.g., landuse with 'kind' or 'Type' fields indicating public/private/river/bridge), two interactive map-clicked start/end points, and generates a route path using an external Python runner (routing_runner.py). Key workflow steps include: (1) exporting the selected vector layer to Shapefile; (2) transforming start/end points to a user-specified EPSG CRS; (3) invoking an external subprocess with parameters including spacing, max distance, clearance, buffer (corridor clipping), and EPSG; (4) loading the resulting GeoJSON route layer into QGIS. The output is a vector line layer named 'Portal Route' added to the QGIS project. No satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or Earth observation data processing occurs — this is purely GIS-based geometric routing and spatial constraint handling. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and EO data sources are not involved or specified.

name: Clip vector layers by selected polygon
desc: The script performs spatial intersection and clipping of QGIS vector layers against a user-selected polygon. It identifies all vector layers in the current QGIS project that intersect the selected geometry, groups them into two QGIS layer groups ('Intersecting Layers' and 'podzon') based on layer name matching (e.g., 'Территории_преимущественно_компактной_застройки', 'Прочие виды использования'), and creates memory-based clipped vector layers for each intersecting feature — preserving original attributes and geometry (intersection only). Clipped layers are named with suffix '_clipped_N_area_X.XX' and added to a third group 'Clipped Layers'. No raster data, satellite imagery, temporal filtering, or classification is involved; the workflow is purely vector-based GIS processing within QGIS Desktop using PyQGIS API. Study area is defined solely by the user-selected feature geometry; no external geospatial datasets (e.g., GEE ImageCollections) are loaded or processed.

name: Generate stage-discharge sensitivity curves
desc: The script performs a dual-zone (channel + floodplain) hydraulic modeling workflow to generate stage-discharge (Q–h) sensitivity curves by systematically varying Manning’s n roughness coefficients per land cover class across 30 water level multipliers (0.1–3.0× base water level). For each stage factor, it computes inundation depth using HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) and base water level rasters, classifies pixels as channel or floodplain using a vector mask, assigns land cover–specific roughness values, calculates cross-sectional hydraulic properties (flow area, wetted perimeter, hydraulic radius), and applies the Manning equation to compute discharge for all combinations of n values. Outputs include: (1) per-stage inundation rasters, (2) individual Excel files containing all n-combination discharges and flow areas, and (3) aggregated discharge values written into a pre-existing summary Excel workbook ('QGIS-Calculations-San-Isidro.xlsx') under the 'Cabula Curve List' sheet for hydrologic curve number (CN) or rating curve analysis.

name: Generate stage-discharge sensitivity curves
desc: The script performs hydraulic modeling to generate stage-discharge (Q) sensitivity curves for the Cabula River reach in San Isidro, using a dual-zone (channel + floodplain) Manning’s n-based approach. It processes QGIS raster and vector layers: water level (PA_WL_Cabula_10_FINAL), HAND-derived elevation-above-stream (HAND_EleveAbvStream_BestSubcatchmentClipped), and slope (Slope_Degrees_NewDEM); applies land cover classification from LandCover_Vector_3984,6m.shp; and uses a channel mask (SmallerChannel_Vector.shp). For each water level multiplier (0.1–3.0 m in 0.1 m increments), it computes inundated area, cross-sectional area, wetted perimeter per land cover class, and composite roughness via Einstein-Horton weighting (n_c = [Σ(P_i·n_i^1.5)/P_total]^(2/3)). Discharge is calculated using Manning’s equation separately for channel and floodplain zones, with floodplain discharge suppressed below critical stage (H_CRIT = 1.8 m). Outputs include: (1) per-stage inundation rasters (Inun_X.X.tif), (2) per-stage Excel files listing all Manning’s n combinations and resulting discharge (Sensitivity_X.X.xlsx), and (3) aggregated Q values written into columnar format in QGIS-Calculations-San-Isidro.xlsx under the 'Cabula Curve List' sheet. The study area is explicitly named as 'San Isidro' and 'Cabula', with reach length fixed at 3984.6 m and valley slope derived from two elevations over 2749.334 m — implying a specific river reach geometry.

name: Generate stage-discharge sensitivity curves
desc: The script generates stage-discharge (Q) sensitivity curves for a hydraulic reach in San Isidro (implied by 'Cabula Curve List' sheet name and 'San-Isidro.xlsx' output path), using QGIS-based HAND (Height Above Nearest Drainage) inundation mapping and dual-zone (channel + floodplain) Manning’s n parameterization. It iterates over 30 water level multipliers (stage factors from 0.1 to 3.0 m), computes pixel-level hydraulic geometry (area, wetted perimeter, hydraulic radius) from HAND-derived inundation depth rasters, slope rasters, and land cover vector data, then calculates discharge for all combinatorial Manning’s n configurations per land cover class (Water, Rangelands, Built Area, Crops, Trees). Outputs include: (1) per-stage flood depth rasters ('Inun_X.X.tif'), (2) per-stage Excel files listing all n-combination discharges ('Sensitivity_X.X.xlsx'), and (3) aggregated discharge values written into columnar format in an existing Excel workbook ('QGIS-Calculations-San-Isidro.xlsx', sheet 'Cabula Curve List'). The study area is bounded by a 3984.6 m hydraulic reach; valley slope is derived from DEM elevation difference (42.80544281 m → 29.117033 m) over horizontal distance 2749.334 m. Data sources include local shapefiles (LandCover_Vector_3984,6m.shp, SmallerChannel_Vector.shp), raster layers loaded in QGIS ('PA_WL_Cabula_10_FINAL', 'HAND_EleveAbvStream_BestSubcatchmentClipped', 'Slope_Degrees_NewDEM'), and no satellite or GEE-hosted datasets are used — this is a desktop QGIS Python script, not a Google Earth Engine script despite the prompt's mischaracterization.

name: Compute Space Syntax integration metrics
desc: The script performs justified graph (J-graph) / Space Syntax analysis on a user-provided point layer (nodes = spaces) and line layer (edges = connections), computing depth-based metrics including depth from base node, total depth, connected node count, mean depth, relative asymmetry, real relative asymmetry, and integration (1/RRA). It matches line endpoints to nodes within a user-defined tolerance, builds an undirected graph, runs BFS for local and global integration calculations, writes results as new attributes to the node layer, and optionally generates tree or radial layout visualizations as temporary memory layers.

name: Clip imagery and DEM to AOI
desc: The script exports a masked and auto-cropped PNG texture tile (Tile__0__0.png) aligned to a user-defined vector clipping layer, and a georeferenced GeoTIFF DEM clipped to the same spatial extent and resolution. It performs coordinate transformations, map rendering, pixel-level masking, opaque-pixel bounding box detection, and GDAL-based DEM reprojection/clipping. Inputs are QGIS layers: a basemap raster (rendered visually), a DEM raster, and a vector AOI — all provided by the user at runtime. No remote sensing data ingestion, time-series processing, or classification occurs; all operations are local, static, and geometry-driven. Study area, time range, satellite sensors, and bands are not specified in the code.

name: Compensate square point geometry
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin tool for geometric compensation of square points: given two orthogonal distances (abscissa and ordinate) and a measured diagonal distance, it computes a corrected point location that satisfies the Pythagorean relationship within a tolerance threshold. It uses rubber bands to visualize a dynamic line and compensated point on the map canvas, snap-to-map functionality for precision, and creates output points in a memory vector layer with cross-shaped symbology. The tool operates only when the project CRS is EPSG:3948 (a French national metric projection), and displays real-time feedback including calculated line length, error magnitude, and pass/fail status against tolerance. No remote sensing data, time-series, or Earth observation inputs are involved — this is a purely geometric, interactive GIS digitizing aid.

name: Apply fuzzy membership transformation
desc: The script applies user-defined fuzzy membership functions (linear, triangular, trapezoidal, sigmoidal, Gaussian) to a single-band QGIS raster layer to transform pixel values into [0,1] membership degrees. It reads the input GeoTIFF via GDAL, performs pixel-wise fuzzy logic mapping using parameters entered by the user (e.g., a,b for linear_inc), clips results to [0,1], writes a new GeoTIFF output (named 'fzy_{basename}.tif'), loads it into QGIS, and applies a fixed 5-class pseudo-color renderer with semantic labels ('mauvais' to 'très bon'). Metadata (function type, parameters, timestamp, username) is saved in a sidecar '.fzy' CSV file. No remote sensing data ingestion, cloud masking, temporal compositing, or classification occurs — all operations are local, deterministic, and raster-based within QGIS. Input source is arbitrary local GeoTIFF; no satellite, sensor, band, time range, or geographic extent is specified or inferred from code.

name: Compute shortest evacuation time
desc: The script computes shortest pedestrian evacuation times from flooded buildings to non-flooded shelters using OpenStreetMap-derived road networks, Tobler’s hiking function (with optional DEM-based slope adjustment), and network shortest-path analysis. It takes as input: (1) a building polygon layer, (2) a shelter point layer, and (3) a flood inundation polygon layer — all in QGIS. It reprojects layers to EPSG:32644, identifies buildings intersecting the flood polygon, extracts an OSM walk network centered on the building layer’s extent (using osmnx.graph_from_point), projects the graph, maps shelters and buildings to nearest network nodes, computes per-building shortest paths to all viable shelters, estimates travel time either via constant walking speed (5.472 km/h ≈ 1.52 m/s) or terrain-adjusted Tobler’s function (if DEM provided), selects the minimum-time route per building, and outputs two geopackage-compatible memory layers: (i) 'buildings_with_clusters' (flooded buildings with assigned shortest evacuation time, shelter ID, and geometry), and (ii) 'Evacuation_Routes' (dissolved line geometries of optimal routes grouped by shelter ID). No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series data is used; all spatial inputs are user-provided vector layers. Study area, time range, and DEM path (dem_path) are not specified in the code — dem_path is referenced but never defined or loaded.

name: Model sound pressure level LpA
desc: The script implements the ISO 9613-2:1996 standard for outdoor sound propagation to compute A-weighted sound pressure level (LpA) raster surfaces from point sources (e.g., industrial equipment, traffic nodes) over terrain. It integrates digital elevation model (DEM)-based geometric spreading, atmospheric absorption (using temperature, humidity, and pressure), ground effect (simplified G parameter), and optional barrier diffraction (via line barriers with height attributes). The core workflow processes each source–receiver path across a grid, computes total attenuation, and sums contributions (logarithmically) to generate a continuous LpA raster (dB re 20 µPa). Optionally, it also computes LpA values at discrete receptor points (e.g., dwellings) and exports them as vector features (GeoPackage/Shapefile).

name: Split monthly climate raster bands
desc: The script splits a multi-band raster into individual single-band GeoTIFF files (monthly mode) or yearly multi-band GeoTIFF files (yearly mode), with automatic labeling using month names and years (e.g., 'tmax_Jan_2023.tif') or year-only labels (e.g., 'ppt_2023.tif'). It applies a consistent pseudocolor renderer (using min/max statistics across bands) to newly created yearly rasters. The input is any multi-band raster (not sensor-specific), but the algorithm’s documentation and group name ('TerraClimate Downloader') strongly indicate it is designed for TerraClimate datasets — gridded, global, monthly climate variables (e.g., precipitation, max temperature) spanning 1958–present at ~4.5 km resolution. No spatial subsetting, reprojection, or classification is performed; only band extraction and file export via GDAL translate. Outputs are georeferenced GeoTIFFs with LZW compression, optionally added to QGIS map canvas with styling.

name: Download TerraClimate climate variable
desc: The script downloads and clips TerraClimate gridded climate data for a user-defined polygon area of interest. It connects to the TerraClimate OPeNDAP server (http://thredds.northwestknowledge.net:8080/thredds/dodsC/TERRACLIMATE_ALL/data) to fetch NetCDF files (e.g., TerraClimate_ppt_2024.nc) for selected variables (e.g., 'ppt', 'tmax', 'pdsi') and years (1958–2025). It subsets spatially using bounding box with optional buffer (in degrees), optionally selects one month or all 12 months per year, concatenates multi-year/multi-month data into a raster stack, writes a temporary GeoTIFF, then clips it precisely to the input polygon using GDAL's cliprasterbymasklayer. The output is a single GeoTIFF file with band(s) corresponding to time steps (e.g., 12 bands for monthly 2024; 24 bands for Jan–Dec 2024 & 2025), styled with variable-specific pseudocolor ramps (e.g., 'precipitation' ramp for 'ppt'), and added to the QGIS map canvas. No study area, satellite, sensor, or custom geometry is hardcoded — the AOI is fully user-provided via input vector layer.

name: Offset itinerary stroke points at intersections
desc: The script processes vector layers representing itinerary strokes (strokes_iti) and intersection nodes (noeuds_graph) to generate displaced (offset) point features at each stroke–node intersection. It buffers nodes, computes line–buffer-boundary intersections, identifies whether each intersecting point lies near the start or end of the corresponding stroke segment (using geometry extremity logic), calculates local line direction and normal vectors, and places offset points perpendicular to the stroke at a distance scaled by an 'offset' attribute and a user-defined 'largeur' parameter. Outputs are: (1) a memory vector layer 'points_offset' containing displaced points with attributes including angle, dx/dy components, offset value, stroke/route IDs, and extremity flag; and (2) a difference layer 'layer_iti_visu' showing itinerary strokes clipped outside node buffers — intended for visual separation of overlapping strokes at junctions in cartographic rendering.

name: Clean polygon topology
desc: The script repairs invalid polygon geometries, harmonizes shared boundaries between adjacent polygons, removes spurious vertices based on short-edge, near-collinearity, and proximity to an optional outline layer, enforces per-feature area-change limits during internal cleanup, and optionally snaps outer boundaries to a reference outline — all without auto-committing changes, writing results to the layer’s edit buffer. It operates on a user-specified input polygon layer (e.g., 'voronoi_topology_errors') and an optional outline layer (e.g., 'Outline'), using QGIS native algorithms ('native:fixgeometries', 'native:snapgeometries') and custom local vertex cleanup logic. No satellite, temporal, or external geospatial data sources are involved; inputs are vector layers already loaded in the QGIS project. Outputs include updated geometries in the edit buffer, plus a printed topology report (invalid count, vertex count, area change, forced moves, etc.).

name: Generate synthetic Voronoi topology errors
desc: The script creates an in-memory polygon layer named 'voronoi_topology_errors' by generating NUM_POINTS=1000 random points in the unit square [0.0,1.0]×[0.0,1.0], computing Voronoi polygons via QGIS's 'qgis:voronoipolygons' algorithm, then deliberately injecting coordinate perturbations (±ERROR_MAGNITUDE=0.0005) and duplicated vertices (with DUPLICATE_VERTEX_PROBABILITY=0.30) into polygon rings to simulate topological defects. The output is a reproducible synthetic dataset for testing topology-cleaning workflows — no real-world geospatial data, satellite imagery, or temporal analysis is involved; all geometry is algorithmically generated and perturbed in memory.

name: Export vector layers to file formats
desc: The script exports selected QGIS vector layers to various geospatial file formats (e.g., GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoPackage, CSV, DXF) with optional reprojection to a user-specified CRS. It handles geometry-preserving and non-geometry formats separately, warns about attribute-only exports (e.g., CSV/XLSX), applies filename sanitization, logs progress and errors, and supports French/English UI localization.

name: Assign recognizers to land parcels
desc: The script implements a QGIS plugin widget for assigning recognizer codes (from a CSV file with columns ID;NOMBRE_RECONOCEDOR;CODIGO) to vector features in land parcel layers. It supports multiple assignment strategies: (1) 'Seleccionado' — assigns the CODIGO from exactly one checked CSV row to currently selected map features; (2) 'Aleatoria' — assigns unique CODIGOs to grouped features (by a user-selected grouping field) either fully or limited by 'Número predios a asignar'; (3) Advanced tab provides 'Asignar' (group-wise random assignment per CODIGO with N elements per group), 'Asignar x C' (cluster-based assignment using centroid proximity), and 'Desasignar Todos' (nulling the destination field). It also supports exporting grouped results to GeoPackage folders (one per CODIGO value) containing both 'terrenos marcados' and spatially proximal 'terrenos base' layers, and QField project packaging. No remote sensing data, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis is involved — all operations are vector attribute and geometry manipulations within QGIS desktop.

name: Extract contour lines
desc: The script extracts contour lines either by filtering vector layers (DXF) using predefined layer code values ('F0017110'–'F0017113') corresponding to Korean topographic contour types (e.g., '주곡선', '계곡선'), or by generating contour vector layers from a user-selected DEM raster using GDAL's contour algorithm with a user-defined elevation interval (in meters). Outputs include: (1) filtered DXF vector layers with subsetString applied (no new layer created — in-place filter), or (2) a newly generated GeoPackage vector layer named '등고선_{interval}m' added to the QGIS project, with metadata set via set_archtoolkit_layer_metadata including tool_id='contour_extract', units='m', and params={'interval_m': float(interval)}. No satellite, time-series, or geographic extent constraints are imposed — all inputs are interactive QGIS layer selections. Study area, time range, and data sources are not specified in the script.

name: Calculate vertex angles and segment lengths
desc: The script dynamically computes interior angles at each vertex of line features (e.g., roads, transmission lines, or routes) and the Euclidean length of each line segment in meters. It creates two real-time memory layers: (1) point layer labeled with rounded angle values (in degrees) at non-terminal vertices, styled in blue Arial 15pt; (2) line segment layer labeled with rounded distance values (in meters), styled in red Arial 15pt. Angle calculation uses azimuth-based difference (absolute turn angle between incoming and outgoing segments). Distance is computed in UTM-projected coordinates when input CRS is geographic (EPSG:4326), otherwise uses native planar units. The workflow responds to live edits (geometryChanged, featureAdded, featureDeleted) on the selected vector line layer. No remote sensing data, time series, or classification is involved — it is a purely geometric, client-side QGIS plugin for route/line topology analysis.

name: Extract land surface features from canvas
desc: The script extracts vector polygon features representing regions of user-selected colors directly from the QGIS map canvas display. It performs pixel-based color matching in HSV space (using hue tolerance and value range filtering), applies region-growing to identify contiguous areas, converts pixel coordinates to map coordinates using the canvas's current map settings and CRS, constructs polygon geometries from horizontal pixel segments, applies optional smoothing and simplification (via buffering and smoothing), unions extracted regions, and appends them as features to a memory vector layer named 'Extracted'. No external geospatial datasets, satellite imagery, or time-series analysis are used—the input is purely the rendered canvas image at the moment of execution. The study area, time range, and data sources are not specified because the script operates on the live QGIS rendering buffer, not on remote sensing data.
